title: Democrats gain control of the House and Senate — What happens now?
text:
Democrats gain control of the House and Senate. What happens now?
Democrats gained control of both the House and Senate in a historic midterm election, marking a significant shift in power for the Trump administration.
Democrats gain control of the House and Senate. What happens now?
Democrats gained control of both the House and Senate in a historic midterm election, marking a significant shift in power for the Trump administration.
Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January after a historic midterm election that shifted the balance of power in Congress.
The party flipped at least seven Senate seats in ruby-red and battleground states and gained more than two dozen House districts, including some that voted for President Donald Trump in 2024 by double digits.
This marks the first time since 2006 that both chambers of Congress have flipped from one party to another during the same midterm election.
Key races that will impact balance of power
Democrat Josh Turek defeated Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson in Iowa, and Adam Hamilton ousted Republican Sen. Roger Marshall in Kansas as part of a cascade of stunning victories. In a historic win, Democrat James Talarico defeated Ken Paxton in Texas and Annie Andrews upset Darline Graham in South Carolina.
In Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown beat Sen. Jon Husted, and Democrat Roy Cooper took an open North Carolina seat. Together, these wins gave Democrats a broad set of gains across the Senate map.
Thirty-six states also elected governors. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa ousted Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seeking a fourth term. Republican Vivek Ramaswamy lost to Democrat Amy Acton in Ohio's gubernatorial race.
History was made on Election Night
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms of Georgia will be the first Black female governor of any state. In Florida, Byron Donalds became the state's first Black Republican to be elected governor.
In Nevada, Democrat Aaron Ford defeated Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo. Ford will be the state's first Black governor.
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won Michigan's U.S. Senate seat, becoming the country's first Muslim senator. El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers.
How do the results impact President Trump's agenda?
With control of both chambers, House Democrats are preparing an ambitious agenda focused on making life more affordable for Americans and conducting oversight of the Trump administration.
"Against all odds, we Democrats have won the Senate, and we have five words for the American people: Relief is on the way," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said.
During an interview with Fox News, Trump congratulated Democrats on their victory, noting that he has already spoken with some of them. He also pointed out that even if both chambers pass legislation, he retains the power to veto their bills.

title: One of three remaining Shakers has died
text:
One of the world’s last remaining Shakers has died.
Sister June Carpenter died early Tuesday morning, according to a statement from the Sabbathday Lake Shaker Village Community.
She was born in Boston in 1938 and first visited the Shakers 50 years later in 1988, where she heard they were seeking a library volunteer. She joined the community in 1989.
Sister June served as cataloger of the Shaker Library where she organized and cataloged generations of Shaker records and history. She also cared for the flower gardens, the barn cats, and was an avid football fan and known as the “queen of trivia” within the community.
“Sister June will be remembered for her steadfast faith, her kindness toward all living things, and her dedication to the Shaker way of life,” the statement reads. “She will be deeply missed by her Shaker family, friends, and the many people whose lives she touched.”
The Sabbathday Lake Shakers community in New Gloucester dates back to 1783 and is the last remaining such community in the world.
There are now only two remaining members of the Shakers: Brother Arnold Hadd, and the newest Shaker, and Sister April Baxter, who joined in the past couple of years.
In accordance with Sister June’s wishes, no funeral services will be held, and in lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Shaker Library.

title: Democrat Aaron Ford defeats Republican incumbent to become Nevada’s first Black governor
text:
LAS VEGAS (AP) — Nevada’s Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford has won the race for governor, ousting Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and becoming the state’s first Black governor.
Ford has served as the state’s top prosecutor since 2019. Throughout his campaign, he described growing up in poverty and going to school hungry. He explained how he became a math teacher before earning his law degree, and highlighted efforts to fight the Trump administration.
“This campaign didn’t happen by accident,” Ford said at a Democratic watch party Tuesday. “It happened because of faith, because of family, because of hard work, and because the people of Nevada decided that our best days are still ahead of us.”
Ford focused his campaign on affordability, promising to tackle student loan debt and crack down on the development of artificial intelligence data centers. He painted his opponent as a staunch loyalist of the president and criticized Lombardo for vetoing bills that Ford said would have helped Nevadans, from restrictions on corporate homeownership to providing free school meals.
Amid voters’ concerns over the impacts of AI data centers, Ford promised to pause new tax abatements for them and oppose projects on federal land in Nevada.
He defended against attacks by the governor, a former sheriff, that tried to paint Ford as soft on crime while he was attorney general. He also deflected Lombardo’s accusations that his policy goals would be too expensive.
Ford got a boost from national Democrats who are eyeing potential 2028 presidential campaigns, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris, who came to the state to campaign for him. Trump won Nevada in 2024 with 50.6% of the vote.
The economy took center stage
During this year’s race, the governor portrayed Ford as a threat to the state’s business-friendly climate. Lombardo sought to tie him to Democrat-controlled California, claiming Ford would bring the “Newsom playbook” of high taxes and more regulations.
Democrats worked to connect Lombardo with President Donald Trump’s tariffs, saying they harmed Las Vegas tourism, which saw a 17% drop in Canadian visitors in 2025. The president has feuded with Canadian leaders, and the two countries are in the middle of a trade dispute.
Ford criticized Lombardo for vetoing legislation the Democrat said would make life more affordable, such as a bill to limit home purchases by corporate investors. Nevadans are grappling with some of the highest gas prices in the country and a shortage of tens of thousands of homes.
The race for governor cast a shadow beyond Nevada
The westernmost battleground state has a distinctive electorate that doesn’t always follow national political trends.
Democratic strength in Las Vegas is counterbalanced by heavily Republican rural areas, and the true wild cards are the nonpartisan voters who make up nearly 40% of the electorate. The steady flow of people into and out of the state, as well as the large number of working-class and Latino voters, make it difficult to predict statewide races.
Although Nevada only has six electoral college votes, both parties have Nevada as an early state in their nominating calendar.
Law enforcement backgrounds were key to the race
Both candidates faced scrutiny for how they exercised their authority in law enforcement.
Ford’s campaign criticized Lombardo after he avoided a traffic ticket in Las Vegas, interrupting the police officer to say “I’m Joe Lombardo.” Meanwhile, the governor’s campaign blasted Ford for sponsoring consideration of a clemency application for a man who killed a pregnant woman in 2017.
Lombardo secured a major boost when the Democratic district attorney for Clark County, which covers Las Vegas, endorsed the governor instead of his fellow Democrat.
The governor served in law enforcement for over 25 years before becoming sheriff of Clark County in 2014. He became well known in 2017 while overseeing the investigation into the Las Vegas mass shooting, the deadliest in modern U.S. history. Lombardo was born in Japan to a U.S. military family stationed overseas and served in the Army and the Nevada National Guard.
Ford, a former state senator, frequently spoke about experiencing poverty as a child and how his father brought home stale candy bars from the grocery store he worked at for the family’s dinner. Since being elected attorney general, he has secured millions in settlements from opioid manufacturers, and he successfully sued a student loan servicer as well as the gaming platform Roblox.

title: Douglas Carlisle Jr. wins Maine House District 5 race
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Republican Douglas C. Carlisle Jr. has won the race for Maine House District 5, defeating Democrat Lori Kenneson in Tuesday’s general election, according to unofficial results with an estimated 99% of ballots counted.
Carlisle, a Presque Isle resident, will succeed Republican Joseph Underwood, who did not seek reelection.
District 5 includes portions of Presque Isle, and Carlisle will serve a two-year term representing the district in Augusta.

title: Very warm today with showers on the way
text:
Very warm today with showers on the way
How’s the weather looking for your Wednesday? Get the latest Maine’s Total Weather video forecast from Meteorologist Ted McInerney.
Very warm today with showers on the way
How’s the weather looking for your Wednesday? Get the latest Maine’s Total Weather video forecast from Meteorologist Ted McInerney.
An unusually warm Wednesday across Maine, with afternoon temperatures reaching at least the mid-70s in many communities, roughly 20 degrees above normal. How quickly the clouds clear will help determine just how high readings climb. Daily records could be challenged in Portland, where the Nov. 4 mark is 74 degrees set in 1987, and Augusta, where it is 74 set in 1990.
Clouds and moisture increase tonight, keeping temperatures mild. Northern Maine drops into the mid- to upper 40s, while southern areas settle into the lower to mid-50s. A cold front approaches Thursday, setting up a wetter stretch late in the week and into the weekend.
My biggest forecast question is where that boundary stalls. Recent models favors a position just offshore, which could concentrate the heaviest rainfall along the coast. A slower front that stops farther west would shift the soaking rain inland.
Unsettled conditions linger into early next week, with additional showers possible through Monday. Rain and snow showers could continue into Tuesday along mountain slopes. I’ll be watching the front’s progress closely to narrow down which parts of Maine receive the most rain.

title: Portland voters decide direction of City Council as two races head to ranked-choice runoff
text:
PORTLAND — Kate Snyder and Ilma López have won their respective races for City Council following a ranked-choice runoff Wednesday, signaling a shift in direction for the nine-member council.
After the 11 a.m. tabulations, Snyder won the councilor at-large seat with 55% of the vote, besting second-place finisher Joey Brunelle, who reached 45%.
“I’m excited to serve, we have a lot of challenges ahead of us,” Snyder said following the announcement of the results. “I’m really looking forward to working collaboratively with members of the council.”
In District 5, López reached 59%. Michael Todd Chretien, in second place, received 40.9%.
In a social media post following the win, López thanked her supporters and opponents.
“I’m not a perfect or career politician,” she said. “I’m a mom, neighbor and small business owner who loves Portland. I’ll bring my experience, stand up for everyone’s rights and work for honest, realistic solutions.”
The tabulations, conducted by third-party vendor MK Elections, were displayed on a large screen for the candidates in the State of Maine Room at City Hall.
In the District 4 race, Councilor Anna Bullett appeared to win reelection by just 12 votes Tuesday over challenger Jake Viola, who is exploring whether to request a recount.
Heading into Election Day, Portland was already guaranteed two new councilors in the coming term after Councilors April Fournier and Kate Sykes opted not to run for reelection, making Bullett the lone incumbent on Portland ballots.
However, the victories by Snyder and López represent a more moderate-leaning shift on the council. Fournier had endorsed Brunelle for the at-large seat, while Sykes had endorsed Chretien in District 5.
Mayor Mark Dion said voters showed a clear desire for moderation on the council, and for officials to make decisions that have broader support.
He said Lopez will bring the perspective of a small business owner, while Snyder has experience as “a consensus builder and someone who wants to see policy that works.” Dion had endorsed both candidates.
During the campaign, candidates attempted to separate themselves and their policy platforms through local forums, candidate questionnaires and endorsements. Top issues on the minds of voters included public safety and homelessness, housing and property taxes.
While candidates largely avoided negative campaigning, a political action committee known as the Campaign for Responsible Government complicated the relative peace by backing three candidates — although as of Election Day, the PAC had only spent money to support Lopez in District 5.
COUNCILOR AT-LARGE
Following the ranked-choice runoff Wednesday, Brunelle said the results show that Portland has “taken a step backwards in its support of working class people,” which he believes stands in “sharp contrast” to election results elsewhere.
After the initial tally Tuesday night, Brunelle trailed Snyder by roughly 4,000 votes, but with the third-place candidate Atiim Boykin eliminated, the election would be decided on whom his supporters ranked second. Snyder picked up roughly 2,000 votes, allowing her to cross the 50% mark.
Boykin, 50, said he was aware of his position in the race: He believed more moderate voters would likely gravitate toward Snyder, while progressives would choose Brunelle. But because some supporters of those candidates instructed voters not to rank the other, Boykin was hoping things could potentially shake out in his favor.
Boykin had raised and spent nearly $11,000 as of the most recent campaign finance reports due Oct. 23.
Brunelle, 41, campaigned on an ability to get multiple factions to collaborate and find solutions, as well as expand community involvement in local government.
As the lone clean elections candidate in the race, he had so far spent about $19,600. Maximum campaign funding for at-large clean elections candidates is $32,498.
Brunelle also received endorsements from Councilor Pious Ali and School Board Chair Sarah Lentz.
As of last week, Snyder, 56, had raised $32,600, and had spent $17,800.
DISTRICT 4
The District 4 race was the only head-to-head contest, and with only a 12-vote margin, it appears likely that Viola will request a recount.
The tally as of Wednesday morning was 3,421 to 3,409 in favor of Bullett. City Clerk Abbey Lombard said she was still confirming the threshold for requesting a recount.
Viola campaigned on providing a fresh approach and more consistent communication with constituents, while Bullett ran on her experience, progressive values and established relationships with staff.
The district includes East Deering and parts of the Back Cove, Deering Center and North Deering neighborhoods.
Bullett and Viola both ran as clean elections candidates, and were able to receive maximum campaign funding of $12,498. Bullett spent roughly half that, while Viola spent nearly all.
DISTRICT 5
The race for District 5, which includes Riverton and portions of North Deering, also hinged on a ranked-choice runoff Wednesday.
Michael Todd Chretien, 57, the Maine DSA-backed candidate who was endorsed by outgoing Councilor Sykes, had called for an aggressive approach to housing development, including a goal of producing 5,000 new units over five years, and promised to push for state solutions to high property taxes.
López, however, garnered broad support within the district. As co-owner of the Ugly Duckling and Chaval restaurants, López campaigned on restoring accountability to the city’s approach to public safety. She also said that as a business owner, it didn’t always feel as though she has councilor support.
López, 44, was born and raised in Venezuela but has lived in Portland for 14 years.
Jakobi Delgado, an economics student at the University of Southern Maine who would’ve been the youngest-ever councilor elected, received 8.1% of the vote. Kevin Gardella, 49, ran on providing better representation for constituents, and for offering a balanced approach to new development. He received 8.3% of first-place votes.
All four candidates ran clean elections campaigns.
Chretien said Wednesday that Mayor Dion made “a strong case for a City Council more in line with his policy preferences.”
“The new council will be judged by how much affordable housing it builds, how it works with our schools to fully fund education, and how consistently it fights to keep our neighbors safe from ICE,” he said.
SCHOOL BOARD
Three newcomers running unopposed for seats on Portland’s school board were also voted in Tuesday.
Lucia Rico, a political newcomer, will be the at-large board member. Alexandra Reissman, a mother of three Portland students, will take the District 4 seat. And newcomer Rich Leone was elected to the District 5 seat.

title: FOR YOUR HEALTH: More ways to get everyday health care
text:
Long waits, rising costs and gaps in primary care are changing where people turn for everyday health needs.
(NAPSI)—The U.S. has some of the finest, most dedicated medical professionals in the world. Yet, according to data from Gallup, 70% of Americans view the U.S. health care system negatively, with 23% saying it is in a “state of crisis” and 47% saying it has “major problems.” Long waits, rising costs and hard-to-get primary care appointments lead many people to delay or skip care. And the nation is projected to be short more than 70,000 primary care physicians by 2038, according to the Health Resources and Services Administration.
Health Care that Works for You
The good news: Everyday care may be closer than you think. Millions of patients have received acute, preventive and chronic care, quickly and conveniently, at retail health clinics across the country. More people are turning to these clinics for routine health needs, and many post prices up front so patients know what a visit costs.
Retail health destinations such as MinuteClinic®, the medical clinics located inside more than 800 CVS Pharmacy® stores nationwide, are one example. Many locations offer convenient evening and weekend hours and can provide preventive and wellness care such as women’s health, vaccinations and routine screenings; chronic condition care such as diabetes and high blood pressure management; treatment for common illnesses such as cold, flu and sore throats; and, in select markets, adult primary care. For patients who prefer not to visit in person, MinuteClinic Virtual Care is available 24/7, including holidays, for common illnesses and chronic condition management. Patients can access care with or without insurance, and an simple, transparent $89 cash-pay option is available. MinuteClinic also offers newer digital options in select states, including message-based care for common conditions and a virtual weight loss program that may include access to GLP-1 medications, when appropriate.
High-Quality Providers Who Care
At MinuteClinic, whether receiving care in-person or virtually, you can find board-certified nurse practitioners and physician associates delivering accessible, high-quality care. These providers can diagnose and treat illnesses, order and interpret tests, manage ongoing care, and refer patients to specialists when needed. They follow nationally recognized standards and are committed to delivering the highest level of care. Virtual mental health counseling is provided by licensed therapists. MinuteClinic was also the first retail health care provider to receive accreditation from The Joint Commission, an independent organization that evaluates health care quality and safety, which it has maintained since 2006.
A Streamlined Experience
In addition, a new in-clinic kiosk simplifies check-in and lets patients see their place in line, so most can get a same-day appointment. Patients can also choose between in-person and virtual visits on the CVS Health® app or MinuteClinic.com. In many places , most primary care appointments are available same or next day.
Staying Healthy
Knowing where to go matters, too: Retail clinics are a good fit for a wide variety of wellness needs, but for chest pain, trouble breathing or other emergencies, call 911. There are four more steps you can take to protect your own health, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention:
1. Stay at a healthy weight, exercise regularly and avoid tobacco.
2. Limit alcohol. Over time, excessive drinking can lead to high blood pressure and various cancers. By not drinking too much, you can reduce these health risks.
3. Get routine health screenings. These tests can catch health problems early, when they may be more easily treated. And many health plans cover recommended screenings, vaccines and annual wellness visits at no cost.
4. Get enough sleep. Insufficient sleep has been linked to development and poor management of conditions like diabetes, heart disease, obesity and depression. Adults should get at least 7 hours of sleep daily.
Learn More
For more information about the 195 services in addition to primary care MinuteClinic offers, visit www.MinuteClinic.com.

title: TechPlace startup positions itself for growth with C-suite promotion
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Salmonics LLC has named co-founder Veronica Achorn president as the Brunswick Landing biotech startup shifts its focus toward veterinary applications.
CEO and co-founder Dr. Cem Giray announced the appointment on social media. He will continue to serve as CEO and chief technology officer.
Salmonics, which converts unused blood from farmed salmon into biomedical products, is housed in Brunswick Landing’s TechPlace incubator. The startup was founded in 2020.
“Veronica has been by my side since day one, and she has been instrumental in building our company from the ground up,” said Giray. “The professional acumen, talent and dedication she brings to our partnership are what enable us to navigate through every challenge and truly power Salmonics LLC to perform at its very best. I have been incredibly fortunate to be working with her.”
Achorn previously served as head of operations, playing a central role in building the startup, from laboratory development and quality management to marketing and business operations.
She holds a bachelor’s and master’s degree in marine science and marine biology from the University of Maine.

title: Old Orchard Beach voters choose school board, Town Council members
text:
Voters in Old Orchard Beach turned out Tuesday to elect candidates in state and local elections, including school board and Town Council.
On the local ballot were three candidates for Town Council, two for school board and one for town clerk.
Here are the results.
TOWN COUNCIL
In a four-way race for three seats, Kenneth Blow won the majority of the votes with 3,434.
The unofficial results show a close tally between the three other candidates: Lori Gramlich received 2,995 votes, Shawn O’Neill received 2,883 and Michael Tousignant received 2,867 votes.
Blow, a local business owner, is a lifelong Old Orchard Beach resident who has served on the Town Council for 13 years. He simultaneously ran for the House District 131 seat.
In his responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Blow said his priorities include providing essential services and infrastructure upgrades in town and maintaining one of the lowest mill rates in southern Maine. He also highlighted the importance of bringing more affordable housing to Old Orchard Beach.
Gramlich, O’Neill and Tousignant did not respond to the voter guide survey.
SCHOOL BOARD
Voters elected Peter Flaherty and Donna Moutsatsos to serve as Regional School Unit 23 directors Tuesday. They received 2,954 and 2,833 votes, respectively. David Boudreau received 1,934 votes.
The newly elected directors will serve three-year terms.
TOWN CLERK
Incumbent Town Clerk Kim McLaughlin was the only candidate on the ballot, receiving 4,571 votes. She was first elected to the position in 2024.
During her first term as town clerk, McLaughlin received the Lorraine Fleury award from the Maine Senate for her election security preparations, her close work with the police department and her dedication to providing a safe, secure polling place.

title: Old Town man accused of assaulting teenager on Halloween weekend
text:
An Old Town man is accused of assaulting a 15-year-old who was walking with friends Friday night.
The teenager and two friends were walking around 10:40 p.m. along Stillwater Avenue to the Old Town Plaza. They were being loud, using profanities and calling each other vulgar names, the trio — ages 15, 16 and 20 — told Old Town police.
Tyron Fox, 32, and his girlfriend were driving by and decided the group was targeting them, according to the police report filed in Penobscot County Superior Court. He exited the vehicle and approached the group, appearing ready to fight, they told police.
The 20-year-old tried to explain the group wasn’t talking to Fox and his girlfriend. Fox then grabbed the 15-year-old around the neck with one hand and applied “immense pressure,” the report said. The teenager told police he was worried he’d lose consciousness.
While still holding the teenager’s neck, Fox then slammed him on the ground over and over while also holding his clothing, the report said. The teenager was also punched on the right side of his face.
When police arrived, an officer could see “clearly discernable” and fresh marks on the side of the teenager’s neck, including visible marks from several fingers and a scratch that was still bleeding, the report said.
Fox is charged with one felony count of aggravated assault and one misdemeanor count of violation of condition of release. His attorney did not respond to a request for comment.
“The group insisted that there was no qualms with the vehicle or it’s [sic] occupants — the attack by all reasonable analysis seemed sporadic and unreasonable,” the officer wrote.
Fox and his girlfriend drove away, but the group had taken a picture of the license plate, the report said. Police went to the girlfriend’s home, where they interviewed her and Fox.
The girlfriend said she couldn’t see what was happening but asserted that because Fox was yelling, he could not be fighting, the report said.
When interviewed by police, Fox maintained he confronted the group but did not use any physical force, the report said.
Fox had his first court appearance Monday. He is being held without bail at the Penobscot County Jail in Bangor because he is accused of violating his bail conditions. In that case, which is still pending, Fox is charged with operating after revocation of his driver’s license.

title: Vance blames war in Iran for Republican midterm losses: ‘If you’d like to argue it was worth it ... then do so’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — JD Vance publicly broke from President Donald Trump ‘s defense of the Iran war Wednesday after the Republican Party’s deep losses in the midterm elections, attempting to distance himself from voters’ clear rebuke of the president as the vice president faces questions about his own political ambitions.
Vance, who has said he would decide after the election whether to run for president in 2028, issued a lengthy social media post blaming the unpopular conflict with Iran for the GOP’s drubbing. Vance said, “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”
But arguing that the war was worth it is what Trump repeatedly did on the campaign trail, continued to do in interviews as election results came in and did again Wednesday morning. As he led reporters on an impromptu visit to the ballroom he’s constructing at the White House, Trump said, “The Iran thing, we had to do and we continue to do it.”
Trump said he spoke to Vance on Wednesday morning and, when asked about the vice president’s post, he called it “good” and said, “I know how he feels about it,” and “I think it was fine.”
The president also said he “knew the war was going to impact” the midterm elections but again defended his actions.
Vance, who had long advocated for restraint in U.S. military intervention overseas, was lukewarm in his defense of the conflict after Trump launched it and even became the face of an unsuccessful attempt to end the fighting.
Democrats plan to hold Vance accountable for the war
Democrats showed they intend to make Vance own the war.
“If Vance has felt this way all along, why didn’t he speak out forcefully?” Democratic National Committee spokeswoman Rosemary Boeglin said in a statement. “Why didn’t he resign? And most importantly, why didn’t he stand up for Americans?”
The vice president, she said, “will always do what’s most politically convenient for him in the moment — even if it means throwing Americans under the bus. Vance owns this administration’s failures.”
Democrats swept control of both the House and the Senate on Tuesday, defeating GOP candidates even in deep-red areas that Trump carried by wide margins two years ago.
“There’s no doubt this is a repudiation of the last two years,” said Marc Short, who was chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence and worked in Trump’s White House in his first term.
He said Vance will still have a big microphone as the sitting vice president, and the election results don’t mean he won’t be the GOP’s nominee for president in two years.
But, Short said, “It certainly doesn’t help his case, that’s for sure. I would argue it does hurt.”
When Pence was in the role, he intentionally tried not to distance himself from Trump and shared his opinions privately, Short said. But Vance’s post Wednesday seemed to be “an intentional separation” from the president despite being inherently linked to him.
“You made that bargain when you agreed to be vice president,” he said.
Vance says reason for loss is ‘obvious to almost everyone’
Vance, in his post, said that Republican voters cast their ballots for Democrats because of the war, the cost of living, America not being prioritized and the U.S. relationship with Israel — a dynamic where he’s also sounded a different note than Trump.
“The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone,” he wrote.
Unlike the president, Vance declined to endorseIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection and this summer publicly chastised members of Israel’s government for opposing Trump’s efforts to resolve the war with Iran.
Vance, who has been a staunch defender of the administration’s immigration policies, also appeared to be seeking some distance from the immigration crackdown that drew a backlash.
“I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance,” he wrote.
But he said he rejected any politicians who might propose amnesty for people living in the country illegally.
Voters made it clear they disapproved of the Iran war
About 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States. Most of those voters dissatisfied with the Iran war backed the Democratic candidate in their U.S. House race, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the leading issue for most voters.
Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to their vote for Congress, well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.
Nearly all voters who backed the Democratic candidate in their U.S. House race said going to war with Iran was the “wrong decision,” while roughly 8 in 10 voters who backed the Republican candidate said it was the “right decision.”
A former Marine who served in Iraq, Vance had been critical of that conflict and said after becoming vice president that a Trump administration would not send troops into the “open-ended conflicts” of the past.
After Trump launched the war with Iran this past spring, Vance was noticeably quiet in speaking about it, a conspicuous change for a politician known for being a pugnacious defender of the president.
This summer, he tried to argue the conflict was worth it, telling conservative podcast host Megyn Kelly in an interview that, “If we transformed the Middle East, this is fundamentally worth it.”
___
Associated Press Writer Linley Sanders in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Bar Harbor Garden Club presents 'Cooking From Your Garden – A Seasonal Approach' with Amy Pollien
text:
BAR HARBOR — The Bar Harbor Garden Club will host Amy Pollien as the guest speaker for its meeting on Thursday, Nov. 12, at Birch Bay Retirement Village in Bar Harbor. Pollien’s presentation will provide ideas and instructions to prepare healthy nutritious dishes from gardens and backyards. Specifically, her presentation will highlight the techniques she uses to eat or preserve the harvest from every season.
Thirty-five years ago, Amy and her husband Rob settled on their 4-acre site, with dreams of building their post-and-beam home and growing plants to supply the fillings for their seven favorite pies. Pollien’s garden, Seven Pies, is a mix of flowers, orchard, and vegetables. Seven Pies began with the goal of producing at least that many ingredients for pie: apple, blueberry, strawberry, raspberry, plum, peach, and pumpkin. However, with time, a lot of effort and the application of natural soil enhancements such as biochar, they have transformed the land into a thriving habitat that supports pollinators, yields abundant edible fruits and plants, and brings them joy and serenity.

title: 🍩 Donut Stop Believing! This Maine Shop Is One of America's Best!
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This Maine Donut Shop Is One of the Best in the U.S.
Have you had Maine's "must try" donut?
National Donut Day, is tomorrow, Thursday, November 5th!
It is one of two observed by donut lovers across the nation. It's the day donuts steal the bakery case spotlight, ready to tease their way into white bakery box and go home!
Maine has so many places to get great donuts, including traditional bakeries and innovative shops, all across the state.
You can get them at the usual places like Dunkin, or Tim Horton, but when they are Maine made, it just hits a little different.
Lovefood is a popular online food platform that provides recipes, cooking guides, food news, restaurant reviews, and meal planning.
They also make lists, which we love, so when it came down to choosing the best donut in each state, we just HAD to know what their choice for Maine was.
Read More: Market Basket Opens New Maine Store This Week: Is Bangor Next?
The Holy Donut is a family-owned donut shop in Portland, Maine, that serves gourmet donuts made with Maine potato flour. The mother, sister, and youngest members of the family are all involved in the business.
They are known for large, dense, "cake" style donuts, using all-natural ingredients, including cage-free eggs, unbleached wheat flour, real potato, and real buttermilk.
When they first opened in Portland, back in 2012, The Holy Donut became an instant hit, making people from other parts of the state extremely jealous, and you also can enjoy this tasty treat right here in the Greater Bangor area.
Tiller & Rye, located at 20 South Main Street in Brewer, is a Maine natural grocery store featuring fresh produce, grass fed meats, cheeses, dietary alternatives, bulk spices and grains, fresh baked breads, craft beers and organic wines, and they stock delicious treats from The Holy Donut!
Stop in and grab a dark chocolate sea salt, fresh lemon, sweet potato coffee cake, or pomegranate donut to start the day, and find out for yourself, why they are one of the best in the United States.

title: Florida authorities say 2 dead at Tampa office complex, including gunman shot by security guard
text:
Florida authorities say 2 dead at Tampa office complex, including gunman shot by security guard
A gunman plowed a car into a courtyard on Citibank's sprawling business campus near Tampa on Wednesday and opened fire with a rifle, killing a woman before a security guard fatally shot him, authorities said.
The Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office did not give a motive for the shooting or say whether the gunman and his lone victim knew each other.
The attack sent workers scrambling as the suspect crashed his car among outdoor tables where people were eating lunch, then started shooting, said Chief Deputy Frank Losat of the sheriff’s office. He said 3,200 people were on the campus at work during the attack.
The gunman fatally shot the woman before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria, Losat said. The guard and the gunman exchanged fire, and the guard killed him, Losat said.
“Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely," Losat told a news conference. "So kudos to that security guard.”
The names of the gunman and the woman killed were not immediately released.
Losat said four other people were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. He didn't know whether any of them had been shot or struck by the gunman's vehicle.
Citibank VP heard ‘incredible clatter’ of gunfire, then screaming
The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant’s employees.
David Dzien, a Citibank vice president, told The Associated Press he was returning to work after lunch when he saw the shooter's sedan crash through a fence about 150 yards away from him, followed by an “incredible clatter” that he later realized was gunfire.
People near the crashed car suddenly dispersed and others began to scream, Dzien said, as he sprinted back into the building and evacuated through a fire escape.
"I can still hear the particular type of scream," he said, "and I’m still trying to process it, frankly."
The attack occurred on a day when “VIPs” who don’t normally work at the complex were present for a “quarterly review,” Dzien said.
More than 360 deputies began arriving immediately
Sheriff's deputies began arriving at the campus within a minute of the first 911 call, Losat said. The response was huge, with more than 360 deputies — many in tactical gear — rushing to the scene.
Those deputies spent 2 1/2 hours searching and clearing the building where the shootings occurred plus adjacent office buildings, Losat said.
Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from responding officers described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search as people were found sheltering in locked rooms and closets, then carefully escorted from the buildings and parking garage.
Citigroup said in a statement that it was “aware of an incident” at the complex and was cooperating with authorities.
Nearby hotel gave shelter to hundreds of fleeing workers
Employees at the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel, a few hundred feet from the Citibank complex, were having a monthly employee luncheon in the hotel’s ballroom when they saw a massive flood of police vehicles headed toward the campus.
General Manager Matt Chauvin said Citibank employees ran over and told the front desk there was an active shooter.
“We at first locked the doors and, you know, went into lockdown, but the employees kept coming over," Chauvin said.
Chauvin estimated the hotel sheltered about 300 Citibank workers. Hotel staff gave them water and lunch, and let some go into hotel rooms “to sort of decompress or make phone calls.”
“Luckily we were far enough away that they were all safe,” he said.

title: Spinnaker Trust named among 2026 Best Places to Work in Maine
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Recognized for the ninth consecutive year as one of Maine’s top small employers
PORTLAND – Spinnaker Trust has been named one of the Best Places to Work in Maine among small employers, a designation recognizing outstanding workplaces that benefit the state’s economy, workforce and businesses.
This achievement marks the ninth consecutive year that Spinnaker Trust has earned this recognition in the small employer category, which includes organizations with 15 to 99 U.S. employees. Based in Portland, Spinnaker has a team of more than 40 professionals.
Celebrating its 25th anniversary this year, Spinnaker has grown from a six-person boutique firm into a team serving individuals, families, institutions and businesses, including ESOP companies, across Maine and beyond. The firm has remained locally owned and independent since its founding in 2001.
“Earning this recognition for the ninth consecutive year is especially meaningful as we celebrate 25 years of Spinnaker Trust,” Amanda V. Rand, Esq., president, CEO and principal of Spinnaker Trust, said. “Our teammates have shaped a workplace where people support one another, share their knowledge and have opportunities to grow. As we develop our next generation of leaders, we want to preserve that spirit and the thoughtful, personal service our clients deserve.”
Best Places to Work in Maine is a survey competition that identifies and recognizes the state’s best employers across small, medium and large employer categories. Best Companies Group, an independent research firm specializing in identifying and recognizing great workplaces, manages the survey and assessment process.
Honorees are selected through a two-part process: an evaluation of each company’s benefits, workplace policies, practices and other organizational information, worth 25% of the score, and a confidential employee survey evaluating the workplace experience, worth 75%. The combined scores determine the final rankings.
Spinnaker Trust is a Maine bank chartered as a non-depository trust company with more than $3.2 billion in assets under management and $2.5 billion under administration for a global clientele. Founded in Portland in 2001, the locally owned, independent firm provides investment management, trust and estate planning, and tax services. Spinnaker also provides ESOP Trustee services to more than 80 organizations throughout the Northeast. The firm helps clients manage and grow their assets and prepare their legacies for future generations. For more information, visit www.spinnakertrust.com.

title: Live updates: Tracking competitive 2026 midterm election races
text:
Tracking competitive 2026 midterm election race results
Democrats won big last night, gaining control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as victories in several gubernatorial races.
The Get the Facts Data Team is tracking competitive Senate, House of Representatives and gubernatorial races.
The data team will update coverage as results are called to see which seats stayed with the same party or flipped.
Democrats make big Senate gains
In the Senate, Democrats flipped seven seats and will hold a majority in the chamber next year.
As of Wednesday morning, Democrats had gained Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Maine. The party also retained seats in Minnesota and Michigan.
The Cook Political Report had rated 11 Senate races as competitive, with six of those being toss-ups. So far, Democrats have won five of those toss-ups.
Alaska is the last of the competitive seats that has not been called as of Wednesday morning.
North Carolina’s Senate race was not rated as competitive and Democratic nominee Roy Cooper flipped that seat.
House flips lead to new Democratic majority
In the House of Representatives, Democrats have flipped more than 20 seats as of Wednesday morning.
All 435 seats in the House were up for election this year, including 54 competitive races.
Of the 54 competitive races, Democrats have flipped 21 seats, including all three competitive races in Iowa’s 1st, 2nd and 3rd districts.
Nine states implemented new district boundaries in a wave of mid-decade redistricting ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. More than 34 million people were assigned new districts as a result.
Democrats hold majority of governorships for the first time since 2010
There were 36 gubernatorial elections in the midterms this year, with 12 of them classified as competitive races.
Democrats have flipped five of those competitive gubernatorial races and retained three. Republicans retained the governorships in Nebraska and Florida.
Alaska and Kansas were also rated as competitive seats but have not been called yet.

title: Waterville Mayor Michael Morris beats Matthew Boulerice again
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Waterville Mayor Michael Morris won a second term in Tuesday’s election, beating Matthew Boulerice for the second time in three years.
Morris, a Democrat, had 4,022 votes to 2,012 for Boulerice, a Republican, according to unofficial results. The city is one of the few in Maine to use parties for local races.
Morris beat Boulerice easily in 2023 to win his first three-year term. This time, Boulerice framed the race around leadership, asking voters at a Morning Sentinel forum last month whether the city is more affordable, safer or more efficient than it was three years ago.
Morris, who works for Bank of America, argued the city was recovering from frequent city manager turnover and that careful leadership takes time. He pointed to economic growth, including Amazon’s planned facility on the Waterville-Sidney line.
He vetoed this year’s budget in July, saying it leaned too heavily on the city’s undesignated fund balance. Boulerice said he would have kept the City Council from passing a budget the mayor had to veto.
Boulerice, a real estate developer, also called for courting developers more aggressively and for more accountability in the city’s approach to addiction and homelessness.
Morris will begin his second term in January.

title: Penobscot County’s 23% increase budget advances without cuts
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Penobscot County’s budget committee approved a budget that would increase county taxes by roughly 23%.
No cuts were made to the county’s 2027 budget during the four and a half hour meeting Wednesday.
Every county department’s expenses rose compared with the 2026 budget. The county’s 2026 budget also increased taxes by roughly 15%.
The budget still needs to be approved by the Penobscot County Commissioners later this month.
Committee members, who are elected officials serving across the county, spoke at length against the tax increase and reviewed the budget by department, but they ultimately accepted the county’s budget as presented. Multiple members voted against specific departmental budgets, but none were changed.
The county commissioner and administration budget was the only to be voted down. But it was passed without changes on a second vote.
Committee members were faced with deciding if the county should be fully funded, which would create a hike in taxes, or if there was room for cuts in the budget.
The final vote to accept the budget was contentious. Brewer City Councilor Jenn Moring, Hampden Councilor Eric Jarvi, Clifton Select Board Member John Williams, Bradley Town Councilor Duane Lugdon and state Rep. James Dill, D-Old Town, voted against the budget.
Committee members said they could not take the tax hike back to their residents.
“If we don’t approve this, we are just kicking the can down the road. We’re going to be in the same spot,” Morin said, adding that the budget process should start in the summer and include more feedback over more time than just one meeting.
If the budget is approved by County Commissioners David Marshall, Andre Cushing and Dan Tremble, county taxes are set to increase by 23.36%. When divided across county residents, it will raise taxes for a property valued at $250,000 by more than $100 next year.
As passed, the county budget fully funds the Penobscot County Jail, which has drained more than $11 million dollars from county reserve accounts. The county has undertaxed residents since 2021, requiring officials to pull from reserves to fund the jail.
Morin said this year’s budget information was the most complete in her three years on the committee, but said the county commissioners have had years to reconcile the budget and properly fund the county.
At times, committee members clashed with county officials over the cost of county services and how Tinkham described the increase, which he likened to the cost of a McDonald’s meal, a six pack of beer, or buying coffee and donuts every month.
“There are folks out there that can’t afford to buy those things today,” Lugdon said. “How are we going to go back and tell them that we’re anticipating now an additional 23% rise in their county tax, which I guarantee is not a huge portion of the town’s budget, but if you stack up the county’s increase, aside the schools’ increase, and the revenues that the towns need to get through the fiscal years, they all add up.”
Multiple members voted against more than one department’s budget. Williams and Jarvi objected to the majority of departments, saying that savings could be found.
Marshall and Cushing recommended the budget to the committee last month. Tremble voted against, saying that it would raise costs at a time when county residents are already paying higher prices for food and fuel.
Multiple committee members agreed with Tremble.
In response, Tinkham said members need to decide what the value of county services are, and the committee could “fund it, defer it or reduce it.”
County Commissioners will hold a public hearing and vote to approve the budget on Nov. 18.

title: UMF celebrates national First-Gen Day Friday
text:
FARMINGTON — The University of Maine at Farmington is honoring the achievements of its students, staff, faculty and members of the community who are first in their families to attend college with its annual First-Generation College Celebration Day at 12:30 p.m. on Friday, Nov. 6, outside on the Mantor Campus Green. Free and open to the public.
The festive event will feature a reading of the First-Gen Proclamation by Larry Tuttle, assistant professor of geology and first-gen college graduate, accompanied by a confetti cannon celebratory salute! Of the more than 1,500 students at UMF 713 or 47% are first-generation students!
“UMF is so proud of all of our students, especially those who are the first in their family to attend a four-year college. Farmington’s Johnson Scholars program is dedicated to providing the right resources and support so first-generation college students can get a quality education, graduate and be successful. First-Gen day is a way to recognize their efforts and celebrate all they’ve accomplished,” Ashlee Fecteau, director of the UMF TRIO Johnson Scholars program, said.
First-generation college students bring unique strengths to their campus and community. They pave the way as role models for others as they pursue the opportunity and personal growth that can come with a college education.
First-Gen Day has been celebrated since 2017, when campuses across the country mark the anniversary of the signing of the Higher Education Act of 1965 by President Lyndon B. Johnson to strengthen access to college resources.

title: Democrat Hakeem Jeffries poised to make history as first Black speaker of the House
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is on the cusp of making history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a generational shift in U.S. politics after Democrats trounced Republicans to win majority control of the chamber in the midterm elections.
Jeffries faces a vote of his colleagues when the new Congress convenes Jan. 3. If nominated and elected, as expected, it would be the first time a Black lawmaker has grasped the powerful House speaker’s gavel, a job second in line to the president and the only leadership position in Congress mandated by the U.S. Constitution.
His rise to the speakership at the nation’s domed Capitol, which enslaved African Americans helped build, would be a milestone more than 150 years in the making, tracing an arc of history that began with the first Black American elected to the U.S. House in the turbulent era of post-Civil War Reconstruction. Jeffries would wield the gavel at a time when many of the landmark gains of the 20th-century Civil Rights era are being challenged anew, often by the Trump administration.
Jeffries was met with cheers of “Speaker! Speaker!” at the Democrats’ watch party in Washington.
“This is not a partisan moment. This is a patriotic one,” Jeffries said.
He said House Democrats understand that this is a change election, and “the American people are crying out for transformational change.”
“We hear you,” he said. “We’re going to work hard to deliver on the dramatic change that you deserve.”
The Brooklyn-born 56-year-old Jeffries, known for sprinkling old-school hip-hop lyrics into his freestyle remarks, would take over the office from Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, as Democrats seek to confront President Donald Trump’s final two years in office.
The president has publicly and privately taunted Jeffries, a New York University-educated lawyer, who has served in Congress since 2013, and is the highest-ranking Black elected official in America. Trump once mocked Jeffries by posting on social media a fake photo of the Democratic leader wearing a sombrero outside the White House.
The whole House votes on its speaker as one of the first orders of business when Congress convenes in January. The parties typically choose their leaders during internal caucus elections in November.
Jeffries thanked House Democrats in a letter Wednesday, making clear his desire to serve as the next speaker.
“America is back!” Jeffries wrote.
He went on to say his goal is to empower them to act decisively in the next Congress in three areas: affordability, accountability and American values.
Jeffries is charting a new course for Democrats after Pelosi
The path ahead has been clear for Jeffries and his leadership team, with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who have often moved as a trio representing a new era of House leadership. Clark is expected to become the majority leader and Aguilar the majority whip.
Jeffries would be the first Democratic speaker since Nancy Pelosi and he has led the party for the past four years, with her support, once she decided to step aside after the Democrats’ election losses in 2022.
But Jeffries and the team of Democratic leaders will be quickly tested in the majority, with all the power and responsibility that comes with running the often unruly House.
They are bracing to confront not only Trump, but also a fresh group of Democrats elected to office, including a handful backed by the Democratic Socialists of America pushing the party leftward, though the largest caucus in the House is expected to remain the more moderate New Democrat Coalition.
Jeffries has promised a robust 100-day agenda to lower the costs of living and launch oversight and investigations to hold the Trump administration accountable. Impeachment is an option.
Promising to show voters that Democrats can govern, Jeffries and the leadership team hope to hold their new majority together and avoid the chaotic disruptions and dysfunction that often left Johnson unable to control the GOP’s razor-thin majority in the House.
Colleagues have praised Jeffries’ collaborative style, a listener who represents a shift from Pelosi’s powerful tenure as the nation’s first female speaker of the House.
But at the same time, his calm-is-a-choice deliberative nature has drawn criticism that Jeffries can be too slow to act in the frenzied political environment when voters are seeking swift reaction to mounting crises and concerns.
Soaring healthcare costs, gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran, Trump’s relationship with Putin over Ukraine and concerns about corruption are all top issues ahead.
His path to power runs from Brooklyn to Washington
The son of an Air Force veteran and a social worker, Jeffries told The Associated Press on the campaign trail that growing up during the crack epidemic in New York shaped his sense of purpose.
His experience led to “a desire to want to improve the quality of life for hardworking people, who could have fled difficult circumstances but remained in the community, worked hard to turn things around,” he said.
A married father of two, Jeffries grew up steeped in Brooklyn’s Cornerstone Baptist Church, and represents parts of the Brooklyn-area district once held by trailblazing Rep. Shirley Chisholm.
He earned a bachelor’s degree from the State University of New York at Binghamton, a master’s degree in public policy at Georgetown and graduated magna cum laude from NYU School of Law. He worked as a corporate lawyer and served in the New York State assembly before being elected to Congress.
An insurgent himself, Jeffries was 29 when he first ran for office, failing twice in his initial campaigns for state government. In 2012, he challenged a 30-year incumbent member of Congress, who stepped aside as Jeffries swooped in to win the seat.
A member of the Congressional Black Caucus, Jeffries follows in the footsteps of those who came before, including Joseph Rainey, the first Black American elected to the House in 1870. While Rainey never became speaker, he was the first Black lawmaker to preside with the gavel over the House chamber.

title: Trump says he’s not considering replacing Defense Secretary Hegseth, despite voter dissatisfaction with the Iran war
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The midterm election blowout delivered a new era in Washington, with Democrats in Congress eager to meet voter demands for change while Republicans watched their majorities evaporate after a revolt against President Donald Trump and his party in power.
Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast, with many surprising places in between, in a decisive rejection of unified GOP control for the promise of something different for the country. Their majorities will be padded by unusually wide margins in both the House and the Senate.
The staggering results are setting up a starkly divided government, with an emboldened Congress poised to reassert itself as a coequal branch when Democrats take over in the new year. They are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower the costs of gas, groceries and healthcare and conduct vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration, with impeachment an option.
“We hear you,” said House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who would make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job when the new Congress begins on Jan. 3, 2027.
Jeffries called the election a “stunning rebuke of MAGA extremism” and “a great victory for the American people.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer acknowledged the political reality that voters may have been more willing to reject Trump’s party than to embrace the Democrats.
“Many of the folks who voted for us yesterday are still skeptical, and that’s OK,” the New York senator said Wednesday at the Capitol.
He said the history-making scale of his party’s wins — picking up long-shot Senate seats in South Carolina, Texas and Kansas — creates “the opportunity to prove ourselves worthy of their trust.”
All told, the results present a fundamental reshaping of power in Washington, with new openings and challenges for governing. The tally was bewildering for the scope of Democratic gains and the depth of Republican losses, which indiscriminately wiped out GOP firebrands, moderates and veteran conservatives nationwide. The swelling majorities, with some races still too early to call, underlined a deep sense of voter anger and concern over the economy and the state of democracy.
Trump struck a conciliatory tone, suggesting he could work with the Democrats, but he also warned of gridlock ahead as he threatened to use the power of the presidential veto to strike down their agenda.
“I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything,” he told Politico.
Later, he acknowledged the Iran war impacted the midterm elections, suggesting voters were frustrated by surging gas prices that have been a byproduct of the 8-month-old conflict.
“The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” Trump told reporters.
He said he was not considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, despite voter dissatisfaction with the war, saying Hegseth was “doing a great job.”
Vice President JD Vance, often eyed as Trump’s likely successor at the White House, pointedly blamed the president’s war in Iran for Republicans’ midterm wipeout.
House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana will not seek reelection as House Republican leader, according to two people familiar with his decision, setting up a potentially brutal leadership battle following the party’s trouncing by the Democrats. The people who told The Associated Press about Johnson’s decision insisted on anonymity to disclose it.
Democrats vow a 100-day agenda and investigations of Trump
House Democrats are planning to quickly launch efforts to reverse Trump’s GOP cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid healthcare programs. They’re also ready to dive into a robust oversight agenda to, as Jeffries says, “hold the crooks accountable.”
The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, issued a one-sentence warning: “Lawyer up.”
Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, issued his own one-word missive: “Subpoenas.”
Democrats will be under pressure to quickly show that they have solutions for voters’ anger and frustration over high prices, the war in Iran and unease about the direction of the country. About 7 in 10 voters nationally say Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency, according to The AP Voter Poll.
For Jeffries and his leadership team, it will be their first time in the majority, managing a class of newcomers including a handful of far-left democratic socialists.
With the majority in the 435-member House growing well past the 218 needed and the Senate Democrats holding at least 54 of 100 seats in that chamber, Jeffries and Schumer will have room to maneuver.
Vance cites the Iran war for Republicans’ losses
For Republicans, their shriveled numbers quickly launched a reckoning of their own, as they try to figure out what went so uniformly wrong.
In a lengthy online post, the vice president seemingly sought to distance himself from election results seen as a referendum on Trump that featured big Republican losses across the country.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote, adding, “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”
A lame-duck session and leadership elections await Republicans
Republicans may be anxious during the post-election lame-duck sprint to accomplish as much as possible in their remaining weeks in power. But hopes for another GOP-only priority package like their big tax breaks and spending cuts bill seem dim as defeated lawmakers prepare to go home at the end of the year.
Conservatives have also eyed the opportunity for Trump to nominate more judges or even a justice to the Supreme Court while Senate Republicans still hold a majority to confirm the picks.
And the government could be headed toward a federal shutdown next month if Congress fails to pass a funding bill to keep operations running.
In the weeks ahead, the parties will hold internal leadership elections.
Johnson will stay on as a rank-and-file lawmaker in the new Congress, but rivals are lining up to replace him as GOP leader.
Jeffries will seek to shore up support as Democratic leader, before the House chooses its speaker as one of the first votes when the new Congress convenes.
In the Senate, Schumer faces a new generation of Democrats including some who have yet to support him as majority leader.
Trailblazers are coming to Congress
Rarely has the president’s party held on to power during midterm elections, but the Democratic tsunami carried echoes of Trump’s first term, when Republicans faced a voter revolt that sent Democrats to the House majority, and the Barack Obama era, when the Republican tea party swept to power.
This new Congress will also mark firsts and welcome trailblazers.
With the election of Democrat Juliana Stratton of Illinois, the Senate will for the first time have three Black women in office.
Democrat Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota will be the first Native American female senator, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire will become the first openly gay male U.S. senator and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan will be the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate.
___
This story has been corrected to show the Illinois Democrat’s name is Juliana, not Julia.
___
Associated Press writers Tom Beaumont, Joey Cappelletti, Jill Colvin, Kevin Freking, Mary Clare Jalonick and Will Weissert contributed to this report.
___

title: Federal Marshals carry out arrest in Rockland
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - Federal marshals arrested a fugitive in Rockland Tuesday afternoon, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.
Andrew D. Secord, 24, of New Hampshire was arrested for failure to appear in court for charges out of Merrimack County. Officials say Secord did not show up to an arraignment for felony sexual assault, assault, domestic violence assault, and criminal threatening.
A warrant was issued for Secord’s arrest on Oct. 20. The DOJ says investigators uncovered information that Secord had fled to Maine, and a thorough investigation with the help of local police led to his arrest on Tuesday.
Secord was apprehended without incident and is being held pending extradition to New Hampshire.

title: Cape Elizabeth elects Town Council, School Board members
text:
Elizabeth Biermann and Christopher Gorski were elected to the Cape Elizabeth Town Council, and Elizabeth Goodspeed and Julie Pelletier were elected to the town’s school board.
Biermann received 3,468 votes, and 2,723 people voted for Gorski. They defeated Stephanie Anderson and Timothy Thompson.
Goodspeed got 3,582 votes, and Pelletier received 3,142. Karen Lechner received 2,553 votes and was not elected.
Town officials said a record number of ballots were cast absentee. Of the 6,334 municipal ballots cast, 4,182 were cast absentee.
TOWN COUNCIL
Elizabeth Biermann, an attorney who has lived in Cape Elizabeth for seven years, is new to public office. She plans to prioritize lowering costs by taking a long-term view, making the town affordable and making decisions efficiently.
Christopher Gorski, a software engineer, plans to prioritize infrastructure improvements like road paving, protecting open spaces and supporting the school board during his first term in municipal office.
SCHOOL BOARD
Elizabeth Goodspeed, who has a background in education and has children in the school district, wants the schools to plan thoughtfully about using technology in the classroom and for future infrastructure needs.
Julie Pelletier, an emergency medicine physician and parent of three Cape Elizabeth students, wants to support educators. She wants to work with school leaders to come up with a plan for technology use in the classroom, retain and recruit more educators and improve school infrastructure when needed.

title: UMaine political science chair cites affordability, Trump in election results
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - University of Maine political science chair Mark Brewer said Wednesday that he and the rest of the nation witnessed a banner night for Democrats.
Brewer said he thought the CD2 race was always going to be tight.
“That’s a race I thought would be closer than the polls were predicting. I always thought that Matt Dunlap was a stronger candidate than some people were giving him credit for,” Brewer said.
“That being said, I also thought that LePage would squeak this one out. He might still, we don’t know the answer to that. That race is a little bit of a surprise. And that is another race that if it ends up, going to Dunlap, did that Republican weight coming from the White House weigh down Governor LePage? Probably,” he said.
Brewer said he was astounded by the amount of blue as he watched the results come in.
He said he thinks there are two main reasons the results broke this way.
“Affordability is one. You look at all the outlets in the studies that were talking to voters who left the polls. Focus groups going into the election. Voters were talking about affordability, affordability, affordability. The cost of energy. The cost of groceries. The cost of housing. That was the big issue, and then there was Donald Trump,” Brewer said.
“Both of those things kind of melted together and the vast majority of Americans blamed the affordability concerns on Donald Trump’s performance as president,” he said.

title: Standish voters pass mobile home rent control, split on charter changes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Standish voters overwhelmingly backed a mobile home park rent stabilization ordinance, 3,949 to 1,315, according to unofficial results from Tuesday’s election.
The ordinance was placed on the ballot through a citizens’ petition in August. Residents of Pine Tree Estates mobile home park, owned by RHP Properties, called for the measure because they say the Michigan-based corporation has raised lot rents to unaffordable rates in recent years.
Standish will now establish a rent stabilization board to enforce the ordinance, which will limit the amount that mobile home park owners can increase rent. Several Maine towns have passed similar measures.
Voters also approved a charter amendment while rejecting another.
The first, which voters approved 2,681 to 2,565, will reduce the number of meetings necessary for the Standish Town Council to adopt an ordinance from three to two.
The second, which was rejected 3,232 to 2,004, would have increased the total cost of the town’s capital expenditures requiring approval by referendum vote from $75,000 to $150,000.
