title: The Latest: Voters give Democrats control of Congress in rebuke to Trump
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Democrats have won control of Congress in Tuesday’s 2026 midterm elections in a widespread repudiation of President Donald Trump and the Republican Party, a drubbing that reached deep into reliable GOP territory.
Democrats flipped at least seven Senate seats in ruby-red states and battlegrounds alike: Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. They held on to battleground seats in Georgia and Michigan. In the House, Democrats flipped more than two dozen districts, some that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.
Democrats Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Amy Acton in Ohio, Rob Sand in Iowa and Gina Hinojosa in Texas won races for governor, flipping GOP-held offices.
Trump faces a profoundly reshaped Washington for the last two years of his presidency. Democrats will have the power to block his legislative agenda, reject his appointees and investigate his administration.
After telling voters repeatedly to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” Trump tried to shift the blame away from himself, saying Democrats “did a good job” in their campaigns and blaming GOP candidates for losses. Most voters appear to blame his administration for high costs and want Congress to impose more checks on him, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Here’s the latest:
Trump has no public events set for Wednesday as Democrats celebrate rout in midterms
Trump has no public events scheduled for Wednesday, according to the White House, following Democrats’ resounding midterm election wins that will give them control of the House and the Senate for his final two years in office.
The Republican president spoke to Fox News Channel for an interview that aired early Wednesday, saying Democrats “did a good job” and faulting GOP candidates for their losses. “I don’t view it as a hit on me,” he said.
Trump had all but guaranteed the results would be seen as a referendum on him by repeatedly urging voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot.” But the results showed how voters rejected his handpicked candidates while airing widespread concerns about high costs following the Iran war and his punishing tariff policy.
The results leave Trump — who watched returns at the White House with his advisers and members of his Cabinet — with dramatically diminished political capital at home and abroad.
UK leader Burnham says cost of living was key to midterm results
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the midterm results show the importance of ending the Iran war, which has sent fuel prices soaring.
“The world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living,” he said.
Burnham said he would be “working for de-escalation” in the Middle East and urging other leaders to do the same.
He said: “I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved (and) the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia. These are the things we have to focus on now, and I hope the world has a moment to do that.”
Speaker Mike Johnson says GOP will keep working ‘to make America great again’
“While the outcome of this midterm is not what we’d hoped and fought for, a new battle is just beginning,” the Republican speaker said overnight on social media.
Johnson is expected to face a challenge from Republican rivals if he tries to stay on as GOP leader in the new Congress, which Democrats will control after the midterm rout. He did not immediately address his plans.
He said, “come 2028, we WILL take back the House and we will finish the job.”
Governor seats also see a wave of historic firsts after US midterm elections
Across the country, states elected a wave of governors who are the first Black, Latina or female leaders of their respective states.
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, the only current Black governor, won reelection on Tuesday. Republican Byron Donalds in Florida and Democrat David Crowley in Wisconsin were elected as the first Black governors in their states.
Latino Democrats also will take on the highest state office in two of the biggest states. Texas voters rejected Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in favor of Gina Hinojosa, who will be the state’s first Latina governor. And Xavier Becerra, a former California attorney general, outpaced Republican Steve Hilton. Becerra will be California’s first Latino governor since Romualdo Pacheco in 1875.
Meanwhile, Tennessee elected its first female governor. Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn beat Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis city councilwoman.
U.S. midterm elections result in a wave of historic firsts
The country’s first Black female governor, the first Native American female governor, the first Native female senator and the first openly gay male U.S. senator had been declared winners on Tuesday.
By early Wednesday, the first Muslim U.S. senator was added to the list of barrier-breaking milestones.
The astonishing Democratic wave also means the United States will likely have its first-ever Black speaker of the House.
“These firsts show how our country is changing,” Alexis Anderson-Reed, president and CEO of State Voices, a network of advocates for civic engagement and equity in democracy, said in an email.
It’s too early to call the outcome of California’s proposal to tax billionaires
A California measure to tax the net worth of billionaires that divided liberal leaders nationally and triggered one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history was too early to call Wednesday morning as the vote tally continued.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the revenue dedicated to replacing federal funding cuts to healthcare. The measure left ultra-rich people, some of whom spent heavily to defeat it, scrambling to figure out whether they would pay the tax or leave California.
How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to The AP Voter Poll
After more than a decade with Donald Trump at the epicenter of U.S. politics, most voters appear exhausted and exasperated by him, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of midterm voters in all 50 states.
The president’s failure to deliver on key promises — most prominently, his vows to tame inflation, which has worsened instead — clearly weighed on his fellow Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm elections for the House and the Senate. The polling shows that voters generally saw Trump as being more focused on his own fortune and gold-leafed existence than their needs.
The president also helped elevate candidates with obvious flaws, amplifying their struggles in an already challenging year.
But the poll also contains a serious note of caution for Democrats. Many voters dislike the party — and while Democrats hold an advantage on key issues such as the economy, their edge is relatively slim. About 7 in 10 voters said that Congress isn’t doing enough to provide checks and balances for the president, setting the bar for Democrats who won back the Senate and the House.
‘A new era in world relations,’ South African leader says
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa says the Democrats taking control of the House and the Senate in the U.S. midterms is going to “introduce a new era in world relations.”
Ramaphosa says he hopes South Africa will be able to improve its bilateral relationship with the United States after his country became a target for criticism during President Donald Trump’s second term.
Trump’s Republican administration has made several moves against South Africa’s government, which he has baselessly accused of discriminating against its white minority. Those moves include excluding South Africa from meetings of the Group of 20 countries this year in the U.S. and suspending it from AGOA, a key U.S.-Africa trade program.

title: Monmouth Academy girls soccer edges Old Orchard Beach for Class D South title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
AUGUSTA — The ball rocketed off the right foot of Monmouth Academy midfielder Hayli Paradis, into the night sky above Fuller Field.
After sailing 35 yards, it went just over a leaping attempt from Old Orchard Beach goalkeeper Amelia Gervais, grazing off her fingertips and into the net.
The goal came with 27:03 remaining in the second half and gave the Mustangs a 1-0 win over the Seagulls for the Class D South championship Wednesday night.
“It feels great,” said Paradis, a senior. “(Old Orchard Beach) came out and worked hard to the end. We knew we had to come in and get it done. At halftime, we all came together and said we were going to work as hard as we could to get it done.”
The top-seeded Mustangs (10-6) will play North champion Penobscot Valley (10-3-4) in the Class D championship game Saturday at Messalonskee High School in Oakland. It’s the first regional championship for the program since 2000, when Monmouth Academy went on to beat Van Buren 2-0 for the Class D title.
No. 2 Old Orchard Beach (8-8) was playing in its first regional final.
“It was a great shot, (Monmouth Academy) earned it,” said Seagulls coach Heath Floyd. “I knew it was going to be a 1-0 or 2-1 game. … We had some opportunities but just didn’t find the back of the net.”
Play went back and forth in the first half, with the Mustangs holding a slight advantage in possession. They had one scoring opportunity, a breakaway by freshman midfielder Julia Goucher, but the ball got away from Goucher and into the hands of Gervais. The late push gave the Mustangs momentum going into halftime.
“The last 10 minutes (of the first half) was our best soccer,” said Monmouth Academy co-head coach Audrey Fletcher. “We just said that we need to continue that in the second half, and whoever scores first will come out with a win.”
Monmouth Academy continued to move the ball into Seagulls territory after the halftime break. Then, 13 minutes into the second half, Paradis struck with the long ball, giving Monmouth Academy the 1-0 lead.
“(A goal) was the hope, but I wasn’t sure if it was going to carry all the way,” Paradis said. “I was just hoping to get it into play and someone else could finish it, but it ended up going all the way. I was watching it, it kept going and it was just there in a split second.”
Gervais, a senior, had four saves for the Seagulls.
“We played a tough schedule in the Western Maine Conference so we were battle-tested,” Floyd said. “We knew it was going to be tight but the girls were ready. … I’m really proud of these seniors. The goal was always to get to this game, and from there it’s gravy. We’re one or two bounces from getting to states, but this was a huge stepping stone for our program.”
Monmouth Academy had a sluggish start to its season, going 4-4 in the first month, including a 2-1 loss at Old Orchard Beach on Oct. 3. The Mustangs have since gone 6-2 and have outscored opponents 4-0 in the playoffs.
“It’s been a different year with new coaches, especially younger coaches,” said Fletcher, who shares coaching duties with her sister, Haley Springer. “But they’ve been very coachable. From the beginning of preseason until now, they’ve been a very different team. That just shows all the work we’ve done in practice.”

title: A 13-year-old Maine girl is missing

title: An election day that was organized, efficient and polite
text:
During three hours in China Tuesday afternoon, from a little after 1 to a little after 4 p.m., democracy worked as it should: organized, efficient and polite.
Organization started in the parking lot, where men in safety vests directed traffic when needed and sent incomers to the portable building where voting was held.
By the town office, a sign said the office was closed and absentee ballots should go in the dropbox. A second sign said no, not the mailbox, the dropbox.
At the portable building, a greeter just inside the door directed voters to the registration and voting tables. There was space for two people at a time to register; over the approximately three hours, about two dozen people either registered for the first time, registered as new China residents or made changes to their registrations.
At the voting table, the first of two women asked for each voter’s name and address to compare with her list of registered voters. They almost always matched; if they didn’t, the voter was sent to the registration table to sort things out, and invariably came back to vote.
The second woman handed each voter two ballots and told each that both ballots were double-sided – a sentence she’ll probably hear in her dreams for weeks.
Other poll workers pointed out empty voting booths, some with chairs, some without, and when a voter finished filling out the ballot, directed him or her to the ballot boxes, where more helpful officials supervised depositing the ballots.
During the three afternoon hours, there was never a delay in finding an empty voting booth. Sometimes the line to the voting table briefly stretched out the door, a matter of seven or eight people. Once or twice there was a short lull when no one came in; but there were voters mulling over their ballots, so the booths were never completely empty.
Around 285 people voted during those three hours, almost half between 3 and 4 p.m. The 140 or so who voted in that hour meant more than two voters every minute.
Throughout, greetings and comments were pleasant and cheerful. Several people said they were glad to be able to vote. Some thanked poll workers; some workers thanked people for voting.
Also at the China polls during those three Tuesday afternoon hours were 16 people too young to vote, from teen-agers to toddlers, and one large service dog.

title: 1 killed and 2 others injured when a helicopter crashes into bay near Miami, officials say
text:
MIAMI (AP) — One man was killed and two others were critically injured on Wednesday when their helicopter crashed into Biscayne Bay near Miami, officials said.
The Robinson R44 II helicopter went down late Wednesday morning near Bill Baggs State Park, off Key Biscayne, while on a trip to film boats on the water, the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said.
Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during an afternoon news conference that the two survivors were taken to a nearby trauma center in critical but stable condition.
Rescue workers from several local agencies, as well as the U.S. Coast Guard and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, responded to the crash.
When the sheriff’s office marine patrol units reached the scene, they reported finding a Good Samaritan trying to help one of the victims and take him to shore. Miami firefighters attempted to save his life, but he didn’t survive, Cordero-Stutz said.
Meanwhile, border protection officers found the two other men from the helicopter and turned them over to Miami-Dade rescue workers for transport to the hospital.
Cordero-Stutz said the cause of the crash remains under investigation. South Florida has experienced heavy showers over the past few days, but it wasn’t known if the weather contributed to the crash.
Television news video of the crash shows the aircraft upside down underwater with two yellow floats attached to the bottom of its landing skids. Those emergency floats are designed to help keep a helicopter afloat in a water landing.
Officials didn’t immediately identify the helicopter’s occupants. The sheriff said they were still working to notify family members.
On Sunday, nine people died when a Learjet plummeted into the ground near West Palm Beach, Florida, with enough force to create a crater and pulverize the airplane. The NTSB is also investigating that crash.

title: Registered sex offender arrested for recording children, ‘concerning’ images found, police say
text:
MERIDIANVILLE, Ala. (WAFF/Gray News) - A registered sex offender is facing 10 counts of first-degree voyeurism after a Huntsville police investigation.
Daren William Mount, 59, was arrested on Monday.
According to the Huntsville Police Department, Mount was on its radar after an employee at a local business reported seeing “concerning” images while helping him transfer digital files.
HPD’s Special Task Force Rescuing and Investigating Kid Exploitation (STRIKE) team began investigating.
During the investigation, the team said it found pictures and videos of children, including some that were taken at angles showing intimate areas of children’s bodies.
Investigators said some of the images were manipulated. They also said some of the recordings found appeared to be taken in public places.
Mount is a registered sex offender, according to the Alabama Law Enforcement Agency Sex Offender Registry.
Federal court records show Mount pleaded guilty to receipt of child pornography in 2013. He was sentenced to 84 months in prison and 240 months of supervised release.
Mount has returned to prison twice since his 2019 release for violating the terms of his release, according to federal court records.
A federal judge decided he should be under supervised release for life after one of those violations.
The 2011 indictment said his crime spanned from 2003 to 2010, when he was viewing child sexual abuse material on a laptop.
HPD seized electronic devices during Mount’s arrest Monday and has forensic specialists examining those devices.
Police said Mount could be facing additional charges.

title: Troy Jackson wins Maine US Senate race; Hannah Pingree elected governor
text:

BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Midterm election results are being calculated across Maine.
The Latest:
Lepage declares victory; Dunlap responds
Former Gov. Paul Lepage declared victory in the race for U.S. House in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District.
During a press conference in Bangor Wednesday afternoon, he said, “there is no path to victory for my opponent.”
Following LePage’s announcement, the Dunlap campaign responded with a statement saying:
“Maine has the most reliable elections staff in the world, and I want to thank them as they diligently finish the count. This race is very close and there are plenty of ballots left to count. Thank you to every volunteer who worked their heart out on this campaign and thank you to every voter. We’ll have more to say as we learn more.”
Too close to call
The race for U.S. House in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District is too close to call. As of 3:24 p.m. Wednesday, Democrat Matt Dunlap is now trailing Republican former Gov. Paul Lepage by over 1,000 votes with 90% of the ballots counted.
Sen. Angus King reacts
Independent Maine Sen. Angus King released a statement Wednesday about Election night victories.
“I want to congratulate Chellie and Hannah Pingree, and Troy Jackson on their hard-earned victories, and look forward to working with them to deliver results for Maine and Maine people for the strong future that lies ahead,” he said. “I also want to thank Susan Collins for her long service to Maine and look forward to working with her to make the upcoming transition smooth for the people we work for in the weeks and months to come.”
Jackson defeats Collins in Maine Senate race
Democrat Troy Jackson has won the race for Senate in Maine, defeating longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
Collins released the following statement early Monday morning:
“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I’m proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years.
I called Troy Jackson tonight to congratulate him and to assure him that my staff and I will work to ensure a smooth transition.”
Collins was first elected in 1996 and has served five terms. Jackson became the nominee in July after Democratic primary winner Graham Platner dropped out. Jackson is a fifth-generation logger and former president of the Maine Senate.
Balance of power in Washington flips
Democrats have won the US Senate, ending Republican dominance in Washington by harnessing voters’ frustration with Trump, according to the Associated Press.
Hannah Pingree declares victory
Democrat Hannah Pingree has declared victory in Maine’s gubernatorial election, defeating Republican Bobby Charles and Independent Rick Bennett on Tuesday night.
Pingree will succeed incumbent Democratic Gov. Janet Mills, who was unable to seek reelection due to Maine’s constitutional term limits.
Chellie Pingree declares victory
Congresswoman Chellie Pingree has been reelected to represent Maine’s First Congressional District in the U.S. House of Representatives. She declared victory Tuesday night in Portland.
U.S. Senate race draws national attention
One race with national attention is for U.S. Senate. Republican Sen. Susan Collins is running for her sixth term against Democrat Troy Jackson.
Candidates gather for election night
Collins is hosting many Republicans running for office in the state. They include former Gov. Paul LePage, who is running for U.S. Representative in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, and Bobby Charles, who is running for governor.
Supporters for Maine Democrats running for office are gathering in Portland Tuesday night, including Jackson, Chellie Pingree, who is running for reelection for U.S. Representative in Maine’s Congressional District 1 and here daughter Hannah Pingree, who is running for governor.
Political expert weighs in
Maine’s U.S. Senate race is close.
WABI spoke with a political expert who says statewide control won’t just be won in Portland or Bangor. A political expert told WABI that statewide control will not be decided only in Portland or Bangor. The outcome could come down to a handful of swing towns across Maine.
“Bucksport is definitely on that list. Ellsworth that’s another one. Wiscassett which makes sense when you think about what Wiscassett is. Brewer is another one. Interesting results there. Hampden if we wanted to stay in Penobscot County that was another interesting place that might give us a little bit of a bellwether,” said Mark Brewer, University of Maine political Science chair.
Ranked-choice voting could decide race
Maine’s ranked-choice voting system means if neither candidate cracks 50% Tuesday night, those second-choice preferences will decide it all.

title: VETERANS CORNER: Presumptive conditions keep coming up with our veterans
text:
Presumptive Conditions keep coming up with our veterans. I am asked all the time about internal disorders because of possible exposure to certain undesirable elements in the air. I’ve addressed this in the past. I am not sure when but it was probably in a last year issue. I have no problem addressing it again as it is a very real and compensable disorder.
As we age we tend to become affected by some medical problem or another. The heart, lungs, throat, stomach and fecal and urinary tract. Can outside chemical, aerial events cause these? The answer is a definite “yes”. A very good example is the well publicized, Camp Lejeunes water contamination that our military consumed for years. Camp Lejeune’s water supply was contaminated with volatile organic compounds (VOC’s) which are industrial solvents, primarily trichloroethylene (TCE), tetrachloroethylene (PCE), benzene, and vinyl chloride. Don’t ask me to say it.
This was derived from leaking underground storage tanks at industrial waste sites. Another example would be the Tarawa Terrace System in Jacksonville, North Carolina. This water supply was contaminated from an off base dry cleaning business. There are many examples but these two give you an idea of the how and what that caused this.
The thousands of Marines that have passed through there now are aware of some of the possible life threatening diseases that have been contracted by this hidden disaster. Some of the problems are neurological and behavioral disorders, liver and kidney conditions, blood and bone marrow disorders, reproductive and developmental issues and the worst of them all, cancer, bladder, breast, cervical, eophageal, kidney, liver, lung, multiple myeloma, non-hodgkins lymphoma and the central nervous system.
These possible situations occurred in certain duty stations in different areas of the world. If you served in zones where contaminants were present you might be a candidate for any of several medical problems.
Good examples would be like the Vietnam conflict that the government refused to call war. However, what would you call a conflict in which 58,220 military personnel died? No men left behind; however, there were 575 that were never recovered. If you were stationed in or around the Vietnam area during the Agent Orange application, a defoliating agent, delivered from the air, you most likely developed some medical problems as a result of this insidious chemical which was used in and around the river to kill vegetation so we could see the enemy. Last count, has the death toll due to having contact with this chemical by touch or aspiration, at 300,000 U.S. veterans. In other words, we even killed our own. The government of Vietnam estimates that 4 million of its people were exposed, men, women and children, with 400,000 deaths or permanent disabilities caused by exposure. Even some of our Navy veterans on ships a few miles off shore were affected. The presumptive mandate was years in coming but finally we acknowledged the hideous movement of this airborne killer.
Last but not least we have the “Burn Pits” killer. If you were a soldier who was exposed to burn pits you were/are in danger of some life threatening diseases or disorders. The U.S. military incinerated millions of tons of waste containing such things as, plastics, rubbers, chemicals, medical supplies, paint, electronics and munitions as well as human waste. These things were eliminated by burning them in open pits using jet fuel as an accelerant. Because burning was done in the open air at low temperatures incomplete combustion occurred. This caused toxic fumes/smoke containing particulate matter, volatile organic compounds, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, dioxins, furans, and heavy metals directly into the air veterans breathed, as well as civilian populations. This also caused such things as lung disease, cancer, cardiovascular and systemic disorders. Even severe mental health disorders were found to be involved in diagnosis.
Thus came the PACT ACT of 2022 which was signed into law; a VA initiative which provided benefits to veterans who were exposed to burn pits, Agent Orange and other toxic substances such as the contaminated water of Camp Lejeune. In 2024 this was expanded to provide health care to millions of veterans, years earlier than called for by the PACT Act.
If you are a surviving spouse, dependent child or even a dependent parent you may be eligible for D.I.C. benefits, even if you were refused in the past, so my advice is to contact your local VA, Togus, and visit VBA, Veterans Benefits Administration on the second floor of Building 248. They are well versed in this problem and they are there to help you. You can call for an appointment or advice, or feel free to just walk-in. You will be treated with a smile and respect. They will be able to walk you through the process. It’s well worth the effort as you might achieve that which you seek. I hope this article has been of some help. God bless and have a happy and safe weekend.

title: Midterm election 2026: Tracking the results of redistricting efforts
text:
Midterm election 2026: Tracking the results of redistricting efforts
The Get the Facts Data Team is tracking how constituents in districts that were targeted in mid-decade redistricting vote in the 2026 midterm elections.
A mid-decade congressional redistricting battle has played out for more than a year now, reassigning millions of people to new districts.
Both Democrats and Republicans targeted specific districts, starting with the five targeted in Texas when President Donald Trump asked the state to redraw boundaries. California followed in response, redrawing boundaries in favor of Democrats to target five districts.
Nine states are using new congressional district boundaries for the 2026 midterm election. There were 15 districts redrawn potentially favoring Republicans, and six districts redrawn to favor Democrats, adding up to a net of nine districts favoring Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives ahead of the election.
So far, Democrats have picked up five House seats due to redistricting ahead of the midterms — four that were targeted in California and one in Utah.
Ten of the districts targeted by Republicans in redistricting have remained Democrat, including three of the four in Florida, both in Ohio, four in Texas and one in Alabama. One had flipped from Democrat to Republican.
Use the map below to see how the results of races for the House of Representatives were called in districts that were targeted during redistricting.
What is redistricting?
Redistricting is the process of redrawing congressional district boundaries every 10 years, which occurs after population counts come out following the decennial census.
Most recently, the regular redistricting process for states occurred after the 2020 decennial census. But ever since, nine states have new congressional districts for the 2026 midterm elections. Multiple other states have attempted to redraw districts.
Only two other states have voluntarily redrawn districts to give a party advantage between census cycles since 1970, according to Pew Research Center.
How many people have new districts?
More than 34 million people were assigned to new districts, according to an analysis from Protect Democracy. That's about one in every 10 Americans.
Utah has the highest share of people reassigned districts, at more than 69% of voters. The new congressional districts were court-ordered after state judges ruled that state Republicans violated anti-gerrymandering laws.
Utah's 1st Congressional District is currently held by a Republican representative, but the district is rated by The Cook Political Report to shift from solid Republican to solid Democrat.
Other states, including Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee and Florida, have roughly one-third of voters being reassigned districts.

title: Amy Acton wins historic Ohio governor’s race following campaign shaken by controversial ad
text:
Amy Acton defeats Vivek Ramaswamy in Ohio governor's race following controversial campaign ad
Dr. Amy Acton delivered a stunning victory in the race for Ohio governor on Tuesday, overcoming more than $100 million spent against her to become the first Democrat to win the seat in 20 years and the first woman ever elected to the state’s top post.
The public health physician and former COVID-19-era state health director defeated Trump-backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire and 2024 presidential candidate. She campaigned relentlessly on affordability and better access to healthcare, appealing to working- and middle-class voters by emphasizing her hardscrabble roots as an Ohio native who spent part of her childhood homeless and, for one winter, living out of a tent.
Related video above: What's at stake for Congress this midterm?
The contest was roiled by Ramaswamy’s decision in the final month to air an attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother saying she had lied about her upbringing and telling Ohioans not to vote for her. The spot sparked national bipartisan backlash on grounds that Acton’s mother had lost custody of her children decades ago after her husband, their stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child.
Acton’s victory was a huge win for a party that had slipped out of power in the former swing state, one that Democrats had all but written off as voters shifted toward Republicans during the Trump era.
Acton, 60, succeeds GOP Gov. Mike DeWine, whom she served alongside during the early months of the pandemic. But she enters office without elective experience, a stark contrast with her 79-year-old former boss, who is term-limited and likely retiring from elective politics after 50 years.
Acton’s victory came despite massive spending by Ramaswamy and his Republican allies. Elon Musk, for example, injected at least $5 million into a Ramaswamy-aligned political action committee.
She also won even after President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, an Ohio native, made repeated trips to the state in the campaign’s final weeks to rally for Ramaswamy and Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was running to retain Vance’s former seat.
Acton’s campaign was able to capitalize on Ramaswamy’s wealth to paint him as out of touch with average voters whose pocketbooks have been hit by Trump’s tariffs, the rising cost of living, and soaring fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran.
Ohio Republicans, energized by Ramaswamy’s high profile, wealth and proximity to Trump, unified around his candidacy early on. His path was facilitated by DeWine, who appointed his lieutenant governor, Husted, then the leading Republican contender for governor, to the Senate. The party’s decision to endorse a newcomer to Ohio politics left a number of veteran Republican politicians — including the attorney general and state treasurer — scrambling to adjust their own plans. And it wasn’t long before the move prompted some anxiety within the party.
Ramaswamy’s earliest headwinds came in the Republican primary, when fierce critic Casey “The Car Guy” Putsch, a vehicle designer and YouTube provocateur, seemed to catch hold with a portion of the party’s working-class base. Putsch also directed veiled ethnic and religious attacks at Ramaswamy, who is Hindu. In the end, Putsch’s $130,000 campaign attracted nearly 18% of the Republican vote. As the general election neared, Putsch announced he planned to vote for Acton.
Acton was one of the out-of-power Ohio Democrats’ most recognizable figures, after spending months during the early days of the pandemic on statewide broadcasts alongside DeWine and Husted. Ramaswamy and his allies had tried to turn that against her, arguing that she harmed Ohio by being too aggressive in shutting down schools and businesses. The governor ultimately defended Acton, his former Cabinet member, saying the buck stopped with him — though his endorsement stood with Ramaswamy throughout the campaign, even after the ad featuring Acton’s mother.
Initially leaked online, the 60-second spot featuring Acton’s mother was quickly claimed by Ramaswamy, who defended it as a fair criticism of a pattern of deception by Acton that was being inaccurately spun by Democrats and the media as questioning whether she was abused as a child.
The ad featured Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, calling her daughter “a liar” with a “serious problem” with being honest about her past. She urged Ohioans not to vote for Acton. But Arthur had been estranged from Acton for nearly 50 years. She lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton as a child, pleaded not guilty and then fled the state before he could be tried.
Both Vance and Trump defended Ramaswamy’s use of the ad. The president even expressed jealousy that he’d never had the opportunity to run such an attack against a political rival.
But others, including five Ohio governors and other top politicians of both parties, women’s groups and several hundred alumni of Ramaswamy’s Catholic high school in Cincinnati, denounced the ad as gutter politics and called for Ramaswamy to take it down. The campaign took it off the air about a week before the election, having spent about a quarter of the $4 million ad buy Ramaswamy had announced.

title: InvestigateTV+: Growing risk behind lithium-ion batteries
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes an in-depth look at the growing risk of lithium-ion batteries, why safe disposal is so difficult, and what tools safety advocates say are needed to prevent fires and explosions.
Plus, the FBI warns online extremists are targeting children in gaming and social spaces, coercing them into disturbing and violent acts. We investigate how these predator networks operate, the warning signs parents should know and how to report suspected activity.
Then, an award-winning sake blends Native American and Japanese cultures.
Hidden Heat
In a matter of seconds, the battery powering any number of devices within arm’s reach of the average consumer has the potential to transform from an efficient energy source into a fire ball the temperature of a volcanic eruption.
Lithium-ion batteries, with their energy-dense chemistry and falling cost of production, have grown to dominate the rechargeable battery market.
As that popularity has increased, experts say the ability of those batteries to ignite or even explode under certain conditions has meant as the number of fires linked to them has also gone up.
What to know about online extremism
Lurking on popular online games and social media are predators that officials with the FBI say are part of a network of extremists.
A look at float therapy
A type of therapy can improve people’s health by allowing anxiety and tension to float away. Studies show that float therapy can improve sleep and reduce pain.
Sake infusing cultures
Atsuo Sakurai and his wife, Heather, make award-winning sake at a shop just off Route 66 in Holbrook.
Sakurai said people are often surprised to learn the sake comes from Holbrook, Arizona, on Route 66.

title: Shorter days and dark afternoons can trigger depression. Here's how to fight back
text:
As winter approaches and daylight hours grow shorter, people prone to seasonal depression can feel it in their bodies and brains.
The millions of people estimated to have seasonal affective disorder, or SAD, typically have episodes of depression that begin in the fall and ease in the spring or summer. One trigger for SAD is when clocks revert to standard time, which happened Sunday across much of the U.S., bringing darker afternoons. A milder form, subsyndromal SAD, is recognized by medical experts, and there’s also a summer variety of seasonal depression, though less is known about it.
In 1984, a team led by Dr. Norman Rosenthal, then a researcher at the National Institutes of Health, first described SAD and coined the term. “I believe that because it is easy to remember, the acronym has stuck,” he said.
Scientists are trying to understand what causes SAD
No single cause for seasonal affective disorder has been identified. The disorder affects many more women than men, according to the NIH. Symptoms can be similar to depression, and can include persistent feelings of hopelessness or pessimism and difficulty concentrating, remembering, or making decisions.
In one effort to better understand what’s going on, scientists are learning how specialized cells in our eyes turn the blue wavelength part of the light spectrum into neural signals affecting mood and alertness.
Sunlight is loaded with the blue light, so when the cells absorb it, our brains’ alertness centers are activated and we feel more wakeful and possibly even happier.
Researcher Kathryn Roecklein at the University of Pittsburgh tested people with and without SAD to see how their eyes reacted to blue light. As a group, people with SAD were less sensitive to blue light than others, especially during winter months. That suggests one possible cause for wintertime depression.
When days get shorter, powerful light can help
Many people with SAD respond to light therapy, said Dr. Paul Desan of Yale University’s Winter Depression Research Clinic. The therapy can involve exposure to bright light for about a half hour in the morning, powered by devices that emit light about 20 times brighter than regular indoor light.
Research supports using a light that’s about 10,000 lux, a measure of brightness. You need to use it for 30 minutes every morning, according to the research. Desan said this can help not only people with SAD but also those with less-severe winter blahs.
Special lights run from $50 to more than $400. Some products marketed for SAD are too dim to do much good, Desan said.
Yale has tested products and offers a list of recommendations, and the nonprofit Center for Environmental Therapeutics has a consumer guide to selecting a light.
If your doctor diagnosed you with SAD, check with your insurance company to see if the cost of a light might be covered.
Talk therapy and medication can also help some with SAD
Antidepressant medications are a first-line treatment for SAD, along with light therapy. Doctors also recommend keeping a regular sleep schedule and walking outside, even on cloudy days.
Light therapy’s benefits can fade when people stop using it. One type of talk therapy — cognitive behavioral therapy, or CBT — has been shown in studies to have more durable effects, University of Vermont researcher Kelly Rohan said.
CBT involves working with a therapist to identify and modify unhelpful thoughts.
Working with a therapist can help people take small steps toward having fun again, Rohan said. Try planning undemanding but enjoyable activities to break out of hibernation mode, including getting out and seeing a friend for coffee.
___
Carla K. Johnson, the principal writer of this story, retired from The Associated Press in 2025.

title: 1 in 1800 Spotlight: Pat Cohen on Bates Rowing and the Importance of Positive Communities
text:
At the rowing boathouse, a few minutes of goofing off before practice capture what one sophomore values most about Bates: the people who make it worth staying for. Pat Cohen ’29 shares his sophomore experience with The Student as part of the 1 in 1800 series.Cohen is an Economics and Digital and Computational Studies double-major. Hailing from Haverford, Pennsylvania, Cohen is on the men’s rowing team and Student-Athlete Advisory Committee.
What was your life like before Bates?
In high school, I was a dual-sport athlete. I played hockey and rowed for three seasons each, which took up a lot of my time. I was also a member of a Pennsylvania congressional district youth cabinet, where we met with Congresswoman Scanlon once a month. During the summer, I interned with a landlord a few times, as I was interested in learning more about finance.
Why did you choose Bates?
I chose Bates because of the people. The rowing team is different from most other teams I’ve been around or seen on official visits. The men’s and women’s teams are treated as one big team under Coach Steenstra, who serves as the head coach for both. We treat each other as teammates, and we sit in class together.
On my official visit, I remember meeting a rower who ended up being one of the women’s captains my freshman year. The guy who was supposed to take me to class was running late because of a meeting. So she stepped in and hosted me at one of her classes instead. That moment resonated with me and showed me that Bates has not only friendly people, but also a rowing team with a unique culture.
What are you involved in here?
Currently, I’m a member of the Bates men’s rowing team and SAAC, the Student Athlete Advisory Committee. I’m still deciding on my subdivision, but I’ll know what it is in about a week. I’m also a double major in Economics and Digital and Computational Studies.
What are you most excited about in the next three years? Why?
The thing I’m most excited about is finishing my Economics major and my DCS major. I’m just excited to see where life takes me, to be honest. I’m also looking forward to meeting my future teammates, getting closer to my current teammates, and keeping in touch with the teammates who are alums. I can’t wait to see how Bates and the rowing team change over the next few years.
Do you have a favorite part of every day? If so, what is it?
I would say my favorite part of every day is the moment right before practice starts. We’ll already be at the boathouse and right before we start stretching, Coach gives us five or 10 minutes to just be kids. We’re not busy with thinking about schoolwork anymore and we’re not in practice yet. We’re able to be stress-free. I think those ten minutes allow us to have a better practice, and let us separate the student part of our lives and the athlete part of our lives. It’s also just a good time for us to get to know our teammates better and to be with others.
Is there anything you’re curious about trying this year?
I’m curious, as I think most sophomores are, looking at study abroad programs. I’m planning to attend the study abroad meetings while I decide whether I want to go abroad or spend that semester at Bates, since being here means so much to me.
I don’t really want to lose one semester because we only get eight. On the other hand, lots of Bates students go through, and I don’t want to lose the opportunity of being able to get that once-in-a-lifetime chance. I’m excited to learn more about studying abroad in the meetings and figure out my decision from there.
How have you gotten involved in the Lewiston Community during your time at Bates?
I’ve actually been involved in the community since my first semester here. A large part of my DCS 109 course was going to the middle school and teaching the students about computer science.
Being able to teach the middle schoolers and learn more about what the students at Lewiston Middle School care about was really cool. Also [so was] being able to see how Bates and Lewiston Middle School are similar and different, and how the Bates and Lewiston communities are important to each other.
Editor’s Note: Cohen’s answers have been edited for length and clarity.

title: ​​Donald Trump stands by Pete Hegseth after midterm rout
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
Much of the post-midterms speculation about potential Cabinet shuffles has centered on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a key architect of President Donald Trump’s unpopular war with Iran who is already shaping up to be a top target of congressional Democrats.
Trump told reporters Wednesday that he is not considering replacing Hegseth, saying “I think he’s doing a very good job.”
Hegseth has also been talked about as a potential appointed senator in Tennessee, where incumbent U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, a Republican, won the governor’s race Tuesday and could pick her interim successor.
“I actually think he’d be very popular if he did that,” Trump said of Hegseth potentially filling Blackburn’s seat.
Hegseth moved to Tennessee with his family in 2022, according to the Knoxville News Sentinel.
Story by Seung Min Kim.

title: Troy Jackson wins U.S. Senate seat; House District 2 still in limbo
text:
BAR HARBOR — Democrat Troy Jackson has unseated five-time United States Sen. Susan Collins.
Jackson, who became the Democratic nominee in July after Graham Platner exited the race, surpassed Collins, a Republican, early Wednesday morning. According to the Bangor Daily News, Jackson received 52.8% of the vote, while Collins trailed with 45.9%. As of 10:50 a.m., 91% of the vote had been tabulated.
Collins conceded, calling Jackson to congratulate him and assure a “smooth transition,” according to a statement issued by her campaign just after midnight on Wednesday morning, Nov. 4.
“It’s has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate,” Collins said. “I’m proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years.”
Collins was first elected to the U.S. Senate in 1996 and has spent 30 years in office. She has chaired the Senate Appropriations Committee, which allocates federal funds, since 2025 and was the first Mainer in 92 years to lead the committee.
Jackson, who touts himself as a fifth-generation logger from Allagash, declared victory soon after 1 a.m. Wednesday morning.
“To every Mainer who voted for Senator Collins: I’m going to be your senator, too. You don’t have to vote for me to have me fight for you,” Jackson said in a campaign statement. “This power was never mine. You gave it to me. My job is to use it for you — and I’m going to spend every day working to give you a government worthy of that trust.”
Jackson served in the Maine Senate from 2008 to 2014 and from 2016 to 2024, representing parts of Aroostook County, and he was Senate president from 2018 to 2024. He unsuccessfully ran in the gubernatorial race this year, losing to Hannah Pingree in the primaries.
He campaigned on passing Medicare for all and lowering the cost of prescription drugs, taxing the rich, dismantling ICE, passing a federal right to abortion and passing comprehensive civil rights legislation, among other issues.
Similar to the rest of the state, Hancock County favored Jackson over Collins, 55% to 45%, with 91% of precincts reporting. 17,217 Hancock County voters chose Jackson, while 14,076 chose Collins, according to unofficial results.
Maine Democratic Party Executive Director Devon Murphy-Anderson congratulated Jackson in a statement soon after he declared victory.
“From working in the woods as a logger to serving as President of the Maine Senate, Troy has spent his career fighting for working Mainers,” Murphy-Anderson said. “In just 101 days, he built a campaign that took on a six-term incumbent and won. He traveled across Maine, answered tough questions, and showed voters exactly the kind of senator he would be: someone who shows up, listens, and fights for them.”
As of Wednesday morning, the U.S. House Congressional District 2 race between former Gov. Paul LePage, a Republican, and State Auditor Matt Dunlap, a Democrat, had not yet been called.
According to the Bangor Daily News, LePage was leading with 49.8% of the vote as of 10:50 a.m., and Dunlap trailed close behind with 49% of the vote. Almost 4,000 votes, 1.2%, were blanks or for write-in candidates. Only 89% of the vote had been counted. According to The Maine Monitor, Gregory A. Ward, a write-in candidate, had gained about 0.05% of the vote.
In Hancock County, with 91% of precincts reporting, Dunlap led with 60.1% (18,836) of the vote, while LePage had garnered 39.9% (12,504).
The U.S. House District 1 race was called early in the night, with Democrat Chellie Pingree holding on to her seat against challenger Ronald Russell, commanding a 66.2% to 33.8% lead as of press time.
If neither candidate in the District 2 race gains more than 50% of the vote in the first round of tabulation, ranked-choice voting will kick in. In ranked-choice voting, the lowest-ranked candidate is eliminated in each round until there are only two candidates left, according to the Secretary of State’s office. The one with the majority of the votes, or more than 50%, will be declared the winner.
If additional counting occurs, the results of the election could be delayed days or weeks. In June, when three races proceeded to ranked-choice voting, the tabulation process stretched into the following week.

title: Midterms launch wave of historic firsts for some states — and for the nation
text:
Midterms launch wave of historic firsts for some states — and for the nation
Yes, the 2026 midterms will be remembered for the astonishing number of losses that Democrats handed to President Donald Trump. But in the background, something perhaps equally seismic unfolded: a wave of firsts that elevated into high office members of groups that had, until now, been kept largely at the margins.
There were cheers and happy tears at election parties from New Mexico to Georgia late Tuesday once it became clear voters had elected the country's first Black female governor, the first Native American female governor, the first Native female senator and the first openly gay male U.S. senator. By early Wednesday, the first Muslim U.S. senator was also added to the list of barrier-breaking milestones. The astonishing blue wave also means the United States will likely have its first-ever Black speaker of the House.
Most of these firsts are Democrats, but the GOP has also broken some new ground.
While some of these candidates have avoided focusing on the inherent historic value of their race, gender, religion or sexual orientation, some voters' rights advocates are celebrating how the electorate has expanded.
Related video: Democrats gain control of the House and Senate. What happens now?
“These firsts show how our country is changing,” Alexis Anderson-Reed, president and CEO of State Voices, a network of advocates for civic engagement and equity in democracy, said via e-mail.
“For years, people of color and LGBTQ+ communities have organized, knocked on doors, talked to voters, held conversations, and done the hard work of saving our democracy," Anderson-Reed said. "These wins are because of them.”
Here are some of the races where history was and could be made.
First Native American female governor
Democrat Deb Haaland reveled in her history-making moment of becoming the first Native American female governor in U.S. history. Haaland was declared the winner over Republican Gregg Hull, a former mayor, to lead New Mexico.
The Laguna Pueblo citizen noted that Native Americans are still here despite past efforts by the federal government to strip them of their languages and culture.
“Tonight, in our nation's 250th year, I stand before you as the first Native American woman elected governor in U.S. history,” Haaland told ecstatic supporters at a victory celebration.
In 2018, Haaland was one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress. Then she became the first Native American Cabinet secretary, running President Joe Biden’s Department of the Interior. Charles Curtis, from the Kaw Nation, was the first Native Cabinet member as President Herbert Hoover’s vice president.
Oklahoma was the only state to elect a tribal citizen for governor — Democrat Johnston Murray in the 1950s and current Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt.
"I want every child watching to know that your dreams matter and that New Mexico is a place where you can build the life you want,” Haaland said, adding that she is living proof.
First Native woman senators
Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan has become the first Native American female U.S. senator, helping Democrats win back the Senate. A citizen of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, Flanagan defeated Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter.
Tafoya would have been the first Republican of Latina heritage to sit in the U.S. Senate.
Mary Peltola, who is Yup’ik and a Democrat, could also become the first Alaska Native U.S. senator. Votes in her race to unseat Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan are still being tabulated.
Peltola was considered a trailblazer in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to the U.S. House of Representatives.
First Black female governor
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was declared the winner Tuesday night in the Georgia governor's race, ending 250 years of U.S. history without a Black woman elected as a state's governor. The former Atlanta mayor was running against Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman.
“Tonight should remind us all that no matter what community we come from, Georgia is not defined by one moment in time or by one person,” Bottoms told euphoric supporters. “It's been defined by all of us, and I will be a governor for everyone in this state."
She will also be Georgia’s first governor of color. All 83 of Georgia’s previous governors have been white men.
Lisa Demuth, however, lost an opportunity to be the first Black female governor. The former Minnesota House speaker was overtaken by longtime Minnesota U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar.
Stacey Abrams had been the only Black woman to come close to winning a governor's race when she got the Georgia Democratic Party's nomination in 2018 and 2022.
First Muslim US senator
Abdul El-Sayed will become the first Muslim American to serve in the U.S. Senate.
The contentious race to be Michigan's next senator was called for him early Wednesday morning. The race between the progressive Michigan Democrat and Republican Mike Rogers has grabbed attention nationally, especially after El-Sayed's primary opponent endorsed Rogers.
“You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed told a Detroit crowd. “Thank you. This is all yours.”
El-Sayed has had to contend with Republicans all the way up to Trump implying or overtly stating that the Michigan-born epidemiologist is not American and supports terrorism. Trump has called him “dangerously radical" and “too extreme” and referred to him as “Mohammed." El-Sayed and his supporters have denounced the attacks as Islamophobic or racist affronts to religious freedom.
First openly gay male US senator
Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas won his U.S. Senate race in New Hampshire and will become the country’s first openly gay male senator. He defeated former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu, a Republican who previously served in both chambers of Congress.
This new benchmark is not something Pappas has dwelled on while campaigning, saying, “I’m not running to make history.” But he also applauded the fact that his sexual orientation was not a huge source of discussion among potential voters.
First Black and Latino governors
The U.S. went from having only three elected Black governors in its 250-year history to gaining several more overnight.
On Tuesday, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, the third one in the U.S. and the only current Black governor, won reelection, while Republican Byron Donalds and Democrat David Crowley were elected as the first Black governor in Florida and Wisconsin, respectively. With Bottoms' victory in Georgia, two Deep South states will be governed by a Black leader for the first time.
Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, has called the presence of so many Black gubernatorial contenders “a unique moment.” It's not “an applause line” but a challenge to make diverse gubernatorial nominees more common, he said.
In addition, Nevada’s Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford won the race for governor, ousting Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and becoming the state’s first Black governor.
This was one of the most closely watched elections in the country, and Ford’s win marks a major victory for Democrats’ efforts to expand their control of state governments in key battlegrounds. Nevada will play a critical role in the next presidential election.
Latinos, both Democrats, will take on the highest state office in two of the biggest states. Texas voters rejected Gov. Greg Abbott in favor of Gina Hinojosa, who will be the state's first Latina governor. Xavier Becerra, former California attorney general, outpaced Republican Steve Hilton. He will be California's first Latino governor since Romualdo Pacheco in 1875.
Record year of women running for governor and Congress
This midterm has been a record-breaker for women vying for state and federal offices. Democrats increased their 2022 number of female candidates to 19 running for governor, according to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. The Republican Party had seven women setting their sights on governor.
Like Minnesota, Tennessee elected its first female governor. Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn beat Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis city councilwoman.
Nearly 300 women, including incumbents, were running for the U.S. Senate and House, as documented by Rutgers' Center for American Women and Politics.
Among them was Democrat Juliana Stratton in Illinois, who defeated Republican Don Tracy on Tuesday. Stratton, the current lieutenant governor, will succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin. With fellow Democrat Sen. Tammy Duckworth, who is of Thai heritage, the pair will make Illinois the first state to be represented by two female senators of color. Stratton's win also means there will be three Black women serving in the Senate.
___
Associated Press writers Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, Susan Montoya Bryan and Savannah Peters in Albuquerque, New Mexico, contributed to this report.

title: Mortgage rates continue quick retreat
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mortgage rates continue quick retreat
Current mortgage rates
The 30-year fixed mortgages in this week’s survey had an average total of 0.35 discount and origination points. Discount points are a way to lower your mortgage rate, while origination points are fees lenders charge to create, review and process your loan.
Shop smarter for mortgage rates
Bankrate connects you to the latest lender offers, tailored to you. Find your low rate today.
Explore mortgage rates
Monthly mortgage payment at today’s rates
The national median family income for 2026 is $106,800, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the median price of an existing home sold in September 2026 was $417,500, according to the National Association of Realtors. Based on a 20% down payment and a 7.26% mortgage rate, the monthly principal and interest payment of $2,281 amounts to about 26% of the typical family’s monthly income.
Meanwhile, home prices are still rising — the National Association of Realtors reports the median home price was up 1.3% over the past year, and the median of $417,500 was an all-time high for the month of September. However, values have begun to dip in many formerly hot markets. Still, signs are mixed. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller index released in late October showed national home prices grew 2.1% in the year ending in August, marking an acceleration.
What will happen to mortgage rates in the rest of 2026?
Inflation rose to 3.7% in September, although the Fed’s preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, was 3.0% for September. Oil prices have spiked amid the conflict in Iran, pushing inflation up and lifting mortgage rates from their 2026 low of 6.09%. Rising inflation has been the main driver of higher mortgage rates — the consumer price index has pushed well above the Fed’s 2% target, although 10-year Treasury yields have fallen below 5%, down from 5.3% last month.
Tuesday’s midterm results also could affect mortgage rates. “The results of the recent U.S. elections should create gridlock and constrain additional federal spending, which could help reduce pressure on Treasury yields,” says Sean Salter, a finance professor at Middle Tennessee State University. “However, persistent inflation and the possibility of further Federal Reserve tightening will likely limit any significant decline.”
Housing economists no longer expect mortgage rates to fall below 6% in the near future, and even a return below 7% seems a stretch. That reality that’s affecting home sales. Higher mortgage rates, still-record home prices and persistent inflation are likely to put the brakes on home sales. Instead, rates have risen sharply, a situation only exacerbated by the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate hike.
-  Methodology The Bankrate.com national survey of large lenders is conducted weekly. title: Mortgage rates continue quick retreat
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Mortgage rates continue quick retreat
Current mortgage rates
The 30-year fixed mortgages in this week’s survey had an average total of 0.35 discount and origination points. Discount points are a way to lower your mortgage rate, while origination points are fees lenders charge to create, review and process your loan.
Shop smarter for mortgage rates
Bankrate connects you to the latest lender offers, tailored to you. Find your low rate today.
Explore mortgage rates
Monthly mortgage payment at today’s rates
The national median family income for 2026 is $106,800, according to the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, and the median price of an existing home sold in September 2026 was $417,500, according to the National Association of Realtors. Based on a 20% down payment and a 7.26% mortgage rate, the monthly principal and interest payment of $2,281 amounts to about 26% of the typical family’s monthly income.
Meanwhile, home prices are still rising — the National Association of Realtors reports the median home price was up 1.3% over the past year, and the median of $417,500 was an all-time high for the month of September. However, values have begun to dip in many formerly hot markets. Still, signs are mixed. The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller index released in late October showed national home prices grew 2.1% in the year ending in August, marking an acceleration.
What will happen to mortgage rates in the rest of 2026?
Inflation rose to 3.7% in September, although the Fed’s preferred measure, the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) index, was 3.0% for September. Oil prices have spiked amid the conflict in Iran, pushing inflation up and lifting mortgage rates from their 2026 low of 6.09%. Rising inflation has been the main driver of higher mortgage rates — the consumer price index has pushed well above the Fed’s 2% target, although 10-year Treasury yields have fallen below 5%, down from 5.3% last month.
Tuesday’s midterm results also could affect mortgage rates. “The results of the recent U.S. elections should create gridlock and constrain additional federal spending, which could help reduce pressure on Treasury yields,” says Sean Salter, a finance professor at Middle Tennessee State University. “However, persistent inflation and the possibility of further Federal Reserve tightening will likely limit any significant decline.”
Housing economists no longer expect mortgage rates to fall below 6% in the near future, and even a return below 7% seems a stretch. That reality that’s affecting home sales. Higher mortgage rates, still-record home prices and persistent inflation are likely to put the brakes on home sales. Instead, rates have risen sharply, a situation only exacerbated by the Fed’s Sept. 16 rate hike.

title: Election day in America
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) -
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) — Control of Congress is at stake as Americans head to the polls Tuesday, joining tens of millions who have already voted early.
From the seats on the ballot to federal election monitoring, here are three things to know.
1. Every House seat is up for election
All 435 seats in the U.S. House and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot, along with hundreds of local races.
The results will determine which party controls Congress and shape President Donald Trump’s ability to advance his agenda during the next two years.
2. Millions voted before Election Day
Nearly 60 million Americans cast ballots before Election Day, either through early in-person voting or by mail.
That’s out of roughly 250 million Americans eligible to vote, according to Pew Research Center.
However, early voting totals alone won’t reveal which party is gaining ground. Even in states that report voters’ party registrations, party affiliations don’t always represent which candidates they supported.
3. Federal monitors are deploying nationwide
The Justice Department has announced it’s deploying approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers across all 50 states, marking the department’s first monitoring effort to reach every state.
Their work includes monitoring compliance with federal voting rights laws, including protections against voter intimidation and requirements ensuring access for voters with disabilities.
Once polls close, close contests and the time needed to count outstanding ballots could leave control of Congress unsettled beyond election night.
