title: Ex-Prince Andrew called to testify in civil case, 1st royal in 156 years to get witness summons
text:
Ex-Prince Andrew called to testify in civil case, 1st royal in 156 years to get witness summons
The former Prince Andrew has been called to testify as a witness in a civil fraud trial, marking what is believed to be the first time in more than 150 years that a member of the royal family has received a witness summons, British media reported on Wednesday.
The summons comes after a judge at the High Court in London gave the green light last month for the former prince, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, to be called to testify about payments he allegedly received from the parties in the case. Mountbatten-Windsor may apply to have the summons set aside, so there is no guarantee he will testify.
The lawsuit was filed by Turkish national Nebahat Evyap Isbilen, who alleges that her former adviser Selman Turk misappropriated tens of millions of pounds of her money. As part of the case, she says Turk misled her about a 750,000-pound ($1 million) payment he arranged for her to make to Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019.
Related video: Former Prince Andrew arrested in wake of Epstein files release
Mountbatten-Windsor, a younger brother of King Charles III, repaid the money in 2021 and he is not a party to the suit.
Turk claims that Isbilen authorized the payment in hopes that Mountbatten-Windsor might be able to use his connections to help her husband, who has been imprisoned in Turkey since 2015. Isbilen alleges that her husband is the victim of political persecution.
Isbilen’s attorneys said last month that they believed this would be the first time since 1870 that a member of the royal family was subject to a witness summons.
At that time, the future King Edward VII, then the Prince of Wales, was called to testify in the divorce case brought by Charles Mordaunt, a baronet and member of Parliament. The prince accepted the summons and denied having improper relations with Mordaunt’s wife, Harriet Mordaunt.
Mountbatten-Windsor is facing his own legal troubles as several British police forces investigate his links to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. British authorities began their inquiries after the U.S. Department of Justice released millions of pages of documents from its investigation of Epstein earlier this year.
Charles stripped Mountbatten-Windsor of his princely title in late 2025 as he tried to shield the royal family from the scandal surrounding his brother’s relationship with Epstein.

title: How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to The AP Voter Poll
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to The AP Voter Poll
After more than a decade with Donald Trump at the epicenter of U.S. politics, most voters appear exhausted and exasperated by him, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of midterm voters in all 50 states.
The president’s failure to deliver on key promises — most prominently, his vows to tame inflation, which has worsened instead — clearly weighed on his fellow Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm elections for the House and the Senate. The polling shows that voters generally saw Trump as being more focused on his own interests than their needs.
The president also helped elevate flawed candidates, amplifying their struggles in an already challenging year. He suggested in a Tuesday evening interview with Fox News Channel that Democrats “fought hard” and that the Republican base “didn’t like the candidates” he had endorsed because some of his picks were not fully loyal to him.
But the poll also contains a serious note of caution for Democrats. Many voters dislike the party — and while Democrats hold an advantage on key issues such as the economy, their edge is relatively slim. About 7 in 10 voters said Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances for the president, setting the bar for Democrats who won back the Senate and the House.
Video below: Democrats gain control of the House and Senate. What happens now?
Inflation crushed Republicans
It was impossible for GOP candidates to hide from inflation. Voters could see it clearly in their receipts from grocery stores and gasoline stations. The financial blow of an auto repair or a utility bill after a sweltering summer was inescapable. And even in Republican strongholds such as Texas, the drag caused by inflation helped Democrats.
About 2 in 10 Texas voters said inflation had imposed “severe” hardship on them and their family — and about three-quarters of this group backed Democrat James Talarico for the Senate. An additional 6 in 10 voters, roughly, said inflation had led to “moderate” hardship, and Talarico won the majority of these voters, too.
That same pattern repeated in state after state. Nationally, voters who said they were “very concerned” about everyday costs — including groceries, healthcare and gas — overwhelmingly said they voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.
But it wasn’t just the inflation itself that mattered. Voters nationwide pinned the blame on Trump for his tariffs, his war in Iran and his unfulfilled campaign promise two years ago to bring down prices.
Asked about the impact of Trump’s policies, about two-thirds of voters nationwide said they had made the economy worse. And out of this group, about 8 in 10 said they backed the Democratic candidate.
Corruption was a major concern
More than half of voters nationally said government corruption was “crucial” for their vote for Congress. That was a little higher than the share who said the cost of living was “crucial,” a striking finding in a year when about 6 in 10 voters said they were personally “very concerned” about the cost of food and groceries.
Meanwhile, despite Republicans’ suggestion that voters cared little about Trump making more than $1 billion last year from meme coins and cryptocurrency, most voters saw Trump as obsessed with his own interests. During his second term, Trump solicited donations from powerful companies to build his desired White House ballroom after having surprised the country by rapidly demolishing what had been the building’s East Wing.
That tenor set at the top spilled over into business deals for his family and other deals by his associates involving pardons and federal policies.
Ultimately, about two-thirds of voters said Trump does not have the right priorities — and the overwhelming majority of these voters supported Democratic House candidates.
Voters want an assertive Congress
For much of the past two years, Trump acted on his own.
Much of the Republican-controlled House and Senate barely objected to his whims. He laid off federal workers, imposed sweeping new tariffs, launched the war with Iran, remodeled Washington in gold paint, threatened the Federal Reserve, the Kennedy Center and the Smithsonian Institution and bullied a bevy of longtime allies.
Voters made it clear that they want more congressional oversight.
About 7 in 10 voters said Congress was not doing enough to provide checks and balances for the presidency, including about 4 in 10 Republicans.
Swing voters don’t really love Democrats, even if they voted for them
Despite Democrats’ victories, voters did not deliver a ringing endorsement of the party as a whole. Many voters expressed frustration with both parties: On the economy, foreign policy, healthcare, taxes and immigration, roughly 2 in 10 voters said “neither” party was better equipped to handle these issues. An even larger share of voters said neither party would be better at addressing government corruption or artificial intelligence.
Those skeptical voters generally broke for Democrats.
But it wasn’t because the party was overwhelmingly popular. Only about half of voters had a “somewhat” or “strongly” favorable view of the Democratic Party. That was higher than the approximately 4 in 10 who viewed the GOP positively, but not by much. About 2 in 10 voters who supported Democratic candidates had a negative view of the party as a whole.
Instead, in key races, voters seemed to be looking to Democratic candidates for change. In Maine, for instance, most voters who said having a candidate with “the right experience” mattered most to their Senate decision chose Republican incumbent Susan Collins. But more voters cared about bringing about “needed change,” and they favored Democrat Troy Jackson.
Republicans chose weak candidates
Trump endorsed Republicans who turned off voters — and that put areas that were once safely with the GOP at risk.
After Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina died in July, the president chose the late senator’s sister, Darline Graham, to fill his seat. The new Sen. Graham then promptly decided to seek election and struggled on foreign policy questions that were once her brother’s forte.
About 6 in 10 voters in the South Carolina Senate race said she lacked the experience to serve in the Senate.
During the Texas Republican primary, Trump ultimately backed the state’s attorney general, Ken Paxton, over its sitting senator, John Cornyn. Paxton was scandal-ridden and had been impeached but not convicted. About two-thirds of Texas Senate voters said he lacked the character to be a senator.
The president prized loyalty in Republican candidates. That hurt Republican candidates in many states.
In North Carolina, as in several other states, about 6 in 10 voters said the state's Republican Senate nominee, Michael Whatley, was “too supportive” of Trump. They chose former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, for the Senate instead.

title: Hannah Pingree speaks after winning governor's race
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Governor-elect Hannah Pingree turns attention to housing and healthcare in Maine
Governor-elect Hannah Pingree held a news conference Wednesday morning following her victory in the Maine gubernatorial election.
The Democrat and former Maine House speaker delivered a similar message to the one she delivered on election night, saying she will focus on housing, healthcare and building stronger communities.
Pingree did not answer any questions after the news conference, and one big question that remains is how she plans on passing a bipartisan budget.
During the news conference, Pingree said she will work with anyone regardless of their political party in order to get things done in Augusta.
"A big majority is not a license to go it alone. It is a promise to get it done well," Pingree said. "I will work with Democrats, Republicans, independents, tribal leaders, local officials, unions, business owners, nurses, teachers, farmers, loggers and fishermen. If you've got a good idea, my door will be open."
You can watch Pingree's news conference in its entirety in the YouTube video embedded below.
According to The Associated Press, Pingree had a decisive lead (55.0%) over Republican candidate Bobby Charles (36.9%) and independent candidate Rick Bennett (8.0%) with 92% of the votes counted as of 1 p.m. Wednesday.
Pingree declared victory in the governor's race late Tuesday night after she received phone calls from Bennett and Charles, who both conceded.
"I wished (Hannah) well and told her that her success is Maine's success," Bennett said Tuesday night. "I know that she's a committed public servant."
"Join me in a commitment to the future tonight and wish good luck to Hannah, as we commit ourselves to a better future in Maine," Charles told his supporters after he conceded the race.
Pingree served in the Maine House of Representatives from 2002 to 2010, including as House Majority Leader from 2006 to 2008 and Speaker of the House from 2008 to 2010.
She recently spent six years in the administration of Gov. Janet Mills, working as the director of the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future. Pingree tackled issues like housing and the environment, and was on the front lines of the 2024 winter storms that devastated parts of Maine's coast.
Pingree said she wants to implement the "science of reading" in Maine, as well as universal pre-K and other education policies that have worked well in other parts of the country.
When it comes to housing, Pingree said she wants to get every homeless veteran off the street and cut red tape so projects can get off the ground faster. She also wants to invest $100 million a year in housing.

title: Celebrity hair stylist and entrepreneur John Frieda dies at 75
text:
(CNN) — Celebrity hairstylist and entrepreneur John Frieda has died at the age of 75, according to an announcement shared Tuesday on his salon’s official Instagram account.
The announcement stated that Frieda passed away peacefully, surrounded by his family. No details, including a cause of death, were released.
“Mr Frieda’s pioneering spirit and dedication to his craft transformed people’s hair and confidence worldwide; one of the most influential figures in hairdressing, he is a true icon who shaped and inspired culture,” the post said.
Frieda was best known for his namesake line of hair care products, most notably the Frizz Ease collection, which launched in the United States in 1990. He is remembered as an icon across the hair and beauty industry.
Frieda is survived by his wife, four children and two grandchildren.

title: Democrats just took back control of Congress. What’s next?
text:
Democrats just took back control of Congress. What’s next?
Democrats took back control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, wins that will allow the party to obstruct President Donald Trump’s legislative agenda, block judicial nominees, and ramp up oversight.
The results set the stage for an era of political gridlock in the final two years of President Trump’s term.
Democrats will also face barriers as they work to advance their own priorities. In the Senate, 60 votes are needed to advance most major legislation, a threshold that requires some degree of bipartisan support, and the president can still veto bills that he doesn’t like.
At a minimum, Democrats will use their newly won majorities to send a message to the American public about how the party would govern ahead of the next presidential election.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries has said that his party will seek to reinstate enhanced premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act enrollees and reverse Medicaid cuts passed by the Republican-led Congress. Democrats are also expected to tee up votes challenging the president’s tariffs and opposing the war in Iran.
Trump has often bypassed Congress during his second term to shrink the federal workforce and slash funding in some areas, with little resistance from Republican allies on Capitol Hill. He’ll have to work with Democrats in some capacity to strike deals on government spending bills. A failure to compromise could risk yet another government shutdown.
Meanwhile, Democrats are expected to leverage control of key committees to launch a slew of investigations into Trump and his allies to rein in what they consider rampant corruption, but there are mixed views in the party about whether or not to pursue impeachment.
The Senate’s Democratic majority could also stand in the way of Trump’s judicial nominees and potential Supreme Court picks, should a seat on the high court open up. Democrats may also obstruct the president’s nominations for unfilled positions within his administration.
As the Democrats enter a new chapter on Capitol Hill, they’ll need to navigate ideological divides within the party. Progressives and moderates may spar over competing stances on Israel. There are also differing views over how far to go on healthcare and immigration reform.
The first test of the Democrats’ ability to unite different factions will come in the opening days of the new Congress with party leadership elections. Jeffries and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer are in line for the top spots, but both leaders have faced criticism at times from within their ranks.

title: Paul Pelosi prohibited from driving after pleading no contest to hit-and-run charge
text:
Paul Pelosi prohibited from driving after pleading no contest to misdemeanor hit-and-run charge
Paul Pelosi, husband of former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, was prohibited from driving for six months and ordered to complete a work program after pleading no contest Tuesday to a misdemeanor hit-and-run charge.
Paul Pelosi, 86, was charged after a collision with a legally parked car on the side of the road July 3, the Napa County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement at the time. He was driving his brown convertible in Yountville, California, a town in the heart of wine country. He briefly stopped and then allegedly drove away. The parked car was unoccupied, and no injuries were reported.
State law requires drivers involved in accidents resulting in property damage to stop and provide their vehicle and license information. Pelosi was charged with a misdemeanor violation of that law. In addition, Pelosi was charged with an infraction for making an unlawful turn, Napa County prosecutors said.
Related video: Close Call: Police car struck by passing driver
Officials have said no alcohol was involved in the collision.
Pelosi pleaded no contest to both the misdemeanor and infraction, prosecutors said Tuesday. He was placed on one year of summary probation, a type of unsupervised release that does not involve reporting to a probation officer, and is prohibited from driving for six months. He was also ordered to complete a 10-day work program.
Pelosi paid about $11,200 in restitution to the owner of the car he struck along with court fines and fees.
“Mr. Paul Pelosi has personally apologized to the owner of the vehicle and assured them that he would take responsibility for the damage to their vehicle," a spokesperson for the Pelosi family told KRON-TV in July.
Pelosi pleaded guilty in 2022 to misdemeanor charges of driving under the influence in Napa County and was sentenced to five days in jail and three years of probation. He served two days in jail and received good conduct credit for two other days, leaving just one day to serve in a work program at the courthouse.
As part of his probation, Pelosi was required to pay thousands in fines and victim restitution, attend a three-month drinking driver class and install an ignition interlock device, which forces drivers to provide a breath sample to prove sobriety before the engine will start.

title: Iranian officials say midterm results show US voters have rejected Trump’s war
text:
(AP) - Iranians on Wednesday struck a defiant tone, celebrating U.S. voters’ rebuke of President Donald Trump in the midterm elections while many in the Middle East waited to see how the results could affect the Iran war.
Concerns about the war, particularly frustration over rising prices for fuel and other goods in the U.S., helped Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s vote, a sharp setback for Trump and his Republican Party.
But Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father and predecessor was killed in the opening strikes of the war in February, dismissed the prospect of any major change in the U.S. approach to the Islamic Republic.
“If there are still those who harbor even a slight hope for a change in behavior or partisan and factional shifts within the system of domination, or who imagine that by giving concessions to America they can dissuade it from hostility toward the Iranian nation, they are gravely mistaken,” he said on his social media account.
There are fears that full-scale fighting could resume
The broader region has been on edge for weeks over the prospect of the U.S. resuming full-scale military operations against Iran. Talks aimed at preventing renewed fighting are continuing, while other U.S. allies in the region urge Washington against resuming a war that began more than eight months ago and has rattled the global economy and devastated Iran.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reportedly pushed for more strikes, while Trump has alternated between threatening major military action and pushing for a deal.
Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, wrote Wednesday on X that “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.” He warned that if the U.S. government ignores the vote for change, “it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare.”
Despite ceasefire agreements and repeated diplomatic efforts, military confrontations have continued in southern Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a social media post that Americans had sent a clear message and warned Washington against ignoring it. If the U.S. continues to ignore reality, the spokesperson said, “the consequences of this grave miscalculation will extend far beyond what you have already witnessed.”
Iran marks anniversary of 1979 seizure of US Embassy
Underscoring the mutual hostility at the heart of the conflict, thousands marched through Tehran on Wednesday at a government-organized demonstration commemorating the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. Embassy.
Pro-government demonstrators burned American and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.” They displayed effigies of Trump and Netanyahu alongside caricatures of the two leaders.
“Trump has gone too far in everything and that’s one reason for his defeat in the election,” said Hananeh Jahed, a demonstrator.
Zahra Nadiminejad praised Iranian resistance, saying U.S. voters “finally figured out that this is Iran, and they can’t just come in here and do whatever the hell they want.”
“They’ve seen the consequences of the war back home, from skyrocketing gas and food prices to all the devastating effects the war has had on their own country. And whether the Democrats win or the Republicans win, our hostility toward America will never come to an end.”
Nearly five decades ago, Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy on Nov. 4, 1979, taking American diplomats and other citizens hostage. Fifty-two Americans were held for 444 days before being released.
The crisis helped cement the rupture between the two countries, which have had no formal diplomatic relations for years.
The United States and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28, killing the country’s longtime supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and triggering a conflict that has disrupted global energy markets and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Addressing the demonstrators on Wednesday, Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani claimed the United States and Israel had suffered a massive defeat, which he said was also reflected in last week’s Israeli elections.
“The decisive defeat of the United States and the Zionist regime in recent developments and elections is the result of the Iranian nation’s steadfastness and strength,” Zakani said.
Iranian targets hit ahead of the midterms
The U.S. elections came just a day after what appeared to be a limited strike on Iranian targets in the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway, which renewed questions about what might come next.
Iranian state media reported explosions Monday on Qeshm and Hengam islands and near the southern port city of Bandar Abbas. Iranian authorities have not publicly identified the specific sites struck or disclosed the extent of the damage.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited before the war, has seen repeated Iranian attacks on commercial shipping. Iran has sought to restrict shipping to pressure the U.S. to lift its blockade on Iranian ports.
Iran’s state TV said Wednesday that four oil tankers caught fire after they struck mines on what it described as unauthorized routes.
Back-channel negotiations have continued.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
Before the latest strikes, the Trump administration’s last known attacks on Iran were in early September. Thousands of U.S. troops remain in waters off Iran to maintain the naval blockade, aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are on their way to the Middle East.
___
This story was corrected to show that the U.S. Embassy siege was nearly five decades ago, not three.
___
Associated Press writers Samy Magdy, Toqa Ezzidin and Aamer Madhani contributed to this report.

title: Republican redistricting sought a midterm edge. It didn’t work
text:
Republican redistricting sought a midterm edge. It didn’t work
At the urging of President Donald Trump, Republicans in eight states redrew the boundaries of dozens of congressional districts over the past year while angling for an edge that could help them hold onto a slim House majority in a tough midterm election.
Ultimately, it didn't work.
Republicans lost most of the Democratic-held seats they had targeted to flip, lost others they had banked on retaining and got swept out of power by a Democratic surge fueled by voter dissatisfaction with Trump, the economy and the war with Iran.
The Republican redistricting plan fell flat in Alabama, Florida and Texas. It got scuttled by courts in Missouri and then firmly defeated by its voters Tuesday. And it got offset in California, where a retaliatory Democratic redistricting flipped previously Republican-held seats.
The Trump redistricting plan “was systematically dismantled,” former Attorney General Eric Holder, chair of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said in an election night statement. “And given the opportunity, voters instead chose to elect a new Democratic majority.”
New districts presumed continuing support for Trump
Congressional voting districts typically are redrawn after a census at the start of each decade to account for population changes. But Trump spurred an unusual mid-decade redistricting battle last year when he urged Texas Republicans to reshape U.S. House districts to give the GOP a shot at winning five additional seats in the midterm election.
A cascade of redistricting followed, spurred along in the South by a Supreme Court ruling that weakened federal Voting Rights Act protections for majority Black districts. Republicans hoped their redistricting could net as many as four more seats in Florida, two in Ohio and one each in Alabama, Louisiana, North Carolina and Tennessee.
In all but one of those revamped districts, Trump would have carried over 54% of the vote had they been in place for the 2024 election, according to Associated Press estimates.
“In normal times, that sort of district is relatively safe,” said Justin Levitt, a professor at the Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who runs the “All About Redistricting” website.
But the presumed Republican districts got undercut by shifting viewpoints of Trump. The AP Voter Poll found about 6 in 10 disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency. Views of Trump’s priorities also were mostly negative.
“It’s foolish to presume that the electorate in one year is going to look like the electorate in another in a time of radical swings in public opinion," Levitt said. “I think it is likely that some line-drawers got cocky.”
Redistricting fell flat in the Rio Grande Valley
In Texas, Republicans reconfigured three heavily Latino districts in the Rio Grande Valley, which had shifted toward Trump in 2024, to try to boost their chances of unseating Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez. But both won reelection Tuesday. And Democrats instead unseated Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, whose district is sandwiched between theirs.
Though De La Cruz's new district retained the same percentage of Trump-inclined voters as the 2024 version, about 3 in 5 voting-age residents were new — making it harder for her to compete against Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido, a well-known Latin Grammy award winner.
The AP Voter Poll indicates a substantial shift in Hispanics moving away from Republicans compared with Trump’s victory just two years ago. Nationally about one-third of Hispanics say they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House race, while roughly 4 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago.
Republicans had “unrealistic assumptions about a shift in Latino voting" remaining in their favor, said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston.
Democrats retained seats in Florida and Alabama
Republicans in Florida tried to tilt four more House seats to the GOP in Trump’s adopted home state. Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz was among their targets, but he decided to run anyway in one of the redrawn districts. He won reelection Tuesday.
“I’ve worked across the aisle. I’ve delivered results for my community, and they spent $26 million trying to beat me,” Moskowitz said after his victory in Florida’s 25th Congressional District. “They lit that money on fire tonight.”
He said voters in his new district, like those nationwide, were most concerned about the economy and their ability to afford a good quality of life. But he said that redistricting angered voters, too.
After redistricting, about two-thirds of voting-age residents were new to the district represented by Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor. But she also won reelection. Democrat Pia Dandiya won yet another district -- an open seat in southern Florida — that Republicans had reshaped for an advantage.
In Alabama, a Supreme Court ruling allowed the Republican-led Legislature to revert to what the GOP considered to be a friendlier map. But Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures won reelection anyway, defying Republicans' plans.
North Carolina redistricting led to costly and close races
Republicans redrew two congressional districts in eastern North Carolina with a goal of unseating Democratic Rep. Don Davis in the 1st Congressional District, which has sent a Black member to Congress for more than 30 years. They made Davis' district a bit more Republican by bringing in thousands of voters from the 3rd Congressional District, held by Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. In exchange, they reassigned thousands of Democratic-leaning areas to Murphy's district.
The ensuing advertising battle for Davis' seat cost well over $50 million, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, ranking among the most expensive House races nationally.
Davis held a slight lead Tuesday night, and the race between Murphy and Democratic challenger Raymond Smith was particularly close.
More redistricting is likely ahead of the 2028 elections
What started as a Republican redistricting effort could become a Democratic redistricting movement ahead of the presidential election.
Maryland voters on Tuesday approved a constitutional amendment that will make it easier for the state's Democratic-led General Assembly to redraw districts to the party's advantage. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, have touted it as a way to “stop Trump.”
Democrats who made gains in numerous state legislatures Tuesday also could use that power for redistricting. And Democratic lawmakers in New York already have taken an initial step toward congressional redistricting before the 2028 elections.
But the recent midterm redistricting revealed it can be difficult to anticipate voter behavior when trying to gerrymander districts for partisan advantage. That could particularly be the case for the next presidential election, which would be the first in a dozen years without Trump's name atop the ballot, making it hard to know how his supporters would realign behind new candidates.
“It’s really tough to pick a political model that accurately shows you who’s likely to show up in 2028,” Levitt said.

title: Maine Democrats add seats in the Legislature, giving Hannah Pingree a bigger majority
text:
A national wave election led Democrats to expand their majorities in both chambers of the Maine Legislature on Tuesday, giving Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree a much firmer hold on the State House than Gov. Janet Mills had in her final two years.
Democrats said they won at least 87 seats in the 151-member House and 22 of 35 Senate seats as of early Wednesday. That is up from the 76 House seats and 20 Senate seats they won in 2024, when the lower chamber was decided by just 60 votes across three districts.
The result extends Democratic control of the Legislature into a ninth and 10th year and hands Pingree, a former House speaker, a large working majority as she confronts a two-year budget gap of more than $1 billion. Narrow margins in 2024 had empowered centrist members who swung some votes despite firm Democratic control of Augusta.
“Democrats see a future where we build upon the strengths of our state: our strong work ethic, our pristine environment, and most of all, neighbors who look after their neighbors,” House Speaker Ryan Fecteau, D-Biddeford, said. “That’s the message that resonated with Mainers.”
The losses left Republicans potentially further from power than they were when Mills was elected in 2018. Rep. Ken Fredette, R-Newport, a former House minority leader, said the party has to reset and govern alongside Pingree and the Democrats.
“I think the reality is that you have to govern, and I don’t think you can just be the party of no,” Fredette said. “I don’t think being the party of no is going to help us rebuild.”
Democrats held or flipped seats along the swing belt between the rural, Republican-leaning north and the more Democratic south, where most of this year’s costliest races were fought. Sen. Mike Tipping, D-Orono, easily won a rematch with Republican Leo Kenney after winning narrowly two years ago.
In the Senate, Democratic-aligned groups led outside spending in seven of the eight costliest races, many of them bids to flip Republican seats. Democrat Michael Scott beat Sen. Bruce Bickford, R-Auburn, in the state’s most expensive legislative race, and Democrat Patric Moore unseated Sen. Scott Cyrway, R-Albion, who had long held his Waterville-area seat.
Two more Republican seats were within reach early Wednesday. Democrat Amanda Heath beat Republican Kati McCormick for an open Augusta-area seat, and Democrat Elizabeth Bosworth was poised to beat former Rep. John Andrews, R-Paris, for the seat Sen. Rick Bennett gave up to run for governor as an independent.
Republicans had focused their money on the House, outspending Democrats in nine of the 10 costliest races there. It largely did not pay off. Democrats won eight of those 10, including holds by Rep. Sally Cluchey, D-Bowdoinham, and Rep. Kilton Webb, D-Durham, two of their narrowest 2024 winners.
Democrats also ousted Reps. Quentin Chapman, R-Auburn, and Marygrace Cimino, R-Bridgton, and flipped Republican-held seats in Raymond and Fryeburg. The latter town showed them pushing deeper than before into red districts.
Both parties also backed independents in districts where their own candidates have struggled, with mixed results. Rep. Amy Roeder, D-Bangor, beat independent Stephen Carey, who was backed by the Senate Republican campaign arm, by more than 20 points. All five independents running for the Senate in districts without a Republican on the ballot lost to Democrats.
But in the Belgrade area, Rep. Sharon Frost, an independent who narrowly ousted a Republican incumbent in 2024, held her seat against Republican Dexter Bridges Jr. after getting help from Democratic-aligned groups.
It appeared that Democrats lost only one House seat they won in 2024. In a race between two former Lewiston city councilors, Republican Lee Clement beat Democrat Luke Jensen by just 38 votes. It followed a tumultuous period in Maine politics.
Outside groups spent more than $4.6 million on legislative races in the final two months of the campaign, according to Maine Ethics Commission filings. Most of that helped Democrats, although Republicans outspent them in the House.
Pingree has pledged to invest $100 million a year in housing, which a larger majority makes easier to pass. Her plan to let towns tax wealthy out-of-state second-home owners at higher rates is a heavier lift, since it would likely require a constitutional amendment needing two-thirds votes in both chambers.
Lawmakers will be sworn in next month, when they will elect a House speaker and Senate president. Pingree must send them a balanced budget proposal by early February.

title: Justice Department identifies potential targets as it escalates Alaska Senate criminal probe
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department has escalated its investigation over an Alaska Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, sending letters advising a prominent Democratic attorney and others that they are considered targets of the criminal inquiry.
The letter to attorney Marc Elias, who for years has represented Democratic presidential campaigns and the party itself in election-related challenges — and has himself been a target of President Donald Trump — is among numerous ones that have been issued, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation. Target letters are sometimes issued to people the department intends to indict, but they do not necessarily mean someone will be charged.
They come as the department has ramped up an investigation into a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. Also on the ballot is retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, whose presence the Trump administration is investigating as a potential effort to spark voter confusion and steal votes from the incumbent Republican.
Criminal investigation has intensified in recent days
The criminal investigation has been quietly unfolding for months but gained new steam after the New York Times reported last week that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan.
The Justice Department has issued more than 100 subpoenas and has also sent letters ordering people to preserve records as part of the investigation, according to one of the people briefed on the probe. The FBI over the weekend also paid home visits to donors of Dan J. Sullivan.
Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage on Friday that the new revelations led to a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.” He declined to say what specific crimes authorities were investigating.
“I’m not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not,” Heyman said last week. “That’s why we are conducting that thorough investigation.”
Peltola has said she didn’t know anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot.
“I am not interested in tricking voters,” Peltola said last week.
Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have also repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest.
Recruiting spoiler candidates to siphon votes from the other major party is a practice that has been used by Republicans and Democrats alike for decades without drawing criminal scrutiny. But Trump’s Justice Department says it is taking the matter seriously.
“Everybody agrees that there is a man running that doesn’t want to run, that doesn’t expect to be senator, that is only running to confuse Alaskan voters,” Attorney General Todd Blanche told the Fox News Channel on Tuesday. “And so that’s why the Department of Justice has been fighting tooth and nail to stop this process.”
Blanche declined to discuss the target letters, saying he was not going to “confirm anything that has to do with an ongoing investigation.”
Elias is a fixture of Democratic politics — and longtime Trump target
Elias has for years been a target of Trump’s ire due in part to his role as general counsel for the 2016 presidential campaign of Trump’s Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton.
During that campaign, he hired a research and intelligence firm to conduct opposition research on Trump — an arrangement that ultimately led to the creation of a dossier of allegations on the Republican candidate’s connections to Russia that contained salacious gossip, unverified rumors and discredited information.
Trump has long been furious about the research, known casually as the “Steele dossier,” and last year announced that he would sanction the law firm of Perkins Coie, where Elias then worked, by revoking security clearances of attorneys at the firm. The punishment was blocked by a judge after a court challenge.
Elias, who did not return messages seeking comment Tuesday, alluded to that history in a statement that said: “No one should be surprised that President Trump’s Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day. This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President’s political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets.”
What is the significance of a target letter?
A target letter is a letter that the Justice Department sometimes sends to individuals whom it sees as at legitimate risk of indictment. The department defines a “target” as a person against whom it has gathered substantial evidence linking them to a possible crime and regards as a potential defendant.
It was not immediately clear exactly how many people received a target letter in connection with the Alaska investigation.
The Justice Department does not typically require targets of its investigations to testify before a grand jury in part because of constitutional protections against self-incrimination.
In this case and others, though, getting a target letter does not necessarily mean that a person will be indicted or has committed a crime. The Trump administration has repeatedly struggled to secure grand jury indictments in politically sensitive cases.
“We will not be intimidated by a sham investigation. We are going to keep working around the clock to support our clients and make sure President Trump and his party enjoy a well-deserved beating at the ballot box,” Elias said in a statement.

title: Three More County Soccer Teams Chase Regional Championships Wednesday
text:
Championship Wednesday: Three County Teams Chase Northern Maine Soccer Titles
Four Northern Maine championships came back to Aroostook County on Tuesday. Now, three more County soccer teams have an opportunity to keep that momentum going.
After Fort Kent and Wisdom swept their regional championship games, the spotlight shifts to Presque Isle, Fort Fairfield and Madawaska for Wednesday's Class B and Class D North finals.
Presque Isle's girls will take on unbeaten John Bapst at Hampden Academy, while both Fort Fairfield teams will compete for Class D North titles in Presque Isle.
And one of those championships is guaranteed to stay in Aroostook County.
For the third consecutive year, Madawaska and Fort Fairfield will meet in the Class D North boys final.
Three games, three championship opportunities, and another big day for County soccer.
Here's a look at Wednesday's matchups.
Girls Soccer
Class B North: Presque Isle Looks to Knock Off Top-Seeded John Bapst
(3) Presque Isle vs. (1) John Bapst
6:30 p.m. | Hampden Academy
Presque Isle's girls are one victory away from a trip to the Class B state championship.
The third-seeded Lady Wildcats enter Wednesday's regional final following an impressive 4-0 semifinal victory over Cony.
And what stood out about that performance was the balance.
Hailey Plant, Carrlyn Buck, Bridgid Schupbach and Willow Bugbee each scored for Presque Isle, giving the Wildcats four different goal scorers in one of their biggest games of the season.
Presque Isle also defeated Skowhegan 3-1 in the quarterfinals, with Peyton Boinske scoring twice and Buck adding another goal.
Now the challenge gets even bigger.
Top-seeded John Bapst enters the championship undefeated at 15-0-1.
The Crusaders reached Wednesday's final after overcoming a halftime deficit against Hermon, rallying for a 3-2 semifinal victory.
Presque Isle comes in at 11-3-2, and the Wildcats have shown throughout the tournament that they can generate offense from several different players.
But Wednesday will require another complete performance against a team that hasn't lost this season.
For the Lady Wildcats, the opportunity is right in front of them.
One more victory, and they're Northern Maine champions.
Class D North: Fort Fairfield Faces Penobscot Valley for Regional Title
(2) Fort Fairfield vs. (1) Penobscot Valley
6:45 p.m. | Presque Isle High School
Fort Fairfield's girls are back in the Class D North championship, and Wednesday's matchup brings together the region's top two seeds.
The second-seeded Tigers earned their spot with a hard-fought 1-0 semifinal victory over Central Aroostook on Saturday.
It was another close meeting between two familiar County opponents, with Fort Fairfield finding the goal it needed and keeping the Lady Panthers off the scoreboard.
The Tigers also shut out Washburn 4-0 in the quarterfinals.
Chloe White scored twice in that victory, while Kendall Ainsworth and Madison Parks each added a goal. Goalkeeper Addison Cole earned the shutout.
Now Fort Fairfield faces top-seeded Penobscot Valley.
The Howlers advanced with a 1-0 semifinal victory over Madawaska, ending the Owls' tournament run.
That means both teams arrive at Wednesday's championship following shutout victories.
Fort Fairfield has shown it can score in bunches, but its defense has also played a major role in getting the Tigers this far.
With a regional championship and a trip to states on the line, Wednesday's game could come down to which team makes the most of its opportunities.
Boys Soccer
Class D North: Madawaska and Fort Fairfield Meet for Third Straight Regional Final
(1) Madawaska vs. (3) Fort Fairfield
4:15 p.m. | Presque Isle High School
Some postseason matchups have a way of becoming traditions.
For the third consecutive year, the Class D North boys championship will feature Madawaska and Fort Fairfield.
The top-seeded Owls and third-seeded Tigers have worked their way through another tournament, and once again, they'll meet with a Northern Maine title on the line.
Madawaska enters Wednesday at 14-2 after defeating Hodgdon 2-0 in the semifinals.
Owen Gagnon and Aiden Gagnon provided the goals for the Owls, who have put together another impressive season.
Earlier in the tournament, Madawaska defeated the Maine School of Science and Mathematics 5-0 in the quarterfinals, a victory that also marked head coach Ben Gagnon's 100th career coaching win.
Fort Fairfield has taken a different path to the championship.
The Tigers enter at 8-6-2 after defeating second-seeded Central Aroostook 3-1 in Friday's semifinals.
They also shut out Washburn 3-0 in the quarterfinals, with Asher Winters scoring twice and Dax Milton adding another goal.
Levi Cole recorded the shutout in that game.
Now the two teams meet again.
There's no shortage of familiarity between these programs, and both know what it takes to reach this stage.
Madawaska enters as the top seed, but Fort Fairfield has already shown it can win difficult tournament games away from home.
And unlike the other County championship matchups Wednesday, this one guarantees an Aroostook County team will be heading to the Class D state final.
One team will celebrate a Northern Maine championship. The other will see its season come to an end.
Either way, another Class D North title is coming back to the County.
Wednesday's Northern Maine Regional Championship Schedule
Class B North Girls — Hampden Academy
6:30 p.m. — (1) John Bapst vs. (3) Presque Isle
Class D North Boys — Presque Isle High School
4:15 p.m. — (1) Madawaska vs. (3) Fort Fairfield
Class D North Girls — Presque Isle High School
6:45 p.m. — (1) Penobscot Valley vs. (2) Fort Fairfield

title: What you need to know about extremists recruiting children through online games
text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. (InvestigateTV) - Lurking on popular online games and social media are predators that officials with the FBI say are part of a network of extremists.
These cybercriminals are known for coercing their victims into self-harm and other acts, according to FBI special agent Heith Janke.
“Many of these actors are motivated by nihilistic violent extremism and what that generally means generally is they want to sow chaos and they want the destruction of our society,” Janke said.
As authorities work to stop this threat, they say parents are the first line of defense for their children.
Because what many children don’t know is who else is playing.
FBI identifies new extremist threat
The threat is called Nihilistic Violent Extremists, or NVEs. In plain terms, it’s online radicalization with a violent, deadly goal.
“It’s basically a hatred for our society’s values and with a drive to cause chaos and destruction in our communities,” said Amy Ramsey, a supervisory Special Agent with the FBI in Kansas City.
NVEs were first documented in 2021. Known groups include the 764 Network and “No Lives Matter.” The FBI describes NVE’s as a rising domestic terrorism threat.
“We have in this country 1,700 domestic terrorism investigations, a large chunk of which are nihilistic violent extremism, NVE — those who engage in violent acts motivated by a deep hatred of society, whatever that justification they see it is,” said Kash Patel, FBI Director.
The federal agency is investigating the deadly shooting at a San Diego Mosque for its connections with NVE’s.
On May 18, two teens opened fire on the Islamic Center of San Diego, killing three people while livestreaming the attack before taking their own lives. The FBI said the young gunmen were radicalized online and motivated by nihilistic violent extremism.
Kansas City area sees rise in NVE activity
Ramsey said the threat is closer than many think.
“Just like our offices nationally, we have seen a rise in NVE activity,” Ramsey said. “We have seen nihilistic violent extremism activity on both sides of the state line.”
Ramsey declined to discuss case specifics but said children between 11 and 18 are exactly who is being targeted. They are often vulnerable youth who may lack strong family or social support. The victims usually spend a significant amount of time in online communications.
“Both boys and girls are targeted, but predominantly female,” Ramsey said. “It really starts in a benign way, just building rapport and building a friendship.”
Once trust is established, predators move their victims to encrypted platforms where they are nearly impossible to track.
How NVEs differ from other online predators
“Nihilistic violent extremism has taken the sexual extortion that we’ve seen for years and sort of ramped it up to be more violent,” Ramsey said.
The violence begins with what Ramsey calls “blood signs,” such as writing names in blood on a notebook or wall, or violence against siblings or pets.
The behavior often escalates quickly.
“The end goal is not sexual gratification or money. It is for a victim to, in fact, commit suicide or to commit an act of mass violence,” Ramsey said. “That is their goal. They want to create chaos and destruction in our society.”
Where do the predators operate
Ramsey said the predators are often global, both inside and outside of the United States.
“They use any platforms with peer-to-peer messaging. Any gaming apps, social media or chat forums.”
Federal agents say the form of deterrence is education.
Parents must know the apps and games their children use and monitor their online activity.
“Be careful not to become complacent,” said Ramsey. “Look at the content on devices. Don’t just restrict and forget. Also, limit communication with any strangers, especially younger kids.”
Ramsey said it is most important for parents to communicate.
“Be ready to have open, calm communication about online dangers,” Ramsey said. “You need to create a safe environment, so they feel comfortable about coming to you.”
If you suspect NVE activity
If parents suspect NVE activity, Ramsey said the most important thing is to remain calm and not shame the child.
“Immediately preserve all evidence, including messages and content, and cease all communication with the predators,” said Ramsey.
Parents can report suspected activity to the FBI at FBI.gov by submitting a tip, calling 1-800-CALL-FBI or contacting their local police department.
“You should report any activity, even if you’re not sure. The FBI will help determine if it is NVE-related,” said Ramsey. “If it is a predator, they have likely victimized other children. Your evidence could help nationwide investigations.”
The FBI said the biggest deterrence is education.
Teaching kids to recognize red flags
Samantha Hausker, Director of Education at the Boys and Girls Club, said the organization is working to arm kids with the tools they need.
“We teach them how to be responsible digital citizens,” Hausker said. “We bring awareness to cyberbullying and how to recognize those red flags online.”
“It can start with one comment or one little interaction with someone online,” Hausker said. “So, make sure we teach them how to be aware of those things.”

title: Kennebunkport residents approve Prelude funding, plus Kennebunk referendum results
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Residents of Kennebunkport on Tuesday passed a widely discussed amendment to the town’s mass gathering ordinance, now allowing the town to fund a portion of the Kennebunkport Business Association’s annual Christmas Prelude event.
The amendment passed with 2,002 votes and 516 residents voting against it.
The town also approved funding up to $17,500 of the cost of the event this December.
The two referendum questions mark a tentative end to the monthslong debate of municipal funding for the event. The topic bubbled up this spring after the discovery of an ordinance that prohibited town funding of Prelude, and as some residents shared concerns about the crowds and traffic that the event creates.
Though Select Board members have briefly discussed the possibility of returning to deliberations over language sometime in the future, the passage of the ordinance now leaves the door open for the town to cover some of the municipal costs going forward.
OTHER RACES
Kennebunkport residents also passed two land use ordinance amendments. The first makes conditional uses in each zone subject to review by the planning board or code enforcement officer, while the second divides home occupations under the zoning ordinance into two types.
In Kennebunk, residents weighed in on eight referendum articles. All eight articles passed, including referendums that would transfer ownership of a portion of town owned property off Factory Pasture Lane to establish a few affordable single-family homes.
Other referendum articles include amendments that will expand the Select Board’s ability to appropriate town funds, increase the amount of time the town manager has to submit a budget proposal, increase the number of signatures required to recall an elected official from office and more.

title: Multiple rollover crashes in Aroostook County Tuesday afternoon
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WABI) - Officials in Aroostook County responded to a pair of rollover crashes yesterday.
The Aroostook County Sheriff’s Office said a 65-year-old Monticello man rolled his vehicle off the road in Littleton just before 6 p.m. Tuesday night.
He was taken to a local hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
Earlier Tuesday afternoon, a 48-year-old Monticello woman also lost control and rolled over along Route 1 in Monticello just after 2 p.m.
Officials say she was treated at the scene for minor injuries.

title: Conservative-backed candidates sweep Bangor City Council seats
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A three-person slate of conservative-backed candidates swept all three open seats on the Bangor City Council on Tuesday, diverging from statewide and national trends that favored Democrats.
Anthony Cote, Terry Dinkins, and Joseph Pratt finished as the top vote-getters in a field of 12 candidates. The trio was endorsed as a bloc by Concerned Citizens of Bangor, a newly formed political action committee seeking to change the council’s makeup.
Slate ran as an endorsed bloc
Despite running together on the endorsed slate, candidates said they had little prior connection.
“We really didn’t know each other prior to running our campaigns,” Dinkins said. “Concerned Citizens of Bangor endorsed three of us. And that was Cote, myself, and Pratt. And that’s how it turned out.”
Concerned Citizens of Bangor members offered interviews to all candidates before making endorsements. The PAC then invested in digital advertising to share their focus on downtown public safety, police department staffing, and restrictions on needle exchange programs, amid other priorities.
“I just think [voters] sent a message that they want something different,” said Philip Henry of Concerned Citizens of Bangor. “They want a safe community, they want accountability, they want economic development, and they want responsible spending.”
Focus on public safety and community needs
Top vote-getter Anthony Cote, a local business owner, said the election outcome reflected community concerns rather than party affiliation.
“My biggest issues is just cleaning up Bangor, making Bangor safe. I want my wife and my kids to be able to walk downtown without being worried about them,” Cote said. “Safety, law and order.”
Dinkins, who serves as pastor of the Mansion Church, will take office as the church prepares to open its winter warming center next week. He said his approach centers on balancing assistance with clear expectations.
“We keep them accountable here,” Dinkins said. “And I think that’s what we need on our streets is to keep them accountable, but help them with the need that they have.”
Transition of council seats
The three newly elected councilors will be sworn into office on Monday.
They will replace outgoing councilors Susan Deane, Carolyn Fish, and Joe Leonard. Deane and Fish did not seek re-election, while Leonard placed fifth in his bid for another term.

title: Maine Voters Elected Hannah Pingree Governor, Troy Jackson to the U.S. Senate
text:
Maine Elects Hannah Pingree Governor, Jackson Unseats Collins
Mainers turned out at the polls on Tuesday to elect Hannah Pingree as the next Governor, and elect new leadership to the U.S.Senate.
Maine's Second Congressional Race Is Too Close to Call
In a contentious campaign season, negative advertising and heated debates between candidates in several key races dominated the airwaves.
The result was a large turnout, as voters cast their ballots for their favorites.
Hannah Pingree has been elected Governor.
In the night's biggest upset, Troy Jackson unseated Maine's longtime Senator Susan Collins.
Most races have been decided, but the second Congressional District will go into ranked-choice results before a winner can be determined.

title: Justice Department identifies potential targets as it escalates Alaska Senate criminal probe
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department has escalated its investigation over an Alaska Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, sending letters advising a prominent Democratic attorney and others that they are considered targets of the criminal inquiry.
The letter to attorney Marc Elias, who for years has represented Democratic presidential campaigns and the party itself in election-related challenges — and has himself been a target of President Donald Trump — is among numerous ones that have been issued, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation. Target letters are sometimes issued to people the department intends to indict, but they do not necessarily mean someone will be charged.
They come as the department has ramped up an investigation into a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. Also on the ballot is retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, whose presence the Trump administration is investigating as a potential effort to spark voter confusion and steal votes from the incumbent Republican.
Criminal investigation has intensified in recent days
The criminal investigation has been quietly unfolding for months but gained new steam after the New York Times reported last week that Peltola’s campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan.
The Justice Department has issued more than 100 subpoenas and has also sent letters ordering people to preserve records as part of the investigation, according to one of the people briefed on the probe. The FBI over the weekend also paid home visits to donors of Dan J. Sullivan.
Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage on Friday that the new revelations led to a “significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska.” He declined to say what specific crimes authorities were investigating.
“I’m not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not,” Heyman said last week. “That’s why we are conducting that thorough investigation.”
Peltola has said she didn’t know anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot.
“I am not interested in tricking voters,” Peltola said last week.
Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have also repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats’ behest.
Recruiting spoiler candidates to siphon votes from the other major party is a practice that has been used by Republicans and Democrats alike for decades without drawing criminal scrutiny. But Trump’s Justice Department says it is taking the matter seriously.
“Everybody agrees that there is a man running that doesn’t want to run, that doesn’t expect to be senator, that is only running to confuse Alaskan voters,” Attorney General Todd Blanche told the Fox News Channel on Tuesday. “And so that’s why the Department of Justice has been fighting tooth and nail to stop this process.”
Blanche declined to discuss the target letters, saying he was not going to “confirm anything that has to do with an ongoing investigation.”
Elias is a fixture of Democratic politics — and longtime Trump target
Elias has for years been a target of Trump’s ire due in part to his role as general counsel for the 2016 presidential campaign of Trump’s Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton.
During that campaign, he hired a research and intelligence firm to conduct opposition research on Trump — an arrangement that ultimately led to the creation of a dossier of allegations on the Republican candidate’s connections to Russia that contained salacious gossip, unverified rumors and discredited information.
Trump has long been furious about the research, known casually as the “Steele dossier,” and last year announced that he would sanction the law firm of Perkins Coie, where Elias then worked, by revoking security clearances of attorneys at the firm. The punishment was blocked by a judge after a court challenge.
Elias, who did not return messages seeking comment Tuesday, alluded to that history in a statement that said: “No one should be surprised that President Trump’s Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day. This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President’s political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets.”
What is the significance of a target letter?
A target letter is a letter that the Justice Department sometimes sends to individuals whom it sees as at legitimate risk of indictment. The department defines a “target” as a person against whom it has gathered substantial evidence linking them to a possible crime and regards as a potential defendant.
It was not immediately clear exactly how many people received a target letter in connection with the Alaska investigation.
The Justice Department does not typically require targets of its investigations to testify before a grand jury in part because of constitutional protections against self-incrimination.
In this case and others, though, getting a target letter does not necessarily mean that a person will be indicted or has committed a crime. The Trump administration has repeatedly struggled to secure grand jury indictments in politically sensitive cases.
“We will not be intimidated by a sham investigation. We are going to keep working around the clock to support our clients and make sure President Trump and his party enjoy a well-deserved beating at the ballot box,” Elias said in a statement.

title: When heating oil surges, Mainers must weather it together
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Tae Chong is the executive director of Furniture Friends, serves on the board of directors of Good Shepherd Food Bank and previously served as the weatherization program officer at MaineHousing and as a Portland city councilor. He lives in Portland.
If you recently received your first heating oil delivery of the season, you likely felt the shock that so many Maine households are facing right now. The current heating oil bill is almost double that of last year, and it may continue to climb this winter.
With wholesale energy pressures pushing fuel prices sharply higher, staying warm this winter feels like an uphill climb. It can seem overwhelming, but for those who remember 2006 to 2008, we have seen this script before.
Back then, crude oil spiked toward record highs and retail heating oil almost doubled in two years. Serving as weatherization program officer at MaineHousing during that crisis, I watched families forced to ration fuel, burning roughly 150 fewer gallons just to get by. LIHEAP applications surged by 25%. Even after Congress doubled Maine’s emergency block grant, the money bought fewer gallons than the prior year because fuel costs outpaced federal formulas.
Maine remains the most heating-oil-dependent state in the country, with over half of our households heating with oil. Because our state is largely rural, an energy price hike never stops at the burner. Crude oil drives diesel and maritime fuel. That means higher freight costs to stock shelves in rural grocery stores, bigger fuel bills for truckers and lobstermen and higher grocery bills for working families.
When fuel spikes collide with rising electricity rates and grocery inflation, traditional safety nets stretch thin. The average low-income family has less than $400 in emergency savings. They cannot absorb thousands in added winter costs. When forced to choose between heat, groceries, or medicine, families cut the only flexible line item they have: food.
Meeting this moment takes collaboration on two fronts: forward-looking policy and grassroots community action.
First, policymakers have an opportunity to lead early. Our congressional delegation can champion supplemental LIHEAP funding that reflects today’s fuel prices. In Augusta, state leaders can safeguard emergency fuel assistance, municipal revenue sharing and vital efficiency and weatherization initiatives through Efficiency Maine, regional community agencies and more.
Maine must also support regional service centers that provide essential shelter for unhoused neighbors. Portland has roughly 5% of the state’s population but more than 40% of its emergency shelter beds. Revenue sharing alone cannot address this imbalance. To keep every neighbor safe from freezing temperatures, the state should partner with communities such as Portland, Lewiston, Bangor, Brunswick, Sanford, Rockland and Presque Isle, which use local tax dollars and facilities to meet statewide shelter needs.
Second, state and federal policy take time, but winter weather does not wait. We can each make an immediate difference by lifting up the frontline organizations keeping Mainers safe.
When family budgets get poured into fuel tanks, food pantries absorb the shortfall. Supporting Good Shepherd Food Bank and local neighborhood pantries keeps families fed. Donating warm coats and heavy blankets to Maine Needs, Catholic Charities, faith organizations and other organizations brings immediate warmth into underheated homes.
At Furniture Friends, we see how fundamental furniture brings warmth and dignity. Mattresses and area rugs add thermal insulation, slowing conductive heat loss from cold floors. Last year alone, we provided nearly 900 beds to 864 families to ensure children and seniors never sleep on a freezing floor.
Mainers have always weathered tough winters by looking out for one another. By championing sound energy policies and supporting the local organizations on the ground, we can ensure every neighbor makes it through this winter with warmth, health and dignity.

title: Dem. Chris Pappas wins Senate seat in New Hampshire, becomes first openly gay male senator
text:
CONCORD, N.H. (AP) — U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu in New Hampshire on Tuesday, keeping a critical open U.S. Senate seat in the hands of Democrats as they regained control of the chamber.
The race to fill the seat being vacated by three-term Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen was one of a handful that helped determine the balance of power in the Senate. Republicans were hoping to regain a foothold in the region while Democrats didn’t want to lose ground.
Pappas told supporters his win was a “victory for Team New Hampshire over the broken status quo.”
“Tonight’s results are a wake-up call for corporate special interests and billionaires who have been rigging the economy, for the cowards in Congress who have enabled health care cuts, tariffs and war, and for the incompetent president who can’t even be bothered to care how people are being hurt,” he said.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
While outsiders were on the ballot elsewhere, the New Hampshire race featured two candidates who tried to tap into anti-establishment angst from the inside. Sununu railed against “career politicians” despite having spent three terms in the U.S. House and one in the Senate before being ousted by Shaheen in 2008. Pappas told voters “Our country is ready for change” while seeking to remain in Washington, where he has represented the state’s 1st Congressional District since 2019.
New Hampshire voters haven’t elected a Republican to Congress since 2010. They also have voted for Democrats for president since 2004, though Republicans have dominated at the state level in recent years. With the win, Pappas will become the first openly gay male U.S. senator. He will be succeeded in the House by Shaheen’s daughter, Stefany Shaheen.
‘Team New Hampshire vs. Team Trump’
Pappas, 46, grew up working in his family’s Manchester restaurant, which opened in 1917 and claims to have invented chicken tenders. After college, he served as a state lawmaker, county treasurer and state executive councilor before being elected to Congress. In September, he defeated a democratic socialist and other opponents by a wide margin to win the Democratic primary.
“This has been a long campaign against the backdrop of chaos, corruption and costs coming out of Washington,” Pappas told supporters Tuesday night in Manchester. “New Hampshire showed up today, you spoke up today, you said in a resounding voice that New Hampshire needs a course correction. Washington needs a new generation at the table to fix things.”
Voters were particularly likely to say government corruption was “crucial” for their vote, and Pappas won most of them, according to The AP Voter Poll. He won an even greater share of voters who said the state of democracy was the most important issue facing the country.
Pappas frequently sought to link Sununu to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu despite Sununu once calling him a loser. He accused Sununu of having “a selective memory about what’s been going on over the last couple of years” and told him, “The guy who gave you his complete and total endorsement is wrecking New Hampshire’s Main Street economy.”
“This election is about Team New Hampshire versus Team Trump,” Pappas said during a debate last week. “This is not a moment to restore someone who was out of step with New Hampshire before and bring them back into power.”
Most New Hampshire voters thought Sununu was “too supportive” of Trump, while only about 4 in 10 said Pappas was “too extreme,” according to The AP Voter Poll.
Mike Bradley, 77, a licensed mental health counselor from Bow, described his vote for Pappas as “almost more anti- than pro-.”
“I’m so disgusted with what Republicans in general are doing with Trump at the helm, and pretty much no one’s standing up to him. The corruption, the homophobia, the transphobia, the endless war,” he said. “ I’m hoping that Democrats can grab a majority and counteract all this negative stuff.”
Only one Chris was on the ballot
Sununu easily defeated former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown and a handful of lesser-known candidates to win the Republican nomination. His first name was conspicuously absent from his green, blue and white campaign signs, and critics said he was counting on voters confusing him with his popular younger brother, Chris Sununu, who served eight years as governor. Their father also is a former governor.
Once the Senate’s youngest member, Sununu is now 62, older than Shaheen was when he bragged in a campaign advertisement about being younger and faster than she was. He derided Pappas as an ineffective and out-of-touch “career politician” despite the fact that Sununu traveled a similar path from the House to the Senate and comes from a family whose name is synonymous with Republican politics in New Hampshire.
“This has been an incredible campaign, but it’s not our night,” Sununu told his supporters, conceding the race about 10 minutes after the last polls closed.
Voters deluged by attack ads and mailers
Campaign cash poured in from all sides, though data compiled by AdImpact and OpenSecrets.org showed Republicans were spending considerably more as the race tightened.
Republicans accused Pappas of catering to Washington lobbyists and party bosses, describing the race as “problem solver Sununu” vs. “puppet Pappas.” “New Hampshire needs a leader, not a lightweight,” one ad from the National Republican Senatorial Committee concluded.
Pro-Pappas ads, meanwhile, accused Sununu of making millions off his political connections and highlighted the Sununu name appearing in the Epstein files. In a 2010 email, Jeffrey Epstein said Sununu “has good stories.” It’s unclear whether he meant the current candidate or his father, John H. Sununu, but Sununu says neither of them ever met or communicated with Epstein or the recipient of the email.

title: Democrat Deb Haaland to become first Native American female governor in US history
text:
(AP) - Democrat Deb Haaland was elected Tuesday governor of New Mexico, defeating Republican Greggory D. Hull.
Haaland is a former U.S. interior secretary and member of Congress.
Haaland reveled in her history-making moment of becoming the first Native American female governor in U.S. history.
The Laguna Pueblo citizen noted that Native Americans are still here despite past efforts by the federal government to strip them of their languages and culture.
“Tonight, in our nation’s 250th year, I stand before you as the first Native American woman elected governor in U.S. history,” Haaland told ecstatic supporters at a victory celebration.
In 2018, Haaland was one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress. Then she became the first Native American Cabinet secretary, running President Joe Biden’s Department of the Interior. Charles Curtis, from the Kaw Nation, was the first Native Cabinet member as President Herbert Hoover’s vice president.
Oklahoma was the only state to elect a tribal citizen for governor — Democrat Johnston Murray in the 1950s and current Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt.
“I want every child watching to know that your dreams matter and that New Mexico is a place where you can build the life you want,” Haaland said, adding that she is living proof.
Hull is a former three-term mayor of one of New Mexico’s largest cities. Outgoing Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham is term-limited.
The Associated Press declared Haaland the winner at 10:40 p.m. EST.
