title: Maine is a bright spot in a new study on loon population
text:
A new study indicates widespread and long-term declines in loon populations across the birds’ southern breeding range.
But Maine appears to be a bright spot, where loon productivity — the number of surviving chicks per breeding pair — is growing slightly, according to the research from Birds Canada.
“We actually found little evidence to suggest decline in productivity in Maine, and it actually showed that over the past 35 years, Maine’s remained relatively stable,” said Matt Fuirst a research ecologist at Birds Canada.
Fuirst and fellow researchers looked at decades of observations on thousands of lakes and ponds across Canada and the northern U.S.
The group found a 40% average decline in chick production across loons’ range, with much steeper declines in the Canadian prairies and Maritime provinces.
Fuirst said that construction and development, pollution and contamination from lead fishing sinkers are threats to loons. But the effects of climate change, including more acidic rainfall and decreased water clarity from increased storm runoff may also be hurting loons’ success at finding and catching fish, Fuirst added.
“We didn’t test what is causing these declines. We know that the threats vary by regions and some of the regions of where loons breed may be experiencing different threats,” Fuirst added.
Maine Audubon, which monitors loon populations in the state, said the population estimate this year was almost 2,800 adults and 276 chicks.
Conservation Director Sally Stockwell said in a statement that the organization is familiar with the Birds Canada study and concerned about widespread declines of the birds in North America.
Stockwell added that Maine’s adult population seems to be doing well and chick production has remained more or less steady over the decades.
But “some more recent limited monitoring of breeding success does suggest that our overall productivity is also below what’s needed to sustain a population long-term,” Stockwell added.
This story appears through a media partnership with Maine Public.

title: US cruise ship that suspended global voyage over fuel costs no passengers
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
US cruise ship that suspended global voyage leaves Cambodia with no passengers
A U.S. cruise ship that forced all its passengers to disembark in Cambodia after suspending its operations last week has departed the Southeast Asian nation with only crew aboard, Cambodian officials said Wednesday.
The MV Odyssey, owned by Florida-based Villa Vie Residences, had been on an around-the-world cruise when it suspended its planned three-year voyage due to the sharp rise in fuel costs.
It had been docked for a scheduled stop at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, when on Oct. 28 its 203 passengers were suddenly told they had to disembark within a few hours.
Related video: Energy experts predict high gas prices will stick around
The ship left Sihanoukville late Tuesday with only crew and other personnel on board, said Tang Sochetkresna, director of the Tourism Department of Preah Sihanouk province. He said he didn't know the ship's next destination.
He said that nearly 100 passengers remained in Sihanoukville, while others were visiting other parts of Cambodia or had traveled on to other countries. Most of the ship's passengers were Americans.
The ship, with its 650-passenger capacity, had 156 crew members on board, but it was not clear how many departed with the ship.
There has been no official announcement of future plans for the cruise ship. Media reports suggested that a creditor had taken over its management and was having it sailed to Singapore, Southeast Asia’s main maritime hub.
The abrupt end to the ship's voyage has drawn widespread attention because it had touted itself as a floating home, combining long-term living at sea with global travel.
Several passengers said they had paid more than $300,000 for a suite for the lifetime of the vessel.
Villa Vie Residences said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran.
The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
Passengers had said the company had been asking them for several months for contributions to keep the ship operating, and there has been an active debate on social media over whether its operation was ever financially viable.
Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before the COVID-19 pandemic, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise, along with the purchase of a second ship to operate in a similar capacity, had already been planned.

title: MAINE-LY GARDENING: What time is it?
text:
A few days ago, we experienced a jumble of notable days: Halloween, All Saints Day, the return of Standard Time, Election Day. We are halfway between the Autumnal Equinox and the Winter Solstice. Some of these special days go back thousands of years, others are marked on our paper or electronic calendars.
Around 5,000 or so years ago our ancestors in different parts of the world found ways to mark the passage of time they observed as the sun and moon moved through the sky. Some carved or painted symbols on rock faces. Other, larger groups built great monuments like the pyramids of Egypt and Central America that still intrigue us. In the last century, more of these ancient structures have been shown to reveal a sophisticated understanding of the seasons.
Without the distractions of the modern world, ancient people really watched the seasons in their regions, whether their societies were still primarily based on a hunting and gathering life that was ruled by nature, or had already settled into societies based on agriculture. They knew when to forage for plants and when to sow seeds. They knew when to expect the return of the wild animals, birds, and fish that ensured their survival.
People were always conscious of the directions: east and west as the sun traveled overhead; north and south as birds and animals migrated. Some traditional languages are so closely tied to the natural world that the speakers refer to a thing or person as being on their north, rather on the right or left, and this changes constantly as they move. This depth of knowledge is almost unimaginable to urban humans who can barely navigate using a map.
How good to be gardeners. – still grounded in the rhythm of the year – planting, tending our gardens, harvesting, and now enjoying a more restful season while looking ahead to next spring. In six months, when a bunch of special days won’t be as clumped together (I checked my 2027 calendar), we gardeners will be as focused on the natural cycle of the sun, moon and earth as our ancient forebears were. We’ll be starting seeds, watching the weather, and wondering if the calendar on the wall or the “smart” phone will provide a reliable indication of planting time.
My favorite TV gardener, British and living in an area closer to our USDA Zone 7, and where Daylight Saving Time ends a week earlier than here in the U.S., reminded gardeners to stop and sit in garden for a while and just notice how the lower sun of this season peaks through the trees. Some leaves still remain but in six months when the sun will be similarly low, but the trees will be at a different stage of growth. It’s that sort of attention to time that we modern folks so often ignore.
To describe the special light through the trees at this time, we might use the English word dappled, or the scientific word crepuscular (not as pretty and really used for dim evening light). But the Japanese language has one word – komoreb – that means exactly what we are seeing: the rays of low sunlight as they filter through the leaves.
Let’s pause for a while – no matter how much Halloween candy we distributed or ate, or how many leaves need to be raked, or who won which election – and take in the fading light of another season.
 © Judith Chute Hsiang
Jude Hsiang is a retired University Extension Master Gardener Program instructor and a member of the China Community Garden.

title: Rollover Crashes Injure Two Monticello Drivers
text:
AROOSTOOK COUNTY, Maine (WAGM) - Rollover crashes injured two Monticello residents Tuesday.
According to the Aroostook County Sheriff’s Office, sheriffs responded to a rollover in Monticello at 2:13 p.m. on Tuesday Nov. 3. The Sheriff’s Office says a 48-year-old Monticello woman lost control of her vehicle while traveling south on Route 1, which caused her vehicle to go off the road and roll over. Sheriffs say she was treated for minor injuries on scene.
Later that evening at 5:53 p.m., the Sheriff’s Office responded to a second roll over in Littleton. Sheriffs say like the first crash, the driver, a 65-year-old Monticello man, lost control of his vehicle while traveling south causing it to go off the roadway and roll over. The driver was transported to Houlton Regional Hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. Both accidents are still under investigation. The Sheriff’s Office says they’d like to thank Southern Aroostook Ambulance, as well as the Littleton and Monticello Fire Departments for their assistance.

title: Democrat Gina Hinojosa elected Texas’ first Latina governor, ousts Republican incumbent Greg Abbott
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — In a stunning upset, Gina Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than 30 years on Tuesday, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott and catapulting a decided underdog to the helm of what has long been the nation’s most populous red state.
She will become Texas’ first Latina governor — and the first Democrat to hold the office since Ann Richards in the 1990s — following a groundbreaking victory that topples one of the nation’s most prominent Republican governors and steadfast supporters of President Donald Trump, possibly accelerating the state’s shift to an emerging battleground.
Her victory was part of an electrifying night for Democrats in Texas, where James Talarico also won election, defeating Republican Ken Paxton in the race for the U.S. Senate.
Hinojosa’s win served as validation for Democrats’ long deferred dream that demographic changes in the state would be followed by a shift in political power. It also elevates Hinojosa, a 52-year-old state legislator from a liberal Austin district since 2017, into a breakout Democratic star, even as she did not have significant support from the national party for her campaign.
“It never bothered me that they doubted me. It bothered me that they doubted us,” Hinojosa told supporters at her victory party in Austin. “Texas, my faith in you never wavered.”
Jumping in the race with little money or name recognition, Hinojosa engineered a plucky and populist challenge, railing against artificial intelligence data centers and corruption to down Abbott. She also proved that money in politics has clear limits. Billionaire Elon Musk had spent tens of millions of dollars to back Republicans, and Abbott’s campaign had spent $180 million since last year in what was thought to be a safe path to a fourth term.
But Hinojosa proved durable while simultaneously riding the tailwinds of Talarico’s hard-charging Senate campaign, one of the nation’s marquee races. Just two years after Trump carried the state by double digits, the upset is also a stark reflection of how a glum national mood dragged down Republicans even in a stronghold where Democrats had not won in decades.
Trump blamed Abbott for the loss in a striking criticism of one of his staunchest supporters, accusing him of becoming a “RINO,” or Republican in name only, in the last months of the race. “He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!” Trump posted on social media.
Abbott, who had been seeking a record fourth term, said he called Hinojosa and pledged to help her transition into office.
“Leading this state has been the greatest honor I’ve ever had,” Abbott told supporters as he conceded the race.
On a national level, the loss will set off alarms for Republicans, who depend on winning Texas in presidential election years to maintain a path to the White House.
The first Democrat elected governor since 1990
How Hinojosa governs is likely to open a dramatic political and cultural shift in the Texas Capitol, which over the last decade has passed one of the nation’s strictest abortion laws and increasingly aggressive immigration crackdowns. Her victory gives Democrats a potent veto pen, but the extent of her power will be tested in a statehouse where Republicans still have a majority.
Abbott, who first took office in 2015, won each of his previous races by double digits.
Then came Hinojosa, who started her campaign last year at a time when bigger-name Democrats seemed uneager to wade into the race.
From the start she accused Abbott of prioritizing the wealthy over everyday people and failing to bring down costs. Abbott said Hinojosa wanted to raise taxes and painted her as a radical and a threat to Texans’ way of life.
One of Hinojosa’s earliest campaign pledges was a one-time $1,500 payment to each of the state’s nearly 32 million residents that she called a “Corruption Tax Refund.” She said the money would come from Texas’ massive emergency savings fund.
Hinojosa also seized on growing national rejection of data centers, accusing Abbott of allowing the energy-guzzling server warehouses to multiply. Abbott responded to public anger with a temporary moratorium on new data center approvals.
Hinojosa distanced herself from the progressive label
Hinojosa was once a proud vice chair of the Texas Legislative Progressive Caucus and defender of transgender rights, which became a centerpiece of Abbott’s attacks.
She tried to shake off the progressive label throughout the campaign and batted away culture-war issues, presenting herself instead as a populist. Her campaign included ads featuring Republican voters saying they would support her.
“They want to run an entire campaign saying that I’m too woke,” Hinojosa said in one spot. “I plan to spend an entire campaign focused on the fact that working people are too broke.”

title: Aging Untold: These are the skin cancer warning signs you may overlook as you age
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we highlight the easily overlooked warning signs of skin cancer and discuss what to ask during a dermatology exam.
Then, we explore the emotional weight of caregiving promises, examining how commitments made in love can lead to guilt when care needs change.
Finally, we visit a retired Vermont couple who turned their family barn into a bustling bakery, finding a sweet new purpose in their second act.
Skin cancer can appear in ways you might not expect, and in places you might not check.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said some of the warning signs that people might overlook include sores that don’t heal or moles that bleed easily.
And while people often are told to check areas that are exposed to the sun, Rogers warns that skin cancer can show up elsewhere.
For aging expert Amy O’Rourke, it was on her scalp. She is sharing her story.
Promising someone you are caring for that you will never put them in a home or that they can always live with you might come from love.
But those promises are often made before families have talked through what caregiving could involve, and feelings of guilt can come when care needs change over time.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing tips on how to navigate these difficult conversations and what caregivers can say instead.
Making a 60-mile drive to a farm call is not unusual for Dr. Rachel Miner, a mixed-animal veterinarian in Kansas. From families’ dogs and cats to herds of cattle, she treats animals of all kinds.
But veterinarians like Dr. Miner are becoming increasingly rare.
The doctors who protect the nation’s livestock and, by extension, its food supply, are a dwindling force, creating a critical gap in the first line of defense against disease and food insecurity.
Top of the Mountain Farm and Bakery just might be the most remote bakery in Vermont.
George Peak and Colleen Willette run it in a converted barn off a long dirt road surrounded by state forest.
From this little slice of heaven, they create homemade whoopie pies made with local maple syrup and “a lot of love,” along with other treats.

title: Gorham elementary school closed again due to gas odor
text:
Narragansett Elementary School in Gorham will reopen Thursday after closing Wednesday due to a reported gas odor, according to school officials.
Wednesday’s closure marks the fourth time in a year that the elementary school has closed due to issues with gas, though no leaks were detected during today’s inspection.
Late last year, students were evacuated and classes were canceled twice within a month after two separate gas leaks. Following another gas leak last month, school officials announced they launched an in-depth investigation into the cause of the repeated leaks.
Assistant Superintendent Quinton Donahue said in a message to families Wednesday morning that the school was closed “out of an abundance of caution” after staff received a report of a gas odor.
In an update to families Wednesday afternoon, Principal Erin Eppler said the Gorham Fire Department, mechanical contractor Johnson & Jordan, and natural gas company Unitil assessed the building using specialized equipment but found no gas leaks and concluded the gas odor was likely caused by an “air handler drawing in gas that vented outside from the building’s regulators.”
Eppler wrote that school staff were not satisfied moving forward without additional precautions and said professionals will come to Narragansett daily starting tomorrow to conduct additional testing.
The district will host a meeting for families to hear additional information from administrators, facilities staff, representatives from contractors and the Gorham Fire Department on Monday, Nov. 9, at 6 p.m. at the school.
“We know another incident involving a gas odor is concerning for our families and staff,” Eppler wrote. “It is just as concerning to us. The safety of our students and staff is paramount, and we take our responsibility to provide a safe learning environment seriously.”

title: Troy Jackson wins Maine US Senate race over GOP Sen. Susan Collins in key Democratic victory
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Late Democratic entry Troy Jackson won Maine’s U.S. Senate seat early Wednesday, defeating longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins, taking advantage of President Donald Trump’s deep unpopularity to dislodge an incumbent who had survived tough challenges in the past.
“For every family doing everything they can and wondering when somebody is going to do something for them, you have gotten me into this and you’re going to have someone who is fighting for you in Washington, D.C.,” Jackson told the crowd at an election night party in Portland.
Jackson, 58, a fifth-generation logger and former president of the state Senate, had a little more than 100 days to sell himself to Maine voters after he replaced Graham Platner as the party’s nominee in July.
He won a hastily convened nominating convention and began barnstorming the state, focusing heavily on economic issues such as the high costs of housing and healthcare. As a former campaign surrogate of independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, he was known to many progressives in the state but lacked the widespread name recognition of Collins.
Collins, 73, was widely perceived as the most vulnerable Senate Republican this election year. She entered Election Day as the only Republican lawmaker in Congress from New England and was seeking her sixth term representing a state that has voted for the Democratic candidate for president since 1992.
“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I’m proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years,” Collins said in a statement after calling Jackson to concede.
Jackson took over the nomination during a time of crisis for Democrats
Jackson hails from rural Aroostook County, among the poorest in the state, where he went to work as a lumberjack at 19.
He first entered politics after leading a weeklong loggers’ blockade along Maine’s border with Quebec in the late 1990s protesting the hiring of Canadian loggers who were coming into Maine and driving down pay rates.
The standoff ended with Jackson being escorted away by police, an unsuccessful ending that spurred him to run for elected office. He served nearly 20 years in the state House, rising up the ranks to become the Senate’s top leader.
Jackson initially didn’t plan to run for Senate this year. Instead, he threw his hat in for the Democratic nomination for governor but lost.
Platner, an oyster farmer and political newcomer, had drawn huge crowds and enthusiasm but also faced a string of controversies. After he announced in July that he would withdraw from the Senate race, Jackson won a special nominating convention later that month.
It made for a rushed start to the campaign for Jackson. Since then, he has held events at churches, union halls and bars to tout issues such as workers’ rights and the cost of living.
At times, his campaign rhetoric is reminiscent of Sanders, who joined Jackson for rallies in October.
“In the end, if you work hard, you should be able to build a decent life,” Jackson said at a campaign event near Portland in September. “But that’s not the reality right now.”
He criticized Collins as not doing enough to stop Trump. Jackson noted she voted to advance Trump’s signature tax cut and budget legislation out of committee, before she was a “no” vote on its final passage.
“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said.
Jackson faced blowback over his temperament during the campaign, and Collins criticized him for telling her to “shut up” during a debate.
Collins attempted to woo voters on her independence
Collins was first elected in 1996 and has touted her independence from Trump and her party. She has said she didn’t vote for Trump in 2016, and she voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot.
In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president’s ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they “should never be elected to office again.”
When Vice President JD Vance made trips to Maine, Collins did not appear with him. Vance told the crowd at a May rally that he sometimes gets frustrated with the senator and wishes she were more partisan.
Collins has been a top target of Democrats before. Many pollsters predicted Collins would lose to former Maine House Speaker Sara Gideon in 2020. Collins won handily during a year that Democrats won the presidential race and both U.S. House seats in Maine.
During this year’s race, Collins touted her longevity in the Senate and her status as a key player in powerful committees and budgeting negotiations. She said those aspects of her service remain critically important for Mainers.
“It has been 92 years since a Maine senator was chair of the Senate appropriations committee, the most powerful committee in the Senate,” Collins told reporters. “When I took over last year, I realized I had a once-in-a-century opportunity to help the state of Maine and pursue national priorities as well.”
___
Kruesi reported from Providence, Rhode Island.

title: Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins election to US Senate from Minnesota
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrat Peggy Flanagan won election Wednesday to the U.S. Senate representing Minnesota, defeating Republican Michele Tafoya.
Flanagan’s win held a seat for Democrats that the party could not afford to lose as it tried to flip Senate control in Washington.
The current lieutenant governor, Flanagan, who is a member of the Ojibwe Native American tribe, will succeed Sen. Tina Smith, a Democrat who did not seek reelection.
Flanagan’s win also gives progressives a notable victory in a year where Democrats’ left flank has been ascendant.
Tafoya was making her bid for political office after gaining fame as a sideline reporter on NFL football broadcasts.

title: LePage claims win in uncalled Maine 2nd District race
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - While the race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District has not been officially called by the Associated Press, one candidate has declared victory.
Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage made the announcement Wednesday afternoon, saying he was confident he had beaten Democrat Matt Dunlap.
“Public numbers have us up about 4,000, and the team has been calling all the towns that haven’t come in yet, and there’s no path to victory for my opponent,” LePage said. “We’re very, very pleased for the outcome. Looking forward to going to Washington and doing what I said I was going to do is work for the Maine people.”
LePage was joined by family, campaign workers, supporters and public officials in celebrating the declared victory.
“This is something that I was looking forward to, and I know a lot of my constituents were looking forward to,” said Rep. Jim Thorne, who represents Carmel and Hermon. “He has an open dialogue with the President of the United States, which bodes well for Maine and some of the things that we want to accomplish.”
In the wake of a cross-country blue wave, this was the only seat in the nation to be flipped by a Republican.
When it comes to working in a now Democratic-majority Congress, LePage said: “If it helps Maine, I’m all in. If it hurts Maine, I’m all out. And I will work with anybody to help make this country a better country.”
Thorne cited LePage’s history as governor and the large conservative base in the 2nd Congressional District as reasons the race was an outlier nationally.
Sofia Pride, 19, who is part of the University of Maine College Republicans club, also pointed to volunteer field work.
“Quite a few of our members volunteered for them and people were really into doing the door knocking and connecting with voters and everything and they just obviously did such a great job and it’s really exciting for them.”
While LePage declared an early victory, Dunlap said the contest remains too close to call.
“Maine has the most reliable elections staff in the world, and I want to thank them as they diligently finish the count,” Dunlap said in a statement. “This race is very close and there are plenty of ballots left to count. Thank you to every volunteer who worked their heart out on this campaign and thank you to every voter. We’ll have more to say as we learn more.”
As of 5 p.m. Wednesday with an estimate 91.7% of votes in, LePage holds 50.3% of the vote with Dunlap at 49.7%.

title: Speaker Johnson won’t seek reelection as House Republican leader after party’s midterm wipeout
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Speaker Mike Johnson will be stepping aside from Republican Party leadership after the GOP’s wipeout in the midterm election, declining to seek support to stay on as House minority leader in the new Congress, according to two people familiar with his decision Wednesday.
Johnson is expected to retain his seat as a rank-and-file member of the House from Louisiana when Congress convenes in January. He won reelection from his Shreveport-area district for a sixth term in office.
It’s a swift rise and fall for Johnson, often seen as an accidental speaker, who nevertheless drew close to President Donald Trump and led the House GOP during a tumultuous era, with one of the slimmest majorities in modern times.
And it sets up a fierce internal party battle for the new GOP leader after Democrats swept to power.
Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the House majority leader, said in a letter to colleagues that “the election was far worse than any of us expected” and he is running for the minority leadership post because “the stakes couldn’t be higher.” Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio sent a letter to colleagues describing himself as “battle-tested” as he announced his bid for the job.
House Republicans are expected to elect their new leader when members-elect gather in Washington next week, in what will likely be a familiar showdown between Scalise and Jordan, who reached for the top spot before, only to lose out, paving the way for Johnson.
The people who told The Associated Press about Johnson’s decision insisted on anonymity to disclose it.
Johnson’s sunny assertions that Republicans would defy history in the midterms, as voters traditionally have punished the president’s party in power, failed to hold. Instead, Republicans were trounced as Democrats swept to the House majority, leaving Johnson without a path to power.
The powerful speaker’s gavel now is expected to pass to Democrats, who are preparing to nominate House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York for the job, second in line to the president. The House speaker’s election is among the first votes of the new Congress, on Jan. 3, 2027.
From Shreveport to Washington
Johnson first won the speaker’s gavel in 2023 after his colleagues ousted the previous GOP speaker, Kevin McCarthy of California, in a first-of-its-kind coup in House history.
A lower-level member of House leadership, Johnson in many ways fell into the job after Republican colleagues could not agree on a successor to McCarthy. He had distinguished himself before the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol by organizing support for Trump’s false claims of widespread fraud in the 2020 election he lost to Democrat Joe Biden.
Once in office, Johnson quickly pulled closer to Trump — so close that Johnson candidly recounts their almost daily phone calls and chats, often offering his impressions in the president’s voice.
Johnson led passage of the GOP’s signature package of tax breaks and social services cuts that Trump signed into law. He protected the president and his administration from embarrassing votes, including a recent effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, by simply sending lawmakers home.
House leadership elections ahead
Johnson’s decision sets up a potential repeat of the leadership battles that have played out in recent years between the House GOP’s conservative and far-right flanks.
Scalise has long courted backing from the House GOP’s conservative wing, particularly business and energy sector lawmakers. Jordan, the brawling former wrestler who helmed the Judiciary Committee, has long been preferred by the hard right, including some from the Freedom Caucus.
Both Scalise and Jordan tried for the speaker’s gavel once McCarthy was forced aside in 2023, but they failed to win majority support from their colleagues, splitting the votes. At the time, Johnson emerged as the consensus candidate who became the House speaker.
___
This story has been corrected to show Johnson won reelection to a sixth, not eighth, term.

title: Trump-backed Republican redistricting sought a midterm edge. It didn’t work.
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
WASHINGTON — At the urging of President Donald Trump, Republicans in eight states redrew the boundaries of dozens of congressional districts over the past year while angling for an edge that could help them hold onto a slim House majority in a tough midterm election.
Ultimately, it didn’t work.
Republicans lost most of the Democratic-held seats they had targeted to flip, lost others they had banked on retaining and got swept out of power by a Democratic surge fueled by voter dissatisfaction with Trump, the economy and the war with Iran.
The Republican redistricting plan fell flat in Alabama, Florida and Texas. It got scuttled by courts in Missouri and then firmly defeated by its voters Tuesday. And it got offset in California, where a retaliatory Democratic redistricting flipped all five of the Republican-held seats it targeted.
“This is a catastrophic rebuke of Donald Trump’s failed effort to gerrymander the country into oblivion to save the U.S. House of Representatives for himself,” John Bisognano, president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said Wednesday.
New districts presumed continuing support for Trump
Congressional voting districts typically are redrawn after a census at the start of each decade to account for population changes. But Trump spurred an unusual mid-decade redistricting battle last year when he urged Texas Republicans to reshape U.S. House districts to give the GOP a shot at winning five additional seats in the midterm election.
A cascade of redistricting followed, spurred along in the South by a Supreme Court ruling that weakened federal Voting Rights Act protections for majority Black districts. Republicans hoped their redistricting could net as many as four more seats in Florida, two in Ohio and one each in Alabama, Louisiana, North Carolina and Tennessee.
In all but one of those revamped districts, Trump would have carried over 54% of the vote had they been in place for the 2024 election, according to Associated Press estimates.
“In normal times, that sort of district is relatively safe,” said Justin Levitt, a professor at the Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who runs the “All About Redistricting” website.
But the presumed Republican districts got undercut by shifting viewpoints of Trump. The AP Voter Poll found about 6 in 10 disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency. Views of Trump’s priorities also were mostly negative.
“If we look across the country, that entire mid-decade redistricting gambit was a complete bust for Republicans,” said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston.
Redistricting fell flat in the Rio Grande Valley
In Texas, Republicans reconfigured three heavily Latino districts in the Rio Grande Valley, which had shifted toward Trump in 2024, to try to boost their chances of unseating Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez. But both won reelection Tuesday. And Democrats instead unseated Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, whose district is sandwiched between theirs.
Though De La Cruz’s new district retained the same percentage of Trump-inclined voters as the 2024 version, about 3 in 5 voting-age residents were new — making it harder for her to compete against Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido, a well-known Latin Grammy award winner.
The AP Voter Poll indicates a substantial shift in Hispanics moving away from Republicans compared with Trump’s victory just two years ago. Nationally about one-third of Hispanics say they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House race, while roughly 4 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago.
The new Texas districts were drawn by Adam Kincaid, executive director of the National Republican Redistricting Trust.
“Trying to pick up five seats in Texas, without putting anything else in serious jeopardy, it was a Herculean task,” Kincaid said Wednesday. He added: “It required the trends that we had been seeing over the past several years to continue, and that did not happen.”
Had Republicans not redrawn the Texas districts, however, they likely would have lost even more seats, Kincaid said.
Democrats retained seats in Florida and Alabama
Republicans in Florida tried to tilt four more House seats to the GOP in Trump’s adopted home state. Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz was among their targets, but he decided to run anyway in one of the redrawn districts. He won reelection Tuesday.
“I’ve worked across the aisle. I’ve delivered results for my community, and they spent $26 million trying to beat me,” Moskowitz said after his victory in Florida’s 25th Congressional District. “They lit that money on fire tonight.”
He said voters in his new district, like those nationwide, were most concerned about the economy and their ability to afford a good quality of life. But he said that redistricting angered voters, too.
After redistricting, about two-thirds of voting-age residents were new to the district represented by Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor. But she also won reelection. Democrat Pia Dandiya won yet another district — an open seat in southern Florida — that Republicans had reshaped for an advantage.
In Alabama, a Supreme Court ruling allowed the Republican-led Legislature to revert to what the GOP considered to be a friendlier map. But Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures won reelection anyway, defying Republicans’ plans.
North Carolina redistricting led to costly and close races
Republicans redrew two congressional districts in eastern North Carolina with a goal of unseating Democratic Rep. Don Davis in the 1st Congressional District, which has sent a Black member to Congress for more than 30 years. They made Davis’ district a bit more Republican by bringing in thousands of voters from the 3rd Congressional District, held by Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. In exchange, they reassigned thousands of Democratic-leaning areas to Murphy’s district.
The ensuing advertising battle for Davis’ seat cost well over $50 million, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, ranking among the most expensive House races nationally.
Davis held a slight lead Wednesday, and the race between Murphy and Democratic challenger Raymond Smith was particularly close.
More redistricting is likely ahead of the 2028 elections
What started as a Republican redistricting effort could become a Democratic redistricting movement ahead of the presidential election.
Maryland voters on Tuesday approved a constitutional amendment that will make it easier for the state’s Democratic-led General Assembly to redraw districts to the party’s advantage. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, have touted it as a way to “stop Trump.”
Democrats who made gains in numerous state legislatures Tuesday also could use that power for redistricting — most notably in Wisconsin, where districts are tilted toward Republicans. And Democratic lawmakers in New York already have taken an initial step toward congressional redistricting before the 2028 elections.
But the recent midterm redistricting revealed it can be difficult to anticipate voter behavior when trying to gerrymander districts for partisan advantage. That could particularly be the case for the next presidential election, which would be the first in a dozen years without Trump’s name atop the ballot, making it hard to know how his supporters would realign behind new candidates.
The midterm election “shows districts aren’t destiny — that if voters actually show up, they can overcome district lines,” Levitt said.
Story by David A. Lieb.

title: Elon Musk spends big on losing efforts in 2026 midterm elections
text:
Elon Musk spent nearly $500M on the midterms, the majority of which went to losing causes, candidates
The 2026 midterms delivered a historic setback for Republicans, as Democrats won both chambers of Congress, made gains in several state legislatures and flipped major battleground governorships. This came despite record GOP campaign spending, led by Elon Musk.
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO spent at least $445 million between January 2025 and October 2026, according to OpenSecrets, the nonpartisan organization that tracks U.S. campaign financing. That was the most by an individual this cycle.
The New York Times, which put Musk’s total spending at $474 million, reported that he directed most of it — $212 million — toward Republican Ken Paxton’s unsuccessful bid for the U.S. Senate. Musk also donated $12.3 million to other Texas political groups, bringing his total in the state to $224 million.
The Times noted that the figure is likely an undercount because it excludes Musk’s dark-money spending and some of America PAC’s individual expenditures in Texas. Nevertheless, Democrats won every statewide race in Texas on Tuesday.
“We just proved that all the money in the world is no match for the people of Texas,” Democratic Sen.-elect James Talarico said in his victory speech Tuesday. Singling out Musk, Talarico added, “We just sent a message to every billionaire megadonor — every trillionaire megadonor."
Musk sought to paint Talarico as a "far-left extremist" who supported open borders and radical transgender policies. Projected to win about double digits, Talarico, a state lawmaker, clearly overcame the attacks and resonated with Texans.
Elsewhere, Musk donated $30 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the House GOP's super PAC that was tasked with maintaining control of the lower chamber. They were also remarkably unsuccessful, as Democrats are projected to win more than 250 seats.
Other unsuccessful candidates he or his PAC donated to include Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio and Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race. Musk also supported Vivek Ramaswamy, who lost Ohio's gubernatorial election to Democrat Amy Acton.
Musk offered a veiled reaction to last night's results on X, writing "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now." He later added, "Guess my election-interfering space lasers didn’t work this time."

title: Israel’s president takes first steps to build new government after accepting election results
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday accepted the certified results of last week’s parliamentary elections as legally binding and began consultations with party representatives on forming a new government.
The move dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to discredit the vote, in which he and his allies lost their majority in parliament, known as the Knesset, while Arab-led parties made historic gains.
“The elections are over. Now is the time to face reality,” Herzog said.
Netanyahu and his supporters have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, possibly with foreign assistance.
Herzog began consultations with party leaders on Wednesday night to determine whom to designate to form a government — a process that could bring Netanyahu’s opponents to power.
Commission finds no fraud in Israel’s election
Israel’s elections commission said earlier on Wednesday that after a thorough investigation of all parties’ claims of fraud, it had found “no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results.”
Netanyahu’s Likud party did not respond to a request for comment.
A separate investigation by the Shin Bet intelligence service, which is headed by David Zini, a Netanyahu appointee and loyalist, into allegations of foreign interference in the election is still ongoing.
In a private meeting Wednesday of the elections committee’s members, its head, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, read out an intelligence assessment from the Shin Bet saying the agency believed there had been a “widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states,” including from countries hostile toward Israel.
The Shin Bet provided no evidence to explain its assertion. The Associated Press obtained a transcript of the assessment from a person who attended the meeting and requested anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.
The committee has previously said that while claims about foreign actors seeking to influence the election are serious and under investigation, it does not believe that any such interference affected the results — even if it had happened.
Sohlberg reiterated that stance on Wednesday. “At this stage, these are merely suspicions, and even if they are substantiated, the scope of their potential impact is limited,” he said during a ceremony to present the certified election results to Herzog.
Sohlberg added that it was dangerous to cast doubt on the results and said they are legally binding.
Public trust in the electoral process is “easy to destroy, yet very difficult to repair,” he warned.
Consultations kick off coalition-building process
In the Oct. 27 vote, neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the bloc of allies of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, secured a parliamentary majority needed to form a new government, raising the possibility of an alliance between the two rivals or an alliance between Eisenkot and some of the Arab-led parties.
Herzog began a series of sit-downs with political parties on Wednesday. Three factions — all aligned with Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist base — recommended Netanyahu be given a chance to form a coalition government, while a fourth — led by a former Netanyahu ally turned rival — recommended Eisenkot. Eight more parties, including the two Arab-led factions, are scheduled to meet Herzog on Thursday, with Eisenkot’s Yashar and Netanyahu’s Likud speaking last.
After the consultations, Herzog will choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes is most likely to be able to form a coalition government. He has several days to announce his decision, which will then set the stage for weeks of negotiations.
If neither man can put together a government, the country would hold a new election early next year.
Intelligence agency’s request to interrogate senior Arab lawmakers is rejected
The Shin Bet sought approval from Israel’s attorney general on Tuesday to interrogate several elected officials as part of its separate investigation, including Ra’am party leader Mansour Abbas and other senior Arab lawmakers, Israeli media reported.
In a statement rejecting the request, Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said: “It is not permissible to interrogate citizens or elected officials without evidence to justify such action.”
The Joint List of Arab parties condemned the request, calling it a “campaign of incitement” by Netanyahu and his allies designed to delegitimize the Arab vote.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right ally of Netanyahu, called on the Shin Bet, over which he has no authority, to “arrest all the leaders of the Arab political parties” and interrogate them in “basement interrogation cells until these suspicions are fully clarified.”
Herzog said Wednesday that the Shin Bet’s investigation into possible foreign interference should proceed, but cautioned that Arab Israeli voters “must not be smeared.”
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” Herzog said.
___
Melzer reported from Nahariya, Israel.

title: Scarborough elects town councilors, passes radio system referendum
text:
Voters elected Jessica Sargent, Sean Flaherty and Isha Agarwal from a field of seven candidates vying to fill three seats on the Scarborough Town Council, according to unofficial election results from Tuesday’s election. Their terms will expire in 2029.
Flaherty got 7,050 votes, while Sargent received 6,617 and Agarwal earned 5,366. Lawrence Cain, Denise Hamilton, Samuel Cofone and Russell Wayne Werts trailed with 4,434, 4,449, 2,348 and 1,815 votes, respectively.
Flaherty, a Democrat, is a lawyer and served as a member of the Maine House of Representatives from 2008 to 2010.
Agarwal, a Democrat, is an emergency room doctor running for office for the first time.
Sargent, a Democrat, is a small business owner and conservation policy consultant running for office for the first time.
Voters elected Andrew Guillerault to the Scarborough School Board. He earned 5,820 votes, while his opponent, Stephen Zamierowski, earned 4,754.
Guillerault is a stay-at-home dad, coach, former district employee and the husband of a teacher.
Voters elected Matthew Garrett, Jason Greenleaf and Benjamin McDougal as the three Scarborough Sanitary District Trustees. They got 7,636, 8,469 and 5,949 votes, respectively. Denis Lafreniere Jr., who was also running, was not elected, with 5,000 votes. The seats have three-year terms expiring in 2029.
RADIO SYSTEM REFERENDUM
Scarborough voters approved the referendum to upgrade the radio communications system used by Scarborough’s and Old Orchard Beach’s public safety, public service and school departments.
The referendum asked residents to approve borrowing up to $6 million, in anticipation of receiving federal grants to help pay for Scarborough’s $9.2 million share. The total project will cost nearly $12.4 million, with Old Orchard Beach contributing $3.2 million.

title: Former chief deputy closes in on Hancock sheriff victory as challenger concedes
text:
Former chief deputy and current Ellsworth detective Corey Bagley is poised to be Hancock County’s next sheriff after rival Lt. Dakota Dupuis conceded Wednesday morning.
As of 9 a.m., Republican nominee Bagley had a roughly 3,000-vote lead on Dupuis, a Democrat, in the divisive election for Hancock County’s top law enforcement officer, according to unofficial results compiled by the Bangor Daily News.
Bagley had 13,884 votes and Dupuis had 10,965 votes with 30 of 37 municipalities having reported unofficial results.
Dupuis conceded Wednesday morning on Facebook, noting that he had congratulated Bagley on his win.
The race for sheriff turned bitter in its final weeks after outgoing sheriff Scott Kane, a Republican who endorsed Dupuis, accused Bagley of steering a county contract to his father, Rudy Bagley, during his time at the sheriff’s department. Kane did not seek re-election.
Bagley has denied involvement in the contract, claiming it was agreed upon between his father and County Commissioner William Clark, who was sheriff at the time. Clark has endorsed Bagley, who served the sheriff’s office for 31 years prior to his departure in 2023.
Four Democratic state legislators crossed party lines to endorse Bagley in the campaign’s final months. County commissioners were split on their support for the candidates.
If elected sheriff, Bagley, 57, and Dupuis, 31, both said they would prioritize community policing and mental health services. Bagley hopes to replicate Bar Harbor’s Good Morning program, a free service that offers daily check-ins on senior residents and adults with disabilities.
Bagley said he wants to mend what he described as the sheriff’s office’s fraught relationships with local law enforcement and first responder agencies.
Outside of his law enforcement career, Bagley spent more than three decades coaching youth sports in Ellsworth and has been involved in various local charities and nonprofits.

title: These are all the Senate, House and gubernatorial seats Democrats flipped
text:
Tracking the election flips: See where each party made gains in midterms
Democrats will hold the majority in the Senate and House of Representatives and several governorships next year after a historic blue wave in the midterm elections.
As of Thursday morning, Democrats will hold 54 Senate seats and 240 House seats in the next term.
The Get the Facts Data Team tracked results in competitive Senate, House and gubernatorial races, as well as other seats that flipped.
Democrats win control of Senate
In the Senate, Democrats flipped seven seats and will hold a majority in the chamber next year.
As of Thursday morning, Democrats had gained Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Maine. The party also retained seats in Minnesota and Michigan.
The Cook Political Report had rated 11 Senate races as competitive, with six of those being toss-ups. So far, Democrats have won five of those toss-ups.
Alaska is the last of the competitive seats and has not been called as of Wednesday morning.
North Carolina’s Senate race was not rated as competitive, and Democratic nominee Roy Cooper flipped that seat.
House flips lead to new Democratic majority
In the House of Representatives, Democrats have flipped more than 30 seats as of Thursday morning. About 48 House races have not been called yet.
All 435 seats in the House were up for election this year, including 54 competitive races.
Of the 54 competitive races, Democrats have flipped 25 seats, including all three competitive races in Iowa’s 1st, 2nd and 3rd districts. Michigan also had three competitive House races in the state's 4th, 7th and 10th districts, all of which were flipped from Republican to Democrat.
Republicans have flipped one House seat, Texas's 32nd district was redistricted to favor Republicans.
Democrats secure majority of governorships in 16 years
There were 36 gubernatorial elections in the midterms this year, with 12 of them classified as competitive races.
Democrats have flipped five of those competitive gubernatorial races and retained three. Republicans retained the governorships in Nebraska and Florida.
Alaska's and Kansas' gubernatorial elections were also rated as competitive but have not been called yet.

title: Democrats’ sweeping state government gains will shift power and bring pressure to deliver results
text:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Democrats in Texas took control of the state House after historic wins for governor and U.S. Senate, part of a series of sweeping gains nationwide in Tuesday’s elections that shifted the balance of power across several battleground and Republican-leaning states.
It will be the first time Democrats control the House in Texas since Republicans took over after the 2002 election. Republicans are keeping control of the Senate in the state — which also elected Gina Hinojosa its first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994.
In this year’s midterm elections, the party took full control — both statehouse chambers and governors’ offices — in at least five states where they previously shared power.
The wins put pressure on the party to answer to an electorate angry over the rising cost of living, high gas prices, inflation and the lack of affordable housing. State governments shape a wide array of policies affecting everyday lives, including tax rates and abortion rights, school choice and education funding, data center development, and the use of artificial intelligence and law enforcement surveillance cameras.
“Now it’s time to deliver,” said Devin Remiker, chairman of Wisconsin’s Democratic Party, which retained the governor’s office and successfully flipped both chambers of the state Legislature, breaking a 16-year Republican majority.
Democrats prevail in battleground states
Democrats also won or retained full control of both chambers of the legislatures in Michigan, Minnesota and Pennsylvania and kept the governor’s office for trifectas in all three.
In Nevada, they gained control by winning the governor’s seat and retaining the legislature.
U.S. HOUSE BALANCE OF POWER
There will be pressure on Democrats in Wisconsin and other battleground states to redraw congressional maps, just as President Donald Trump successfully urged eight Republican-led states to do ahead of this election. But that backfired, with Republicans losing most of the Democratic-held seats they had targeted to flip and others they had banked on winning.
The Republican congressional redistricting in Texas may have mobilized additional Democratic voters in some parts of the state who helped drive gains in the statehouse, said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston.
But “when we’re trying to think about why Democrats won, it’s one man in the White House and his policies — Donald Trump,” Jones said.
Even under maps that favored Republicans in Wisconsin, Democrats picked up two congressional seats in Tuesday’s races. That means the state will have an evenly divided congressional delegation in 2027.
Democrats also break up Republican trifectas and supermajorities
Democrats will also hold at least 28 governorships in 2027, with pickups in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — states long held by Republicans.
And the party broke or prevented Republican supermajorities in nine legislative chambers in eight states: Florida, South Carolina, Indiana, Missouri, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and North Carolina.
That means Republicans would need help from Democratic lawmakers to override a Democratic governor’s veto in Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina. The Associated Press has not called the governor’s race in Kansas.
The wins come after Democrats lost nearly 1,000 state legislative seats during President Barack Obama’s tenure, a slide they’ve been trying to reverse for several cycles.
It’s the biggest single-election change of partisan power in state governments since 2010, said Katie Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting at the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Lawmakers who will soon be in the majority say the change brings expectations. “We know that people will be counting on us to deliver, and we take that incredibly seriously,” said Wisconsin state Rep. Greta Neubauer, currently the minority leader of state Assembly Democrats.
Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said the party won “historic levels of power in statehouses.” She said they hadn’t flipped this many seats nationwide since the 1980s.
This time, she said, Democrats will have to focus on issues that matter to middle-class voters such as improving educational opportunities and increasing access to healthcare, particularly in rural areas.
“This election is about kitchen-table issues; it’s about economic opportunities,” she said Wednesday. “That is what the mandate is about.”
Wins put spotlight on Democratic priorities in 2027
The cost of groceries, housing, healthcare, gas and utility bills were campaign talking points after legislative sessions packed with bills aiming to make life more affordable for Americans, while also providing tax relief and reining in data center development and the use of artificial intelligence.
The coming legislative session could see major efforts to lighten the tax burden on the middle class, relax housing regulations, expand access to healthcare, and force utilities and data center developers to do more to stop electricity bills from rising.
Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who won reelection, told his supporters Tuesday night that people want him and lawmakers to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, invest in infrastructure, kids, police and communities, and enshrine abortion rights for women in the state constitution.
Other newly elected governors, including Wisconsin’s David Crowley and Minnesota’s Amy Klobuchar, said they wanted to work with Republicans.
“I am not interested in moving Minnesota to the left or the right; I want to move us forward,” Klobuchar said.
She even had a warning for her Democratic supporters.
“Spoiler alert: You may not like every single thing I do,” she said.

title: Gorham elects Maine’s first openly nonbinary state lawmaker
text:
Seven Siegel will become Maine’s first openly nonbinary state lawmaker after winning the House District 109 seat in Gorham on Election Day. The Democrat received 3,229 votes, overcoming Republican Diana Kushnar’s 2,101 votes.
Siegel, a 37-year-old computer science teacher at Kennebunk High School serving their second term on the Gorham Town Council, moved to Maine six years ago. They ran for Maine House on reining in costs of living, modernizing technology policy and ending tax relief for corporations.
“I don’t make a big deal of (being nonbinary), because the policies and the work are more important,” Siegel said. “But I also think an important part is representation and having people see that nonbinary people exist, and they’re good policymakers, too.”
Siegel said the adult they would have needed as a kid would not be afraid to make their identity known and work hard. Now, they want to be that adult.
“I’m excited to work for the people of Maine,” they said, adding that they have found their long-term home in Gorham after living in multiple states. They and their wife, Becky Wartell, have a 3-year-old daughter.
Siegel will stay on the Gorham Town Council until their term ends in November 2028 because they want to help update the town’s comprehensive plan next year.
The Democrat was endorsed by Equality Maine, an organization that advocates for pro-LGBTQ+ legislation and policy reform in Maine.
“Seven will join the Maine Legislature at a time when LGBTQ+ rights are under attack here in Maine and nationwide — and their victory is a milestone moment for our community,” said Heide Lester, interim executive director at Equality Maine. “Elected officials like Seven are not only critical in the ongoing fight to protect the rights of all Mainers; they also inspire others to run and win.”
While Siegel will be the first openly nonbinary member of the Maine Legislature, Ambureen Rana is a Democrat representing House District 21 in Bangor who identifies as genderqueer. Siegel said they already spoke with Rana after being elected Tuesday.
WABI reported in 2023 that about 32 LGBTQ+ people have served in the Maine Legislature in the past 38 years.

title: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer says Democrats will work to lower costs with or without Trump
text:
(Gray News/AP) – Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday’s 2026 midterm elections in a widespread repudiation of President Donald Trump and the Republican Party, a drubbing that reached deep into reliable GOP territory.
“Oh man, wow, wow, wow,” Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said in his victory speech. “Against all odds, we Democrats have won the Senate!”
Schumer said Democrats recruited great candidates who focused their campaigns on costs, chaos and corruption, while Republicans embraced “the worst president ever.”
“Republicans made a choice and followed Trump over the cliff,” Schumer said. “We listened, they didn’t. And the American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks.”
Schumer closed his victory speech with a warning to his own party: “Americans voted for change and now, Democrats must deliver.”
He held a post-election news conference in Washington Wednesday, where he spoke about the high costs of fuel, electricity and the corruption of the Trump administration. Schumer said Democrats are determined to lower costs for the American people.
“We are going to work hard to drive costs down, with the president or without him,” Schumer said Wednesday to close his news conference.
Democrats flipped at least seven Senate seats in ruby-red states and battlegrounds alike: Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. They held on to battleground seats in Georgia and Michigan.
In the House, Democrats flipped more than two dozen districts, some that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.
Trump faces a profoundly reshaped Washington for the last two years of his presidency. Democrats will have the power to block his legislative agenda, reject his appointees and investigate his administration.

title: This might be the most remote bakery in all of Vermont
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WALDEN, Vt. (Aging Untold)- Up a long dirt road in Vermont, George Peak and Colleen Willette live on a little slice of heaven, operating perhaps the most remote bakery in the state.
“How could you not love it up here? You look around and trees are covered,” said Peak, who just turned 80.
The husband and wife team run Top of the Mountain Farm and Bakery from a converted barn surrounded by state forest.
The barn was originally built for Peak’s tractor before Willette outgrew her home kitchen two years ago.
“It just took off,” Willette said.
A favorite treat is the homemade whoopie pie made with local maple syrup and “a lot of love,” Willette said. “It’s quite a treat.”
On weekends, the bakery transforms into a diner that serves as a must-stop for hungry snowmobilers traveling the trail just feet away from the building.
Peak handles deliveries, coming off the hill to bring sweet treats to 10 stores in northern Vermont, putting in about 60 miles a day.
“He’s holding up pretty good. Yeah, he does well,” said the 69-year-old Willette of her delivery partner. “He has to take a nap after his lunch break.”
The couple of 30 years say their friends have questioned their decision to keep working in retirement.
“‘It’s crazy,’ my friends will say, ‘What are you doing, you’re retired. Why don’t you just enjoy yourself?’ I’m enjoying myself,” Willette said.
“And the other thing, we don’t have time to argue,” Peak said.
“But I’m always right, so there’s no arguing,” Willette added.
“And I know it,” Peak responded.
The couple said the rural life fits them perfectly despite what others might think.
“People say we’re crazy for being way up here, but I wouldn’t want to be anywhere else,” Peak said.

title: Candidates elected to Brunswick council, school board

Voters in Brunswick elected four town councilors and three school board members on Tuesday.
The only contested local races were for two at-large council seats.
Newcomer Jennifer Navarro won a special election to serve the remaining year of the term vacated by former Councilor Katherine Wilson by 338 votes, according to unofficial results from Tuesday’s election.
