Two council seats in Districts 5 and 7, went to unopposed incumbents Jennifer Hicks and Steven Weems, respectively.
All three candidates for the Brunswick school board were seeking reelection to their seats and were running unopposed. W. Benjamin Walsh was reelected in District 5, Sarah Singer was reelected to the District 7 seat and William Thompson will serve another term at-large.

title: Iranian officials say midterm results show US voters have rejected Trump's war
text:
Iranian officials say midterm results show US voters have rejected Trump's war
Iranian officials on Wednesday celebrated U.S. voters’ rebuke of the Republican Party and President Donald Trump in the midterm elections, as the region waited to see how the results could affect the Iran war.
Concerns about the war’s effects, particularly frustration over rising prices for fuel and other goods in the U.S., helped Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s vote.
“Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, wrote on X. “If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare.”
The broader region has been on edge over the prospect of the U.S. resuming full-scale military operations against Iran for the first time in almost two months. Talks aimed at preventing renewed fighting continue, while other U.S. allies in the region are urging Washington against resuming full-scale operations in the war, now more than eight months old, which has rattled the global economy and devastated Iran.
Related video: White House official calls election night mood "defiant"
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reportedly pushed for more strikes, while Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal.
Despite ceasefire agreements and repeated diplomatic efforts, military confrontations have continued in southern Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz, raising concerns about a return to full-scale fighting.
Iran’s supreme leader said those who think partisan changes in the United States can change its enmity toward the Islamic Republic are “gravely mistaken.”
In a letter shared on his social media account, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who hasn’t been seen publicly since the war began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28, said: “If there are still those who harbor even a slight hope for a change in behavior or partisan and factional shifts within the system of domination, or who imagine that by giving concessions to America they can dissuade it from hostility toward the Iranian nation, they are gravely mistaken.”
Iranian targets hit ahead of the midterms
The midterms came after the U.S. carried out what appeared to be a limited strike on Iranian targets in the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway, which raised questions about what might come next.
Iranian state media reported explosions Monday on Qeshm and Hengam islands and near the southern port city of Bandar Abbas. Iranian authorities have not publicly identified the specific sites struck or disclosed the extent of the damage.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world’s oil supply passed before the war, has also witnessed repeated incidents involving commercial shipping. Iran has severely restricted shipping through the strait since the conflict began, while the United States has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Ali Nikzad, Iran’s deputy parliament speaker, linked Republican election losses to Washington’s policy toward Iran. He told lawmakers Wednesday that U.S. sanctions had failed to break Iran’s economy or force its people to surrender.
“The enemy’s efforts to bring down Iran’s economy have failed time and again,” Nikzad said, adding: “These defeats are the aftershocks of defeat at the hands of the Iranian people.”
Iran marks anniversary of 1979 seizure of US Embassy
The anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. Embassy in Tehran was marked in Iran on Wednesday, with thousands of people parading through the Iranian capital to commemorate the event.
Demonstrators burned American and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.” Effigies of Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu were displayed alongside caricatures of the two leaders. One depicted Trump as a ferocious dog poised to attack, with Netanyahu holding its leash.
Addressing the demonstrators, Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani claimed the United States and Israel had suffered a decisive defeat, including in the U.S. midterms.
“The decisive defeat of the United States and the Zionist regime in recent developments and elections is the result of the Iranian nation’s steadfastness and strength,” Zakani said. “Even political rivals in the United States have acknowledged that this failure was the result of the Iranian people’s ingenuity and perseverance.”
On Nov. 4, 1979, Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy, taking American diplomats and other citizens hostage. Fifty-two Americans were held for 444 days before being released on Jan. 20, 1981.
The crisis helped cement the rupture between the two countries, which have had no formal diplomatic relations for decades.
Iran’s influential hard-line judiciary chief, Gholam Hossein Mohseni Ejehi, linked the election results to the war and the anniversary of the hostage crisis in a post on X.
“Trump failed both in war and in politics. We will certainly impose even more defeats upon him,” he wrote.
The United States and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28, killing the country’s longtime supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and triggering a conflict that has disrupted global energy markets and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Back-channel negotiations continue
Back-channel negotiations have continued as Israel and some Middle Eastern allies lobby Trump.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday, before news of the strikes in the Strait of Hormuz emerged, that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
Before the latest strikes, the Trump administration’s last known attacks on Iran were in early September. Thousands of U.S. troops remain in waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are on their way to the Middle East.
Netanyahu pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections during a weekend call with Trump, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. The two officials said diplomatic efforts had made progress and mediators were trying to advance a framework under which Iran would halt its attacks in the strait in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade.
The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American officials and, in one case, Israeli officials. The third person, who was briefed on the call, also spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly.
___
Associated Press writers Samy Magdy and Aamer Madhani contributed to this report.

title: Democrats secure majority of governorships for first time in decades
text:
Democrats secure majority of governorships for first time in decades
Democrats scored victories in governor’s races in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia, riding a wave of voter discontent in Tuesday’s midterm elections to deliver a rebuke to President Donald Trump and GOP policymaking.
The wins delivered a majority of governorships to Democrats for the first time in two decades, allowing them to put up a stronger defense against Trump's second-term agenda.
Related video above | Democrats pledge affordability reforms as they prepare to take control of Congress
The number of states in play was surprisingly large — a reflection of Trump’s poor approval ratings dragging on his party, with Democrats rolling up victories in presidential battleground states, heavily populated states and states that Trump won easily in 2024.
They landed a historic victory, as Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia — a presidential battleground state — made her the first Black woman to be elected governor in the U.S.
Democrats won in Iowa, Ohio and Texas, all states where Republicans have controlled state government for years, as well as all six presidential battleground states that Trump flipped in 2024 to win the White House.
Democrats also will preside over the nation's dozen most heavily populated states, except for Florida.
In the weeks leading up to Election Day, Trump traveled to heavily Republican areas to headline rallies attended by GOP gubernatorial candidates looking for a boost, in a sign of the impending losses.
All told, 36 states that are home to about 80% of the nation’s population were electing a governor Tuesday. In 19 states, the office was open. Heading into the elections, Democratic governors represented 60% of the nation’s population, but Republicans held 26 of the nation's 50 governors’ offices.
In 2027, Democrats will hold at least 28 governorships.
Democrats last gained a majority of governorships in 2006, flipping six governors’ offices in the last midterm under a second-term Republican president. Republicans recaptured the majority four years later.
More states under Democratic leadership could mean more governors fighting — or ignoring — Trump's agenda.
Trump has tested the power of states, clashing primarily with Democratic-led states over call-ups of National Guard troops, immigration operations, conditions on federal aid and efforts to assert federal control over election requirements, including restricting mail voting.
Democratic victories in Georgia, Texas, Iowa and Ohio
Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and onetime White House adviser to former President Joe Biden, overcame GOP attacks on her management of the city during the COVID-19 pandemic to defeat Rick Jackson, a billionaire who plunged more than $200 million of his own money into the race.
She accused him of getting rich off a broken healthcare system and profiting off pain.
Her victory breaks GOP control of state government in Georgia, as does Democrat Amy Acton’s victory in Ohio, in a campaign that made national headlines when Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, aired a widely criticized attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother.
In two other GOP-controlled states, Democrat Rob Sand defeated Republican Zach Lahn in Iowa, while Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa beat third-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas, where no Democrat had been elected to statewide office since 1994.
Hinojosa was seen as a long shot after she emerged from a primary with a fraction of Abbott’s cash total and no statewide name recognition.
But as misgivings grew louder among rural Republicans over Abbott's policies on data centers, water rights and public schools, fellow Latino politicians and politicos wrote to the Democratic Governors Association to request $10 million in campaign aid, saying Hinojosa had made it a close race.
The DGA gave $1 million — far less than it spent in Arizona, Georgia, Iowa, Michigan, Nevada, Ohio and Wisconsin — and Hinojosa won despite being outspent 5-to-1 on ads, according to AdImpact data.
Notably, Abbott skipped Trump’s rally in Texas, a sign of the president’s unpopularity.
More races were seen as competitive
Democrats also saw an opportunity to pick up a governor’s office in Alaska, where the incumbent was term-limited. Like Georgia, Alaska hasn't elected a Democratic governor since 1998.
Republicans' best chance to pick up an executive suite was in Kansas, a normally deep red state where Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly was term-limited.
Republicans hung onto control in Florida, where U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds defeated David Jolly, a former Republican congressman-turned-independent who ran as a Democrat in the nation’s third-most populous state. Donalds will be Florida's first Black governor.
Republicans also had an eye on Oregon, but Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek fended off a second straight challenge from Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan.
Contests are in big states and swing states, too
Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York won reelection, and Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former U.S. health and human services secretary, cruised to victory in California.
Democrats also swept control of the executive branch in the six swing states from the 2024 presidential election: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
In Nevada, state Attorney General Aaron Ford knocked off Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. Ford will be the state’s first Black governor after campaigning on his record of challenging the Trump administration in court and tying Lombardo to the president.
In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection, as did Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs of Arizona. Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, won the open governor's job in Wisconsin, and Michigan’s secretary of state, Jocelyn Benson, won her state's open governor’s office.
The winners could have substantial influence over election administration during the 2028 presidential election. That could be important, considering Trump’s interest in expanding federal control over elections.
Meanwhile, three Democratic governors who are considered possible presidential candidates in 2028 all won reelection: Wes Moore of Maryland, JB Pritzker of Illinois and Shapiro, of Pennsylvania.
Demonstrating a big margin of victory, fundraising prowess and the electoral strength to help other Democrats win sends a strong signal to donors and party activists, analysts say.
The 2026 election produced some firsts
In Texas, Hinojosa will be the state's first Latina governor, while Deb Haaland 's victory in New Mexico made her the first Native American woman elected to lead a state.
More states elected Black governors, as well. Eight Black major party gubernatorial nominees were on ballots. In the past 250 years, only three elected governors have been Black, including Moore. Victories by Bottoms, Crowley, Donalds and Ford more than doubled that number in just one election.
Meanwhile, states were on course to possibly beat the record number of 14 female governors.

title: Holiday Craft Fair at the Canton Historical Society
Chemical plant explosion in Mississippi prompts shelter-in-place order
text:
GREENVILLE, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - A chemical plant explosion in Mississippi prompted a massive emergency response Wednesday morning.
According to Washington County emergency officials, crews were called to the Loveland facility, formerly known as Platte Chemical, just after 7 a.m. for an initial blast involving a chemical herbicide stored inside a “hot box.”
Multiple agencies responded as thick smoke spread from the facility, prompting a shelter-in-place order for the surrounding area.
Firefighters and emergency personnel were able to contain the flames once at the scene while undergoing decontamination protocols due to potential chemical exposure.
Greenville Mayor Errick Simmons praised the swift coordination of local and state responders.
“Our first priority is the safety of our residents, our first responders, and everyone working at or near the facility,” Simmons said. “I ask our citizens to remain calm, avoid the immediate area, and allow our firefighters and emergency personnel the space they need to do their jobs safely and effectively.”
Officials confirmed no injuries were reported in the explosion while lifting the shelter-in-place order.
The cause of the blast remained under investigation.

title: Crews respond to early morning explosion at a Mississippi chemical plant
text:
GREENVILLE, Miss. (AP) — Emergency crews responded Wednesday to an explosion at a Mississippi chemical plant that sent a large plume of black smoke into the air.
Crews were notified just after 7 a.m. of an explosion at the Loveland Products plant in Greenville, city officials said in a news release. The city in the Mississippi Delta region has a population of about 26,000 people. It’s about 120 miles (193 kilometers) northwest of Jackson, the capital.
No injuries were immediately reported, said Sara Moreland Hester, a deputy emergency management director for Washington County and a local firefighter. She said that as of midmorning, the fire was controlled but not fully extinguished.
The city news release said that according to preliminary information provided by the plant management, the explosion involves a fire associated with a herbicide chemical.
Nutrien, the parent company of Loveland, said the fire was “being managed,” and that plant leadership was working with first responders. Loveland — based in Loveland, Colorado — makes fertilizer, plant nutrition and crop protection products.
Greenville Mayor Errick D. Simmons said in the news release that residents are asked to avoid the immediate area as officials monitor the situation.
“We are coordinating with emergency response agencies to assess the situation, contain the fire, and determine whether additional protective measures are necessary,” Simmons said.
City officials said the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality has dispatched personnel to the area.

title: Pedestrian dies after being hit by Amtrak train in NH
text:
A person died in Rollinsford, New Hampshire, on Wednesday after being struck by an Amtrak train, police say.
First responders were dispatched to the tracks in the area of Main and Mechanic streets just before 3 p.m., the Rollinsford Police Department said in a news release.
A pedestrian was located deceased. Their identity was being withheld pending notification of next of kin, police said.
The department said its preliminary investigation “indicates that the pedestrian was walking southbound on the tracks and did not see or hear the Amtrak train approaching behind them, due to wearing headphones, and was struck by the train.”
The Amtrak Police Department and area fire departments assisted in the response, Rollinsford police said.
Spokespeople for Amtrak did not respond to a request for information about the incident on Wednesday.
A southbound Downeaster train was stopped in Rollinsford shortly after the incident, according to Amtrak’s train tracking webpage, and wound up arriving in Boston roughly two hours behind schedule, shortly after 6:30 p.m.
Two northbound trains were also delayed Wednesday night, according to the tracker: one by more than an hour and the other by nearly two hours.

title: Wildfire near Maine border grows to about 1,000 acres
text:
A wildfire about a mile from Maine’s border with New Hampshire has grown to about 1,000 acres, the White Mountain National Forest said Wednesday.
The Wild River fire is 11% contained and burning about 7 miles southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire. More than 50 firefighters and two helicopters are assigned to the fire.
Dry leaf litter and a lingering drought in the area are helping the fire spread through what officials said was “steep, hard-to-reach terrain.”
Crews are clearing vegetation to build fire lines where they can safely work, and helicopters are dropping water in areas that may be inaccessible to firefighters.
Officials are preparing a closure order that would bar public entry to the area and keep it accessible to firefighters and emergency crews.
The fire was first reported Sunday afternoon. Its cause is under investigation.

title: Fort Kent and Wisdom Sweep Four Northern Maine Soccer Championships
text:
Four Games, Four Championships: Fort Kent and Wisdom Sweep Northern Maine Soccer Finals
Four games. Four victories. Four Northern Maine championships.
Tuesday was a remarkable day for Aroostook County high school soccer, as both Fort Kent and Wisdom sent their boys and girls teams into regional championship games and all four came away with victories.
And they did it in four very different ways.
Fort Kent's boys needed just 36 seconds of overtime to knock off top-seeded Orono, Wisdom's boys survived a nine-goal championship game, Wisdom's girls got a hat trick from Ellie Cyr, and Fort Kent's girls captured their fourth consecutive regional championship with another impressive defensive performance.
By the end of the evening, four more County teams had punched their tickets to Saturday's state championships.
Here's how Tuesday's Northern Maine regional finals played out.
Girls Soccer
Class C North: Fort Kent Captures Fourth Straight Regional Championship
(1) Fort Kent 3, (2) Orono 0
Four years. Four regional championships.
The Fort Kent Lady Warriors are heading back to the Class C state championship after defeating second-seeded Orono 3-0 Tuesday evening at Hampden Academy.
Fort Kent struck early, and its defense took care of the rest.
Reece Doucette scored twice for the Lady Warriors, while Hayden Plourde added the other goal.
Goalkeeper Trinity Daigle and the Fort Kent defense kept Orono off the scoreboard, securing the shutout and another Northern Maine title.
It was a complete performance from a Fort Kent team that has been one of the most consistent programs in Northern Maine girls soccer.
The Lady Warriors entered the championship after defeating Houlton 5-0 in the semifinals, and Tuesday's victory gave them another shutout against one of the region's top teams.
Now Fort Kent will have an opportunity to bring home a state championship.
The Lady Warriors will face Maranacook, which advanced out of Class C South with a 1-0 victory over Mount Abram.
Four consecutive regional titles are an impressive accomplishment for any program, and Fort Kent has another opportunity to add to that success Saturday.
Eight-Player North: Ellie Cyr's Hat Trick Sends Wisdom to States
(2) Wisdom 3, (1) Dexter 1
Wisdom's girls are Northern Maine champions.
The second-seeded Lady Pioneers earned a 3-1 victory over top-seeded Dexter Tuesday evening at Brewer High School, completing an impressive tournament run and securing their place in Saturday's Eight-Player state championship.
Ellie Cyr delivered another outstanding performance, scoring all three Wisdom goals.
Lakiah Lee scored Dexter's lone goal.
Wisdom's defense was a major part of the victory, limiting the Tigers to one goal and protecting the lead throughout the championship matchup.
The Lady Pioneers had entered Tuesday after defeating previously unbeaten Sumner 5-0 in the semifinals.
That meant Wisdom had to get past two of the region's strongest teams to bring home the Northern Maine championship.
And they did exactly that.
Wisdom will now play for the Eight-Player state championship Saturday in Presque Isle against Southern Maine champion Bangor Christian.
For a program from the St. John Valley, the opportunity to compete for a state championship in Aroostook County makes the next game even more special.
Boys Soccer
Class C North: Dominic Cyr Delivers Overtime Winner for Fort Kent
(3) Fort Kent 2, (1) Orono 1 (Overtime)
Some championship games are decided by a single moment.
For Fort Kent's boys, that moment came just 36 seconds into overtime Tuesday afternoon.
Dominic Cyr converted a penalty kick to give the third-seeded Warriors a dramatic 2-1 victory over top-seeded Orono in the Class C North regional championship at Hampden Academy.
It was an exciting finish to a well-played game between two teams that had battled throughout the afternoon.
Orono struck first when Gabe Lule scored in the 18th minute, giving the Red Riots a 1-0 advantage.
Fort Kent continued to battle, and Cyr delivered the equalizer in the second half to send the game into overtime.
The extra period barely had time to get started before Cyr came through again.
His penalty kick sent Fort Kent into celebration and secured the Northern Maine championship.
It was the second consecutive dramatic tournament finish for the Warriors, who had advanced past George Stevens Academy in the semifinals on penalty kicks.
This time, Fort Kent didn't need a shootout.
The Warriors will now face Hall-Dale in Saturday's Class C state championship after Hall-Dale defeated Mount Abram 2-1 in the Southern Maine final.
And with the Fort Kent girls also winning their regional championship Tuesday, both Warrior soccer teams will be playing for state titles on Saturday.
Eight-Player North: Wisdom Boys Win Nine-Goal Championship Game
(3) Wisdom 5, (4) Piscataquis 4
Wisdom's boys made sure the Pioneers would have two teams heading to the state championships.
The third-seeded Pioneers defeated fourth-seeded Piscataquis 5-4 Tuesday afternoon at Brewer High School to capture the Eight-Player North regional championship.
It was a high-scoring championship matchup, with nine goals between the two teams and Wisdom coming away with the one-goal victory.
The Pioneers had already survived a dramatic semifinal against Calais, advancing on penalty kicks after goalkeeper Bentley Nadeau stopped the final Calais attempt.
Tuesday brought another close finish, but the result was the same.
Wisdom found a way to win.
The Pioneers will now face Telstar in Saturday's Eight-Player state championship after Telstar defeated Pine Tree Academy 5-1 to capture the Southern Maine title.
And just like Fort Kent, Wisdom will have both its boys and girls teams competing for state championships.
That's quite an accomplishment for a small school, and another reason Saturday is shaping up to be a memorable day for the St. John Valley.
The 2026 MPA Soccer Championships on 101.9 The Rock are proudly presented by Pineland Farms in Mars Hill.

title: This might be the most remote bakery in all of Vermont
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WALDEN, Vt. (Aging Untold)- Up a long dirt road in Vermont, George Peak and Colleen Willette live on a little slice of heaven, operating perhaps the most remote bakery in the state.
“How could you not love it up here? You look around and trees are covered,” said Peak, who just turned 80.
The husband and wife team run Top of the Mountain Farm and Bakery from a converted barn surrounded by state forest.
The barn was originally built for Peak’s tractor before Willette outgrew her home kitchen two years ago.
“It just took off,” Willette said.
A favorite treat is the homemade whoopie pie made with local maple syrup and “a lot of love,” Willette said. “It’s quite a treat.”
On weekends, the bakery transforms into a diner that serves as a must-stop for hungry snowmobilers traveling the trail just feet away from the building.
Peak handles deliveries, coming off the hill to bring sweet treats to 10 stores in northern Vermont, putting in about 60 miles a day.
“He’s holding up pretty good. Yeah, he does well,” said the 69-year-old Willette of her delivery partner. “He has to take a nap after his lunch break.”
The couple of 30 years say their friends have questioned their decision to keep working in retirement.
“‘It’s crazy,’ my friends will say, ‘What are you doing, you’re retired. Why don’t you just enjoy yourself?’ I’m enjoying myself,” Willette said.
“And the other thing, we don’t have time to argue,” Peak said.
“But I’m always right, so there’s no arguing,” Willette added.
“And I know it,” Peak responded.
The couple said the rural life fits them perfectly despite what others might think.
“People say we’re crazy for being way up here, but I wouldn’t want to be anywhere else,” Peak said.

title: UMaine Political Science chair calls Jackson campaign ‘impressive’ even with ‘blue wave’ help
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - WABI spoke to University of Maine Political Science Chair Mark Brewer on Wednesday to get his take on how the national environment played a role in deciding Maine’s senate race.
He said that the “Blue Wave” does serve as an indictment on the Trump Presidency and that perhaps being lost in the mix is the 101 day sprint to the finish of the Troy Jackson campaign.
Jackson became the Democratic nominee when Graham Platner’s scandal plagued campaign came to an end following an allegation of sexual assault, which Platner denies.
“It was an impressive piece of organizing starting with what they did to get the nomination at that convention. They had that thing locked up days in advance. Even the competitors were like wow I can’t believe that just happened to us. They followed that up raising $20 million in that short period of time. He was on message. He rarely had any gaffs on the trail. They got him ready for debates where he held his own. I think that their campaign was incredibly impressive but all that being said obviously Trump plays a big role here not just for Collins but there’s lots of Republican losers today Who are grumbling over their morning coffee or cereal about Donald Trump,” said Brewer.

title: Democrat Josh Turek wins election to US Senate from Iowa
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Josh Turek won Iowa’s rare open U.S. Senate race in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping a Republican-held seat and helping Democrats end GOP dominance in Washington.
Turek’s victory over Republican Ashley Hinson made him the first Democrat since Barack Obama to win a statewide federal race in Iowa. Turek will be one of four Democratic members of Iowa’s federal delegation after years of exclusively Republican representation in Washington.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
Iowa reemerged as a political battleground this year as Democrats seized on high fuel prices, tariffs and a war overseas that caused turmoil in the state’s dominant agricultural industry. The retirements of Republican Sen. Joni Ernst and Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds made for the first cycle without incumbents seeking the top-of-the-ticket seats since 1968, breathing new life into Democrats’ efforts to reverse years of electoral failure in the state.
Turek told supporters Tuesday that his underdog race seemed far-fetched in a state that elected Trump by double digits just two years ago.
“They told me it was impossible to win this Senate race, but tonight, Iowa, we have once again proved that the impossible is possible,” he said.
Iowa became one of Democrats’ targets as they looked to take over majority control of the Senate, and the campaign drew hundreds of millions of dollars.
Hinson thanked her staff and supporters Tuesday, saying she will “continue to fight for common sense.”
“I think we ran an absolutely fabulous campaign across the state,” she said. “Lots of late nights and lots of miles.”
Pressure on Republicans reached Iowa
Although many Republicans walked a political tightrope this cycle, Hinson had a more challenging balancing act than most. Iowa has faced manufacturing job losses, healthcare clinic closures and shrunken farm profits since Trump returned to the White House. There was loud unrest over poor water quality and rising cancer rates.
Hinson launched her campaign last year promising to be Trump’s “top ally” in the Senate. Almost a year later, she instead focused her message on being “Iowa’s best bipartisan fighter.”
In September, after House members were sent home, Hinson said Iowans “shouldn’t have to foot the bill” for the Iran war.
She did not, however, join two fellow Iowa Republicans in battleground districts — U.S. Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks — in voting with Democrats earlier in September on a resolution intended to halt Trump’s ability to continue military action without lawmakers’ approval.
Hinson said the resolution was not the way to allow Trump to bring the war to an immediate and successful end.
While Hinson pointedly critiqued the president on specific issues in the final months of the race, she still appeared beside him when he made two visits to Iowa in the last two weeks of the campaign.
A majority of Iowa voters saw Hinson as “too supportive” of Trump, according to The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of the electorate.
Nunn also lost Tuesday to Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, and Miller-Meeks lost to Democrat Christina Bohannan, a former state representative. The congressional seat that Hinson left open when she ran for Senate also flipped to Democrat Lindsay James.
Turek taps into desire for change
About 3 in 10 Iowa voters said the quality that most mattered for their vote was that their chosen candidate would “bring needed change,” and Turek overwhelmingly won those voters.
Turek said he heard stories of people hurting as he crisscrossed the state.
About 7 in 10 Iowa Senate voters said they are “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way things are going in the country, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Iowa Senate voters were more likely to say government corruption was “crucial” for their vote for Congress than the cost of living, although both rose above other issues. About half of Iowa voters said government corruption was “crucial” for their vote, while about 4 in 10 said this about the cost of living.
And while Hinson cast Turek as “too liberal” for Iowa, less than half of Iowa voters said Turek’s views were “too extreme.”
Like many other Republican candidates across the country, Hinson lost significant ground among young voters, compared to Trump in 2024. Hinson also appeared to have lost ground among white women, a group that Trump narrowly won in 2024.
Hinson did outperform Turek among white voters without a college degree, winning about half of these voters, but she fell short of Trump’s 2024 performance.
Democrats were eager to revive Iowa’s bipartisan tradition
Then-President Obama was the last Democrat to win a statewide federal election in Iowa with his reelection victory in 2012. State Auditor Rob Sand was the lone Democrat in statewide elected office over the last four years. He won the governor’s race on Tuesday.
For three decades, Iowans sent a bipartisan pair to the Senate. That included current Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley and former Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin, who decided not to seek reelection in 2014. Ernst won Harkin’s seat.
Turek, a state representative and former Paralympian, wanted to follow in Harkin’s path. Born with spina bifida, believed to be from his father’s exposure to chemicals during the Vietnam War, Turek credits Harkin’s work to enact the Americans with Disabilities Act for his own achievements.
Turek called Harkin up to join him on stage Tuesday, saying Harkin gave him and so many other Americans “an on-ramp” to society.
“One senator’s ability to work across the aisle and pass good public policy changed my life,” Turek said. “He fought for the little guy, the same people I’m fighting for.”

title: 7 private schools sue state over new rule for special ed student placements
text:
A group of private schools in Maine is suing the state Department of Education over a new rule that impacts the rights of students with special needs to a free and appropriate education.
The schools take issue with an emergency order imposed over the summer, saying it was adopted without the required public input and didn’t meet the standards for an emergency. They also dispute the substance of the rule, which they argue leaves private schools with no recourse but costly federal litigation if they believe they can’t safely educate a student.
“These schools work with the highest-needs population that we have. We should be encouraging them to work with students, and encouraging them to accept placements,” said Tara Walker, an attorney representing the private schools. “A rule that forces all the liability to go to them, and gives them no opportunity to make their own safety assessments — I just think it’s bad policy.”
Every disabled student in Maine is guaranteed a public education, per federal law. If a student with a disability like autism, dyslexia or behavior issues does not have their particular needs met at the public school, they may instead attend a special private school, paid for with public tuition dollars.
Most of the time, those placements occur without issue, through an agreement between the public district and the parents. But sometimes the parties disagree about the best location for the student.
When that happens, Maine offers recourse through what’s called a due process hearing, after which an administrative officer will issue a decision. Families also have the option to resolve the matter through mediation. If the dispute is still not settled, one of the parties may appeal to federal court.
Until this summer, the only parties named in those hearings or cases were the parents and the public school district. To address disputes that arise when private schools remove students in conflict with the public district and parents, the Maine Department of Education passed a new rule that allows private schools to be named as parties.
Seven private schools from around the state say that decision will restrict their ability to serve students by “forcing those schools into litigation every time there is an issue regarding student behavior.”
A Department of Education spokesperson declined to comment, citing active litigation.
EMERGENCY RULE
In July, the department released its new rule on an “emergency” basis, meaning it went into effect immediately and did not require the typical public comment process.
In a document laying out its decision, the department said it became concerned in 2021 that private schools believed they could unilaterally remove a disabled student for any reason without going through the legal process. After issuing a letter that clarified that schools were breaking the law if they terminated a student without going through the proper process, the department believed the issue was resolved, until a 2025 lawsuit.
In that case, Spurwink, a nonprofit that operates private schools for students with disabilities, alleged that a pair of parents and the Lewiston School Department were misinterpreting the state law by ordering Spurwink to keep teaching a student who had injured staff. The student, who has nonverbal autism and behavior issues, had bitten three staff members, requiring emergency medical care.
That student’s parents, who spoke anonymously with the Portland Press Herald, said Spurwink was aware of their son’s behavior issues when they accepted him, and argued the school violated the legal process by discharging him without any consultation. After that, he lacked structure and learning opportunities.
“He’s regressing,” the student’s father said.
That case was ultimately dismissed, but the department determined it needed a clearer policy on removal of students by private schools.
The department first worked to find a contractual solution. It proposed a plan last October and sought comment from public districts, private schools and the general public. Following an unfavorable response, the department then proposed another plan in January, modeled off Massachusetts’ process, which it said was also met with negative feedback from public schools.
“At this point, despite the department and representatives of the (districts) and private schools working hard to come to a contractual solution, there remain obstacles to bringing it to a mutually agreeable end, primarily due to the continued lack of a regulatory enforcement mechanism,” the department wrote in its reasoning document.
It then issued its emergency ruling, which stands for one year and did not require any notice or public comment. The department is seeking to make the rule permanent during the incoming legislative session.
‘THEY DON’T LIVE WITH THOSE RESULTS’
Rather than providing a clearer process for disputes, as the department said when it announced the rule change, the private schools feel it had the opposite effect.
Walker, the attorney for the private schools, said the department’s abandonment of the contractual solutions, which required public input, allowed it to adopt a rule without hearing from the affected parties, and she described the action as a “misuse of the emergency process.”
After taking more than a year to develop the contractual solution, the lawsuit argues, the issue hardly met the definition of an emergency.
Walker also disputed the idea that any private school she works with has “unilaterally” removed a student. Instead, she said, private schools end up bearing all of the burden for a student’s safety, but lack any mechanism to express that they can’t safely educate a student.
It’s the public school districts that hold the power to make the placement decisions, she said, but they don’t bear the liability of keeping that student safe. “If a district is keeping a student in an environment that isn’t working, they don’t live with those results,” Walker said.
She said the rule change leaves private schools with essentially only one option if they don’t think they can safely educate a student: costly and time-consuming federal litigation. In the meantime, she said, a dangerous situation might arise if they’re forced to continue teaching the student.
The schools bringing the lawsuit include two organizations that operate special purpose private schools — Central Aroostook Association in Presque Isle and Spurwink — as well as the town academies of Thornton in Saco, Washington in East Machias, Lincoln in Newcastle, Foxcroft in Dover-Foxcroft and Fryeburg Academy. The Maine Association of Independent Schools, which represents private schools across the state, is also a plaintiff.
As of Wednesday, no deadline has been set for the department to file a response.

title: Time sensitivities are simply greater in Maine
text:
Matthew Tzuker is an executive coach and writer who lives in Portland.
One of the more charming features of the American calendar is that we clump Halloween, Election Day and change the clocks all within a few days of each other. This year they were all particularly close, creating a chaos sandwich.
Grouping Halloween and Election Day together makes sense. If Halloween originated to chase away evil spirits before the long, dark winter or to get out our last sins before we turn good again (kind of like “The Purge” movies), a few days before we vote is a perfect time for some cathartic release.
But deciding that, between the two, we are all going to agree to take an hour of daylight from the back end and tack it onto the morning feels like a dare that we don’t have to take. Yet here we are, hungover from both Halloween and watching election returns, plunged into self-imposed darkness well before dinner time when we should be getting some sunshine.
To paraphrase Kurt Vonnegut, “because we are earthlings, we have to believe what clocks tell us.” Twice a year, we prove Vonnegut wrong briefly and then go right back to proving him right, falling in line with whatever the clock says after we just told it what to say.
This is a bigger deal in Maine than it is elsewhere, jutting out into the Atlantic as we do, teetering on the edge of Eastern Standard Time and whatever mystery lies east of that. Moving that hour spirals us into a darkness the rest of the country doesn’t understand.
Besides Alaska, Maine has the earliest winter sunsets. I can’t speak for Alaskans, but our sunlight in Maine is too special to be messed with. It’s part of our aura (see Homer, Winslow). Based on a 2019 vote, Maine is ready to move to permanent Daylight Savings Time — once the federal government allows such free thinking.
But waking up in utter darkness to begin the day well before sunrise is its own kind of struggle.
Health and sleep advocates lean toward a permanent Standard Time (that’s the one we just switched to). It feels like the early risers, with their air of superiority, are telling the rest of us what to do with the precious few hours of sunlight we have. We would lose an hour of late sun in the luscious Maine summer, only to be blinded by it in the early morning. Not a great deal for us either.
Meanwhile, changing the clocks as if time were our arbitrary plaything has been proven to result in more car accidents, worsened sleep and a host of other health problems, not to mention the havoc it wreaks on the sleep schedules of young children. National politicians have also tried to change this semiannual madness. Then Sen. Marco Rubio made a big push for it in 2018, but now he has more important global problems to fail to solve. Other politicians have made noise, including Donald Trump, yet every year nothing changes. I suspect the proximity to Election Day has intimidated our leaders, not wanting to take the blame for any inevitable backlash.
Maybe we should think more broadly, since it doesn’t seem like we really need to follow laws anymore.
Newfoundland, I just found out, made its own time zone, just half an hour ahead of its western neighbors. Maybe there’s something there. Or maybe, rather than plunging, we could step into darkness gradually. Fall back 30 minutes one week, then 30 minutes a week or two later.
Or perhaps we are thinking about this all wrong. Maybe in the winter, regardless of what the clock says, we honor the darkness, and simply agree to do less. Obviously, progress must march on (it’s America, after all), but would it be so bad if, for the coldest darkest months, we simply started things later and ended them earlier? Instead of powering through with extra coffee, we could follow the example of the trees and animals: shed some things, fatten up, sleep longer.
Winter in Maine is long and dark, but it shouldn’t take an act of Congress to make it more bearable. We can just do it. All it takes is giving ourselves and each other a little break, just until the light returns.

title: US stocks surge, Dow soars 1,500 points as Brent oil’s price drops below $95 per barrel after Democrats take control of Congress
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. stocks are soaring Wednesday after President Donald Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections.
Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.8%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1,519 points, or 2.9%, as of 2:06 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.9% higher.
Stocks of solar-power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell below $100 for the first time in nearly a month. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices, for Republicans’ midterm losses.
Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington.
“Earnings trump elections,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.
Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy.
Much remains impossible to predict, of course, and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defense, foreign policy and in some instances trade.
A downbeat forecast could be that “Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck” who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies’ levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank.
An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes “a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words.”
Here’s a look at some of the moves rippling through financial markets:
Trump Media and Tesla are down
Trump’s social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market’s bigger losers, down 16.6%.
Since briefly touching a peak of $175 five years ago, it’s dropped toward $5. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump’s postings on the platform.
Elon Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 2.4%, and SpaceX sank 4.8%. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress.
AI companies in general are under pressure
Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories across the country could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general.
Investors see Democratic wins in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the build out of further AI data centers. AI-related stocks came into Election Day already under pressure because of worries their prices had shot too high.
Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the poster child of the frenzy around AI-related stocks, sank 1.8% and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, dropped 10.2%
Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, held up better. It rose 0.1% after reporting much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
Companies that have been spending heavily on AI chips also did better. Alphabet rose 4%, for example, after it tumbled more than 12% Thursday to its worst loss ever on worries that it was spending too much on AI investments.
Defense stocks are down
A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the war with Iran.
That helped send down stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the U.S. military, including drops of 7% for Lockheed Martin, 4.2% for Northrop Grumman and 2.4% for General Dynamics.
Green power companies are up, and oil prices are down
Democratic control of Congress could light the way for companies in the solar and wind industries. First Solar jumped 5.8%, and Enphase Energy climbed 4.7%.
Stocks of big oil companies, meanwhile, sank. ExxonMobil fell 4.9%, and ConocoPhillips dropped 5.6%. They had been rallying for much of the year after Trump and Israel began the war with Iran, which sent crude prices much higher.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, plunged 8.6% Wednesday to $94.70.
The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $70 and $120 per barrel since just before the war with Iran began.
Healthcare stocks and dollar stores also rallied
A Democratic-led Congress could try to reverse some of the cuts to federal healthcare and food assistance that Republicans approved during the summer in their “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”
That helped stocks climb across the healthcare industry, including a rise of 9.6% for HCA Healthcare, which runs hospitals and ambulatory sites.
Retailers also benefited on hopes that Democrats may push policies to help Americans struggling to keep up with the fast-rising cost of living. Dollar Tree, which focuses in particular on lower-income Americans, had one of the market’s bigger leaps and rose 8.9%.
Bond yields are down
In the bond market, Treasury yields eased. That could be a signal investors see less risk of Washington piling even more debt onto its already big mountain with the coming end to one-party control.
Treasury yields had surged through the summer and reached their highest levels in decades because of worries about the U.S. government’s big debt, along with higher inflation and other concerns. A Congress controlled by Democrats could provide a check against more spending and cuts to taxes that would widen Washington’s deficit.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.89% from 4.95% late Tuesday.
Stocks jump in much of the world
Indexes climbed across most of the world. Stocks leaped 2% in Paris, 2.2% in Shanghai and 1.8% in London. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was an outlier and fell 1.4%.
___
AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report from Hong Kong, and McHugh contributed from Frankfurt, Germany.

title: Three More County Soccer Teams Chase Regional Championships Wednesday
text:
Championship Wednesday: Three County Teams Chase Northern Maine Soccer Titles
Four Northern Maine championships came back to Aroostook County on Tuesday. Now, three more County soccer teams have an opportunity to keep that momentum going.
After Fort Kent and Wisdom swept their regional championship games, the spotlight shifts to Presque Isle, Fort Fairfield and Madawaska for Wednesday's Class B and Class D North finals.
Presque Isle's girls will take on unbeaten John Bapst at Hampden Academy, while both Fort Fairfield teams will compete for Class D North titles in Presque Isle.
And one of those championships is guaranteed to stay in Aroostook County.
For the third consecutive year, Madawaska and Fort Fairfield will meet in the Class D North boys final.
Three games, three championship opportunities, and another big day for County soccer.
Here's a look at Wednesday's matchups.
Girls Soccer
Class B North: Presque Isle Looks to Knock Off Top-Seeded John Bapst
(3) Presque Isle vs. (1) John Bapst
6:30 p.m. | Hampden Academy
Presque Isle's girls are one victory away from a trip to the Class B state championship.
The third-seeded Lady Wildcats enter Wednesday's regional final following an impressive 4-0 semifinal victory over Cony.
And what stood out about that performance was the balance.
Hailey Plant, Carrlyn Buck, Bridgid Schupbach and Willow Bugbee each scored for Presque Isle, giving the Wildcats four different goal scorers in one of their biggest games of the season.
Presque Isle also defeated Skowhegan 3-1 in the quarterfinals, with Peyton Boinske scoring twice and Buck adding another goal.
Now the challenge gets even bigger.
Top-seeded John Bapst enters the championship undefeated at 15-0-1.
The Crusaders reached Wednesday's final after overcoming a halftime deficit against Hermon, rallying for a 3-2 semifinal victory.
Presque Isle comes in at 11-3-2, and the Wildcats have shown throughout the tournament that they can generate offense from several different players.
But Wednesday will require another complete performance against a team that hasn't lost this season.
For the Lady Wildcats, the opportunity is right in front of them.
One more victory, and they're Northern Maine champions.
Class D North: Fort Fairfield Faces Penobscot Valley for Regional Title
(2) Fort Fairfield vs. (1) Penobscot Valley
6:45 p.m. | Presque Isle High School
Fort Fairfield's girls are back in the Class D North championship, and Wednesday's matchup brings together the region's top two seeds.
The second-seeded Tigers earned their spot with a hard-fought 1-0 semifinal victory over Central Aroostook on Saturday.
It was another close meeting between two familiar County opponents, with Fort Fairfield finding the goal it needed and keeping the Lady Panthers off the scoreboard.
The Tigers also shut out Washburn 4-0 in the quarterfinals.
Chloe White scored twice in that victory, while Kendall Ainsworth and Madison Parks each added a goal. Goalkeeper Addison Cole earned the shutout.
Now Fort Fairfield faces top-seeded Penobscot Valley.
The Howlers advanced with a 1-0 semifinal victory over Madawaska, ending the Owls' tournament run.
That means both teams arrive at Wednesday's championship following shutout victories.
Fort Fairfield has shown it can score in bunches, but its defense has also played a major role in getting the Tigers this far.
With a regional championship and a trip to states on the line, Wednesday's game could come down to which team makes the most of its opportunities.
Boys Soccer
Class D North: Madawaska and Fort Fairfield Meet for Third Straight Regional Final
(1) Madawaska vs. (3) Fort Fairfield
4:15 p.m. | Presque Isle High School
Some postseason matchups have a way of becoming traditions.
For the third consecutive year, the Class D North boys championship will feature Madawaska and Fort Fairfield.
The top-seeded Owls and third-seeded Tigers have worked their way through another tournament, and once again, they'll meet with a Northern Maine title on the line.
Madawaska enters Wednesday at 14-2 after defeating Hodgdon 2-0 in the semifinals.
Owen Gagnon and Aiden Gagnon provided the goals for the Owls, who have put together another impressive season.
Earlier in the tournament, Madawaska defeated the Maine School of Science and Mathematics 5-0 in the quarterfinals, a victory that also marked head coach Ben Gagnon's 100th career coaching win.
Fort Fairfield has taken a different path to the championship.
The Tigers enter at 8-6-2 after defeating second-seeded Central Aroostook 3-1 in Friday's semifinals.
They also shut out Washburn 3-0 in the quarterfinals, with Asher Winters scoring twice and Dax Milton adding another goal.
Levi Cole recorded the shutout in that game.
Now the two teams meet again.
There's no shortage of familiarity between these programs, and both know what it takes to reach this stage.
Madawaska enters as the top seed, but Fort Fairfield has already shown it can win difficult tournament games away from home.
And unlike the other County championship matchups Wednesday, this one guarantees an Aroostook County team will be heading to the Class D state final.
One team will celebrate a Northern Maine championship. The other will see its season come to an end.
Either way, another Class D North title is coming back to the County.
Wednesday's Northern Maine Regional Championship Schedule
Class B North Girls — Hampden Academy
6:30 p.m. — (1) John Bapst vs. (3) Presque Isle
Class D North Boys — Presque Isle High School
4:15 p.m. — (1) Madawaska vs. (3) Fort Fairfield
Class D North Girls — Presque Isle High School
6:45 p.m. — (1) Penobscot Valley vs. (2) Fort Fairfield

title: Mom, daughter killed in suspected grizzly bear attack after vanishing on walk, officials say
text:
(Gray News) - A mother and her 20-year-old daughter were killed in a suspected grizzly bear attack on a popular trail in Canada, officials said.
On Sunday, the family reported them missing.
Officials discovered the bodies on the Snooka West Trail near Bella Coola, British Columbia, following a multi-day search, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service.
The victims were identified as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter, Selah Reed, 20, the CBC reported.
Josh Balcarras, Jennifer’s brother, told the CBC his sister and niece were familiar with the path, describing it as a “casual walk.”
The BC Conservation Officer Service has urged the public to avoid the Snooka West Trail. Officers are investigating and working to track and capture any bears involved in the attack.

title: Poverty among older Americans has risen five years in a row, data shows
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Poverty among older Americans has climbed for the fifth year in a row, according to new Census data, even as overall poverty went down.
Claire Casey, president of the AARP Foundation, said affordability is now a top concern for older adults.
“So it’s actually risen 20%, the rate of poverty for people over 65,” Casey said.
AARP Foundation’s new Economic Security Monitor found 70% of older households saw their expenses go up in three months.
Anthony Hamalainen, 67, of Marquette, Michigan, said older adults on fixed incomes are among those hit hardest.
“I mean, I’m sure there’s other people are struggling too, but the seniors are really hitting it really super bad because they live on a fixed income. Most of them do,” Hamalainen said.
Hamalainen owned a wireless installation company, but a fall from a roof in 2006 left him unable to work. When he was ready to return to work in his 50s, he struggled to find a job because of his disability and his age.
He began receiving Social Security after the accident, but medical bills and other expenses piled up. He gets by on just over $1,000 a month, plus $40 in SNAP benefits. He says it gets harder every year.
“I run out of money each month. I mean, it’s just ridiculous. It’s really hard for us to live,” Hamalainen said.
Casey offered this advice to older adults who are concerned about making it through right now.
“I would say don’t think about an age. Think about what you want in your life and what you can do and then seek out the resources that are out there to help you,” Casey said.
Hamalainen is now training with AARP to help other seniors find jobs.
AARP offers free resources for older adults who are struggling to pay bills. The group also recommends checking with local, state and federal programs that may be able to help.

title: Incumbent, newcomer elected to Orono Town Council
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
An incumbent and one new member were elected to the Orono Town Council Tuesday.
Daniel Demeritt, the board’s current chair, and Colleen Marzilli were elected to the council. The race saw four candidates vying for two seats on the board.
Demeritt received 1,987 votes, while 2,129 were cast for Marzilli, according to results submitted by Orono Town Clerk Shelly Crosby. Orono voters cast 6,279 ballots Tuesday.
Their opponents, Devon Biggie and Daniel LaPoint, received 1,287 and 876 votes, respectively.
The two electees said they want to maintain affordability for Orono residents and find ways for the town to bring in new businesses and create new public policy.
Demeritt, an incumbent and chair of the outgoing council, will continue his time on the council, which has made decisions on Orono’s long-term vision and enacted reactive policy based on public feedback.
Running for reelection, Demeritt said he has “more to do” as a councilor.
Marzilli, who ran for a council seat in 2025, wants to bring ideas to the council that would highlight Orono’s natural beauty and public services, she said last month. As a councilor, Marzilli said she wants Orono to be affordable while investing in housing and business.

title: New month, new crop of films at Maine indie movie theaters
text:
A new month, new films. And a few old films, as Maine’s indie movie houses continue to nimbly counter-program against ubiquitous streaming slop and ho-hum blockbusters. This month, we’ve got a little-seen Charlie Chaplin, even lesser-known 1960s underground rock, a fresh look at a folk legend, an Australian classic, next year’s Oscar bait and some Maine-made goodness.
‘La Bola Negra’
Starts Friday, Nov. 6, Maine Film Center, 93 Main St., Waterville, watervillecreates.org
Oscar buzz is already circulating for this time-hopping tale of love, sex, war and queer history, loosely built around the unfinished play of the same name from legendary Spanish writer Federico Garcia Lorca, who was killed by government forces in 1936 for his leftist politics, his homosexuality — or both. The visually stunning, sumptuously dramatic film takes in three interconnected tales of forbidden gay love and desire from three different time periods in Spanish history. A mysterious letter, a hidden affair, a political prisoner, a stunning cabaret singer (the great Penelope Cruz), a dogged scholar of Lorca’s life and works (Glenn Close) all intertwine in what looks like a Best Foreign Film Oscar nominee, at least.
‘Dust Bowls and Jewish Souls: Another Side of Woody Guthrie’
Sunday, Nov. 8, One Longfellow Square, Portland, onelongfellowsquare.com
Folk music legend and socialist icon Woody Guthrie famously brandished a guitar labeled “This machine kills fascists.” Apart from that sentiment being both timely and timeless, this documentary from director Steven Pressman also examines the little-known Jewish roots of Guthrie’s art and activism. Through his renowned mother-in-law, the poet and songwriter Aliza Greenblatt, Guthrie incorporated Jewish songs, references and history through his prolific musical career.
The film is presented with a live performance by none other than Guthrie’s granddaughter (and daughter of Arlo Guthrie) Sarah Lee Guthrie, who’ll talk about her famous relatives and the film, and sing selections from their work and her own. There will be refreshments on hand from Lewiston’s own She Doesn’t Like Guthrie’s restaurant in support of the event sponsors, the Maine Jewish Film Festival.
‘Growing Old Together in Belfast’
Tuesday, Nov. 10, Colonial Theatre, 163 High St., Belfast, colonialtheatre.com
Written and directed by Belfast, Maine’s own Jeff Edwards, this feature film follows an eclectic group of aging Mainers as they confront, well, growing old together in Belfast. Starring locals Edwards, Joanna Young, Linda Garson Smith, Tycelia Santoro, Ned Lightner, Lisa Kushner, Kristin Frangoulis, George Frangoulis and Sarah Edwards, the all-Maine production is described as “a whimsical tale of eight characters coming to terms with aging, offering a hopeful message regarding the possibilities of transformation and connection in the home stretch of life.”
‘A King in New York’
Nov. 11 and 14, Kinonik, Wednesday, 121 Cassidy Point Drive, Portland, kinonik.org
Charles Chaplin was in his 60s when he undertook his last starring role in this bitter but still inventively funny sound film about a deposed king forced to fend for himself in Red Scare America. Chaplin himself had been exiled from the United States and, furious and still uncompromisingly brilliant, he turned his spite and ire into a broadside attack on America’s growing fascism under McCarthyism. (At one point, his monarch literally douses the anti-Communist witch hunters with a firehose in their own kangaroo courtroom.) Still nimble and clever in his comic set pieces and physical gags, the aging Chaplin wrote and directed what the blessed movies-on-film freaks at Kinonik rightly call “one of the great screw-yous in movies.”
‘Walkabout’
Nov. 14, PMA Films, 7 Congress Square, Portland, portlandmuseum.org/
PMA Films is running a series they’re calling “A Few Small Odysseys,” and there’s no movie that better encapsulates the contradiction of that phrase like Nicolas Roeg’s mesmerizing 1971 masterpiece. On the surface, it’s a simple story: The teen daughter (“An American Werewolf in London’s” Jenny Agutter) and young son of a seemingly ordinary Australian man are stranded in the outback after the man tries to kill them all. Lost and delirious from hunger and thirst, the children are found by a teenage Aboriginal boy (the extraordinary David Gulpilil) who leads them back toward “civilization.”
The children bond, the young teens are drawn to each other, and the impossible, ancient landscape looms all around them in majestic, implacable silence. Their odyssey carries them through the story of their country, of colonialism, of bigotry and young love, of friendship and, ultimately, tragedy, all while I (who’ve seen this movie a dozen times) can only watch in spellbound awe. Young Gulpilil (who most know from “Crocodile Dundee”) is a revelation, as the cultural divide slowly erodes the friends’ bond the closer they get to the white children’s homeland.
‘Fugs Film!’
Nov. 16, Space, 538 Congress St., Portland, space.538.org
As the trailer for director Chuck Smith’s rockumentary about 1960s-era band The Fugs explains, both The Fugs and The Velvet Underground came out of the same downtown New York art scene — except you’ve heard of The Velvet Underground. A product of the unlikely confluence of Beat poetry, outsider art, garage rock, folk, photo punk and counterculture anti-war prankishness, The Fugs songs are as rough as they are witty. The film traces the band’s unlikely rise to the rock ‘n’ roll fringe and more predictable retreat from it, all while applauding the band founders for never abandoning the grungy, disreputable ethics that have made them cult favorites of everyone from Bob Dylan to Frank Zappa to Sonic Youth. (Listen for their still resonant protest song “CIA Man” over the end credits of the Coen Brothers’ “Burn After Reading”).
Dennis Perkins is a freelance writer who lives in Auburn with his wife and his cat.

title: It’s too early to call the outcome of California’s proposal to tax billionaires
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — A California measure to tax the net worth of billionaires that divided liberal leaders nationally and triggered one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history was too early to call Wednesday morning as the vote tally continued.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the revenue dedicated to replacing federal funding cuts to healthcare. The measure left the ultra-rich, some of whom spent heavily to defeat it, scrambling to figure out whether they would pay the tax or leave California.
Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders framed the proposal as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality by ensuring the ultra-rich pay their fair share. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom warned it would prompt the state’s wealthiest to move out of California and take their tax money with them.
With almost 6 million votes yet to be counted, the AP Decision Team will wait for additional vote results before declaring a winner.
Opponents of the proposed one-time tax on billionaires have outnumbered supporters across most of the state. “No” has sizable leads in the Inland/Central Valley region and the San Diego and Orange County area, and smaller leads along the central coast and in the Bay Area. “Yes” votes led narrowly in Los Angeles County and the northern coast.
The “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side, thanks in large part to tech moguls and venture capitalists, who poured millions into a political action committee fighting the measure. Some billionaires, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the proposed tax. Mark Zuckerberg said he would stay in California for eight years and made a deal with Meta that would help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.
Backers of the proposed tax, led by the powerful labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, said it was needed to help the state backfill the federal funding cuts. The union estimates the state will lose $100 billion in federal healthcare funding over five years.
“It’s time to collect those taxes so we can ensure that our healthcare system is still safe,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions.
But some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Teachers Association, are part of a coalition that opposed it. They’re concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there’s a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents.
Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said he planned to vote against it.
“Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.”
Anthony Serrano, a Democrat living in Folsom who works for Kaiser Permanente, one of the nation’s largest not-for-profit healthcare plans, said he was leaning toward voting for the tax because he tends to support “anything that is a positive for healthcare.”
Even if the measure wins approval from a majority of voters, it would be blocked from taking effect if at least one of two measures designed to nullify it — Propositions 41 and 42 — passes and receives more “yes” votes. The proposals, which are backed by the political action committee Building a Better California, include a ban on new taxes on financial assets and other personal property, a category that excludes real estate. The committee raised more than $333 million, about 30% of it from Brin.
Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom said a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million.
Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month urging voters to support the state measure, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”
Even if the proposed billionaire tax fails in California, the battle over the measure ignited a crucial dialogue on the issue, Gonzalez said.
“We are taking a step forward, and we are showing other states that you can look them in the eye — you can look these billionaires in the eye — and take them on,” she said.

title: Bob Dylan comes knockin' on pope's door as Leo welcomes legend to Vatican
text:
Bob Dylan comes knockin' on pope's door as Leo welcomes legend to Vatican
Bob Dylan came knockin’ on Pope Leo XIV’s door Wednesday, as the American singer-songwriter and poet visited with the American pope at the Vatican during a break between concert dates in Italy.
Video above from last month: Pope Leo XIV leads Sunday prayers as he recovers from lung surgery
The Vatican said the encounter was brief, with Leo giving Dylan a rosary and Dylan presenting the pope with a copy of his autobiography, “Chronicles: Volume One.”
Leo had quoted from an unpublished protest song Dylan penned in 1963, “Go Away You Bomb,” in his 2026 book “Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift.”
Leo was warning against the race to rearm and the recourse to nuclear weapons and quoted the lyric, addressed to a hypothetical atomic bomb: “I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an’ man-handled.”
Two Vatican officials accompanied Dylan: the Rev. Antonio Spadaro, a Vatican culture ministry official who also accompanied Patti Smith to a July audience with Leo; and Andrea Monda, the editor of the Vatican newspaper, L’Osservatore Romano.
Spadaro said Dylan had wanted to speak with Leo, and the two met in private for a few minutes. In an essay in L'Osservatore Romano, he recalled that the former Robert Prevost, who was born in Chicago in 1955, grew up familiar with Dylan's music.
He also noted that Dylan was very familiar with St. Augustine of Hippo, the inspiration for Leo's spirituality and Augustinian religious order, penning “I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine” for the 1967 album "John Wesley Harding."
Dylan, who won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 2016, wore a black hoodie and a loose tie. Vatican photos of the encounter showed him with the hood over his head.
It wasn’t Dylan’s first papal encounter: He played for Pope John Paul II, and thousands of other people, in 1997 during a concert capping a religious congress in Bologna, Italy.
Dylan, who changed his name from Robert Zimmerman, was born to a Jewish family in Minnesota. He famously became a born-again Christian in 1979 and alienated some of his longtime fans with songs like “Gotta Serve Somebody” and “Saved.”
In more recent years, Dylan has been more circumspect about his religious beliefs. In a 2022 interview with the Wall Street Journal, Dylan said that he was a “religious person” who reads the scriptures, meditates and prays.
Dylan met with Leo in between concert dates in Italy. He played in Milan on Monday and is playing Rome on Thursday. In his most recent concert before the meeting with the pope, Dylan sang his 1997 song “Tryin’ to Get to Heaven” that contains the lyric, “I’ve been all around the world, boys/Now I’m trying to get to heaven before they close the door."

title: Star NASCAR driver suspended by own team for final race of season
text:
MOORESVILLE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A star NASCAR driver has been suspended by his own team for the final race of the 2026 season.
Drivers in all three of NASCAR’s top series will wrap up the racing slate this weekend at Homestead-Miami Speedway.
However, Carson Hocevar, driver of the No. 77 car, will not be among them.
Spire Motorsports announced on Tuesday that Hocevar would be suspended for the Nov. 8 season finale race.
The team-induced suspension comes after some accused Hocevar of intentionally spinning himself to cause a caution during the Nov. 1 race at Martinsville.
The 23-year-old also had a run-in with Austin Cindric as he upheld his reputation as an aggressive driver.
“A decision like this has a lot of variables and a cascading effect across an organization like ours,” Spire Motorsports said in a statement. “The easy thing would have been to leave this in NASCAR’s hands. To us, however, this isn’t about money or points. We believe in respect. Our integrity matters. This is the right decision. Sometimes the right decision for someone you care about hurts in the short term.”
NASCAR veteran and former Spire driver Justin Haley will race in Hocevar’s place.
In a statement of his own, Hocevar called the suspension “an embarrassing day” for him.
“I let the people down that gave me the opportunity of a lifetime to drive a Cup car,” he wrote. “I crossed the line with my on-track actions and gave [owner] Jeff [Dickerson] and Spire Motorsports no option but to put someone else in the 77 car this weekend.”
Hocevar became one of NASCAR’s more popular drivers this season, in part because of his aggressive driving style and charisma.
But he has had numerous incidents involving other drivers in his young career, and was also involved in a viral brawl at Bristol in September.
Hocevar earned his first Cup race win at Talladega on April 26, and advanced to NASCAR’s postseason for the first time this season.
In 35 races this season, Hocevar won a race and recorded 12 top-10 finishes and six top-fives. He sat 12th in the points standings heading into the final race.
