title: REVIEW POTPOURRI: From Charles Munch to Fritz Weaver
text:
Charles Munch
Piston: 6th Symphony; Martinu: Fantaisies Symphoniques – Charles Munch conducting the Boston Symphony. RCA Victor Red Seal, LM-2083, LP, recorded 1956 at Symphony Hall.
Charles Munch (1891-1968) had been a very gifted violinist and concertmaster of orchestras that included the Leipzig Gewandhaus before he decided, at the age of 40 in 1931, to devote himself to conducting. Certain friends laughed at him even considering such a ridiculous pipe dream.
Munch laughed with them, pushed forward, and, after much success with the Paris Conservatory Orchestra and guest conducting the New York Philharmonic, became music director of the Boston Symphony in 1949 for 13 very eventful years, before resigning in 1962 to take up a fully busy Indian summer six years of both guest conducting engagements and taking on the music-director responsibilities of the newly-created Orchestre de Paris. In September 1968, the Maestro was touring in the U.S. with his new Orchestre and died at a hotel, in Richmond, Virginia, shortly after finishing a concert there.
The above record features two different 6th Symphonies that were commissioned by the BSO in 1956 to celebrate its 75th anniversary.
Composers Walter Piston (1894-1976) and Bohuslav Martinu (1890-1959) both shared a close professional relationship with Munch and his BSO predecessor Serge Koussevitzky (1874-1951), but otherwise had dissimilar personalities, world views and styles. Piston was born in Rockland and his 6th Symphony had a certain granite quality in its emotional reserve, perhaps rooted in the New England soil, its veiled beauty peeled away only through repeated listening.
Martinu was a native of the Czech Republic and spent many years in Paris. His 6th Symphony has certain primitive sonorities, possibly inspired by the primitive eerie details of Czech composer Leos Janacek while the sprightly, beguiling and at times abrasive beauties could be tied to studying composition with the phenomenal French composer Albert Roussel, whose own music puts him in the same category as his contemporaries Debussy and Ravel.
Both performances can be accessed via YouTube.
A personal note – Uncle George Fletcher Cates (1915-1999) resided in Paris from 1945 to 1947 doing humanitarian relief work for the American Friends Service Committee, founded by South China’s most famous native Rufus Jones (1863-1948) and he told me about attending a concert of the Paris Conservatory Orchestra conducted by Maestro Munch.
During the Nazi occupation from 1940 to 1944, Munch conducted concerts and donated most of his money to the French Resistance, putting his life on the line.
Sarasate
Sarasate: Zigeunerweisen and Carmen Fantasy; Dvorak: Violin Concerto and Mazurek. Akiko Suwanai, violin with Ivan Fischer conducting the Budapest Festival Orchestra, Philips 289464531-2, compact disc, recorded 2000.
For some strange reason, I have never been particularly moved by Antonin Dvorak’s Piano Concerto but I consider his Violin and Cello Concertos masterpieces. The Violin Concerto was finally premiered in Prague in 1883 after four years of constant revisions.
It has been beautifully played and recorded several times – these include Isaac Stern/Eugene Ormandy, Edith Peinemann/Peter Maag, Josef Suk/Karel Ancerl, Georg Kulenkampf/Eugen Jochum, Pamela Frank/Charles Mackerras, three different Nathan Milsteins with respectively William Steinberg, Rafael Fruhbeck de Burgos and Paul Kletzki; this CD contains the phenomenally exquisite playing of Akiko Suwanai with the unfortunately bland, smoothed out conducting of Ivan Fischer with the Budapest Festival Orchestra.
Interestingly, while Suwanai has stayed below the radar in recent years, Fischer has been one of the very few conductors, in this age of ignorance/dislike of classical music among the many, to make the news currently. After a huge success with guest engagements in both the States and Europe, the Maestro was booked with the Berlin Philharmonic and wanted his own seating plan with the players but they refused to even consider cooperating. So a cancelation of any Berlin Philharmonic engagements. And the media, even with all the other world events, gave this story lots of press.
Upon looking at the pairing of Dvorak (1841-1904) and Spanish composer/violinist Pablo de Sarasate (1844-1908), one might wonder what the two have in common besides similar life spans.
First, Dvorak’s publisher Fritz Simrock was also acquainted with Sarasate and urged Dvorak to dedicate the very pleasant Mazurek to him. In return, Sarasate did express some admiration for passages in the Violin Concerto, but would only perform pieces that showed off his technical virtuosity in a narcissistic manner.
The two Sarasate pieces on this CD, however, are very captivating listening and, along with the Dvorak Mazurek, are played very nicely, Fischer even showing more electricity in his conducting.
Fritz Weaver
Actor Fritz Weaver (1926-2016) had a fierce charisma and resonant command, helped by a booming speaking voice in his characterization of villains, one of the most vivid being the leader of a deadly money laundering syndicate in the 1967 made for TV movie, The Borgia Stick, with a fine cast that included Don Murray, Inger Stevens, Marshall Thompson, Ralph Waite, Barnard Hughes and the playwright Marc Connelly as a syndicate operative under the guise of a grandfatherly gentleman patronizing the local coffee shop. And accessible via YouTube.

title: How float therapy is helping some improve sleep and reduce anxiety
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (InvestigateTV) - A type of therapy can improve people’s health by allowing anxiety and tension to float away. Studies show that float therapy can improve sleep and reduce pain.
Float therapy involves lying in a tub filled with nearly a thousand pounds of magnesium dissolved in skin-temperature water. The solution is dense enough that the body cannot sink.
Sessions typically last an hour or more, with the option to turn off all lights and block out all sound.
Nia Linbravo referees women’s basketball games four to five nights a week. She has also worked as a juvenile probation officer and now works in project management. She said the physical and mental demands of her schedule made it difficult to slow down.
“It was hard to relax,” Linbravo said.
A herniated disk and trouble sleeping led her to try float therapy. She said the experience has also helped her manage a diagnosis of depression and anxiety.
“I talked to my doctor about doing this. I wanted to talk about different strategies and they were saying it would be helpful for me, and it has been,” Linbravo said.
She described the sensation of floating as a form of release.
“I think it’s the weightlessness and the feeling of the water supporting me, and I’m literally just letting go,” Linbravo said. “Being in the floating tank, it is a space for me to just talk to myself and reflect on what’s happening — calm my mind and be in the moment.”
Dana Highfill has worked as a massage therapist for 17 years and operates Float North in Northeast Portland. She said most clients come in seeking relief of some kind.
“There’s that physical component — you’re getting relief because it feels like you’re turning off gravity. You’re laying there fully supported, your joints open up, and it helps reduce inflammation,” Highfill said.
She said float therapy can also support mental health care routines.
“You have reduced stimulation to your nervous system. You can go from fight or flight, which most of us live in, to a rest and repair state,” Highfill said.
Highfill also addressed a common concern about the experience, noting that the tanks are not as confining as some expect. A single tank measures eight feet long, four feet wide, with a seven-foot ceiling. The water is approximately 10 inches deep.

title: Hawk rescued after being found grounded in a driveway. The 'mystery diagnosis' now solved
text:
Hawk rescued after being found grounded in a driveway. The 'mystery diagnosis' now solved
A hawk found grounded in a Virginia driveway was evaluated by wildlife experts, who said they've recently solved the mystery behind why it was unwilling to fly.
The Southwest Virginia Wildlife Center of Roanoke said in a post on Facebook that a mature, adult red-shouldered hawk was found grounded in a driveway about a mile away from the center's facility.
Upon arrival, the hawk was checked out for the "usual suspects" such as "broken bones, lead toxicity, eye issues, head trauma, emaciation, and bruising from any kind of collision or altercation," the wildlife center said.
Related video: Kitten rescued by California Highway Patrol
All were within normal limits.
Further examination later determined that the hawk had an unusual diagnosis.
"At over 910g (two pounds) in weight, she was too darn fat to fly," the wildlife center said. "We couldn't even palpate her keel due to the heavy layer of fat covering it."
The person who found the hawk told officials that neighbors reported their free-roaming chickens had disappeared at an "alarming rate" over the last few weeks, leading officials to believe this was how the animal gained weight.
"Our mystery was very likely solved! This queen was picking off the buffet of easy prey set out before her, eating her fill, and then snoozing in the trees nearby until she was ready to eat again," the post said. "The chickens were let out in the morning, she ate another, and repeat."
The post continued, saying, "This story is kinda funny (unless you're the chickens getting eaten), but there is a sobering reality: This is a man-made issue, and this could have had a sadder ending if she had been found by a larger predator instead of the finder. Without flight, she is extremely vulnerable."
The wildlife center said the incident serves as a warning to not feed wildlife, directly or indirectly.

title: Florida sheriff says 2 dead, including suspect, as witnesses report shooting at Tampa office complex
text:
TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — A gunman plowed a car into a courtyard on Citibank’s sprawling Tampa business campus on Wednesday and opened fire with a rifle, killing a woman before a security guard fatally shot him, authorities said.
The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office did not give a motive for the shooting or say whether the gunman and his lone victim knew each other.
The attack sent workers scrambling as the suspect crashed his car among outdoor tables where people were eating lunch, then started shooting, said Chief Deputy Frank Losat of the sheriff’s office. He said 3,200 people were on the campus at work during the attack.
The gunman fatally shot the woman before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria, Losat said. The guard and the gunman exchanged fire, and the guard killed him, Losat said.
“Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely,” Losat told a news conference. ”So kudos to that security guard.”
The names of the gunman and the woman killed were not immediately released.
Losat said four other people were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. He didn’t know whether any of them had been shot or struck by the gunman’s vehicle.
Citibank VP heard ‘incredible clatter’ of gunfire, then screaming
The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant’s employees.
David Dzien, a Citibank vice president, told The Associated Press he was returning to work after lunch when he saw the shooter’s sedan crash through a fence about 150 yards (137 meters) away from him, followed by an “incredible clatter” that he later realized was gunfire.
People near the crashed car suddenly dispersed and others began to scream, Dzien said, as he sprinted back into the building and evacuated through a fire escape.
“I can still hear the particular type of scream,” he said, “and I’m still trying to process it, frankly.”
The attack occurred on a day when “VIPs” who don’t normally work at the complex were present for a “quarterly review,” Dzien said.
More than 360 deputies began arriving immediately
Sheriff’s deputies began arriving at the campus within a minute of the first 911 call, Losat said. The response was huge, with more than 360 deputies — many in tactical gear — rushing to the scene.
Those deputies spent 2 1/2 hours searching and clearing the building where the shootings occurred plus adjacent office buildings, Losat said.
Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from responding officers described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search as people were found sheltering in locked rooms and closets, then carefully escorted from the buildings and parking garage.
Citigroup said in a statement that it was “aware of an incident” at the complex and was cooperating with authorities.
Nearby hotel gave shelter to hundreds of fleeing workers
Employees at the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel, a few hundred feet from the Citibank complex, were having a monthly employee luncheon in the hotel’s ballroom when they saw a massive flood of police vehicles headed toward the campus.
General Manager Matt Chauvin said Citibank employees ran over and told the front desk there was an active shooter.
“We at first locked the doors and, you know, went into lockdown, but the employees kept coming over,” Chauvin said.
Chauvin estimated the hotel sheltered about 300 Citibank workers. Hotel staff gave them water and lunch, and let some go into hotel rooms “to sort of decompress or make phone calls.”
“Luckily we were far enough away that they were all safe,” he said.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. AP journalists Cybele Mayes-Osterman in Chicago, R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this story.

title: Cornell rape investigation will be led by former prosecutor in Sean 'Diddy' Combs case
text:
Cornell rape investigation will be led by former prosecutor in Sean 'Diddy' Combs case
A reopened criminal investigation into gang rape allegations at Cornell University will be led by a former Manhattan federal prosecutor who oversaw high-profile sex crimes cases against music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs and fashion executive Peter Nygård, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced on Wednesday.
Jacqueline Kelly, a Cornell alumna and partner at the law firm Boies Schiller Flexner, will serve as outside counsel for James' investigation, which was spurred by a former student’s allegations in a September lawsuit that several men raped her at a fraternity party in October 2024.
Kelly and a team of lawyers and investigators from her firm and the attorney general's office will be responsible for gathering evidence, interviewing witnesses, reviewing investigative records and reports, and analyzing the facts and applicable law, James said.
They will report to James, who was appointed last month by Gov. Kathy Hochul as a special prosecutor overseeing the Cornell probe. James, a Democrat, made the announcement a day after winning election to a third term.
Separately, two men named as defendants in the former student's lawsuit want the attorney general removed from the investigation. They argue James is biased because of a social media post she made before her appointment that expressed support for the accuser. A judge has yet to rule.
“Jacqueline Kelly is a seasoned prosecutor who has overseen numerous cases from investigation through trial,” James said in a statement. “With her criminal legal expertise, commitment to public service, and judicial experience, I am confident that she will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation.”
Kelly, a Columbia Law School graduate, was a prosecutor in the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office for nearly a decade and led the civil rights unit in the office’s criminal division. She oversaw investigations and prosecutions of civil rights offenses, voting rights violations, sex crimes and hate crimes.
She left last year to join Boies Schiller Flexner and will remain at the firm while she conducts the Cornell investigation.
“All New Yorkers deserve a fair and thorough inquiry into the facts of this case,” Kelly said. “I look forward to lending my years of experience as a federal prosecutor to the Office of the Attorney General as we examine all available evidence.”
Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor on Oct. 1, saying she had lost faith in the local prosecutor, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who declined to bring charges in 2024.
Van Houten said he would restart the investigation following the former student's lawsuit, but a lawyer for the accuser said the district attorney was preparing to bring the matter to a grand jury within two weeks.
James has said her investigation will take months.
The former Cornell student, identified in court papers as Jane Doe, alleged in her lawsuit that some of the men pressured her into using ketamine and marijuana and that she drank alcohol that left her too intoxicated to consent. A few weeks later, she said, she made reports to campus police and the university's Title IX office.
The case roiled the Ivy League institution, raising questions about how universities, police departments and local prosecutors respond to campus sexual assaults.
Last month, Cornell hired former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to review how the school investigates sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the campus police response and more.
As a federal prosecutor, Kelly supervised the prosecutions of former Manhattan neurologist Ricardo Cruciani, who killed himself in jail while awaiting trial on federal charges after his conviction in state court for molesting patients, as well as Bronx music teacher Jesus Concepcion, who was sentenced in 2024 to 30 years in prison for sexually abusing five students. She also took on the mafia, prosecuting a dozen members of the Lucchese crime family.
At Boies Schiller Flexner, she focuses on regulatory and criminal investigations and represents victims of sexual assault and other crimes. The firm, co-founded by lawyer David Boies, is known for representing victims of the late Jeffrey Epstein, as well as corporate clients including Amazon and the defunct health technology company Theranos.
James, whose office is geared toward civil litigation and consumer protection, has turned to outside counsel in the past to assist in investigations.
In 2021, she appointed two outside lawyers, former Manhattan U.S. Attorney Joon Kim and employment lawyer Anne Clark, to conduct a non-criminal investigation into sexual harassment allegations against then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo, leading to his resignation. Cuomo denied the findings in their report.

title: Democrat Gina Hinojosa elected Texas’ first Latina governor, ousts Republican incumbent Greg Abbott
text:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — In a stunning upset, Gina Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than 30 years on Tuesday, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott and catapulting a decided underdog to the helm of what has long been the nation’s most populous red state.
She will become Texas’ first Latina governor — and the first Democrat to hold the office since Ann Richards in the 1990s — following a groundbreaking victory that topples one of the nation’s most prominent Republican governors and steadfast supporters of President Donald Trump, possibly accelerating the state’s shift to an emerging battleground.
Her victory was part of an electrifying night for Democrats in Texas, where James Talarico also won election, defeating Republican Ken Paxton in the race for the U.S. Senate.
Hinojosa’s win served as validation for Democrats’ long deferred dream that demographic changes in the state would be followed by a shift in political power. It also elevates Hinojosa, a 52-year-old state legislator from a liberal Austin district since 2017, into a breakout Democratic star, even as she did not have significant support from the national party for her campaign.
“It never bothered me that they doubted me. It bothered me that they doubted us,” Hinojosa told supporters at her victory party in Austin. “Texas, my faith in you never wavered.”
Jumping in the race with little money or name recognition, Hinojosa engineered a plucky and populist challenge, railing against artificial intelligence data centers and corruption to down Abbott. She also proved that money in politics has clear limits. Billionaire Elon Musk had spent tens of millions of dollars to back Republicans, and Abbott’s campaign had spent $180 million since last year in what was thought to be a safe path to a fourth term.
But Hinojosa proved durable while simultaneously riding the tailwinds of Talarico’s hard-charging Senate campaign, one of the nation’s marquee races. Just two years after Trump carried the state by double digits, the upset is also a stark reflection of how a glum national mood dragged down Republicans even in a stronghold where Democrats had not won in decades.
Trump blamed Abbott for the loss in a striking criticism of one of his staunchest supporters, accusing him of becoming a “RINO,” or Republican in name only, in the last months of the race. “He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!” Trump posted on social media.
Abbott, who had been seeking a record fourth term, said he called Hinojosa and pledged to help her transition into office.
“Leading this state has been the greatest honor I’ve ever had,” Abbott told supporters as he conceded the race.
On a national level, the loss will set off alarms for Republicans, who depend on winning Texas in presidential election years to maintain a path to the White House.
The first Democrat elected governor since 1990
How Hinojosa governs is likely to open a dramatic political and cultural shift in the Texas Capitol, which over the last decade has passed one of the nation’s strictest abortion laws and increasingly aggressive immigration crackdowns. Her victory gives Democrats a potent veto pen, but the extent of her power will be tested in a statehouse where Republicans still have a majority.
Abbott, who first took office in 2015, won each of his previous races by double digits.
Then came Hinojosa, who started her campaign last year at a time when bigger-name Democrats seemed uneager to wade into the race.
From the start she accused Abbott of prioritizing the wealthy over everyday people and failing to bring down costs. Abbott said Hinojosa wanted to raise taxes and painted her as a radical and a threat to Texans’ way of life.
One of Hinojosa’s earliest campaign pledges was a one-time $1,500 payment to each of the state’s nearly 32 million residents that she called a “Corruption Tax Refund.” She said the money would come from Texas’ massive emergency savings fund.
Hinojosa also seized on growing national rejection of data centers, accusing Abbott of allowing the energy-guzzling server warehouses to multiply. Abbott responded to public anger with a temporary moratorium on new data center approvals.
Hinojosa distanced herself from the progressive label
Hinojosa was once a proud vice chair of the Texas Legislative Progressive Caucus and defender of transgender rights, which became a centerpiece of Abbott’s attacks.
She tried to shake off the progressive label throughout the campaign and batted away culture-war issues, presenting herself instead as a populist. Her campaign included ads featuring Republican voters saying they would support her.
“They want to run an entire campaign saying that I’m too woke,” Hinojosa said in one spot. “I plan to spend an entire campaign focused on the fact that working people are too broke.”
___
This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Elon Musk’s last name.

title: Brightening Skies This Afternoon... Rain Chances Return Thursday Afternoon
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Outside of a few lingering spotty showers over Northern Aroostook County... the bulk of the rain has exited as of noontime today. We’ll dry things out and brighten up as the afternoon progresses. The best for sunshine will be over areas south of Greenville and Millinocket while clouds remain prevalent to the north. Temperatures will be quite a bit warmer than yesterday with highs in the 60s to near 70° for most locales... even some low 70s possible closer to Bangor and points southward. We’ll see partly cloudy skies tonight with lows dropping to the mid-40s to low 50s.
An approaching cold front will bring us increasing clouds for our Thursday with some scattered light rain showers during the afternoon. Mild air ahead of the front will allow temperatures to top off in the 60s to near 70°. The cold front will move into the state Thursday night into Friday and will play a role in bringing some rainfall to the state later Friday into Saturday. The exact position of the front will determine where the heaviest rain will fall but some spots certainly could see 1″ or more of rainfall Friday night through Saturday morning. Upper-level energy coming out of the Great Lakes Region Friday night will cause a new area of low pressure to develop near the Mid-Atlantic Region Saturday morning. Depending on the track of that new low... we could see some more rainfall Saturday night into Sunday. There’s still some uncertainty with regard to how this will all play out so stay tuned for updates.
Today: Brightening skies. Lingering rain this morning across areas especially north and east of Millinocket. Warmer with highs in the 60s to around 70°.... a few upper 50s possible along the coast. Southwest wind 5-10 MPH.
Tonight: Partly cloudy. Lows in the mid-40s to low 50s. Light and variable wind.
Thursday: Partly to mostly cloudy. Scattered showers possible during the afternoon. Highs in the 60s to near 70°. South/southwest wind 5-15 MPH.
Friday: Mostly cloudy with rain possible later in the day... especially closer to the coast. Highs in the 60s.
Saturday: Mostly cloudy with rain possible... mainly during the morning. Cooler with highs in the 50s to near 60°.
Sunday: Showers possible during the morning then brightening skies during the afternoon. Cooler with highs in the 40s to around 50°.

title: DNC Chairman shares party goals after ‘blue wave’
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Following a sweeping “blue wave” that saw Democrats flip long-held Republican seats across the country, party leaders in Washington are preparing an aggressive legislative and oversight agenda focused squarely on lowering everyday costs.
Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) hailed the outcome as a “generational remake of the Senate map,” pointing to victories in states long considered untouchable for Democrats.
According to Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin said voters responded to their pitches of affordability, but also rebuked President Trump.
“They were sending a message to Donald Trump,” Martin said, using stiff language, in an interview on Capitol Hill. “‘Get off your ass and do something to help me. Get off your ass and do something to help our country.’”
Policy Priorities: Healthcare, Tariffs, and Ending the Iran War
Martin emphasized that Democrats’ top priority will be delivering on economic promises, beginning with efforts to roll back Trump administration tariffs and reverse federal cuts to social safety nets.
Specifically, Martin targeted recent legislation that scaled back federal assistance programs to fund tax cuts.
“Repeal the ‘Big Ugly Bill,’ which cut Medicaid and SNAP benefits to give tax breaks to the wealthiest in this country,” Martin said.
Foreign policy is also set to take center stage, with Democratic lawmakers planning legislative maneuvers to force an end to the ongoing war in Iran.
Oversight and Accountability
Beyond legislative policy, Democrats plan to use their new committee gavels to launch investigations into alleged corruption within the executive branch.
“We can walk and chew gum at the same time,” Martin said. “Meaning that we can both deliver on that agenda and also hold people accountable in this country, and the reality is we’re seeing massive corruption with this administration.”
While members in both parties have floated the potential impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the handling of the Iran War, Martin stopped short of endorsing formal proceedings, stating only that Hegseth “will be held accountable.”

title: Why Paul LePage is on track to be Maine Republicans’ lone bright spot, but barely
text:
Former Gov. Paul LePage was in position early Wednesday to hand Maine Republicans their only major win of a bruising night, even as he trailed State Auditor Matt Dunlap by about 1,000 votes in the 2nd Congressional District.
The rest of the ballot went the other way. Democrat Troy Jackson ousted U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, helping his party take control of the Senate. Democrat Hannah Pingree won the governor’s race, and Democrats expanded their majorities in both chambers of the Legislature.
That leaves LePage as the only Republican with a chance to be part of Maine’s congressional delegation next year. A win would flip a seat Democrats have held since 2018 and make him New England’s only Republican in the U.S. House.
It will be close. A Bangor Daily News analysis of the returns rates the race as likely to go to LePage. That is not a call. Decision Desk HQ, the BDN’s national partner, had not called the race as of 3 a.m. Wednesday and rated it a toss-up before Tuesday. But LePage is clearly favored, and the race also looks unlikely to need a ranked-choice count.
An estimated 57,000 votes remained to be counted in 111 towns as of early Wednesday, with Dunlap leading by just 1,000. To hold on, Dunlap would need the remaining towns to favor LePage by no more than about 2 points.
The problem for Dunlap is that there are much more Republicans than that. Those towns backed Republicans by about 9 points in 2024, when the district as a whole was roughly even.
In 2026, they are running redder. Based on towns already counted, the BDN’s model expects the outstanding towns to favor LePage by about 13 points. At that rate, he would net about 7,700 votes and win by roughly 6,700. Even at the low end of the model’s range, he would net about 5,800, more than five times what he needs.
Dunlap’s best remaining town is likely to be Farmington, the only large Democratic-leaning town still out, which is expected to net him about 740 votes. Sabattus, Oxford and Pittsfield together are expected to net LePage about 1,100, and most of his projected margin comes from roughly 105 small, rural towns that have not yet reported.
Blank ballots and 149 write-ins could still leave the winner just short of a majority and trigger a ranked-choice count, as in 2024. The BDN could still call the race if those ballots cannot change the outcome.

title: I Ate Everything on Dunkin’s ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Menu
text:
I Ate and Drank Everything on Dunkin’s ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Menu
Avengers: Assemble!
(To be clear: By “Avengers,” I mean donuts. By “Assemble,” I mean congregate inside my mouth. And by “!” I mean “Some really questionable life choices brought me to this moment, but I am a middle-aged father two children and it’s too late to start over.”)
With about six weeks to go before the big debut of Avengers: Doomsday, the rollout of what is sure to be a multiverse of tie-in products and foods is fully underway. Today, Dunkin’ Donuts launched an incursion of baked goods and caffeinated beverages upon our world with the debut of their Avengers: Doomsday themed foods and drinks.
And now I will eat and drink all of it.
This is my gift and my curse. Like the members of the X-Men, I was born with a remarkable mutant power. No, I can’t shoot lasers out of my eyes or speak telepathically or gain knowledge by touching my hand to a television set, rolling my eyes back in my head, and hissing “LLLLEEEEARNINGGG.”
Instead, I have the superhuman ability to consume extreme amounts of fast food inspired by movies. For over a decade, whenever a chain restaurant releases a menu of food inspired by a movie —no matter how tangentially — I eat all of it and report back on my findings. (My secondary mutation is my total lack of shame, as I will clearly debase myself — and destroy my body — for the sake of content.)
Much like Earth’s Mightiest Heroes of the Avengers, I stand as the first line of defense against these menus. I do it so you can decide for yourself whether you want to try something called a “Doom Cloud Latte.”
My own anxiety notwithstanding, Dunkin’ clearly believes their Doomsday menu will be a big driver of traffic to their stores; they even made an TV spot for it, starring Marvel’s three biggest stars of the moment: Channing Tatum, H.E.R.B.I.E. the Fantastic Four’s adorable robot sidekick, and Channing Tatum’s baffling Cajun accent as the suave X-Man Gambit.
Okay Gambit, you convinced me. I’m about to make a name for myself by eating two different donuts and a couple of Munchkins while guzzling down not one, not two, not even three or four or five, but six different energy drinks. (Hey, quick question for a friend: How many milligrams of caffeine can a person safely ingest before it becomes toxic? My friend is my cardiologist, by the way.)
All I know is this: If this be doomsday at least I died the way I lived: Making really bad decisions in order to entertain people.

title: Aroostook County communities report results from 2026 general election
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Aroostook County communities report results from 2026 general election
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) – Communities across Aroostook County are reporting results from Tuesday’s general election, with voters weighing in on municipal races, local ballot questions and several closely contested state legislative races.
Election returns received from Caribou, Presque Isle, Van Buren, Fort Fairfield, Sherman, Castle Hill, Chapman and Mapleton provide a closer look at how residents voted in their respective communities.
We are still awaiting election results from several communities.
Caribou
In Caribou, voters approved a proposal authorizing the city to spend up to $2.9 million on a replacement aerial ladder truck for the Caribou Fire and Ambulance Department.
The measure passed with 1,800 votes in favor and 1,085 opposed. The funding may come from a combination of municipal funds, reserves, grants, bonds, lease-purchase agreements or bank financing, as determined by the City Council.
In the race for Caribou City Council, Tamara Lovewell received 1,990 votes, followed by Jeff Whitney with 1,591 and George LaCasse Jr. with 1,553. All three candidates ran unopposed for the three available seats.
For the two available RSU 39 school board seats, Melissa Swanberg received 1,873 votes and Dale Gordon received 1,224, securing both positions. Christina Peterson finished third with 1,192 votes.
Tiffany Stewart received 2,563 votes for the Jefferson Cary Memorial Hospital Fund position.
Caribou voters also favored Republican Susan Collins in the U.S. Senate race, giving her 2,056 votes compared with 1,114 for Democrat Troy Jackson.
Presque Isle
In Presque Isle, voters elected two at-large City Council members, with Jeffery Willette receiving 1,859 votes and Eugene Cronin receiving 1,808, according to the election returns provided to WAGM. Jeremiah Harris followed with 1,331 votes.
Willette, the current City Council chairperson, secured another term, while Cronin, a former city recreation and parks director, will join the council for the first time.
In local school board races, John Harvell received 442 votes for the MSAD 1 Section 5 seat, while Lori Kenneson received 172 votes for the Section 9 seat. Both ran unopposed.
Presque Isle voters also weighed in on several state races.
In Maine House District 5, Republican Douglas Carlisle Jr. received 1,778 votes compared with 1,512 for Democrat Lori Kenneson.
In State Senate District 2, Republican Trey Stewart received 1,951 votes, while Democrat Janel Underwood-Charette received 1,353.
The city’s U.S. Senate results showed Collins receiving 1,931 votes compared with 1,398 for Jackson.
Van Buren
Several races were closely contested in Van Buren, including the State Senate District 1 race.
Democrat Vaughn McLaughlin received 344 votes, narrowly edging Republican Lucien Daigle, who received 341 votes in the municipality.
In the Maine House District 2 race, Democrat Roland Martin received 368 votes compared with 322 for Republican Roger Albert.
Van Buren voters also favored Democrat Hannah Pingree in the governor’s race, giving her 355 votes compared with 284 for Republican Robert Charles and 53 for independent Rick Bennett.
In the U.S. Senate race, Collins received 375 votes compared with 327 for Jackson.
Fort Fairfield
Fort Fairfield voters also reported results from several state and federal races.
In Maine House District 3, Republican Susan Bernard received 728 votes, compared with 667 for Democrat David McCrea.
In the State Senate District 1 race, Republican Lucien Daigle received 711 votes, while Democrat Vaughn McLaughlin received 663.
For governor, Republican Robert Charles received 674 votes, followed by Democrat Hannah Pingree with 573 and independent Rick Bennett with 127.
In the U.S. Senate race, Collins received 834 votes compared with 547 for Jackson.
Fort Fairfield reported 1,406 ballots cast.
Mapleton, Chapman and Castle Hill
Results from several smaller Aroostook County communities showed support for Republican candidates in multiple statewide and congressional contests.
In Mapleton, Collins received 702 votes compared with 271 for Jackson. Republican Robert Charles received 588 votes in the governor’s race, while Pingree received 304 and Bennett received 79.
In the Maine House District 6 race, Republican Donald Ardell received 563 votes in Mapleton, compared with 401 for Democrat Melanie Tompkins.
Chapman reported 149 votes for Collins and 71 for Jackson. In the governor’s race, Charles received 126 votes, Pingree received 74 and Bennett received 17.
In the House District 6 race, Ardell received 123 votes in Chapman, while Tompkins received 89.
Castle Hill reported 128 votes for Collins and 71 for Jackson. The governor’s race saw Charles receive 110 votes, followed by Pingree with 78 and Bennett with 13.
The House District 6 race was tied in Castle Hill, with Ardell and Tompkins each receiving 99 votes.
Sherman
In Sherman, voters favored Republican candidates in several state and federal races.
Collins received 320 votes compared with 71 for Jackson in the U.S. Senate race.
Republican Paul LePage received 294 votes in the 2nd Congressional District race, compared with 89 for Democrat Matthew Dunlap.
For governor, Charles received 287 votes, Pingree received 82 and Bennett received 20.
In State Senate District 2, Republican Trey Stewart received 296 votes compared with 80 for Democrat Janel Underwood-Charette.
Republican Tracy Quint received 325 votes in the Maine House District 8 race.
Results remain unofficial
While these municipal returns provide a look at voting trends across Aroostook County, they represent only the votes cast in the individual communities and do not necessarily reflect the final outcome of districtwide or statewide races. Results remain unofficial pending certification.
For the latest election results from across Maine, visit WAGM’s Election Results page.

title: Bangor man arrested for Sunday morning assault
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Bangor man has been arrested after officials say he assaulted a woman and left her unconscious.
Bangor Police said they were called to an altercation outside of a Franklin Street bar just before 1 a.m. on Sunday morning.
An officer said they witnessed Detrayvious Calvin, 30, run up to another man and punch him from behind.
Calvin was placed into custody when officers noticed a woman lying on the ground and bleeding from her face.
As a result of the investigation, officers learned that the woman was attempting to break up a fight between Calvin and another person when she was hit in the face by Calvin.
The woman was transported to an area hospital.
Calvin was arrested and taken to Penobscot County Jail and has been charged with assault and disorderly conduct.

title: Mississippi Senate candidates Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde-Smith both ‘confident’ in winning race as it remains too close to call

BILOXI, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) — The Mississippi Senate race between Democratic candidate Scott Colom and Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is still too close to call.
As of Wednesday morning, Colom and Hyde-Smith have both said they are “confident” that they will win.
“Where we are, where the ballots are, we’re gonna win,” Colom said as he addressed supporters at a 10 a.m. news conference. “This is our election. We’ve won it. The people have done it. They’ve decided to go in a new direction. I’m confident of that.”
In a statement, Hyde-Smith’s campaign said, “Our campaign is closely monitoring the remaining count. We remain confident that when every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted, Mississippians will have reelected Cindy Hyde-Smith.”
As of 11:30 a.m. Wednesday, 95.6% of votes had been counted. Colom narrowly leads Hyde-Smith, taking 462,857 (48.9%) of the vote compared to Hyde-Smith’s 462,792 (48.9%) votes. Independent Ty Pinkins has received 19,938 (2.1%) votes.
Because the race is a general congressional race, there will be no runoff, and the top vote-getter will take the seat.
No Democrat has represented Mississippi in the Senate since 1989.

title: Here’s who won in Saco municipal elections
text:
Voters in Saco on Tuesday reelected the city’s mayor and two incumbent city councilors, while residents of Ward 2 will send a new member to the council.
Residents also returned two incumbent members of the school board to office.
CITY COUNCIL
In Ward 2, Trevor Nason was elected, with a total of 927 votes. He beat out incumbent Joshua Parks, who received 535. Ward 2 covers the area closest to Scarborough, including Saco Heath Preserve.
Voters in Ward 3 chose Sandra Guay, with a total of 916 votes. Guay, an attorney, was appointed to the council in August to fill a vacancy. She beat out John Shannon III, who received 374 votes. Ward 3 covers much of the area around Route 1.
Incumbent Nathan Johnston won an uncontested race in Ward 7, which covers downtown Saco.
SCHOOL BOARD
Both incumbent candidates for Saco school board seats in Wards 2 and 6 will be returning to their positions.
In Ward 2, Jennifer Preble, who received 919 votes, beat out Arianna Parks, who received 524.
A total of 681 voters selected incumbent Sarah Truman in Ward 6, while Maureen “Moe” Cahill received 401 votes.
In the run-up to the election, the challengers had argued that their background as educators was needed on the board.
Donald Pilon was the only candidate on the ballot for Ward 4, receiving 1,352 votes. Ward 4 covers the oceanfront section of Saco.
In his response to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Pilon — who is a former Saco mayor and Maine House representative — said he decided to run for school board because the education of Saco students is “the most important charge” of city government, and he believes his experience in state and local government will help support the board’s mission.
MAYOR
Incumbent Jodi MacPhail was the only candidate on the ballot, receiving 8,977 votes. This will be her second consecutive term as mayor.
In an August news release announcing her candidacy, MacPhail touted her achievements as creating a consistent and stable environment for staff, working with the City Council on key initiatives, working closely with the school department, and investing in local projects.

title: Troy Jackson wins Maine US Senate race over GOP Sen. Susan Collins in key Democratic victory
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Late Democratic entry Troy Jackson won Maine’s U.S. Senate seat early Wednesday, defeating longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins, taking advantage of President Donald Trump’s deep unpopularity to dislodge an incumbent who had survived tough challenges in the past.
“For every family doing everything they can and wondering when somebody is going to do something for them, you have gotten me into this and you’re going to have someone who is fighting for you in Washington, D.C.,” Jackson told the crowd at an election night party in Portland.
Jackson, 58, a fifth-generation logger and former president of the state Senate, had a little more than 100 days to sell himself to Maine voters after he replaced Graham Platner as the party’s nominee in July.
He won a hastily convened nominating convention and began barnstorming the state, focusing heavily on economic issues such as the high costs of housing and healthcare. As a former campaign surrogate of independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, he was known to many progressives in the state but lacked the widespread name recognition of Collins.
Collins, 73, was widely perceived as the most vulnerable Senate Republican this election year. She entered Election Day as the only Republican lawmaker in Congress from New England and was seeking her sixth term representing a state that has voted for the Democratic candidate for president since 1992.
“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I’m proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years,” Collins said in a statement after calling Jackson to concede.
Jackson took over the nomination during a time of crisis for Democrats
Jackson hails from rural Aroostook County, among the poorest in the state, where he went to work as a lumberjack at 19.
He first entered politics after leading a weeklong loggers’ blockade along Maine’s border with Quebec in the late 1990s protesting the hiring of Canadian loggers who were coming into Maine and driving down pay rates.
The standoff ended with Jackson being escorted away by police, an unsuccessful ending that spurred him to run for elected office. He served nearly 20 years in the state House, rising up the ranks to become the Senate’s top leader.
Jackson initially didn’t plan to run for Senate this year. Instead, he threw his hat in for the Democratic nomination for governor but lost.
Platner, an oyster farmer and political newcomer, had drawn huge crowds and enthusiasm but also faced a string of controversies. After he announced in July that he would withdraw from the Senate race, Jackson won a special nominating convention later that month.
It made for a rushed start to the campaign for Jackson. Since then, he has held events at churches, union halls and bars to tout issues such as workers’ rights and the cost of living.
At times, his campaign rhetoric is reminiscent of Sanders, who joined Jackson for rallies in October.
“In the end, if you work hard, you should be able to build a decent life,” Jackson said at a campaign event near Portland in September. “But that’s not the reality right now.”
He criticized Collins as not doing enough to stop Trump. Jackson noted she voted to advance Trump’s signature tax cut and budget legislation out of committee, before she was a “no” vote on its final passage.
“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said.
Jackson faced blowback over his temperament during the campaign, and Collins criticized him for telling her to “shut up” during a debate.
Collins attempted to woo voters on her independence
Collins was first elected in 1996 and has touted her independence from Trump and her party. She has said she didn’t vote for Trump in 2016, and she voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot.
In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president’s ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they “should never be elected to office again.”
When Vice President JD Vance made trips to Maine, Collins did not appear with him. Vance told the crowd at a May rally that he sometimes gets frustrated with the senator and wishes she were more partisan.
Collins has been a top target of Democrats before. Many pollsters predicted Collins would lose to former Maine House Speaker Sara Gideon in 2020. Collins won handily during a year that Democrats won the presidential race and both U.S. House seats in Maine.
During this year’s race, Collins touted her longevity in the Senate and her status as a key player in powerful committees and budgeting negotiations. She said those aspects of her service remain critically important for Mainers.
“It has been 92 years since a Maine senator was chair of the Senate appropriations committee, the most powerful committee in the Senate,” Collins told reporters. “When I took over last year, I realized I had a once-in-a-century opportunity to help the state of Maine and pursue national priorities as well.”
___
Kruesi reported from Providence, Rhode Island.

title: Supreme Court to hear dispute over death row inmate sentence
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S. Supreme Court is scheduled to hear a case Wednesday centering on a dispute over a Texas death row inmate’s sentence.
It came before the justices after the legal team for the inmate, Dexter Johnson, challenged his death sentence, under a claim of intellectual disability. And it was a claim that not brought up during his initial trial.
“What’s happened here is that in the last 10 to 20 years, the medical community’s understanding of intellectual disability has changed,” said Ethan Nutter, a lawyer who filed an amicus brief in the case, on behalf of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers.
Johnson was convicted of capital murder for the 2006 killing of 23-year-old Maria Aparece. He was scheduled to be executed in May 2019 but his sentence was stayed because of a federal court’s finding, after the challenge was raised.
“Under the current understanding, Mr. Johnson meets that definition of intellectual disability,” said Nutter. “And that’s important because the Supreme Court has said that it’s unconstitutional to execute someone who is intellectually disabled.”
Johnson’s litigators raised the intellectual disability claim just days before his scheduled execution because of the 2013 update to the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5). The update presented a change to the way clinicians view IQ.
“Only later did the DSM-5 displace the rigid IQ threshold, replacing it with a standard focused more on adaptive functioning deficits,” Johnson’s legal team wrote in a Supreme Court filing. “Under that framework, Mr. Johnson’s trial expert withdrew the premise that had previously foreclosed a disability diagnosis, and two additional experts concluded that Mr. Johnson is intellectually disabled.”
The Texas Department of Criminal Justice’s Correctional Institutions later asked the Supreme Court to review the Fifth Circuit’s finding for Johnson’s case, in February 2026.
In the department’s brief, it wrote that the lower court’s holding “erases the strict limits on claims based on new evidence.” It also wrote, “For the people of Texas in general and for the families of Johnson’s victims in particular, justice delayed is justice denied.”
In another amicus brief filed by Aparece’s father, Protasio Aparece, his legal team wrote, “Protasio has an interest in seeing justice carried out for his daughter, and in doing everything he can to ensure that no other family endures the decades of excessive delays in obtaining justice that he and his family have suffered.”
However, the question before the justices is not only about Johnson’s case, but also how strict federal courts should be when prisoners challenge their sentences.
Nutter said the court is deciding a specific procedural issue.
“The narrow issue in this case that the Supreme Court is actually deciding is whether the federal court can address this, what’s called a second or successive habeas petition,” Nutter said.
The court is expected to issue a decision in the case by June 2027.

title: This sake combines Japanese and Navajo culture together
text:
HOLBROOK, Ariz. (InvestigateTV) — Atsuo Sakurai and his wife, Heather, make award-winning sake at a shop just off Route 66 in Holbrook.
Sake is a traditional Japanese alcohol made from fermented rice. Its history spans thousands of years. Sakurai’s shop, Arizona Sake, makes the beverage in a 200-gallon vat.
Sakurai said people are often surprised to learn the sake comes from Holbrook, Arizona, on Route 66.
“Oh, yeah. Initially, nobody believed,” he said.
Sakurai is from Tokyo, about 6,000 miles from Holbrook. He worked in the sake industry there before moving to Arizona.
“Initially, I had a dream. Starting a business, establishing a business. Sake manufacturing somewhere in the world,” Sakurai said.
Heather Sakurai is from the Navajo Nation. The couple combine their cultures in the bottle. Sakurai said one of the sakes uses Navajo tea.
“Navajo tea, Navajo tea sake. This is Navajo tea itself, a plant,” he said.
At the shop, workers wash and heat rice in baskets and then put it in vats to ferment.
“When fermentation is done, we press the sake like mash,” Sakurai said.
The sake is squeezed out under pressure. Sakurai said it takes about three months to make one bottle from start to finish.
Sakurai’s sake has won competitions in Japan and around the globe. He makes traditional styles of sake. Some of his creations are sold only in Holbrook.
“The aroma is really beautiful. People describe it as pear or blueberry,” he said.
One taster said she could taste prickly pear in one of the sakes.
“Oh my God, I can really taste the prickly pear. This is about as Arizona as it gets,” the taster said.
Sakurai said the slow, hands-on process brings him peace in a world of AI and automation.
“That kind of business, industry, I want to save,” he said.
Technology threatens how some industries operate, much like the interstate did to some businesses along Route 66. Sakurai said he is confident the story he has written in Holbrook will endure.
Asked whether Arizona Sake will be around in 100 years, Sakurai said, “Hopefully.”

title: Mainers, test your well water
text:
My family is dealing with contaminated water — specifically uranium and arsenic in our well water. We tested the water eight years ago when we moved in but the levels of these chemicals have changed dramatically and now pose a serious health risk. We have no idea how long we have been drinking this poisonous water. Our two children have been drinking this water their whole lives. We’re in the midst of a lot of medical testing for all of us. Waiting for the results has been incredibly stressful.
I urge everyone on well water to test their water regularly. Google tells me that the levels of these chemicals can change due to many factors, including drought (we’ve experienced several drought seasons). Note: while our radon isn’t elevated, we should test for that too.
Unfortunately the solutions to treat these chemicals are incredibly expensive. I wish Maine had a program to help people who cannot afford to install these expensive water systems, we really should. This message is also for anyone who has influence over this type of thing, as much as for folks drinking well water.
I also ask that pediatricians tune into this issue. When they ask their patients about lead, seatbelts and smoke alarms, they should also remind families — especially those on well water — to test it periodically for contamination.
I hope this letter will prevent the type of scary and stressful situation we’re experiencing from happening to others. Take care out there.
Ashley Bahlkow
North Yarmouth

title: Democrat David Crowley defeats Trump ally to become Wisconsin’s first Black governor
text:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Democrat David Crowley defeated a Republican with close ties to President Donald Trump on Tuesday, rising from a childhood in one of the nation’s poorest neighborhoods to become the first Black person to lead the battleground state.
Crowley’s win over U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany marks the first time in Wisconsin’s 178-year history that Democrats will hold the governor’s office for more than eight consecutive years. He will replace Gov. Tony Evers, who decided to retire instead of seeking a third term.
Crowley told his supporters in his victory speech that he would be a governor for everyone, including those who didn’t vote for him.
“Wisconsin isn’t a red state or a blue state,” he said. “We never have been. In a state this close, nobody gets to govern alone.”
He promised to work with Democrats and Republicans on lowering costs in Wisconsin. Democrats were hoping to flip control of the Legislature for the first time in 16 years.
The victory blunts Republican efforts to claw back control of a state that Trump won in two of his three presidential campaigns. It also ensures that a Democrat will be leading Wisconsin during the next race for the White House, when the state will likely continue its role as a key battleground.
Crowley, 40, was born in the north side of Milwaukee in one of the country’s poorest neighborhoods, and his parents battled substance abuse and evictions. But Crowley turned to community organizing and politics, winning election to the Legislature at age 30. He served just over three years before being elected in 2020 as Milwaukee County executive.
His path to the governor’s office was tumultuous. He dropped out of the race when he appeared unlikely to win the Democratic nomination, only to rejoin at Evers’ urging. He defeated a democratic socialist in the August primary, then faced off with Tiffany, who received most of his financial support from just three billionaires.
Tiffany, who survived a small plane crash while campaigning, was weighed down by the president’s record-low approval numbers in Wisconsin, a state that Trump won twice.
Democrats were hoping for a trifecta — winning the governor’s office and flipping both legislative chambers. They have not had full control of Wisconsin state government since 2010.
U.S. GOVERNORS BALANCE OF POWER
An open governor’s race for the first time in 16 years
Wisconsin’s governor’s race was open for the first time in 16 years after Evers decided against seeking a third term.
The last open race for governor was in 2010, when Democratic incumbent Jim Doyle, similar to Evers, opted not to seek a third term. Republican Scott Walker won that year, and over the next eight years enacted a wide array of Republican priorities that dramatically scaled back union rights, slashed taxes and started requiring voters to show identification at the polls.
Evers, who normally doesn’t endorse in primaries, got behind Crowley in an effort to blunt the rising campaign of democratic socialist Francesca Hong. Crowley won by less than half a percentage point.
Wisconsin is used to close races.
Trump, who endorsed Tiffany, won Wisconsin in 2016 and 2024 and lost in 2020. Those three presidential elections are among five of the past seven in Wisconsin that have been decided by less than a percentage point.
In 2018, Evers defeated then-Gov. Scott Walker by 1.1 percentage points. Evers won reelection by 3.4 points in 2022, a landslide by Wisconsin standards.
Tiffany cast Crowley as pro-data center; Crowley ran on affordability
Tiffany tried to portray Crowley as an advocate for building data centers in Wisconsin, referring to him as “Data Center David Crowley.” Tiffany ran an ad that included a clip of Crowley saying Wisconsin could become the “AI and data hub not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe.”
But Tiffany also said positive things about data centers in the past. Crowley changed his position on data centers late in the campaign, coming out in favor of a moratorium in October. Tiffany did not call for a moratorium on construction.
Tiffany also tried to portray Crowley as weak on crime and said Crowley would increase taxes as governor to pay for his agenda, which included expanding healthcare and fully funding public schools.
Crowley hammered Tiffany on economic issues, saying his loyalty to Trump and support of the war in Iran was to blame for the high gas prices that were hurting Wisconsin residents, particularly farmers. Crowley also ran in support of overturning the 15-year-old state law known as Act 10 that effectively ended collective bargaining rights for most public workers.
Tiffany, 68, voted for that law when he was a member of the Legislature. Tiffany was elected to Congress in 2020, representing a mostly rural district after nine years in the Legislature.
Crowley also called for expanding Medicaid coverage, increasing funding for public schools and increasing access to child care.

title: Poverty among older Americans has risen five years in a row, data shows
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(InvestigateTV) — Poverty among older Americans has climbed for the fifth year in a row, according to new Census data, even as overall poverty went down.
Claire Casey, president of the AARP Foundation, said affordability is now a top concern for older adults.
“So it’s actually risen 20%, the rate of poverty for people over 65,” Casey said.
AARP Foundation’s new Economic Security Monitor found 70% of older households saw their expenses go up in three months.
Anthony Hamalainen, 67, of Marquette, Michigan, said older adults on fixed incomes are among those hit hardest.
“I mean, I’m sure there’s other people are struggling too, but the seniors are really hitting it really super bad because they live on a fixed income. Most of them do,” Hamalainen said.
Hamalainen owned a wireless installation company, but a fall from a roof in 2006 left him unable to work. When he was ready to return to work in his 50s, he struggled to find a job because of his disability and his age.
He began receiving Social Security after the accident, but medical bills and other expenses piled up. He gets by on just over $1,000 a month, plus $40 in SNAP benefits. He says it gets harder every year.
“I run out of money each month. I mean, it’s just ridiculous. It’s really hard for us to live,” Hamalainen said.
Casey offered this advice to older adults who are concerned about making it through right now.
“I would say don’t think about an age. Think about what you want in your life and what you can do and then seek out the resources that are out there to help you,” Casey said.
Hamalainen is now training with AARP to help other seniors find jobs.
AARP offers free resources for older adults who are struggling to pay bills. The group also recommends checking with local, state and federal programs that may be able to help.

title: Democrats reversed Donald Trump's inroads with Hispanic, Black and young voters
text:
WASHINGTON — Democratic candidates made up significant ground among key demographic groups in the 2026 midterms, according to The AP Voter Poll, reversing many of the gains President Donald Trump made with the traditional Democratic coalition in the 2024 presidential election.
The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of more than 100,000 voters in all 50 states, showed that young voters swung sharply left. Democratic candidates’ performance among voters under 30 this year far exceeded the support this group gave Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 AP VoteCast survey.
Hispanic voters, who shifted toward Trump in 2024 as well, moved toward Democrats this year, as did Black voters — particularly Black men. Many Moderates — who overwhelmingly said Congress was not doing enough to put checks and balances on the presidency — backed Democratic candidates nationally and were important for Democratic victories in several key Senate races.
And as most voters said inflation had caused them and their family at least “moderate” hardship over the past year, voters with a 2025 household income of less than $50,000 also shifted away from Republicans, compared to 2024.
Here is how five key demographic groups moved in the 2026 election, according to The AP Voter Poll:
Voters under 30 swung toward the Democratic Party
After relatively high support for Trump in the 2024 election, young voters snapped back toward the Democratic Party in this year’s midterms.
The AP Voter Poll showed about 7 in 10 voters under 30 nationally said they supported the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, while about 3 in 10 said they voted for the Republican. That was a dramatic shift from 2024, when the youngest voters were roughly split between Trump and Harris.
Most first-time midterm voters, who skew younger, also mostly supported the Democratic candidate.
Both young voters and first-time voters made up a fairly small share of voters. Only about 1 in 10 voters in the 2026 national electorate are under 30, for instance, which limited the impact of the shift.
But young voters’ displeasure with the country and its leadership was clear. About half of young voters said they were “angry” about the way things were going in the country today, compared with only about one-third of voters ages 65 and older. And about 6 in 10 voters under 30 said one reason for their vote for the U.S. House was to express opposition to Trump, compared to about half of voters ages 30-44, and about 4 in 10 voters ages 45 and older.
Young voters shifted toward the Democrats in each of the Senate races where the Democratic Party picked up a seat, including in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina.
Republicans lost ground with Hispanic voters, particularly in Texas
Republicans appeared to lose most — if not all — of Trump’s gains with Hispanic voters in 2024.
Only about one-third of Hispanic voters said they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House race, while roughly 4 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago. About 6 in 10 Hispanic voters nationally said they voted for the Democratic candidate in their local House race.
This shift was evident in the Texas Senate race that Democrat James Talarico won over Republican Ken Paxton. The AP Voter Poll showed roughly 6 in 10 Hispanic voters in the Texas Senate race supported Talarico, while only about 3 in 10 voted for Paxton. The group was more closely split between Trump and Harris in the 2024 presidential election, according to AP VoteCast.
And even in the Florida Senate race, where Republican Sen. Ashley Moody managed to narrowly win reelection, less than half of Hispanic voters supported Moody, while Trump definitively won this group two years earlier.
Republican inroads with Black voters appear fleeting
Black voters, particularly Black men, were another group where Trump’s 2024 gains didn’t stick.
Only about 1 in 10 Black men voters nationally backed the Republican candidate in their local U.S. House race, down from the roughly one-quarter who supported Trump in the last presidential election, according to AP VoteCast. About 9 in 10 Black voters supported the Democratic House candidate, up from the roughly 8 in 10 who cast their ballot for Harris.
These shifts were particularly important in some major races. Black men shifted significantly in the Georgia race for governor, where Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected as a governor. About 9 in 10 Black men voted for Bottoms, according to The AP Voter Poll. Only about three-quarters supported Harris in 2024.
About 9 in 10 Black women supported Bottoms, roughly the same share that supported Harris.
Republican Byron Donalds, who was elected Florida’s first Black governor, did not have the same level of success with Black voters. About one-quarter of Black men in the state voted for Donalds over Democrat David Jolly, while only about 1 in 10 Black women supported Donalds.
Democrats increased their support with moderate voters
Democrats increased their support with moderate voters, particularly in key Senate races where Democrats flipped Republican-held seats.
Roughly two-thirds of moderates supported the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race, an uptick from the approximately 6 in 10 moderate voters who backed Harris.
A large majority of moderate voters, about 8 in 10, said Congress was not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency, and a similarly high share said they had experienced at least a “moderate” hardship in the past year because of inflation.
Many Democratic candidates in key Senate upset races benefitted from significant moderate support. In Kansas, for instance, Democrat Adam Hamilton won about 7 in 10 moderate voters, a substantial rise from the roughly half that Harris won in 2024.
In Iowa, there was a similar pattern as Democrat Josh Turek won about two-thirds of moderates, up from about half for Harris.
And in North Carolina, Democrat Roy Cooper won about three-quarters of moderates, improving on the slimmer majority that backed Harris.
Amid concern about costs, lower income voters move toward Democrats
In a year when economic concerns drove many voters’ choices, the AP Voter Poll found lower-income voters shifted toward the Democrats.
More than half of voters with a 2025 household income under $50,000 voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race. These voters were about evenly split between Trump and Harris in 2024. About 3 in 10 U.S. voters nationally report having a family income that falls under $50,000 each year.
The survey suggests that these voters were more likely than voters with a higher income to say they were concerned about the cost of food and groceries, gas prices and utilities. About 6 in 10 voters with a household income under $50,000 said the cost of living was “crucial” to their vote, compared to about half of voters who earned $50,000 or more.
Story by Linley Sanders, Humera Lodhi and Amelia Thomson-Deveaux.

title: Democrats capture governorships in Texas, other GOP-controlled states in rebuke to Republicans
text:
U.S. GOVERNORS BALANCE OF POWER
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — Democrats scored victories in governor’s races in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia, riding a wave of voter discontent in Tuesday’s midterm elections to deliver a rebuke to President Donald Trump and GOP policymaking.
The wins put Democrats on their way to taking a majority of governorships for the first time in two decades, allowing them to put up a stronger defense against Trump’s second-term agenda.
They also landed a historic victory, as Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia — a presidential battleground state — made her the first Black woman to be elected governor in the U.S.
Democrats also won in Iowa, Ohio and Texas, all states where Republicans have controlled state government for years.
The number of states in play was surprisingly large — a reflection of Trump’s poor approval ratings dragging on his party, with Democrats rolling up victories in presidential battleground states, heavily populated states and states that Trump won easily in 2024.
In the weeks leading up to Election Day, Trump went to heavily Republican areas to headline rallies attended by GOP gubernatorial candidates looking for a boost.
All told, 36 states that are home to about 80% of the nation’s population were electing a governor Tuesday. In 19 states, the office was open. Heading into the elections, Democratic governors represented 60% of the nation’s population, but Republicans held 26 of the nation’s 50 governors’ offices.
Democrats last gained a majority of governorships in 2006, flipping six governors’ offices in the last midterm under a second-term Republican president. Republicans recaptured the majority four years later.
More states under Democratic leadership could mean more governors fighting — or ignoring — Trump’s agenda.
Trump has tested the power of states, clashing primarily with Democratic-led states over call-ups of National Guard troops, immigration operations, conditions on federal aid and efforts to assert federal control over election requirements, including restricting mail voting.
Democratic victories in Georgia, Texas, Iowa and Ohio
Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and onetime White House adviser to former President Joe Biden, overcame GOP attacks on her management of the city during the COVID-19 pandemic to defeat Rick Jackson, a billionaire who plunged more than $200 million of his own money into the race.
She accused him of getting rich off a broken healthcare system and profiting off pain.
Her victory breaks GOP control of state government in Georgia, as does Democrat Amy Acton’s victory in Ohio, in a campaign that made national headlines when Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, aired a widely criticized attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother.
Iowa Democrat Rob Sand defeated Republican Zach Lahn, while Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa beat third-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas, where no Democrat had been elected to statewide office since 1994.
Hinojosa was seen as a long shot after she emerged from a primary with a fraction of Abbott’s cash total. But as Republicans began to express misgivings over Abbott, fellow Latino politicians and politicos wrote to the Democratic Governors Association to request $10 million in campaign aid, saying Hinojosa had made it a close race.
The DGA gave $1 million — far less than it spent in Arizona, Georgia, Iowa, Michigan, Nevada, Ohio and Wisconsin — and Hinojosa won despite being badly outspent 5-to-1 on ads, according to AdImpact data.
Notably, Abbott skipped Trump’s rally in Texas, a sign of the president’s unpopularity.
More races were seen as the most competitive
Democrats also saw opportunities to pick up a governor’s office in Alaska, where the incumbent was term-limited, and in Nevada, where state Attorney General Aaron Ford was challenging Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo.
Like Georgia, Alaska hadn’t elected a Democratic governor since 1998.
Republicans’ best chance to capture an executive suite was in Kansas, a normally deep red state where Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly was term-limited.
Republicans hung onto control in Florida, where U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds defeated David Jolly, a former Republican congressman-turned-independent who ran as a Democrat in the nation’s third-most populous state.
Republicans also had an eye on Oregon, where Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek was trying to fend off a second challenge from Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan.
Contests are in big states and swing states, too
Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York won reelection, and Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former U.S. health and human services secretary, cruised to victory in California.
Control of the executive branch was on the line in the six swing states from the 2024 presidential election, and Democrats were making a bid to control all six: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection, while Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, won the governor’s job in Wisconsin, and Michigan’s secretary of state, Jocelyn Benson, won her state’s open governor’s office.
The winners could have substantial influence over election administration during the 2028 presidential election. That could be important, considering Trump’s interest in expanding federal control over elections.
Meanwhile, three Democratic governors who are considered possible presidential candidates in 2028 all won reelection: Wes Moore of Maryland, JB Pritzker of Illinois and Shapiro, of Pennsylvania.
Demonstrating a big margin of victory, fundraising prowess and the electoral strength to help other Democrats win sends a strong signal to donors and party activists, analysts say.
The 2026 election produced some firsts
In Texas, Hinojosa was elected to be the state’s first Latina governor, while Deb Haaland ‘s victory in New Mexico made her the first Native American woman elected to lead a state.
More states elected Black governors, as well. Eight Black major party gubernatorial nominees were on ballots. In the past 250 years, only three elected governors have been Black, including Moore. Victories by Bottoms, Crowley and Donalds ensured that voters would double that number in just one election.
Meanwhile, states were on course to possibly beat the record number of 14 female governors.
___
Follow Marc Levy at http://twitter.com/timelywriter

title: Midterm election results
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, breaking through in Republican strongholds.
Here are three things to know as counting continues.
1. Democrats capture the House and Senate
Democrats flipped seven Senate seats and dozens of Republican-held House districts, as of Wednesday morning. The Democrats victories extended into “red” states with surprising wins in Texas and South Carolina.
Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska were still considered “too close to call” on Wednesday.
The new Democratic majorities take office in January, giving President Trump’s opponents greater power to investigate the administration, challenge Trump’s legislative agenda and block his nominees.
More than 124 million ballots were cast, with counting still underway, according to the University of Florida Election Lab. That surpasses the previous midterm record of nearly 119 million ballots cast in 2018.
2. Trump distances himself from losses
Trump offered mixed messages as the results came in, congratulating Democrats while distancing himself from Republican defeats.
In an election-night interview with Fox News, he credited Democrats for working hard. In a separate phone interview with Politico, he argued that Republicans struggled to turn out his supporters because he was not on the ballot.
The president also posted an image of a red hat bearing the word “VETO,” highlighting his authority to reject legislation passed by a Democratic-controlled Congress.
But he also expressed a willingness to negotiate and work with Democrats, leaving room for potential agreements despite the coming partisan battles.
3. Leadership votes still lie ahead
Democrats must still choose who will lead their new majorities.
Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York currently lead their party in the Senate and House, respectively. Both need support from their Democratic colleagues to retain those roles.
Jeffries would also need to win a vote of the full House to become speaker when the new Congress convenes Jan. 3. If elected, he would become the first Black speaker in U.S. history.
Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has endorsed Jeffries, praising his leadership following the Democratic victory.
