title: Lions linebacker Jack Campbell says he has full movement in lower body after suffering neck injury
text:
ALLEN PARK, Mich. (AP) — Detroit Lions All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell said he has full movement in his lower body and is “continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body,” in his first comments since he was carted off the field on a backboard during a game against Minnesota.
“I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic,” Campbell said Wednesday in a statement released by the team. “I’m taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better.”
Campbell suffered a neck injury early in the fourth quarter of a 19-15 win over the Vikings on Sunday. He was alert when he was taken to the hospital, where he has been recovering since his injury.
Lions coach Dan Campbell said it was powerful that Jack Campbell updated his improving condition himself, shortly before the team’s previously scheduled news conferences with coaches and players.
“That’s good news. That’s positive news,” Dan Campbell said. “We’re all thankful for that.”
Jack Campbell was face down on the turf and not moving after hitting Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson. He was evaluated by medical personnel before being strapped to a board and carefully lifted onto the cart to a round of applause.
“I especially want to thank the athletic trainers and medical personnel who responded and cared for me on the field,” Jack Campbell said. “I know those were difficult moments, and I’m incredibly grateful for the professionalism, compassion, and care you showed me. The way you handled everything and looked after me when I needed it most is something I’ll never forget.”
The former Iowa star was drafted by the Lions with the 18th overall pick in 2023. Last season, he was an All-Pro selection after becoming the first NFL player in seven years to have 150-plus tackles and at least five sacks and three forced fumbles.
Jack Campbell’s condition has been closely followed since Sunday, a fact that he has felt.
“My family and I want to sincerely thank everyone for the overwhelming amount of love, prayers, and support we’ve received over the past few days,” he said. “It means more to us than words can express.”
The Lions (5-2) play at Miami (1-6) on Sunday.
“The best thing we can do is play the way he would want us to play and honor him that way,” Lions quarterback Jared Goff said.

title: Democrats pledge affordability reforms as they prepare to take control of Congress
text:
Democrats pledge affordability reforms as they prepare to take control of Congress
Democrats are preparing to take control of Congress in January after overwhelming victories in both the Senate and the House of Representatives.
"Against all odds, we Democrats have won the Senate. And we have five words for the American people: relief is on the way," said Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.
Until then, Republicans will remain in control of both chambers during a period known as a lame-duck session.
Lame duck sessions
A lame-duck session is the period of time when Congress is in session after a November election and before the new Congress begins the following January.
Political analysts expect the lame-duck session will remain largely inactive, and Democrats are expected to filibuster or stall any last-minute Republican bills.
Despite that, there are significant priorities that need to be addressed before the year ends, including government funding, Farm Bill provisions, and some health care programs through Veterans' Affairs. Those items are set to lapse on Dec. 11.
Party agendas
Democrats now face a dilemma: whether to focus their political capital on prioritizing their legislative agenda or impeachment efforts.
Party leaders have pledged to address affordability issues on day one of the 120th Congress. Democrats have also promised to reverse Medicaid cuts, restore Affordable Care Act tax credits, repeal President Donald Trump's tariffs, and end the ongoing conflict in Iran.
"We now have a responsibility to govern on affordability, to lower the high cost of all the things, the high cost of groceries, the high cost of housing, the high cost of gas," said House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.
Other Democrats have suggested filing motions to impeach Trump. Political analysts say the Senate lacks the two-thirds majority needed to convict him.
Tuesday night's overwhelming rejection of the Republican agenda may also influence GOP lawmakers' actions.
"There are an awful lot of Republicans in Congress who are going to take this as a rebuke, and who are going to move much more cautiously as a result," said Marc Sandalow, political analyst.
Trump said Wednesday that he has spoken with Democrats, but did not specify who. The president said he is willing to work with the Democrats provided they do not try to pass any "insane" legislation.

title: US Marshals arrest man in Rockland wanted in NH
text:
Federal marshals arrested Andrew D. Secord, 24, in Rockland on Tuesday on a charge of failing to appear in court.
Secord had been wanted in New Hampshire on charges of aggravated felonious sexual assault, second-degree assault, two counts of criminal threatening and domestic violence assault, according to a press release from the U.S. Marshals Service.
On Oct. 20, 2026, investigators with the U.S. Marshals Service in New Hampshire received an arrest warrant for Secord.
Investigators received information suggesting Secord had fled New Hampshire and might be staying in Rockland. They alerted marshals in Maine.
Federal agents, working with Rockland police, found Secord and apprehended him.
He has been charged as a fugitive from justice and is awaiting extradition back to New Hampshire.

title: Federal judge dismisses case against Russian-born scientist accused of smuggling frog embryos
text:
BOSTON (AP) — A federal judge on Wednesday granted a government motion to dismiss all charges against a Russian-born scientist who was accused of smuggling frog embryos into the United States.
Kseniia Petrova, who was conducting cancer research for Harvard Medical School, was indicted last year on one count of concealment of a material fact, one count of false statement and one count of smuggling goods into the United States. She had been charged with the smuggling before that.
She told The Associated Press in an interview that she did not realize the items needed to be declared and was not trying to sneak anything into the country.
The case began to fall apart in April, after a federal judge ruled a customs officer improperly canceled Petrova’s visa over the incident. Petrova had been briefly detained by immigration officials and feared being deported to Russia and imprisoned there.
Then, Petrova’s lawyers filed a motion to dismiss, arguing the government was selectively and vindictively prosecuting her and that was unconstitutional. They argued that the government only filed criminal charges after it looked like she would win her immigration case. They also argued it was rare for anyone to be charged criminally for what Petrova did.
Federal District Judge Leo Sorokin, who was nominated by former President Barack Obama, dismissed all the charges against Petrova on Wednesday without a hearing.
“The DOJ never should have brought this highly unusual “smuggling” prosecution against Kseniia Petrova, a talented scientist at Harvard,” one of Petrova’s attorneys Daniel Marx said in a statement. “Ms. Petrova only sought to advance medical research into aging that could benefit everyone, and her handling of scientific samples — inert, non-living, non-toxic, frog embryos — never posed any danger to anyone.”
In early 2025, Petrova was returning from a vacation in France, where she had stopped at a lab specializing in splicing superfine sections of frog embryos and obtained a package of samples for research. She was questioned about the samples while passing through a customs checkpoint at Boston Logan International Airport.
Petrova was “lawfully detained after lying to federal officers about carrying substances into the country,” a spokesperson for Department of Homeland Security said earlier this year. The Trump administration was committed to “restoring the rule of law and common sense to our immigration system,” the statement said. The department includes Customs and Border Protection.
But on Tuesday night, U.S. Attorney Leah Foley filed a motion to dismiss the case “based on developments in this case and an assessment of the office’s priorities and resources.”
“At this stage, the resource costs of continuing this prosecution outweigh the public interest in its resolution,” she wrote, adding that the “defendant’s claims of vindictive and selective prosecution are meritless.”
Among the reasons for the dismissal, Foley wrote, was an April court ruling which granted the “defendant broad discovery in support of a selective prosecution” as well as documents related to comparable cases and also Customs and Border Protection policies and procedures.
“The government must supply the defendant with information pertaining to any number of passenger encounters involving undeclared items that could be considered comparable, without regard for the manner in which those items were carried, the presence or absence of planning, or the strength of the evidence of a passenger’s fraudulent intent,” Foley wrote.

title: Conservative slate takes all 3 open Bangor City Council seats
text:
The conservative slate for Bangor City Council — Anthony Cote, Terry Dinkins and Joseph Pratt — swept all three open seats on Tuesday, beating out nine other contenders in the city’s largest candidate pool in at least four decades.
The outcome is a sign that an uptick in local organizing on the right, backed by tens of thousands in spending on ads, paid off in a city that typically votes blue, and on a midterms night where Democrats have won nearly all the big-ticket federal races in Maine and across the country.
Cote was the most popular candidate, with 4,758 votes, and Dinkins and Pratt earned 4,615 and 4,099 votes, respectively.
Cote and Pratt are Republicans, while Dinkins is unenrolled in a political party. All three were endorsed by the Concerned Citizens of Bangor PAC, which formed this year and spent more than $15,000 on the election.
The nine unsuccessful candidates, in order of most to least votes received, were Adam Baker 3,331, Joe Leonard 3,165, Andrei Yermakov 3,102, Jennifer McGinley Maskala 1,833, James Gallagher 1,798, Michael Furrow 1,712, Katherine Devine 1,658, John King 1,640, and Dawson Nevells 1,485.
The new councilors will be sworn in Monday, Nov. 9, at 10 a.m. They will replace Leonard as well as outgoing councilors Susan Deane and Carolyn Fish.
Cote owns a construction business and has described himself as a centrist. He said his top priority as a councilor would be to make Bangor more business-friendly. He also wants to cut the city budget and further restrict the number of needles someone can get when visiting a syringe exchange program due to his belief that those programs enable addiction.
Cote was excited to hear the news, and also “a little surprised,” but said he thinks the results are a sign that residents feel they haven’t been listened to by the current council. There were “a lot of good candidates,” Cote said, but he thinks the Concerned Citizens of Bangor’s organizing helped voters unite behind three candidates.
Dinkins is the pastor of the Mansion Church on Center Street, the chaplain at the Penobscot County Jail and a branch manager for an armored car company. He’s run a winter warming center out of his church since 2020 and named reducing homelessness and cutting down on drugs and needles as priorities. He’d like Bangor to focus on improving mental health care and drastically reducing the number of needles distributed in the city. He’s drawn criticism in local circles online for counter-protests his church has held at LGBTQ+ pride events in the past.
“I think the citizens of Bangor want a change,” Dinkins said shortly after results came in. “The voters spoke, and we’re gonna do our best to make that change.”
Pratt oversees the wealth management group at Bar Harbor Bank and Trust and serves on the boards of several nonprofits, including the Bangor Public Library. He said his top priority would be to restore civility and decorum to the council. He also wants to expand the tax base to ease the burden on property owners. He’s opposed to harm reduction programs like syringe services and has said he believes those programs perpetuate drug abuse.
Pratt was a little surprised by the sweep as well, saying he expected one of the more liberal candidates to make the cut. The race’s results, and the large candidate field this year, were a sign to him that residents were unhappy with the direction in which the city has been going, he said.
Several Republican voters at Bangor’s polling place on Tuesday told the Bangor Daily News they thought those three candidates were the best choice for Bangor.
Jen Potter, a Bangor resident and nurse, said she was looking for local candidates who felt strongly about cleaning up the city, pointing to public drug use in particular. “I literally can look out my window and see people shooting up,” she said.
Electrician Kevin Peary saw his vote for the three as a vote for the council to “curve and come back to center” after skewing too far to the left. Peary said he was concerned about the housing market, the economy and drug use locally and wanted to see city leaders give people “a hand up rather than a hand out.”
The three winning candidates were by far the top fundraisers in the race. Dinkins raised nearly $15,000 by the most recent campaign finance filing deadline, while Cote and Pratt collected about $8,000 and $5,000 in campaign donations, respectively. The trio raised more than double the nine other candidates combined.
The PAC supporting them also spent more than $15,000 to support its preferred candidates, mostly via social media advertising. The group got most of its money from real estate investors and companies in the Bangor area and hired a conservative social media strategist who also worked for Republican Bobby Charles’s gubernatorial campaign.
All three winners said they thought the group’s work played some role in the decisive victory.
Separately, the wealthy tech entrepreneur and Cape Elizabeth Republican Jonathan Bush spent tens of thousands through his nonprofit, Maine for Keeps, on ads targeting voters in Bangor, Lewiston and Waterville this election cycle, although those ads didn’t name specific candidates.
On the left, the progressive, labor-aligned nonprofit Food and Medicine rallied about Leonard, Baker and Yermakov, although the group only spent about $300 on municipal candidates this year. The nonprofit took money this year from a national Democrat-aligned PAC and also supported candidates for offices further up on the ballot, including U.S. Senate and governor.
Katie Brydon, Emily Tilton and Jamie Beck were elected to the school committee with 7,593, 7,233 and 7,147 votes, respectively, after running unopposed for three open seats.

title: Florida sheriff says 2 dead, including suspect, as witnesses report shooting at Tampa office complex
text:
TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — A gunman plowed a car into a courtyard on Citibank’s sprawling Tampa business campus on Wednesday and opened fire with a rifle, killing a woman before a security guard fatally shot him, authorities said.
The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office did not give a motive for the shooting or say whether the gunman and his lone victim knew each other.
The attack sent workers scrambling as the suspect crashed his car among outdoor tables where people were eating lunch, then started shooting, said Chief Deputy Frank Losat of the sheriff’s office. He said 3,200 people were on the campus at work during the attack.
The gunman fatally shot the woman before a security guard confronted him in a cafeteria, Losat said. The guard and the gunman exchanged fire, and the guard killed him, Losat said.
“Was there a potential for further violence? Absolutely,” Losat told a news conference. ”So kudos to that security guard.”
The names of the gunman and the woman killed were not immediately released.
Losat said four other people were taken to a hospital with non-life-threatening injuries. He didn’t know whether any of them had been shot or struck by the gunman’s vehicle.
Citibank VP heard ‘incredible clatter’ of gunfire, then screaming
David Dzien, a Citibank vice president, told The Associated Press he was returning to work after lunch when he saw the shooter’s sedan crash through a fence about 150 yards (137 meters) away from him, followed by an “incredible clatter” that he later realized was gunfire.
People near the crashed car suddenly dispersed and others began to scream, Dzien said, as he sprinted back into the building and evacuated through a fire escape.
“I can still hear the particular type of scream,” he said, “and I’m still trying to process it, frankly.”
The attack occurred on a day when “VIPs” who don’t normally work at the complex were present for a “quarterly review,” Dzien said.
More than 360 deputies began arriving immediately
Sheriff’s deputies began arriving at the campus within a minute of the first 911 call, Losat said. The response was huge, with more than 360 deputies — many in tactical gear — rushing to the scene.
Those deputies spent 2 1/2 hours searching and clearing the building where the shootings occurred plus adjacent office buildings, Losat said.
Radio traffic on Broadcastify.com from responding officers described an exhaustive floor-by-floor search as people were found sheltering in locked rooms and closets, then carefully escorted from the buildings and parking garage.
Nearby hotel gave shelter to hundreds of fleeing workers
Employees at the Sheraton Tampa Brandon Hotel, a few hundred feet from the Citibank complex, were having a monthly employee luncheon in the hotel’s ballroom when they saw a massive flood of police vehicles headed toward the campus.
General Manager Matt Chauvin said Citibank employees ran over and told the front desk there was an active shooter.
“We at first locked the doors and, you know, went into lockdown, but the employees kept coming over,” Chauvin said.
Chauvin estimated the hotel sheltered about 300 Citibank workers. Hotel staff gave them water and lunch, and let some go into hotel rooms “to sort of decompress or make phone calls.”
“Luckily we were far enough away that they were all safe,” he said.
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. AP journalists Cybele Mayes-Osterman in Chicago, R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this story.

title: Trump-backed Republican redistricting sought a midterm edge. It didn’t work
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — At the urging of President Donald Trump, Republicans in eight states redrew the boundaries of dozens of congressional districts over the past year while angling for an edge that could help them hold onto a slim House majority in a tough midterm election.
Ultimately, it didn’t work.
Republicans lost most of the Democratic-held seats they had targeted to flip, lost others they had banked on retaining and got swept out of power by a Democratic surge fueled by voter dissatisfaction with Trump, the economy and the war with Iran.
The Republican redistricting plan fell flat in Alabama, Florida and Texas. It got scuttled by courts in Missouri and then firmly defeated by its voters Tuesday. And it got offset in California, where a retaliatory Democratic redistricting flipped all five of the Republican-held seats it targeted.
“This is a catastrophic rebuke of Donald Trump’s failed effort to gerrymander the country into oblivion to save the U.S. House of Representatives for himself,” John Bisognano, president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said Wednesday.
New districts presumed continuing support for Trump
Congressional voting districts typically are redrawn after a census at the start of each decade to account for population changes. But Trump spurred an unusual mid-decade redistricting battle last year when he urged Texas Republicans to reshape U.S. House districts to give the GOP a shot at winning five additional seats in the midterm election.
A cascade of redistricting followed, spurred along in the South by a Supreme Court ruling that weakened federal Voting Rights Act protections for majority Black districts. Republicans hoped their redistricting could net as many as four more seats in Florida, two in Ohio and one each in Alabama, Louisiana, North Carolina and Tennessee.
In all but one of those revamped districts, Trump would have carried over 54% of the vote had they been in place for the 2024 election, according to Associated Press estimates.
“In normal times, that sort of district is relatively safe,” said Justin Levitt, a professor at the Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who runs the “All About Redistricting” website.
But the presumed Republican districts got undercut by shifting viewpoints of Trump. The AP Voter Poll found about 6 in 10 disapprove of how Trump is handling the presidency. Views of Trump’s priorities also were mostly negative.
“If we look across the country, that entire mid-decade redistricting gambit was a complete bust for Republicans,” said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston.
Redistricting fell flat in the Rio Grande Valley
In Texas, Republicans won just one of the five seats they had targeted to flip. But Democrats flipped two Republican-held districts, putting the GOP at a net loss.
Republicans reconfigured three heavily Latino districts in the Rio Grande Valley, which had shifted toward Trump in 2024, to try to boost their chances of unseating Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez. But both won reelection Tuesday. And Democrats instead unseated Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, whose district is sandwiched between theirs.
Though De La Cruz’s new district retained the same percentage of Trump-inclined voters as the 2024 version, about 3 in 5 voting-age residents were new — making it harder for her to compete against Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido, a well-known Latin Grammy award winner.
The AP Voter Poll indicates a substantial shift in Hispanics moving away from Republicans compared with Trump’s victory just two years ago. Nationally about one-third of Hispanics say they backed the Republican in their local U.S. House race, while roughly 4 in 10 voted for Trump two years ago.
The new Texas districts were drawn by Adam Kincaid, executive director of the National Republican Redistricting Trust.
“Trying to pick up five seats in Texas, without putting anything else in serious jeopardy, it was a Herculean task,” Kincaid said Wednesday. He added: “It required the trends that we had been seeing over the past several years to continue, and that did not happen.”
Had Republicans not redrawn the Texas districts, however, they likely would have lost even more seats, Kincaid said.
Democrats retained seats in Florida and Alabama
Republicans in Florida tried to tilt four more House seats to the GOP in Trump’s adopted home state. Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz was among their targets, but he decided to run anyway in one of the redrawn districts. He won reelection Tuesday.
“I’ve worked across the aisle. I’ve delivered results for my community, and they spent $26 million trying to beat me,” Moskowitz said after his victory in Florida’s 25th Congressional District. “They lit that money on fire tonight.”
He said voters in his new district, like those nationwide, were most concerned about the economy and their ability to afford a good quality of life. But he said that redistricting angered voters, too.
After redistricting, about two-thirds of voting-age residents were new to the district represented by Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor. But she also won reelection. Democrat Pia Dandiya won yet another district -- an open seat in southern Florida — that Republicans had reshaped for an advantage.
In Alabama, a Supreme Court ruling allowed the Republican-led Legislature to revert to what the GOP considered to be a friendlier map. But Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures won reelection anyway, defying Republicans’ plans.
North Carolina redistricting led to costly and close races
Republicans redrew two congressional districts in eastern North Carolina with a goal of unseating Democratic Rep. Don Davis in the 1st Congressional District, which has sent a Black member to Congress for more than 30 years. They made Davis’ district a bit more Republican by bringing in thousands of voters from the 3rd Congressional District, held by Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. In exchange, they reassigned thousands of voters in Democratic-leaning areas to Murphy’s district.
The ensuing advertising battle for Davis’ seat cost well over $50 million, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, ranking among the most expensive House races nationally.
Davis held a slight lead Wednesday, and the race between Murphy and Democratic challenger Raymond Smith was particularly close.
More redistricting is likely ahead of the 2028 elections
What started as a Republican redistricting effort could become a Democratic redistricting movement ahead of the presidential election.
Maryland voters on Tuesday approved a constitutional amendment that will make it easier for the state’s Democratic-led General Assembly to redraw districts to the party’s advantage. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, have touted it as a way to “stop Trump.”
Democrats who made gains in numerous state legislatures Tuesday also could use that power for redistricting — most notably in Wisconsin, where districts were tilted toward Republicans. And Democratic lawmakers in New York already have taken an initial step toward congressional redistricting before the 2028 elections.
But the recent midterm redistricting revealed it can be difficult to anticipate voter behavior when trying to gerrymander districts for partisan advantage. That could particularly be the case for the next presidential election, which would be the first in a dozen years without Trump’s name atop the ballot, making it hard to know how his supporters would realign behind new candidates.
The midterm election “shows districts aren’t destiny – that if voters actually show up, they can overcome district lines,” Levitt said.

title: Aging Untold: These are the skin cancer warning signs you may overlook as you age
text:
(Aging Untold) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we highlight the easily overlooked warning signs of skin cancer and discuss what to ask during a dermatology exam.
Then, we explore the emotional weight of caregiving promises, examining how commitments made in love can lead to guilt when care needs change.
Finally, we visit a retired Vermont couple who turned their family barn into a bustling bakery, finding a sweet new purpose in their second act.
Skin cancer can appear in ways you might not expect, and in places you might not check.
Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said some of the warning signs that people might overlook include sores that don’t heal or moles that bleed easily.
And while people often are told to check areas that are exposed to the sun, Rogers warns that skin cancer can show up elsewhere.
For aging expert Amy O’Rourke, it was on her scalp. She is sharing her story.
Promising someone you are caring for that you will never put them in a home or that they can always live with you might come from love.
But those promises are often made before families have talked through what caregiving could involve, and feelings of guilt can come when care needs change over time.
The Aging Untold experts are sharing tips on how to navigate these difficult conversations and what caregivers can say instead.
Making a 60-mile drive to a farm call is not unusual for Dr. Rachel Miner, a mixed-animal veterinarian in Kansas. From families’ dogs and cats to herds of cattle, she treats animals of all kinds.
But veterinarians like Dr. Miner are becoming increasingly rare.
The doctors who protect the nation’s livestock and, by extension, its food supply, are a dwindling force, creating a critical gap in the first line of defense against disease and food insecurity.
Top of the Mountain Farm and Bakery just might be the most remote bakery in Vermont.
George Peak and Colleen Willette run it in a converted barn off a long dirt road surrounded by state forest.
From this little slice of heaven, they create homemade whoopie pies made with local maple syrup and “a lot of love,” along with other treats.

title: Vassalboro voting results (November 2026)
text:
Vassalboro voters turned down two of the five articles on their Nov. 3 local ballot, the two intended to help fund revitalization of the town office staff.
The first rejected article asked approval to use up to $20,000 from the town’s unassigned fund balance for costs associated with hiring a new town manager, from seeking the right person to “salary adjustments necessary to meet current market conditions.”
The article was supported by 1,063 voters, opposed by 1,223.
The other defeated article asked for up to $30,000 from unassigned fund balance for options to provide financial services for the town. Listed options were paying a new bookkeeper more generously; contracting for outside “accounting support services”; or “hiring administrative support staff to assist with financial and human resources functions.”
This article was supported by 1,027 voters and opposed by 1,150.
The three articles approved authorize up to $8,000 from the unassigned fund balance to pay the town’s auditor to provide necessary information to finish the 2024-2025 audit; authorize the select board to transfer funds between accounts to avoid overdrafts; and accept a new Budget Committee Ordinance.
The select board authorization, a standard article that was accidentally omitted from the June town meeting warrant, was most popular: 1,504 in favor, 633 opposed.
The Budget Committee Ordinance was favored by 1,441 voters, opposed by 627. The vote to pay the auditor was 1,295 in favor to 887 opposed.
On the state ballot, Vassalboro voters favored Republican candidates, not by wide margins. They supported Susan Collins over Troy Jackson for the United States Senate by 386 votes, out of 2,266 ballots cast in that race.
They favored Robert Charles over Hannah Pingree for Governor of Maine by 141 votes; and Ronald Russell over Chellie Pingree for the U. S. House of Representatives by 94 votes.
For State Senate District 15, Vassalboro voters favored Republican Kati McCormick over Democrat Amanda Ann Heath by 174 votes. For House District 61, Republican Alicia Carol Collins had a 310-vote margin over Democrat Robin G. Crawley.

title: CVS to split into two companies in major breakup of its $117 billion healthcare empire
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
CVS to split into two companies in major breakup of its $117 billion healthcare empire
CVS Health said Wednesday it is splitting into two companies, marking one of the largest shakeups in the healthcare industry. It’s a major reversal of the mergers that brought together the nation’s largest drugstore retailer along with health insurance giant Aetna and pharmacy benefit manager Caremark.
The breakup unwinds a strategy that began in 2007, when CVS merged with Caremark, which handles prescription benefits available to people with health insurance. In 2018, CVS acquired Aetna for $69 billion.
“We’re basically taking what I believe is one great company and making it two,” said CEO David Joyner in a statement.
Shares of CVS Health, which had been up about 15% so far this year, fell by 2% in premarket trading after initially ticking up. Shareholders will get shares of both companies in a tax-free transaction expected to close in early 2028, according to the company.
CVS also reported higher third-quarter earnings and revenue Wednesday, due primarily to better results from its Health Care Benefits segment. The company also raised its earnings guidance for the rest of this year.
CVS has 9,000 locations across the United States, 800 of which operate “MinuteClinics” staffed by nurse practitioners and physician assistants.

title: Ashland residents support police but still want lower taxes
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ashland residents packed a public hearing Wednesday to debate whether or not to close the town’s police department.
Nearly 200 people attended the session, a precursor to a Thursday night town vote.
The possibility of closing the department arose during an Oct 19 Town Council meeting because of residents’ concerns about property taxes.
If the vote to close should pass, Ashland would be the sixth rural police force Maine has lost in the last six years — three of those in Aroostook County — due to money and staffing problems. It would leave the region with six municipal police departments and add another town to the jurisdiction of state troopers and sheriff’s deputies.
Speakers overwhelmingly favored keeping the department, but some hoped for a compromise to lower taxes.
“Ashland used to be a boom town. It’s not that way anymore,” Boyd Tibbetts said. “It’s like a retirement community. It’s getting tough to pay my taxes and other bills and the cost of living has gone sky high. Yet I realize we have to have a police department.”
Numerous residents said they chose to come to Ashland because it’s a small, safe community. Several said drug crime has decreased during Montpetit’s tenure.
“We have worked with the Ashland Police Department and our crime has gone down tremendously,” said Brenda Clark of nearby Garfield, which contracts with Ashland for police services. “Crime has calmed down. Elderly people feel safer. That’s what we need. If we give up our police department, we’re going to be one hurting unit.”
Town Council Chairperson Sherri Calhoun served as moderator. Ashland Councilors Tyler Michaud, Kevin Robinson, Sharon Everett and Tom Raymond formed a panel, which also included Maine State Police Lt. Brian Harris, Aroostook County Sheriff Peter Johnson and Ashland Police Chief Michael Montpetit.
Should sheriffs and state police take over services, response time averages 30 minutes, Harris and Johnson said. Both forces are understaffed and can’t give the attention a local police department can, including checking on elderly residents or being near schools, Harris said.
“That’s the things you’re going to lose. You’re not going to be able to call Mike at 11 p.m.,” he said. “Nothing against us, it’s just that we are spread thin.”
Tom Wood asked if, should the town vote to keep the department, the council would be willing to create a steering committee to examine other ways to cut the budget. Councilors said they would consider such a committee.
“We see the work the police department does and recognize that a town vote to disband the department is likely to have a negative impact on the community,” Council Chairperson Sherri Calhoun said at the hearing. “This is a question about taxes and sustainability of services as our population decreases.”
Residents will vote at 7 p.m. Thursday, also at the recreation center, on whether they want to continue funding the police.

title: Republican redistricting failed to flip most targeted districts
text:
Republican redistricting failed to flip most targeted districts
Many of the districts targeted in mid-decade redistricting by Republicans failed to flip parties.
So far, 10 of the 15 districts targeted by Republicans in seven states have kept a Democrat in the seat. Republicans have picked up one seat, while Democrats have picked up six House seats as a result of redistricting.
Democrats ended up with six seats targeted when districts were redrawn — five in California as a result of Republican efforts in Texas and one more in Utah. Redistricting in Utah was court-ordered after state judges ruled that state Republicans violated anti-gerrymandering laws.
Now, all six of those were flipped.
Republicans have failed to flip 10 of their targeted seats and still have more pending in Tennessee, North Carolina, Louisiana and Florida. One seat was flipped by Republicans in Texas.
Use the map below to see how the results of races for the House of Representatives were called in districts that were targeted during redistricting.
What is redistricting?
Redistricting is the process of redrawing congressional district boundaries every 10 years, which occurs after population counts come out following the decennial census.
Most recently, the regular redistricting process for states occurred after the 2020 decennial census. But ever since, nine states have new congressional districts for the 2026 midterm elections. The process has played out for more than a year now, reassigning millions of people to new districts.
Both Democrats and Republicans targeted specific districts, starting with the five targeted in Texas when President Donald Trump asked the state to redraw boundaries. California followed in response, redrawing boundaries in favor of Democrats to target five districts.
Nine states are using new congressional district boundaries for the 2026 midterm election. Fifteen districts were redrawn potentially favoring Republicans, and six districts were redrawn to favor Democrats, adding up to a net of nine districts favoring Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives.
Only two other states have voluntarily redrawn districts to give a party advantage between census cycles since 1970, according to Pew Research Center.
How many people have new districts?
More than 34 million people were assigned to new districts, according to an analysis from Protect Democracy. That's about 1 in every 10 Americans.
Utah has the highest share of people reassigned districts, at more than 69% of voters.
Utah's 1st Congressional District is currently held by a Republican representative, but the district is rated by The Cook Political Report as shifting from solid Republican to solid Democrat.
In other states, including Texas, Louisiana, Tennessee and Florida, roughly one-third of voters were reassigned districts.

title: FIRST ALERT WEATHER: Rain Continues Tonight, with More Substantial Rainfall Possible Heading into the Weekend
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Good evening everyone and happy Tuesday. It’s certainly been a bit of a gloomy Election Day across Aroostook County, with cloudy skies and rain showers working their way across the region throughout the day today. The good news is that this is exactly the kind of weather we’ve been needing, as our ongoing drought conditions have continued to worsen over the last several weeks. Rain is expected to continue overnight tonight into tomorrow morning, before we get a bit of a break from the wet weather. Temperatures are also expected to warm considerably over the next couple of days, with highs Thursday potentially reaching the upper 60s for some locations.
Rain showers will continue across much of Aroostook County throughout the overnight hours tonight, with periods of steadier rainfall expected as a warm front gradually works its way northward through the region. Temperatures won’t be particularly cold tonight, with most locations expected to remain in the upper 30s to lower 40s. Caribou, Presque Isle and Houlton are all expected to see low temperatures around 39 degrees, while some of our western and southern locations could remain in the lower to mid 40s. Southeasterly winds around 5 to 10 MPH will also help introduce some warmer air into the region overnight. I think some of our more substantial rainfall from this first round will occur during the overnight hours, particularly across northern portions of Aroostook County.
Rain is expected to continue into Wednesday morning, but the good news is that we should begin to see showers gradually tapering off as we work our way through the day. I think locations further south will have the best opportunity to see the rain come to an end earlier in the morning, while northern and northeastern portions of Aroostook County could continue to see showers into the early afternoon hours. The exact timing will depend on how quickly our warm front can push northward through the region. Behind that front, temperatures will begin to climb considerably compared to what we’ve been experiencing today. Highs Wednesday are expected to reach the upper 50s to lower 60s for most locations, with Caribou around 59 degrees, Presque Isle near 60 degrees and Houlton closer to 62 degrees. Some of our southern and western locations could even reach the mid 60s.
The latest rainfall potential map from the Weather Prediction Center is certainly a welcome sight given just how dry conditions have been across northern Maine. Widespread measurable rainfall is finally expected across much of Aroostook County, with some of the greatest amounts from this first round of rain occurring across northern portions of the region. The National Weather Service in Caribou is now forecasting rainfall totals approaching an inch across portions of northern Maine through Wednesday, with lesser amounts expected the further south you travel. While an inch of rain isn’t going to eliminate the significant rainfall deficit we’ve accumulated over the last several months, I do think it’s enough to provide at least some limited drought relief, especially for our northern communities. What I’m particularly encouraged by is that this won’t be our only opportunity for rain over the next several days. The rainfall potential map only extends through Friday, meaning it doesn’t even account for the potentially more substantial rainfall we’re watching for the upcoming weekend.
Thursday looks to feature another significant jump in temperatures across the region, although I wouldn’t expect to see a particularly sunny day. Mostly cloudy skies are expected for much of the day, with some rain showers potentially returning during the afternoon hours, especially across northern and western portions of Aroostook County. Despite the cloud coverage, temperatures will have no problem climbing well above average for this time of year. Highs Thursday are expected to reach the mid to upper 60s, with Presque Isle around 66 degrees, Caribou near 64 degrees and Houlton potentially reaching 68 degrees. That’s nearly 20 degrees above the average high temperature in Caribou for this time of year! Southerly winds will be responsible for helping bring that warmer air into the region, although I don’t expect particularly strong winds during the day. For more details on what to expect through the remainder of the work week and our increasing rainfall chances heading into the weekend, make sure to check out my First Alert Video Forecast attached to this article. Have a great evening!

title: MDI voters reject long-discussed plan to reorganize school system
text:
A plan to restructure the Mount Desert Island region’s public school system that’s been under discussion for years failed in multiple member towns Tuesday.
AOS 91 includes Bar Harbor, Mount Desert, Southwest Harbor, Tremont, Trenton and the offshore islands of the Cranberry Isles, Frenchboro and Swan’s Island. If voters had approved the new structure, it would have become a more conventional, centrally organized school district with one board — a regional school unit, or RSU.
Bar Harbor, Mount Desert, Southwest Harbor and Tremont all voted against the plan, according to results collected by the Mount Desert Islander newspaper.
“The vote showed a need for continued conversation,” said Superintendent Michael Zboray, who was surprised by what he called tight margins showing some support for the plan.
Maine towns generally adopted AOS systems, or alternative organizational structures, in an effort to retain local control over their schools while following then-Gov. John Baldacci’s 2007 school consolidation law. An AOS includes multiple committees, boards or even smaller administrative units governing their local schools, plus a larger board.
Almost all of them have since split apart, reorganized or considered doing so, often seeking more efficiency than the administrative load of numerous budgets and duplicated work in business offices. Only eight AOS systems remain, according to the Maine School Management Association.
That operational redundancy was a motivating factor in AOS 91, which has to pass 10 budgets each year, according to Zboray. An RSU would consolidate those boards into one unit with weighted votes.
In materials presented before the vote, school officials also said the reorganization would make access to education more equitable and provide specialized services that are hard to staff in small schools, give more support to teachers and staff, and save money.
Major reservations Zboray heard included how member towns would have voting representation on a regional board and whether the plan went far enough to reorganize students across school buildings, such as by creating a middle school.
It also would have spread out the debt for a new elementary school under construction in Bar Harbor, which some pushed back on, Zboray said.
He said local boards have worked well together and thanked participants, saying the process also provided data about local priorities that could inform any future reorganization discussion.
A reorganization process would have to start over again from scratch if elected officials chose to try again, and he would work with them in that case.

title: Trump talks about the White House ballroom project, not the midterms, in extended public comments
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump reacted Wednesday to Republicans’ midterm election losses by showing off the White House ballroom he’s building as he demonstrated the kind of detached behavior that voters around the country said was a key reason they opted to punish his party.
In an extraordinary scene, Trump summoned reporters to the hulking construction site that he demolished the East Wing to make room for and the Republican president spoke for nearly 20 minutes about minute building details. He did not mention his party losing control of Congress after defeats in some of the country’s deepest GOP strongholds, including Texas and South Carolina, or voter concerns about the high cost of living and federal corruption that helped cause the election losses.
“This has been a structure the likes of which has never been seen anywhere,” Trump said, speaking into a microphone that sent loud feedback echoing around the cavernous space.
He talked at length about how the ballroom would be the ”safest place in Washington" upon completion, stretching five stories underground and featuring a cut of marble that he called “a vein that people have been after for 50 years.”
“We have large staircases coming from the kitchen. If I put the kitchen on top, you would lose three walls, because a kitchen takes about 30% of the space,” Trump said of his choice to make the ballroom’s kitchen subterranean.
“It’s going to be top of the line,” he added.
This is not what presidents normally talk about the day after an election
Presidents usually speak with reporters the day after the midterms. It’s normal for those whose party endured big losses to shoulder publicly at least part of the responsibility.
But not Trump.
He began the day with a schedule that showed only private meetings, then suggested he had decided at the last minute to invite the press to watch as the final steel beam — topped with a small evergreen tree symbolizing growth and luck — was hoisted into place on the ballroom roof.
Trump signed the beam with a marker during the ceremony, writing “Love!” followed by his name in supersize letters.
His appearance came after midterm voters said they thought the president was focused on the wrong issues. About two-thirds of voters said Trump does not have the right priorities, according to The AP Voter Poll, and the overwhelming majority of these voters supported Democratic House candidates.
The post-midterm ceremony might also reinforce voter concerns about whether Trump, 80, is up for the rigors of the presidency.
Biden dropped out of his reelection race in 2024 after a disastrous debate with Trump, who even today frequently mocks Biden’s mental and physical acuity.
Trump seeks to shift blame for the midterms
Trump eventually took questions at the ballroom site and attempted to duck responsibility for the broad Republican losses. He insisted he didn’t lead the party into an Election Day drubbing despite staging a flurry of rallies where he implored supporters to pretend that he was on the ballot.
“If I were on the ballot I would have won,” Trump insisted.
He said campaign rallies in mostly Republican states or conservative parts of more closely divided ones featured enthusiastic crowds “but we weren’t able to transfer love to the candidates.”
The beam-raising was not his first baffling political moment this week. On Monday, Trump gave his closing message of the midterm cycle in a long speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, shining a spotlight at a pivotal time on a project marred by algae, leaks and delays.
“I heard it was a very good speech, got great reviews,” he said on Wednesday.
Ducking responsibility is common with Trump
An Associated Press analysis of the 39 Trump speeches and rallies that Trump staged between Sept. 1 and Election Day showed the president used phrasing suggesting he was on the ballot in 30 of them. In some addresses he returned to the subject more than once, though, meaning there were at least 40 instances where he appealed to voters to engage in that bit of make-believe.
But as the extent of his party’s defeat became apparent on election night, Trump was deflecting blame.
“I don’t like to consider it a defeat for me. I wasn’t on the ballot,” he told Fox News Channel. Voters, he said, just “didn’t like the candidates” on the ballot. The Voter Poll suggests Trump himself was a drag on GOP politicians and that in some races, candidates were seen as too supportive of the unpopular president.
Trump has a long history of passing the buck, on issues large and small, especially when there are ballot-box failures.
After Republicans lost the House in the 2018 midterms during Trump’s first term, he blamed defeated members of his own party.
Utah Rep. Mia Love, who had tried to distance herself from him, “gave me no love, but then she lost. Too bad,” the president said, while also mocking other losing lawmakers for not embracing him — Florida’s Carlos Curbelo, Colorado’s Mike Coffman, Virginia’s Barbara Comstock, and Illinois’ Peter Roskam.
That’s in contrast to how Democrat Barack Obama described his party’s losses in 2010 as “a shellacking” or Republican George W. Bush described Democratic victories in the 2006 midterms as “a thumping.”
But Trump, known for defying all kinds of presidential norms, began laying the groundwork for avoiding blame this cycle well before balloting began.
He told Punchbowl News in August that voters were angry at Republicans “but they’re not angry at me.”
The president posted on his social media site last month that should Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton lose — and he did — “it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove.” That’s despite Trump’s risky endorsement of scandal-marred Paxton in the primary over incumbent Cornyn, who first got to the Senate in 2002 and was considered the safer bet. Rove is a political strategist who helped Bush win the White House.
Also losing Tuesday was Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a longtime Trump ally.
Trump posted on social media that if Abbott “hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost,” suggesting the governor had backed away from his staunchly conservative credentials and become “Republican in Name Only.”
__
Associated Press writers Amelia Thomson DeVeaux, Linley Sanders, Josh Boak and Aaron Kessler contributed to this report.

title: How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON — After more than a decade with Donald Trump at the epicenter of U.S. politics, most voters appear exhausted and exasperated by him, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of midterm voters in all 50 states.
The president’s failure to deliver on key promises — most prominently, his vows to tame inflation, which has worsened instead — clearly weighed on his fellow Republicans in Tuesday’s midterm elections for the House and the Senate. The polling shows that voters generally saw Trump as being more focused on his own fortune and gold-leafed existence than their needs.
The president also helped elevate candidates with obvious flaws, amplifying their struggles in an already challenging year. He suggested in a Tuesday evening interview with Fox News Channel that Democrats “fought hard” and that the Republican base “didn’t like the candidates” he had endorsed because some of his picks were not fully loyal to him.
But the poll also contains a serious note of caution for Democrats. Many voters dislike the party — and while Democrats hold an advantage on key issues such as the economy, their edge is relatively slim. About 7 in 10 voters said Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances for the president, setting the bar for Democrats who won back the Senate and the House.
Inflation crushed Republicans
It was impossible for GOP candidates to hide from inflation. Voters could see it clearly in their receipts from grocery stores and gasoline stations. The financial blow of an auto repair or a utility bill after a sweltering summer was inescapable. And even in Republican strongholds such as Texas, the drag caused by inflation helped Democrats.
About 2 in 10 Texas voters said inflation had imposed “severe” hardship on them and their family — and about three-quarters of this group backed Democrat James Talarico for the Senate. An additional 6 in 10 voters, roughly, said inflation had led to “moderate” hardship, and Talarico won the majority of these voters, too.
That same pattern repeated in state after state. Nationally, voters who said they were “very concerned” about everyday costs — including groceries, healthcare and gas — overwhelmingly said they voted for the Democratic candidate in their local U.S. House race.
But it wasn’t just the inflation itself that mattered. Voters nationwide pinned the blame on Trump for his tariffs, his war in Iran and his unfulfilled campaign promise two years ago to bring down prices.
Asked about the impact of Trump’s policies, about two-thirds of voters nationwide said they had made the economy worse. And out of this group, about 8 in 10 said they backed the Democratic candidate.
Corruption was a major concern
More than half of voters nationally said government corruption was “crucial” for their vote for Congress. That was a little higher than the share who said the cost of living was “crucial,” a striking finding in a year when about 6 in 10 voters said they were personally “very concerned” about the cost of food and groceries.
Meanwhile, despite Republicans’ suggestion that voters cared little about Trump making more than $1 billion last year from meme coins and cryptocurrency, most voters saw Trump as obsessed with his own interests. During his second term, Trump solicited donations from powerful companies to build his desired White House ballroom after having surprised the country by rapidly demolishing what had been the building’s East Wing.
That tenor set at the top spilled over into business deals for his family and other deals by his associates involving pardons and federal policies.
Ultimately, about two-thirds of voters said Trump does not have the right priorities — and the overwhelming majority of these voters supported Democratic House candidates.
Voters want an assertive Congress
For much of the past two years, Trump acted on his own.
Much of the Republican-controlled House and Senate barely objected to his whims. He laid off federal workers, imposed sweeping new tariffs, launched the war with Iran, remodeled Washington in gold paint, threatened the Federal Reserve, the Kennedy Center and the Smithsonian Institution and bullied a bevy of longtime allies.
Voters made it clear that they want more congressional oversight.
About 7 in 10 voters said Congress was not doing enough to provide checks and balances for the presidency, including about 4 in 10 Republicans.
Swing voters don’t really love Democrats, even if they voted for them
Despite Democrats’ victories, voters did not deliver a ringing endorsement of the party as a whole. Many voters expressed frustration with both parties: On the economy, foreign policy, healthcare, taxes and immigration, roughly 2 in 10 voters said “neither” party was better equipped to handle these issues. An even larger share of voters said neither party would be better at addressing government corruption or artificial intelligence.
Those skeptical voters generally broke for Democrats.
But it wasn’t because the party was overwhelmingly popular. Only about half of voters had a “somewhat” or “strongly” favorable view of the Democratic Party. That was higher than the approximately 4 in 10 who viewed the GOP positively, but not by much. About 2 in 10 voters who supported Democratic candidates had a negative view of the party as a whole.
Instead, in key races, voters seemed to be looking to Democratic candidates for change. In Maine, for instance, most voters who said having a candidate with “the right experience” mattered most to their Senate decision chose Republican incumbent Susan Collins. But more voters cared about bringing about “needed change,” and they favored Democrat Troy Jackson.
Republicans chose weak candidates
Trump endorsed Republicans who turned off voters — and that put areas that were once safely with the GOP at risk.
After Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina died in July, the president chose the late senator’s sister, Darline Graham, to fill his seat. The new Sen. Graham then promptly decided to seek election and struggled on foreign policy questions that were once her brother’s forte.
About 6 in 10 voters in the South Carolina Senate race said she lacked the experience to serve in the Senate.
During the Texas Republican primary, Trump ultimately backed the state’s attorney general, Ken Paxton, over its sitting senator, John Cornyn. Paxton was scandal-ridden and had been impeached but not convicted. About two-thirds of Texas Senate voters said he lacked the character to be a senator.
The president prized loyalty in Republican candidates. That hurt Republican candidates in many states.
In North Carolina, as in several other states, about 6 in 10 voters said the state’s Republican Senate nominee, Michael Whatley, was “too supportive” of Trump. They chose former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat, for the Senate instead.
Story by Josh Boak, Hyojin Yoo and Humera Lodhi.

title: Kennebunkport voters approve funding for annual Christmas Prelude
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Kennebunkport voters approve funding for annual Christmas Prelude
On Tuesday, Kennebunkport voters approved up to $17,500 in town funding to help support the annual Christmas Prelude celebration, following months of debate over whether taxpayers should help cover costs associated with the popular holiday event.
The funding was approved alongside a change to the town’s mass gathering ordinance, allowing Kennebunkport to help cover municipal expenses associated with the event.
The Kennebunkport Business Association has argued that Christmas Prelude provides an economic boost to local businesses, not only during the annual celebration but throughout the year.
“Over the last several months, we've been working on proving the community component of the KBA and the Christmas Prelude event in general, and all of the support that it provides the businesses over the course of the whole year, not just over the two weeks of December that the event actually happens,” Catie Seavey, vice president of the Kennebunkport Business Association said.
This year's Christmas Prelude is scheduled to begin Dec. 3 and run through Dec. 13, bringing thousands of visitors to Kennebunkport for the annual holiday celebration.

title: Mississippi Senate race is still too close to call
text:
Scott Colom widens his lead over Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi Senate race
Thousands of absentee and affidavit ballots are still being counted in Mississippi, leaving the outcome of the close U.S. Senate race between Democratic candidate Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith undecided.
The race remains too close to call, with Colom currently holding a lead over Hyde-Smith. If Colom wins, he would be the first African American elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since Reconstruction.
Colom's lead has widened slightly since Wednesday, when he was ahead by only a few dozen votes.
The ballots left to be counted include provisional ballots cast by voters who didn’t immediately meet voting requirements at the polls. The final results may take days to determine.
Election officials said Tuesday’s scanned ballots have been counted, as have absentee ballots that were cast in person. The ballots that are still being counted are affidavit ballots and mail-in ballots that were postmarked no later than Nov. 3.
Affidavits are filed by voters who could not show I.D. at the polls. Those voters must show an approved form of I.D. at their circuit clerk's office by Nov. 10 for their vote to be counted.
Once all the ballots are in, they will be processed by election commissioners across the state. They will either be accepted and added to the vote count, or they will be rejected. That process can take a few days.
Candidates may have representatives present for the vote count.
Every county in Mississippi has a Nov. 10 deadline for all votes to be counted and submitted. They must be certified by Nov. 13.
Mississippi does not have a recount provision in state law, and there's no automatic recount process. But a challenger can seek a court order for a recount.
"We prepared for this moment," Colom told Hearst sister station WAPT in Mississippi. "Our campaign, our volunteers, the people of Mississippi are not surprised."
The race remains tight, with experts unable to make a final projection.
Cheikh Taylor, chair of the Mississippi Democratic Party, urged patience.
"I think the race is close. Everyone should just hold their horses for a little while and wait for those affidavit votes to come in. They're going to be very important," Taylor said.

title: Political response to gas prices shows contempt for the average American
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
One question: Why? Two of the major gas companies just reported they have made massive profits this year and Trump has said we are “making a freaking fortune” on gas. Unfortunately the “we” is not the American people but the gas companies. Again I ask: Why?
Why can’t the gas companies get by on just profits, rather than “massive” profits? Trump and his cronies may be making a fortune — but at what cost to the American people? Already, many cannot heat their homes or use their cars normally. Trucking costs have increased. And the gas companies can make billions? It is just wrong.
No one in Washington, D.C., will regulate the gas companies; too many are tied to Big Oil. Gas prices could be cut in half, meaning those greedy gas companies and politicians would have to try to get by on normal profits, but our political leaders do not care about the average American.
I am disgusted with the oil companies, I am disgusted with Trump enriching himself as president, I am tired of our government not working on behalf of the American people.
What is truly disgusting is that it will not change. So very wrong and very sad.
Gary Phillips
Wells

title: Bangor Symphony Orchestra And Gary Sinise Honor Veterans At Collins Center With Graceful Warrior Concert
text:
Actor Gary Sinise Brings The Lt. Dan Band To Play With The Bangor Symphony Orchestra For Veterans Day Concerts This Weekend
This weekend will mark a first-of-it's-kind Veterans Celebration between the Bangor Symphony Orchestra and award-winning actor/writer/humanitarian Gary Sinise.
Read More: ‘Northern Lights’ Holiday Display Returns to L.L.Bean This Friday
The Symphony is joining with Sinise and his 'Lt. Dan Band', to honor those who serve/served in the armed forces with a unique and powerful weekend of music and literature!
Sinise, his band and the Bangor Symphony Orchestra will perform a pair of Veterans Day Special concerts called Graceful Warrior at the Collins Center for the Arts.
According to the BSO, while there will be lots of music folks will recognize, this concert will also feature new music created to honor Sinise's son, Mac.
"Inspired by his late son Mac's music, most of which was discovered shortly after Mac's passing at a young age from a rare spinal cancer on January 5, 2024, Gary has curated this concert to honor the power of music and healing. The concert features the Bangor Symphony Orchestra in the first half, including Gary Sinise narrating Aaron Copland's 'Lincoln Portrait', and Gary Sinise & The Lt. Dan Band in the second half, with Mac's music transcribed by Oliver Schnee, a musical composer and old college friend of Mac's who is also helping bring Mac's music to life."
Aside from his memoir, Grateful American: A Journey from Self to Service, which Sinise published in 2019, he just wrote another book, this one about his son, Mac, called Graceful Warrior: The True Story of a Son, a Father, and a Family Who Carried Each Other Through.
Graceful Warrior is expected to launch November 10th of this year, the day before Veterans Day.
According to the Collins Center for the Arts website, incorporating the book and the music helps to further the mission of helping support veterans.
"Presented in conjunction with Gary’s upcoming book Graceful Warrior, this one-of-a-kind event is a profound reflection on love, loss, resilience, and hope. Graceful Warrior will be available for sale at the events, and all proceeds from the book sales go to the Gary Sinise Foundation, to help further their mission of 'serving our nation by honoring our defenders, veterans, first responders, their families, and those in need … by creating and supporting unique programs designed to entertain, educate, inspire, strengthen, and build communities.'"
BSO Music Director and Conductor, Lucas Richman, says he feels a special privilege in being able to perform these pieces with Sinise in attendance.
“As a father, I was incredibly touched by Mac Sinise’s journey and Gary’s dedication to bringing the treasure trove of his son’s music to light. It will be a great honor to have Gary here with the BSO playing his son’s music, as well as paying tribute to the generations of veterans who are the focal point of the work done by the Lt. Dan Band and the Gary Sinise Foundation."
The Graceful Warrior performances will be held this Saturday November 7th at 7 PM and Sunday November 8th at 1 PM at the Collins Center for the Arts.
You can purchase tickets through the Collins Center Box Office or the Bangor Symphony Orchestra. BSO Season ticket holders, this will be an add-on to the subscription package.
Read More: Bangor Mall Christmas Craft Fair Still Happening This Weekend
Veterans, active military members, and first responders can get two tickets for free by calling the Collins Center Box Office at (207) 581-2787.
They will also launch the The Graceful Warrior book during the performances, with advance copies for sale at each event in Orono.

title: Sherrod Brown flips Senate seat in Ohio for Democrats by ousting Sen. Jon Husted
text:
Democrat Sherrod Brown will return to Senate after ousting Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio race
Former Sen. Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio on Tuesday, flipping a seat that was crucial to Democrats' strategy to retake the chamber and providing a ray of hope for the party's longer-term prospects in a former swing state that had turned sharply to the right over the last decade.
Brown won after hammering Husted relentlessly throughout one of the nation's most expensive races, drawing attention to the Republican's support for artificial intelligence data centers, his ties to a bribery scandal at the statehouse and campaign donations he'd taken from billionaire retail magnate Les Wexner, who once employed the late sexual predator Jeffrey Epstein.
Husted argued that Brown, who has spent five decades in politics, was out of date and too liberal for Ohio voters. Late in the campaign, President Donald Trump — who made several Ohio visits on Husted's behalf — became fixated on Husted's athletic physique, promoting the former college football player as the better-looking candidate.
Brown's victory caps a remarkable turnaround for the longtime Democrat. He lost his Senate seat just two years ago, defeated by newcomer Bernie Moreno, only to jump back into the political fray for a successful comeback. The campaign featured a rush of more than $500 million in spending from both sides and their allies.
Since Tuesday was technically a special election in Ohio, Brown now serves out the final two years of the Senate term won by JD Vance in 2022. Husted — a former lieutenant governor, secretary of state and state House speaker — was appointed to replace Vance when he ascended to the vice presidency last year.
Brown's victory could reshape Democrats' perspective headed forward on Ohio, which many had largely written off as out of reach. The state's electorate had swung strongly toward Republicans in the decade since Trump entered the political arena, prompting analysts to declare an end to the state's traditional bellwether status.
But the president's tariffs, trade war with Canada and the war with Iran that sent fuel prices soaring gave Brown, 73, a fresh opening with rural and working-class voters.
Trump stumped for Husted without success
The landscape this year was significantly different than it was two years ago, when Brown lost to Moreno in a bitter campaign where spending topped $500 million.
For one thing, Trump was not on the ballot to drive Republican turnout, and the president's low approval ratings complicated the impact of his once-coveted endorsements for candidates such as Husted. The president and vice president — with an advertising boost from technology companies — pressed a positive message on artificial intelligence data centers during their multiple rallies for Husted, keen on reversing one of his key vulnerabilities. Ultimately, it wasn't enough.
This was Ohio's third U.S. Senate race in as many election cycles, with another coming in two years, and it also notably featured no political newcomer. Running as an "outsider" with Trump's endorsement had worked as a winning formula for both Moreno and Vance.
Instead, both Brown and Husted had long records in public office that the other could exploit. Husted, 59, has never been accused of any crime associated with the $60 million bribery scandal involving FirstEnergy, but he had been called to testify in the criminal trial of two former executives — footage Brown and his allies used to blanket the airwaves.
Husted also donated all the donations from Wexner left in his political accounts to an anti-sex trafficking charity, but the fact he received them was used by Brown to jab at a vulnerability for Republicans over their votes on releasing the Epstein files.
Meanwhile, to highlight Brown's many years in Washington, Husted ran one ad noting that he was a 7-year-old playing pee wee football when Brown first went to Congress. Another cited Brown's vote in favor of the bank bailout of 2008, nearly two decades ago, to paint him as beholden to Wall Street.
Brown's longevity in politics did come with a key upside: strong name recognition. He didn't have to work to identify himself to voters as Husted had to do, airing a variety of positive biographical ads.

title: Holden-area school to close following voter approval
text:
An elementary school in Eddington will close after three communities — Eddington, Clifton and Holden — voted for it to shut down at the end of the school year.
More than twice as many voters favored the closure than those who were opposed, with 2,530 votes to approve cast across the three communities and 1,114 against.
With the vote, residents in the communities, which make up Regional School Unit 63, agreed to consolidate students in two buildings. The RSU School Board has not decided what will happen with the closed elementary school.
The closure will save the district $669,950 by cutting multiple positions and reducing maintenance and fueling costs, according to the district. Although there will be a drop in costs, it’s unclear if the closure will lower local taxes.
Ahead of the vote, residents were told that their communities would have to pay the cost to keep the school open, roughly $670,000, if they denied the referendum. Under state law, any community that requires a school to stay open has to pay the fee to operate it for a year. That fee would have been split by two communities if both voted against the measure.
Residents in Eddington spoke out against the closure in a school board meeting earlier this year and on social media leading up to election day, but Eddington voters approved the closure in a 732-564 vote.
The RSU School Board can now review how the building can be used.

title: 2 college students whose bodies were found in the Colorado mountains fell to their deaths
text:
(AP) - The two college students whose bodies were recovered last week in the Colorado mountains were rappelling and fell a “substantial distance” when a rock they were anchored to likely gave way, authorities said Tuesday.
Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20, died instantly from multiple blunt force injuries, an autopsy found, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office and coroner’s office. Their bodies were found in a snow-filled basin of West Apostle Mountain, about 100 miles (160 kilometers) southeast of Aspen.
The heavy snowstorm was not a direct factor, according to the statement, which commended the college students for their love of the outdoors and preparation for the climbing trip.
“In most similar cases that have led to a devastating conclusion we find it easy to pick apart what was done wrong,” said Chaffee County Sheriff Andy Rohrich. “That was not the case with Kaden and Jackson.”
The pair had set out from Colorado Mountain College’s Leadville campus for what was supposed to be a weekend trip. While they were originally aiming for Ice Mountain, a 13,958-foot (4,254-meter) peak, Rohrich said they appeared to switch to the 13,597-foot (4,144-meter) West Apostle Mountain.
Donlon was starting to rappel from an anchor point backed up by other protections when the rock likely gave way, according to Rohrich. Matsuda was attached to the same anchor, and they both fell a long distance, although the exact length was not known, according to the statement.
“While their lives were far too short, they spent their final moments together surrounded by the majestic beauty of Chaffee County’s high peaks that they loved,” Rohrich said. “There is also relief knowing neither of them suffered.”
Colorado Mountain College, which has campuses throughout the Colorado Rockies, is known for its programs focusing on the state’s robust outdoor recreation economy, including mountaineering, ski patrol and guiding careers.
Matsuda, of Ridgway, Colorado, and Donlon, of Queensbury, New York, became fast friends at the small campus in Leadville, which bills itself as America’s highest city at 10,119 feet (3,084 meters) above sea level. Located about 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of Denver, the city is home to about 2,600 people and is flanked by some of Colorado’s tallest mountains.
Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter. Donlon, an avid climber and skier, was studying outdoor recreation leadership and had come to Colorado to pursue his love of the mountains.
It was raining when they started hiking, according to the sheriff’s office, and later a severe storm arrived, dumping up to 2 feet (0.6 meters) of snow.
___
Associated Press writer Wufei Yu contributed.

title: Bangor Mall condemned due to electrical issues, lack of working bathrooms, city says
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The City of Bangor has released a statement explaining why code enforcement abruptly shuttered most of the Bangor Mall on Monday.
City of Bangor spokesperson David Warren says the city has tried to work with the mall’s owners for years to resolve their concerns, and while some have been addressed, others remain. Warren cited “significant health and safety-related code violations,” pointing specifically to unsafe electrical conditions, inoperable heating systems, and a lack of working general-use restrooms.
“As of Monday, portions of the mall did not have properly operating heating systems,” Warren said. “The City was compelled to shut off electric service to both corridor entrances due to a roof that continues to leak. The lack of proper illumination creates additional safety issues.”
Placards deeming the property “unfit for human habitation or use” were posted at general entrances Monday afternoon, surprising tenants and shoppers.
Multiple mall tenants and workers told WABI and posted on social media that they received no advance notice from the city. The city’s statement confirmed that Namdar Realty Group, the New York-based firm that owns the property, was notified the day of the closure. Warren said Namdar has 30 days to appeal by filing a written petition for a hearing before the City’s Board of Appeals. WABI reached out to Namdar for comment but has not received a response.
Anchor stores Dick’s Sporting Goods and JCPenney remain open via their exterior entrances. The former Furniture, Mattresses & More space—recently vacated following its owners’ retirement—is privately owned and unaffected by the condemnation order.
Kathy Harvey, who owns the furniture store space also organizes says the mall’s annual holiday craft fair, which is scheduled for this weekend and next. Harvey and the city say the craft fair will go on, and the event will proceed as planned inside the former store rather than in the mall concourses.
The Sears wing was previously cordoned off for code violations last winter. City officials said the affected areas will remain closed until Namdar resolves outstanding violations. Tenants told WABI that repairs have been ongoing, with roof work among several projects underway.
The City says their economic development team is assisting displaced businesses as much as they can.
