title: Democrat leads controversial ex-prosecutor for Hancock County probate judge seat
text:
Democratic nominee Brian Thomas has a more than 3,000-vote lead on Republican and controversial former District Attorney Matthew Foster for Hancock County’s probate judge seat.
As of 10:30 a.m. Wednesday, Thomas had 16,822 votes and Foster had 13,619 votes with 34 of 37 municipalities having reported unofficial results.
“I’m certainly encouraged, and I think it’s likely that it’ll hold based on what hasn’t been counted yet,” Thomas told the Bangor Daily News Wednesday morning. “I’m honored that people have given me the chance to serve as the probate judge.”
The candidates are vying to fill a seat that’s been largely in limbo since April 2025, when current Probate Judge William B. Blaisdell was suspended from practicing law after facing multiple contempt orders over overdue child support payments to his ex-wife.
The county’s probate judge handles cases often involving sensitive familial matters like estates, guardianships and name changes. Since Blaisdell’s suspension, those cases have been overseen by probate judges from nearby counties.
Thomas, a Lamoine land trust lawyer and former archaeologist, won the Democratic nomination as a write-in candidate after learning no one was challenging Foster.
The Republican nominee and former local district attorney lost reelection in 2022 after he was caught lying in a candidates forum about whether he ever had been investigated by the state attorney general’s office.
Foster was investigated by state officials in 2017 and 2018, while he was the top prosecutor in Hancock and Washington counties, for allegedly inappropriately touching a 13-year-old child who was living with him at the time. He has denied the allegations and was never charged with a crime.
Foster also came under scrutiny in 2020 after he was accused of posting a racist meme on Facebook that mocked looters during protests over the death of George Floyd, according to the Ellsworth American. He later denied having posted the memes, saying his account may have been hacked.
Foster runs Downeast Legal Services on State Street in Ellsworth.

title: Man indicted on arson, attempted murder charges in connection with Harrington fire
text:
WASHINGTON COUNTY, Maine (WABI) - A Harrington man has been indicted by a Washington County grand jury on several charges, including attempted murder, in connection with a July house fire.
Arthur Langley faces charges of attempted murder, arson, and reckless conduct.
Investigators with the Maine State Fire Marshal’s Office say Langley intentionally set fire to a home on Main Street in Harrington on July 17.
When authorities initially arrested Langley, he was only charged with arson and reckless conduct. The grand jury later added the attempted murder charge in the formal indictment.

title: Democrats make sweeping gains at the state level, taking control of legislatures and shifting power
text:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Democrats made sweeping gains in state governments during the midterm elections, taking control of several legislatures and shifting the balance of power across some battleground and historically Republican-leaning states.
The party took full control — both statehouse chambers and governors’ offices — in Minnesota and Wisconsin and could pick up more states to earn additional trifectas.
The wins put pressure on the party to answer to an electorate angry over the price of gas, inflation, affordable housing and the rising cost of living. State governments shape a wide array of policies affecting everyday lives, including tax rates and abortion rights, school choice and education funding, data center development, and the use of artificial intelligence and law-enforcement surveillance cameras.
“Now it’s time to deliver,” Wisconsin Democratic Party Chairman Devin Remiker said.
Democrats take full control in battleground states
Democrats succeeded in flipping control of both chambers of the Legislature in battleground Wisconsin, breaking a 16-year Republican majority, and retained the governor’s office. They also won back full control of the Legislature in neighboring Minnesota and retained the governor’s office for another trifecta.
Democrats also were in position to win trifectas in the presidential battlegrounds of Pennsylvania and Michigan.
And the party broke or prevented Republican supermajorities in nine legislative chambers in eight states: Florida, South Carolina, Indiana, Missouri, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and North Carolina.
There will be pressure on Democrats in Wisconsin and other battleground states to redraw congressional maps, just as President Donald Trump successfully urged eight Republican states to do ahead of this election. But that backfired, with Republicans losing most of the Democratic-held seats they had targeted to flip and others they had banked on winning.
Even under maps that favor Republicans in Wisconsin, Democrats picked up two congressional seats in Tuesday’s races. That means the state will have an evenly divided congressional delegation in 2027.
Democrats also break up Republican trifectas and supermajorities
Democrats will also hold at least 28 governorships in 2027, with pickups in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — states long held by Republicans.
The wins come after Democrats lost nearly 1,000 state legislative seats during President Barack Obama’s tenure, a slide they’ve been trying to reverse for several cycles.
Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said Democrats won “historic levels of power in statehouses.” She said Democrats hadn’t flipped this many seats nationwide since the 1980s.
“The shift in the balance of power in our statehouses will have some of the longest-lasting impacts of this election,” she said.
Wins put spotlight on Democratic priorities in 2027
The cost of groceries, housing, healthcare, gas and utility bills were major campaign talking points after legislative sessions packed with bills aiming to make life more affordable for Americans, while also providing tax relief and reining in data center development and the use of artificial intelligence.
The coming legislative session could see major efforts to lighten the tax burden on the middle class, relax housing regulations, expand access to healthcare, and force utilities and data center developers to do more to stop electricity bills from rising.
Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who won reelection, told his supporters on Tuesday night that people want him and lawmakers to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, invest in infrastructure, kids, police and communities, and enshrine abortion rights for women in the state Constitution.
Other newly elected governors, including Wisconsin’s David Crowley and Minnesota’s Amy Klobuchar, said they wanted to work with Republicans.
“I am not interested in moving Minnesota to the left or the right; I want to move us forward,” Klobuchar said.
She even had a warning for her Democratic supporters.
“Spoiler alert: You may not like every single thing I do,” she said.
___
Mulvihill reported from Haddonfield, New Jersey. Associated Press reporter Marc Levy contributed.

title: Democrat David Crowley defeats Trump ally to become Wisconsin’s first Black governor
text:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Democrat David Crowley defeated a Republican with close ties to President Donald Trump on Tuesday, rising from a childhood in one of the nation’s poorest neighborhoods to become the first Black person to lead the battleground state.
Crowley’s win over U.S. Rep. Tom Tiffany marks the first time in Wisconsin’s 178-year history that Democrats will hold the governor’s office for more than eight consecutive years. He will replace Gov. Tony Evers, who decided to retire instead of seeking a third term.
Crowley told his supporters in his victory speech that he would be a governor for everyone, including those who didn’t vote for him.
“Wisconsin isn’t a red state or a blue state,” he said. “We never have been. In a state this close, nobody gets to govern alone.”
He promised to work with Democrats and Republicans on lowering costs in Wisconsin. Democrats were hoping to flip control of the Legislature for the first time in 16 years.
The victory blunts Republican efforts to claw back control of a state that Trump won in two of his three presidential campaigns. It also ensures that a Democrat will be leading Wisconsin during the next race for the White House, when the state will likely continue its role as a key battleground.
Crowley, 40, was born in the north side of Milwaukee in one of the country’s poorest neighborhoods, and his parents battled substance abuse and evictions. But Crowley turned to community organizing and politics, winning election to the Legislature at age 30. He served just over three years before being elected in 2020 as Milwaukee County executive.
His path to the governor’s office was tumultuous. He dropped out of the race when he appeared unlikely to win the Democratic nomination, only to rejoin at Evers’ urging. He defeated a democratic socialist in the August primary, then faced off with Tiffany, who received most of his financial support from just three billionaires.
Tiffany, who survived a small plane crash while campaigning, was weighed down by the president’s record-low approval numbers in Wisconsin, a state that Trump won twice.
Democrats were hoping for a trifecta — winning the governor’s office and flipping both legislative chambers. They have not had full control of Wisconsin state government since 2010.
U.S. GOVERNORS BALANCE OF POWER
An open governor’s race for the first time in 16 years
Wisconsin’s governor’s race was open for the first time in 16 years after Evers decided against seeking a third term.
The last open race for governor was in 2010, when Democratic incumbent Jim Doyle, similar to Evers, opted not to seek a third term. Republican Scott Walker won that year, and over the next eight years enacted a wide array of Republican priorities that dramatically scaled back union rights, slashed taxes and started requiring voters to show identification at the polls.
Evers, who normally doesn’t endorse in primaries, got behind Crowley in an effort to blunt the rising campaign of democratic socialist Francesca Hong. Crowley won by less than half a percentage point.
Wisconsin is used to close races.
Trump, who endorsed Tiffany, won Wisconsin in 2016 and 2024 and lost in 2020. Those three presidential elections are among five of the past seven in Wisconsin that have been decided by less than a percentage point.
In 2018, Evers defeated then-Gov. Scott Walker by 1.1 percentage points. Evers won reelection by 3.4 points in 2022, a landslide by Wisconsin standards.
Tiffany cast Crowley as pro-data center; Crowley ran on affordability
Tiffany tried to portray Crowley as an advocate for building data centers in Wisconsin, referring to him as “Data Center David Crowley.” Tiffany ran an ad that included a clip of Crowley saying Wisconsin could become the “AI and data hub not only for the entire country, but for the entire globe.”
But Tiffany also said positive things about data centers in the past. Crowley changed his position on data centers late in the campaign, coming out in favor of a moratorium in October. Tiffany did not call for a moratorium on construction.
Tiffany also tried to portray Crowley as weak on crime and said Crowley would increase taxes as governor to pay for his agenda, which included expanding healthcare and fully funding public schools.
Crowley hammered Tiffany on economic issues, saying his loyalty to Trump and support of the war in Iran was to blame for the high gas prices that were hurting Wisconsin residents, particularly farmers. Crowley also ran in support of overturning the 15-year-old state law known as Act 10 that effectively ended collective bargaining rights for most public workers.
Tiffany, 68, voted for that law when he was a member of the Legislature. Tiffany was elected to Congress in 2020, representing a mostly rural district after nine years in the Legislature.
Crowley also called for expanding Medicaid coverage, increasing funding for public schools and increasing access to child care.

title: Revolve data breach exposed shoppers' saved card numbers and expiration dates
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Revolve data breach exposed shoppers' saved card numbers and expiration dates
Revolve is notifying customers after a breach exposed saved card numbers and expiration dates. State filings list at least 197,072 affected residents across five states.
Revolve data breach exposed shoppers' saved card numbers and expiration dates
Revolve is notifying customers after a breach exposed saved card numbers and expiration dates. State filings list at least 197,072 affected residents across five states.
Revolve Group, Inc., which operates the online fashion retailers Revolve and FWRD, is notifying customers that a data breach involved names, addresses, payment card numbers and expiration dates, according to breach notices filed with state officials.
The company said an unauthorized actor accessed its online shopping platform on Sept. 11. The data involved customers who had saved a payment method to their account.
The National Consumer Unit reviewed publicly available state breach notices to assess the scope of the breach. The filings list 127,200 affected Texas residents, 46,813 in Massachusetts, 17,813 in South Carolina, 3,918 in Iowa, and 1,328 in Vermont. Data returned by the Texas attorney general’s site for Revolve’s filing includes a separate field listing 1,515,073 people affected nationwide, though that figure does not appear in the public search results. Revolve has not publicly disclosed a nationwide total. Not all states make breach notices available to search.
Customers who receive a notice should review their card statements and promptly report unfamiliar charges to the card issuer. They can also contact the issuer and ask for a replacement card with a new number.
Revolve says customers who have questions about the breach can call 888-517-6458, Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern Time, excluding some major U.S. holidays.
What else can you do?
One of the best ways to protect yourself before a data breach happens is to proactively freeze your credit. While a freeze won't stop unauthorized charges on an exposed card, it can make it harder for someone to open a new credit account in your name using stolen information by restricting access to your credit report. A freeze is free to place and lift, but you must contact Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion separately.

title: Husband and wife drown in river while using inflatable kayak
text:
PHOENIX (KPHO/Gray News) — A married couple drowned on Halloween while floating on the lower Salt River in an inflatable kayak.
Arizona authorities said they were called to the river Saturday afternoon for reports of a man yelling that his wife couldn’t swim as the two floated downstream.
According to investigators, both the man and woman went missing underwater.
The woman’s body was found just after 2 p.m., with her husband’s body located upstream about an hour later.
Deputies identified the couple as Cindy Bowers, 68, and Anthony Beringer, 59. They were sharing one kayak, and neither was wearing a life jacket, the sheriff’s office said.
The couple’s deaths remain under investigation.

title: Portland’s famed department store comes alive in historian’s new book
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Department store historian Michael Lisicky wants you to remember Porteous.
Although the space at 522 Congress St. has been home to the Maine College of Arts and Design (MECA&D) for over three decades, the space was, for nearly nine decades before that, the flagship Porteous department store. The college’s Free Street entrance even still bears the department store’s original signage.
“What’s interesting about Porteous is that the building is still so alive,” said Lisicky. “You don’t get that a lot in these old districts and structures. These department stores struggled when the buildings became too antiquated.”
Lisicky’s new book, “You’ll Enjoy Shopping at Porteous,” covers the rise and closure of the Porteous, Mitchell & Braun department store chain throughout the 20th century, painting a picture of Portland’s Congress Street as it changed over the decades in response to burgeoning consumer trends.
The Porteous, Mitchell, and Braun firm, founded in 1873 in Connecticut, took over its Portland space from a previous department store and established itself as a mainstay in downtown Portland, especially around the holidays.
The book touches on topics such as Porteous’ yearly Christmas traditions, the development of the Maine Mall and other retail competitors, the Porteous chain’s expansion across three states, and what remains of these institutions today, long after they’ve shuttered their doors. The Portland store closed in February 1991.
The chronological account is accompanied by a variety of archival photos and newspaper advertisements related to the store. The book was released on Oct. 27.
“When department stores closed when they were at their most personal in the ’80s, there were eulogies. Papers were posting all these memories,” said Lisicky. “Now there will be maybe a blip (in the paper) because (department stores) are no longer part of our culture.”
For Lisicky, a career oboeist in the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra until he retired from the instrument and moved to Portland last year, department stores had been a part of his life since childhood. He remembers fond memories of accompanying his mother to local department stores — institutions that he believed would always be around, but ultimately discovered to be finite.
“They’re anchoring cities. They’re employing thousands. So you think they’re going to be there forever,” said Lisicky.
When department stores across the country began rapidly disappearing in the ’80s, Lisicky turned to libraries and microfilm machines to dig up all he could on these vanishing establishments. His research soon turned into travels around the country to document the final days of local department stores.
“I wanted to know their stories,” said Lisicky. “I was sad to see them go.”
When the internet made it easy to connect historians with curious readers, Lisicky found himself answering readers’ questions as a writer for a column on departmentstorehistory.net, a website run by Jan Whitaker. The columns eventually attracted the interest of a publisher and led to Lisicky’s first book about the former Baltimore department store Hutzler’s. Since then, Lisicky has authored 10 more books on department stores.
While Lisicky hopes this new book will preserve the legacy of Porteous, he also wants the book to connect with Mainers and hopes it will rekindle fond memories.
“A person gets the book, and they look at it, and then their mind starts to open up,” said Lisicky. “Their stories come out, and then people like to tell you these stories.”
Alongside his use of archival material, Lisicky also conducted interviews with former Porteous employees, alongside notable Mainers with fond memories of the store, including Portland Mayor Mark Dion and Gov. Janet Mills.
“As a child, my eyes widened with awe to see the mannequins decked out in the latest styles and the professional displays of colorful kitchenware, rugs, and housewares,” said Mills in the book. “But for my mother and me, it was the women’s and girls’ clothing and shoes that always caught our attention. Porteous, Mitchell, and Braun offered something for everyone.”
His most memorable interview was with 106-year-old Sally Wigon, the owner of Wigan Office Supply in downtown Portland, whom he described as “spitfire of a lady” able to recall memories of Portland and Porteous from the ’20s and ’30s.
“My mother was a bit of a snob. Her favorite stores were Porteous, Springer’s Jewelers, and L.H. Schlosberg furs. Porteous had everything: cosmetics, hair salon, dresses. They were like Macy’s, but they didn’t have any food, no little coffee shop,” Wigon recalled. “J.R. Libby was located in the next block past Porteous, but I don’t think my mother ever bought anything in there. It didn’t seem like a ‘big beautiful store,’ and it carried a ‘low high-grade’ level of merchandise. Talk about being a snob!”
Lisicky doesn’t limit his book to just Porteous and the city of Portland. In fact, he also talks about Bangor and Lewiston and their former department stores: Freese’s and Peck’s, respectively.
“You should not write a book about a retailer in Maine without doing your due diligence and discussing (other retailers),” said Lisicky. “Portland, Bangor and Lewiston are all different, and they had their iconic stores.”
IF YOU GO
Lisicky will give two talks about his book, “You’ll Enjoy Shopping at Porteous,” in the coming months:
Nov. 14, Falmouth Memorial Library, 5 Lunt Road, Falmouth, 2-3:30 p.m. in the Russell Room. Registration encouraged but not required. falmouthmemoriallibrary.org.
Dec. 3, Thomas Memorial Library, 6 Scott Dyer Road, Cape Elizabeth, 6:30-8 p.m. in Community Room A&B. thomas-me.whofi.com/calendar/event/467709.

title: Registered sex offender arrested for recording children, ‘concerning’ images found, police say
text:
MERIDIANVILLE, Ala. (WAFF/Gray News) - A registered sex offender is facing 10 counts of first-degree voyeurism after a Huntsville police investigation.
Daren William Mount, 59, was arrested on Monday.
According to the Huntsville Police Department, Mount was on its radar after an employee at a local business reported seeing “concerning” images while helping him transfer digital files.
HPD’s Special Task Force Rescuing and Investigating Kid Exploitation (STRIKE) team began investigating.
During the investigation, the team said it found pictures and videos of children, including some that were taken at angles showing intimate areas of children’s bodies.
Investigators said some of the images were manipulated. They also said some of the recordings found appeared to be taken in public places.
Mount is a registered sex offender, according to the Alabama Law Enforcement Agency Sex Offender Registry.
Federal court records show Mount pleaded guilty to receipt of child pornography in 2013. He was sentenced to 84 months in prison and 240 months of supervised release.
Mount has returned to prison twice since his 2019 release for violating the terms of his release, according to federal court records.
A federal judge decided he should be under supervised release for life after one of those violations.
The 2011 indictment said his crime spanned from 2003 to 2010, when he was viewing child sexual abuse material on a laptop.
HPD seized electronic devices during Mount’s arrest Monday and has forensic specialists examining those devices.
Police said Mount could be facing additional charges.

title: Collins Dictionary has chosen its 2026 word of the year: How it 'outshines' the others
text:
Collins Dictionary chooses 'mogging' as its 2026 word of the year
Collins Dictionary has named "mogging” — a slang word meaning to outshine someone or something — as its word of the year.
Dictionary experts said Tuesday that the word, most often used by young people “in a playful and ironic way when someone is upstaged," has entered mainstream language and saw a 210% increase in usage in 2026.
Other new and notable entries include “firewaves," defined as a series of urban wildfires in a short space of time, and “P(doom),” an estimation of the probability that artificial intelligence will bring about the collapse of human civilization.
Related video: Letters from a WWII soldier to his sweetheart offer an intimate picture of love during wartime
Alex Beecroft, Collins managing director, said that choosing "mogging" shows how “each generation leaves its mark on language.”
“It’s a great example of how Gen Z and Gen Alpha have adopted a word and turned it into humorous slang, making the language their own and ‘mogging’ the rest of us," he said.
The dictionary said that its experts monitor the 27-billion-word database, which draws from sources including social media, to create its annual list of words that reflect the ever-evolving English language.
The 2026 list includes “carspreading,” which refers to the tendency of manufacturers to build cars that are longer, wider and heavier, and “fricy,” describing trendy food or drinks that are both fruity and spicy.
Other new entries were “ghost jobs” — jobs that are advertised without any intention to appoint anyone — and “friendslop,” a type of low-budget, independently produced video game played among friends.

title: Chris Pappas to become first openly gay male US senator with win in New Hampshire
text:
Chris Pappas wins US Senate election in New Hampshire to become first openly gay male senator
U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu in New Hampshire on Tuesday, keeping a critical open U.S. Senate seat under Democratic control.
The race to fill the seat being vacated by three-term Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen was one of a handful that could determine the balance of power in the Senate. Republicans were hoping to regain a foothold in a region long dominated by Democrats in Congress while Democrats sought to hold the seat as part of their effort to win control of the chamber.
While outsiders were on the ballot elsewhere, the race for the seat being vacated by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen featured two candidates who tried to tap into anti-establishment angst from the inside. Sununu railed against "career politicians" despite having spent three terms in the U.S. House and one in the Senate before being ousted by Shaheen in 2008. Pappas told voters "Our country is ready for change" while seeking to remain in Washington, where he has represented the state's 1st Congressional District since 2019.
New Hampshire voters haven't elected a Republican to Congress since 2010. They also have voted for Democrats for president since 2004, though Republicans have dominated at the state level in recent years. With the win, Pappas will become the first openly gay male U.S. senator.
'Team New Hampshire vs. Team Trump'
Pappas, 46, grew up working in his family's Manchester restaurant, which opened in 1917 and claims to have invented chicken tenders. After college, he served as a state lawmaker, county treasurer and state executive councilor before being elected to Congress. In September, he defeated a democratic socialist and other opponents by a wide margin to win the Democratic primary.
"This is a time for a new generation of leadership in the United States Senate who understands the problems New Hampshire is facing, who will stand up to the recklessness of this administration, lower costs and make life better for Granite Staters," he said in a debate last week.
Pappas frequently sought to link Sununu to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu despite Sununu once calling him a loser. He accused Sununu of having "a selective memory about what's been going on over the last couple of years" and told him, "The guy who gave you his complete and total endorsement is wrecking New Hampshire's Main Street economy."
"This election is about Team New Hampshire versus Team Trump," Pappas said. "This is not a moment to restore someone who was out of step with New Hampshire before and bring them back into power."
Mike Bradley, 77, a licensed mental health counselor from Bow, described his vote for Pappas as "almost more anti- than pro-."
"I'm so disgusted with what Republicans in general are doing with Trump at the helm, and pretty much no one's standing up to him. The corruption, the homophobia, the transphobia, the endless war," he said. " I'm hoping that Democrats can grab a majority and counteract all this negative stuff."
Only one Chris was on the ballot
Sununu easily defeated former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown and a handful of lesser-known candidates to win the Republican nomination. His first name was conspicuously absent from his green, blue and white campaign signs, and critics said he was counting on voters confusing him with his popular younger brother, Chris Sununu, who served eight years as governor. Their father also is a former governor.
Once the Senate's youngest member, Sununu is now 62, older than Shaheen was when he bragged in a campaign advertisement about being younger and faster than she was. He derided Pappas as an ineffective and out-of-touch "career politician" despite the fact that Sununu traveled a similar path from the House to the Senate and comes from a family whose name is synonymous with Republican politics in New Hampshire.
"Chris Pappas talks about all the things he wants to do and wants to accomplish, but he's been there for eight years and he hasn't gotten the job done," Sununu said during the debate. "I'll focus on the right issues. I'll stand up to my party and the president when it's right for New Hampshire, and I'll get things done."
Voters deluged by attack ads and mailers
Campaign cash poured in from all sides, though data compiled by AdImpact and OpenSecrets.org showed Republicans were spending considerably more as the race tightened.
Republicans accused Pappas of catering to Washington lobbyists and party bosses, describing the race as "problem solver Sununu" vs. "puppet Pappas." "New Hampshire needs a leader, not a lightweight," one ad from the National Republican Senatorial Committee concluded.
Pro-Pappas ads, meanwhile, accused Sununu of making millions off his political connections and highlighted the Sununu name appearing in the Epstein files. In a 2010 email, Jeffrey Epstein said Sununu "has good stories." It's unclear whether he meant the current candidate or his father, John H. Sununu, but Sununu says neither of them ever met or communicated with Epstein or the recipient of the email.

title: Iranian officials say midterm results show US voters have rejected Trump’s war
text:
(AP) - Iranians on Wednesday struck a defiant tone, celebrating U.S. voters’ rebuke of President Donald Trump in the midterm elections while many in the Middle East waited to see how the results could affect the Iran war.
Concerns about the war, particularly frustration over rising prices for fuel and other goods in the U.S., helped Democrats win control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s vote, a sharp setback for Trump and his Republican Party.
But Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father and predecessor was killed in the opening strikes of the war in February, dismissed the prospect of any major change in the U.S. approach to the Islamic Republic.
“If there are still those who harbor even a slight hope for a change in behavior or partisan and factional shifts within the system of domination, or who imagine that by giving concessions to America they can dissuade it from hostility toward the Iranian nation, they are gravely mistaken,” he said on his social media account.
There are fears that full-scale fighting could resume
The broader region has been on edge for weeks over the prospect of the U.S. resuming full-scale military operations against Iran. Talks aimed at preventing renewed fighting are continuing, while other U.S. allies in the region urge Washington against resuming a war that began more than eight months ago and has rattled the global economy and devastated Iran.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reportedly pushed for more strikes, while Trump has alternated between threatening major military action and pushing for a deal.
Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, wrote Wednesday on X that “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message.” He warned that if the U.S. government ignores the vote for change, “it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare.”
Despite ceasefire agreements and repeated diplomatic efforts, military confrontations have continued in southern Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson said in a social media post that Americans had sent a clear message and warned Washington against ignoring it. If the U.S. continues to ignore reality, the spokesperson said, “the consequences of this grave miscalculation will extend far beyond what you have already witnessed.”
Iran marks anniversary of 1979 seizure of US Embassy
Underscoring the mutual hostility at the heart of the conflict, thousands marched through Tehran on Wednesday at a government-organized demonstration commemorating the anniversary of the 1979 takeover of the U.S. Embassy.
Pro-government demonstrators burned American and Israeli flags and chanted “Death to America” and “Death to Israel.” They displayed effigies of Trump and Netanyahu alongside caricatures of the two leaders.
“Trump has gone too far in everything and that’s one reason for his defeat in the election,” said Hananeh Jahed, a demonstrator.
Zahra Nadiminejad praised Iranian resistance, saying U.S. voters “finally figured out that this is Iran, and they can’t just come in here and do whatever the hell they want.”
“They’ve seen the consequences of the war back home, from skyrocketing gas and food prices to all the devastating effects the war has had on their own country. And whether the Democrats win or the Republicans win, our hostility toward America will never come to an end.”
Nearly five decades ago, Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy on Nov. 4, 1979, taking American diplomats and other citizens hostage. Fifty-two Americans were held for 444 days before being released.
The crisis helped cement the rupture between the two countries, which have had no formal diplomatic relations for years.
The United States and Israel launched the war against Iran on Feb. 28, killing the country’s longtime supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, and triggering a conflict that has disrupted global energy markets and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Addressing the demonstrators on Wednesday, Tehran Mayor Alireza Zakani claimed the United States and Israel had suffered a massive defeat, which he said was also reflected in last week’s Israeli elections.
“The decisive defeat of the United States and the Zionist regime in recent developments and elections is the result of the Iranian nation’s steadfastness and strength,” Zakani said.
Iranian targets hit ahead of the midterms
The U.S. elections came just a day after what appeared to be a limited strike on Iranian targets in the crucial Strait of Hormuz waterway, which renewed questions about what might come next.
Iranian state media reported explosions Monday on Qeshm and Hengam islands and near the southern port city of Bandar Abbas. Iranian authorities have not publicly identified the specific sites struck or disclosed the extent of the damage.
The Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited before the war, has seen repeated Iranian attacks on commercial shipping. Iran has sought to restrict shipping to pressure the U.S. to lift its blockade on Iranian ports.
Iran’s state TV said Wednesday that four oil tankers caught fire after they struck mines on what it described as unauthorized routes.
Back-channel negotiations have continued.
U.S. Vice President JD Vance said Monday that he and Trump “both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
Before the latest strikes, the Trump administration’s last known attacks on Iran were in early September. Thousands of U.S. troops remain in waters off Iran to maintain the naval blockade, aimed at preventing tankers carrying Iranian oil from reaching the global market. Another aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are on their way to the Middle East.
___
This story was corrected to show that the U.S. Embassy siege was nearly five decades ago, not three.
___
Associated Press writers Samy Magdy, Toqa Ezzidin and Aamer Madhani contributed to this report.

title: Dem. Chris Pappas wins Senate seat in New Hampshire, becomes first openly gay male senator
text:
CONCORD, N.H. (AP) — U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu in New Hampshire on Tuesday, keeping a critical open U.S. Senate seat in the hands of Democrats as they regained control of the chamber.
The race to fill the seat being vacated by three-term Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen was one of a handful that helped determine the balance of power in the Senate. Republicans were hoping to regain a foothold in the region while Democrats didn’t want to lose ground.
Pappas told supporters his win was a “victory for Team New Hampshire over the broken status quo.”
“Tonight’s results are a wake-up call for corporate special interests and billionaires who have been rigging the economy, for the cowards in Congress who have enabled health care cuts, tariffs and war, and for the incompetent president who can’t even be bothered to care how people are being hurt,” he said.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER

Sununu railed against “career politicians” despite having spent three terms in the U.S. House and one in the Senate before being ousted by Shaheen in 2008. Pappas told voters “Our country is ready for change” while seeking to remain in Washington, where he has represented the state’s 1st Congressional District since 2019.
New Hampshire voters haven’t elected a Republican to Congress since 2010. They also have voted for Democrats for president since 2004, though Republicans have dominated at the state level in recent years. With the win, Pappas will become the first openly gay male U.S. senator. He will be succeeded in the House by Shaheen’s daughter, Stefany Shaheen.
‘Team New Hampshire vs. Team Trump’
Pappas, 46, grew up working in his family’s Manchester restaurant, which opened in 1917 and claims to have invented chicken tenders. After college, he served as a state lawmaker, county treasurer and state executive councilor before being elected to Congress. In September, he defeated a democratic socialist and other opponents by a wide margin to win the Democratic primary.
“This has been a long campaign against the backdrop of chaos, corruption and costs coming out of Washington,” Pappas told supporters Tuesday night in Manchester. “New Hampshire showed up today, you spoke up today, you said in a resounding voice that New Hampshire needs a course correction. Washington needs a new generation at the table to fix things.”
Voters were particularly likely to say government corruption was “crucial” for their vote, and Pappas won most of them, according to The AP Voter Poll. He won an even greater share of voters who said the state of democracy was the most important issue facing the country.
Pappas frequently sought to link Sununu to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu despite Sununu once calling him a loser. He accused Sununu of having “a selective memory about what’s been going on over the last couple of years” and told him, “The guy who gave you his complete and total endorsement is wrecking New Hampshire’s Main Street economy.”
“This election is about Team New Hampshire versus Team Trump,” Pappas said during a debate last week. “This is not a moment to restore someone who was out of step with New Hampshire before and bring them back into power.”
Most New Hampshire voters thought Sununu was “too supportive” of Trump, while only about 4 in 10 said Pappas was “too extreme,” according to The AP Voter Poll.
Mike Bradley, 77, a licensed mental health counselor from Bow, described his vote for Pappas as “almost more anti- than pro-.”
“I’m so disgusted with what Republicans in general are doing with Trump at the helm, and pretty much no one’s standing up to him. The corruption, the homophobia, the transphobia, the endless war,” he said. “ I’m hoping that Democrats can grab a majority and counteract all this negative stuff.”
Only one Chris was on the ballot
Sununu easily defeated former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown and a handful of lesser-known candidates to win the Republican nomination. His first name was conspicuously absent from his green, blue and white campaign signs, and critics said he was counting on voters confusing him with his popular younger brother, Chris Sununu, who served eight years as governor. Their father also is a former governor.
Once the Senate’s youngest member, Sununu is now 62, older than Shaheen was when he bragged in a campaign advertisement about being younger and faster than she was. He derided Pappas as an ineffective and out-of-touch “career politician” despite the fact that Sununu traveled a similar path from the House to the Senate and comes from a family whose name is synonymous with Republican politics in New Hampshire.
“This has been an incredible campaign, but it’s not our night,” Sununu told his supporters, conceding the race about 10 minutes after the last polls closed.
Voters deluged by attack ads and mailers
Campaign cash poured in from all sides, though data compiled by AdImpact and OpenSecrets.org showed Republicans were spending considerably more as the race tightened.
Republicans accused Pappas of catering to Washington lobbyists and party bosses, describing the race as “problem solver Sununu” vs. “puppet Pappas.” “New Hampshire needs a leader, not a lightweight,” one ad from the National Republican Senatorial Committee concluded.
Pro-Pappas ads, meanwhile, accused Sununu of making millions off his political connections and highlighted the Sununu name appearing in the Epstein files. In a 2010 email, Jeffrey Epstein said Sununu “has good stories.” It’s unclear whether he meant the current candidate or his father, John H. Sununu, but Sununu says neither of them ever met or communicated with Epstein or the recipient of the email.

title: Troy Jackson won’t back Chuck Schumer. Will that affect his influence?
text:
Super PACs aligned with Democratic Senate Leader Chuck Schumer of New York spent tens of millions of dollars in ads aimed at toppling Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
WinSenate and Majority Forward spent more than $46 million to benefit Jackson, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact. The figure represented more than half of the ad spending by Democratic allies since Jackson became the nominee on July 25.
But that investment — largely on attack ads that chipped away at the image Collins tried to cultivate of a moderate, independent public servant — isn’t generating any newfound loyalty from Troy Jackson.
Jackson, who decisively beat Collins on Tuesday, said throughout the campaign that he would not support Schumer as Senate leader. Instead, he’s largely aligned himself with the progressive wing of the party led by Sens. Bernie Sanders, I-Vermont, and Elizabeth Warren, D-Massachusetts.
Jackson reaffirmed his opposition to Schumer when asked by national press on Tuesday.
“I’ve told Sen. Schumer I’m going to support somebody else, so it’s no different now,” Jackson said in a video posted by CBS News.
Jackson’s unwillingness to support Schumer could affect his prospects for committee assignments or influence within the party as a freshman, said Mark Brewer, chair of political science at the University of Maine in Orono.
“But if Jackson is out (in) front of what turns out to be a larger Democratic rebellion against Schumer that results in a different leader, that could really benefit Jackson both inside and outside of the chamber,” Brewer said.
A spokesperson for Jackson said Wednesday that it was premature to talk about who the senator-elect wants to become Democratic leader.
Other possible leadership candidates include Sens. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Cory Booker of New Jersey.
Schumer only needs the support of a majority of his caucus to be reelected leader. He told reporters on Wednesday that he expects to win another term as leader.
“The issue is not me. I’ll be reelected as majority leader. But the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want,” Schumer told reporters in a video posted by CNN.
With Democrats projected to win 54 to 56 seats, the party will set the legislative agenda in Washington, D.C., and control key committees that set spending and policy priorities. A poor relationship with leadership could hinder Jackson’s ability to get the committee assignments he wants.
A Jackson spokesperson said Wednesday that it was also premature to talk about what committees assignments he would like.
But Politico reported that Jackson expressed interest in serving on the finance; commerce; and Health, Education, Labor and Pensions committees. He also expressed interest in the Senate Appropriations Committee, which Collins chaired.
“I know it’s based on seniority, but I think if I beat the appropriations chair, then I should be on appropriations. That’s going to be my argument, anyways,” Jackson said on Tuesday, according to Politico.

title: Democrats’ sweeping state government gains will shift power and bring pressure to deliver results
text:
MADISON, Wis. (AP) — Democrats in Texas took control of the state House after historic wins for governor and U.S. Senate, part of a series of sweeping gains nationwide in Tuesday’s elections that shifted the balance of power across several battleground and Republican-leaning states.
It will be the first time Democrats control the House in Texas since Republicans took over after the 2002 election. Republicans are keeping control of the Senate in the state — which also elected Gina Hinojosa its first Democratic governor since George W. Bush ousted Ann Richards in 1994.
In this year’s midterm elections, the party took full control — both statehouse chambers and governors’ offices — in at least five states where they previously shared power.
The wins put pressure on the party to answer to an electorate angry over the rising cost of living, high gas prices, inflation and the lack of affordable housing. State governments shape a wide array of policies affecting everyday lives, including tax rates and abortion rights, school choice and education funding, data center development, and the use of artificial intelligence and law enforcement surveillance cameras.
“Now it’s time to deliver,” said Devin Remiker, chairman of Wisconsin’s Democratic Party, which retained the governor’s office and successfully flipped both chambers of the state Legislature, breaking a 16-year Republican majority.
Democrats prevail in battleground states
Democrats also won or retained full control of both chambers of the legislatures in Michigan, Minnesota and Pennsylvania and kept the governor’s office for trifectas in all three.
In Nevada, they gained control by winning the governor’s seat and retaining the legislature.
U.S. HOUSE BALANCE OF POWER
There will be pressure on Democrats in Wisconsin and other battleground states to redraw congressional maps, just as President Donald Trump successfully urged eight Republican-led states to do ahead of this election. But that backfired, with Republicans losing most of the Democratic-held seats they had targeted to flip and others they had banked on winning.
The Republican congressional redistricting in Texas may have mobilized additional Democratic voters in some parts of the state who helped drive gains in the statehouse, said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston.
But “when we’re trying to think about why Democrats won, it’s one man in the White House and his policies — Donald Trump,” Jones said.
Even under maps that favored Republicans in Wisconsin, Democrats picked up two congressional seats in Tuesday’s races. That means the state will have an evenly divided congressional delegation in 2027.
Democrats also break up Republican trifectas and supermajorities
Democrats will also hold at least 28 governorships in 2027, with pickups in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and Texas — states long held by Republicans.
And the party broke or prevented Republican supermajorities in nine legislative chambers in eight states: Florida, South Carolina, Indiana, Missouri, Iowa, Ohio, Kansas and North Carolina.
That means Republicans would need help from Democratic lawmakers to override a Democratic governor’s veto in Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina. The Associated Press has not called the governor’s race in Kansas.
The wins come after Democrats lost nearly 1,000 state legislative seats during President Barack Obama’s tenure, a slide they’ve been trying to reverse for several cycles.
It’s the biggest single-election change of partisan power in state governments since 2010, said Katie Owens Hubler, director of elections and redistricting at the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Lawmakers who will soon be in the majority say the change brings expectations. “We know that people will be counting on us to deliver, and we take that incredibly seriously,” said Wisconsin state Rep. Greta Neubauer, currently the minority leader of state Assembly Democrats.
Heather Williams, president of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said the party won “historic levels of power in statehouses.” She said they hadn’t flipped this many seats nationwide since the 1980s.
This time, she said, Democrats will have to focus on issues that matter to middle-class voters such as improving educational opportunities and increasing access to healthcare, particularly in rural areas.
“This election is about kitchen-table issues; it’s about economic opportunities,” she said Wednesday. “That is what the mandate is about.”
Wins put spotlight on Democratic priorities in 2027
The cost of groceries, housing, healthcare, gas and utility bills were campaign talking points after legislative sessions packed with bills aiming to make life more affordable for Americans, while also providing tax relief and reining in data center development and the use of artificial intelligence.
The coming legislative session could see major efforts to lighten the tax burden on the middle class, relax housing regulations, expand access to healthcare, and force utilities and data center developers to do more to stop electricity bills from rising.
Democratic Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who won reelection, told his supporters Tuesday night that people want him and lawmakers to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, invest in infrastructure, kids, police and communities, and enshrine abortion rights for women in the state constitution.
Other newly elected governors, including Wisconsin’s David Crowley and Minnesota’s Amy Klobuchar, said they wanted to work with Republicans.
“I am not interested in moving Minnesota to the left or the right; I want to move us forward,” Klobuchar said.
She even had a warning for her Democratic supporters.
“Spoiler alert: You may not like every single thing I do,” she said.

title: Northern Light Health to regionalize services and expand outpatient care
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Northern Light Health plans to regionalize its services and expand outpatient care as the system works to regain its footing following disastrous financial losses in 2024.
System leaders see the move as a sweeping change that will fundamentally alter how the healthcare network operates at its highest levels and help patients get appointments more easily. Dr. Guy Hudson, president and CEO of Northern Light Health, wants to swap the system’s current setup, where hospitals are the center of care, for a new one that instead prioritizes services around patients.
Inpatient care includes the services people typically imagine when they think of a hospital stay, like overnight care after a major surgery. Anything that can be done in one day, such as X-rays, annual physicals or routine tests, such as a mammogram or colonoscopy, is considered outpatient.
“The way things have been built in Maine is all services kind of center around hospitals,” Hudson said in an exclusive interview Tuesday with the Bangor Daily News. “We have to evolve.”
Northern Light’s leaders believe that shifting this approach is the best path toward financial sustainability as hospitals across the state are struggling in the face of high costs and Medicaid cuts, though they could provide few concrete details of what this plan will entail, and it seems that patients will see the effects gradually.
Hudson started in his role one year ago, putting the health system on a three-year plan aiming to claw Northern Light out of its financial hole. He reported that the system is on track toward that goal, and returns from the end of 2025 already showed far smaller losses than the previous year.
“We’re stable, but it doesn’t necessarily mean sustainability,” Hudson said, adding that there is still work to be done to protect the hospital system’s future.
Northern Light needs to make more money in order to fund the significant infrastructure improvements its aging facilities need, Hudson said. He also noted that the system is not planning for layoffs at this time. Northern Light did recently hire its first chief clinical officer, Dr. Dean Kindler, and chief nursing officer, Dena Keilman, both of which are positions that will oversee the entire system.
The system’s planned shift will “improve access, and it will improve timeliness of care for patients that need it,” Hudson said. Part of that will include regionalizing hospital operations and governance into three regions covering the entire state: north, central and south. That means regional leaders will oversee multiple hospitals in an area, and will absorb some of the administrative responsibilities from those who are in charge of individual hospitals.
To do this, Northern Light will need to expand outpatient networks so patients “only come into hospitals when they actually need that higher level of care,” said Hudson, who added that the top complaint he hears from the public is people having trouble getting appointments at Northern Light facilities.
The system is aiming to get patients in to see a provider quicker when they need it. That means even if a patient can’t get in at their usual primary care office, there will be more flexibility to be seen somewhere else in the system and avoid a hospital visit.
“In other words, it’s getting the organization to connect with itself,” Hudson said.
Outpatient services are generally cheaper than inpatient services. Bolstering them at Northern Light could mean expanding the system’s own outpatient services or finding a partner that’s more established in that realm, Hudson said, but the CEO didn’t share what steps the system will take to achieve this when asked follow-up questions.
Such a partnership would fit into Hudson’s broader vision for healthcare in Maine, where he thinks providers need to work more closely together, starting by building a statewide electronic healthcare record system. Doing so would acknowledge the reality that many people shift between facilities run by different providers, he said.
“Maine is perfectly positioned to actually make these transitions,” Hudson said, adding that he was part of creating a similar model in western Washington earlier in his career.
Numerous financial challenges are looming for Maine healthcare providers, including low MaineCare reimbursement rates and planned changes to a federal drug pricing program that hospitals say would cost them millions. Northern Light is part of a lawsuit filed last month by the American Hospital Association against Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the federal Department of Health and Human Services over those changes.
“Maine is very, very dependent on 340B revenue,” Hudson said, referring to the name of the program that sets discounts on prescription drugs for safety-net healthcare providers.
Congress’ nonrenewal of the Affordable Care Act subsidies that helped make health insurance more affordable for millions of Americans has also presented challenges for the healthcare system and its patients, according to Hudson.
“We’ve already seen this increase in bad debt, with people not being able to pay,” he said.

title: China voting results (November 2026)
text:
China voters re-elected three select board members, running without opposition, and approved the other four questions on their local ballot, notably supporting an expenditure for a new fire truck.
The truck will be owned by the town and used by the China Village Volunteer Fire Department. Voters authorized spending up to $750,000 for the vehicle, including $200,000 previously appropriated and any grants or gifts received.
The vote was 1,596 in favor to 488 opposed.
In the following article, voters authorized issuing up to $550,000 in bonds, through the Maine Bond Bank or another appropriate institution, to pay for the truck. That vote was 1,587 to 482.
By slightly wider margins, voters repealed an outdated solid waste ordinance and replaced it with a new one, 1,703 in favor to 403 opposed; and amended sections of the town’s Land Development Code, 1,669 to 428.
The votes for the three select board members were as follows: Edwin Bailey, 1,292; Blane Casey, 1,510; and Thomas Rumpf, 1,289.
A total of 2,241 ballots were cast in the local election.
On the state ballot, 2,247 China residents voted as follows:
— For United States Senate, Republican Susan Collins 1,333 votes; Democrat Troy Jackson, 871 votes.
— For governor, Republican Robert B. Charles, 1,104; Democrat Hannah Pingree, 942; and Independent Rick Bennett, 178.
— For representative to Congress, Republican Ronald Russell, 1,168; Democrat Chellie Pingree, 1,041.
— For District 15 State Senator, Republican Kati McCormick, 1,212; Democrat Amanda Ann Heath, 996.
— For District 62 Representative to the state legislature, Republican Katrina Smith, 1,252; Democrat Pamela Jo Swift, 954.

title: Hakeem Jeffries poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House
text:
Hakeem Jeffries poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House
Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is on the cusp of making history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a generational shift in U.S. politics after Democrats trounced Republicans to win majority control of the chamber in the midterm elections.
Jeffries faces a vote of his colleagues when the new Congress convenes Jan. 3. If nominated and elected, as expected, it would be the first time a Black lawmaker has grasped the powerful House speaker’s gavel, a job second in line to the president and the only leadership position in Congress mandated by the U.S. Constitution.
His rise to the speakership at the nation’s domed Capitol, which enslaved African Americans helped build, would be a milestone more than 150 years in the making, tracing an arc of history that began when the first Black American was elected to the U.S. House in the turbulent era of Reconstruction after the Civil War. Jeffries would wield the gavel at a time when many of the landmark gains of the 20th century Civil Rights era are being challenged anew, often by the Trump administration.
Jeffries was met with cheers of “Speaker! Speaker!” at the Democrats’ watch party in Washington.
“This is not a partisan moment. This is a patriotic one,” Jeffries said.
He said House Democrats understand that this is a change election, and “the American people are crying out for transformational change.”
“We hear you,” he said. “We’re going to work hard to deliver on the dramatic change that you deserve.”
The Brooklyn-born 56-year-old Jeffries, who is known to sprinkle old-school hip hop lyrics in his freestyle remarks, would take over the office from Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, at a time when Democrats are eager to confront President Donald Trump’s final two years in office.
The president has publicly and privately taunted Jeffries, a New York University-educated lawyer, who has served in Congress since 2013, and is the highest-ranking Black elected official in America. Trump once mocked Jeffries by posting on social media a fake photo of the Democratic leader wearing a sombrero outside the White House.
The whole House votes on its speaker as one of the first orders of business when Congress convenes in January. The parties typically choose their leaders during internal caucus elections in November.
Jeffries is charting a new course for Democrats after Pelosi
The path ahead has been clear for Jeffries and his leadership team, with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who have often moved as a trio representing a new era of House leadership. Clark is expected to become the majority leader and Aguilar the majority whip.
Jeffries would be the first Democratic speaker since Nancy Pelosi and he has led the party for the past four years, with her support, once she decided to step aside after the Democrats’ election losses in 2022.
But Jeffries and the team of Democratic leaders will be quickly tested in the majority, with all the power and responsibility that comes with running the often unruly House.
They are bracing to confront not only Trump, but also the fresh group of Democrats elected to office, including a handful backed by the Democratic Socialists of America pushing the party leftward, though the largest caucus in the House is expected to remain the more moderate New Democrat Coalition.
Jeffries has promised a robust 100-day agenda to lower the costs of living and launch oversight and investigations to hold the Trump administration accountable. Impeachment is an option.
Promising to show voters that Democrats can govern, Jeffries and the leadership team hope to hold their new majority together and avoid the kinds of chaotic disruptions and dysfunction that often left Johnson unable to control the GOP’s razor-slim majority in the House.
Colleagues have praised Jeffries’ collaborative style, a listener who represents a shift from Pelosi’s powerful tenure as the nation’s first female speaker of the House.
But at the same time, his calm-is-a-choice deliberative nature has drawn criticism that Jeffries can be too slow to act in the frenzied political environment when voters are seeking swift reaction to mounting crises and concerns.
Soaring healthcare costs, gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran, Trump’s relationship with Putin over Ukraine and concerns about corruption are all top issues ahead.
His path to power runs from Brooklyn to Washington
The son of an Air Force veteran and a social worker, Jeffries told The Associated Press on the campaign trail that growing up during the crack epidemic in New York shaped his sense of purpose.
His experience led to “a desire to want to improve the quality of life for hardworking people, who could have fled difficult circumstances but remained in the community, worked hard to turn things around,” he said.
A married father of two, Jeffries grew up steeped in Brooklyn’s Cornerstone Baptist Church, and represents parts of the Brooklyn-area district once held by trailblazing Rep. Shirley Chisholm.
He earned a bachelor’s degree from the State University of New York at Binghamton, a master's degree in public policy at Georgetown and graduated magna cum laude from NYU School of Law. He worked as a corporate lawyer and served in the New York state assembly before being elected to Congress.
An insurgent himself, Jeffries was 29 when he first ran for office, failing twice in his initial campaigns for state government. In 2012 he challenged a 30-year incumbent member of Congress, who stepped aside as Jeffries swooped in to win the seat.
A member of the Congressional Black Caucus, Jeffries follows in the footsteps of those who came before, including Joseph Rainey, the first Black American elected to the House in 1870. While Rainey never became speaker, he was the first Black lawmaker to preside with the gavel over the House chamber.

title: The Best New Movies to Watch at Home This Weekend
text:
The Best New Movies You Can Watch at Home This Weekend
New movies are coming to streaming this week and every week, at a faster pace than ever before. As always, ScreenCrush has your back, with a weekly guide to the latest releases on streaming (and digital rental or purchse) that deserve your attention. Sit back, relax, and check out what’s coming to a TV or computer (or, sigh, a phone) near you.
Then you’ve got all weekend to watch up with these titles. The theater is still the best, of course, but some weekends you just can’t muster the energy to get off the couch and haul yourself to the multiplex.
New Movies Streaming This Week and Weekend
This week you can watch Zach Cregger’s terrific adaptation of Resident Evil, watch Robert Pattinson take on Chris Hansen and To Catch a Predator, or go back to the 1300s with Andrew Garfield and Paul Greengrass.
If these titles don’t do it for you, you can also check out some other recent streaming releases here. Or just keep scrolling, and see the new movies you can stream or rent on digital at home this weekend.
Resident Evil
There have been so many Resident Evil movies to date, and some of them have their defenders. But at least for me, Zach Cregger’s recent adaptation is far and away the best of them all — and it isn’t even close. Like the classic games, it starts from a relatively grounded place, when a medical courier (Austin Abrams) sets out on a snowy night to deliver an important package to Raccoon City. By the end, it is out-and-out monster madness.
Where to watch Resident Evil: Prime Video, Apple TV, Fandango.
The Uprising
Is this movie a sneaky, gritty Robin Hood tale? That depends on who you ask! (Some U.S. ads called it “The Uprising: The Rise of Robin Hood” while its U.K. distributor stated publicly “The Uprising is a historical epic about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, not Robin Hood.“ Either way, it stars Andrew Garfield, and was written and directed by The Bourne Ultimatum and Captain Phillips’ Paul Greengrass, in a story inspired by the Peasants’ Revolt in 1380s England.
Where to watch The Uprising: Premieres on November 6 on Peacock.
Possible Love
South Korea’s official entry in this year’s race for the Academy Award for Best International Film is this drama from Lee Chang-dong, the gifted filmmaker behind titles like Poetry and Burning. Per Netflix, Possible Love “follows two married couples — a laid-off worker and his wife, and a documentary filmmaker and her husband — whose paths cross when the filmmaker sets out to film them, bringing both marriages face to face with their different lives and hidden desires.”
Where to watch Possible Love: Premieres on November 6 on Netflix.
Primetime
Robert Pattinson plays a twisted version of NBC journalist Chris Hansen in Primetime, Lance Oppenheim’s fictionalized account of the behind-the-scenes drama of the infamous series To Catch a Predator. Between this and his work co-directing You Can See Everything, Oppenheim is having one hell of a fall.
Where to watch Primetime: Prime Video, Apple TV, Fandango.
Motor City
This thriller starring Reacher’s Alan Ritchson played at the Venice and Toronto Film Festivals; Ritchson stars as a “1970s Detroit a working-class romantic” who is “framed by a ruthless gangster after falling for his girlfriend. After years in prison, he returns with only one mission: revenge.” Uh oh.
Where to watch Motor City: Premieres on November 6 on AMC+.

title: Trump responds as voters deliver rebuke by flipping key GOP-held Senate seats
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — For Donald Trump, his party’s resounding midterm losses pave the way for investigations and potential impeachments that will put the Republican president on the defensive in his final two years in office.
The results shift the center of gravity closer to Capitol Hill, where Democrats will be angling to check Trump’s power after two years of acquiescence from congressional Republicans. It not only resurfaces a dynamic from his first term in office, when House Democrats took power in Trump’s first midterms and ultimately impeached him twice, but with control as well of the Senate, Democrats can now stymie Trump’s nominations to Cabinet posts and lifetime federal judgeships.
Trump had all but guaranteed the results would be seen as a referendum on himself by repeatedly urging voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” as he went into primarily conservative states to shore up Republican candidates and warned of a Washington where Democrats were in power.
But the results showed how voters rejected Trump’s handpicked candidates while airing widespread concerns about high costs in the wake of his war against Iran and his punishing tariff policy.
Trump tried to shift the blame away from himself during a Fox News interview that aired early Wednesday, saying Democrats “did a good job” in their campaigns and faulting GOP candidates for their losses. “I don’t view it as a hit on me,” he said.
The results leave Trump — who watched returns at the White House with his advisers and members of his Cabinet — with dramatically diminished political capital at home and abroad.
From investigations to impeachment, the stakes for Trump are high
Senior Democrats, as they anticipated a majority in at least one chamber of Congress, have been telegraphing what their top investigative targets would be: the Trump administration’s policies, the conduct of its personnel, and interactions between government officials and private corporations who’ve tried to wield influence with the White House.
Among their priorities are the Trump family’s business dealings, the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and broader allegations of corporate corruption.
A Democratic majority will be armed with control of committees, bigger budgets and staff, and subpoena powers that could compel the administration to be responsive to Congress. In response, the White House could reprise its strategy from the first Trump administration, when it slow-walked congressional requests for documents and testimony and asserted executive privilege over certain information.
The president is also bracing for major legislative fights, saying he has a “strong veto.” On Tuesday night, Trump posted a picture of his signature red ball cap with “VETO” stitched on it.
Voters blame Trump’s economic policies
Placing himself front and center on voters’ minds was a major gamble by the president and his political team, who believed it would drive “Make America Great Again” supporters to the polls. Democrats were eager to watch the unpopular president insert himself so fully in the campaign, believing it served as an effective reminder of who should be blamed for the state of the economy.
“Trump’s desire to have everyone think that he’s on the ballot? Like, it’s happening,” said Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., who campaigned in key battlegrounds this fall, including Iowa, Georgia and Texas. “Everyone is thinking about him and the harm that he has done to them directly.”
The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of the midterm electorate, showed relatively few voters had positive things to say about Trump’s performance on the economy. About two-thirds of voters nationally say Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., while only about 3 in 10 say they’ve improved economic conditions. Similarly, about two-thirds of voters said Trump’s tariff policies have “hurt” the national economy, or the economy in their local area.
Views of Trump’s priorities more broadly — and his capabilities as a leader — were also mostly negative. More than half of voters say Trump is not a strong leader, does not fight for people like them, does not have the right priorities and does not have the mental capability to serve effectively as president. About 6 in 10 voters say Trump places a higher priority on his own personal interests than he does the country’s interests, while about 4 in 10 said he puts more weight on the country’s interests.
The president — who faced a Democratic-led House for the latter half of his first term — campaigned aggressively in the final weeks to keep the Republican majorities on Capitol Hill because he knows what the consequences would be if Democrats seize power.
But the president at times shrugged off the prospect of a Republican loss of power in Congress. The president is also keenly aware of the political power he draws from having a foil, leveraging opposition to consolidate support in his party and boost fundraising.
Trump’s choices for GOP races had their own baggage
In the House, Democrats flipped districts that voted for Trump by as much as 18 points in 2024. Democrats won at least seven Senate seats in ruby-red states and battlegrounds alike: Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina.
Despite urging voters to use their imagination when reading names on the ballot, Trump’s hand-picked Republican candidates in Texas and South Carolina faced deep skepticism.
Republican Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina after a campaign in which she faced questions about her inexperience.
Republican Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico in Texas, was impeached by his own party over corruption accusations and stained by a very public divorce. But Trump backed him instead of powerful incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, whom he viewed as not sufficiently supportive.
Trump’s loyalty pressures also led incumbent Republican Sen. Thom Tillis in North Carolina to decide to retire after clashing with the president. To try to keep that seat in GOP hands, Trump backed his close ally Michael Whatley, who lost to Democrat Roy Cooper.
Trump was also dealt twin defeats in two Midwestern states that had borne the brunt of high diesel prices and his tariff war. Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Roger Marshall in Kansas, while Republican Ashley Hinson lost to Democrat Josh Turek.
In another sign of Republican weakness, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, whom Trump had endorsed and repeatedly praised. On Tuesday night, Trump posted on social media that Abbott was to blame for his loss, calling him a “RINO” — a Republican in name only.
