title: Looking a bit scruffy for a good cause during No Shave November
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Joshua Bridges is a nurse practitioner who lives and works in Bangor.
If you see me this month, please forgive my scruffy appearance. It’s for a good cause! No Shave November began in 2009 as a grassroots effort to raise awareness and funds for cancer research and men’s health. The idea is simple: Put down the razor, grow some facial hair, start a conversation, and donate what you might have spent on grooming to a worthy cause.
One of the most striking health disparities is that women in the United States live nearly five years longer than men, on average. In 2024, life expectancy was 81.4 years for women and 76.5 years for men in the U.S.
There are many reasons for this difference, including biology, but some are within our control. Men are more likely to engage in risky behaviors, smoke, drink excessively, delay routine medical care, and neglect preventive health measures. We can’t control everything, but we can do better.
The insurance companies and actuaries know something about risk, too. If you’ve ever purchased automobile insurance for a young man, you know that it can be expensive. Young men are statistically more likely to engage in risky driving behaviors.
Unfortunately, risk-taking doesn’t necessarily end in our twenties. Consider ladders. Falls from ladders cause thousands of workplace injuries every year, and men experience higher rates of these injuries. (In fact, spending some time on a ladder at my house last weekend helped inspire this column.)
Two male friends of mine died in their twenties. One was a college student killed in an interstate automobile accident. He wasn’t wearing a seatbelt. The other was a friend and coworker who died from complications of testicular cancer just weeks after the birth of his second child. Could either death have been prevented? I don’t know. But their stories have stayed with me.
Soon after my fortieth birthday, I had my own encounter with cancer. A routine eye examination detected a rare but potentially lethal cancer called uveal melanoma in my right eye. It was treated with radiation, and I’ve been undergoing ongoing surveillance for metastatic disease.
Thankfully, three years later, I remain healthy, with no evidence of metastases. Multiple experts have told me that detecting it early probably saved my life.
That experience prompted me to take a fresh look at how I care for myself. For me, that means eating well, exercising, nurturing social and spiritual wellness, and being a little more careful when I’m on a ladder.
I’m not suggesting we live in a shell. In fact, I believe one of the secrets to a fulfilling life is learning to be adventurous while managing risk. Am I going to avoid the outdoors because I had a rare melanoma in my eye? Absolutely not. But if you see me outside, chances are I’ll be wearing a hat and sunglasses.
Science is also opening exciting new doors. The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, helped launch a new era of genetic research. We now know much more about how inherited genetic variations influence disease risk. Research into epigenetics, which examines how genes are regulated, is expanding our understanding of how biology and the environment interact. Personalized medicine holds considerable promise, although we still have much to learn.
So what can men do today? Start with the basics. Eat more vegetables, exercise regularly, avoid tobacco, moderate alcohol consumption, and take sensible precautions when participating in potentially dangerous activities. Establish a relationship with a primary care provider and don’t ignore symptoms or unusual changes in your body. Discuss your individual cancer risks and appropriate screening schedules. Colorectal cancer screening should begin at age 45 for most adults. Decisions about prostate cancer screening should be made with your healthcare provider after discussing the potential benefits and risks. Don’t neglect dental and eye care.
No Shave November is a fun way to start a serious conversation. This month, let’s do more than grow a beard. Let’s make a commitment to taking better care of ourselves. We may not be able to control how long we live, but we can do a lot to influence how well we live.

title: El-Sayed says Michigan rejected ‘hateful, spiteful campaign’ by Republicans after being labeled ‘jihadist’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed told The Associated Press on Wednesday that Michigan voters had rejected “a hateful, spiteful campaign” after months of Republican attacks on his Muslim identity in one of the nation’s most closely watched Senate races.
El-Sayed said he was “running on adrenaline and caffeine” after his race with Republican Mike Rogers was called early Wednesday, giving Democrats another significant victory in a premier swing state as they won a substantial majority in the Senate in Tuesday’s midterms.
Throughout the cycle, Republicans sought to demonize El-Sayed, who was born in the U.S. after his parents immigrated from Egypt. President Donald Trump repeatedly called him a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists.”
“Michigan proved just how big we are. Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face,” El-Sayed said. “Michiganders rejected that. Every single county, every single one, pushed against that.”
In a sign of how combative the race had become, Rogers and El-Sayed had not spoken as of Wednesday afternoon, even after Rogers issued a statement conceding the race. In 2024, Rogers called then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin to concede on Wednesday morning, before the AP had even called the race.
El-Sayed, who will become the nation’s first Muslim senator, told the AP by phone that the morning was “a moment of reflection,” including about what his victory would mean to his two young daughters. His 3-year-old, he said, has no idea what happened, while his 8-year-old understands but sees it as normal.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
“Now, this is something they read about in the history books,” he said.
With approximately 97% of the vote in, El-Sayed held a 7 percentage point lead over Rogers. Every county in the state shifted toward Democrats compared with 2024, according to AP voting data.
The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of more than 4,500 voters in Michigan, showed that Michigan Senate voters were roughly split on whether El-Sayed’s views were “too extreme,” with about half saying they were.
El-Sayed rose from a double-digit defeat eight years ago in the state’s Democratic gubernatorial election to an upset victory of an establishment-backed candidate in the primary after being outspent by tens of millions. He said his campaign proved that “old-fashioned politics can work if you’re willing to do the work.”
El-Sayed quickly pivoted, though, toward the future, saying his victory is “not the success” and that “the success is what you’re able to do with the seat.”
He would not commit to supporting Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer for another term, saying he did not yet know who else might run. Schumer is expected to retain the leadership position.
“I do believe we need new leadership and I think people are hungry for it,” El-Sayed added.
___

title: Hannah Pingree wants you to apply to join her governor administration
text:
Fresh off Tuesday’s election victory, Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree has launched a transition website that allows people to apply to serve in her administration.
The Democrat plans to move swiftly to assemble a team of commissioners who will oversee more than a dozen departments and a group of staffers who will work within the governor’s office.
Pingree, 50, will succeed Gov. Janet Mills, her fellow Democrat who is termed out of office. Numerous commissioners under Mills have already stepped down or announced plans to do so, which is typical during transitions.
The shift from Mills, a 78-year-old Farmington native, to Pingree, a former Maine House speaker from North Haven who led Mills’ policy office from 2019 until launching her gubernatorial bid last year, is unique in that Maine has not seen a two-term Democratic governor pass the baton to a fellow Democrat since 1850. Maine last elected Republican governors to more than two consecutive terms in 1952.
During a Wednesday news conference in Fort Allen Park by Portland’s Eastern Promenade, Pingree invited Mainers to visit her new website — hannahpingreetransition.com — and to apply to join her team.
All applications are confidential, and Pingree’s team has asked applicants to share a resume and cover letter along with an indication of one office or department they are interested in. Pingree’s team will review applications on a rolling basis this month. No deadline for applying was provided.
Pingree spoke about how Democrats expanded their majorities in each chamber of the Legislature in Tuesday’s election. Still, she said, she wants to work with Mainers of all stripes and has often pointed to her bipartisan accomplishments when she served as speaker of the Maine House from 2008-10.
“I’m grateful to the voters who sent a strong group of leaders to the State House, and I look forward to working with every one of them, Democrats, Republicans and independents, to get things done for Maine people,” Pingree said. “We’re heading into a hard winter and we’re going to need to get to work.”
Pingree’s transition website says she “is committed to building an administration that reflects the very best of Maine — integrity, compassion, service and shared optimism about improving the lives of Maine people.”
“She’s assembling a team of the most capable and collaborative leaders devoted to Maine’s future,” the website states.
Pingree, who will become Maine’s 76th governor and the second woman to lead the state after Mills, is also preparing for her Jan. 6 inauguration in Augusta. Maine law requires the governor-elect to establish a transition committee that helps assemble the Cabinet and staff, and a committee that plans the inauguration.
The state provides the incoming governor with $5,000 to support the inauguration and transition process, and the governor-elect is allowed to fundraise to cover other costs. Pingree’s transition website has a donation option for the inauguration.
Pingree comfortably beat Republican Bobby Charles, a Leeds lawyer, and independent Rick Bennett, a former Maine Republican Party chair and state senator from Oxford, in Tuesday’s election.
With about 92% of votes counted as of Wednesday afternoon, Pingree had received 55% of the vote to 36.9% for Charles and 8% for Bennett.

title: Republican Pete Ricketts wins reelection to US Senate over independent challenger in Nebraska
text:
(AP) - Republican Pete Ricketts won election Wednesday to the U.S. Senate representing Nebraska, defeating independent candidate Dan Osborn.
Ricketts will now serve his first full six-year term, following his 2023 appointment to replace Republican Sen. Ben Sasse and 2024 special election victory.
Osborn, an industrial mechanic and military veteran, also ran in 2024 against the state’s other Republican senator, Deb Fischer.
Democrat Cindy Burbank won her party’s primary earlier this year but served as a stalking horse candidate for Osborn, campaigning on her intention to withdraw and clear the way for the independent candidate, who was backed by Democratic leaders.
Ricketts is a former Nebraska governor and a wealthy investor.
The Associated Press declared Ricketts the winner at 3:27 a.m. EST.

title: Husband and wife drown in river while using inflatable kayak
text:
PHOENIX (KPHO/Gray News) — A married couple drowned on Halloween while floating on the lower Salt River in an inflatable kayak.
Arizona authorities said they were called to the river Saturday afternoon for reports of a man yelling that his wife couldn’t swim as the two floated downstream.
According to investigators, both the man and woman went missing underwater.
The woman’s body was found just after 2 p.m., with her husband’s body located upstream about an hour later.
Deputies identified the couple as Cindy Bowers, 68, and Anthony Beringer, 59. They were sharing one kayak, and neither was wearing a life jacket, the sheriff’s office said.
The couple’s deaths remain under investigation.

title: Midterm election results
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterm elections, breaking through in Republican strongholds.
Here are three things to know as counting continues.
1. Democrats capture the House and Senate
Democrats flipped seven Senate seats and dozens of Republican-held House districts, as of Wednesday morning. The Democrats victories extended into “red” states with surprising wins in Texas and South Carolina.
Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska were still considered “too close to call” on Wednesday.
The new Democratic majorities take office in January, giving President Trump’s opponents greater power to investigate the administration, challenge Trump’s legislative agenda and block his nominees.
More than 124 million ballots were cast, with counting still underway, according to the University of Florida Election Lab. That surpasses the previous midterm record of nearly 119 million ballots cast in 2018.
2. Trump distances himself from losses
Trump offered mixed messages as the results came in, congratulating Democrats while distancing himself from Republican defeats.
In an election-night interview with Fox News, he credited Democrats for working hard. In a separate phone interview with Politico, he argued that Republicans struggled to turn out his supporters because he was not on the ballot.
The president also posted an image of a red hat bearing the word “VETO,” highlighting his authority to reject legislation passed by a Democratic-controlled Congress.
But he also expressed a willingness to negotiate and work with Democrats, leaving room for potential agreements despite the coming partisan battles.
3. Leadership votes still lie ahead
Democrats must still choose who will lead their new majorities.
Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York currently lead their party in the Senate and House, respectively. Both need support from their Democratic colleagues to retain those roles.
Jeffries would also need to win a vote of the full House to become speaker when the new Congress convenes Jan. 3. If elected, he would become the first Black speaker in U.S. history.
Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi has endorsed Jeffries, praising his leadership following the Democratic victory.

title: Election day in America
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) -
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) — Control of Congress is at stake as Americans head to the polls Tuesday, joining tens of millions who have already voted early.
From the seats on the ballot to federal election monitoring, here are three things to know.
1. Every House seat is up for election
All 435 seats in the U.S. House and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot, along with hundreds of local races.
The results will determine which party controls Congress and shape President Donald Trump’s ability to advance his agenda during the next two years.
2. Millions voted before Election Day
Nearly 60 million Americans cast ballots before Election Day, either through early in-person voting or by mail.
That’s out of roughly 250 million Americans eligible to vote, according to Pew Research Center.
However, early voting totals alone won’t reveal which party is gaining ground. Even in states that report voters’ party registrations, party affiliations don’t always represent which candidates they supported.
3. Federal monitors are deploying nationwide
The Justice Department has announced it’s deploying approximately 1,000 election monitors and observers across all 50 states, marking the department’s first monitoring effort to reach every state.
Their work includes monitoring compliance with federal voting rights laws, including protections against voter intimidation and requirements ensuring access for voters with disabilities.
Once polls close, close contests and the time needed to count outstanding ballots could leave control of Congress unsettled beyond election night.

title: Debut novelist explores a remote Maine island as a ‘crucible for character’
text:
In her debut novel, “The Shared Life of Egan and Lucian,” Rose Smith explores the intersection of family, art and the natural world. Inspired by time spent in Casco Bay and her lifelong fascination with the “Odyssey,” Smith explores motherhood, creativity, homecoming and the pull of a place. In her first-ever interview, she spoke with the Portland Press Herald about the remote island that sparked the novel, the artists who shaped her imagination and the years she spent bringing the story to life.
The novel’s remote setting gives the story a timeless quality. How did you decide when to set this family’s story, and what did that time period allow you to explore?
I went to a birthday party on an island in Casco Bay. There are no stores or businesses there, but it’s only a 45-minute ferry ride from Portland. The idea that you would be so close to a big city, but also be in this remote place — that was exciting as a kind of crucible for character.
My visit was pre-pandemic, and back then, services weren’t delivering groceries there yet. So by setting the novel at a time when cellphones weren’t a big part of life, we could really feel the island community as something special, protected and insular. And then, as the characters grew, so too did the connection that not only they felt, but the whole world started to feel.
The ‘Odyssey’ is fresh in my mind, as I’m sure it is for many readers who have recently seen the Christopher Nolan film. What inspired you to weave so much of the ‘Odyssey’ through this novel?
I first read the “Odyssey” when I was a teenager, and I felt connected to the story of Telemachus, of his rage and disillusionment and confusion about being abandoned by his father. Then I read it again in my 20s, when I was traveling all over the world, and I was really connected to Odysseus’ sense of adventure. And then I read it again once I was a mother and wife, and Penelope was the focus of my attention. In “The Shared Life of Egan and Lucian,” it was impossible to write about life on an island without thinking of the “Odyssey.”
A lot of the same kinds of themes find their way in: fathers and sons, mothers and sons, long marriages. Of course, “nostos,” the ancient Greek term for homecoming, is crucial to my story because of the way that Lucian comes home.
It’s a poem I am deeply connected to and think about a lot, and it felt natural to give my obsession to Ian. I love the way he exists in the world as this very devoted father, but also a self-taught intellectual.
Without giving anything away, I want to ask about the relationship between water and tragedy in the novel. There are echoes of the ‘Odyssey,’ but there’s also the very real ruggedness and danger of the New England landscape — something that can get lost in today’s highly aestheticized, social media version of the region. What interested you about bringing those two ideas together?
I’m interested in an unmitigated experience with the natural world. The experience that we tend to have now with the natural world, because of the ubiquity of our phones as cameras, is creating a distance between us as humans and the natural world that we live in. And, obviously, there are dire ramifications to that kind of disconnection. But if you live in a place like my fictional Shep’s Island, there’s no getting around it — you are subject to nature and the environment and how it can shape and change you.
The setting feels so specific and intimately observed. What is your connection to this part of Maine, and how did that relationship shape this novel? Does it go beyond your friend’s birthday party?
My friend, who was born, raised and still lives in Casco Bay, invited a few friends to a weeklong gathering to celebrate her birthday. She’s a talented painter, and she was building a studio attached to her barn. I was in a busy time in my life with work, and I had little kids. I was not thinking about writing — life sometimes stands in the way of that. And my friend gave me this lovely gift one morning, saying, “Go to my studio and write.” I sat down and started writing. The character of Lea came to me whole, and I wrote those first few pages.
I have gone back to experience the region at different points of the year. My cousin lives in Maine, and she has been extraordinarily game to go to remote islands in the dead of winter with me so that I can have that sensory experience. You don’t have to go to a place to write about it, but I felt like I was going to be able to write the kind of novel I wanted to write by having those sensory details at my fingertips.
Can you tell me a bit more about your career and the path that led you to ‘The Shared Life’?
I wrote those first few pages, and then I set it aside — I was a busy film producer. During a career break, I pulled out those early pages, and that’s when it took off.
I was a few drafts in when I realized I needed to learn more about fiction writing, so I got an MFA in creative writing. Then I came back and rewrote the novel in a year, using everything I had learned in school. My experience in producing documentaries also taught me so much about storytelling.
In total, I spent seven years on “The Shared Life.”
Seven years, wow — what does it feel like to publish your first book of fiction?
It is unbelievably thrilling. Working with my publisher has been a dream. And the early responses have been so kind. My first love is reading — there’s no place I’d rather be than in a bookstore or library — so knowing that my book will be in both is unbelievably gratifying.
What drew you to explore the role of art and creativity in your characters’ lives?
I was raised in an artists’ commune and sat at my godfather’s feet as he painted giant canvases — being a small child in these environments created a lifelong interest in art. But, throughout my life, there was always this awareness that all of the artists were men. I would wonder, what would life have been like if the women had been artists? As an artist who has children, I wanted to explore that question through Sheila and Lea — two different women from different generations and with different approaches to being a mother and artist.
I’m very interested in the tension that occurs in an artist’s life, as they require focus and solitude, but also connection and relationship, and how those things get negotiated and resolved.
Samara Brass is a writer and editor based outside Boston.

title: Adam Hamilton ousts GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, Democrats’ 1st Senate win in Kansas in 94 years
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (AP) — Adam Hamilton, a Democrat and Methodist megachurch pastor, won a startling upset in Kansas over Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, flipping a seat once believed to be safely red in another example of how far unhappiness with President Donald Trump has spread throughout the nation.
Hamilton’s victory was historic for snapping a 94-year losing streak in Senate races for Kansas Democrats — the nation’s longest — and because spending on the campaign was around $110 million, easily a record in low-cost Kansas. Republicans attempted a massive rescue effort for Marshall, including two Trump rallies in the state in October, but weren’t able to save his attempt at a second term.
“This is amazing. We really did make history,” Hamilton told his supporters. “We’re not flyover country. We’re the heart of the country.”
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
In his concession speech in Wichita, Marshall said, “I don’t have any answers” and promised to “keep fighting for this great nation.” He called serving in the Senate “the great honor of my life.”
Hamilton won among the state’s moderate voters, with roughly 7 in 10 backing him over Marshall. Marshall only won about one-quarter of this group, down from about 4 in 10 in 2020, according to the AP Voter Poll.
Also, roughly 8 in 10 voters under 30 backed Hamilton. Marshall split that group with his Democratic opponent during his first Senate race in 2020.
Hamilton appealed to voters frustrated with the rising cost of living and unhappy with Trump’s handling of the economy and the war with Iran. He also promised to combat the intense partisanship in Washington. In his victory speech from a Kansas City-area hotel, Hamilton said people were also upset with cuts in health care and food assistance, and President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
“I think the people in Kansas, Republicans and Democrats, are saying that what’s happening in Washington is not OK,” Hamilton said. “Kansans are also fed up with the way politicians divide us.”
Hamilton’s fundraising far outstripped Marshall’s — particularly when it came to contributions from Kansas residents — and Democratic groups poured tens of millions of dollars into the state. It helped the party overcome efforts by Trump and Vice President JD Vance to animate Trump’s political base with rallies down the stretch in Kansas.
Hamilton is the founding pastor of the 25,000-member Church of the Resurrection in the Kansas City area, the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation. He brought to the race a centrist persona, a knack for fundraising and a public profile as the author of several dozen books.
Democrats flip a longtime GOP Senate seat in Kansas
Marshall, a retired obstetrician, was elected to the House in 2016 and won his Senate seat in 2020. He remained loyal to Trump throughout the campaign, defending both the war and Trump’s tariffs.
Republicans spent the final few weeks of the campaign pounding home a traditionally winning message for them: that voting for the Democratic nominee would put liberal Democrats in charge of the Senate. While visiting Topeka, Vance called Hamilton “Chuck Schumer’s stooge,” though Hamilton said repeatedly that he would not support keeping the New York senator as Democratic leader.
With only a nominal primary challenge, Marshall’s campaign didn’t start its ads until late August and his fundraising lagged. Republicans, worried about the national attention that Hamilton was drawing, shifted millions of dollars from North Carolina to Kansas.
Echoing Trump, Marshall blamed high fuel prices on Ukrainian attacks on Russian infrastructure in their war. He repeatedly told voters that the economy was strong and has improved under Trump.
He also faced attacks alleging he had abandoned Kansas to live in Florida. Marshall said he owned a vacation home in Florida so he could spend time with family. Marshall sold the property last month.
Hamilton’s victory bucked decades of Kansas history
The last Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas was George McGill, a Wichita attorney, in 1932. There hadn’t even been a truly close race since 1974, when future Republican icon Bob Dole won a second term by less than 2 percentage points following the Watergate scandal that forced President Richard Nixon from office.
Republicans portrayed Hamilton as too “woke” for Kansas, in part by highlighting his church’s support for LGBTQ rights. In the campaign’s final weeks, they also focused on two cases of alleged sexual abuse of teenage boys by an adult leader at annual camps for Hamilton’s church, one each in 2005 and 2006.
The church investigated the first incident in 2005 but did not report it to law enforcement when the victims couldn’t positively identify the perpetrator, and the man returned for the 2006 camp. The second incident was reported to law enforcement and the church turned over its records on the first case, but the local prosecutor did not pursue criminal charges.
The church changed its child protection policies and since the 2005 case has required all incidents to be reported to law enforcement. Hamilton acknowledged that it was a mistake for the church not to report the first incident in 2005 and for him to not personally check to see that the man didn’t return in 2006.
However, along with Trump’s drop in popularity nationally, Hamilton benefitted from a recent shift in Kansas politics.
Although the state is often viewed as ruby red, there’s a sizable bloc of moderate voters who have regularly swung governor’s races to Democrats. Suburbs near Kansas City, Missouri, have become increasingly blue, making it easier for Democrats to win statewide races by carrying just the most populous counties.
Hamilton positioned himself in the political center
Hamilton’s comments about Schumer demonstrated the balance he sought to strike in wooing independent and Republican voters. He made a point of describing himself as “independent-minded” and positioned himself as a potential moderate counterweight in Washington.
In another example, he criticized U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement during an event in Topeka but stopped short of calling to abolish the agency.
“They were formed to make sure that people didn’t fly airplanes into buildings again,” he said, referencing the Sept. 11 terror attacks. “If they stick to what they were created for, I’m grateful for them.”
His campaign also hammered Marshall — who uses “Doc” on his stationery — over questions about how he pursued unpaid patient bills before he won a U.S. House seat in 2016.
The New York Times reported that Marshall and his practice sued more than 700 patients during his decades-long medical career. In 81 cases, patients were arrested for missing court dates, and two experts called his tactics extreme, according to the report. During a televised debate, Marshall called attacks on him a “gross mischaracterization” of his professional record.
Many voters appeared concerned about Marshall’s character because of questions about his past debt-collection practices, AP VoteCast found. A slim majority said Marshall did not have the right personal character to serve in the Senate.
—-
This story has been updated to correct that Marshall was elected to the House in 2016, not 2017.

title: Vance blames Iran War for Republican midterm losses
text:
Vance blames Iran War for Republican midterm losses
Vice President JD Vance blamed Republicans’ sweeping midterm losses on the Iran War, which Israel and the U.S. jointly launched in February, in a statement Wednesday morning.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote on X. “The president himself said so last night.”
Video above: White House official calls election night mood "defiant"
In a post of more than 600 words analyzing the midterm election results, the vice president played down the role of the economy in the overwhelming Democratic wins across the country.
“One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true,” Vance said. “But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone.”
For his part, Trump said Wednesday that Vance's take was "largely true, because it drove up the gasoline a little bit short-term."
In his remarks the morning after Election Day, after spending nearly 20 minutes discussing his White House ballroom project and signing a beam, Trump reiterated multiple times that the U.S. couldn't let Iran have a nuclear weapon, or "everything that you see here someday might not exist."
When asked if he believed the Iran war was worth losing the Senate, Trump said he did, saying he'd pursue the war again if he had to.
As recently as Monday, Trump had downplayed the situation, saying “this isn’t a war” with Iran. “There’s no war raging," he said on Fox News.
The most recent U.S. military action against Iran, in the form of what appeared to be a limited strike on islands in the Strait of Hormuz and in the nearby mainland area of Bandar Abbas, came just hours before the midterm elections. Days before then, the Pentagon had provided an updated estimate to Congress that the Iran war had cost taxpayers $47.1 billion so far.
“If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” Vance said in his Wednesday post. He attributed Democrats’ successes to 2024 Trump voters opting to vote for Democrats in 2026.
Besides the Iran War, Vance listed “Focus on cost of living/inflation,” “Put America First,” and “Change our relationship to Israel” as other critical issues that drove people to, by and large, elect Democrats in key races, giving them a majority in the House and Senate.
About 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States. Most of the voters dissatisfied with the war supported the Democratic candidate in their U.S. House races, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the leading issue for most voters.
Vance has been tied to the unpopular war in Iran in the public’s eye because of his role in negotiations and policy decisions, which Trump tasked him with. A former Marine who served in Iraq, Vance said when he became vice president that the Trump administration would not pursue “open-ended conflicts." He was initially a critic of joining Israel’s war with Iran, having built his political brand in part on opposing wars like the current one.
Vance was reportedly concerned about the conflict ballooning across the region and about America’s munitions being depleted. The New York Times called him “the figure inside the White House most opposed to a full-scale war.” But ultimately, he has deferred to Trump’s decisions, defending the war as "worth it" on Megyn Kelly's podcast.
In June, Trump joked that he would blame Vice President Vance if a preliminary deal with Iran fell through.
“I like that idea, sure,” Trump said when Fox News’s Peter Doocy asked if the vice president would take the fall if the deal failed. “If it works out, I’m going to take the credit. If it doesn’t work out, I’m blaming JD. You better be careful, JD.”
The 60-day window established in that deal ended in August 2026 without a final formal peace treaty. The prospect of a return to full-scale fighting has left the Middle East uneasy in recent weeks as peace talks resume. Trump has alternated between embracing diplomacy and threatening to use the “mother of all bombs” on Iran in public comments in recent weeks.
The New York Times reported last week that Vance had sent a letter to a top Iranian political and military official to propose renewed “comprehensive peace negotiations,” citing a senior U.S. official and an Iranian official.
“To the people who are pissed off and want to say, 'I told you so': you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview,” Vance wrote.

title: South Portland considers early learning campus at former Kaler Elementary
text:
The South Portland School Department is considering reopening James O. Kaler Elementary School as a consolidated early learning center less than six months after it closed.
Johanna Prince, the assistant superintendent, recommended moving six pre-kindergarten classes to the now shuttered elementary school, and using it as the home base for educating 3-year-old students with special needs. The move would free up capacity at the four elementary schools and possibly allow Dora L. Small Elementary to get rid of its portable classrooms.
The district is expecting that the early learning campus will serve more than 130 3-year-old and pre-kindergarten students. Prince said there is potential for outside partnerships because the academic programming would not require the full building footprint.
The buildings and grounds committee will explore the viability of using Kaler, and the district released a request for proposals for potential on-site partnerships. The School Board would have final say over what happens to the now mothballed school building.
Prince estimates that staffing an early learning campus at Kaler would cost about $3.03 million, not including $320,000 in one-time costs to move the classrooms, and renovate the space to accommodate younger students, and age-appropriate play spaces.
About $1.7 million of the total cost is estimated to be covered by state funding as part of the transition of responsibility for young students with special needs from Child Development Services to the schools. By next school year, South Portland schools must provide services to 3-year-old students with special needs who live in the city. Fifteen such students have been identified as of last month, with 32 more in the referral process, according to Prince.
The state will pay for some specialized staff members, like special education teachers and educational technicians. But the district will need to foot the $1.2 million bill to cover utilities and additional staff members, like custodians, food service workers, a nurse and other preschool teachers and ed techs. Prince anticipates that ongoing local costs will be about $422,842.
Prince also estimates that about $130,000 of those costs can be covered by future on-site partnerships.
If the district does not reopen Kaler for an early learning campus, the remaining elementary schools may face capacity issues in the future, regardless of how the board ultimately divides up students between schools.
The Maine Department of Education advises a minimum of six hours of programming per week for 3-year-old students with special needs to engage with general education with peers without special needs, so the district would need to partner with off-site providers to meet state-mandated obligations, which would involve additional consideration and travel.
The early learning campus proposal has received strong community support with a majority of caregivers and staff members who completed surveys in the last few months saying they were interested in the district pursuing this option.
In response to potential criticism that reopening Kaler would seem to be a whiplash response after the school was closed less than six months ago as a cost-saving measure, Prince said that reopening as an early learning campus carries different financial considerations, given the available state funding.

title: Dow jumps by 1,000 points as Democrats take control of Congress
text:
Stocks surge and the Dow soars 1,500 points as oil prices tumble following midterm elections
U.S. stocks soared Wednesday after President Donald Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections.
Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.6% for its best day in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,569 points, or 3%, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.4%.
Stocks of hospital owners and dollar stores serving low-income Americans helped lead the widespread rally following the nationwide losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil also tumbled below $95 and touched its lowest level in two months. Vice President JD Vance blamed Republicans' midterm losses on the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices.
Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington.
“Earnings trump elections,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.
Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy.
Much remains impossible to predict, of course, and Trump retains executive authority over key areas such as defense, foreign policy and in some instances trade.
A downbeat forecast could be that “Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck” who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies’ levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank.
An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes “a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words.”
All told, the S&P 500 rose 119.70 points to 7,688.62. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rallied 1,569.40 to 53,356.12, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 364.50 to 25,736.51. Here’s a look at some of the moves that rippled through financial markets:
Trump Media and Tesla sank
Trump’s social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market’s bigger losers, down 24.5%.
Since briefly touching a peak of $175 five years ago, it’s dropped to $4.49. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump’s postings on the platform.
Elon Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 3.3%, and SpaceX sank 3.8%. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress.
AI companies in general are under pressure
Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general.
Investors see Democratic wins in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the further build out of AI data centers. AI-related stocks came into Election Day already under pressure because of worries their prices had shot too high.
Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the poster child of the frenzy around AI-related stocks, sank 3.2% and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, dropped 9.9%.
Companies that have been spending heavily on AI chips held up better. Alphabet rose 3.2%, for example. The parent company of Google had tumbled to its worst loss ever last Thursday on worries that it was spending too much on AI investments.
Defense stocks are down
A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the war with Iran.
That hurt stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the U.S. military, including drops of 6.9% for Lockheed Martin, 4.5% for Northrop Grumman and 2.6% for General Dynamics.
Oil prices tumbled, and green energy companies rose
The possibility of pressure to pull back on the war sent the price for a barrel of Brent crude oil plunging 8.7% to $94.62. That in turn hurt stocks of big oil companies, which had been rallying for much of the year. ExxonMobil fell 4.6%, and ConocoPhillips dropped 5.2%.
Falling oil prices usually hurt stocks of renewable-energy companies because they can lessen the incentive to switch to other energy sources. But Democratic control of Congress could light the way for companies in the solar and wind industries.
First Solar rose 4.6%, and Enphase Energy climbed 3.7%.
Healthcare stocks and dollar stores also rallied
A Democratic-led Congress could try to reverse some of the cuts to federal healthcare and food assistance that Republicans approved in their “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”
That helped stocks climb across the healthcare industry, including a 10.3% rise for HCA Healthcare, which runs hospitals and ambulatory sites.
Retailers also benefited on hopes that Democrats may push policies to help Americans who are struggling to keep up with the fast-rising cost of living. Dollar Tree, which focuses in particular on lower-income Americans, rose 9.6%.
Bond yields are down
In the bond market, Treasury yields sank as oil prices dropped and took pressure off inflation. The move could also be a signal that investors see less risk of Washington piling more debt onto its already big mountain with the coming end to one-party control.
Treasury yields had climbed through the summer and reached their highest levels in decades because of worries about the U.S. government’s big debt, along with high inflation and other concerns. A Congress controlled by Democrats could provide a check against more spending and cuts to taxes that would widen Washington’s deficit.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury dropped to 4.88% from 4.95% late Tuesday.
Stocks jump in much of the world
Indexes climbed across most of the world. Stocks leaped 2% in Paris, 2.2% in Shanghai and 1.8% in London. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was an outlier and fell 1.4%.

title: InvestigateTV+: Growing risk behind lithium-ion batteries
text:
(InvestigateTV) — InvestigateTV+ takes an in-depth look at the growing risk of lithium-ion batteries, why safe disposal is so difficult, and what tools safety advocates say are needed to prevent fires and explosions.
Plus, the FBI warns online extremists are targeting children in gaming and social spaces, coercing them into disturbing and violent acts. We investigate how these predator networks operate, the warning signs parents should know and how to report suspected activity.
Then, an award-winning sake blends Native American and Japanese cultures.
Hidden Heat
In a matter of seconds, the battery powering any number of devices within arm’s reach of the average consumer has the potential to transform from an efficient energy source into a fire ball the temperature of a volcanic eruption.
Lithium-ion batteries, with their energy-dense chemistry and falling cost of production, have grown to dominate the rechargeable battery market.
As that popularity has increased, experts say the ability of those batteries to ignite or even explode under certain conditions has meant as the number of fires linked to them has also gone up.
What to know about online extremism
Lurking on popular online games and social media are predators that officials with the FBI say are part of a network of extremists.
These cybercriminals are known for coercing their victims into self-harm and other acts, according to FBI special agent Heith Janke.
“Many of these actors are motivated by nihilistic violent extremism and what that generally means generally is they want to sow chaos and they want the destruction of our society,” Janke said.
A look at float therapy
A type of therapy can improve people’s health by allowing anxiety and tension to float away. Studies show that float therapy can improve sleep and reduce pain.
Float therapy involves lying in a tub filled with nearly a thousand pounds of magnesium dissolved in skin-temperature water. The solution is dense enough that the body cannot sink.
Sessions typically last an hour or more, with the option to turn off all lights and block out all sound.
Sake infusing cultures
Atsuo Sakurai and his wife, Heather, make award-winning sake at a shop just off Route 66 in Holbrook.
Sake is a traditional Japanese alcohol made from fermented rice. Its history spans thousands of years. Sakurai’s shop, Arizona Sake, makes the beverage in a 200-gallon vat.
Sakurai said people are often surprised to learn the sake comes from Holbrook, Arizona, on Route 66.

title: What’s next in investigation of Learjet crash in Florida that killed 9?
text:
(AP) - Investigators are just beginning the lengthy process of determining why a business jet plummeted from the sky in Florida after encountering a thunderstorm and slammed into the ground with such force that it created a crater and shattered the plane.
The experts at the National Transportation Safety Board will lead the investigation into the crash that killed all nine people abord the Learjet, but it will likely take more than a year to determine exactly what caused this tragedy.
Dramatic videos from witnesses — combined with the disturbing final radio transmissions as the pilots realize their fate — will give investigators important clues. The cockpit voice recorder would also help if investigators can find it intact.
“Our mission is to understand not just what happened, but why it happened, and to recommend changes to prevent it from happening again,” NTSB member Tom Chapman said.
Here’s what investigators are doing now and what comes next:
Investigators are gathering critical evidence
An NTSB team will spend days collecting every piece of the plane they can find. Investigators said Tuesday that pieces of a key part of the tail called the elevator that controls the angle of the nose were found more than a mile away from the main crater. That confirms the plane started to break apart before impact.
Chapman said investigators are searching for the Learjet’s cockpit voice recorder because it could provide crucial details about what the pilots were talking about as they lost control of the plane after it encountered turbulence and ice started to build up on the wings.
“That will be very important data,” Chapman said. But being unable to find that recorder won’t doom the investigation. “Without it, our folks are very, very good. We’re still able to do some incredible detective work and determine how things transpired.”
The co-pilot told air traffic controllers that the plane was being thrown up and down more than 700 feet (213 meters) as she asked them for a better route through the area. It’s not clear why the pilots hadn’t flown around the storms.
But torrential rains in Florida over the past week are making investigators’ work more difficult. The crater was filling with rainwater that likely left some pieces of the plane submerged, and a utility pole had to be removed.
The NTSB asked anyone who finds part of the plane to report it for investigators to collect.
Initial NTSB report takes about a month
Two news conferences have provided some initial details. But the NTSB will spend most of the next month developing a preliminary report describing what happened.
Crash evidence will be taken to a secure hanger where investigators can test intact components and even try to reassemble parts to get a better idea of what happened.
But the force of the crash and the fire destroyed much of the plane, so that will make investigators work harder.
Retired airline pilot and aviation safety expert John Cox said he also doesn’t understand why the plane descended from its previous cruising altitude of 41,000 feet (12,497 meters) as it approached the storms. The pilots steered around a larger storm cell but appeared to head directly into a rapidly developing smaller one, Cox said.
“If I’m looking at thunderstorms, I’d rather be at 41 than at 35. You’ve got a better view, you’re more likely to be on top of it, or at least, in the very wispy tops of it,” Cox said. “I don’t understand why they came down.”
Investigators will try to determine whether they knew that storm cell was there, what the plane’s weather radar showed and whether the pilots checked any other weather services.
Preliminary reports provide factual details but don’t include any analysis or cause. That takes much more time.
Investigators will dig deeper
Weather will be a key early focus of the investigation. NTSB experts will work with the National Weather Service and Federal Aviation Administration to get a better idea of what the plane encountered as it was cruising at 35000 feet (10,668 meters).
Maps that overlay the flight path on top of colorful weather maps show the Learjet flying directly into a small red storm cell that worsened quickly.
But the board considers everything that may have contributed to a crash.
Investigators will review maintenance records and any history of problems with the plane. They will also interview officials at the Upper Jets company that operated the flight as well as air traffic controllers and people who work at the Texas airport the plane took off from.
Videos and photos shot by bystanders can also provide crucial clues about what happened. The NTSB will also collect copies of any surveillance footage that might show the crash.
In certain high-profile crashes, the NTSB may also hold several days of investigative hearings where investigators can question key people involved to learn more and share details with the public as they did after last year’s UPS plane crash.
The final report could take more than a year
Generally, it takes 12-18 months for the NTSB to complete a crash investigation, but it can take longer in complicated cases. NTSB’s roughly 400 workers are pursuing over 1,200 active investigations.
Final reports include details about what happened and explain probable causes.
The NTSB also develops recommendations to prevent similar crashes and improve safety. But the independent agency doesn’t have power to require those changes to be made.
Instead, it is up to regulators like the FAA, the industry and Congress to adopt the NTSB recommendations.
But there is a long history of NTSB recommendations being ignored because regulators or the industry decide making the change would be more costly and cumbersome than it is worth.
Even when the FAA or Congress agrees with the suggestions it might take years to approve new rules.

title: Bangor Symphony Orchestra And Gary Sinise Honor Veterans At Collins Center With Graceful Warrior Concert
text:
Actor Gary Sinise Brings The Lt. Dan Band To Play With The Bangor Symphony Orchestra For Veterans Day Concerts This Weekend
This weekend will mark a first-of-it's-kind Veterans Celebration between the Bangor Symphony Orchestra and award-winning actor/writer/humanitarian Gary Sinise.
Read More: ‘Northern Lights’ Holiday Display Returns to L.L.Bean This Friday
The Symphony is joining with Sinise and his 'Lt. Dan Band', to honor those who serve/served in the armed forces with a unique and powerful weekend of music and literature!
Sinise, his band and the Bangor Symphony Orchestra will perform a pair of Veterans Day Special concerts called Graceful Warrior at the Collins Center for the Arts.
According to the BSO, while there will be lots of music folks will recognize, this concert will also feature new music created to honor Sinise's son, Mac.
"Inspired by his late son Mac's music, most of which was discovered shortly after Mac's passing at a young age from a rare spinal cancer on January 5, 2024, Gary has curated this concert to honor the power of music and healing. The concert features the Bangor Symphony Orchestra in the first half, including Gary Sinise narrating Aaron Copland's 'Lincoln Portrait', and Gary Sinise & The Lt. Dan Band in the second half, with Mac's music transcribed by Oliver Schnee, a musical composer and old college friend of Mac's who is also helping bring Mac's music to life."
Aside from his memoir, Grateful American: A Journey from Self to Service, which Sinise published in 2019, he just wrote another book, this one about his son, Mac, called Graceful Warrior: The True Story of a Son, a Father, and a Family Who Carried Each Other Through.
Graceful Warrior is expected to launch November 10th of this year, the day before Veterans Day.
According to the Collins Center for the Arts website, incorporating the book and the music helps to further the mission of helping support veterans.
"Presented in conjunction with Gary’s upcoming book Graceful Warrior, this one-of-a-kind event is a profound reflection on love, loss, resilience, and hope. Graceful Warrior will be available for sale at the events, and all proceeds from the book sales go to the Gary Sinise Foundation, to help further their mission of 'serving our nation by honoring our defenders, veterans, first responders, their families, and those in need … by creating and supporting unique programs designed to entertain, educate, inspire, strengthen, and build communities.'"
BSO Music Director and Conductor, Lucas Richman, says he feels a special privilege in being able to perform these pieces with Sinise in attendance.
“As a father, I was incredibly touched by Mac Sinise’s journey and Gary’s dedication to bringing the treasure trove of his son’s music to light. It will be a great honor to have Gary here with the BSO playing his son’s music, as well as paying tribute to the generations of veterans who are the focal point of the work done by the Lt. Dan Band and the Gary Sinise Foundation."
The Graceful Warrior performances will be held this Saturday November 7th at 7 PM and Sunday November 8th at 1 PM at the Collins Center for the Arts.
You can purchase tickets through the Collins Center Box Office or the Bangor Symphony Orchestra. BSO Season ticket holders, this will be an add-on to the subscription package.

Veterans, active military members, and first responders can get two tickets for free by calling the Collins Center Box Office at (207) 581-2787.
They will also launch the The Graceful Warrior book during the performances, with advance copies for sale at each event in Orono.

title: Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeats incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas race
text:
Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeats incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas race
In a stunning upset, Gina Hinojosa was elected the first Democratic governor of Texas in more than 30 years on Tuesday, ousting Republican incumbent Greg Abbott and catapulting a decided underdog to national prominence leading what has long been the nation's most populous red state.
She will become Texas' first Latina governor — and the first Democrat to hold the office since Ann Richards in the 1990s — following a groundbreaking victory that topples one of the nation's most prominent Republican governors and steadfast supporters of President Donald Trump, possibly accelerating the state's shift to an emerging battleground.
Above video | Analysis from Gromer Jeffers, political reporter at the Dallas Morning News
Her victory was part of an electrifying night for Democrats in Texas, where James Talarico won election to the U.S. Senate over Republican Ken Paxton.
Hinojosa's win served as validation for Democrats' long deferred dream that demographic changes in the state would be followed by a shift in political power. It also elevates Hinojosa, a 52-year-old state legislator from a liberal Austin district since 2017, into a breakout Democratic star, even as she did not have significant support from the national party for her campaign.
"It never bothered me that they doubted me. It bothered me that they doubted us," Hinojosa told supporters at her victory party in Austin. "Texas, my faith in you never wavered."
Jumping in the race with little money or name recognition, Hinojosa engineered a plucky and populist challenge, railing against artificial intelligence data centers and corruption to down Abbott. She also proved that money in politics has clear limits. Billionaire Elon Musk had spent tens of millions of dollars to back Republicans, and Abbott's campaign had spent $180 million since last year in what was thought to be a safe path to a fourth term.
But Hinojosa proved durable while simultaneously riding the tailwinds of Talarico's hard-charging Senate campaign, one of the nation's marquee races. Just two years after Trump carried the state by double digits, the upset is also a stark reflection of how a glum national mood dragged down Republicans even in a stronghold where Democrats had not won in decades.
On a national level, the loss will set off alarms for Republicans, who depend on winning Texas in presidential election years to maintain a path to the White House.
The first Democrat elected governor since 1990
How Hinojosa governs is likely to open a dramatic political and cultural shift in the Texas Capitol, which over the last decade has passed one of the nation's strictest abortion laws and increasingly aggressive immigration crackdowns. Her victory gives Democrats a potent veto pen, but the extent of her power will be tested in a statehouse where Republicans still have a majority.
Abbott, who first took office in 2015, won each of his previous races by double digits.
Then came Hinojosa, who started her campaign last year at a time when bigger-name Democrats seemed uneager to wade into the race.
From the start she accused Abbott of prioritizing the wealthy over everyday people and failing to bring down costs. Abbott said Hinojosa wanted to raise taxes and painted her as a radical and a threat to Texans' way of life.
One of Hinojosa's earliest campaign pledges was a one-time $1,500 payment to each of the state's nearly 32 million residents that she called a "Corruption Tax Refund." She said the money would come from Texas' massive emergency savings fund.
Hinojosa also seized on growing national rejection of data centers, accusing Abbott of allowing the energy-guzzling server warehouses to multiply. Abbott responded to public anger with a temporary moratorium on new data center approvals.
Hinojosa distanced herself from the progressive label
Hinojosa was once a proud vice chair of the Texas Legislative Progressive Caucus and defender of transgender rights, which became a centerpiece of Abbott's attacks.
She tried to shake off the progressive label throughout the campaign and batted away culture-war issues, presenting herself instead as a populist. Her campaign included ads featuring Republican voters saying they would support her.
"They want to run an entire campaign saying that I'm too woke," Hinojosa said in one spot. "I plan to spend an entire campaign focused on the fact that working people are too broke."

title: What's next in the investigation of the Learjet crash in Florida that killed 9?
text:
What's next in the investigation of the Learjet crash in Florida that killed 9?
Investigators are just beginning the lengthy process of determining why a business jet plummeted from the sky in Florida after encountering a thunderstorm and slammed into the ground with such force that it created a crater and shattered the plane.
The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the investigation into the crash that killed all nine people aboard the Bahamas-bound Learjet, and it will likely take more than a year to determine the cause.

Dramatic bystander videos combined with the disturbing final radio transmissions as the pilots realize their fate will give investigators important clues. The cockpit voice recorder could also help if investigators can find it intact.
“Our mission is to understand not just what happened, but why it happened, and to recommend changes to prevent it from happening again,” NTSB member Tom Chapman said.
Here's what investigators are doing now and what comes next:
Investigators are gathering critical evidence
The NTSB team will spend days collecting every piece of the plane they can find. Investigators said Tuesday that pieces of a key part of the tail called the elevator, which controls the plane's pitch, were found more than a mile away from the main crater. That confirms the plane started to break apart before impact.
Chapman said investigators are searching for the Learjet's cockpit voice recorder because it could provide crucial details about what the pilots said to each other as they encountered turbulence, ice formed on the wings and they lost control of the aircraft.
“That will be very important data,” Chapman said. But being unable to find that recorder won't doom the investigation. “Without it, our folks are very, very good. We’re still able to do some incredible detective work and determine how things transpired.”
The co-pilot told air traffic controllers that the plane was being thrown up and down more than 700 feet, and she asked them for a better route through the area. It's not clear why the pilots didn't fly around the storms.
Torrential rains in Florida over the past week have hindered the investigators' work. The crater filled with rainwater, possibly concealing parts of the wreckage under water, and a utility pole had to be removed.
The NTSB asked anyone who finds part of the plane to report those findings for investigators to collect.
The initial NTSB report will take about a month
The agency’s findings so far are limited, but its experts will publish a preliminary report about 30 days after the crash describing what happened. It won’t include analysis or a cause, which will come in a later, more detailed report.
The force of the crash and the fire destroyed much of the plane. Any evidence investigators are able to gather will be taken to a secure hangar where they can test or try to reassemble smashed components to better understand what happened.
Retired airline pilot and aviation safety expert John Cox said he doesn’t understand why the plane descended from its cruising altitude of 41,000 feet (12,500 meters) as it approached the storms. The pilots steered around a larger storm cell but appeared to head directly into a rapidly developing smaller one, Cox said.
“If I’m looking at thunderstorms, I’d rather be at 41 than at 35. You’ve got a better view, you’re more likely to be on top of it, or at least, in the very wispy tops of it,” Cox said. “I don’t understand why they came down.”
Investigators will try to determine whether they knew that storm cell was there, what the plane’s weather radar showed and whether the pilots checked any other weather services.
Investigators will dig deeper
Weather will be a key early focus of the investigation. NTSB experts will work with the National Weather Service and the Federal Aviation Administration to get a better idea of what the plane encountered at around 35,000 feet (11,000 meters).
Images that overlay the flight path atop weather radar maps show the Learjet flew directly into a small red storm cell that quickly worsened.
But the agency will consider a myriad of factors that may have contributed to the crash.
Investigators will review maintenance records and any history of problems with the plane. They will also interview officials at Upper Jets, the company that operated the flight, as well as air traffic controllers and people who work at the airport in Austin, Texas, from where the plane departed.
Videos and photos shot by bystanders can also provide crucial clues about what happened. The NTSB will also collect surveillance footage that might show the crash.
In certain high-profile crashes, the NTSB can hold investigative hearings during which investigators question people, as it did after last year's UPS plane crash.
The final report could take more than a year
Generally, it takes 12 to 18 months for the NTSB to complete a crash investigation, but complicated cases can take longer. NTSB's roughly 400 workers are pursuing more than 1,200 active investigations.
Final reports include extensive details about what happened and identify the probable causes.
The NTSB recommends changes to prevent similar crashes and improve safety, but it doesn't have the power to require those changes to be installed or enforced.
The responsibility for adopting those falls to the FAA, the industry and Congress, all of which have historically ignored NTSB recommendations, deeming such changes too costly and cumbersome.
Even when the FAA or Congress agree with the suggestions, it can take years to approve new rules.

title: Critical shortage of vets could threaten America’s food supply
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — A silent crisis is unfolding across America’s heartland.
The veterinarians tasked with protecting the nation’s livestock, and by extension, its food supply, are a dwindling force, creating a critical gap in the first line of defense against disease and food insecurity.
For Dr. Rachel Miner, a mixed-animal veterinarian in eastern Kansas, a 60-mile drive to a farm call isn’t unusual. It has become a reality of the job.
She treats everything from household pets to herds of 1,500 cattle, understanding that her work is about more than just animal welfare.
“We’re not only taking care of the animal, but we’re providing for the industry,” Dr. Miner explains. “And the industry that is, supplies us, beef, pork, chicken, all those things.”
But veterinarians like Dr. Miner are becoming increasingly rare. A 2023 Johns Hopkins report reveals a staggering statistic: since the end of World War II, the U.S. has lost 90% of its food-animal vets. The U.S. government has designated official “shortage areas” in 46 out of 50 states, where a small number of vets are responsible for a massive number of animals.
The consequences are dire. In a two-county area in New Mexico, a single veterinarian is responsible for 40,000 cattle. In Pike County, Illinois, the number of full-time vets has plummeted from five to just one, serving 1,000 farms. The Illinois Department of Agriculture reports that cattle have died simply because veterinary services were not available in time.
The high cost of a shrinking workforce
The shortage has profound implications for the safety and stability of America’s food supply.
“It’s absolutely critical,” Brad White, director of the Beef Cattle Institute at Kansas State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, said. He stresses that healthy livestock, cared for by veterinarians, are essential to protecting both the animals and the people who depend on them.
Without enough vets to monitor herds, vaccinate against illness and respond to outbreaks, the risk of widespread disease increases. The 2022 bird flu outbreak serves as a stark reminder. As the virus swept through poultry farms, millions of chickens were culled to prevent its spread, causing egg prices to skyrocket by 96% in one year. While the vet shortage didn’t cause the outbreak, experts say robust veterinary care is key to preventing and containing such events.
Several factors are driving vets away from rural, large-animal practices. The cost of veterinary school can run into the hundreds of thousands of dollars, yet salaries in rural areas are often lower than those for small-animal vets in cities. The work is also physically and mentally demanding, with long hours and extensive travel.
“It can be exhausting, especially in those shortage areas, because you don’t have another veterinarian beside yourself,” Bryant Karlin, a student at K-State’s veterinary college, said.
Investing in a solution
To combat the crisis, federal and state governments are stepping in with solutions aimed at easing the financial burden. The federal Veterinary Medicine Loan Repayment Program offers up to $25,000 in student loan reimbursement for vets who commit to working in a designated shortage area for at least three years. However, the program is highly competitive, with fewer than half of applicants receiving the award each year.
Seeing the need, institutions like Kansas State University have created their own localized incentives. K-State’s program forgives 25% of a graduate’s loan for each year they practice in rural Kansas, for up to four years. The results are promising.
“There’s been 93% of them that have completed their four-year obligation,” White said. “More importantly, 15 years going, 83% of them are in rural practice in Kansas today. So they’re staying.”
For students like Emma McClure, who grew up in a rural area, the program provides peace of mind and a path to serve her community. “I have witnessed a lot of people, especially when they have emergencies, have to drive an hour or more to get the help that they need,” she said. “That’s something that’s definitely made an impact on my decision.”
Despite these efforts, the challenge remains immense. The American Veterinary Medical Association reported that the number of mixed and food-animal vets shrank by another 15% in 2023. While programs like K-State’s are a vital step, experts agree that a broader, sustained effort is needed to ensure the health of America’s livestock and the security of the food on its tables.

title: James Talarico notches historic U.S. Senate win, a first for Texas since 1988
text:
James Talarico notches historic U.S. Senate win, a first for Texas since 1988
Democrat James Talarico flipped a U.S. Senate seat in Texas on Tuesday, defeating Republican Ken Paxton to pull off the first statewide victory in more than 30 years and sending a jolt through a longtime GOP stronghold that President Donald Trump carried by double digits just two years ago.
The 37-year-old state legislator, former middle school teacher and Presbyterian seminarian will become Texas’ first Democratic senator since 1993, laying bare how voter frustration midway through Trump’s second term imperiled Republicans deep inside typically safe turf. The victory is a rejection of Trump’s pick for the seat and threatens Republicans’ control of the Senate, where Democrats needed to gain four seats to retake the majority.
Talarico will become the Senate’s youngest member and replace longtime Sen. John Cornyn, 74, who lost a bruising GOP primary to the scandal-plagued Paxton, whose nomination bolstered Talarico’s appeal to Republican and independent voters.
Related video above: What's at stake for Congress this midterm?
The heated campaign in Texas, one of the most expensive of the midterms, became partly a referendum on Paxton’s legal, personal and ethical troubles that have shadowed much of his three terms as the state’s attorney general. That included a federal corruption investigation, which did not result in charges, and impeachment by his own party in the Texas House over accusations of abusing his office to help a political donor. He was later acquitted in the state Senate.
Democrats have spent much of this century on a sputtering quest to win in Texas, and finally achieving victory could offer a roadmap in states where the party has struggled to compete. Talarico found success in a campaign with scant partisanship, TikToks that racked up millions of views and a railing against billionaires he said were corrupting politics at the expense of everyday Americans — a target that included Elon Musk, the world’s richest person and a Texas resident, who spent heavily backing Paxton.
For Republicans, whose governance in Texas has seen the rollback of abortion rights and offered the Trump administration a blueprint for immigration crackdowns, the defeat to a Democrat who once ran as a proud Austin progressive threatens to deepen partisan infighting.
Senate GOP leaders warned early on that Paxton and his baggage would jeopardize the seat in an already difficult midterm landscape for Republicans.
But Trump, trusting his instincts, endorsed his loyal ally in the primary over Cornyn.
The first Democrat to win a Texas Senate race since 1988
Talarico, the grandson of a Baptist preacher, ran a campaign that sidestepped culture-war battles and instead emphasized an economic populist message while skewering Paxton’s history of scandal.
He told crowds that the biggest divide in U.S. “is not left versus right, it’s top versus bottom.” Rarely maligning the Republican Party as a whole, the Democrat, whose path to victory required converting GOP voters, focused on the top issue of a frustrated electorate: the rising cost of living.
Talarico drew a causal line from high prices to corruption — billionaires seeding politics with gobs of money — and used it to attack Paxton’s reliance on megadonors. Meanwhile relentless television ads flashed headlines from a federal corruption investigation into Paxton after his aides reported him to the FBI in 2020, although prosecutors ultimately decided to not bring charges.
It was still an uphill climb. Democratic candidates in past years, most notably Beto O’Rourke’s 2018 campaign against Sen. Ted Cruz, have ignited enthusiasm that was swiftly doused on election night. Texas last sent a Democrat to the Senate when Lloyd Bentsen was reelected in 1988 — the year before Talarico was born.
Paxton’s durability faded in a heated race
Paxton’s defeat shatters a decade of political resilience in the face of legal and personal troubles, including a 2015 indictment on securities fraud charges and a divorce filing last year by his wife, state Sen. Angela Paxton, on “biblical grounds” over accusations of adultery.
That durability withered in the biggest race of his career. Paxton, who avoided debating Talarico, staked his candidacy on painting his opponent as a liberal extremist while framing the race as a battle for the direction of the nation.
He unleashed a tidal wave of attacks highlighting statements Talarico made as a legislator for his liberal Austin district, including calling God “nonbinary” and saying there were six genders. Talarico now says he considers those comments “cringey.”
But Paxton struggled to unify Republicans after the primary against Cornyn. Trump campaigned in Texas in a final stretch bid to drive GOP turnout, but facing deep unpopularity across much of the country, his efforts fell short.
It was a very pricey campaign
The race was one of the most expensive in the country, as both sides blanketed the airwaves with more than a half-billion dollars in combined campaign ads, according to AdImpact.
Most of that was aimed at boosting Paxton in the nation’s second-most populous state, home to 31 million residents and for years a conservative counterweight to California’s liberal influence.
Musk contributed a total of $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the same amount that the fund then gave to Texas PAC, the largest contributor to Paxton’s campaign. Musk also gave $10 million to the Paxton-supporting Lone Star Liberty PAC.
Talarico argued that the inflated spending blitz made clear the urgent need for checks on powerful interests, saying often on the campaign trail: “Texas is not for sale.”
