"John was more than a mentor to us; he was a true icon of the hair industry. He was the person who taught us everything, believed in us, and made us better."
Related video above | Remembering those we lost in 2026
A cause of death was not immediately clear.
Frieda was one of London's best-known hairdressers, styling models for British Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar and building a celebrity clientele that included Twiggy, Jackie Kennedy Onassis, Mick Jagger and Diana, Princess of Wales.
In 1976, he opened his first salon and created the “Purdey” cut for Joanna Lumley’s character in the television series “The New Avengers,” according to his bio. He later expanded his salons to New York and Los Angeles.
Working with American hair care executive Gail Federici, he developed the Frizz-Ease line, launched in 1988, and later introduced Sheer Blonde products.

title: Mississippi Democratic candidate Scott Colom says he’s ‘confident’ he’ll win Senate race as it remains too close to call
text:
BILOXI, Miss. (WLOX/Gray News) — The Mississippi Senate race between Democratic candidate Scott Colom and Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is still too close to call.
As of Wednesday morning, Colom and Hyde-Smith have both said they are “confident” that they will win.
“Where we are, where the ballots are, we’re gonna win,” Colom said as he addressed supporters at a 10 a.m. news conference. “This is our election. We’ve won it. The people have done it. They’ve decided to go in a new direction. I’m confident of that.”
In a statement, Hyde-Smith’s campaign said, “Our campaign is closely monitoring the remaining count. We remain confident that when every legally cast vote is fully and accurately counted, Mississippians will have reelected Cindy Hyde-Smith.”
As of 11:30 a.m. Wednesday, 95.6% of votes had been counted. Colom narrowly leads Hyde-Smith, taking 462,857 (48.9%) of the vote compared to Hyde-Smith’s 462,792 (48.9%) votes. Independent Ty Pinkins has received 19,938 (2.1%) votes.
Because the race is a general congressional race, there will be no runoff, and the top vote-getter will take the seat.
No Democrat has represented Mississippi in the Senate since 1989.

title: 2 college students whose bodies were found in the Colorado mountains fell to their deaths
text:
(AP) - The two college students whose bodies were recovered last week in the Colorado mountains were rappelling and fell a “substantial distance” when a rock they were anchored to likely gave way, authorities said Tuesday.
Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20, died instantly from multiple blunt force injuries, an autopsy found, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office and coroner’s office. Their bodies were found in a snow-filled basin of West Apostle Mountain, about 100 miles (160 kilometers) southeast of Aspen.
The heavy snowstorm was not a direct factor, according to the statement, which commended the college students for their love of the outdoors and preparation for the climbing trip.
“In most similar cases that have led to a devastating conclusion we find it easy to pick apart what was done wrong,” said Chaffee County Sheriff Andy Rohrich. “That was not the case with Kaden and Jackson.”
The pair had set out from Colorado Mountain College’s Leadville campus for what was supposed to be a weekend trip. While they were originally aiming for Ice Mountain, a 13,958-foot (4,254-meter) peak, Rohrich said they appeared to switch to the 13,597-foot (4,144-meter) West Apostle Mountain.
Donlon was starting to rappel from an anchor point backed up by other protections when the rock likely gave way, according to Rohrich. Matsuda was attached to the same anchor, and they both fell a long distance, although the exact length was not known, according to the statement.
“While their lives were far too short, they spent their final moments together surrounded by the majestic beauty of Chaffee County’s high peaks that they loved,” Rohrich said. “There is also relief knowing neither of them suffered.”
Colorado Mountain College, which has campuses throughout the Colorado Rockies, is known for its programs focusing on the state’s robust outdoor recreation economy, including mountaineering, ski patrol and guiding careers.
Matsuda, of Ridgway, Colorado, and Donlon, of Queensbury, New York, became fast friends at the small campus in Leadville, which bills itself as America’s highest city at 10,119 feet (3,084 meters) above sea level. Located about 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of Denver, the city is home to about 2,600 people and is flanked by some of Colorado’s tallest mountains.
Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter. Donlon, an avid climber and skier, was studying outdoor recreation leadership and had come to Colorado to pursue his love of the mountains.
It was raining when they started hiking, according to the sheriff’s office, and later a severe storm arrived, dumping up to 2 feet (0.6 meters) of snow.
___
Associated Press writer Wufei Yu contributed.

title: How float therapy is helping some improve sleep and reduce anxiety
text:
PORTLAND, Ore. (InvestigateTV) - A type of therapy can improve people’s health by allowing anxiety and tension to float away. Studies show that float therapy can improve sleep and reduce pain.
Float therapy involves lying in a tub filled with nearly a thousand pounds of magnesium dissolved in skin-temperature water. The solution is dense enough that the body cannot sink.
Sessions typically last an hour or more, with the option to turn off all lights and block out all sound.
Nia Linbravo referees women’s basketball games four to five nights a week. She has also worked as a juvenile probation officer and now works in project management. She said the physical and mental demands of her schedule made it difficult to slow down.
“It was hard to relax,” Linbravo said.
A herniated disk and trouble sleeping led her to try float therapy. She said the experience has also helped her manage a diagnosis of depression and anxiety.
“I talked to my doctor about doing this. I wanted to talk about different strategies and they were saying it would be helpful for me, and it has been,” Linbravo said.
She described the sensation of floating as a form of release.
“I think it’s the weightlessness and the feeling of the water supporting me, and I’m literally just letting go,” Linbravo said. “Being in the floating tank, it is a space for me to just talk to myself and reflect on what’s happening — calm my mind and be in the moment.”
Dana Highfill has worked as a massage therapist for 17 years and operates Float North in Northeast Portland. She said most clients come in seeking relief of some kind.
“There’s that physical component — you’re getting relief because it feels like you’re turning off gravity. You’re laying there fully supported, your joints open up, and it helps reduce inflammation,” Highfill said.
She said float therapy can also support mental health care routines.
“You have reduced stimulation to your nervous system. You can go from fight or flight, which most of us live in, to a rest and repair state,” Highfill said.
Highfill also addressed a common concern about the experience, noting that the tanks are not as confining as some expect. A single tank measures eight feet long, four feet wide, with a seven-foot ceiling. The water is approximately 10 inches deep.

title: Caregiving is essential to Maine
text:
November is National Family Caregivers Month, a time to recognize those who provide care for family members and friends and to consider how prepared our communities are to support them.
Maine is the oldest state in the nation. Many of us are already caregivers, and many more will become caregivers in the future. The question isn’t whether caregiving will touch our lives, but whether we will have the support we need when it does.
Imagine having the flexibility to care for someone we love without worrying about losing income or jeopardizing our job. Caregiving brings enough challenges without having to navigate systems that make it harder. Legislation supporting caregivers can make a meaningful difference for both those receiving care and those providing it.
Our newly elected legislators will be making decisions on bills that directly affect caregivers and their families. We have an opportunity to let them know that supporting caregivers matters.
I have had the privilege of caring for members of my own family. I know firsthand that caregiving can be deeply rewarding, but it also comes with sacrifices and difficult decisions. We should support those who need care as well as those who provide it.
Reach out to our newly elected legislators. Congratulate them and ask them to make caregiving a priority. Caregivers should also share their stories. Personal experiences can help legislators understand the real-life impact of their decisions.
We are all in this together. Let’s make Maine a state prepared to care for its people.
Star Pelsue
Portland

title: Paul LePage declares victory in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District race
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WAGM) - Former Maine Gov. Paul LePage has declared victory in the race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, despite the race remaining too close to call.
Speaking at a news conference Wednesday, LePage said his campaign believes there is no path to victory for his Democratic opponent, Matthew Dunlap, based on the outstanding votes.
“Well, the public numbers have us up about 4000 and we the team has been calling all the towns that haven’t come in yet and there’s no path to victory for my opponent. I am declaring victory,” LePage said.
However, The Associated Press has not called the race, and Dunlap has not conceded.
LePage, who served two terms as Maine’s governor from 2011 to 2019, thanked his campaign team for their work throughout the election and said he looks forward to representing Maine in Washington.
“We’re very, very pleased for the outcome. Looking forward to going to Washington and doing what I said I was going to do is work for the main people and this is my gig. If it’s for if it helps Maine, I’m going to be all over it. If it hurts Maine, I’m going to be all against it. And I will work with anyone and everyone that wants to put Maine first,” LePage said.
When asked about the possibility of working in a Democratic-controlled Congress, LePage emphasized his willingness to work across party lines.
“I’m going to tell you, it’s like I said, if it helps Maine, I’m all in. If it hurts Maine, I’m all out. And I will work with anybody to help make this country a better country,” LePage said.
The 2nd Congressional District covers much of Maine geographically, including Aroostook County.
While LePage has declared victory, the outcome of the race remains undecided as election officials continue counting outstanding ballots.

title: Midterms bring in wave of historic firsts for some states — and for the nation
text:
(AP) - Yes, the 2026 midterms will be remembered for the astonishing number of losses that Democrats handed to President Donald Trump. But in the background, something perhaps equally seismic unfolded: a wave of firsts that elevated into high office members of groups that had, until now, been kept largely at the margins.
There were cheers and happy tears at election parties from New Mexico to Georgia late Tuesday once it became clear voters had elected the country’s first Black female governor, the first Native American female governor, the first Native female senator and the first openly gay male U.S. senator. By early Wednesday, the first Muslim U.S. senator was also added to the list of barrier-breaking milestones. The astonishing blue wave also means the United States will likely have its first-ever Black speaker of the House.
Most of these firsts are Democrats, but the GOP has also broken some new ground.
While some of these candidates have avoided focusing on the inherent historic value of their race, gender, religion or sexual orientation, some voters’ rights advocates are celebrating how the electorate has expanded.
“These firsts show how our country is changing,” Alexis Anderson-Reed, president and CEO of State Voices, a network of advocates for civic engagement and equity in democracy, said via e-mail.
“For years, people of color and LGBTQ+ communities have organized, knocked on doors, talked to voters, held conversations, and done the hard work of saving our democracy,” Anderson-Reed said. ”These wins are because of them.”
Here are some of the races where history was and could be made.
First Native American female governor
Democrat Deb Haaland reveled in her history-making moment of becoming the first Native American female governor in U.S. history. Haaland was declared the winner over Republican Gregg Hull, a former mayor, to lead New Mexico.
“Tonight, in our nation’s 250th year, I stand before you as the first Native American woman elected governor in U.S. history,” Haaland told ecstatic supporters at a victory celebration.
“I want every child watching to know that your dreams matter and that New Mexico is a place where you can build the life you want,” Haaland said, adding that she is living proof.
First Native woman senators
Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan has become the first Native American female U.S. senator, helping Democrats win back the Senate. A citizen of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, Flanagan defeated Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter.
Tafoya would have been the first Republican of Latina heritage to sit in the U.S. Senate.
Mary Peltola, who is Yup’ik and a Democrat, could also become the first Alaska Native U.S. senator. Votes in her race to unseat Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan are still being tabulated.
Peltola was considered a trailblazer in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to the U.S. House of Representatives.
First Black female governor
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was declared the winner Tuesday night in the Georgia governor’s race, ending 250 years of U.S. history without a Black woman elected as a state’s governor. The former Atlanta mayor was running against Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman.
“Tonight should remind us all that no matter what community we come from, Georgia is not defined by one moment in time or by one person,” Bottoms told euphoric supporters. “It’s been defined by all of us, and I will be a governor for everyone in this state.”
She will also be Georgia’s first governor of color. All 83 of Georgia’s previous governors have been white men.
Lisa Demuth, however, lost an opportunity to be the first Black female governor. The former Minnesota House speaker was overtaken by longtime Minnesota U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar.
Stacey Abrams had been the only Black woman to come close to winning a governor’s race when she got the Georgia Democratic Party’s nomination in 2018 and 2022.
First Muslim US senator
Abdul El-Sayed will become the first Muslim American to serve in the U.S. Senate.
The contentious race to be Michigan’s next senator was called for him early Wednesday morning. The race between the progressive Michigan Democrat and Republican Mike Rogers has grabbed attention nationally, especially after El-Sayed’s primary opponent endorsed Rogers.
“You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed told a Detroit crowd. “Thank you. This is all yours.”
El-Sayed has had to contend with Republicans all the way up to Trump implying or overtly stating that the Michigan-born epidemiologist is not American and supports terrorism. Trump has called him “dangerously radical” and “too extreme” and referred to him as “Mohammed.” El-Sayed and his supporters have denounced the attacks as Islamophobic or racist affronts to religious freedom.
First openly gay male US senator
Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas won his U.S. Senate race in New Hampshire and will become the country’s first openly gay male senator. He defeated former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu, a Republican who previously served in both chambers of Congress.
This new benchmark is not something Pappas has dwelled on while campaigning, saying, “I’m not running to make history.” But he also applauded the fact that his sexual orientation was not a huge source of discussion among potential voters.
First Black and Latino governors
The U.S. went from having only three elected Black governors in its 250-year history to gaining several more overnight.
On Tuesday, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, the third one in the U.S. and the only current Black governor, won reelection, while Florida Republican Byron Donalds, Wisconsin Democrat David Crowley and Nevada’s Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford were all elected as the first Black governor in their respective states. With Bottoms’ victory in Georgia, there will be five Black governors serving simultaneously.
Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, has called the presence of so many Black gubernatorial contenders “a unique moment.” It’s not “an applause line” but a challenge to make diverse gubernatorial nominees more common, he said.
Latinos, both Democrats, will take on the highest state office in two of the biggest states. Texas voters rejected Gov. Greg Abbott in favor of Gina Hinojosa, who will be the state’s first Latina governor. Xavier Becerra, former California attorney general, outpaced Republican Steve Hilton. He will be California’s first Latino governor since Romualdo Pacheco in 1875.
Record year of women running for governor and Congress
This midterm has been a record-breaker for women vying for state and federal offices. Democrats increased their 2022 number of female candidates to 19 running for governor, according to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. The Republican Party had seven women setting their sights on governor.
Like Minnesota, Tennessee elected its first female governor. Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn beat Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis city councilwoman.
Nearly 300 women, including incumbents, were running for the U.S. Senate and House, as documented by Rutgers’ Center for American Women and Politics.
Among them was Democrat Juliana Stratton in Illinois, who defeated Republican Don Tracy on Tuesday. Stratton, the current lieutenant governor, will succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin. With fellow Democrat Sen. Tammy Duckworth, who is of Thai heritage, the pair will make Illinois the first state to be represented by two female senators of color. Stratton’s win also means there will be three Black women serving in the Senate.
___
Associated Press writers Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, Susan Montoya Bryan and Savannah Peters in Albuquerque, New Mexico, contributed to this report.

title: For Maine, as for America, a bright new political day
text:
Douglas Rooks has been a Maine editor and columnist for 42 years. His biography of Gov. Ken Curtis, “Transformational,” is now available. He welcomes comment at [email protected].
The morning after a major election is a new day — and this day is newer than most.
The national midterm election results are an unquestionable a rejection of President Donald Trump’s policies and politics – and present a big opportunity for Democrats, in the nation and in Maine.
And the outcome of this election amounts to even more than that. It’s a repudiation of the billionaire class and its attempts to not only rule the American economy but to run the federal government.
This effort began in the first days of Trump’s second administration, when the president loosed the world’s richest man to wreak havoc within the executive branch, setting off a struggle in the courts that continues today.
How else to explain a remarkable turn of events almost no one could have anticipated? In Michigan, the first Muslim senator, Abdul El-Sayed, with a deeply thoughtful approach to policy, joins New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as a rising star in the national party.
There are many such stories.
There’s Methodist megachurch minister Adam Hamilton, a Democrat winning a Kansas Senate seat for the first time since the depths of the Great Depression. There’s devout Christian James Talarico, the Democrat who won in Texas — the ultimate Republican stronghold, where the party has been uninterrupted in its Senate delegation since 1988.
And yes, here in Maine, Troy Jackson defeated Sen. Susan Collins in one of the nation’s most closely watched and debated races. Jackson is also the first Democrat to win here since 1988. The logger-turned-legislator will join independent Sen. Angus King, now Maine’s senior senator, in one of the most interesting U.S. Senate duos ever.
Sen. Collins, like her childhood idol, Margaret Chase Smith, ran one too many times. In seeking a sixth term, she has become just the third popularly elected U.S. senator from Maine defeated in reelection.
There wasn’t really any good news for Maine Republicans.
Their last hope, former Gov. Paul LePage, supposedly a lock to become a 78-year-old freshman, still narrowly trailed Democrat Matt Dunlap in the 2nd Congressional District Wednesday morning.
At the State House, Democrats will add to House and Senate majorities, where current Minority Leader Trey Stewart may see his caucus shrink below two-thirds. Democrats won seats mostly represented by Republicans for the last two decades in Augusta, Auburn and Waterville. Republicans’ only possible consolation? Two former House leaders, Billy Bob Faulkingham and Joel Stetkis, won open seats.
The Legislature’s geography will change little. Republicans hold a shrinking demographic base in Maine’s rural counties, while Democrats increasingly dominate populous Cumberland and York counties. This could be a challenge for Maine’s next governor, Hannah Pingree.
Pingree won the gubernatorial race decisively and even more impressively than Gov. Janet Mills, who was the first governor since Ken Curtis (1967 to 1975) to win majorities in both her campaigns. Maine will now have its second woman as governor following its first. It’s also the first time the same party has maintained control of the Blaine House since the four-year term was inaugurated in 1959.
Pingree won about 55% against two competitive opponents, Republican Bobby Charles and Republican-turned-independent Rick Bennett. This is about a large a mandate as a Maine governor ever gets.
Between now and January, major decisions will be made. Pingree’s Cabinet choices will be an important indication of how she plans to govern, just as Democrats’ choices for House and Senate leaders, and selection of committee chairs, will signal their intentions.
Fortunately, Republican attempts to save their seats by engaging in personal attacks on Democratic candidates — peaking in the Ohio governor’s race, and from which, regrettably, Sen. Collins did not remain immune — were repaid in full measure by voters.
Newly elected governors, senators, representatives and legislators should listen carefully not only to what voters said, but to what they expect.
Partisan, litmus-test issues that dominated our campaigns for too long must now be swept away, with a renewed focus what really matters to an aroused, focused electorate.
Nationally, Congress must reestablish itself as a separate branch of government, with particular attention to mammoth income inequality that produced the attempted billionaire takeover.
Americans need secure access to health care, the opportunity for good jobs and careers, and environmental policies that our halt our march toward catastrophic climate change. It’s a tall order, but first steps aren’t hard to envision now.
In Maine, state government needs to become more effective and better organized so it can be more responsive. Republican complaints on that score aren’t groundless. Fortunately, we have a lot of new and mostly younger talent to guide us as we attempt these feats.
If we succeed, we can reestablish American leadership in the world, and better government at home. A new day, indeed.

title: Mt. Ararat field hockey storms back, beats Skowhegan to earn A North title
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
OAKLAND — As her players celebrated with their family members, Krista Chase finally had a moment to decompress from the wild game her team had just played.
“First time,” the Mt. Ararat field hockey coach said as she watched a blue-clad sea of players and fans embrace outside the fence lining Messalonskee High School’s Veterans Stadium. “I can’t believe it.”
Believe it — even if it’s hard to believe the way Mt. Ararat won. The Eagles came back from two goals down to knock off reigning Class A North champ Skowhegan on Wednesday, winning the first regional title in program history.
“We’ve been down before, but we just get back up again,” said Mt. Ararat’s Maddy Sweet, who sparked the comeback with the first of the Eagles’ three goals. “It feels amazing because it’s my senior year, and it’s just really surreal.”
Cali LeClair also scored for top-seeded Mt. Ararat (17-0), which got the winner from Kamryn Chase with 6 minutes, 2 seconds as it advanced to Saturday’s state final against South champion Cheverus (17-0) at Edward Little High School in Auburn. Kaitlyn Dufour and Sydney Perkins scored for Skowhegan.
Dufour opening the scoring with 2:44 remaining in the opening quarter,r dribbling through the Mt. Ararat defense and firing into the bottom-right corner. Second-seeded Skowhegan (15-2) added another goal early in the second quarter, as Faith Pease assisted Perkins, who tapped it in from close range.
Mt. Ararat got on the board with 4:30 left in the third quarter, as Sweet scored on an assist from Addison Chubbuck. The Eagles nearly scored on shots just wide late in the third quarter and early in the fourth, and finally, with 11:04 to play, they tied it on a goal from LeClair.
“Typically, that’s how our goals have come this season,” Kamryn Chase said. “Once one goal starts, we just keep going — we keep that momentum up, and we just keep pushing, keep scoring, and keep on hammering the cage.”
Continue to push Mt. Ararat did, and with six minutes to play, Chase was called upon as the Eagles were awarded a penalty stroke. The junior fired a hard shot to the right side of the cage, and Skowhegan goalie Michelle Williams got her glove on the ball but could not keep it out of the goal.
“We’ve been working our whole season for this, so when I got up to the line, I knew that I just needed to execute and do what I know and what I’ve been practicing all year long,” Chase said. “I work on really getting low, and even if they anticipate the ball going there, (it’s often) so quick that it just goes in.”
Skowhegan couldn’t recover from going a goal down, falling to its second defeat against Mt. Ararat this year, along with a 4-1 loss on Oct. 12. It’s the second time in three years the River Hawks have failed to win the regional title after the program earned a stunning 22 straight from 2001-23.
This victory came much tougher for Mt. Ararat than the showdown three weeks ago in Skowhegan. The Eagles knew the River Hawks would be hungrier Wednesday, Krista Chase said, and after a first half in which she thought her team was too tense, Chase course-corrected at halftime.
“We did not have fun in the first half, and we all said, ‘Let’s make a commitment to having fun,’” Chase said. “I said at halftime that nothing worth doing and achieving comes easy. We want adversity, and we want challenge — it makes the victory all the more celebratory and satisfying and worth it.”
It was the second regional final appearance in program history for Mt. Ararat, which lost to Skowhegan in last year’s A North title game. Now, the Eagles get a Cheverus team that is unbeaten (70-0-1) in its last 71 games since losing the 2022 state championship game to the River Hawks.
“Regionals really separate the good teams from the great teams, and the great teams make it to states,” Sweet said. “We’ll see you on Saturday. … I cannot wait.”

title: US stocks rally, Dow soars more than 1,000 points after Democrats take control of Congress
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. stocks are soaring Wednesday after President Donald Trump’s party lost its sole control of Washington in the midterm elections.
Stocks generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, and the S&P 500 jumped 1.8%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1,519 points, or 2.9%, as of 2:06 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1.9% higher.
Stocks of solar-power companies, dollar stores and hospital owners helped lead the way as Wall Street tried to sort the winners from losers following the widespread losses for Republicans. Investors, meanwhile, see risks ahead for Trump’s social-media company, the artificial-intelligence industry and businesses owned by Elon Musk, who donated heavily to Republicans.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil fell below $100 for the first time in nearly a month. Vice President JD Vance blamed the war with Iran, which caused a spike in oil prices, for Republicans’ midterm losses.
Strategists along Wall Street had been urging investors not to get swept up in the election because it may not matter much for the broad market in the long term. Prices for stocks depend more on where profits for companies and interest rates are heading than on who controls what in Washington.
“Earnings trump elections,” according to Brian Jacobsen, chief economic strategist at Annex Wealth Management.
Still, Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario as Democrats are set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives. Wall Street generally prefers split control of Washington because it lessens the risk of transformative changes to the economy.
A downbeat forecast could be that “Trump is not now a lame duck, but an angry duck” who might restart tensions over tariffs and NATO allies’ levels of military spending, said Carsten Brzeski, global chief of macro at ING Bank.
An optimistic view, Brzeski said, is that Trump becomes “a tame duck ... that he will slow down any disruptive efforts and that he will put more focus on trying to win the Nobel Peace Prize by ending the two big wars without big disruption, and on trade, nothing happens but a few words.”
Here’s a look at some of the moves rippling through financial markets:
Trump Media and Tesla are down
Trump’s social-media company, Trump Media & Technology Group, was one of the market’s bigger losers, down 16.6%.
Since briefly touching a peak of $175 five years ago, it’s dropped toward $5. Its main business is Truth Social, which is most well known for Trump’s postings on the platform.
Elon Musk’s businesses also struggled. Tesla fell 2.4%, and SpaceX sank 4.8%. Musk, a former top Trump adviser, is among the possible targets for investigations by a Democratic-controlled Congress.
AI companies in general are under pressure
Trump has been a big backer of the AI industry, and Democratic victories across the country could mean more regulation or restrictions. Concerns have grown across political parties about AI in general.
Investors see Democratic wins in Texas in particular as possibly slowing the build out of further AI data centers. AI-related stocks came into Election Day already under pressure because of worries their prices had shot too high.
Nvidia, the chip company that quickly became the poster child of the frenzy around AI-related stocks, sank 1.8% and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. CoreWeave, a company that rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, dropped 10.2%
Advanced Micro Devices, another chip giant, held up better. It rose 0.1% after reporting much stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected.
Companies that have been spending heavily on AI chips also did better. Alphabet rose 4%, for example, after it tumbled more than 12% Thursday to its worst loss ever on worries that it was spending too much on AI investments.
Defense stocks are down
A Democratic-led Congress could push Trump to pull back on the war with Iran.
That helped send down stocks of companies that make weapons and other equipment for the U.S. military, including drops of 7% for Lockheed Martin, 4.2% for Northrop Grumman and 2.4% for General Dynamics.
Green power companies are up, and oil prices are down
Democratic control of Congress could light the way for companies in the solar and wind industries. First Solar jumped 5.8%, and Enphase Energy climbed 4.7%.
Stocks of big oil companies, meanwhile, sank. ExxonMobil fell 4.9%, and ConocoPhillips dropped 5.6%. They had been rallying for much of the year after Trump and Israel began the war with Iran, which sent crude prices much higher.
The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, plunged 8.6% Wednesday to $94.70.
The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $70 and $120 per barrel since just before the war with Iran began.
Healthcare stocks and dollar stores also rallied
A Democratic-led Congress could try to reverse some of the cuts to federal healthcare and food assistance that Republicans approved during the summer in their “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”
That helped stocks climb across the healthcare industry, including a rise of 9.6% for HCA Healthcare, which runs hospitals and ambulatory sites.
Retailers also benefited on hopes that Democrats may push policies to help Americans struggling to keep up with the fast-rising cost of living. Dollar Tree, which focuses in particular on lower-income Americans, had one of the market’s bigger leaps and rose 8.9%.
Bond yields are down
In the bond market, Treasury yields eased. That could be a signal investors see less risk of Washington piling even more debt onto its already big mountain with the coming end to one-party control.
Treasury yields had surged through the summer and reached their highest levels in decades because of worries about the U.S. government’s big debt, along with higher inflation and other concerns. A Congress controlled by Democrats could provide a check against more spending and cuts to taxes that would widen Washington’s deficit.
The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.89% from 4.95% late Tuesday.
Stocks jump in much of the world
Indexes climbed across most of the world. Stocks leaped 2% in Paris, 2.2% in Shanghai and 1.8% in London. Japan’s Nikkei 225 was an outlier and fell 1.4%.
___
AP Writer Elaine Lai contributed to this report from Hong Kong, and McHugh contributed from Frankfurt, Germany.

title: Voters overwhelmingly reject data centers in their communities on Election Day
text:
Voters overwhelmingly reject data centers in their communities on Election Day
The tally for all ballots across the country on whether to restrict data centers was 45-1
Voters overwhelmingly reject data centers in their communities on Election Day
The tally for all ballots across the country on whether to restrict data centers was 45-1
Voters overwhelmingly rejected a variety of artificial intelligence data center projects and initiatives across the country on Tuesday at the ballot box.
This year has seen around 50 local data center-related ballot measures across the U.S., according to Ballotpedia. On Nov. 3 alone, 47 ballot measures were set to be decided by voters on the issue of data centers.
Related video above: The data center debate
The site datacentersontheballot.com, provided by Redbud Consulting, breaks down the measures that were decided on Tuesday. To simplify often complicated ballot language, the site classifies measures as either Restrict or Allow, meaning that a measure would restrict (or ban) an AI data center or allow a data center to be built in the community. The result: 45-1.
Facing the 47 ballot measures across the country, 45 communities voted to restrict data centers, and just one community voted to allow construction. One is still yet to be decided.
Twenty-one of the measures were in towns and cities in Ohio alone. The next state with the most measures was Maine, with eight ballot measures.
The measures consisted of varied language involving data center construction. Some asked about an outright ban. Some asked for a 180-day moratorium. Others asked about imposing technical limitations, such as on a site's electricity or water usage. A ballot measure in Maine asked, "Shall an ordinance entitled, 'An Ordinance to Establish a Retroactive Moratorium on Data Centers' be enacted?" An Ohio measure asked, "Shall the resolution enacting approval of a development and supply agreement term summary with EdgeConneX be approved?" And a Florida ballot asked, "Should the City Charter prohibit new data centers within the City?" The winning answers, respectively, were: Yes, No, and Yes. These all count as votes to restrict data center development.
The measure with the highest proportion voting to restrict was in Morgan County, Illinois, with 88.3% of the 10,663 votes cast stopping data center development. The closest vote was in Sprigg Township, Adams County, Ohio, with 52.6% voting to restrict construction of data centers. On average, the pro-restriction vote percentage was over 70%.
The lone measure that passed to allow data center construction was in Harwood, North Dakota, where the measure netted 75.6%. Notably, the ballot language seemed to be about whether to approve "additional review" of certain developments, which would include data centers, and whether to add a lengthy amendment to the city's Home Rule Charter to effect this review.
The opposition to data centers comes amid the Democratic Party's historic blue wave, marking a stiff rebuke of President Donald Trump and the Republican agenda, which has broadly been very positive toward AI and data centers.
"The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," the president posted to Truth Social at the end of August, saying that communities must "let data reign" in order to become "successful and rich." "The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame."

title: It’s too early to call the outcome of California’s proposal to tax billionaires
text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — A California measure to tax the net worth of billionaires that divided liberal leaders nationally and triggered one of the most expensive ballot fights in state history was too early to call Wednesday morning as the vote tally continued.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians whose net worth exceeds $1 billion, with most of the revenue dedicated to replacing federal funding cuts to healthcare. The measure left the ultra-rich, some of whom spent heavily to defeat it, scrambling to figure out whether they would pay the tax or leave California.
Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders framed the proposal as a monumental step toward reining in deep wealth inequality by ensuring the ultra-rich pay their fair share. But Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom warned it would prompt the state’s wealthiest to move out of California and take their tax money with them.
With almost 6 million votes yet to be counted, the AP Decision Team will wait for additional vote results before declaring a winner.
Opponents of the proposed one-time tax on billionaires have outnumbered supporters across most of the state. “No” has sizable leads in the Inland/Central Valley region and the San Diego and Orange County area, and smaller leads along the central coast and in the Bay Area. “Yes” votes led narrowly in Los Angeles County and the northern coast.
The “no” side raised roughly 10 times as much as the “yes” side, thanks in large part to tech moguls and venture capitalists, who poured millions into a political action committee fighting the measure. Some billionaires, including Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, started cutting ties with the state in anticipation of the proposed tax. Mark Zuckerberg said he would stay in California for eight years and made a deal with Meta that would help him pay the tax without losing his ownership stake in the company.
Backers of the proposed tax, led by the powerful labor union SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, said it was needed to help the state backfill the federal funding cuts. The union estimates the state will lose $100 billion in federal healthcare funding over five years.
“It’s time to collect those taxes so we can ensure that our healthcare system is still safe,” said Lorena Gonzalez, president of the California Federation of Labor Unions.
But some traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Teachers Association, are part of a coalition that opposed it. They’re concerned about how the tax revenue would be divvied up and about the potential impact on the state’s budget if there’s a mass exodus of wealthy taxpayers. California’s budget relies heavily on the income tax of the state’s richest residents.
Robert Swonger, an auto glass technician living near Sacramento who’s politically independent, said he planned to vote against it.
“Obviously, I would like billionaires not to have as much money as they do,” he said. “But I don’t believe taxing them out of existence is going to work.”
Anthony Serrano, a Democrat living in Folsom who works for Kaiser Permanente, one of the nation’s largest not-for-profit healthcare plans, said he was leaning toward voting for the tax because he tends to support “anything that is a positive for healthcare.”
Even if the measure wins approval from a majority of voters, it would be blocked from taking effect if at least one of two measures designed to nullify it — Propositions 41 and 42 — passes and receives more “yes” votes. The proposals, which are backed by the political action committee Building a Better California, include a ban on new taxes on financial assets and other personal property, a category that excludes real estate. The committee raised more than $333 million, about 30% of it from Brin.
Progressive politicians, including Sanders and Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren, have long supported a federal wealth tax. Newsom said a California wealth tax would disadvantage the state, but he supports a national minimum tax on anyone with a net worth above $100 million.
Days before Sanders held rallies in California cities last month urging voters to support the state measure, Newsom told reporters that the senator’s focus on wealth inequality was “spot-on.” But he said that “on this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”
Even if the proposed billionaire tax fails in California, the battle over the measure ignited a crucial dialogue on the issue, Gonzalez said.
“We are taking a step forward, and we are showing other states that you can look them in the eye — you can look these billionaires in the eye — and take them on,” she said.

title: 16 midterm races are within 1%. What could happen next?
text:
16 midterm races are within 1%. What could happen next?
Most races in the 2026 midterm election have been called. However, a few remain close enough that recounts or court action could follow.
Working with the Get the Facts Data Team, the Hearst National Investigative Unit reviewed races where 95% of the votes have been counted. The teams found 16 contests in which the candidates are separated by 1% or less.
What could happen next depends on each state's rules.
Where are the close races?
One governor's race, one Senate race and 14 House races make up the 16 close races.
In the closest race, Mississippi's Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom leads incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 65 votes, per AP as of Wednesday afternoon. That's with 96% of the votes counted.
In Florida, there are five close races for U.S. House seats. The margins range from 0.4% to 0.8%, as of Wednesday afternoon.
In Minnesota, the U.S. House race between Jake Johnson and Brad Finstad has a margin of 0.1%. Just under 350 votes separate the two candidates.
The Kansas governor's race between Cindy Holscher and Ty Masterson is separated by 0.6%, or a few thousand votes.
Close margins don't mean something is wrong
Pamela Smith, president and CEO of Verified Voting, said a narrow result by itself is not evidence of a counting problem
"A narrow margin just indicates that of all the people that turned out to vote for that contest, they're pretty evenly divided on what they wanted to see happen," Smith said.
Election officials still have to complete the canvass, a review to make sure valid votes are included in the final results, before results are certified. States also conduct post-election audits, though their methods and timing vary.
Differences between audits and recounts
A close result may trigger a recount in some states. Audits, however, are different.
Smith said an audit is a routine check of how voting equipment functioned and whether votes were counted accurately. Audits are not necessarily tied to close races.
"An audit is something that happens every election as a matter of course," Smith said.
A recount focuses on a specific contest and retallies its votes.
"If you have a close margin in some states, that will trigger a recount to happen depending on how close it is, and that varies by state. But it's about a particular contest," Smith said.
Verified Voting has a summary of the differences.
You can also look at Audit Law Database and Recount Law Database to see what it says about the laws in your state.
What happens in Mississippi?
Mississippi does not have a standard recount process. A person who disputes an election result may seek remedy in court under state law.
Smith said a court order may direct a recount to examine whether the outcome was correct and whether votes were counted and included properly.
Smith said audits and recounts can provide additional information that may be used in a court proceeding
As of Wednesday afternoon, we had found no court filings in Mississippi or the other close races in our review. That could change as officials finish counting and certify the results.
This story was shot and edited by Hearst National Investigative Photojournalist Reid Bolton.

title: Up and Down the Kennebec Valley: Medical history in central Kennebec Valley (Augusta), Part 1
text:
Augusta doctors, part one
On the front page of the July 31, 1875, issue of Augusta’s Daily Kennebec Journal, nine doctors chose to list themselves under the heading “Professional Cards.” In the order of the cards, they were:
— James B. Bell, M.D., and Thos. M. Dillingham, M.D., with offices at the corner of Oak and State streets. Dr. Bell’s office hours were 10 to 12 a.m.; Dr. Dillingham’s, 8 to 10 a.m. and 1 to 2 p.m. A note said that Dr. D. was “obliged to withdraw his office in Hallowell” because he was so busy in Augusta.
— Dr. J. O. Webster, 128 State Street (south of Episcopal Church). His office hours were until 9 a.m.; 1 to 3 and 6 to 7 p.m.
— J. W. Toward, M.D., Physician and Surgeon. Office on State Street, lot next south of Free Baptist church. No office hours listed.
— W. L. Thompson, M.D., Corner State and Green streets. Office hours 1 to 3 p.m.
— L. J. Crooker, M.D., residence and office Winthrop Street, “one door east of Baptist Church, (the church with the town clock) In rear of Court House, Augusta, Maine.” Office hours 9 a.m. to 12 m.
— Drs. Brickett & Bolan, Copartnership. Office, Cushnoc House, State St. Dr. Brickett’s office hours 9 to 12 a.m., Dr. Bolan’s 2 to 5 p.m. Dr. Brickett’s residence, Spring St. Bolan’s residence, State St., opposite Dr. H. H. Hill. Office open from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m.
[Cushnoc House was a well-known 19th-century hotel and tavern, on the corner of State and Winthrop streets where Lithgow Library now stands.]
— W. Scott Hill, M.D. Residence and Office, 182 State St. Augusta Maine Office hours 7:30 to 9 a.m., 1 to 3 and 7 to 9 p.m.
* * * * * *
An on-line biography of James Bachelder Bell, from a book on lives of practitioners of homeopathic medicine (see box number one), says Bell was born Feb. 21, 1838, in Monson, and attended Monson Academy. Because of ill health, instead of going to college he studied medicine with an uncle in Middletown, Connecticut.
In 1859, Bell graduated from the Homeopathic Medical College of Pennsylvania. In June 1860, he went to Europe to begin a year’s “diligent study” at Vienna’s Allgemeines Krankenhaus (General Hospital), “with occasional visits to the Homeopathic Hospitals.”
Bell traveled for a while before practicing in Skowhegan, his father’s home town, for 10 months and then settling in Augusta. In 1862, he apparently tried to enlist in the military, but “circumstances [unexplained] hindered his engagement.”
The biographer said Bell established a successful practice, with a preference for surgery. The pension office and then the City of Augusta employed him in the late 1860s: “During this time he examined several thousand discharged soldiers, and was obliged to resign his office on account of his private practice.”
The undated article, apparently written in the 1870s, called Bell “Hahnemannian” and mentioned his 1869 work titled “Homeopathic Treatment of Diarrhoea.”
The book was republished, no date given, by an Indian publisher whose on-line site calls it “The Homeopathic Therapeutics of Diarrhoea.” Yet another site gave a third title – or perhaps referred to a second published work — and praised Bell’s contributions to the understanding and treatment of gastrointestinal disorders and to modern homeopathy
In 1863, Bell and Mary Pauline Robinson, of Skowhegan, were married. Their three children were Florence, Samuel Robinson and James Hudson.
Around 1880, the Bells moved to Boston. An elaborate brick double house at 176 and 178 Commonwealth Avenue was designed and built for them and another homeopathic physician, William Palmer Wesselhoeft.
Each house had two entrances. The two close together where the houses joined were for each doctor’s patients, two more toward the far side of each half were family entrances.
Mary Bell died in January, 1909; her widower died in September 1914.
* * * * * *
Thomas Manley Dillingham, another homeopathic doctor, was Bell’s partner in Augusta about 1877, Henry Kingsbury said in his Kennebec County history. A variety of on-line sources say he was born in 1850 (FamilySearch says Sept. 17, 1850, in Boothbay), second of four children of William Addison Pitt Dillingham and Caroline Price (Townsend) Dillingham.
He attended Philips Exeter Academy, in New Hampshire, in the 1860s and then completed (unspecified) medical training. At some point, he practiced in Gardiner. In 1874, he moved his practice (from an unspecified place) to Augusta and became Dr. Bell’s partner for five years.
Dillingham then moved to Boston, opening a Boylston Street office.
On Jan. 4, 1897, he married Harriet Ashby Carleton (1865 – 1959). There is no record of any children. In 1900, the couple lived in New York City; in 1910, in Cheshire, New Hampshire.
Dillingham died Oct. 26, 1925, in Santa Barbara, California; his widow died there on Feb. 15, 1959. Dillingham is buried in Augusta’s Forest Grove Cemetery, with his parents, brother and sisters. Although FamilySearch says Harriet is buried in Augusta, Find a Grave does not list her in Forest Grove Cemetery.
* * * * * *
An on-line Webster genealogy says Dr. John Ordway Webster was named after his grandfather, who was born in Chester, New Hampshire, in 1777, moved to Vassalboro around 1800 and died in Mobile, Alabama, in February 1828.
The second John Ordway Webster was born in Augusta Feb. 27, 1842, first of three children of John Milton and Sarah Hayes (Hussey) Webster. The genealogy says he was listed as a private in the Eighth Maine Regiment in 1861 and in 1865. Kingsbury wrote that he studied medicine under Dr. George E. Brickett and took “one course of lectures at Bowdoin,” whether before or after his military service is unclear.
Both sources agree that Webster graduated from Harvard Medical School in 1868. In 1879-70, he was a surgeon in Maine’s National Soldiers’ Home at Togus (see box number two); from 1870 to 1877, he practiced medicine in Lynn, Massachusetts; and then came back to Augusta.
FamilySearch says Webster married Anna Maria Bartlett (1844 – 1942) on May 21, 1870, in Portland. They had four children: John Milton (1871 – 1935), Margaret Bartlett (1872 – 1958), Erastus Bartlett (1874 – 1928) and Mary Clifford (1876 – 1970).
Back in Augusta, the genealogy says Webster was on the state Board of Health and “an active and useful member” of the Augusta school board. Kingsbury wrote a summary history of Augusta school districts from 1797 to 1887 based on an address Webster delivered March 26, 1887. Augusta’s J. O. Webster School (originally an elementary school, now the Webster Head Start center) was named in his honor.
In 1892, the family moved to San Diego. Webster died there Sept. 6, 1896, leaving behind his widow and the four adult children. The genealogy says younger daughter Mary was by then Mary Kraemer.
* * * * * *
Dr. J. Warren Toward is among the more elusive research subjects on this list of Augusta doctors.
His office on State Street was fairly new in July 1875. In the March 1, 1870, issue of the Daily Kennebec Journal, he listed his residence on Green Street opposite the Methodist Church. If his house was indeed his office, he listed no office hours.
Dr. Toward evidently died in the summer or early fall of 1894. The Oct. 15, 1894, issue of the Masonic Token, has a short article saying that his will, filed on Sept. 24 in probate court, made Maine General Hospital (in Augusta?) his residuary legatee “for the purpose of providing free beds for Masons in Maine, giving preference to those from Kennebec County.”
(The Masonic Token “Whereby one brother may know another,” was published four times a year in Portland, starting in March 1867. Its last issue was in 1917 or 1918.
* * * * * *
Also in that March 1, 1870, issue was a card from Dr. Farrar, located at 18 State Street, first house south of the Augusta House, who wrote that he specialized in “chronic or long-standing diseases,” and claimed no other doctor was more successful in treating diseases “peculiar to women and children.” Dr. Farrar offered free consultations.
A news item in the same issue said the doctor had treated some of “our first citizens” successfully and added, “We commend him to the afflicted.”
In the Feb. 23, 1870, issue of the same newspaper, Dr. Farrar, still without a first name or initials, had explained that he came from Hartford, Connecticut, where he was resident physician and surgeon. Before that, he had practiced for seven years in New York City and Brooklyn. He was in Augusta for a month before going on to Bangor and then back to Hartford.
He added a copy of a Feb. 1, 1870, letter from Mrs. E. Chandler Wheeler, who said she had been his assistant for two years. She praised him as a “kind, careful and judicious medical advisor,” who did not discriminate between rich and poor patients.
The doctor noted that “Mrs. Dr. Farrar, the Medical Lecturer to Women” was always present during “office hours for Ladies.”
* * * * * *
After this diversion from the initial list, your writer plans to continue this topic next week.
National Soldiers Home
Maine’s National Soldiers’ Home, the first of several established to care for wounded Civil War soldiers, was originally named the Eastern Branch of the National Asylum for Disabled Volunteer Soldiers.
It was located at Togus, in the former Togus Springs Resort, which the federal government bought for $50,000 (and in which it later invested thousands more dollars). The first resident arrived in October of that year. An on-line site says there were 442 residents a year later; 993 by 1878; and in 1904, almost 2,800.
Because “asylum” seemed to imply “dependence and a lack of manliness,” the name was changed to “home” in 1872.
The website includes a long list of places where veterans capable of working could learn and practice trades, from the butcher shop and the bakery to the harness shop and the brickyard. Togus had its own fire station, store, library and opera house.
Nonetheless, the website says, Togus and similar facilities in other states were “not homelike.” Abuse and corruption led to Congressional investigation; and an atmosphere of gloom and hopelessness prevailed, as men in all degrees of ill health saw no future except “the grave-yard in sight of the home.”
Many of the veterans drowned their despair. The website says all the National Homes “were surrounded by places to buy alcohol, eager to take veterans’ pensions and earnings.”
Wikipedia lists 14 homes, the first nine established between 1866 and 1898 and the last two in 1929 and 1930. Togus was the only one in New England. In July 1930, the national homes became part of the new Veterans Administration.
Main sources
Kingsbury, Henry D., ed., Illustrated History of Kennebec County Maine 1625-1892 (1892)
Websites, miscellaneous.

title: QUINN QUESTIONS: Do you remember your first love interest?
text:
The first romantic interest in my life was a new girl in my first-grade class. She had the best-looking tennis shoes on the planet.
Even better, she was a world-class runner. All us kids raced every day during recess and – except for the time some guy tripped her – she won every race.
Because boys and girls stayed on different sides of the playground, it took all my courage to cross the dividing sidewalk to ask where she got those shoes. Once I got those footwear details, she no longer interested me.
I did briefly admire a girl in a third-grade square dance class, because she knew the do-se-do.
But then I met Charlotte, my seventh-grade English teacher.
To this 12-year-old boy, she seemed gorgeous. She was an older woman…probably 23. In class she teased me, and we kidded around a lot.
By the third six weeks I was profoundly in love, and that had never happened before. But at the height of my passion, spring came around.
A couple of friends and I got tickets to the local sports event. While there, I saw my 20-something instructor with a man about her age.
After we exchanged greetings, she said, “I’d like for you to meet my fiancé’.” What? She was engaged?
I shook the guy’s hand and talked to them a couple minutes, but I was emotionally destroyed. How could she?
I felt really bad for at least nine days. Then baseball season started.

title: Israel’s president accepts certified election results, will start consultations for new government
text:
Israel’s president accepts certified election results, will start consultations for new government
Israeli President Isaac Herzog accepted on Wednesday the certified results from last week’s vote, and said he would begin consultations with party representatives regarding the formation of a new government.
Neither the party of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor that of his main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, secured an outright majority in parliament. The two sides are now in hard-fought negotiations to convince smaller parties to join forces to create a new government.
THIS IS A BREAKING NEWS UPDATE. Check back for updates. AP’s earlier story follows below.
Israel’s election commission said Wednesday it has found no fraud in last week’s vote, dealing a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s attempts to discredit the results.
Netanyahu and his supporters have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, possibly with foreign assistance.
The results showed Netanyahu's religious-nationalist bloc losing its parliamentary majority,while Arab-led parties made substantial gains.
“The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the committee said in a statement.
The acting director of the elections committee, Dean Livne, said its investigation examined every complaint “individually and thoroughly,” but found no evidence to support allegations that the election results were invalid.
The results, which are set to be formally certified Wednesday, “accurately reflect the choices voters made at the ballot box,” Livne added. A separate investigation by the Shin Bet intelligence service into allegations of foreign interference in the election is ongoing, according to a spokesperson for the elections committee.
The elections committee has said that while allegations that foreign actors may have sought to influence the election are serious, it does not believe any such interference affected the results of the election.
“Our position is that even if the suspicions are substantiated, this would not undermine the integrity of the electoral process or the election results as a whole,” the head of the committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said Sunday.
Netanyahu’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
After receiving the certified results, Israel’s President Isaac Herzog will begin to meet Wednesday with each of the parties elected to parliament.
Following two days of consultations, he will choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot — who he believes is best positioned to form a coalition government, setting the stage for weeks of negotiations.
Neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Eisenkot's bloc of allies secured a parliamentary majority needed to form a new government. That raises the possibility of an alliance between the two rivals or an alliance between Eisenkot and some of the Arab-led parties. If neither man can put together a government, the country would hold a new election early next year.

title: 1 killed and 2 others injured when a helicopter crashes into bay near Miami, officials say
text:
MIAMI (AP) — One person was killed and two others were injured on Wednesday when a helicopter crashed into Biscayne Bay near Miami, officials said.
The Robinson R44 II helicopter went down late Wednesday morning while occupants were taking photos of boats near Bill Baggs State Park, off Key Biscayne, the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said.
Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during a news conference Wednesday afternoon that all three occupants were adult males, and the two survivors were taken to a nearby trauma center in critical but stable condition.
Rescue workers from several local agencies, as well as the U.S. Coast Guard and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, responded to the crash.
When the sheriff’s office marine patrol units reached the scene, they reported finding a Good Samaritan trying to help one of the victims and take him to shore. Miami firefighters attempted to save his life, but he didn’t survive, Cordero-Stutz said.
Meanwhile, border protection officers found the two other men from the helicopter and turned them over to Miami-Dade rescue workers for transport to the hospital.
Cordero-Stutz said the cause of the crash remains under investigation. South Florida has experienced heavy showers over the past few days, but it wasn’t known if the weather contributed to the crash.
Television news video of the crash shows the aircraft upside down underwater with two yellow floats attached to the bottom of its landing skids. Those emergency floats are designed to help keep a helicopter afloat in a water landing.
Officials didn’t immediately identify the helicopter’s occupants. The sheriff said they were still working to notify family members.

title: Speaker Johnson won’t seek reelection as House Republican leader after party’s midterm wipeout
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Speaker Mike Johnson will be stepping aside from Republican Party leadership after the GOP’s wipeout in the midterm election, declining to seek support to stay on as House minority leader in the new Congress, according to two people familiar with his decision Wednesday.
Johnson is expected to retain his seat as a rank-and-file member of the House from Louisiana when Congress convenes in January. He won reelection from his Shreveport-area district for a sixth term in office.
It’s a swift rise and fall for Johnson, often seen as an accidental speaker, who nevertheless drew close to President Donald Trump and led the House GOP during a tumultuous era, with one of the slimmest majorities in modern times.
And it sets up a fierce internal party battle for the new GOP leader after Democrats swept to power.
Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana, the House majority leader, said in a letter to colleagues that “the election was far worse than any of us expected” and he is running for the minority leadership post because “the stakes couldn’t be higher.” Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio sent a letter to colleagues describing himself as “battle-tested” as he announced his bid for the job.
House Republicans are expected to elect their new leader when members-elect gather in Washington next week, in what will likely be a familiar showdown between Scalise and Jordan, who reached for the top spot before, only to lose out, paving the way for Johnson.
The people who told The Associated Press about Johnson’s decision insisted on anonymity to disclose it.
From Shreveport to Washington
Johnson first won the speaker’s gavel in 2023 after his colleagues ousted the previous GOP speaker, Kevin McCarthy of California, in a first-of-its-kind coup in House history.
A lower-level member of House leadership, Johnson in many ways fell into the job after Republican colleagues could not agree on a successor to McCarthy. He had distinguished himself before the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol by organizing support for Trump’s false claims of widespread fraud in the 2020 election he lost to Democrat Joe Biden.
Once in office, Johnson quickly pulled closer to Trump — so close that Johnson candidly recounts their almost daily phone calls and chats, often offering his impressions in the president’s voice.
Johnson led passage of the GOP’s signature package of tax breaks and social services cuts that Trump signed into law. He protected the president and his administration from embarrassing votes, including a recent effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, by simply sending lawmakers home.
House leadership elections ahead
Johnson’s decision sets up a potential repeat of the leadership battles that have played out in recent years between the House GOP’s conservative and far-right flanks.
Scalise has long courted backing from the House GOP’s conservative wing, particularly business and energy sector lawmakers. Jordan, the brawling former wrestler who helmed the Judiciary Committee, has long been preferred by the hard right, including some from the Freedom Caucus.
Both Scalise and Jordan tried for the speaker’s gavel once McCarthy was forced aside in 2023, but they failed to win majority support from their colleagues, splitting the votes. At the time, Johnson emerged as the consensus candidate who became the House speaker.
___
This story has been corrected to show Johnson won reelection to a sixth, not eighth, term.

title: Democrat Deb Haaland to become first Native American female governor in US history
text:
(AP) - Democrat Deb Haaland was elected Tuesday governor of New Mexico, defeating Republican Greggory D. Hull.
Haaland is a former U.S. interior secretary and member of Congress.
Haaland reveled in her history-making moment of becoming the first Native American female governor in U.S. history.
The Laguna Pueblo citizen noted that Native Americans are still here despite past efforts by the federal government to strip them of their languages and culture.
“Tonight, in our nation’s 250th year, I stand before you as the first Native American woman elected governor in U.S. history,” Haaland told ecstatic supporters at a victory celebration.
In 2018, Haaland was one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress. Then she became the first Native American Cabinet secretary, running President Joe Biden’s Department of the Interior. Charles Curtis, from the Kaw Nation, was the first Native Cabinet member as President Herbert Hoover’s vice president.
Oklahoma was the only state to elect a tribal citizen for governor — Democrat Johnston Murray in the 1950s and current Republican Gov. Kevin Stitt.
“I want every child watching to know that your dreams matter and that New Mexico is a place where you can build the life you want,” Haaland said, adding that she is living proof.
Hull is a former three-term mayor of one of New Mexico’s largest cities. Outgoing Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham is term-limited.
The Associated Press declared Haaland the winner at 10:40 p.m. EST.

title: Trump touts ballroom after GOP suffers historic midterm losses
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump continued to insist Wednesday that his supporters have tremendous love for him, even as fellow Republicans blame his policies for the party’s midterm election losses.
With votes still being counted, Democrats have won at least 7 Senate seats and 28 House seats in the 2026 midterm elections. Wednesday at the White House, Trump wanted to talk primarily about his ballroom project.
“It’s going to be here for many, many years and serving our country well,” Trump said.
Vice President JD Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X, “The reason we lost is the war.” He was referring to the conflict with Iran, which Vance has opposed from the outset.
Trump, standing in the ballroom that is still being constructed, said he agreed with that assessment.
“Well, I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” Trump said. “And probably that’s probably it’s true. But at the same time, if I had to do again, I’d have to do it again, because long term it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
In several post-election interviews, Trump said he is absolutely willing to accept the election results and work with congressional Democrats.
Trump also said he will use his veto power to block Democratic legislation. He said that will force Democrats to negotiate with the White House to find a path forward.

title: ‘Camp Out Hunger’ collecting donations for locals ahead of Thanksgiving

Eighth annual event

Organizers say that despite a financially difficult year for families, the drive has seen record-breaking turnout and donations of all sizes from local residents and companies. They attribute it to the generosity of Central Mainers.

title: Florida sheriff says 2 dead, including suspect, as witnesses report shooting at Tampa office complex
text:
TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — Florida authorities said two people were dead, including a suspect, after witnesses reported a shooting Wednesday at Citibank’s sprawling business complex that employs thousands in the Tampa area.
Officers swarmed the campus Wednesday afternoon, and TV video showed long lines of workers streaming out of the office buildings. The Hillsborough County Sheriff’s Office said in a post on social media that it had “responded to an active threat and is currently clearing the building.”
The sheriff’s office said a suspect and one other person were dead. It was not immediately known whether anyone else was injured.
“We believe this is a targeted incident,” Sheriff Chad Chronister posted on the social platform X.
The Citibank campus in suburban Tampa includes four three-story office buildings that house thousands of the banking giant’s employees.
Citigroup said in a statement that it was “aware of an incident” at the complex and was cooperating with authorities.
Doug Merritt said he was startled when his son called him from the Citibank campus Wednesday, saying he had fled after hearing gunshots.
“He was very close to it,” Merritt told The Associated Press. “He left all this stuff where he was at and he was able to get out of there.”
For around an hour, Merritt said, he didn’t know whether his son was safe as he struggled to get in touch over a bad internet connection.
“I wanted him to get to safety,” he said. “I was upset.”
___
Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia. AP journalists R.J. Rico in Atlanta and Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia contributed to this story.

title: Windham votes down every referendum question
text:
Windham voters elected Marjorie Govoni and Megan Potter to the Regional School Unit 14 school board and voted against three ballot questions — regarding its town meeting, a proposed community center and approving expenditures.
In a four-way race for two of the town’s six seats on the RSU 14 school board, Govoni and Potter won with 3,769 and 3,617 votes, respectively, defeating Joe Kellner and Adam Zajac.
On whether to switch from an in-person town meeting format to a secret ballot, the town voted “no,” with 3,943 in favor and 5,310 against.
The proposal to put $19.5 million toward converting Windham Middle School to a community center failed with 4,548 in favor and 5,267 against.
Voters rejected, 5,637-3,821, raising the threshold for supplemental appropriations that require full town meeting approval from $25,000 to $500,000.

title: Mom, daughter killed in suspected grizzly bear attack after vanishing on walk, officials say
text:

Officials discovered the bodies on the Snooka West Trail near Bella Coola, British Columbia, following a multi-day search, according to the BC Conservation Officer Service.
