title: Analysis: Trump has defied political consequences for years. The midterms changed that.
text:
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
WASHINGTON — For more than a decade, Donald Trump defied the rules of politics that applied to everyone else.
No more.
Tuesday’s elections were a categorical repudiation of a Republican president who has spent the first half of his second term governing without regard to consequences, imposing unilateral tariffs that undermined the economy and starting a war that spiked fuel prices and angered Americans who did not approve of U.S. involvement in the kind of Middle East conflict he had promised to avoid. On top of that, he earned billions in outside investments and focused on Washington renovations that showed little empathy for those struggling financially.
Having survived scandal, impeachments and a criminal conviction, Trump approached the midterms as yet another hurdle he could clear with the sheer force of his personality, insisting the economy was fine and the war in Iran was needed to avoid nuclear war.
This time, he couldn’t make the sale and voters forcefully rejected him.
“Let’s just be clear about what happened last night,” outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, said Wednesday morning. “This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country.”
In the Senate, Democrats will soon represent longtime Republican bastions such as South Carolina, Texas and Kansas. A Black woman will hold the governorship of Georgia, a state that was both the heart of the Confederacy and the soul of the Civil Rights Movement. A Latina will become governor of Texas, where Trump’s strict immigration enforcement has rocked communities from the Rio Grande Valley to Houston.
For Democrats who have learned to temper their expectations after painful losses, the magnitude of Tuesday’s results was hard to comprehend.
As votes were still being counted, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Gina Hinojosa in Texas posted dominant victories in governor’s races where even the rosiest outlooks found them narrowly winning. James Talarico similarly dispatched Republican Ken Paxton with relative ease to become the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Texas since 1988.
A profound pivot in American politics
The victories were of such a scale that they might mark a profound pivot in American politics.
Even Trump, who still refuses to accept his loss in the 2020 presidential election to Democrat Joe Biden, didn’t dispute the results. Democrats who will control the House and Senate beginning in 2027 can claim a mandate to shift Washington in a new direction.
“We knew that the chaos and corruption in Washington [was] hurting our people,” said Roy Cooper, the Democrat who flipped a Senate seat in North Carolina. “Today, you said this has to stop. And as your new United States senator, I am ready to take that message to Washington.”
Claiming a mandate and executing on it, though, are two very different things and Democrats will have difficulty delivering on policy promises so long as Trump holds the power of the veto.
But Trump can no longer rely on compliant Republican leaders to acquiesce. Those in his party who lost are likely to become more openly critical in their remaining months in office.
The reordering of power in Washington has the potential to be the signal that the era of Trump’s dominance is waning.
Republicans whom Trump expressly lifted to the ballot and campaigned fiercely for, including Darline Graham in South Carolina, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and Paxton, lost. The coalition of young, Black and Latino voters that propelled Trump two years ago swung decisively to Democrats.
Trump pumped more than $250 million into Republican campaigns, and millions more came from donors like Elon Musk, and it wasn’t enough to fend off losses. The coarse brand of politics that the president has long heralded met its limits, notably in Ohio, where Vivek Ramaswamy, the Republican candidate for governor, hoped an ad featuring negative comments from the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, would revive his campaign.
Acton won and Ramaswamy was not particularly gracious in defeat.
“I have to tell you I have some serious concerns about the future direction of our country,” he said.
Republicans accept election results
That was the exception to the Republican tenor on Tuesday.
In Wisconsin, Tom Tiffany, who objected to certification of the 2020 presidential election, conceded defeat to David Crowley in the governor’s race. Trump was also unusually congratulatory of Democrats, saying the party did a “good job” and blaming GOP candidates for their loss.
Sen. John Cornyn, whom Trump refused to endorse in the Texas primary against Paxton, applauded Talarico and pledged to try to help him.
Voters nationwide were in the mood for change, according to The AP Voter Poll, which found that roughly three-quarters of voters feel “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the direction of the country.
Among those who had Trump in mind when they voted, about twice as many wanted to express opposition to him as those who wanted to support him. Most also blamed his administration for high costs: About 6 in 10 said higher than usual prices are “more because of Trump’s policies.”
Democrats will face pressure to govern
After a decisive victory, the burden will soon be on Democrats to prove they can govern effectively.
The party has pledged to investigate Trump but will have to navigate calls to also impeach him, which could drain valuable time. At the same time, there will also be pressure to prove they can pass significant legislation to address healthcare, high prices and measures to rein in presidential power.
“We have to deliver for the American people on getting costs down,” said Jared Moskowitz, a Florida Democrat who won reelection to a House seat that Republicans sought to redraw in their favor. “That is the mandate” for Democrats on Capitol Hill.
Asked what happens should the president simply veto Democratic legislation, Moskowitz said: “Let him do that. Let him still tell the American people affordability is a hoax.”
Story by Steven Sloan. Associated Press writer Bill Barrow contributed to this report.

title: Democrats usher in a new era with their resounding sweep of the House and the Senate
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The midterm election blowout delivered a new era in Washington, with Democrats in Congress eager to meet voter demands for change while Republicans watched their majorities evaporate after a revolt against President Donald Trump and his party in power.
Democrats ousted Republicans from coast to coast, with many surprising places in between, in a decisive rejection of unified GOP control for the promise of something different for the country. Their majorities will be padded by unusually wide margins in both the House and the Senate.
The staggering results are setting up a starkly divided government, with an emboldened Congress poised to reassert itself as a coequal branch when Democrats take over in the new year. They are ready to launch a 100-day agenda to lower the costs of gas, groceries and healthcare and conduct vast oversight and investigations into Trump and his administration, with impeachment an option.
“We hear you,” said House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who would make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job when the new Congress begins on Jan. 3, 2027.
Jeffries called the election a “stunning rebuke of MAGA extremism” and “a great victory for the American people.”
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer acknowledged the political reality that voters may have been more willing to reject Trump’s party than to embrace the Democrats.
“Many of the folks who voted for us yesterday are still skeptical, and that’s OK,” the New York senator said Wednesday at the Capitol.
He said the history-making scale of his party’s wins — picking up long-shot Senate seats in South Carolina, Texas and Kansas — creates “the opportunity to prove ourselves worthy of their trust.”
All told, the results present a fundamental reshaping of power in Washington, with new openings and challenges for governing. The tally was bewildering for the scope of Democratic gains and the depth of Republican losses, which indiscriminately wiped out GOP firebrands, moderates and veteran conservatives nationwide. The swelling majorities, with some races still too early to call, underlined a deep sense of voter anger and concern over the economy and the state of democracy.
Trump struck a conciliatory tone, suggesting he could work with the Democrats, but he also warned of gridlock ahead as he threatened to use the power of the presidential veto to strike down their agenda.
“I don’t want to be just sitting there for two years vetoing everything,” he told Politico.
Later, he acknowledged the Iran war impacted the midterm elections, suggesting voters were frustrated by surging gas prices that have been a byproduct of the 8-month-old conflict.
“The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it,” Trump told reporters.
He said he was not considering replacing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, despite voter dissatisfaction with the war, saying Hegseth was “doing a great job.”
Vice President JD Vance, often eyed as Trump’s likely successor at the White House, pointedly blamed the president’s war in Iran for Republicans’ midterm wipeout.
House Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana will not seek reelection as House Republican leader, according to two people familiar with his decision, setting up a potentially brutal leadership battle following the party’s trouncing by the Democrats. The people who told The Associated Press about Johnson’s decision insisted on anonymity to disclose it.
Democrats vow a 100-day agenda and investigations of Trump
House Democrats are planning to quickly launch efforts to reverse Trump’s GOP cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid healthcare programs. They’re also ready to dive into a robust oversight agenda to, as Jeffries says, “hold the crooks accountable.”
The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Rep. Robert Garcia of California, issued a one-sentence warning: “Lawyer up.”
Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, issued his own one-word missive: “Subpoenas.”
Democrats will be under pressure to quickly show that they have solutions for voters’ anger and frustration over high prices, the war in Iran and unease about the direction of the country. About 7 in 10 voters nationally say Congress is not doing enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency, according to The AP Voter Poll.
For Jeffries and his leadership team, it will be their first time in the majority, managing a class of newcomers including a handful of far-left democratic socialists.
With the majority in the 435-member House growing well past the 218 needed and the Senate Democrats holding at least 54 of 100 seats in that chamber, Jeffries and Schumer will have room to maneuver.
Vance cites the Iran war for Republicans’ losses
For Republicans, their shriveled numbers quickly launched a reckoning of their own, as they try to figure out what went so uniformly wrong.
In a lengthy online post, the vice president seemingly sought to distance himself from election results seen as a referendum on Trump that featured big Republican losses across the country.
“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote, adding, “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”
A lame-duck session and leadership elections await Republicans
Republicans may be anxious during the post-election lame-duck sprint to accomplish as much as possible in their remaining weeks in power. But hopes for another GOP-only priority package like their big tax breaks and spending cuts bill seem dim as defeated lawmakers prepare to go home at the end of the year.
Conservatives have also eyed the opportunity for Trump to nominate more judges or even a justice to the Supreme Court while Senate Republicans still hold a majority to confirm the picks.
And the government could be headed toward a federal shutdown next month if Congress fails to pass a funding bill to keep operations running.
In the weeks ahead, the parties will hold internal leadership elections.
Johnson will stay on as a rank-and-file lawmaker in the new Congress, but rivals are lining up to replace him as GOP leader.
Jeffries will seek to shore up support as Democratic leader, before the House chooses its speaker as one of the first votes when the new Congress convenes.
In the Senate, Schumer faces a new generation of Democrats including some who have yet to support him as majority leader.
Trailblazers are coming to Congress
Rarely has the president’s party held on to power during midterm elections, but the Democratic tsunami carried echoes of Trump’s first term, when Republicans faced a voter revolt that sent Democrats to the House majority, and the Barack Obama era, when the Republican tea party swept to power.
This new Congress will also mark firsts and welcome trailblazers.
With the election of Democrat Juliana Stratton of Illinois, the Senate will for the first time have three Black women in office.
Democrat Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota will be the first Native American female senator, Chris Pappas of New Hampshire will become the first openly gay male U.S. senator and Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan will be the first Muslim to serve in the U.S. Senate.
___
This story has been corrected to show the Illinois Democrat’s name is Juliana, not Julia.
___
Associated Press writers Tom Beaumont, Joey Cappelletti, Jill Colvin, Kevin Freking, Mary Clare Jalonick and Will Weissert contributed to this report.

title: Byron Donalds wins Florida governor’s race, becoming state’s first Black governor
text:
Byron Donalds wins Florida governor’s race, becoming state’s first Black governor
Republican Rep. Byron Donalds was elected Florida’s first Black governor on Tuesday in a race that was seen as unexpectedly competitive down the stretch, defeating Democratic nominee David Jolly.
Donalds will succeed outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, who used the office to fan presidential ambitions and steer President Donald Trump’s adopted home state further to the right.
Related video above: Midterm elections to decide the president's path forward
The race presented a test of whether Trump’s unpopularity, which has dragged down Republicans across the U.S., would extend to his backyard and endanger an office in Florida that a Democrat hasn’t won in more than 30 years.
Jolly is a former Republican congressman who switched parties and ran a centrist campaign. Donalds had sought to define him as an out-of-touch liberal, and he reached out to Black voters who traditionally side with Democrats.
Beyond the national political environment, the race centered on issues including high prices and the cost of homeowners insurance, a particularly salient issue in a state with a history of being ravaged by hurricanes.
Florida spent a generation as America’s prized political battleground, where the interests of big cities, agricultural towns, freshly arrived retirees and diverse Latino communities collided in elections often decided by fractions of a percentage point.
That reputation faded under DeSantis, who won his first race in 2018 by less than half a percentage point. But once he was in office, he leaned into culture wars centered on race and gender — signing, for instance, legislation often labeled by critics as “ Don’t Say Gay ” that bars instruction on sexual orientation and gender identity in kindergarten through the third grade. By the time he ran for reelection in 2022, DeSantis won in a nearly 20-point landslide that left the state’s Democrats in shambles.
Jolly faced steep hurdles in his effort to lead the party’s rebound. Republicans have a roughly 1.5 million voter registration advantage, and Donalds dominated Jolly in fundraising.
Seeking to overcome those challenges, Jolly campaigned in Florida’s Democratic strongholds, like Broward County, along with traditionally Republican parts of central Florida and the state’s Panhandle.
Donalds maintained a steady confidence throughout the campaign, balancing his support for Trump with efforts to create some distance, including minimizing references to the president on his website.

title: North Berwick bans data centers, South Berwick elects Select Board members
text:
Voters in North Berwick cast their votes for two referendum items, while South Berwick residents elected two new town councilors and a couple additions to the school board.
Berwick joined both towns in voting for federal, state and county races but considered no local candidates.
NORTH BERWICK
Residents voted 2,114-582 to adopt an ordinance which defines and bans data centers.
In June, the Select Board decided to skip a data center moratorium and instead write ordinance language to take straight to voters. The ordinance applies to facilities with an aggregate data center area of at least 25,000 square feet.
It prevents all new proposals from being considered, and would halt development, though there are none active in town.
Voters also considered a change to the town’s comprehensive plan, which they approved in a 1,653-924 decision.
The amendment expands the town’s growth area — zones for future development or land use — in an effort to make use of public infrastructure, like water and sewer resources.
Both the data center ban and the growth area amendment are effective immediately.
SOUTH BERWICK
Residents in South Berwick elected Jane Brekke and Anthony Palazzaetti to the Select Board, replacing Chair John James and Vice Chair Mallory Cook, who was elected as a House District 149 representative.
Brekke earned 2,140 votes, while Palazzetti earned 1,785, besting Dorothy Maguire and Ronald Fousek who garnered 1,424 and 604 votes, respectively. The newly elected officials will join the five-person board immediately.
Joined by voters in Eliot, residents elected Perrin Chick to serve a one-year term on the Maine School Administrative District 35 school board and Heather Holland for another full term. Both ran unopposed for their terms.

title: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer says Democrats will work to lower costs with or without Trump
text:
(Gray News/AP) – Democrats won control of Congress in Tuesday’s 2026 midterm elections in a widespread repudiation of President Donald Trump and the Republican Party, a drubbing that reached deep into reliable GOP territory.
“Oh man, wow, wow, wow,” Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, said in his victory speech. “Against all odds, we Democrats have won the Senate!”
Schumer said Democrats recruited great candidates who focused their campaigns on costs, chaos and corruption, while Republicans embraced “the worst president ever.”
“Republicans made a choice and followed Trump over the cliff,” Schumer said. “We listened, they didn’t. And the American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks.”
Schumer closed his victory speech with a warning to his own party: “Americans voted for change and now, Democrats must deliver.”
He held a post-election news conference in Washington Wednesday, where he spoke about the high costs of fuel, electricity and the corruption of the Trump administration. Schumer said Democrats are determined to lower costs for the American people.
“We are going to work hard to drive costs down, with the president or without him,” Schumer said Wednesday to close his news conference.
Democrats flipped at least seven Senate seats in ruby-red states and battlegrounds alike: Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina. They held on to battleground seats in Georgia and Michigan.
In the House, Democrats flipped more than two dozen districts, some that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024.
Trump faces a profoundly reshaped Washington for the last two years of his presidency. Democrats will have the power to block his legislative agenda, reject his appointees and investigate his administration.

title: Sanford residents elect Peter Tranchemontagne as mayor
text:
Sanford residents have elected City Councilor Peter Tranchemontagne as their new mayor, according to unofficial results from the city.
Tranchemontagne received 4,051 votes to beat out Deputy Mayor Maura Herlihy, who received 2,748.
Matthew Dupuis received 860 votes, and Daniel White received 713.
In an email Wednesday afternoon, Tranchemontagne said he was honored that the people of Sanford had chosen him, and that he was grateful to everyone who took the time to vote, regardless of who they supported. He also gave a special thanks to the city staff and poll workers.
“It means a great deal to have the chance to serve the city I call home,” he said. “I look forward to listening to residents, working alongside the council and city staff, and working hard for everyone in Sanford.”
Herlihy said in an email that Sanford is headed in the right direction and wished the new officials well.
“We have worked hard to get here and I hope the new Council will continue to build upon our successes,” she wrote.
Though the mayoral race is technically nonpartisan, Tranchemontagne campaigned alongside some state Republicans and emphasized public safety as one of his priorities. He will take over and serve a two-year term after current Mayor Becky Brink finishes her term on Dec. 31.
Voters also selected two out of seven candidates to serve on the Sanford City Council. Meagan Crawford won the most votes, 2,829, while Shawn Goodwin received 1,958.
Crawford said in an email Wednesday that she was blown away by the support from her community, saying, “This win is for all of us to share!”
“I am honored to represent my community on the City Council, and I am so proud of the voting turnout yesterday,” she said. “There is so much positive energy to progress Sanford, let’s hold on to it, and work together to build the community we want to live in.”
Goodwin thanked the city’s residents and everyone who ran for office.
“As for myself going forward, I can’t wait till January,” Goodwin said in an email. “It’s time to get to work.”
The winning council members will take over starting Jan. 1.
Among unsuccessful candidates, Jonathan Martell — the only incumbent on the ballot — got 1,783 votes. Bryce Lambert received 1,747, while Victoria Pariyar and Michael Perry each earned just over 1,500. Alexander Clary finished last, with just over 1,300.
Paula Tatiana Cote and Lisa Pritchett were elected to the Sanford School Committee.
Brian Samia was elected unopposed as Sanford Water District trustee, and Kevin Eaton was elected unopposed as Sanford Sewerage District trustee.

title: Paul LePage declares victory in tight race for Maine's CD2 seat
text:
Paul LePage declares victory in tight race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat
The Associated Press has yet to call the U.S. House race between the Republican former governor and Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap
Paul LePage declares victory in tight race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat
The Associated Press has yet to call the U.S. House race between the Republican former governor and Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap
Former Gov. Paul LePage declared victory in the race for Maine's 2nd Congressional District seat on Wednesday, although The Associated Press has yet to call the U.S. House race in the Republican's favor.
The AP had LePage with a lead of 2,653 votes over Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap with 94% of votes counted as of 10:52 a.m. Thursday. Independent candidate Gregory Ward, a declared write-in, has received 0.05% of the vote.
"The public numbers have us up about 4,000 and the team has been calling all the towns that haven't come in yet, and there's no path to victory for my opponent," LePage said Wednesday afternoon from Sea Dog Brewing Company in Bangor. "I am declaring victory."
You can watch LePage's announcement in the YouTube video embedded below.
The Dunlap campaign has informed Maine's Total Coverage that Dunlap has not called LePage to concede the race.
"No news yet, lots of votes to count," the Democrat's campaign said.
Dunlap and LePage are vying to replace outgoing Congressman Jared Golden, a Blue Dog Democrat who announced nearly a year ago that he would not be running for reelection.
LePage has nearly 30 years of political experience, as he was first elected to the Waterville City Council in 1997 and served two terms before being elected mayor of Waterville in 2003. He served as mayor for seven years and stepped down in January 2011, when he was sworn in as governor after winning the 2010 gubernatorial election. He was reelected governor in 2014 and left office in January 2019, as anyone who holds the Maine governor's office cannot serve more than two consecutive terms. LePage ran for a third nonconsecutive term as governor in 2022, but he was unable to defeat incumbent Gov. Janet Mills.
Before his time as state auditor, Dunlap served as Maine's secretary of state for two separate terms (2005-11, 2013-21). He also served in the Maine House of Representatives from December 1996 to January 2005.
Maine's 2nd Congressional District is the largest congressional district by area east of the Mississippi River. CD2 includes all of Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Somerset, Waldo and Washington counties, as well as the Kennebec County communities of Augusta, Belgrade, Chelsea, Farmingdale, Fayette, Gardiner, Hallowell, Manchester, Monmouth, Mount Vernon, Oakland, Randolph, Readfield, Rome, Sidney, Vienna, Wayne and Winthrop.

title: Susan Collins concedes race to Democrat Troy Jackson in stunning political upset
text:
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins conceded the race to Democrat Troy Jackson early Wednesday morning in a seismic move that ends the Republican’s 30-year tenure in the Senate.
Jackson had 53.1% of votes to 45.7% for Collins when the Bangor Daily News and its national partner, Decision Desk HQ, called the race at 1:10 a.m. Wednesday.
“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I’m proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years,” Collins said in a statement Wednesday morning, adding that she called Jackson to congratulate him and ensure a smooth transition.
The election all but ends the political career of one of Maine’s most famous and scrutinized elected officials. Collins, who rose to a top position in the U.S. Senate touting her centrism and skills as a dealmaker, was ultimately toppled by divisive national politics she could no longer navigate.
It was the first time Maine voters ousted a sitting senator since 1978, when Republican U.S. Rep. William S. Cohen, Collins’ mentor, beat Democratic Sen. Bill Hathaway. Hathaway had won the seat six years earlier by unseating Sen. Margaret Chase Smith, Collins’ role model.
Jackson’s win helps Democrats take decisive control of the Senate. Democrats had already flipped six Senate seats earlier Tuesday night, including North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas, Texas, Iowa and Ohio.
“A little more than 100 days ago, I stood in front of our convention and asked you to put your faith in a logger from Allagash. I told you that we had a party to unite, a movement to build, and a senator to defeat. Well tonight, this morning, the people of Maine have elected that logger to the United States Senate,” Jackson said in a victory speech Wednesday morning.
“If you’re watching this after getting home from a shift or sitting at the table wondering how you’re going to pay the next bill, I want you to hear something very clearly: You are sending somebody to Washington who knows exactly what that feels like. More importantly, I am going to remember who sent me there.”
The progressive former Allagash logger and Maine Senate president led in almost every public poll since late September. But supporters stayed anxious because Collins beat former Maine House Speaker Sara Gideon in 2020 after trailing in every poll, and fewer than half of Jackson’s own backers thought he would win, according to the final University of New Hampshire poll.
Jackson was not supposed to be on this ballot. Democrats entered the summer behind Graham Platner, a populist oyster farmer who weathered controversies over old Reddit posts and a tattoo resembling a Nazi symbol to push Gov. Janet Mills out of the primary, only to quit the race in July after a Maine woman accused him of sexual assault, an allegation he denied.
The party then built a nominating process from scratch with no precedent in Maine politics. Jackson, who revived a campaign that finished third in the June gubernatorial primary, rallied labor organizers and Platner’s progressive base to win 566 of 571 delegates at a July 25 convention in Bangor, leaving him barely 100 days to campaign.
He overcame a wide spending gap by tying Collins to President Donald Trump, pointing to votes he said paved the way for the end of federal abortion rights and deep health care cuts. About 60 percent of likely voters disapproved of Trump’s job performance in final polls.
The race broke Maine spending records. The 2020 race between Collins and Gideon topped $200 million in total spending, and this one passed that on the airwaves alone, with $284 million in ads aired or booked through year’s end, according to AdImpact. Republicans held a $46 million edge, led by the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate Republican leaders.
Collins ran on her seniority as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee and her breaks with Trump on tariffs and the Iran war. Her allies attacked Jackson’s lack of polish and federal experience and his history of testy exchanges with colleagues in Augusta.
Her 2018 vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who later helped overturn federal abortion rights, and her vote to bring Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act to the Senate floor became major flashpoints. She voted against the bill’s final passage, citing its cuts to Maine’s Medicaid program.
Jackson also seized on a September ProPublica report that FBI agents had sought as late as 2024 to widen a bribery investigation that could have involved Collins. She called the allegations false.
Jackson has said his top priorities in Washington will include ending the Iran war and working toward Medicare for All. He will be sworn in in January, ending a Senate career for Collins that began in 1997 and in which she never missed a roll-call vote.
Jackie Cassida, a 55-year-old self-employed independent voter in Belfast, voted for Jackson, citing women’s health and Collins’ vote to confirm Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh.
“I believe it’s time for Maine to see a change, and I think Sen. Collins is due to have a happy retirement,” she said.
BDN writer Elizabeth Walztoni contributed to this report.

title: Democrats poised to control US House after winning key battleground races
text:
Democrats poised to control US House after winning key battleground races
Democrats are poised to control the U.S. House after winning key battleground races.
The Associated Press has called key races for the Democrats, but will not officially declare a majority party until all races are called.
This will likely end a four-year Republican hold on the lower chamber.
Related video above: Midterm elections to decide the president's path forward
Also, this will almost certainly be a major roadblock to President Donald Trump’s agenda in his final two years in office. With Democrats in control, they could block legislation they don’t support and use their power as the controlling party to ramp up oversight of Trump and his administration.
It hasn’t been confirmed, but many believe current Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries will take the Speaker’s gavel from Republican Rep. Mike Johnson.

title: What comes after Election Day? Plus Midcoast events
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The day after elections is always interesting for us. As a chamber we don’t endorse candidates, but we meet many, if not all, of the candidates for our statehouse offices and many others, too, and we build relationships with them, and hear their visions for the world they want to help build. Yet we know, especially when we speak with two great candidates for the same seat, that some good people — thoughtful Mainers who want to do their best to serve us — won’t win. Yet others do win, and carry with them the responsibility to make life better for all Mainers.
There are a couple of lessons from this election that I want to share with you, followed by my idea for what can come next. The caveat I always give when I mention anything political is that these are my views and are not in any way a stance by the chamber of commerce I represent (though these won’t get “too” political where I think that is even a problem). Additionally, if it even matters, I’m registered as Unenrolled, or commonly referred to as Independent, so I’m not a part of either major political party.
First, I was struck — absolutely and completely struck — by the candidate interviews we did this year for statehouse candidates. Every one of them mentioned the need for working across the aisle to just find the best solutions for Mainers regardless of who hatched the idea. They also all addressed affordability, which is the major issue for voters according to nearly any poll you read, but also is the obvious need as we are all experiencing that. Heating oil is a primary immediate concern that needs an immediate solution, and now that Election Day has passed, I hope meetings for affordability and heating oil begin this very week by those elected.
My takeaway from this is very positive, in that, from what I heard from these candidates they understand the urgency of this moment, and the stresses and strains on Mainers. I strongly encourage you to reach out to these legislators right now and let them know your concerns. The biggest issues will not be solved by one single bill, but if legislators can stand by their word and work together regardless of party, they can help us chip away at the affordability issues that we are all being anchored by — that would be a huge victory for everyone.
Secondly, and I say this every election, these are your legislators, and your governor now. Whether you voted for them or not, they are your representative, and you should be rooting for them to do the best job anyone has ever done in the positions they hold. I hope the governor is the best to ever do it; and the new U.S. senator; and our U.S. representatives; and our state legislators. I want them to be life-changingly successful, and you should, too. So maybe, just maybe, don’t rip them down before they even start just because they weren’t your first choice. Maybe, just maybe, listen to what they say, and if you have a different idea, then send them a message in a constructive way, rather than resorting to unproductive name-calling and vitriol. Like it or not, they have their seats for two, four, or six years — that’s a long time. If you want to make Maine successful, maybe start by trying to work with them, instead of against them.
Lastly, and in a way to transition away from politics, my last takeaway is very simple: We have more in common than what divides us, and we need to lean into that. How do we do it? By local engagement. Go have some fun with your neighbors, and maybe you will see they have a lot of the same wants you do, including having fun with their family, supporting local fundraisers, and making our region a place that welcomes guests from around the Midcoast and beyond to experience joyful things.
That transitions us to some incredible local events that you should attend, promote, and have fun with locally, including (get out your calendars to save these dates):
Big Brothers Big Sisters Big Night Out, Nov. 6:
This Friday, BBBS of Bath/Brunswick is having its annual awards night at Maine Maritime Museum in Bath. You may still be able to get tickets, but I know you can also support them by participating in its online auction which closes the night of the event. For more information, check out the events tab on their homepage at BBBSBathBrunswick.org.
MCHPP Harvest Craft and Food Fair, Nov. 7:
Mid Coast Hunger Prevention Program is holding its annual food drive and craft fair this Saturday at Harriet Beecher Stowe School in Brunswick from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Start your holiday shopping with handmade crafts, or bring some nonperishable food by to support your neighbors. The event is presented by Bath Savings and will also feature three food trucks. If you want to bring nonperishable items, the top of the program’s list includes peanut butter, beans, pasta and pasta sauce, canned chicken and tuna, diapers, and cereal.
Early bird sales in Bath, Nov. 7, and Brunswick, Nov. 14
Main Street Bath is hosting its early bird sale this Saturday, Nov. 7, from 6 to 9 a.m. (with some stores going even longer). Get started early and support the downtown merchants. A full list of participants is available online at VisitBath.com.
The following Saturday, Nov. 14, is when the Brunswick Downtown Association hosts its early bird sale, also beginning at 6 a.m. Its list of participating businesses is available online at BrunswickDowntown.org.
OTHER EVENT DATES
• Gardens Aglow (Boothbay Harbor): Nov. 14-Jan. 2
• Chamber After Hours: Nov. 19 at the Brunswick Landing Y, 5 to 7 p.m.
• Merrymeeting Tree Fest: Nov. 20-22 and 27-29
• Burpees for Turkeys: Nov. 21, 2 p.m.

More on these events next week!
Cory King is executive director of the Bath-Brunswick-Topsham Regional Chamber of Commerce.

title: Hannah Pingree wins governor’s race, puts focus on housing, health care
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Democrat Hannah Pingree won a resounding victory in the race to become Maine’s next governor Tuesday night, defeating two opponents to succeed Janet Mills.
With 86% of votes counted by 5:30 a.m. Wednesday, Pingree had received 55.2%, according to the Associated Press. Republican Bobby Charles received 36.8% and Independent Rick Bennett received 8%.
Pingree, 50, was declared the winner by 11 p.m. Tuesday, on a night that saw Democrats regain control of the U.S. House and Senate and win 28 gubernatorial races.
Joined by her family on stage, Pingree — who will become Maine’s second woman governor and second-youngest in the state’s history — said she plans to put a priority on housing and health care when she takes office in January.
“The work ahead of us cannot wait,” she told a gathering of 1,000 Maine Democrats at the Holiday Inn By the Bay that erupted in applause and shouts every time a Democratic victory flashed across the TV screen.
“I believe every Mainer deserves a home they can afford, health care close to home and a community where good jobs, great public schools and small businesses can thrive,” Pingree said.
‘Maine people stepping up’
During her 17-month campaign with stops in “every single corner of the state,” Pingree said she heard people expressing worries from the rising cost of everything to keeping homes warm this winter and wondering whether their kids will be able to afford a home and build a life here. Many voters expressed anxiety about the future of the country.
“And yet, I saw Maine people stepping up again and again for each other, from neighbors banking firewood so nobody in town goes cold to business owners and clergy members standing up for their immigrant neighbors,” Pingree said.
Pingree said she observed much of the same community spirit growing up on an island, where
“you have to dig in and figure out how to solve problems together.”
Well past midnight, into Wednesday morning, the hotel ballroom room was a joyful party zone, with nonstop music from the likes of Tom Petty, Beyoncé and John Cougar Mellencamp. Some were garbed in patriotic attire, including one fellow in a star-spangled suit and another with a Statue of Liberty crown on his head. O
Proud mother
U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine 1st District, spoke earlier in the evening after cruising to victory in her race against Republican challenger Ronald C. Russell. In a quick interview with Mainebiz, she said she was proud of her daughter.
“She worked really hard,” Chellie Pingree said. “She has an amazing team and I think she’s going to do a great job for Maine.”
Asked about her No. 1 advice for the incoming governor, Pingree said, “Honestly, she’s really the one giving me advice. She is my bossy oldest daughter, and that’s a great skill to bring to the job.”
Democrat Troy Jackson was the final speaker of the night after an unexpectedly decisive victory over U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, the longtime Republican incumbent. Union representatives were in full force.
Economic concerns
An oversized media presence included journalists from national news outlets.
In between the official festivities, a few supporters in attendance who spoke with Mainebiz said they were concerned about issues from the economy to immigration.
Lisa Freeman, who works as a palliative care nurse in Portland, said her key economic concern is “anything that gets us out of the Iran War, and anybody that will stand up to Trump and support everyday Americans with the high cost of living.”
What she sees as the biggest challenge for Maine’s next governor: “I would love to support our asylum seekers and people here legally and helping them settle in a life here in Maine. We need them, we need the work they can do.”
Beth Edmonds, a retired librarian from Freeport, said, “I want us to stop spending money on wars, and actually spend money on human interest things, things that matter to people — gas, groceries, health care, child care. Because I think people can make a huge difference in their life if they just have basics. They’re not asking for the moon. They’re asking for a fair place to stand, live their lives well.”
She sees housing as the top challenge for Maine. “I talked to a kid who works in Freeport. He was driving from Rumford.” Though the young man had recently found a place to move to in Hallowell, she said, “Well, it’s closer. But I mean really, that’s crazy.”
Elizabeth Ahlgren, an attorney with a Maine state agency, also cited tariffs as a top concern, along with the wider damage to America’s image in the world.
“Not just the tariffs themselves, in terms of how their impact on goods and the cost of living, but also the impact on foreign relations,” Ahlgren said.
Ahlgren said that while tariffs are not really an issue for a state governor, “you have to look out how businesses are doing that are heavily dependent on tourism and trading.”

title: Authorities are trying to piece together how an escaped Tennessee inmate evaded capture for 10 days
text:
Authorities on Wednesday were still trying to piece together how an escaped Tennessee prisoner convicted of murder evaded capture for more than a week before being tracked down hundreds of miles away in Missouri.
Jacob Morley, who was serving a life sentence for killing a co-worker four years ago, was apprehended Tuesday near Kansas City, Missouri, authorities said. Morley was found after troopers used roadside cameras and a helicopter to track him down and his truck got stuck in the mud. Two rifles and a shotgun were recovered from the truck.
Authorities believe Morley found his way to a farm near Marion, Illinois — about 127 miles (204 kilometers) away — in the days after his escape, spending some time in a shed that was used periodically by hunters.
Investigators found evidence that he drank beer and prepared garlic bread and other food — and that he left behind an apologetic handwritten note after stealing a truck from the farm, according to Williamson County Sheriff Jeff Diederich. Morley is also suspected of stealing clothes and the three firearms from the property.
He was believed to have walked about 3 miles (5 kilometers) to the farm after abandoning a different truck he had driven after his escape. Security cameras captured Morley walking away from the truck and at a couple locations along Route 13, but the terrain — which includes fields and woods — would have made it tough for him to be spotted, Diederich said.
It’s unclear why Morley traveled to Marion and why he was driving near Kansas City, more than 350 miles (563 kilometers) away.
“How he ended up in Marion is kind of a mystery,” Diederich said.
Diederich said there’s no evidence Morley had help from anyone.
Morley, 28, escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tennessee’s far northwestern corner on Oct. 25, after he slipped through a fence in his prison clothes. Surveillance video showed him stealing a truck from a farm near the prison, which he abandoned in Marion.
Kim Wheeler-Elder, a spokesperson for the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, wrote in a text message that all “available information” regarding Morley’s whereabouts when he was on the run has been released.
The Missouri State Highway Patrol says it was informed Tuesday morning that Morley was possibly traveling west on Interstate 70 in the Kansas City area. Authorities said he was compliant when he was arrested.
Morley was transported Tuesday to the Lafayette County Jail in Lexington, Missouri, according to Justin Ewing, a spokesperson for the Missouri State Highway Patrol. The Lafayette County Sheriff’s Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. No charges have been filed against him in Missouri courts, according to online court records.
District Attorney General Danny Goodman Jr. in Tennessee said in a phone interview that Morley could be charged in Missouri and Illinois, as well as in federal court. He plans to file additional charges but it’s unclear when Morley will be returned to Tennessee.
Morley was convicted of killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield’s body was found in a box under Morley’s home after he had been missing for a few weeks.
When Morley saw deputies at his home, he led officers on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said. Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest.
___
Kelety reported from Phoenix. Associated Press writer Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas, contributed.

title: Troy Jackson wins the Maine US Senate race over Sen. Susan Collins in a key Democratic victory
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) — Late Democratic entry Troy Jackson won Maine’s U.S. Senate seat early Wednesday, defeating longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins, taking advantage of President Donald Trump’s deep unpopularity to dislodge an incumbent who had survived tough challenges in the past.
“For every family doing everything they can and wondering when somebody is going to do something for them, you have gotten me into this and you’re going to have someone who is fighting for you in Washington, D.C.,” Jackson told the crowd at an election night party in Portland.
Jackson, 58, a fifth-generation logger and former president of the state Senate, had a little more than 100 days to sell himself to Maine voters after he replaced Graham Platner as the party’s nominee in July.
He won a hastily convened nominating convention and began barnstorming the state, focusing heavily on economic issues such as the high costs of housing and healthcare. As a former campaign surrogate of independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, he was known to many progressives in the state but lacked the widespread name recognition of Collins.
Collins, 73, was widely perceived as the most vulnerable Senate Republican this election year. She entered Election Day as the only Republican lawmaker in Congress from New England and was seeking her sixth term representing a state that has voted for the Democratic candidate for president since 1992.
“It has been the honor of my life to serve the people of Maine in the United States Senate. I’m proud of all I have been able to accomplish for our state and for our country in the past 30 years,” Collins said in a statement after calling Jackson to concede.
Jackson took over the nomination during a time of crisis for Democrats
Jackson hails from rural Aroostook County, among the poorest in the state, where he went to work as a lumberjack at 19.
He first entered politics after leading a weeklong loggers’ blockade along Maine’s border with Quebec in the late 1990s protesting the hiring of Canadian loggers who were coming into Maine and driving down pay rates.
The standoff ended with Jackson being escorted away by police, an unsuccessful ending that spurred him to run for elected office. He served nearly 20 years in the state House, rising up the ranks to become the Senate’s top leader.
Jackson initially didn’t plan to run for Senate this year. Instead, he threw his hat in for the Democratic nomination for governor but lost.
Platner, an oyster farmer and political newcomer, had drawn huge crowds and enthusiasm but also faced a string of controversies. After he announced in July that he would withdraw from the Senate race, Jackson won a special nominating convention later that month.
It made for a rushed start to the campaign for Jackson. Since then, he has held events at churches, union halls and bars to tout issues such as workers’ rights and the cost of living.
At times, his campaign rhetoric is reminiscent of Sanders, who joined Jackson for rallies in October.
“In the end, if you work hard, you should be able to build a decent life,” Jackson said at a campaign event near Portland in September. “But that’s not the reality right now.”
He criticized Collins as not doing enough to stop Trump. Jackson noted she voted to advance Trump’s signature tax cut and budget legislation out of committee, before she was a “no” vote on its final passage.
“Sen. Collins is like an arsonist who helps set the fire and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said.
Jackson faced blowback over his temperament during the campaign, and Collins criticized him for telling her to “shut up” during a debate.
Collins attempted to woo voters on her independence
Collins was first elected in 1996 and has touted her independence from Trump and her party. She has said she didn’t vote for Trump in 2016, and she voted to convict the president after his 2021 impeachment over his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol riot.
In January, Collins joined a handful of Republican colleagues in backing a failed effort to limit the president’s ability to unilaterally use force in Venezuela. The move prompted Trump to say on social media that they “should never be elected to office again.”
When Vice President JD Vance made trips to Maine, Collins did not appear with him. Vance told the crowd at a May rally that he sometimes gets frustrated with the senator and wishes she were more partisan.
Collins has been a top target of Democrats before. Many pollsters predicted Collins would lose to former Maine House Speaker Sara Gideon in 2020. Collins won handily during a year that Democrats won the presidential race and both U.S. House seats in Maine.
During this year’s race, Collins touted her longevity in the Senate and her status as a key player in powerful committees and budgeting negotiations. She said those aspects of her service remain critically important for Mainers.
“It has been 92 years since a Maine senator was chair of the Senate appropriations committee, the most powerful committee in the Senate,” Collins told reporters. “When I took over last year, I realized I had a once-in-a-century opportunity to help the state of Maine and pursue national priorities as well.”

title: York County likely to reelect King sheriff, Mills treasurer
text:
By 10:30 a.m. Wednesday morning, all but two towns posted results for the York County Sheriff race between incumbent William King and David Corbett.
King received 55,674 votes to Corbett’s 33,138. Corbett, a Republican, faced an uphill battle in the historically blue southern Maine county.
The Democratic incumbent was first elected to the position overseeing the county sheriff’s office in 2014 and will serve his fourth term.
Independent candidate Brian Pellerin, who dropped out of the race in September but still appeared on the ballot, had received 2,380 votes by mid-morning. He has been hired as Wells’ new police chief.
Earlier this year, Pellerin and the county’s Republican Party chair, Heidi Sampson, accused Corbett of misrepresenting his qualifications for the position. Sampson also suggested that Corbett was a “paper candidate” intended to siphon votes away from Pellerin, thus clearing King’s path to reelection.
Secretary of State Shenna Bellows ruled in April that Corbett met the qualifications, and that his name could appear on the ballot.
With five York County municipalities left to record results on an item that could have abolished a longstanding elected county treasurer, voters are swinging toward rejection.
By mid-morning, 43,845 had voted to keep the position, while 22,448 voted to abolish it. The position is likely to stay, which means votes cast for Bobby Mills will count. He’ll return to the position after stepping down years ago.
Mills told the Press Herald in October that he was seeking reelection in hopes of saving residents money by getting rid of a full-time, salaried deputy treasurer position, which costs the county $90,000 annually.

Clouds roll in Thursday morning, and a passing shower or two is possible during the afternoon. After a quiet Thursday evening, a few spotty showers are possible overnight and into Friday morning.
On Friday night, coastal Maine has the best chance this week for a soaking rainfall. The storm system has trended east in recent days, with the heaviest rain expected to fall over the ocean.

title: Wells voters approve mobile home lot rent stabilization, data center moratorium
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Voters in Wells on Tuesday approved a mobile home lot rent stabilization ordinance and a moratorium on data center development.
The mobile home rent ordinance will limit the amount of times park owners can increase rents and by how much per year. The referendum passed with 5,594 votes, and a total of 1,494 votes against it.
Residents also voted to pass a retroactive moratorium on data center development, with 5,818 votes in favor and 1,282 against. The 180-day moratorium is retroactive to June 16 and will end on Dec. 13.
An article seeking to create 14 full-time emergency medical service positions passed, with 6,081 votes in favor and 1,197 votes against. The measure follows the dissolution of Wells Emergency Medical Service, which ceased operations this year following a settlement involving alleged Medicare fraud. The average cost per position will amount to $99,148 per person.
The Wells Board of Selectmen was authorized to issue general obligation bonds to renovate the existing fire station on Log Cabin Lane, with 5,306 votes in favor and 1,844 against. Residents also approved a referendum for relocation of a drainage easement with 4,582 votes in favor and 1,955 against.

title: Midterms may bring in wave of historic firsts for some states and the country
text:
(AP) - Yes, the 2026 midterms will be remembered for the astonishing number of losses that Democrats handed to President Donald Trump. But in the background, something perhaps equally seismic unfolded: a wave of firsts that elevated into high office members of groups that had, until now, been kept largely at the margins.
There were cheers and happy tears at election parties from New Mexico to Georgia late Tuesday once it became clear voters had elected the country’s first Black female governor, the first Native American female governor, the first Native female senator and the first openly gay male U.S. senator. By early Wednesday, the first Muslim U.S. senator was also added to the list of barrier-breaking milestones. The astonishing blue wave also means the United States will likely have its first-ever Black speaker of the House.
Most of these firsts are Democrats, but the GOP has also broken some new ground.
While some of these candidates have avoided focusing on the inherent historic value of their race, gender, religion or sexual orientation, some voters’ rights advocates are celebrating how the electorate has expanded.
“These firsts show how our country is changing,” Alexis Anderson-Reed, president and CEO of State Voices, a network of advocates for civic engagement and equity in democracy, said via e-mail.
“For years, people of color and LGBTQ+ communities have organized, knocked on doors, talked to voters, held conversations, and done the hard work of saving our democracy,” Anderson-Reed said. ”These wins are because of them.”
Here are some of the races where history was and could be made.
First Native American female governor
Democrat Deb Haaland reveled in her history-making moment of becoming the first Native American female governor in U.S. history. Haaland was declared the winner over Republican Gregg Hull, a former mayor, to lead New Mexico.
First Native woman senators
Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan has become the first Native American female U.S. senator, helping Democrats win back the Senate. A citizen of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe, Flanagan defeated Republican Michele Tafoya, a former NFL sideline reporter.
Tafoya would have been the first Republican of Latina heritage to sit in the U.S. Senate.
Mary Peltola, who is Yup’ik and a Democrat, could also become the first Alaska Native U.S. senator. Votes in her race to unseat Republican incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan are still being tabulated.
Peltola was considered a trailblazer in 2022 when she became the first Alaska Native elected to the U.S. House of Representatives.
First Black female governor
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was declared the winner Tuesday night in the Georgia governor’s race, ending 250 years of U.S. history without a Black woman elected as a state’s governor. The former Atlanta mayor was running against Republican Rick Jackson, a billionaire businessman.
“Tonight should remind us all that no matter what community we come from, Georgia is not defined by one moment in time or by one person,” Bottoms told euphoric supporters. “It’s been defined by all of us, and I will be a governor for everyone in this state.”
She will also be Georgia’s first governor of color. All 83 of Georgia’s previous governors have been white men.
Lisa Demuth, however, lost an opportunity to be the first Black female governor. The former Minnesota House speaker was overtaken by longtime Minnesota U.S. Sen. Amy Klobuchar.
Stacey Abrams had been the only Black woman to come close to winning a governor’s race when she got the Georgia Democratic Party’s nomination in 2018 and 2022.
First Muslim US senator
Abdul El-Sayed will become the first Muslim American to serve in the U.S. Senate.
The contentious race to be Michigan’s next senator was called for him early Wednesday morning. The race between the progressive Michigan Democrat and Republican Mike Rogers has grabbed attention nationally, especially after El-Sayed’s primary opponent endorsed Rogers.
“You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates,” El-Sayed told a Detroit crowd. “Thank you. This is all yours.”
El-Sayed has had to contend with Republicans all the way up to Trump implying or overtly stating that the Michigan-born epidemiologist is not American and supports terrorism. Trump has called him “dangerously radical” and “too extreme” and referred to him as “Mohammed.” El-Sayed and his supporters have denounced the attacks as Islamophobic or racist affronts to religious freedom.
First openly gay male US senator
Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas won his U.S. Senate race in New Hampshire and will become the country’s first openly gay male senator. He defeated former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu, a Republican who previously served in both chambers of Congress.
This new benchmark is not something Pappas has dwelled on while campaigning, saying, “I’m not running to make history.” But he also applauded the fact that his sexual orientation was not a huge source of discussion among potential voters.
First Black and Latino governors
The U.S. went from having only three elected Black governors in its 250-year history to gaining several more overnight.
On Tuesday, Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, the third one in the U.S. and the only current Black governor, won reelection, while Florida Republican Byron Donalds, Wisconsin Democrat David Crowley and Nevada’s Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford were all elected as the first Black governor in their respective states. With Bottoms’ victory in Georgia, there will be five Black governors serving simultaneously.
Moore, chair of the National Governors Association, has called the presence of so many Black gubernatorial contenders “a unique moment.” It’s not “an applause line” but a challenge to make diverse gubernatorial nominees more common, he said.
Latinos, both Democrats, will take on the highest state office in two of the biggest states. Texas voters rejected Gov. Greg Abbott in favor of Gina Hinojosa, who will be the state’s first Latina governor. Xavier Becerra, former California attorney general, outpaced Republican Steve Hilton. He will be California’s first Latino governor since Romualdo Pacheco in 1875.
Record year of women running for governor and Congress
This midterm has been a record-breaker for women vying for state and federal offices. Democrats increased their 2022 number of female candidates to 19 running for governor, according to the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. The Republican Party had seven women setting their sights on governor.
Like Minnesota, Tennessee elected its first female governor. Republican U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn beat Democrat Jerri Green, a Memphis city councilwoman.
Nearly 300 women, including incumbents, were running for the U.S. Senate and House, as documented by Rutgers’ Center for American Women and Politics.
Among them was Democrat Juliana Stratton in Illinois, who defeated Republican Don Tracy on Tuesday. Stratton, the current lieutenant governor, will succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Dick Durbin. With fellow Democrat Sen. Tammy Duckworth, who is of Thai heritage, the pair will make Illinois the first state to be represented by two female senators of color. Stratton’s win also means there will be three Black women serving in the Senate.
___
Associated Press writers Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, Susan Montoya Bryan and Savannah Peters in Albuquerque, New Mexico, contributed to this report.

title: Report: LIV Golf's financial backer dropping plan for new league in 2027
text:
Report: LIV Golf's financial backer dropping plan for new league in 2027
LIV Golf's main investor set to help it emerge from Chapter 11 bankruptcy is scrapping plans for a new version because it lacked enough player support, The Financial Times reported Wednesday.
BC Partners Credit had pledged as much as $300 million for what was called “LIV Golf 2.0,” which wanted at least 10 tournaments and an emphasis on teams. But it required enough players — at least the right players — sticking around for it.
A previously scheduled hearing Thursday in U.S. Bankruptcy Court would shift toward LIV Golf seeking liquidation of its assets, The Financial Times reported.
Related video above: Judge bans Trump from removing trees on public D.C. golf course
LIV Golf did not immediately return phone calls seeking comment.
The Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia was behind LIV Golf when it launched in 2022 by luring away several big names — Dustin Johnson, Brooks Koepka, Bryson DeChambeau and eventually Jon Rahm — with signing bonuses of nine figures.
Even run-of-the-mill players with only one PGA Tour victory signed for $30 million, more than they had earned in their careers.
The league, originally run by Greg Norman, spent more than $5 billion. But a few months after the start of the Iran war, PIF changed its investment strategy and said it would no longer pay for LIV Golf after the 2026 season.
Even as it was trying to emerge from bankruptcy, filed on Sept. 8, the European tour laid down a crushing ultimatum by saying anyone who signed with LIV 2.0 need not apply for membership — making European players ineligible for the Ryder Cup.

title: Federal Marshals carry out arrest in Rockland
text:
ROCKLAND, Maine (WABI) - Federal marshals arrested a fugitive in Rockland Tuesday afternoon, according to the U.S. Department of Justice.
Andrew D. Secord, 24, of New Hampshire was arrested for failure to appear in court for charges out of Merrimack County. Officials say Secord did not show up to an arraignment for felony sexual assault, assault, domestic violence assault, and criminal threatening.
A warrant was issued for Secord’s arrest on Oct. 20. The DOJ says investigators uncovered information that Secord had fled to Maine, and a thorough investigation with the help of local police led to his arrest on Tuesday.
Secord was apprehended without incident and is being held pending extradition to New Hampshire.

title: Mike Johnson won’t seek reelection as House Republican leader
text:
Politics
Our political journalists are based in the Maine State House and have deep source networks across the partisan spectrum in communities all over the state. Their coverage aims to cut through major debates and probe how officials make decisions. Read more Politics coverage here.
WASHINGTON — House Speaker Mike Johnson will be stepping aside from Republican Party leadership after the GOP’s wipeout in the midterm election, declining to seek support to stay on as House minority leader in the new Congress, according to two people familiar with his decision Wednesday.
Johnson is expected to retain his seat as a rank-and-file member of the House from Louisiana when the Congress convenes in January. He won reelection from his Shreveport-area district for an eighth term in office.
It’s a swift rise and fall for Johnson, often seen as an accidental speaker, who nevertheless drew close to President Donald Trump and led the House GOP during a tumultuous era, with one of the slimmest majorities in modern times. And it sets up a fierce internal party battle for the new GOP leader after Democrats swept to power.
Johnson’s sunny assertions that Republicans would defy history in the midterms, as voters traditionally have punished the president’s party in power, failed to hold. Instead, Republicans were trounced as Democrats swept to the House majority, leaving Johnson without a path to power.
The people who told The Associated Press about Johnson’s decision insisted on anonymity to disclose it.
House Republicans are expected to elect their new leader when members-elect gather in Washington next week, in what will likely be a familiar showdown between two who reached for the top spot before — Reps. Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Jim Jordan of Ohio.
The powerful speaker’s gavel now is expected to pass to Democrats, who are preparing to nominate House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York for the job, second in line to the president. The House speaker’s election is among the first votes of the new Congress, on Jan. 3, 2027.
From Shreveport to Washington
Johnson first won the speaker’s gavel in 2023 after his colleagues ousted the previous GOP speaker, Kevin McCarthy of California, in a first-of-its-kind coup in House history.
A lower-level member of House leadership, Johnson in many ways fell into the job after Republican colleagues could not agree on a next-in-line successor to McCarthy. He had distinguished himself before the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol by organizing support for Trump’s false claims of widespread fraud in the 2020 election he lost to Democrat Joe Biden.
Once in office, Johnson quickly pulled closer to Trump — so close that Johnson candidly recounts their almost daily phone calls and chats, often offering his impressions in the president’s voice.
Johnson led passage of the GOP’s signature package of tax breaks and social services cuts that Trump signed into law. He protected the president and his administration from embarrassing votes, including a recent effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, by simply sending lawmakers home.
House leadership elections ahead
Johnson’s decision sets up a potential repeat of the leadership battles that have played out in recent years between the House GOP’s conservative and far-right flanks.
Scalise, the majority leader, has long courted backing from the House GOP’s conservative wing, particularly business and energy sector lawmakers. Jordan, the brawling former wrestler who helmed the Judiciary Committee, has long been preferred by the hard right, including some from the Freedom Caucus.
Both Scalise and Jordan reached for the speaker’s gavel once McCarthy was forced aside in 2023, but they failed to win majority support from their colleagues, splitting the votes. At the time, Johnson emerged as the consensus candidate who became the House speaker.
Story by Lisa Mascaro and Kevin Freking.

title: School reorganization plan rejected by voters
text:
MOUNT DESERT ISLAND — Residents of MDI, Trenton, Frenchboro and Cranberry Isles weighed in on a proposed school district reorganization plan on Tuesday and soundly voted to reject it.
With 361 yes votes and 525 no votes, the town of Tremont was the first to report its results, and by 9:30 p.m. on election night it was clear the plan had failed.
Voters in Mount Desert rejected the reorganization referendum, 542-672. Bar Harbor voters (1,231-1,825) and Southwest Harbor voters (475-540) also rejected the plan.
Frenchboro voters favored the reorganization 12-10, as did Trenton voters, 525-318.
The plan needed majority approval from voters in Trenton, Bar Harbor, Mount Desert, Southwest Harbor and Tremont to pass.
Swan’s Island is not reporting any polling data due to a clerical issue that left the town without a clerk to file the paperwork needed to get the referendum on the ballot. The error was not noted until after the 60-day deadline for questions to be added to the ballot. According to Superintendent Mike Zboray, the town will not vote on the reorganization now that it failed to pass.
Zboray told the Islander that he is grateful for the effort that the Reorganization Planning Committee put into the planning process.
“I just want to share my recognition for them and the hard work and the tough questions that they had to answer to come up with the plan that they did,” said Zboray. “There is certainly work that still needs to be done.”
The referendum and reorganization proposal came after four years of work by the RPC. The RPC has worked on different versions of the plan and spent the past year sharing the plan at public forums around the island.
One version included a proposed island-wide middle school. Another idea to release pressure on towns that recently invested in capital improvements on their respective elementary schools was floated but ultimately scrapped.
Before the issue went out to voters, a handful of island towns weighed in with a mixed bag of responses, mostly leaning towards rejection of the plan. The Bar Harbor School Board voted 3-2 to recommend the town approve the reorganization plan in August. The Mount Desert Warrant Committee, Bar Harbor Town Council and Tremont Selectboard all recommended their respective towns reject the plan.
Zboray sees the years-long process of planning, hosting community forums, gaining feedback and ultimately the vote as evidence that residents are engaged with the idea of reorganizing the district.
“People are definitely interested in reorganization. How that looks, you know, needs some deeper conversation.”
Now that the referendum has failed, the RPC will disband and the process of bringing another reorganization plan forward will need to start from the beginning.
“I think in the end the fact that we’ve moved the needle a little bit and that we’re having these conversations is really important,” said Zboray. “I hope that we will continue to talk about what’s in the best interest of kids within the district and how we can make sure that we’re meeting all students’ needs. The bottom line is we want to make sure kids are ready for high school, and you know our plan was to try to address some of those disparities in the funding … but we’re going to continue to focus on what’s best for kids and make that happen.”

title: Yarmouth boys soccer squeaks past Cape Elizabeth in penalty kicks
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
FALMOUTH — The powerhouse Yarmouth High boys soccer team was pushed all the way by underdog Cape Elizabeth in the Class B South final Wednesday.
Two players who weren’t on Yarmouth’s 16th state championship team in 2025 were the penalty kick difference-makers, and now the Clippers can go for championship No. 17 on Saturday.
Goalkeeper Gabe Janczuk, previously a member of the golf team, stopped two attempts by Cape Elizabeth, and James Hartnett, who chose not to play in 2025, scored the clincher as Yarmouth advanced to another state final with a 2-1 victory (4-1 in penalty kicks).
“It was definitely a gritty win, but never a doubt, though,” Hartnett said. “They made it hard on us tonight and we earned it.”
PENALTY-KICK DRAMA
After Lucas Hayner converted Yarmouth’s first penalty kick, Janczuk stopped a shot by Max Hayward. Joel Butler and Angus Mailhot scored for Yarmouth, bracketing a successful PK by Cape’s Bennett Hooper. That brought up Cape’s Aidan Marks, with Yarmouth ahead 3-1 in the round of five penalty kicks.
It was Marks who scored on the rebound of his own penalty kick with 13:30 left in regulation to tie the game. With Yarmouth trying to protect a 1-0 lead, Janczuk stopped Marks’ first bid with a dive to his left, but Marks banged in the rebound.
“I thought, he’s going to expect me to go (right) and I’m going right back to the left where he put it last time,” Janczuk said.
Janczuk made the save, giving Hartnett a chance to end the game. He coolly put the ball into the right side of the goal for the clincher.
Yarmouth (15-1-1) will face North champion John Bapst at 11 a.m. Saturday at Cameron Stadium in Bangor.
Cape Elizabeth, which was trying to reach its first state final since winning Class A in 1997, finished its season at 8-7-2, with three losses to Yarmouth.
SETTING THE STAGE
As the defending state champion and top seed, Yarmouth was expected to reach the regional final. The Clippers had won 12 straight, including a 7-0 drubbing of Freeport in the semifinals. Yarmouth entered Wednesday’s game with a 93-8 scoring margin.
No. 7 seed Cape Elizabeth was the surprise team. After a 6-6-2 regular season, including 4-1 and 4-0 losses to Yarmouth, Cape posted a pair of 3-2 playoff wins at No. 2 Fryeburg Academy and No. 6 York.
CAPE CAME TO COMPETE
In the first half, the Capers were focused on playing “tight, tight, tight,” as coach Ben Raymond repeatedly implored, not allowing Yarmouth time to build its offense deliberately from the back.
Cape nearly matched Yarmouth in terms of shots (9 to 7 in favor of Yarmouth) and corner kicks (4-3), but Yarmouth scored the only goal of the first half.
Hayner, the Clippers’ standout attacking midfielder, timed his run well enough to stay onside and receive a Hartnett through ball. Hartnett had carried it in rare open space from the defensive zone. Hayner ran onto the ball, sidestepped Cape goalie Cam Branch’s attempted slide tackle and deposited the ball into the open net in the seventh minute.
The trend of even play continued throughout the game, including the two 15-minute overtimes.
“It takes a lot of energy, it takes a lot of focus. We worked a lot on how we want to defend them coming out of the back and how to limit their long services that we got burned on earlier in the year,” said Cape coach Ben Raymond.
STATISTICS
Cape Elizabeth: Aidan Marks (goal), Cam Branch (9 saves); Team ( 14 shots, 7 on goal, 12 corner kicks)
Yarmouth: Lucas Hayner (goal), James Hartnett (assist), Gabe Janczuk (7 saves); Team ( 17 shots, 10 on goal, 7 corner kicks)

title: Maine Ski Season Is Almost Here as Sugarloaf Eyes November Opening
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Ski Season Is Almost Here as Sugarloaf Eyes November Opening
Let the countdown begin.
For all you Mainers dreaming of mountain air, fresh powder, and carving up the slopes, I've got some exciting news for you. Ski season is within sight.
It's hard to believe we're already gearing up for another winter on the mountains, but here we are. And if you're anything like Maine's countless skiing and snowboarding enthusiasts, the anticipation is probably reaching an all-time high. So, let's bring on the snow.
It always amazes me how much we collectively complain about winter, yet still love getting outside and playing in the snow. I guess we Mainers will never lose that kid inside of us.
When Do Maine Ski Mountains Open for the Season?
It’s time to swap out the golf clubs for ski boots and get your gear tuned up. Maine’s stunning slopes are calling, and one mountain has already announced its opening day... well, sort of.
Let the season begin.
While the snow hasn’t started falling yet, and the snowmaking machines remain idle, that hasn’t slowed down Sugarloaf’s plans to announce a tentative opening. The mountain has posted November 20-22 as its opening weekend, marking the start of its 76th year in operation.
When Did Sugarloaf Mountain First Open for Skiing?
Ever since the first trail was cut back in 1950, Sugarloaf has been one of the true ski gems of the Northeast. It attracts visitors from far and wide with its massive terrain, iconic snowfields, and stunning natural beauty. Experts can even enjoy above-treeline glades, a rarity for East Coast skiing. As the second-tallest mountain in Maine, it can get pretty gnarly up there.
The mountain has also introduced many other outdoor activities over the years. They include Nordic skiing, fat biking, tubing, and even cat skiing. Yes, there's plenty of Après ski choices, too.
With that tentative opening date just around the corner, it's no surprise that ticket packages and other deals are already available on Sugarloaf's website. You can find more details here.
Here's hoping its a nice, snowy year for Sugarloaf and the other ski resorts here in Maine and beyond. A healthy ski season is good for everyone.
