title: UMaine’s Spanish point guard looking forward to season after impactful freshman campaign
text:
ORONO, Maine — Last season, in order for University of Maine women’s basketball coach Amy Vachon to give point guard Asta Blauenfeldt some time at the shooting guard position, she had to find a reliable point guard.
And she did.
In fact, freshman Olivia Alvarez from Spain became the full-time point guard, allowing Blauenfeldt to shoot more and become a more productive supplemental scorer. Now, as Thursday’s season opener approaches, Alvarez said she worked on her shooting over the summer and will be ready to take a shot if opponents leave her open.
“I have way more confidence than I had last year,” said Alvarez. “I’m going to be more aggressive. I need to know when people are open and make the right pass.”
Blauenfeldt’s 11 points per game, up from 9.7 the previous year, made her the team’s second-leading scorer behind America East Player of the Year Adrianna Smith, who averaged 22.8 points per contest.
Alvarez averaged 29.6 minutes of playing time per game, fifth highest on the team, and was second in assists with 58 and tied for third in steals with 41. She averaged 3.7 points and 2.6 rebounds per game.
In three America East playoff games, she averaged 5.3 points, 2.7 rebounds, 2 assists and a steal and had only four turnovers in 104 minutes of play.
“Last year was a great year for her,” said Vachon. “As a freshman, she played a lot and I don’t know if anyone expected that or if she was expecting it.”
Alvarez said she received a lot of guidance from seniors Smith, Blauenfeldt and Sarah Talon.
“They taught me how to play, especially in the hard [close] games,” Alvarez said. “I got a lot of experience from that. Now, even though I’m just a sophomore, I can try to teach the newcomers.”
Alvarez played well in a big role last year and handled it with grace, UMaine redshirt sophomore Maddie Fitzpatrick of Cumberland said.
“She has improved a lot over the offseason and will be taking on an even bigger role this season. And she has been handling it very well through the preseason,” Fitzpatrick said. “I’m excited for everyone to watch her play.”
“Her basketball IQ is really high,” senior center Lizzy Gruber of Gardiner said. “As a freshman, you can know what to do but you can’t execute it and do it at a fast rate. One thing Liv has mastered is being able to think fast.”
Alvarez is also an incredible defender, Gruber said, noting that adapting to college basketball during your freshman season is “really, really hard.”
Alvarez takes pride in defense.
“Ever since I was little, all my coaches told me I had to lock in (on defense). I would always guard the best player on the other team so I had to lock in,” Alvarez said.
Alvarez was both a shooting guard and a point guard growing up. She preferred being the point guard, she said.
Vachon’s offense is complicated, but Alvarez got used to running it over the course of the season.
“I pick things up quickly. It wasn’t that hard,” said the 5-foot-8 Alvarez, a native of Las Rozas de Madrid.
She joins an impressive cast of Spaniards who have played for Vachon, including two-time America East Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year Blanca Millan, third team All-America East pick Alba Orois and all-AE Rookie Team selections Laia Sole and Paula Gallego.
“She is a great defender. She is the head of the snake on defense for us,” Vachon said, noting Alvarez is more comfortable with offense and defense.
“She is in charge of controlling the offense and deciding what we’re going to run and when we’re going to run it,” Vachon said. “She has really worked on her shot and her 3-point shot looks really good. She is finishing a lot better.”
But Vachon, a former standout point guard herself at UMaine and the school’s all-time assists leader, recently told Alvarez that scoring “shouldn’t be the first thing you think about when you step onto the court.”
“I told her some games you’re going to score two points and other games you’re going to score 15,” said Vachon. “It’s not always about scoring. Her job as a point guard is to do what the team needs.”
UMaine graduated its top three scorers from last year’s team in Smith, Blauenfeldt and Talon and was picked to finish fourth in the America East preseason coaches poll.
But Alvarez said she feels the team will surprise people.
“It is a different team but we have a lot of people who can do a lot of different things,” said Alvarez. “Everyone has their own role.”
She said they won’t have to rely on just one or two players to score.
“Everyone can score,” Alvarez said.
She is thoroughly enjoying her time in Orono, she said. She really likes her teammates and roommates and noted that they all “hang out together.”
“We’re having a really good time,” Alvarez said.
Alvarez and the Black Bears will open the season at 6 p.m. on Thursday when they host Siena College of New York on the Skip Chappelle Court in the Memorial Gym in Orono.

title: Westbrook consulting firm taps leader to carry out parent company's growth strategy
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
St.Germain, a Westbrook consulting firm, found its new leader from within its own ranks.
Patrick Coughlin has been with St.Germain since 2002 and will take the helm from Mark St.Germain, who founded the company in 1992 and had served as president.
The transition comes nearly two years after St.Germain was acquired by Aventia, an environmental service firm in Lakewood, Colo.
Dual roles
Coughlin retains his role as vice president of St.Germain and takes on the role of business unit leader for Aventia, overseeing operations, staff, client services and growth.
Mark St.Germain transitions to the role of founder and strategic growth advisor and will assist Coughlin to ensure a seamless transition, strengthen client relationships and connect clients with St.Germain and Aventia’s expertise and resources.
“This transition builds on the strong foundation Mark has established over more than 30 years,” said Coughlin.
Coughlin has over 20 years of experience in the environmental industry and received his bachelor’s degree in chemistry and environmental studies from Bowdoin College. His environmental chemistry and public relations experience goes back to 1989.
Environmental consulting
St.Germain is an environmental consulting and engineering firm providing senior level management to clients in the areas of site planning and development, energy, petroleum and waste management, site investigation and remediation, water resources and environmental, health and safety compliance. Clients include energy suppliers, waste and recycling companies, manufacturers, financial institutions, aggregate producers, affordable housing developers and state and local governments.
St.Germain has 25 employees at its office at 846 Main St. in Westbrook, where the company has been since 2003.
Aventia, with over 400 employees, is an environmental firm that offers consulting, field services and technology-driven solutions to public and private sector clients in more than 40 states. Aventia is in the portfolio of Bernhard Capital Partners, a private equity firm based in Baton Rouge, La., with $4.4 billion in assets under management. In addition to St.Germain,
The acquisition was expected to benefit St. Germain by enabling it to offer services to clients of other Aventia subsidiaries and by reducing costs through the centralization of some purchases and back-office functions.

title: In hotly contested Senate race, Jackson unseats incumbent Collins
text:
Troy Jackson, a Democrat and logger from Aroostook County, pulled off what in July would have seemed an improbable upset — unseating U.S. Sen. Susan Collins, who was running for her sixth term in the U.S. Senate.
Jackson, 58, won the Senate seat with 53.8% of the vote, the Associated Press reported with 86% of the vote tallied through Wednesday morning.
He was part of a blue wave of victories, with Democrats flipping Senate seats in seven states to take control of the governmental body. In addition to Maine, Democrats won seats in Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas. Kansas had not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932.
Democrats also gained control of the House of Representatives.
Jackson, who is from Allagash, has significant experience in the state Legislature, but none at the federal level.
His win might have seemed improbable in July when he was chosen by state Democrats to challenge Collins, a Caribou native who has served in the Senate for nearly three decades and is chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
Jackson was thrust into the role after Graham Platner’s campaign came to a halt amid sexual assault allegations.
Speaking to supporters in Portland after midnight following a 101-day campaign, Jackson pledged to fight for Medicare for all, affordable housing and individuals’ freedom to make their own health care decisions. He also said he would represent all Mainers no matter whom they voted in this election.
“If you’re watching this after getting home from a shift or sitting at the table wondering how you’re going to pay the next bill, I want you to hear something very clearly,” he said. “You are sending somebody to Washington who knows exactly what that feels like. But more importantly, I am going to remember who sent me here.”
Deputy Editor Renee Cordes contributed to this report.

title: County Students Learn Budgeting at Financial Fair
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - The Aroostook Chapter of Credit Unions hosted a Financial Fitness Fair at Northern Maine Community College today.
Local businesses and organizations work year-round to fundraise and plan for the Aroostook Financial Fitness Fair. This year, the fair was held at Northern Maine Community College. Students picked a career and were given a budget based on that career. The goal of the event was to teach local students about finances and budgeting.
Dan Bagley, a Committee Member for the Aroostook Credit Union Financial Fitness Committee said: “I think that there’s a financial need, you know. The schools do the best they can to provide the curriculum that they have to deliver and this is kind of a bonus. It’s an intentional act to manage your finances. You need to be diligent and we’re just trying to give these kids just a glimpse of what their future looks like. I think everybody has fun. Again, they’re just scratching the surface with a one-day event but it’s a lifestyle and a choice to manage your finances and we’re just trying to enlighten them a little bit today.”
Students said the event was fun and showed them how their jobs affect their budgets. Mackenzie Davis, one fair attendee said: “Whatever career you choose it’s kind of like your budget for your future. They didn’t have forensic science or criminology. So, I chose police officer and sheriff. That was the closest I could find. We’re going around and we’re kind of learning our budget for the year for our adult life. They have different stations like housing, fun. There’s extras and transportation. So, it’s kind of getting an idea of what our future’s gonna look like in budgeting.”
The fair also served as an opportunity for students to learn about and apply for local scholarships. Students who attended left the college with a better understanding of how to manage their finances after graduation.

title: The Gracie Theatre celebrates Veterans Day with Springsteen tribute
text:
BANGOR — A powerhouse band of professional musicians will perform the music of Bruce Springsteen at The Gracie Theatre on Saturday, Nov. 7 and tickets are available now.

title: Elementary school budget talks begin in Mount Desert
text:
MOUNT DESERT — Preliminary budget conversations began in Mount Desert Tuesday night at the Mount Desert Elementary School Board meeting.
Principal Heather Dorr and Superintendent Mike Zboray shared preliminary budget findings for fiscal year 2026-27 with the board.
The unaudited carryover, which is unspent budget funds, so far for the current fiscal year is $710,000, $98,000 more than was estimated last year. Zboray explained that there were some savings in salaries across areas from open ed tech and bus driver positions. There were also savings in health insurance from employees moving off their plans to join their spouses’ instead.
Some places where spending has so far exceeded what was budgeted included bus leases which were $19,000 over the budgeted amount. According to Zboray, those costs were due to increased interest rates and the leases ended up being more expensive than expected. Food service is another area where spending exceeds the budgeted amount by $8,000.
In terms of cost centers, the special education teachers line of the budget is anticipated to exceed the budgeted amount by $152,292. Dorr explained that a teacher was moved into the special education line.
The school is also contracted with ProCare Therapy to provide fifth through eighth grade special education case management. However, according to Dorr, ProCare is no longer providing a case manager, so she anticipates saving money in that cost center.
“So, if we were to continue with ProCare then it would be, this number would stay as is, but we currently don’t have a person to be under contract with,” said Dorr regarding the amount exceeding the budget. She elaborated saying that they haven’t paid ProCare for the last month because they haven’t received services. “So, we’ve saved there, but we also haven’t had a case manager.”
There was another unexpected expense for the school for a student who recently moved to the district with needs for an alternative educational program. The tuition costs are $45,000, and since it was an unexpected expense, the school can use reserve funds to pay for it, according to Dorr. The emergency special education reserve account currently totals $163,433.
Other items that exceed the budget include $3,000 for the summer school homework club cost center and $1,851 for the social worker budget.
Zboray said they are expecting to go over budget on heating oil by $12,500 due to increased oil prices.
“All this stuff is difficult because you are trying to plan 18 months ahead of time on these budgets,” said school board chair Brian Henkel.
Principal Dorr shared some goals for the next budget including, “Trying to keep things going the way they’re going and presenting a budget that is palatable.” She went on to share that there are no significant equipment needs currently that would impact the budget. The school greenhouse needs repairs that Dorr said are estimated at $10,000 but that there are donated funds that may be available for use.
In other business, the board discussed renewing their memorandum of understanding or MOU with the Bar Harbor and Mount Desert Police Department to hire a school resource officer. The MOU is shared by Bar Harbor, Mount Desert and MDI High School departments.
The MDES board agreed to the MOU last year and a resource officer currently visits the school on a regular basis.
The school resource officer is an employee of the Bar Harbor and Mount Desert Police Department. Candidates were interviewed by administrators, according to Zboray, to ensure that they were a good fit for the school.
The MOU states that the mission of the student resource officer or SRO program is, “To promote school safety and the educational climate at the school, not to enforce school discipline or punish students.”
One member of the board opposed the MOU sharing disagreement with having police officers in school.
Board member Gail Marshall shared her support for the MOU but only with an officer who fits the role.
“I think this is a very person-specific assignment,” said Marshall. “If you don’t have those right people, you should not have that program.”
The board voted to renew the MOU in a 4-1 decision.

title: Couple who took in 16 foster kids convicted of abuse ‘under the guise of discipline’
text:
LANSING, Mich. (Gray News) - A Michigan couple is accused of abusing their adopted and foster children under the “guise of discipline” for financial gain, according to authorities.
Jurors found 59-year-old Tamal Flore guilty of six counts of first-degree child abuse, two counts of second-degree child abuse and three counts of third-degree child abuse, a press release said.
Her husband, 61-year-old Jerry Flore, was convicted of a single count of second-degree child abuse, which carries up to 10 years in prison. Jurors acquitted him on nine other abuse charges.
The Office of the Michigan Attorney General prosecuted the case, alleging the couple routinely mistreated children brought into their home since 2007.
According to a report from The Detroit News, the Flores were accused of abusing seven of the 16 children they fostered or adopted. The children reportedly described being whipped with a belt, beaten with metal and wooden spoons, and locked in rooms or the garage for days.
Children were also forced to sleep in a marked kitchen area called “the square” for weeks at a time, perform strenuous punishment exercises and had food withheld if they did not complete daily housework.
Sentencing is scheduled for Jan. 11.

title: Read the poem ‘Ode to Soup’ by Ruby Van Dyk
text:
This week’s poem, by Ruby Van Dyk, asks to consider soup and all that it might mean to us — not just a comfort food during a cold, but a talisman of culture, memories and myriad emotions and resiliencies. I love this poem’s vivid, leaping list of soup’s meanings, and how the poem is fueled by questions that simmer our own meditations.
Van Dyk (she/her), who now attends Stanford University, was a senior at Casco Bay High School at the time of writing this poem. She is very passionate about everything related to food. She spends her time outside of school engaged in Portland’s local food systems and in nature. Her poetry book, published in 2025 through the Telling Room’s Young Emerging Authors Fellowship Program, is centered around why we should all care about food: how it impacts us and the environment, and ways we must change this system.
Poets, please note that submissions to Deep Water are open now and through the end of the year. Deep Water is especially eager to share poems by Black writers, writers of color, indigenous writers, LGBTQ+ writers, and other underrepresented voices. Submit your credits at mainewriters.org
Ode to Soup
To me it’s my grandmother’s hands chopping celery.
What is it to you? Sickness?
Does it remind you of grainy purple
syrup and stomach aches?
The bathroom which fogs up to clear
the sharpness in your chest?
To me it’s the prickle of my skin. Sparks,
burns. It’s that temporary scar, wrapped in white fabric.
It’s that man I saw every day across the restaurant.
Always alone. What was it to him?
To me it is the curve of the fake china spoon,
the yell of the beer drunk mahjong players.
What was it to them? It’s the steam printed across my forehead,
writing out stories in untamed chicken scratch.
It’s the dip of my finger in candle wax,
the yell of my mother.
The apology.
What is it to her?
I live while the smell remains, in that creaky house,
disguising conversations in claustrophobic heat.
The scent of campfire hiding in my braided hair,
my hand hovering over the blue burner, a cruel joke.
It sits in my stomach and it doesn’t spin.
I lay myself against the cold tile floor
and listen to the whistling of the water,
the gurgle of the boil. An inhale and an exhale,
rice noodles like long gangly limbs,
onions chopped in haphazard effort.
Is it only sickness to you?
— Ruby Van Dyk
Megan Grumbling is a poet and writer who lives in Portland. title: Susan Collins’ Senate Career Lasted Far Longer Than She Originally Promised
text:
Susan Collins’ Senate Career Lasted Far Longer Than She Originally Promised
Let’s take a look back at the pledge the senator from Caribou made when she was seeking election 30 years ago.
👇 KEEP READING: Best counties to retire to in Maine 👇
During her first U.S. Senate campaign in Maine in 1996, Republican Susan Collins pledged to serve no more than two six-year terms.
She made the commitment publicly during a televised WMTW debate while answering a question about congressional term limits.
Collins said she would honor the pledge regardless of whether a term limits law or constitutional amendment passed.
At the time, she argued that two terms would provide enough time to contribute in Washington before returning home and allowing someone else to serve.
Collins later said she changed her position after learning how Senate seniority could increase her ability to advocate for Maine.
She went on to defeat Democratic challengers Tom Allen in 2008, Shenna Bellows in 2014, and Sara Gideon in 2020, extending her Senate career well beyond the two terms she originally pledged to serve.
Democrat Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and logger, defeated Collins in the Nov. 3 election, denying her a sixth term and ending her nearly 30-year tenure in the Senate.
Jackson campaigned on lowering housing and health care costs and supporting workers, while criticizing Collins for not doing enough to oppose President Donald Trump.
And there you have it! A pledge made during Collins’ first Senate campaign remained part of the political conversation all the way through her final race three decades later.

title: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, will become first Muslim senator
text:
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed wins Michigan Senate race, will become first Muslim senator
Progressive favorite Abdul El-Sayed has defeated Republican Mike Rogers in a bitter campaign for Michigan’s open Senate seat, giving the Democratic Party’s left wing a breakthrough victory in one of the nation’s most important swing states.
El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, will become the nation’s first Muslim senator. A former public health official who has never held elected office, he rose from a double-digit defeat in Michigan’s Democratic gubernatorial primary eight years ago to win a seat in the U.S. Senate.
El-Sayed overcame massive outside spending in both the Democratic primary and general election with a grassroots campaign built around universal health care, removing outside money from elections and sharp criticism of Israel.
Backed by progressive leaders including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, his victory will bolster the movement ahead of the 2028 presidential election, offering evidence that candidates embracing its agenda can win in critical battleground states.
Republicans had cleared the field for Rogers, a former congressman who narrowly lost a Senate race to then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin two years ago. But Rogers struggled to balance his loyalty to President Donald Trump with concerns over rising prices tied to the war in Iran and economic turmoil from the president’s tariffs.
The campaign also featured bitter attacks over El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel. Trump and other Republicans repeatedly sought to link him to terrorist organizations, despite no evidence of such ties, and questioned his loyalty to the United States.
El-Sayed faced questions about whether he could unite Democrats after a contentious primary, particularly among Black voters in Detroit and Jewish voters in its suburbs. El-Sayed’s primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, shocked Democrats by endorsing Rogers on Nov. 1, saying the Democratic candidate hadn’t done enough to address her and the Jewish community’s concerns.
El-Sayed overcame concerns about a divided Democratic coalition
The race became a focal point in the national battle for Senate control after two-term Democratic Sen. Gary Peters decided not to seek reelection.
El-Sayed emerged from a bruising August primary against the establishment-backed Stevens that drew nearly $60 million in outside spending. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, spent nearly $30 million opposing El-Sayed, its largest investment in a single race. El-Sayed has been a staunch critic of Israel.
The contentious primary exposed divisions within the Democratic coalition. El-Sayed faced criticism from some in Michigan’s Jewish community over his rhetoric, including his statement that “hurt people hurt people” following an attack on a Michigan synagogue earlier this year. He later apologized, saying he was “sorry” to “anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful.”
His campaign appearances with Hasan Piker, a popular political streamer who has made inflammatory comments about Israel, Jews and the Sept. 11 attacks, also became a target of criticism.
Some Democrats worried about Black voter turnout in Detroit after Stevens carried Wayne County in the primary. Former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris were among the high-profile Democrats who campaigned with El-Sayed in the city to help mobilize voters.
Progressive agenda breaks through in Michigan
El-Sayed campaigned on an unapologetically progressive platform that made some moderate Democrats uneasy. Central to his campaign was Medicare for All, which would replace the current mix of private and public health insurance with a government-run, single-payer system.
Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders helped build momentum for El-Sayed early in the campaign, while Ocasio-Cortez joined him for a final campaign swing through Michigan’s Upper Peninsula and the Detroit area.
The victory will give progressives a powerful argument heading into the 2028 presidential election that their agenda can win, even in the nation’s most competitive battleground states.
Republicans opted to run it back with Rogers after his razor-thin 2024 loss, when Slotkin prevailed even as Trump won Michigan by more than a percentage point. Once a CNN contributor who criticized Trump, Rogers has aligned himself more closely with the president in recent years.
Rogers tried to expand his support among Democrats and independents, particularly Black and Jewish voters.
But the political environment raised a fresh challenge for the Republican nominee. Rogers, who chaired the House Intelligence Committee and built much of his career around national security, had to navigate high fuel prices and an unpopular war with Iran while remaining aligned with Trump.
“The war with Iran needs to end, and end quickly,” Rogers wrote on social media in September.

title: Grohoski cruises to reelection in State Senate, all other local incumbents also victorious in legislative races
text:
ELLSWORTH — State Senator Nicole Grohoski, Democrat of Ellsworth, cruised to reelection Tuesday in Senate District 7 that covers the most populous part of Hancock County.
She defeated Republican challenger Cheryl Hewes of Ellsworth, 14,382 votes to 7,912 votes, in the 21 Hancock County municipalities that make up Senate District 7. That includes Bar Harbor, Blue Hill and Ellsworth.
In a statement late Wednesday night, Grohoski thanked voters for their support.
“I was raised here in Ellsworth, and Hancock County is my home,” she said. “There is no greater honor than serving our community in the State House, and it is a responsibility that I do not take lightly.”
Grohoski had large margins of victory in multiple communities (2,532 to 672 in Bar Harbor, 1,340 to 521 in Blue Hill). Hewes won in Frenchboro (13 votes to Grohoski’s 9) and Verona Island (158 votes to Grohoski’s 124). In Ellsworth, Grohoski got 2,268 votes while Hewes received 1,887.
Senate District 7 also includes the Knox County town of Isle au Haut, where Grohoski bested Hewes, 39-10. This will be Grohoski’s third full term in the State Senate, and she previously served two terms in the House of Representatives. All legislative seats in Maine have two-year terms.
State Senate District 6
Senator Marianne Moore (R-Calais) could not run for re-election after serving four consecutive terms in the Senate due to Maine’s term limits. Competing to replace her were State Representative Billy Bob Faulkingham, Republican of Winter Harbor, and Aaron Dana of Indian Township, who was not enrolled in a political party. Dana currently serves in the Legislature as the Passamaquoddy Tribe’s representative.
District 6 includes 13 towns in Hancock County (Amherst, Aurora, Eastbrook, Franklin, Gouldsboro, Great Pond, Hancock, Mariaville, Osborn, Sorrento, Sullivan, Waltham and Winter Harbor) and all of Washington County.
With 12 of the 13 Hancock County towns reporting as of Wednesday morning (results were not immediately available from Amherst), Faulkingham won in all of them. The total margin in Hancock County was 3,056 for Faulkingham to 2,070 for Dana.
Statewide news agencies, which also did not have results from all towns, showed Faulkingham leading Dana by about 60% to 40% as of Wednesday morning.
In a statement posted on his Facebook page, Faulkingham expressed gratitude for the support.
”Thank you to the people of Downeast Maine for choosing me to be your Senator!” he wrote. “Jesus is still King, the sun rose this morning, and I still have a lot of fight left in me. Now let’s get to work!”
This will be Faulkingham’s first term in the State Senate, after serving four consecutive terms in the House of Representatives (where he served as minority leader).
State Senate District 10
In Senate District 10, incumbent Republican David Haggan fended off a challenge from Democrat Jaric Fontaine by about 10 percentage points. Both men are from Hampden.
Hancock County towns in District 10 are Bucksport, Dedham and Otis. Haggan won in all three. Haggan won in all nine Penobscot County communities as well.
This will be Haggan’s second term in the Senate, after four consecutive terms in the House.
State House District 12
In House District 12, two newcomers to state politics vied to replace Faulkingham.
Republican Thomas A. Hart Jr. defeated Roy D. Gott, who was not enrolled in any political party, 2,156 (52.3%) to 1,964 (47.7%). Hart won four of the six towns in the district (Gouldsboro, Hancock, Sorrento and Winter Harbor), while Gott won his hometown of Franklin and Sullivan. Hart also prevailed in the Washington County town of Steuben, 345-228.
The contest was close in Sorrento, where Hart defeated Gott, 86-81.
State House District 13
Incumbent Republican Russell White of Ellsworth defeated Democrat Michael Cunningham of Ellsworth, 2,262 to 2,153. The district is made up of Ellsworth, Waltham and Fletcher’s Landing (whose residents vote in Ellsworth, and their numbers are included with the city’s).
It was very, very close in Ellsworth, where White got seven more votes (2,098) than Cunningham (2,091). The margin was wider in Waltham, where voters split 164-62 in favor of White.
This will be White’s second term in the House.
State House District 14
In House District 14, made up of the towns of Bar Harbor, Cranberry Isles, Lamoine and Mount Desert, incumbent Democrat Gary Friedmann of Bar Harbor ran unopposed for reelection. He received a total of 4,556 votes in the four towns in the district. This will be his second term in the House.
State House District 15
In House District 15, incumbent Democrat Holly Eaton of Deer Isle defeated challenger Clifford Noyes of Southwest Harbor, who was not enrolled in any political party. Eaton received more than double the number of votes Noyes received districtwide, 3,534 (70.6%) to 1,474 (29.4%).
Eaton won all seven Hancock County communities in the district (Brooklin, Deer Isle, Frenchboro, Southwest Harbor, Stonington, Swan’s Island and Tremont). The margin was closest in Frenchboro, where Eaton received 10 votes and Noyes got 8.
District 15 also includes two Knox County towns, and Eaton won handily there, too (41-8 in her favor in Isle au Haut and 486-171 in Vinalhaven).
This will be Eaton’s third term serving in the House.
State House District 16
In House District 16, incumbent Democrat Nina Milliken of Blue Hill defeated Republican challenger Eric White of Trenton 3,633 to 1,943, 65.2% to 34.8%.
Milliken bested White in all six of the district’s towns (Blue Hill, Brooksville, Castine, Sedgwick, Surry and Trenton). This will be her third term in the House.
State House District 17
House District 17 saw a rematch of the 2024 contest there, with Republican Steve Bishop of Bucksport and Democrat Ron Russell of Verona Island vying to represent the four-town district.
In 2024, Russell was the incumbent (he was first elected to the House in 2022) and Bishop was the challenger. Bishop won. This year, Bishop was the incumbent, and Russell was seeking to unseat him. Bishop won again.
It was a close race: out of just under 5,000 ballots cast (4,959 in total), Bishop received 2,528 votes (51%) to 2,431 (49%) for Russell — a difference of 97 votes.
The contest was close in all four towns, with Bishop winning two (Bucksport and Orland) and Russell winning two others (Penobscot and Verona Island). But Russell’s victory in Verona Island was only by four votes (147 to 143 for Bishop), while Bishop’s margin in Bucksport was large enough (1,343 to 1,200 for Russell) to carry him to victory.
This will be Bishop’s second term in the House.
State House District 18
In House District 18, incumbent Republican Mathew McIntyre of Lowell was on track for re-election over Democratic challenger Jonathan Goble of Cherryfield. With results available in seven of the eight Hancock County municipalities as of Wednesday morning, McIntyre had won in all of them (Aurora, Dedham, Eastbrook, Great Pond, Mariaville, Osborn and Otis). His margin of victory was wide in some places (302 votes in Otis to Goble’s 131 votes there) and narrow in others (McIntyre bested Goble 22 to 20 in Great Pond).
District 18 is also made up of the Penobscot County towns of Burlington, Clifton, Greenbush, Lowell and Passadumkeag and the Washington County towns of Beddington, Cherryfield and Deblois. The district also includes multiple swaths of unorganized territory.
With more than 75% of the total district reporting results as of Wednesday morning, the Portland Press Herald reported that McIntyre looked to be headed to a comfortable re-election win, 63% to 37% over Goble (with about 1,000 votes more than Goble).
This will be McIntyre’s second term in the House.

title: Political analyst says Senate-elect Jackson should follow Collins’ lead on constituent services
text:
WATERVILLE, Maine (WABI) - Democrat Troy Jackson flipped Sen. Susan Collins’ Maine Senate seat after her 30 years in office. Jackson’s win was powered by strong turnout and by cutting into Collins’ margins across rural communities.
Political analyst Dan Shea, a Colby College government professor, said as voters look to Jackson to tackle major issues like health care and the cost of living, Jackson’s transition also will hinge on mastering what experts call the “bread and butter” of Washington politics: constituent services.
Shea said matching Collins’ reputation for local casework will be critical.
“Susan Collins did that well. You may have disagreed with her on policy matters, but her constituent service operation was excellent. I think Senator-elect Jackson would do well to follow her lead,” Shea said.
Shea suggested Jackson sit down with Collins’ transition team to seek guidance on navigating the federal bureaucracy. He said that would help ensure local towns and everyday Mainers continue receiving direct federal assistance.

title: Lions linebacker Jack Campbell says he has full movement in lower body after suffering neck injury
text:
Lions linebacker Jack Campbell says he has full movement in lower body after suffering neck injury
Detroit Lions All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell said he has full movement in his lower body and is “continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body," in his first comments since he was carted off the field on a backboard during a game against Minnesota.
“I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic,” Campbell said Wednesday in a statement released by the team. “I’m taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better.”
Campbell suffered a neck injury early in the fourth quarter of a 19-15 win over the Vikings on Sunday. He was alert when he was taken to the hospital, where he has been recovering since his injury.
Lions coach Dan Campbell said it was powerful that Jack Campbell updated his improving condition himself, shortly before the team's previously scheduled news conferences with coaches and players.
“That’s good news. That’s positive news,” Dan Campbell said. “We’re all thankful for that.”
Jack Campbell was face down on the turf and not moving after hitting Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson. He was evaluated by medical personnel before being strapped to a board and carefully lifted onto the cart to a round of applause.
“I especially want to thank the athletic trainers and medical personnel who responded and cared for me on the field,” Jack Campbell said. “I know those were difficult moments, and I’m incredibly grateful for the professionalism, compassion, and care you showed me. The way you handled everything and looked after me when I needed it most is something I’ll never forget.”
The former Iowa star was drafted by the Lions with the 18th overall pick in 2023. Last season, he was an All-Pro selection after becoming the first NFL player in seven years to have 150-plus tackles and at least five sacks and three forced fumbles.
Jack Campbell's condition has been closely followed since Sunday, a fact that he has felt.
“My family and I want to sincerely thank everyone for the overwhelming amount of love, prayers, and support we’ve received over the past few days,” he said. “It means more to us than words can express.”
The Lions (5-2) play at Miami (1-6) on Sunday.

title: Volleyball ends season as runners-up in Class C
text:

title: What will Susan Collins’ loss mean to Maine? Voters say it’s ‘up in the air’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
This story is for subscribers only. Subscribers and donors help fund BDN’s in-depth political analysis, campaign finance investigations, and first-in-the-nation race calls. All election results, live analysis and voting information are free to access as a public service. Subscribe for $1 for 3 months right now.
Troy Jackson’s surprise election win means Maine will lose one of its most powerful political figures after he unseated the longtime Republican U.S. Sen. Susan Collins as part of a national wave of Democratic victories.
A day after Tuesday’s election, Mainers reacted with a mix of excitement and concern over what losing Collins could mean to the state and its small towns that have benefited from the federal dollars she’s directed to local projects.
Collins, who was first elected to the chamber in 1996, made her stature in Washington, including as the chair of the Senate’s appropriations committee, central to her campaign pitch. Her power over the federal pursestrings allowed her to divert millions of federal dollars to Maine communities. Through earmarks, a process that allows legislators to request federal money for specific projects, she brought windfalls to numerous municipalities across Maine.
“That’s all up in the air right now,” said Mike Scott, the president of Professional Firefighters of Maine. The group endorsed Collins. Scott said he was “still processing” her defeat on Wednesday morning.
Fire departments have been among the main beneficiaries of Collins’ largesse. She frequently helped small towns pay for fire trucks and safety equipment, which have grown increasingly expensive. More than $60 million in earmarks went to Maine’s public safety projects this year.
Still, Scott said he looked forward to a positive relationship with Jackson, whom he called a “longtime friend” of firefighters. The group had endorsed Jackson in his run for governor earlier this year.
Collins’ appropriations power and past ability to survive tough political headwinds has helped her dominate Maine politics. A New York Times story published Saturday outlined how even some Democrats have been hesitant to cross Collins.
Lewiston’s Democratic Mayor Carl Sheline told the Times that projects supported by Collins’ appropriations contributed to his decision against endorsing Jordan Wood, her first Democratic challenger, last year. He later endorsed Jackson, and on Wednesday, he expressed relief at Collins’ loss.
“We need real moral leadership for our state and country, and Sen. Collins was asking us to forgo that for something as common as money,” he told the Bangor Daily News.
Rural conservative areas have benefited heavily from federal cash. Paul Davis, a former Republican state legislator and current Piscataquis County commissioner, said Collins helped bring dollars to the area for transportation projects.
“We’ve lost that revenue source,” he said. “We’ve lost that influence.”
Aroostook County Administrator Justin Tibbetts said that even before Election Day he heard from people concerned that the region will lose funding with Collins out.
“Just having somebody — it doesn’t matter which party — as chair of the appropriations committee that’s able to bring that [money] to Maine, a lot of folks that I’ve talked to are concerned about that,” Tibbetts said Wednesday.
Tibbetts referenced the North Lakes Fire and Rescue’s new fire station that is under construction, for which Collins secured roughly $3 million. The county couldn’t have built the station without those funds, he said.
“Certainly it’s too early to tell what Mr. Jackson will be able to help the state of Maine with,” he said. “There is a level of the unknown, but we’ll see how things go, and I look forward to meeting with Sen.-elect Jackson.”
Multiple voters in downtown Bangor said Wednesday they were surprised by Jackson’s victory, especially because of Collins’ track record of bringing funds to the state. One voter, Matt Finch, blamed the senator’s loss on Trump.
Her 30-year record “amounted to nothing” when she was lumped in with Trump, Finch said.
Despite saying that they supported a change in Maine politics, multiple voters said they’re worried that Jackson won’t be able to bring the same funding back to the state. Jackson might “ruffle feathers in the wrong way,” and not have the same power that Collins had, Finch said.
Others are unconcerned. John Merrill, the owner of Merrill’s Bookstore in Hallowell, said he hasn’t felt this good about the state of the country in a long time. He dismissed Collins’ funding prowess as campaign rhetoric.
“Anyone who represented Maine has brought federal dollars to Maine,” he said, noting that he is 80 years old. “[Bath Iron Works] has been building ships long before Susan Collins was ever thought of in Congress, so that’s a specious argument.”
He likened her promises to bring money to Maine to President Donald Trump’s suggestion that he would pay everyone $5,000 if Republicans kept control of Congress.
“I don’t react well to people who try to bribe me,” he said.
BDN writers Kasey Turman and Paula Brewer contributed reporting.

title: Wildfire in White Mountain National Forest more than doubles to roughly 1,000 acres
text:
The wildfire just over the Maine border in New Hampshire has more than doubled in size since Tuesday to nearly 1,000 acres, according to the U.S. Forest Service.
The Forest Service first responded to the fire in an area of White Mountain National Forest about seven miles southeast of Gorham, New Hampshire, on Sunday afternoon. The fire grew to roughly 300 acres on Monday and more than 375 acres on Tuesday. It was estimated to be 982 acres as of Wednesday night.
The fire is on the northwest side of the Wild River in Coos County, New Hampshire, just west of Mount Hastings, which is in Oxford County, Maine. It’s estimated to be 11% contained.
The spread since Tuesday has been mainly toward the north and west and through inaccessible terrain, Sarah Hankens, a spokesperson for the Forest Service at White Mountain National Forest, said in a news release Wednesday morning.
She said the fire does not pose any immediate threats to life or property, but officials will work to identify “potential values at risk” and implement suppression tactics accordingly. A forest closure prohibiting public entry was ordered for the area of the fire Wednesday night.
As of Wednesday, the outskirts of the wildfire were less than a half-mile from the Maine border. It is just over 4 miles southwest of the center of Gilead, Maine, and about 2 miles up Wild River from the historic Oxford County logging village of Hastings.
The ongoing drought, which has impacted parts of New Hampshire — and was recently declared a disaster in Maine — has been a key factor in the fire’s rapid growth, Hankens said.
The Forest Service’s response grew from 40 assigned personnel on Monday to 50 on Tuesday, supported by helicopters and drones. Hankens said Wednesday morning that the Forest Service was coordinating with local and state agencies, and 89 personnel were assigned by Wednesday night, with more “en route.”
Hankens said firefighters’ focus Wednesday morning was on setting fire lines and removing vegetation to limit the fire’s spread. But by Wednesday night, Hankens indicated firefighters were getting more aggressive, calling it a “full suppression fire.”
“The objective is to keep the fire in its current footprint and limit fire spread to the greatest extent possible,” she said.
The cause of the fire is under investigation.
A public meeting will be held regarding the fire in Shelburne, New Hampshire, on Thursday, Hankens said.
The wildfire and associated smoke can be tracked online via maps produced by government agencies, such as NASA or the U.S. Department of Environmental Protection, in partnership with the Forest Service.

title: John Bapst boys soccer claims 4th Class B North title in 5 years with win over Oceanside
text:
HAMPDEN, Maine — The John Bapst High School boys soccer team from Bangor had its run of three consecutive Class B North championships snapped by Oceanside of Rockland, 2-1, in overtime last fall.
But the top-seeded Crusaders avenged that loss on Wednesday night as senior striker Kapser Hansen scored a pair of goals and junior wing Gavin Rogers scored the other as John Bapst blanked third seed Oceanside 3-0 at the Hampden Academy field.
John Bapst, now 16-0-1, will take on defending state champ Yarmouth, 15-1-1, in Saturday’s 11 a.m. state title game at Cameron Stadium in Bangor.
Oceanside, a 2-1 loser to Yarmouth in overtime in last year’s state game, concluded a 13-4 season.
It was just the second time all season that the Mariners had been shut out. They entered the game averaging 4.25 goals per game.
But the Crusaders have been very stingy, allowing only nine goals all season long with Wednesday’s game being their 10th shutout and 15th game in which they allowed one goal or less.
“Our defense really held them. They have been super strong for us all year long, minimizing the shot opportunities,” said John Bapst coach Jason Pangburn. “(Oceanside) has some really dangerous players. Our defense played well.”
“Our defense is always solid,” said John Bapst senior midfielder Rafa Rentosa. “You can always trust them to take care of strong attackers like (Oceanside’s Guy) Yamba and Lucas Novicka.”
John Bapst goalie Bode Phillips made five saves on 20 Oceanside shot attempts while Oceanside’s Grady Geretz and Cayden Gray combined for five stops on 16 Crusder attempts.
Hansen scored what proved to be the game-winner just 9:46 into the game.
The ball was misplayed by an Oceanside defender and Hansen took full advantage by poking the ball away from the defender, breaking in down the left channel of the penalty area and beating Geretz with a low left-footed shot to the far corner.
“I was able to tap it (free) and I took a few big touches toward the goal,” said Hansen. “I saw the goalie coming toward me and I saw that the right side was open so I was able to shift my hips and get it as far away from the ‘keeper as possible.
“To start off the game with an early goal felt really good,” said Hansen.
“We expected it to be a great game and for Kasper to be able to put in that early one really helped us get things going,” said Pangburn.
The highly-skilled Yamba made a nifty run to maneuver past a pair of defenders and attack the net from a sharp angle to Phillips’ left but he shot it into the side netting.
A few minutes later, Phillips had to be alert to get his hands and chest on a quickly-taken one-hop free kick by Thomas Geddis from the edge of the penalty area.
Rogers expanded the lead 2:58 into the second half off a perfect feed from Ewan Tunney, who made a clever 180-degree spin at the top of the area and then slid the ball right into his path as he broke free down the left channel in the penalty area.
“We practice a lot on making bending runs around the defenders instead of making a flat run and that was a great pass from Ewan,” said Rogers, who neatly slotted a right-footed shot into the far corner past the helpless Geretz.
Just 4:27 later, Hansen scored his second when again he broke free.
Geretz raced off his line to get his chest on the shot but, unfortunately for him, the ball popped into the air off his body and rolled into the goal.
“I tried to place it a little wider than where it went,” said Hansen. “I was very fortunate it went into the goal. I was very happy about that.”
He nearly completed a hat trick later in the game on another break-in but Geretz made a terrific save to rob him.
Phillips’ best save of the night came in the second half as he sprinted off his line to smother Quinn Commeau’s break-in chance.
Pangburn said his senior son Josh and his center back partner Jake Monnier did a stellar job marking Yamba and communicated very well; holding midfielder Luke Derosier turned in an impressive performance keeping an eye on Oceanside midfielder Lucas Novicka and that right back Hayden Pepin created a lot of good offensive opportunities to keep things going in the second half.
“Overall, it was really a team effort,” said Pangburn.
Oceanside head coach Robbie Krul said the first half had “plenty of little moments.
“We had a game plan and we executed it but, unfortunately, we made one error and we were down 1-0,” said Krul. “Typically, we’re a second half team. But they got another quick transition goal early in the second half.”
He noted that his team never panicked and that he was very proud of them.
“I knew John Bapst deserved to be here. I knew it was going to be a tough match. We had a great game with them in Orono. They beat us in overtime (2-1),” said Krul. “We needed a little bit of soccer fortune.
“We gave them a run for the money and I hope they do well in the final,” Krul added.

title: SBA disaster assistance available

text:
The U.S. Small Business Administration announced the availability of low-interest federal disaster loans for eligible small businesses and private nonprofit organizations impacted by drought beginning Sept. 15.
Eligible Counties
Maine: Androscoggin, Cumberland, Franklin, Hancock, Kennebec, Knox, Lincoln, Oxford, Penobscot, Sagadahoc, Somerset, Waldo, Washington, and York.
Who Can Apply
• Small businesses.
• Private nonprofits & faith-based organizations.
• Small agricultural cooperatives & nurseries.
• Small aquaculture enterprises.
Loan Assistance Available
Economic Injury Disaster Loans: Working capital assistance for operational expenses caused by the disaster.
Key Loan Details
• Up to $2 million in loan funding.
• Interest rates as low as 4 percent for small businesses and 3.625 percent for private nonprofit organizations.
• Loan terms of up to 30 years.
• No interest or required payments during the first 12 months following disbursement

Applicants may call the SBA National Support Network Center with questions regarding their application at (866) SBA-HELP or email disastercustomerservice@sba.gov. For people who are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.

title: From party control to voter turnout: These charts explain the 2026 midterm election results
text:
8 charts that explain the 2026 midterms
8 charts that explain the 2026 midterms
Democrats swept races in the House of Representatives and Senate during Tuesday's midterm election. Democrats will control Congress next term and hold a majority in governorships.
The Get the Facts Data Team compiled a list of charts to explain the 2026 midterm election results.
Control of the House and Senate
Democrats have won control of the U.S. Senate, holding 54 seats as of Wednesday evening.
Democrats have also gained control of the House of Representatives, holding 237 seats on Wednesday.
Which seats flipped in Congress and states?
Democrats flipped five gubernatorial races and now make up the majority of state governors. It's the first time since 2010 that Democratic governors held a majority of governorships.
The Cook Political Report rated 12 gubernatorial races as competitive. Democrats flipped five, retained three and Republicans retained two.
Democrats flipped seven Senate seats and will hold a majority in the chamber next year.
The Cook Political Report rated 11 Senate races as competitive, with six of those being toss-ups. As of Wednesday afternoon, Democrats had flipped five of those toss-up seats.
Democrats gained Senate seats in Texas, Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Maine. Some of these states, like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina, had not elected a Democratic senator in decades.
Democrats also flipped Republican-held seats in the House of Representatives. More than 25 House seats shifted to Democrats, including some in districts redrawn to favor Republicans.
What were the closest races?
Sixteen races were within a margin of 1% or less as of Wednesday afternoon, among races with 95% or more of the ballots counted.
In the closest race, Mississippi Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom leads Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by just 65 votes, per AP. That's with 95% of the votes counted.
Alaska's Senate race is also close, with candidate Democratic nominee Mary Peltola leading Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan by just over 600 votes. Only 74% of the ballots have been counted in that race as of Wednesday.
The governor's race in Kansas is within a margin of 0.6%, and 14 House races are within a margin of 1% or less.
What were the results where redistricting took place?
A mid-decade congressional redistricting battle has played out for more than a year now, reassigning millions of people to new districts.
Both Democrats and Republicans targeted specific districts, starting with the five targeted in Texas when President Donald Trump asked the state to redraw boundaries. California followed in response, redrawing boundaries in favor of Democrats to target five districts.
So far, Democrats have picked up five House seats due to redistricting — four that were targeted in California and one in Utah.
Ten seats targeted by Republicans in redistricting have remained Democrat, including three of the four in Florida, both in Ohio, four in Texas and one in Alabama. One seat targeted in Texas was flipped to Republican.
How was voter turnout different?
About 124 million people voted in the 2026 midterm elections, according to preliminary data from the University of Florida Election Lab. That's up from the 112 million in 2022 and 118.6 million in 2018.
While the over number of votes cast is up, the voter turnout rate for 2026 still lags behind both the 2022 and 2018 midterms, which saw a 69% and 79% voter turnout rate, respectively. In 2026, the preliminary voter turnout rate was 63%.
Voter turnout was calculated using voter registration data from L2 and the U.S. Census Bureau. Voter registration has increased from 153 million in 2018 to 196 million in 2026.

title: Chemical plant explosion in Mississippi prompts shelter-in-place order
text:
GREENVILLE, Miss. (WMC/Gray News) - A chemical plant explosion in Mississippi prompted a massive emergency response Wednesday morning.
According to Washington County emergency officials, crews were called to the Loveland facility, formerly known as Platte Chemical, just after 7 a.m. for an initial blast involving a chemical herbicide stored inside a “hot box.”
Multiple agencies responded as thick smoke spread from the facility, prompting a shelter-in-place order for the surrounding area.
Firefighters and emergency personnel were able to contain the flames once at the scene while undergoing decontamination protocols due to potential chemical exposure.
Greenville Mayor Errick Simmons praised the swift coordination of local and state responders.
“Our first priority is the safety of our residents, our first responders, and everyone working at or near the facility,” Simmons said. “I ask our citizens to remain calm, avoid the immediate area, and allow our firefighters and emergency personnel the space they need to do their jobs safely and effectively.”
Officials confirmed no injuries were reported in the explosion while lifting the shelter-in-place order.
The cause of the blast remained under investigation.

title: Couple who took in 16 foster kids convicted of abuse ‘under the guise of discipline’
text:
LANSING, Mich. (Gray News) - A Michigan couple is accused of abusing their adopted and foster children under the “guise of discipline” for financial gain, according to authorities.
Jurors found 59-year-old Tamal Flore guilty of six counts of first-degree child abuse, two counts of second-degree child abuse and three counts of third-degree child abuse, a press release said.
Her husband, 61-year-old Jerry Flore, was convicted of a single count of second-degree child abuse, which carries up to 10 years in prison. Jurors acquitted him on nine other abuse charges.
The Office of the Michigan Attorney General prosecuted the case, alleging the couple routinely mistreated children brought into their home since 2007.
According to a report from The Detroit News, the Flores were accused of abusing seven of the 16 children they fostered or adopted. The children reportedly described being whipped with a belt, beaten with metal and wooden spoons, and locked in rooms or the garage for days.
Children were also forced to sleep in a marked kitchen area called “the square” for weeks at a time, perform strenuous punishment exercises and had food withheld if they did not complete daily housework.
Sentencing is scheduled for Jan. 11.

title: Lawsuit and ranked choice voting: Why Alaska could be slow — and controversial — to decide
text:
Why the Alaska Senate race could be slow — and controversial — to decide
'Alaska does it different than everyone'
Why the Alaska Senate race could be slow — and controversial — to decide
'Alaska does it different than everyone'
After Election Day, all eyes in the political world could turn to Alaska.
Alaska has already been at the center of a roiling political controversy this week over how the second Dan Sullivan ended up on the state’s Senate ballot, which has sparked lawsuits, criminal investigations and threats to block certification of the election if incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan is defeated by Democrat Mary Peltola.
Related video above — Ballot stacking: what is it and is it legal?
But the uproar about the Alaska Senate race could ratchet up to 11 if control of the Senate comes down to who wins in the state, one that election officials and experts say is unlike any other when it comes to voting.
That’s because it might take two weeks before a winner can be determined.
"Alaska does it different than everyone," said Derek Tisler, counsel with the Brennan Center’s Elections and Government Program. "It’s such a unique state given its geography, given how remote it is and how expansive it is. So voters in all other 49 states are going to be a little confused about how things are done in Alaska when paying attention for the first time."
There are several reasons why Alaska’s vote count could take longer than other states. For one, the state gives between 10 to 15 days for mailed ballots to be returned to the elections office (10 days if mailed within the US and 15 days from overseas). Secondly, the state uses a system called ranked choice voting to count votes, a process where the results won’t be finalized until after that 15-day period if no candidate receives 50% of the vote on the first ballot.
Should that occur, election officials and experts say it’s important for voters to remember that the process is supposed to take that long — especially because the waiting period can allow close elections to become a hotbed for misinformation over claims of cheating.
"If it does take these two weeks to find out the actual composition [of the results], this isn’t a ballot manipulation — it’s not an attempt to alter the results of the election," said Russell Luke, a political science professor at the University of Alaska Fairbanks. "It’s simply how long it takes in Alaska. This is to be expected — it’s not extraordinary or outside the norm."
Threats to block certification
Controversy swirled this week after The New York Times reported new details about Democratic involvement in getting Daniel J. Sullivan onto the Alaska Senate ballot, with the same name as the incumbent. Alaska GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy launched an investigation into whether Democrats sought to confuse voters, and he said Thursday that if the probe finds "wrongdoing," then certification of the Senate race results could be "stopped or changed."
"We’re going to investigate," Dunleavy, who launched a probe into the matter, told NewsNation. "We find out there’s wrongdoing and if that means that the certification then is stopped or changed, then that’s what happens."
Election law experts say there is a path for Republicans to contest the results of the election through the courts, but that the governor’s certification of legitimate election results is not the way to do so.
"If any state authority — whether it’s a canvassing board or secretary of state or governor — wants to interfere with the rights of the voters by delaying or denying certification, the same thing will happen what’s happened in the past: Parties with standing are going to go to the court," said David Becker, a former DOJ attorney and founder of the Center for Election Innovation & Research. "They’re going to get immediate relief."
Derek Muller, an elections law professor at Notre Dame, said there’s a statute in Alaska law for a defeated candidate to contest an election in the event of misconduct, fraud or corruption to change the result of the election or "any corrupt practice as defined by law sufficient to change the results of the election."
That standard would likely be a high bar for a defeated candidate to meet with the courts, Muller said, while also noting that it was a different process entirely than the governor trying not to certify the election.
If the governor refuses certification, Muller said, "the court can order somebody else to do it."
Trump’s lawsuit and Senate questions
The Trump administration has also threatened to block certification if Sullivan loses, with a preemptive lawsuit that was filed even before this week’s developments.
The Justice Department is leaning into the Times’ reporting about Democrats’ involvement in recruiting Daniel J. Sullivan to run, arguing it will confuse voters, though the lawsuit is seen as a long shot likely to fail. The state Supreme Court previously ruled ahead of the primary that the non-incumbent Sullivan could be on the ballot.
The judge in the case is considering requests from Alaska election officials, Democrats and outside groups to dismiss the lawsuit, and a ruling could come as soon as this weekend.
There is also speculation about whether some Senate Republicans might try to prevent Peltola from being sworn in should her victory be certified by the state and she show up January 3 when the new session of Congress convenes.
Such a dramatic move has never happened before. President Donald Trump has been vocally complaining about the Alaska race, something that could spur like-minded senators to try to act. But there is no evidence at this point that it might happen.
Senate GOP aides refused to address the possibility that there might be an objection to or effort to block Peltola’s swearing-in should she win the Alaska Senate race — or even say if there is a procedural mechanism they could use to block her.
Senate practices dictate that when a state certifies an election, the senator-elect provides that certification to the Secretary of the Senate for review. That person is then sworn in, typically by the vice president, with the other members who won their races.
If a challenge is made to the accuracy of the election results, the matter is referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration for investigation. The committee’s eventual findings and recommendations would then go back to the full Senate, which could expel the individual on a majority vote should they find there was wrongdoing or an inaccurate count in the election.
This was last an issue when Sen. Mary Landrieu, a Democrat from Louisiana, was first elected in 1996. She was sworn in even as her opponent alleged voter fraud. A lengthy Senate investigation cleared her.
A more recent controversial race decision played out in the courts: In 2008, Sen. Norm Coleman, a Republican, had a 215-vote lead after the initial vote count in Minnesota. A recount gave a 312-vote lead to Democrat Al Franken. Months of legal wrangling followed. It wasn’t until June 2009 that the Minnesota Supreme Court declared Franken the winner.
Alaska’s slow vote count
Alaska has long been one of the slowest states for reporting election results.
It’s a simple matter of geography: The state is massive, with residents in far-flung areas where ballots have to be flown in to be counted because communities aren’t on the state’s roadway network.
"This was common in Alaska to wait weeks on end for results in close races, even before ranked choice voting," said David de la Fuente, deputy director for politics and research at the moderate think tank Third Way. "Alaska is one of the few states in the country that a substantial part of their population does not get to their job via personal vehicle."
That remoteness is why the state gives mail ballot deadlines of 10 and 15 days after the election, so long as they are postmarked by Election Day.
The U.S. Supreme Court took up a case this year that could have ended that practice, requiring all ballots to arrive by Election Day, but the court ruled against a Republican challenge to the practice of accepting ballots arriving after Election Day in Mississippi.
Luke, the University of Alaska professor, said that while vote counting in Alaska has always been slow, ranked choice voting "certainly exacerbates the issue," because the state waits for the 15-day deadline to run out before running the ranked choice voting tabulation, which is required if no candidate receives 50% of the votes.
Here’s how the process works: The votes of the fourth-place finisher are distributed among the top three vote-getters, based on how voters rank the four candidates on the ballot. Then the votes of the third-place finisher are distributed to the top two vote-getters, which will put a candidate above the 50% threshold. (There is one other Republican, Gerald Heikes, on the ballot along with the two Sullivans and Peltola.)
"In this particular Senate race, that is the likeliest outcome — that neither candidate clearly receives a majority in the first round," Luke said.
The same process could also play out in the state’s gubernatorial and House contests.
Ranked choice voting has been criticized by Republicans, including the president, who has questioned whether Peltola should be seated if she wins.
While some experts have argued that ranked choice voting actually protects the incumbent Sullivan — because voters can rank both Sullivans — the controversy could fuel efforts to end the use of ranked choice voting in Alaska.
In 2024, voters narrowly approved keeping the practice in a referendum. But it’s back on the ballot again in the state, meaning Alaska voters will be using ranked choice voting in the Sullivan-Peltola contest while deciding whether to keep the method for future elections.

title: New schools underway for Cape Elizabeth and Cumberland/North Yarmouth
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Great Falls Construction is involved in southern Maine elementary school projects, with two in the works and a third just finished.
The Gorham-based firm broke ground on a new 111,000-square-foot, $89 million middle school for Cape Elizabeth in October, on a parcel of land off Scott Dyer Road, between the existing middle school and the high school.
The project team is wrapping up ledge removal and foundation work is scheduled to start this week.
The new school will have 25 classrooms, along with rooms for band, chorus and art programs, multiple small collaboration and specialty rooms, a library, cafeteria, gym, dual-sided stage and offices.
Joey Smith, Great Falls’ business development and marketing manager, told Mainebiz the team will demolish most of the current middle school addition that was built in the early 1990s, but protect the original 1934 school building, as the town decides on potential future uses.
“Once the demolition is complete, we’ll construct a new multipurpose athletic field in place of the old middle school building,” Smith said.
R.J. Grondin, based in Gorham, has handled sitework, and the project was designed by Harriman, which is headquartered in Portland.
The Great Falls team will also create a 5,000-square-foot addition and interior renovations to the town’s elementary school, which is connected to the current middle school.
Both school projects are expected to be completed by fall 2028.
Cumberland/North Yarmouth projects
A half-hour north in Cumberland, Great Falls has wrapped up a 6,600-square-foot, four-classroom addition to the Mabel I. Wilson school, topping it off with a new roof.
The school is part of the expanded school campus off of Tuttle Road and currently serves students in grades pre-K through third from Cumberland and North Yarmouth.
Still under construction on the campus is a 76,700-square-foot, $35 million school which will serve students in pre-K through first grade. Great Falls broke ground on the Carolyn F. Small school in June 2025, on a 2.3-acre lot adjacent to the School Administrative District No. 51 campus. It’s expected to have capacity for 550 students in 30 classrooms when completed in June 2027 and will have the ability to be expanded in the future.
“We’re working on getting the building enclosed for the winter so that work on the interior can happen throughout the cold weather,” Smith said. “The roof is nearing completion, along with interior rough-ins, with drywall going up in some areas.”
“These projects for SAD No. 51 are a commitment to the district’s mission of ‘one campus’ where a student can enter pre-K and remain within the same proximity throughout their educational career,” Smith added.
“Great Falls Construction has been engaging with students too, through their ‘Hard Hat Chats’ series where an older student interviews our construction team. The interviews are filmed and shared to spotlight the crew.” Six episodes can be viewed on YouTube.
North Yarmouth-based A.H. Grover Inc. is managing site work on the Small School and Stephen Blatt Architects, based in Portland, is the design team.

title: Maine Ski Season Is Almost Here as Sugarloaf Eyes November Opening
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maine Ski Season Is Almost Here as Sugarloaf Eyes November Opening
Let the countdown begin.
For all you Mainers dreaming of mountain air, fresh powder, and carving up the slopes, I've got some exciting news for you. Ski season is within sight.
It's hard to believe we're already gearing up for another winter on the mountains, but here we are. And if you're anything like Maine's countless skiing and snowboarding enthusiasts, the anticipation is probably reaching an all-time high. So, let's bring on the snow.
It always amazes me how much we collectively complain about winter, yet still love getting outside and playing in the snow. I guess we Mainers will never lose that kid inside of us.
When Do Maine Ski Mountains Open for the Season?
It’s time to swap out the golf clubs for ski boots and get your gear tuned up. Maine’s stunning slopes are calling, and one mountain has already announced its opening day... well, sort of.
Let the season begin.
While the snow hasn’t started falling yet, and the snowmaking machines remain idle, that hasn’t slowed down Sugarloaf’s plans to announce a tentative opening. The mountain has posted November 20-22 as its opening weekend, marking the start of its 76th year in operation.
When Did Sugarloaf Mountain First Open for Skiing?
Ever since the first trail was cut back in 1950, Sugarloaf has been one of the true ski gems of the Northeast. It attracts visitors from far and wide with its massive terrain, iconic snowfields, and stunning natural beauty. Experts can even enjoy above-treeline glades, a rarity for East Coast skiing. As the second-tallest mountain in Maine, it can get pretty gnarly up there.
The mountain has also introduced many other outdoor activities over the years. They include Nordic skiing, fat biking, tubing, and even cat skiing. Yes, there's plenty of Après ski choices, too.
With that tentative opening date just around the corner, it's no surprise that ticket packages and other deals are already available on Sugarloaf's website. You can find more details here.
Here's hoping its a nice, snowy year for Sugarloaf and the other ski resorts here in Maine and beyond. A healthy ski season is good for everyone.

title: El-Sayed says Michigan rejected ‘hateful, spiteful campaign’ by Republicans after being labeled ‘jihadist’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed told The Associated Press on Wednesday that Michigan voters had rejected “a hateful, spiteful campaign” after months of Republican attacks on his Muslim identity in one of the nation’s most closely watched Senate races.
El-Sayed said he was “running on adrenaline and caffeine” after his race with Republican Mike Rogers was called early Wednesday, giving Democrats another significant victory in a premier swing state as they won a substantial majority in the Senate in Tuesday’s midterms.
Throughout the cycle, Republicans sought to demonize El-Sayed, who was born in the U.S. after his parents immigrated from Egypt. President Donald Trump repeatedly called him a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists.”
“Michigan proved just how big we are. Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face,” El-Sayed said. “Michiganders rejected that. Every single county, every single one, pushed against that.”
In a sign of how combative the race had become, Rogers and El-Sayed had not spoken as of Wednesday afternoon, even after Rogers issued a statement conceding the race. In 2024, Rogers called then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin to concede on Wednesday morning, before the AP had even called the race.
El-Sayed, who will become the nation’s first Muslim senator, told the AP by phone that the morning was “a moment of reflection,” including about what his victory would mean to his two young daughters. His 3-year-old, he said, has no idea what happened, while his 8-year-old understands but sees it as normal.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
“Now, this is something they read about in the history books,” he said.
With approximately 97% of the vote in, El-Sayed held a 7 percentage point lead over Rogers. Every county in the state shifted toward Democrats compared with 2024, according to AP voting data.
The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of more than 4,500 voters in Michigan, showed that Michigan Senate voters were roughly split on whether El-Sayed’s views were “too extreme,” with about half saying they were.
El-Sayed rose from a double-digit defeat eight years ago in the state’s Democratic gubernatorial election to an upset victory of an establishment-backed candidate in the primary after being outspent by tens of millions. He said his campaign proved that “old-fashioned politics can work if you’re willing to do the work.”
El-Sayed quickly pivoted, though, toward the future, saying his victory is “not the success” and that “the success is what you’re able to do with the seat.”
He would not commit to supporting Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer for another term, saying he did not yet know who else might run. Schumer is expected to retain the leadership position.
“I do believe we need new leadership and I think people are hungry for it,” El-Sayed added.
___

title: Mount Desert welcomes new Fire Chief
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MOUNT DESERT — Fire Chief Kyle Stewart was officially welcomed to the role this week in Mount Desert after Chief Mike Bender set off on retirement.
The Mount Desert Selectboard acknowledged the appointment of Chief Stewart in the informational portion of their meeting Monday night.
Chief Stewart joined the department in June as Assistant Chief to learn the ropes under Chief Bender before taking over this fall. He moved to MDI from Utah with his family, driving across the country to get here.
“I can’t tell you how thrilled we all are and how much, I think pretty much since the day you’ve arrived, we’ve all been saying just ‘yay’ and really thankful,” said Town Manager Alex Kimball. “And thank you not just to you but to everyone whose really helped him along the as well to really transition over into this role, without that it makes it a lot tougher, so thank you.”
Chief Bender announced his retirement in early 2026, after serving over 40 years in the fire service. His last day was Tuesday.
In July Chief Stewart told the Islander how thankful he was for the time to work with Chief Bender before he stepped down.
“It’s really valuable to me to come in under Chief Bender’s tutelage, learn the back history, learn why the processes are in place that he’s put in place, and have these next couple of months to really just glean from his wealth of information because, quite frankly, he’s built this department from the ground up,” said Stewart. “I’m really grateful to have the time with him.”
In other business, the Selectboard briefly discussed their interest in collecting more data on short-term rentals in the town.
The decision to inventory short-term rentals is in response to a law that was passed in April which increases density and minimum lot sizes in certain areas and goes into effect in July 2027.
Members of the Selectboard agreed that they would like Kimball to look into firms that would help gather this information so they can move forward with inventorying short-term rentals.
The Selectboard also authorized a payment of $12,497 out of the Marina CIP account to pay for repairs to the public dock ramp in Northeast Harbor. The repairs will be made to the center section of the ramp and will prevent future damage of this nature, according to a memo from Harbormaster John Lemoine. The current damage has built up over the last two summers
Town Finance Director Nancy Parsons was appointed as Acting Town Manager for November to handle managerial responsibilities in case Kimball must step away due to an emergency. In a memo from Kimball, Parsons was nominated because Public Works Director Brian Henkel will be out during the month of November.
