title: The Maine 2nd District race is still uncalled. Paul LePage is declaring victory.
text:
BANGOR — Former Gov. Paul LePage said there was no path to victory for his Democratic opponent, State Auditor Matt Dunlap, in the race for Maine’s 2nd Congressional District seat.
“I’m declaring victory,” LePage said at a Wednesday news conference.
LePage, who occupied the Blaine House from 2011-19, said that although The Associated Press has not yet called the race and public vote totals show him up by less than 300 votes, his team had contacted towns yet to report their totals to confirm his victory.
Based on the towns yet to publicly report their results, he appeared to be accurate in predicting a victory, a Portland Press Herald analysis showed.
If the results bear out as his team expects, the former governor’s return to elected office is remarkable in the context of this cycle election: LePage would become the only Republican so far in this “blue wave” midterm to flip a Democratic-held U.S. House seat.
All of Maine’s other elections appear to heavily favor Democrats, with Troy Jackson defeating Sen. Susan Collins and Hannah Pingree easily winning the governor’s race.
The 78-year-old would be one of the oldest freshman congressmen in American history — a back-bencher with little individual lawmaking power in a heavily Democratic Congress.
During the news conference at Sea Dog Brewery in Bangor, LePage repeated a version of a line he’s used often during the campaign about his future in a congressional minority: “If it helps Maine, I’m going to be all for it. If it hurts Maine, I’m going to be all against it.”
“Now I’m going home to sleep,” LePage continued, drawing laughs from gathered supporters. “Going to sleep for the next 20 hours.”
LePage’s path to victory ran through red, rural towns in Maine. After numbers in the second district’s biggest municipalities — Auburn, Lewiston, Augusta and Bangor — came in Tuesday night, LePage’s numbers slowly climbed above Dunlap’s as solidly Republican areas tallied votes.
At 1 a.m. Wednesday, Dunlap held a 1,200-vote lead over LePage.
By noon, that had narrowed to just 269 votes. When the small town of Strong reported its tally at 12:18 p.m., LePage took a 62-vote lead, according to The Associated Press.
Vote-watchers can expect that trend to continue: most of the remaining 30,000 or so votes are in deep red, rural Maine.
The bigger cities in the district, key to Democratic Rep. Jared Golden’s victories in recent elections, reported their votes late last night: Bangor with its 4,100-vote margin for Dunlap, Lewiston with its 2,200-vote margin and Augusta with its 1,500-vote margin.
Now, the outstanding votes sit in small towns like Aroostook County’s Fort Fairfield, which went for Republican congressional nominee Austin Theriault by 10 percentage points two years ago. The results so far suggest LePage is slightly outperforming Theriault in these small, rural, Republican towns.
For instance, in Strong — the western Maine town that flipped results in LePage’s favor Wednesday afternoon — LePage won with a 239-vote margin, while Theriault won it by 166 votes.
In some ways, LePage’s win would not be a particularly surprising result. LePage is a self-described “Trump-before-Trump” in a district where President Donal Trump has won in three consecutive elections. He’s a former governor running against a Democrat who swings further to the left than his predecessor in a district dominated by rural, white voters — exactly the demographic Republicans have leaned on over the past decade.
And the former governor apparently has substantial pull among voters who chose Golden, a moderate Democrat, in recent elections.
Importantly, either candidate would need a margin larger than a couple hundred votes to be declared the winner without a ranked-choice runoff.
As of 4:00 p.m., declared write-in Gregory A. Ward had 163 votes; either candidate would need to win by more than Ward’s total to get 50% of the vote.
If the votes continue as expected, a Republican will hold the 2nd District seat for the first time since 2019, when Golden assumed office after narrowly defeating Republican Bruce Poliquin.

title: The robotext evolution
text:
Cell phone users were hard pressed to forget to vote this year. How could they with the steady drumbeat of text alerts leading up to the election?
Some of the mobile missives advocated individual candidates; others encouraged voting in general. Many were personalized to the recipients with details from their voting records, including physical address, participation in past elections and whether another household member had already voted. Replying “STOP” or deleting and reporting the messages as spam proved about as effective as swatting mosquitos on a muggy summer evening. You might stop one pest in its tracks, but there are more where it came from.

title: Freeport field hockey returns to Class B final with 2-1 victory over Yarmouth
text:
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
SCARBOROUGH — Entering the season, it seemed the Freeport field hockey team’s time had passed. The Falcons had made three of the past four Class B finals, but the core of those teams was gone. Twelve seniors, including eight of 11 starters, had graduated. The Falcons needed to rebuild.
Turns out, a rebuilt roster can still be a championship one.
Freshman Charlotte Sikorski netted the tying goal, sophomore Ava Emmons scored the winner, and second-seeded Freeport rode a dominant second half to a 2-1 victory over No. 1 Yarmouth in the Class B South final Wednesday at Scarborough High School.
The Falcons (14-3), who won the Class B title in 2023, will face North champion Nokomis (16-1) in the state final Saturday at Edward Little High School in Auburn.
Wednesday was the fourth straight regional final between Western Maine Conference rivals Freeport and Yarouth. Freeport (14-3) also won in 2023 and ’25.
“I’m just feeling so grateful for our team, to come together so quick, (after) losing so many seniors last year,” junior midfielder Dalila McCarthy said. “We just have a brand-new team, and we’re all playing together so well.”
After leading the Falcons to those first three regional title games, coach Marcia Wood wasn’t sure at the beginning of the season that Freeport’s success could continue.
“We had no expectations. We just played all year,” she said. “We had fun, we played, we saw what would happen. We didn’t have that pressure, we didn’t have everyone looking at us like, ‘It has to be you.’ We just played. And we battled.”
Freeport looked outclassed in a 5-2 loss to the similarly rebuilt Clippers (15-2) in early October, but the Falcons took a 4-3 victory in the regular-season finale and were prepared again Wednesday. Their plan centered on swarming defense against Yarmouth’s skilled midfielders and forwards, in particular Maya Nasveschuk, who had McCarthy, Sikorski and Briella Boudreau on her much of the afternoon and was frequently doubled.
“She’s an amazing player,” McCarthy said. “We had to mark her the entire game.”
Still, the Clippers controlled play in the first half, outshooting the Falcons 9-1 and going up when Julie Nasveschuk scored with 12:54 left in the second quarter. Freeport evened the score less than two minutes later off a corner when McCarthy hammered a shot toward the goal and Sikorski directed it in.
“I didn’t even know if it went in for a second. I fell to the ground and then I looked and it was in,” she said. “It was amazing getting that goal. We needed that.”
Freeport took the lead in the fourth quarter. Emmons, from 12 yards, flipped the ball toward the cage, and the shot hit a Yarmouth stick and went in with 9:31 to play.
“I was just kind of (thinking) get it toward the goal, because I’m not the best shooter. But I just sent it and hoped someone could get in there,” Emmons said.
“We definitely had the mentality that we could do this, we’ve got this.”
Freeport controlled play in the second half, putting nine shots on net to none for the Clippers. Asked how the Falcons did it, Wood gave a bewildered smile.
“I don’t know,” she said. “We just talk about, ‘No regrets, no regrets, no regrets.’ Give it everything you’ve got.”
Lydia Costa made eight saves for Freeport, as did Stella Murdoch for Yarmouth.
“I think we played as well as we could for 60 minutes. We had so many kids sick today. You just do what you can,” Yarmouth coach Bre Page said. “I think we gave it all we got.”
The Clippers, who had to replace nine starters after last year, are set up well for the future with 10 starters due back, including the Nasveschuk sisters and high-scoring forward Vivienne Corriveau.
Asked if that provided any consolation, a misty-eyed Page chuckled.
“No,” she said. “This team is a great team. … I couldn’t have asked anything more from this group.”

title: Democrats press to win a majority of governors’ offices in midterms after power struggles with Trump
text:
U.S. GOVERNORS BALANCE OF POWER
HARRISBURG, Pa. (AP) — Democrats scored victories in governor’s races in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia, riding a wave of voter discontent in Tuesday’s midterm elections to deliver a rebuke to President Donald Trump and GOP policymaking.
The wins put Democrats on their way to taking a majority of governorships for the first time in two decades, allowing them to put up a stronger defense against Trump’s second-term agenda.
They also landed a historic victory, as Keisha Lance Bottoms’ victory in Georgia — a presidential battleground state — made her the first Black woman to be elected governor in the U.S.
Democrats also won in Iowa, Ohio and Texas, all states where Republicans have controlled state government for years.
The number of states in play was surprisingly large — a reflection of Trump’s poor approval ratings dragging on his party, with Democrats rolling up victories in presidential battleground states, heavily populated states and states that Trump won easily in 2024.
In the weeks leading up to Election Day, Trump went to heavily Republican areas to headline rallies attended by GOP gubernatorial candidates looking for a boost.
All told, 36 states that are home to about 80% of the nation’s population were electing a governor Tuesday. In 19 states, the office was open. Heading into the elections, Democratic governors represented 60% of the nation’s population, but Republicans held 26 of the nation’s 50 governors’ offices.
Democrats last gained a majority of governorships in 2006, flipping six governors’ offices in the last midterm under a second-term Republican president. Republicans recaptured the majority four years later.
More states under Democratic leadership could mean more governors fighting — or ignoring — Trump’s agenda.
Trump has tested the power of states, clashing primarily with Democratic-led states over call-ups of National Guard troops, immigration operations, conditions on federal aid and efforts to assert federal control over election requirements, including restricting mail voting.
Democratic victories in Georgia, Texas, Iowa and Ohio
Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor and onetime White House adviser to former President Joe Biden, overcame GOP attacks on her management of the city during the COVID-19 pandemic to defeat Rick Jackson, a billionaire who plunged more than $200 million of his own money into the race.
She accused him of getting rich off a broken healthcare system and profiting off pain.
Her victory breaks GOP control of state government in Georgia, as does Democrat Amy Acton’s victory in Ohio, in a campaign that made national headlines when Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, a biotech billionaire, aired a widely criticized attack ad featuring Acton’s estranged mother.
Iowa Democrat Rob Sand defeated Republican Zach Lahn, while Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa beat third-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas, where no Democrat had been elected to statewide office since 1994.
Hinojosa was seen as a long shot after she emerged from a primary with a fraction of Abbott’s cash total. But as Republicans began to express misgivings over Abbott, fellow Latino politicians and politicos wrote to the Democratic Governors Association to request $10 million in campaign aid, saying Hinojosa had made it a close race.
The DGA gave $1 million — far less than it spent in Arizona, Georgia, Iowa, Michigan, Nevada, Ohio and Wisconsin — and Hinojosa won despite being badly outspent 5-to-1 on ads, according to AdImpact data.
Notably, Abbott skipped Trump’s rally in Texas, a sign of the president’s unpopularity.
More races were seen as the most competitive
Democrats also saw opportunities to pick up a governor’s office in Alaska, where the incumbent was term-limited, and in Nevada, where state Attorney General Aaron Ford was challenging Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo.
Like Georgia, Alaska hadn’t elected a Democratic governor since 1998.
Republicans’ best chance to capture an executive suite was in Kansas, a normally deep red state where Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly was term-limited.
Republicans hung onto control in Florida, where U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds defeated David Jolly, a former Republican congressman-turned-independent who ran as a Democrat in the nation’s third-most populous state.
Republicans also had an eye on Oregon, where Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek was trying to fend off a second challenge from Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan.
Contests are in big states and swing states, too
Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul of New York won reelection, and Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former U.S. health and human services secretary, cruised to victory in California.
Control of the executive branch was on the line in the six swing states from the 2024 presidential election, and Democrats were making a bid to control all six: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro won reelection, while Democrat David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, won the governor’s job in Wisconsin, and Michigan’s secretary of state, Jocelyn Benson, won her state’s open governor’s office.
The winners could have substantial influence over election administration during the 2028 presidential election. That could be important, considering Trump’s interest in expanding federal control over elections.
Meanwhile, three Democratic governors who are considered possible presidential candidates in 2028 all won reelection: Wes Moore of Maryland, JB Pritzker of Illinois and Shapiro, of Pennsylvania.
Demonstrating a big margin of victory, fundraising prowess and the electoral strength to help other Democrats win sends a strong signal to donors and party activists, analysts say.
The 2026 election produced some firsts
In Texas, Hinojosa was elected to be the state’s first Latina governor, while Deb Haaland ‘s victory in New Mexico made her the first Native American woman elected to lead a state.
More states elected Black governors, as well. Eight Black major party gubernatorial nominees were on ballots. In the past 250 years, only three elected governors have been Black, including Moore. Victories by Bottoms, Crowley and Donalds ensured that voters would double that number in just one election.
Meanwhile, states were on course to possibly beat the record number of 14 female governors.
___
Follow Marc Levy at http://twitter.com/timelywriter

title: Paul LePage declares victory over Matt Dunlap in 2nd District race
text:
This story is for subscribers only. Subscribers and donors help fund BDN’s in-depth political analysis, campaign finance investigations, and first-in-the-nation race calls. All election results, live analysis and voting information are free to access as a public service. Subscribe for $1 for 3 months right now.
Former Gov. Paul LePage declared victory Wednesday afternoon over Democrat Matt Dunlap in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District, which would flip the seat to Republicans and hand his party its only win in the state’s marquee races on a night of sweeping Democratic gains.
LePage, a Republican, had 49.9% of votes to 48.8% for Dunlap, the state auditor, with an estimated 93% of votes tallied at 2:30 p.m. Wednesday. The Bangor Daily News and its national partner, Decision Desk HQ, have not yet called the race.
If the results hold, his victory will stand almost alone for Maine Republicans. Democrat Troy Jackson ousted U.S. Sen. Susan Collins in a kept the governor’s office in her party’s hands for the first time since 1958, and Democrats expanded their majorities in the Legislature.
LePage will be the only Republican in Maine’s congressional delegation and the only one in New England’s House delegation. But it was close in a district President Donald Trump carried three times. LePage trailed Dunlap by about 1,000 votes early Wednesday before late returns from small, Republican-leaning rural towns pushed him ahead.
The 78-year-old who grew up homeless in Lewiston served two terms as governor before losing a 2022 comeback bid to Gov. Janet Mills by 13 points, although he carried the 2nd District in that race. He will be one of the oldest freshmen in the history of the House and returns to elected office for the first time since leaving the Blaine House in 2019.
The seat opened when U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, a centrist Democrat who won four terms in the district by winning over ticket-splitting Republicans, announced last November that he would not seek reelection. National Republicans made it a top target, and House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, campaigned twice in Maine for LePage.
LePage ran on his record of cutting taxes as governor and on protecting Social Security. He touted his personal relationship with Trump, saying he could get into the Oval Office, while saying he opposed the president’s tariffs on Canada in their current form and did not support the Iran war. Trump, Johnson and the National Rifle Association endorsed him.
Dunlap, 61, of Old Town, is a former secretary of state and onetime head of the Sportsman’s Alliance of Maine. He ran a progressive campaign, backing Medicare for All and a war powers resolution to end the Iran war.
He attacked LePage over his age, his alignment with Trump and his support for parts of the Republican tax-and-spending law that cut federal Medicaid funding. He also questioned whether LePage truly lives in Maine, prompting LePage to call himself a “snowbird” who spends winters in Florida during their second and final debate.
But Dunlap’s path to the nomination was rocky. National Democrats warned him against challenging Golden and backed state Sen. Joe Baldacci, D-Bangor, in the June primary, only rallying behind Dunlap after he won the four-way race in a ranked-choice count. Late in the campaign, he drew attention for faulting Golden more over votes with Republicans.
The race drew heavy national money, though the $35 million in advertising from outside groups fell short of the $42 million spent on Golden’s 2024 race against former state Rep. Austin Theriault, according to AdImpact. A group tied to Trump’s political operation and the Johnson-aligned Congressional Leadership Fund backed LePage, while House Majority PAC backed Dunlap.
LePage led Dunlap by 5 points in final polls from The New York Times/Siena College and the University of New Hampshire, but the margin on Election Day was slimmer. Marie Johnson, a 79-year-old Republican in Bangor, said she voted for LePage because he cares, citing his famous life story.
“He’s been through a lot in his own life,” she said.

title: Kale chips recalled nationwide due to potential thallium contamination
text:
Kale chips recalled nationwide due to potential thallium contamination
Kale chips have been recalled nationwide over potential thallium contamination, which officials warn could cause nerve damage or hair loss.
Snack Right Super Foods is recalling certain bags of Brad’s kale chips because they may contain the naturally occurring metal.
Related video above | Recalls explained: How to stay ahead of recalls
The affected products were distributed nationwide from October through December 2025, officials with the Food and Drug Administration announced Tuesday.
The recall covers specific lots of Brad’s Crunchy Kale in Original, Cheeze It Up and Radical Ranch flavors, plus Brad’s Veggie Chips Kale.
The bags are 2 or 3 ounces, and the affected lots have best-by dates from Dec. 21, 2026, through Feb. 17, 2027. You can check the lot numbers and UPCs in the company’s recall notice.
Thallium can cause serious health problems at high levels of exposure, including stomach and intestinal illness, nerve damage and hair loss.
The company says the metal was not introduced during manufacturing.
Rather, kale can take up elements from soil, and drying the kale removes water and concentrates elements already present.
The recall follows testing by the FDA and an earlier investigation by California health officials, who found elevated thallium in samples of several Brad’s products.
If you have an affected bag, stop eating it and throw it away. The company says it is not offering refunds, and asks consumers not to return the product to the store. If you think you have had a health effect after eating the chips, contact a health care provider.

title: 24-year-old runner Rachel Apa dies after collapsing during New York City Marathon
text:
24-year-old runner Rachel Apa dies after collapsing during New York City Marathon
A young Pennsylvania woman running the New York City Marathon for the first time to raise money for charity collapsed in Central Park, just over two miles from the finish line, and later died.
Rachel Apa, 24, of Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, was approaching the 24-mile mark of the 26.2 mile race Sunday when she collapsed, according to the New York Police Department. The city medical examiner's office said Tuesday it was investigating the cause of Apa's death.
Her father told sister station WGAL that she'd been stricken with rhabdomyolysis, a rare condition in which muscles can break down during exertion, poisoning the body. It was her first marathon, Steve Apa said.
New York Road Runners, the nonprofit club that stages the race, said in a news release that a bystander administered CPR to Apa, and event medical staffers also did CPR and used a defibrillator. Paramedics arrived and took Apa to a hospital but were unable to save her.
Apa, an industrial-technology product manager and former college field hockey player, had run to raise money for Parkinson's disease in honor of her grandfather.
“It's unfathomable,” her father told The Times. He said his daughter, who had just begun a master's program at Charleston Southern University, had been in “perfect health.”
Michaela Nicholas was watching the race, cheering on any runners whose names she could discern from their bibs, when Apa passed. Nicholas recalled Tuesday that she called out a message of encouragement, then saw Apa collapse about 15 yards (14 meters) further along the route.
Nicholas, a hospital social worker, said she tried to comfort Apa while two other race spectators performed CPR.
“I just held Rachel’s hand and talked to her and told her that she wasn’t alone and that she’s loved, and I prayed for her,” Nicholas, a clinical social worker, said by phone.
The death occurred as the marathon marked 50 years in its five-borough format. Early editions of the race had been run only in Central Park. A record 61,000 runners reached the finish line.
“We are deeply saddened by Rachel’s passing following running in Sunday’s race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with her family, friends and the entire running community,” New York Road Runners said in its statement.
As word of Apa's death spread on Tuesday, money poured into her “Parkinson's Champions” fundraising page, quickly exceeding her $4,000 goal. The fundraiser was sponsored by the Parkinson's Foundation.
On the page, Apa said her grandfather, who had Parkinson's disease and died in 2022, “taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement.”
Apa worked for TE Connectivity, which makes various electrical components and electronics. The company was grappling with the news Tuesday and expressed condolences. So did Bucknell University, from which Apa graduated in 2024 with a degree in markets, innovation and design -- and a total of 17 goals for the school’s field hockey team.
USA Field Hockey, the sport’s governing body, said on social media that “Rachel’s impact on the sport and those around her will not be forgotten.”

title: Trump touts ballroom after GOP suffers historic midterm losses
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump continued to insist Wednesday that his supporters have tremendous love for him, even as fellow Republicans blame his policies for the party’s midterm election losses.
With votes still being counted, Democrats have won at least 7 Senate seats and 28 House seats in the 2026 midterm elections. Wednesday at the White House, Trump wanted to talk primarily about his ballroom project.
“It’s going to be here for many, many years and serving our country well,” Trump said.
Vice President JD Vance wrote in a lengthy post on X, “The reason we lost is the war.” He was referring to the conflict with Iran, which Vance has opposed from the outset.
Trump, standing in the ballroom that is still being constructed, said he agreed with that assessment.
“Well, I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit short term,” Trump said. “And probably that’s probably it’s true. But at the same time, if I had to do again, I’d have to do it again, because long term it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
In several post-election interviews, Trump said he is absolutely willing to accept the election results and work with congressional Democrats.
Trump also said he will use his veto power to block Democratic legislation. He said that will force Democrats to negotiate with the White House to find a path forward.

title: Democrat Hakeem Jeffries poised to make history as first Black speaker of the House
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries is on the cusp of making history as the nation’s first Black speaker of the House, a generational shift in U.S. politics after Democrats trounced Republicans to win majority control of the chamber in the midterm elections.
Jeffries faces a vote of his colleagues when the new Congress convenes Jan. 3. If nominated and elected, as expected, it would be the first time a Black lawmaker has grasped the powerful House speaker’s gavel, a job second in line to the president and the only leadership position in Congress mandated by the U.S. Constitution.
His rise to the speakership at the nation’s domed Capitol, which enslaved African Americans helped build, would be a milestone more than 150 years in the making, tracing an arc of history that began with the first Black American elected to the U.S. House in the turbulent era of post-Civil War Reconstruction. Jeffries would wield the gavel at a time when many of the landmark gains of the 20th-century Civil Rights era are being challenged anew, often by the Trump administration.
Jeffries was met with cheers of “Speaker! Speaker!” at the Democrats’ watch party in Washington.
“This is not a partisan moment. This is a patriotic one,” Jeffries said.
He said House Democrats understand that this is a change election, and “the American people are crying out for transformational change.”
“We hear you,” he said. “We’re going to work hard to deliver on the dramatic change that you deserve.”
The Brooklyn-born 56-year-old Jeffries, known for sprinkling old-school hip-hop lyrics into his freestyle remarks, would take over the office from Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, as Democrats seek to confront President Donald Trump’s final two years in office.
The president has publicly and privately taunted Jeffries, a New York University-educated lawyer, who has served in Congress since 2013, and is the highest-ranking Black elected official in America. Trump once mocked Jeffries by posting on social media a fake photo of the Democratic leader wearing a sombrero outside the White House.
The whole House votes on its speaker as one of the first orders of business when Congress convenes in January. The parties typically choose their leaders during internal caucus elections in November.
Jeffries thanked House Democrats in a letter Wednesday, making clear his desire to serve as the next speaker.
“America is back!” Jeffries wrote.
He went on to say his goal is to empower them to act decisively in the next Congress in three areas: affordability, accountability and American values.
Jeffries is charting a new course for Democrats after Pelosi
The path ahead has been clear for Jeffries and his leadership team, with Rep. Katherine Clark of Massachusetts and Rep. Pete Aguilar of California, who have often moved as a trio representing a new era of House leadership. Clark is expected to become the majority leader and Aguilar the majority whip.
Jeffries would be the first Democratic speaker since Nancy Pelosi and he has led the party for the past four years, with her support, once she decided to step aside after the Democrats’ election losses in 2022.
But Jeffries and the team of Democratic leaders will be quickly tested in the majority, with all the power and responsibility that comes with running the often unruly House.
They are bracing to confront not only Trump, but also a fresh group of Democrats elected to office, including a handful backed by the Democratic Socialists of America pushing the party leftward, though the largest caucus in the House is expected to remain the more moderate New Democrat Coalition.
Jeffries has promised a robust 100-day agenda to lower the costs of living and launch oversight and investigations to hold the Trump administration accountable. Impeachment is an option.
Promising to show voters that Democrats can govern, Jeffries and the leadership team hope to hold their new majority together and avoid the chaotic disruptions and dysfunction that often left Johnson unable to control the GOP’s razor-thin majority in the House.
Colleagues have praised Jeffries’ collaborative style, a listener who represents a shift from Pelosi’s powerful tenure as the nation’s first female speaker of the House.
But at the same time, his calm-is-a-choice deliberative nature has drawn criticism that Jeffries can be too slow to act in the frenzied political environment when voters are seeking swift reaction to mounting crises and concerns.
Soaring healthcare costs, gas and grocery prices, the war in Iran, Trump’s relationship with Putin over Ukraine and concerns about corruption are all top issues ahead.
His path to power runs from Brooklyn to Washington
The son of an Air Force veteran and a social worker, Jeffries told The Associated Press on the campaign trail that growing up during the crack epidemic in New York shaped his sense of purpose.
His experience led to “a desire to want to improve the quality of life for hardworking people, who could have fled difficult circumstances but remained in the community, worked hard to turn things around,” he said.
A married father of two, Jeffries grew up steeped in Brooklyn’s Cornerstone Baptist Church, and represents parts of the Brooklyn-area district once held by trailblazing Rep. Shirley Chisholm.
He earned a bachelor’s degree from the State University of New York at Binghamton, a master’s degree in public policy at Georgetown and graduated magna cum laude from NYU School of Law. He worked as a corporate lawyer and served in the New York State assembly before being elected to Congress.
An insurgent himself, Jeffries was 29 when he first ran for office, failing twice in his initial campaigns for state government. In 2012, he challenged a 30-year incumbent member of Congress, who stepped aside as Jeffries swooped in to win the seat.
A member of the Congressional Black Caucus, Jeffries follows in the footsteps of those who came before, including Joseph Rainey, the first Black American elected to the House in 1870. While Rainey never became speaker, he was the first Black lawmaker to preside with the gavel over the House chamber.
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

title: A 3,200-pound NASA observatory is careening back toward Earth. Here’s what to know
text:
A 3,200-pound NASA observatory plunged back to Earth after 22 years studying cosmic explosions
NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory met a fiery end on Wednesday morning, nearly 22 years after it launched to study the most powerful explosions in the universe.
Data from the U.S. Space Force estimates the 3,200-pound spacecraft plunged into Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia around 7:39 a.m. ET.
While most of the observatory was expected to burn up as it blazed through the thick inner band of Earth’s atmosphere, NASA predicted some pieces of the vehicle would survive.
It was not immediately clear whether any surviving debris hit land. Previously, NASA had predicted that the “risk of harm coming to anyone on Earth is unlikely, approximately 1 in 2,100.”
A risky reentry
If Swift were launched today, it would likely have to adhere to far stricter safety guidelines regarding end-of-life planning, according to The Aerospace Corporation, which is a federally funded research and development center.
Current orbital debris mitigation standards, which were updated in 2019, mandate that “uncontrolled reentries have an expected casualty of less than 1 in 10,000,” said Parker Wishik, a spokesperson for The Aerospace Corporation. He noted in an email that, in this context, “casualty” refers to “serious injury or death.”
While NASA has long known that Swift would likely have to make an unpredictable plunge back to Earth, the agency had hoped that a daring rescue mission launched in July could latch on and boost the Swift Observatory as atmospheric drag gradually pulled it from a once-stable orbit. It could have extended Swift’s operating life by a decade or more, but ultimately the effort failed. The spacecraft eventually dropped down to just 171 miles (275 kilometers) above the planet, and the observatory officially stopped gathering scientific data.
“At this point, the spacecraft was no longer able to compensate for the effects of the increased drag and entered safe mode,” NASA said in a news release.
A team of researchers at Penn State — NASA’s partner on the project and home to the observatory’s Mission Operations Center — sent the final kill-switch command to Swift on October 20.
Swift’s demise was hastened by an increase in solar activity over the past couple of years as the sun reached the peak of its 11-year cycle in 2024.
Intense flares and coronal mass ejections caused Earth’s atmosphere to expand, which intensified the drag on Swift, leading scientists to predict it would descend toward our planet this fall.
Arizona-based Katalyst Space Technologies scrambled to put together the last-ditch effort to stabilize the Swift observatory earlier this year, getting the rescue mission off the ground in only nine months. The company rapidly produced a spacecraft called LINK, which aimed to grapple the telescope and lift it back into a stable orbit. But the mission failed a few weeks after LINK’s launch in July as the satellite spun out of control in space before reaching the Swift observatory.
Another rescue attempt
As Swift’s fate was sealed, mission scientists slowly turned the telescope’s instruments back on to collect data and observations right up until the end. The instruments had been shut off for months to save power and mitigate how quickly the spacecraft sank out of orbit.
The Swift Observatory, which does not have an established observational replacement waiting in the wings, has served as an astrophysics multi-tool in low-Earth orbit since it launched in November 2004.
Named after fast-flying birds, the telescope could quickly pivot to observe blink-and-you-miss-it cosmic events such as flaring black holes. The telescope was originally designed to study the most powerful explosions in the universe, called gamma-ray bursts, but scientists have also used it to monitor other types of cosmic flashes as well as asteroids and comets.
Despite the failed attempt to rescue Swift, NASA has signaled it may try similar lifeline-extension missions for other valuable space-based instruments. Last week, the agency issued a solicitation — formally called a Request for Proposals or RFP — to commercial companies, asking how they might boost, service or otherwise prolong the life of the iconic Hubble Space Telescope.
NASA’s analysis shows that there’s a 10% chance Hubble will plunge out of orbit by 2032 and a 50% it will deorbit by 2033, according to the RFP. The beloved telescope, launched in 1990, has delivered some of the most recognizable images in astronomy and has transformed scientists’ understanding of the cosmos. There is no replacement for Hubble expected before the 2040s, the RFP states.

title: Trump-backed Republican redistricting sought a midterm edge. It didn’t work
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — At the urging of President Donald Trump, Republicans in eight states redrew the boundaries of dozens of congressional districts over the past year while angling for an edge that could help them hold onto a slim House majority in a tough midterm election.
Ultimately, it didn’t work.
The Republican redistricting plan fell flat in Alabama, Florida and Texas. It got scuttled by courts in Missouri and then firmly defeated by its voters Tuesday. And it got offset in California, where a retaliatory Democratic redistricting flipped all five of the Republican-held seats it targeted.
“This is a catastrophic rebuke of Donald Trump’s failed effort to gerrymander the country into oblivion to save the U.S. House of Representatives for himself,” John Bisognano, president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said Wednesday.
New districts presumed continuing support for Trump
“If we look across the country, that entire mid-decade redistricting gambit was a complete bust for Republicans,” said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University in Houston.
Redistricting fell flat in the Rio Grande Valley
In Texas, Republicans won just one of the five seats they had targeted to flip. But Democrats flipped two Republican-held districts, putting the GOP at a net loss.
Republicans reconfigured three heavily Latino districts in the Rio Grande Valley, which had shifted toward Trump in 2024, to try to boost their chances of unseating Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez. But both won reelection Tuesday. And Democrats instead unseated Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz, whose district is sandwiched between theirs.
Though De La Cruz’s new district retained the same percentage of Trump-inclined voters as the 2024 version, about 3 in 5 voting-age residents were new — making it harder for her to compete against Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido, a well-known Latin Grammy award winner.
The new Texas districts were drawn by Adam Kincaid, executive director of the National Republican Redistricting Trust.
“Trying to pick up five seats in Texas, without putting anything else in serious jeopardy, it was a Herculean task,” Kincaid said Wednesday. He added: “It required the trends that we had been seeing over the past several years to continue, and that did not happen.”
Had Republicans not redrawn the Texas districts, however, they likely would have lost even more seats, Kincaid said.
Democrats retained seats in Florida and Alabama
After redistricting, about two-thirds of voting-age residents were new to the district represented by Democratic Rep. Kathy Castor. But she also won reelection. Democrat Pia Dandiya won yet another district -- an open seat in southern Florida — that Republicans had reshaped for an advantage.
In Alabama, a Supreme Court ruling allowed the Republican-led Legislature to revert to what the GOP considered to be a friendlier map. But Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures won reelection anyway, defying Republicans’ plans.
North Carolina redistricting led to costly and close races
Republicans redrew two congressional districts in eastern North Carolina with a goal of unseating Democratic Rep. Don Davis in the 1st Congressional District, which has sent a Black member to Congress for more than 30 years. They made Davis’ district a bit more Republican by bringing in thousands of voters from the 3rd Congressional District, held by Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. In exchange, they reassigned thousands of voters in Democratic-leaning areas to Murphy’s district.
The ensuing advertising battle for Davis’ seat cost well over $50 million, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, ranking among the most expensive House races nationally.
Davis held a slight lead Wednesday, and the race between Murphy and Democratic challenger Raymond Smith was particularly close.
More redistricting is likely ahead of the 2028 elections
Maryland voters on Tuesday approved a constitutional amendment that will make it easier for the state’s Democratic-led General Assembly to redraw districts to the party’s advantage. Democratic proponents, backed by former President Barack Obama, have touted it as a way to “stop Trump.”
Democrats who made gains in numerous state legislatures Tuesday also could use that power for redistricting — most notably in Wisconsin, where districts were tilted toward Republicans. And Democratic lawmakers in New York already have taken an initial step toward congressional redistricting before the 2028 elections.
But the recent midterm redistricting revealed it can be difficult to anticipate voter behavior when trying to gerrymander districts for partisan advantage. That could particularly be the case for the next presidential election, which would be the first in a dozen years without Trump’s name atop the ballot, making it hard to know how his supporters would realign behind new candidates.
The midterm election “shows districts aren’t destiny – that if voters actually show up, they can overcome district lines,” Levitt said.
___
Associated Press writer Bill Barrow contributed to this report.

title: OBITUARIES for Thursday, November 5, 2026
text:
CINDY CASWELL
FAIRFIELD – Cindy Caswell, 76, passed away peacefully on Saturday, October 3, 2026. She was born February 25, 1950, to Raymond and Pearl Wyman of Benton.
Cindy married the love of her life, Robert “Bob” Caswell. Together they raised their sons James Gooldrop and Randy Caswell.
Cindy cherished her family and was known for her sense of humor, love of country music, and warm heart.
She was predeceased by her parents; sister, Lillian Coffin, and son, James.
Cindy is survived by her husband, Bob; son, Randy and his wife Johnna; grandchildren Annabel, and Xavier; brother, Brian and his wife Donna; eight grandchildren; nieces, nephews; and dear friends.
A celebration of Cindy’s life will be held Sunday, November 15, 2026, from 1 to 4 p.m., at the Waterville VFW, Water St., Waterville. Burial will take place Tuesday, November 17, 2026, Maine Veterans Memorial Cemetery chapel, on Mount Vernon Road, in Augusta, at 1 p.m.
ROGER C. DOWNS SR.
WHITEFIELD – Roger Chase Downs Sr., 82, passed away unexpectedly at his home on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, following ongoing cardiac and lung complications. He was born on July 1, 1944, in Rochester, New Hampshire, the second son of Pearl E. and Warren E. Downs.
Roger grew up in Whitefield and attended the Alamo School, a two-room schoolhouse, from kindergarten through eighth grade. He then graduated from Gardiner High School in 1962, where he enjoyed playing football more than any academic class. It was there he met his wife, Rochelle. After marrying in 1961, they welcomed their children, Vicki, Roger Jr., and Daniel, over the next three years.
After graduating, Roger began working for Dessler’s Meat Market, in Gardiner, honing his skills as a meat cutter. From there, he moved on to First National Stores, quickly becoming the regional meat manager. The family moved many times over the years as he climbed the ranks. In 1970, Roger and Rochelle moved their family to Freeport to open Downs Food Store. Together, they worked tirelessly over many years, making many friends and business acquaintances along the way. Thanks to Roger’s expertise, the store became known for its meat and fish department, also selling goods from local farmers and bakers. If you ever eat a country-style spare rib, you can thank Roger for contributing to its cut and design. Many years later, customers still remarked that they would only use Downs Foods clams for their clam chowder.
In 1982, Roger and Rochelle retired from the grocery business, becoming proprietors of several Freeport properties. This allowed them to move back to Roger’s childhood hometown of Whitefield, where he would pursue his longtime dream of becoming a farmer. They built their dream home on their 126-acre property, a former apple orchard, beginning many years of haying, gardening, and raising livestock. Over the years, he became a self-taught master of the fields, selling hay to local farmers and Agway for over four decades. He was a skilled gardener, harvesting countless crops of beautiful fruits and vegetables from White Heart Farm over the years, using them in the home-cooked meals, treats, and preserves he and Rochelle enjoyed preparing for family and friends. Countless memories were made on the farm: harvesting pumpkins for Halloween, picking apples, sleigh rides with the tractor, and many Thanksgiving, Christmas and Easter holidays spent together as a family enjoying each other’s company – and always, delicious food.
Following Rochelle’s passing in 2015, Roger was fortunate to meet his current partner of nearly five years, Mary Ellen Anderson, of Nobleboro, at a cribbage event. She and Roger enjoyed many memories together, including gardening, baking and cooking, and playing many games of cribbage together at home and at the Wiscasset Community Center. Their last cribbage game was played the morning of Roger’s passing. As Roger’s health began to decline, Mary Ellen was instrumental in his care, allowing him to remain at home and continue to do many of the things he enjoyed. She became his eyes, his ears, his travel companion and confidante, and she became a beloved member of his family.
Roger was a jack of all trades, with many hobbies, passions, and interests, many of which he mastered. He was a skilled outdoorsman who enjoyed deer hunting, and participated in the Maine Moose Hunt three times. He traveled many places to fly fish, including Alaska, Labrador, and Nova Scotia, and wetted a fly in many ponds and lakes throughout Maine. Another hobby that he learned from his grandfather, Harry Chase, was the art of tapping maple trees. He was known for his famous black maple syrup, which he made by collecting sap and boiling it in the same evaporator used by Gramp Chase. He passed on this tradition to his granddaughters, Carly, Blair, and Grace, by collecting sap with them over many chilly afternoons and educating them on how to boil the perfect batch.
He was a lifelong football fan and remained loyal to the New England Patriots and Boston Red Sox through thick and thin. He was also a licensed pilot for many years, flying his Cessnas throughout northern Maine and Canada. He was a true tinkerer, maker, and jury-rigger, always repairing broken farm equipment with whatever happened to be lying around. He loved sharing his passions with his family, whether it was explaining the mechanical structure of an engine or the timing of the first rain on a hay crop. He was a lifelong learner, attending mycology classes and business classes through Cornell University.
He was a passionate personal financier and follower of the stock market, and read many favorite books over the years (Benjamin Franklin was one of his favorite authors). He always enjoyed the daily paper every morning over a cup of black coffee with just a bit of milk. He was a voracious cribbage player throughout his entire life, with countless games and laughs over the years. He especially loved playing against his son-in-law, Claude, who became one of his best friends over the past several years. He was an active community member who cared deeply about giving back to the place he called home. He was a lifetime member of the Freeport Lions Club, served on the Whitefield Planning Board, and was a trustee of the Shin Pond Road Association. He contributed generously over the years to the Whitefield Historical Society, the Whitefield Cemetery Corporation, and the Sheepscot Valley Community Church. Due to his generosity, many historic sites and areas of Whitefield were maintained and refurbished. He will be remembered for his mischievous sense of humor, his generosity to the community, and his constant hospitality to friends and family.
He was predeceased by his wife, Rochelle Parlin Downs; their sons Roger Chase Jr. and Daniel Howard Downs; his brothers James Warren and Harry Leonard Downs; his sister, Sallie Ann Curtis; and their parents, Warren Edward and Pearl Emma Downs.
He is survived by his daughter Vicki L. Legere and her husband Joseph, of Falmouth; granddaughters Blair E. Legere and her partner, Warren M. Blood, of Manhattan, New York, Grace V. Hawkes and her husband, Carter, of Norfolk, Virginia, Carly M. Downs and her daughter, Elise Danielle, of Waltham, Massachusetts; son-in-law, Claude A. Castonguay, of Biddeford; brother, John Haley Down,s of Jefferson; and daughter-in-law, Peggy Flanagan, of Whitefield; countless beloved cousins, nieces, and nephews.
A service will take place at Sheepscot Valley Community Church, in Whitefield, on Saturday, November 7, at noon.
Arrangements and guidance are under the direction of Staples Funeral Home and Cremation Care, 53 Brunswick Ave., Gardiner. Condolences, photos and memories may be shared with the family by visiting the Staples Funeral Home website http://www.StaplesFuneralHome.com.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made to the Whitefield Cemetery Corporation, the Whitefield Historical Society or the Whitefield Union Hall in Kings Mills.
GERALD SAINT AMAND JR.
WINSLOW – Gerald “Jerry the Saint” Saint Amand Jr., 83, passed away peacefully at his home on Wednesday, October14, 2026. Jerry was born in Winslow on June 28, 1943, the only child of Doris Saint Amand and Gerald Saint Amand. He attended Winslow public schools, graduating from Thomas College, in Waterville, in 1967.
In 1966, Gerald created and worked at the New England Sports Enterprises as the editor of the boxing newsgrams for five years. Beginning in 1975 he began his career at Ware-Butler, in Waterville, as a credit account manager, wherein he created numerous working relationships with community members and local businesses. Alongside his time at Ware-Butler, in 1986 he became the president of the Central Maine Striders, a state-wide running club of which he was already a very active member. Throughout his time with the club, he directed numerous marathons and runs such as the Colby 5 Mile Classic, Sentinel 10K Classic, and Pine Tree Marathon.
Around 1993, he created the UU Coffeehouse, a chance for the community to hear acoustic and folk artists in an intimate setting. His wife Ruth was often the whiz in the kitchen creating assorted baked goods for attendees to enjoy. He spent almost every Sunday morning at the Waterville Universalist Unitarian Church where he was an integral part of the community and involved in many projects focused on bettering the accessibility of the church grounds.
His involvement in his community did not stop there as he became a Winslow town council member in 2000. For 15 years he attended monthly meetings, actively learned about town budgets and helped to make decisions that benefited the town and its people.
In the early 2000s he also became a DJ on the Colby College radio station WMHB 89.7 where he enjoyed sharing his love of the ’40s, ’50s and ’60s music alongside acoustic and folk musicians tracks. Throughout his years volunteering was an integral part of his life, shown by becoming an honoree of the Spirit of America for his work with the Hospice in 2017. Gerald was the president of the Hospice Volunteers of Waterville from 2015 until 2018.
His family was always his top priority, made clear by years of Sunday night family dinners and always answering the phone. He enjoyed traveling with his wife Ruth and together they visited many parts of the United States and beyond. Jerry will be remembered for his thoughtful demeanor, his ability to create community, a great love of music, many jokes and his warm smile.
He is survived by his wife, Ruth E. Saint Amand; his two daughters, Lisa Jamison and TerryAnn Towers Saint Amand; his two granddaughters, Samantha Jamison and Tessa Saint Towers; and many relatives.
His celebration of life will be held on Saturday, November 14, 2026, at the Waterville Universalist Unitarian Church, 69 Silver St., at 1:30 p.m.
Arrangements are under the direction and care of Gallant Funeral Home, 10 Elm St., Waterville. An online guestbook may be signed, condolences and memories shared at http://www.gallantfh.com.
In lieu of flowers, donations can be made in Gerald Saint Amand’s memory to Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research at https://www. michaeljfox. org/.
ROLAND E. PELLETIER SR.
CHINA – Roland E Pelletier Sr., 87, of China, passed away on Thursday, October 15, 2026. He was born in Gardiner on September 26, 1939.
He lived a long and remarkable life marked by hard work resilience and an endless love of good conversation. He served in the National Guard for 10 years. He also took pride in his work. He did work at Disney in Florida with their underground city. He was very proud that he was 31 years sober and over 40 years smoke free. Roland was an avid fisherman with his buddies in the Kennebec Valley Bassmasters for over 20 years. Roland was also about reading a good book which was one of his many passions. He was also a storyteller, and he had the most infectious smile that could light up the room.
Roland had a special bond with his grandson William Dow, especially when they would go have lunch and then a movie.
Roland was predeceased by his wife Darlene Pelletier of 48 years, two brothers Richard Pelletier and Robert Pelletier as well as both parents Ernest and Blanche Pelletier.
Roland is survived by his son Roland E. Pelletier Jr. and wife, Cynthia Pelletier, of China; daughter, Rhonda, Dow, and husband William Dow, Augusta;, daughters, Pauline Pelletier, and partner Ronald Benedict, of Vassalboro, Paula Pelletier and wife Terri (tee) Pelletier, of China; three grandchildren. William Dow II, of Augusta, Brianna Benedict, of Massachusetts and Richard Malachi Tilson, of China; many nieces and nephews and cousins.
In lieu of flowers, please give to the Saint Joseph’s Indian school, in Chamberlain South Dakota. Service will be a graveside at the China Friends cemetery, on Dirigo Road, in China, on Saturday, November 14, 2026, at 11 a.m., followed by a reception at China Community Church, at 1p.m.
NANCY J. SMITH
CLINTON – Nancy Jane Smith, 82, passed away on Thursday, October 15, 2026. Nancy was born on May 4, 1944, to the late Richard and Irene King.
A service to honor and celebrate Nancy’s life will be held on Thursday, November 5, at 10 a.m. at Saint John Church, 26 Monument St., Winslow.
J. P. DEVINE
LOS ANGELES, California – J.P. Devine, passed away on Friday, October 16, 2026, in Los Angeles, California, the city where he and his wife, Katherine Joly Devine, of Waterville, had raised their daughters, Dawn Devine and Jillana Devine-Knickel.
After 41 years as a member of the Waterville community, he had returned to Los Angeles last December after Katherine’s passing to be closer to his daughters.
Born and raised in St. Louis, Missouri, as the seventh of the eight children of Naval officer Mathias Devine and Veronica Conlon Devine, J.P. grew up with five brothers in the Navy and served in the U.S. Air Force Intellligence, in Japan, during the Korean War. He became fascinated by the Japanese culture and learned to speak and cook like a local.
As a young actor, he studied and performed at the renowned Cleveland Playhouse and moved to New York City, New York in the 1950s, where he was a proud part of the birth of off-Broadway theatre alongside such luminaries as Jerry Orbach, Anne Bancroft, and Geraldine Paige. It was in New York that he met Katherine Joly, of Waterville, and in 1961 they drove cross country with friends to stake their claim in Hollywood. He became a successful commercial and television actor there, and began his career as a columnist at the Los Angeles Times.
In the early 1980s, Katherine asked him, “Why don’t we move back to my little town in Maine, and you can be a real writer?” They selflessly waited until both daughters had graduated from high school and started their own adult lives, and in 1984 they sold their house in Los Angeles and bought a house on First Rangeway, in Waterville, where they would live for the next 41 years.
As a columnist and film critic for the Central Maine newspapers for over 35 years, he won several awards from the Maine Press Awards, including a first prize for his review of the film Revolutionary Road in 2009.
In 2015, North Country Press published Will Write For Food, a collection of his columns for the Morning Sentinel. Enormously proud that his writing was so beautifully compiled in one volume, Devine gave copies to new friends when he returned to Los Angeles as a way of introducing himself and his remarkable life.
During his time in Waterville, Devine also formed Last Laugh Productions, his theatrical company through which he wrote, directed and produced original plays, classic plays and musicals, and taught acting and improvisation classes to teens and adults at the Waterville Opera House. Always passionate about sharing his theatrical skills and experience with young artists, he also visited Katherine’s acting classes and play rehearsals at Waterville Junior High, where he quickly became a favorite guest.
A gifted painter and cartoonist as well, Devine studied at the Arts Students League, in New York, and created sketches for Katherine’s classrooms as well as paintings for his home and for exhibition at The Last Unicorn restaurant, in Waterville. His painting “Justice,” which he painted for his best friend, Maine Supreme Judicial Court Justice Joseph Jabar, can be seen outside the judges chambers at the Maine Supreme Court office, in Augusta.
Devine is survived by his daughters, Dawn Devine and Jillana Devine-Knickel, and their husbands, Richard Sieloff and Wayne Knickel; along with nieces and nephews including Kevin Devine, Lisa Pisciotta, Matheo Pisciotta, Ann Joly, Michael Joly, Margot Joly and Megan Macauley.
In lieu of flowers, the family asks that you consider a donation to one of J.P.’s favorite charities, The Entertainment Community Fund. (entertainment community.org).
SUSAN J. DEMERS
Susan Jean (Hewett) Demers, 70, passed away on Tuesday, October 20, 2026, at Eastern Maine Medical Center, in Bangor. Born May 1, 1956, she was the first of four children to Walter and Jean (Wheeler) Hewett.
Growing up in Fayette, Susan helped her family run the Fayette Country Store. She often recalled fond memories of working there and living above the store with her parents and siblings. She graduated from Livermore Falls High School in 1974. After graduation, she attended the University of Maine in Augusta for accounting.
In 1987, she married her husband, Ron Demers and had three children, whom she dedicated her time to home schooling until high school. Her lessons emphasized creativity and encouraged them to create from their own imaginations.
During the late ‘90s and early 2000s, she attended Calvary Bible Baptist Church, in Whitefield, and was very active in her church community. As Sunday School Superintendent, she helped teach Sunday school classes, and tirelessly put together arts and crafts projects for the children to make with their lessons each week. She also took pride in contributing to the Girls Alive and Daughters of the King clubs, and was in charge of crafts for Vacation Bible School each summer.
She had a passion for art, and created many seasonal and holiday displays for herself and her family to enjoy around the home. She also enjoyed knitting and crocheting, often giving her completed projects to friends and family members as gifts. Each year, she knitted a variety of mittens to donate to local charities for the cold winter months. She was skilled at knitting mittens and scarves, as well as crocheting afghans.
To her family and friends, she is remembered as having a heart of gold. She loved caring for people and often went the extra mile to help others when she could. In later years, she took up card making and hosted small groups to teach others how to make their own greeting cards. She found joy in sending her homemade cards to others for birthdays and special events.
She had an appreciation for the simple pleasures in life and loved spending time with her grandchildren, often providing fun outdoor and indoor activities to encourage the same creativity and imagination she instilled in her own children.
Susan is survived by her husband of 39 years, Ron Demers; two sons, Josh Demers and his wife, Tiffany, of Windsor, and Matt Demers and his wife, Allison McKeen, of Gardiner; one daughter, Katie Blanchette and her husband, Graham, of Whitefield; one brother, Ronnie Hewett and his wife, Orra Lee, of Fayette; two sisters, Linda Elliot and her husband, Bob, of Mount Vernon, and Marcia Millet and her husband, Tim, of Whitefield; grandchildren Mack, Landon, Emmaline and Blakelynn Demers.
Family and friends are encouraged to honor her memory by spending time with those you love and appreciating the small moments of friendship and fellowship.
WILLIAM D. GARD
WATERVILLE – William Douglas Gard, 95, also known as Doug, passed away peacefully at home on Friday, October 23, 2026. “Doug” was born in Attleboro, Massachusetts, on May 23, 1931, to Alport and Frances Gard, of Prince Edward Island, Canada.
He is survived by his bride of 75 years, Ann; son, Jeffrey D. Gard, of San Jose, California, and his partner Chengwei Li; daughters, Robin L. Doody, of Benton, and her husband Michael, and Cynthia A. O’Neill, of Haddam, Connecticut, and her husband Brian; six grandchildren, Jessica Maguire and her husband, Shawn, Elizabeth Hollingdale and her husband, James, Justin Gard and his wife, Robyn, Alexander Corkum and his wife Helen, Kristen Durnan and her husband Patrick, and Katherine Martin and her husband, Kyle; 18 great-grandchildren; and two great-great-grandchildren.
A service was held on Monday, November 2, 2026, at Veilleux-Redington-Lawry Brothers Funeral Home, 8 Elm St., in Waterville.
JOHN W. MILLER
WINSLOW – John W. Miller passed away peacefully on Saturday, October 24, 2026.
He is leaving behind a legacy of adventure, hard work, and family. A proud U.S. Air Force combat medic who served in Vietnam, he later built a career in materials management at MaineGeneral Medical Center, retiring in 2012. An avid outdoorsman who loved fishing, boating, and exploring, his greatest joy was being Papa to his grandchildren.
He is survived by his wife of 39 years, Helen; daughters and their husbands, Danielle and Michael Zemrak, Robyn and Erik Maheu; four grandchildren, Maddox and Julien Maheu, and Isla and Brighde Zemrak; his sister, Virginia Price and her husband William Price; brother, Charles Miller and his wife Mary Trumbauer; and many nieces, nephews and cousins.
A memorial visitation at 10 a.m. and brief service at noon, will be held on Friday, November 6, 2026, at Veilleux’s Funeral Home, Elm St., in Waterville. A military service at the Veterans Cemetery, in Augusta, will be held at 2 p.m.
We invite those who knew and loved him to take a moment to appreciate a sunset, spend time on the water, and share a truly good belly laugh when you think of him.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made to the Maine Audubon Society in his memory.
Services
HARLAND BRAGG
SIDNEY – There will be an open memorial service for Harland and Shirley Bragg, of Sidney, on Saturday, November 14, 2026, at 2 p.m., at Centerpoint Community Church, 155 West River Road, Waterville. Please join us in celebrating their lives.

title: Democrat Josh Turek wins election to US Senate from Iowa
text:
DES MOINES, Iowa (AP) — Josh Turek won Iowa’s rare open U.S. Senate race in Tuesday’s midterm elections, flipping a Republican-held seat and helping Democrats end GOP dominance in Washington.
Turek’s victory over Republican Ashley Hinson made him the first Democrat since Barack Obama to win a statewide federal race in Iowa. Turek will be one of four Democratic members of Iowa’s federal delegation after years of exclusively Republican representation in Washington.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
Iowa reemerged as a political battleground this year as Democrats seized on high fuel prices, tariffs and a war overseas that caused turmoil in the state’s dominant agricultural industry. The retirements of Republican Sen. Joni Ernst and Republican Gov. Kim Reynolds made for the first cycle without incumbents seeking the top-of-the-ticket seats since 1968, breathing new life into Democrats’ efforts to reverse years of electoral failure in the state.
Turek told supporters Tuesday that his underdog race seemed far-fetched in a state that elected Trump by double digits just two years ago.
“They told me it was impossible to win this Senate race, but tonight, Iowa, we have once again proved that the impossible is possible,” he said.
Iowa became one of Democrats’ targets as they looked to take over majority control of the Senate, and the campaign drew hundreds of millions of dollars.
Hinson thanked her staff and supporters Tuesday, saying she will “continue to fight for common sense.”
“I think we ran an absolutely fabulous campaign across the state,” she said. “Lots of late nights and lots of miles.”
Pressure on Republicans reached Iowa
Although many Republicans walked a political tightrope this cycle, Hinson had a more challenging balancing act than most. Iowa has faced manufacturing job losses, healthcare clinic closures and shrunken farm profits since Trump returned to the White House. There was loud unrest over poor water quality and rising cancer rates.
Hinson launched her campaign last year promising to be Trump’s “top ally” in the Senate. Almost a year later, she instead focused her message on being “Iowa’s best bipartisan fighter.”
In September, after House members were sent home, Hinson said Iowans “shouldn’t have to foot the bill” for the Iran war.
She did not, however, join two fellow Iowa Republicans in battleground districts — U.S. Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks — in voting with Democrats earlier in September on a resolution intended to halt Trump’s ability to continue military action without lawmakers’ approval.
Hinson said the resolution was not the way to allow Trump to bring the war to an immediate and successful end.
While Hinson pointedly critiqued the president on specific issues in the final months of the race, she still appeared beside him when he made two visits to Iowa in the last two weeks of the campaign.
A majority of Iowa voters saw Hinson as “too supportive” of Trump, according to The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of the electorate.
Nunn also lost Tuesday to Democratic state Sen. Sarah Trone Garriott, and Miller-Meeks lost to Democrat Christina Bohannan, a former state representative. The congressional seat that Hinson left open when she ran for Senate also flipped to Democrat Lindsay James.
Turek taps into desire for change
About 3 in 10 Iowa voters said the quality that most mattered for their vote was that their chosen candidate would “bring needed change,” and Turek overwhelmingly won those voters.
Turek said he heard stories of people hurting as he crisscrossed the state.
About 7 in 10 Iowa Senate voters said they are “angry” or “dissatisfied” with the way things are going in the country, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Iowa Senate voters were more likely to say government corruption was “crucial” for their vote for Congress than the cost of living, although both rose above other issues. About half of Iowa voters said government corruption was “crucial” for their vote, while about 4 in 10 said this about the cost of living.
And while Hinson cast Turek as “too liberal” for Iowa, less than half of Iowa voters said Turek’s views were “too extreme.”
Like many other Republican candidates across the country, Hinson lost significant ground among young voters, compared to Trump in 2024. Hinson also appeared to have lost ground among white women, a group that Trump narrowly won in 2024.
Hinson did outperform Turek among white voters without a college degree, winning about half of these voters, but she fell short of Trump’s 2024 performance.
Democrats were eager to revive Iowa’s bipartisan tradition
Then-President Obama was the last Democrat to win a statewide federal election in Iowa with his reelection victory in 2012. State Auditor Rob Sand was the lone Democrat in statewide elected office over the last four years. He won the governor’s race on Tuesday.
For three decades, Iowans sent a bipartisan pair to the Senate. That included current Republican Sen. Chuck Grassley and former Democratic Sen. Tom Harkin, who decided not to seek reelection in 2014. Ernst won Harkin’s seat.
Turek, a state representative and former Paralympian, wanted to follow in Harkin’s path. Born with spina bifida, believed to be from his father’s exposure to chemicals during the Vietnam War, Turek credits Harkin’s work to enact the Americans with Disabilities Act for his own achievements.
Turek called Harkin up to join him on stage Tuesday, saying Harkin gave him and so many other Americans “an on-ramp” to society.
“One senator’s ability to work across the aisle and pass good public policy changed my life,” Turek said. “He fought for the little guy, the same people I’m fighting for.”
