title: Nevada Democrat Aaron Ford defeats Republican Joe Lombardo to become state’s first Black governor
text:
Nevada Democrat Aaron Ford defeats Republican Joe Lombardo to become state’s first Black governor
Nevada’s Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford has won the race for governor, ousting Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and becoming the state’s first Black governor.
This was one of the most closely watched elections in the country, and Ford’s win marks a major victory for Democrats’ efforts to expand their control of state governments in key battlegrounds. Nevada will play a critical role in the next presidential election.
Ford has served as the state’s top prosecutor since 2019. Throughout his campaign, he described growing up in poverty and going to school hungry. He explained how he became a math teacher before earning his law degree, and highlighted efforts to fight the Trump administration.
Related video:
“This campaign didn’t happen by accident,” Ford said at a Democratic watch party Tuesday. “It happened because of faith, because of family, because of hard work, and because the people of Nevada decided that our best days are still ahead of us.”
Ford focused his campaign on affordability, promising to tackle student loan debt and crack down on the development of artificial intelligence data centers. He painted his opponent as a staunch loyalist of the president and criticized Lombardo for vetoing bills that Ford said would have helped Nevadans, from restrictions on corporate homeownership to providing free school meals.
Amid voters’ concerns over the impacts of AI data centers, Ford promised to pause new tax abatements for them and oppose projects on federal land in Nevada.
He defended against attacks by the governor, a former sheriff, that tried to paint Ford as soft on crime while he was attorney general. He also deflected Lombardo’s accusations that his policy goals would be too expensive.
Ford got a boost from national Democrats who are eyeing potential 2028 presidential campaigns, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris, who came to the state to campaign for him. Trump won Nevada in 2024 with 50.6% of the vote.
The economy took center stage
During this year’s race, the governor portrayed Ford as a threat to the state’s business-friendly climate. Lombardo sought to tie him to Democrat-controlled California, claiming Ford would bring the “Newsom playbook” of high taxes and more regulations.
Democrats worked to connect Lombardo with President Donald Trump’s tariffs, saying they harmed Las Vegas tourism, which saw a 17% drop in Canadian visitors in 2025. The president has feuded with Canadian leaders, and the two countries are in the middle of a trade dispute.
Ford criticized Lombardo for vetoing legislation the Democrat said would make life more affordable, such as a bill to limit home purchases by corporate investors. Nevadans are grappling with some of the highest gas prices in the country and a shortage of tens of thousands of homes.
The race for governor cast a shadow beyond Nevada
The westernmost battleground state has a distinctive electorate that doesn’t always follow national political trends.
Democratic strength in Las Vegas is counterbalanced by heavily Republican rural areas, and the true wild cards are the nonpartisan voters who make up nearly 40% of the electorate. The steady flow of people into and out of the state, as well as the large number of working-class and Latino voters, make it difficult to predict statewide races.
Although Nevada only has six electoral college votes, both parties have Nevada as an early state in their nominating calendar.
Law enforcement backgrounds were key to the race
Both candidates faced scrutiny for how they exercised their authority in law enforcement.
Ford’s campaign criticized Lombardo after he avoided a traffic ticket in Las Vegas, interrupting the police officer to say “I’m Joe Lombardo.” Meanwhile, the governor’s campaign blasted Ford for sponsoring consideration of a clemency application for a man who killed a pregnant woman in 2017.
Lombardo secured a major boost when the Democratic district attorney for Clark County, which covers Las Vegas, endorsed the governor instead of his fellow Democrat.
The governor served in law enforcement for over 25 years before becoming sheriff of Clark County in 2014. He became well known in 2017 while overseeing the investigation into the Las Vegas mass shooting, the deadliest in modern U.S. history. Lombardo was born in Japan to a U.S. military family stationed overseas and served in the Army and the Nevada National Guard.
Ford, a former state senator, frequently spoke about experiencing poverty as a child and how his father brought home stale candy bars from the grocery store he worked at for the family’s dinner. Since being elected attorney general, he has secured millions in settlements from opioid manufacturers, and he successfully sued a student loan servicer as well as the gaming platform Roblox.

title: Debris from Florida jet crash falls through woman's roof and into her kitchen
text:
Debris from Florida jet crash falls through woman's roof and into her kitchen
Exclusive pictures show suspected aircraft wreckage inside a West Palm Beach woman's kitchen as investigators confirm critical pieces of the jet broke off before the crash that killed nine people
Debris from Florida jet crash falls through woman's roof and into her kitchen
Exclusive pictures show suspected aircraft wreckage inside a West Palm Beach woman's kitchen as investigators confirm critical pieces of the jet broke off before the crash that killed nine people
Following a deadly jet crash near West Palm Beach, Florida, officials said they have discovered debris miles away, with a suspected piece of the wreckage said to have crashed through the roof of a woman's home, landing in her kitchen.
The debris discovery comes as federal investigators confirmed that critical parts of the aircraft's tail separated before the jet slammed into the ground along a popular street.
Hearst sister station WPBF obtained exclusive pictures of what appeared to be twisted aircraft metal lying on the kitchen floor of Ana Escobar's home, less than a mile from the crash scene.
Watch video in the playfinder above
Escobar said the object tore through her roof and landed inside her kitchen. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office retrieved the suspected wreckage Tuesday as evidence.
Another discovery was made nearly four miles from the crash site.
Peter DiMaira found what appeared to be pieces of the aircraft's tail at his workplace, exactly 3.8 miles from where the jet went down. He contacted the sheriff's office.
The National Transportation Safety Board confirmed Tuesday that investigators recovered three pieces of the jet's left elevator, a critical control surface on the tail that helps control the aircraft's up-and-down movement.
Those pieces were discovered between 1.3 and 3.8 miles from the crash site.
NTSB board member Tom Chapman said the distance confirms the components separated from the aircraft before impact.
But investigators don't yet know whether the loss of those pieces contributed to the crash or whether the violent forces acting on the aircraft caused them to break away.
"The function of the elevator is to control pitch up and down," Chapman said. "At those speeds, I don't know if it would be effective even if it had still been attached to the aircraft. But knowing that it was lost is a very important piece of evidence in terms of pointing us toward other things to investigate."
The discovery raises a critical question: Was the aircraft already out of control when parts of its tail broke off, or did losing those components contribute to the deadly descent?
Investigators are examining weather conditions and other possible factors as they work to determine what happened.
Pilot identified as investigation continues
WPBF confirmed that Jeff Gregory was the pilot of the Learjet when it crashed Sunday.
Copilot Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras was also aboard.
The crash killed all nine people on the aircraft.
Investigators preparing to search massive crater
Meanwhile, NTSB investigators continued combing through the wreckage Tuesday as part of the road where the jet crashed remains blocked to traffic.
Crews removed a dangerous utility pole near the massive impact crater, clearing the way for investigators to begin accessing the site.
The NTSB plans to begin pumping water out of the crater Wednesday so investigators can search for additional critical aircraft components buried in the wreckage.
Among the evidence, they hope to find is a cockpit voice recorder.
Chapman said aircraft maintenance records indicate a recorder had been installed on the Learjet, but investigators have not yet confirmed whether it was still aboard when the plane crashed.
A surviving recording could provide valuable information about what was happening inside the cockpit during the aircraft's final moments.
Investigators are also reviewing dashcam video and eyewitness accounts as they attempt to reconstruct the flight.
The NTSB has not determined what caused the crash.
Additional updates are expected as investigators analyze the recovered wreckage and continue searching the impact crater.

title: Cornell rape investigation will be led by a former prosecutor in the Sean 'Diddy' Combs case
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A reopened criminal investigation into gang rape allegations at Cornell University will be led by a former Manhattan federal prosecutor who oversaw high-profile sex crimes cases against music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs and fashion executive Peter Nygård, New York Attorney General Letitia James announced on Wednesday.
Jacqueline Kelly, a Cornell alumna and partner at the law firm Boies Schiller Flexner, will serve as outside counsel for James’ investigation, which was spurred by a former student’s allegations in a September lawsuit that several men raped her at a fraternity party in October 2024.
Kelly and a team of lawyers and investigators from her firm and the attorney general’s office will be responsible for gathering evidence, interviewing witnesses, reviewing investigative records and reports, and analyzing the facts and applicable law, James said.
They will report to James, who was appointed last month by Gov. Kathy Hochul as a special prosecutor overseeing the Cornell probe. James, a Democrat, made the announcement a day after winning election to a third term.
Separately, two men named as defendants in the former student’s lawsuit are want the attorney general removed from the investigation. They argue James is biased because of a social media post she made before her appointment that expressed support for the accuser. A judge has yet to rule.
“Jacqueline Kelly is a seasoned prosecutor who has overseen numerous cases from investigation through trial,” James said in a statement. “With her criminal legal expertise, commitment to public service, and judicial experience, I am confident that she will lead a fair and comprehensive investigation.”
Kelly, a Columbia Law School graduate, was a prosecutor in the Manhattan U.S. Attorney’s Office for nearly a decade and led the civil rights unit in the office’s criminal division. She oversaw investigations and prosecutions of civil rights offenses, voting rights violations, sex crimes and hate crimes.
She left last year to join Boies Schiller Flexner and will remain at the firm while she conducts the Cornell investigation.
“All New Yorkers deserve a fair and thorough inquiry into the facts of this case,” Kelly said. “I look forward to lending my years of experience as a federal prosecutor to the Office of the Attorney General as we examine all available evidence.”
Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor on Oct. 1, saying she had lost faith in the local prosecutor, Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, who declined to bring charges in 2024.
Van Houten said he would restart the investigation following the former student’s lawsuit, but a lawyer for the accuser said the district attorney was preparing to bring the matter to a grand jury within two weeks.
James has said her investigation will take months.
The former Cornell student, identified in court papers as Jane Doe, alleged in her lawsuit that some of the men pressured her into using ketamine and marijuana and that she drank alcohol that left her too intoxicated to consent. A few weeks later, she said, she made reports to campus police and the university’s Title IX office.
The case roiled the Ivy League institution, raising questions about how universities, police departments and local prosecutors respond to campus sexual assaults.
Last month, Cornell hired former U.S. Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates to review how the school investigates sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the campus police response and more.
As a federal prosecutor, Kelly supervised the prosecutions of former Manhattan neurologist Ricardo Cruciani, who killed himself in jail while awaiting trial on federal charges after his conviction in state court for molesting patients, as well as Bronx music teacher Jesus Concepcion, who was sentenced in 2024 to 30 years in prison for sexually abusing five students. She also took on the mafia, prosecuting a dozen members of the Lucchese crime family.
At Boies Schiller Flexner, she focuses on regulatory and criminal investigations and represents victims of sexual assault and other crimes. The firm, co-founded by lawyer David Boies, is known for representing victims of the late Jeffrey Epstein, as well as corporate clients including Amazon and the defunct health technology company Theranos.
James, whose office is geared toward civil litigation and consumer protection, has turned to outside counsel in the past to assist in investigations.
In 2021, she appointed two outside lawyers, former Manhattan U.S. Attorney Joon Kim and employment lawyer Anne Clark, to conduct a non-criminal investigation into sexual harassment allegations against then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo, leading to his resignation. Cuomo denied the findings in their report.

title: Penobscot Valley Ski Club to host annual ski sale Sunday at Hermon Mountain
text:
HERMON, Maine (WABI) - The Penobscot Valley Ski Club is hosting its annual ski sale Sunday at Hermon Mountain.
The sale is consignment only. No vendors will be on site selling new gear this year.
Sale and registration times
Equipment can be brought in to register for sale from 10 to 11:30 a.m. The sale will be open from noon to 3 p.m.
Acceptable items include downhill and Nordic skis, poles, boots, snowboards and outerwear. The sale will not take old bindings or damaged gear.
Consignment payouts and unsold gear returns will be from 3:30 to 4:30 p.m.
Partnership with Hermon Mountain’s new owners
Organizers are partnering with the new owners of Hermon Mountain. The new owners have been a big help to the club.
Dan Baumert, president of the Penobscot Valley Ski Club, spoke about the partnership.
“They’re pretty instrumental in our youth alpine racing program so we’re trying to keep those relationships up and improve that program as well. It’s been kind of exciting. We’re working with them and they’ve got some new ideas so we decided to just have it out there and have a consignment sale and have it smaller and not be so much work as it has been in the past for the ski club,” Baumert said.
Lunch and snacks are available at Scenic Eats during the sale.
More information on this year’s sale can be found at pvskiclub.org.

title: DNC Chairman shares party goals after ‘blue wave’
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Following a sweeping “blue wave” that saw Democrats flip long-held Republican seats across the country, party leaders in Washington are preparing an aggressive legislative and oversight agenda focused squarely on lowering everyday costs.
Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) hailed the outcome as a “generational remake of the Senate map,” pointing to victories in states long considered untouchable for Democrats.
According to Democratic National Committee Chairman Ken Martin said voters responded to their pitches of affordability, but also rebuked President Trump.
“They were sending a message to Donald Trump,” Martin said, using stiff language, in an interview on Capitol Hill. “‘Get off your ass and do something to help me. Get off your ass and do something to help our country.’”
Policy Priorities: Healthcare, Tariffs, and Ending the Iran War
Martin emphasized that Democrats’ top priority will be delivering on economic promises, beginning with efforts to roll back Trump administration tariffs and reverse federal cuts to social safety nets.
Specifically, Martin targeted recent legislation that scaled back federal assistance programs to fund tax cuts.
“Repeal the ‘Big Ugly Bill,’ which cut Medicaid and SNAP benefits to give tax breaks to the wealthiest in this country,” Martin said.
Foreign policy is also set to take center stage, with Democratic lawmakers planning legislative maneuvers to force an end to the ongoing war in Iran.
Oversight and Accountability
Beyond legislative policy, Democrats plan to use their new committee gavels to launch investigations into alleged corruption within the executive branch.
“We can walk and chew gum at the same time,” Martin said. “Meaning that we can both deliver on that agenda and also hold people accountable in this country, and the reality is we’re seeing massive corruption with this administration.”
While members in both parties have floated the potential impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the handling of the Iran War, Martin stopped short of endorsing formal proceedings, stating only that Hegseth “will be held accountable.”

title: Maine enters bye week at 1-8 after 14-13 overtime loss to Rhode Island
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - Maine football’s losing streak reached eight games in Saturday’s 14-13 overtime loss to Rhode Island.
The Black Bears took the lead in O-T, but their missed extra point led to the loss after the Rams scored and converted theirs in the first overtime.
Head coach Jordan Stevens spoke on the loss and moving forward.
“Our defensive swarm, and just the presence they had in the field, you can’t deny how hard our guys were playing. Unfortunately, that’s how things go in the game of football, so we’ve got to play through the entire game. Obviously, we had extra time to do that in this game and just came up short,” said Stevens.
Maine is now 1-8 on the season.
The Black Bears are on a bye week before traveling to UAlbany on Nov. 14 before hosting New Hampshire to finish their schedule the Saturday after.

title: Janeese Lewis George is Washington's next mayor. Now come the challenges, starting with Trump
text:
Janeese Lewis George is Washington's next mayor. Now come the challenges, starting with Trump
It’s official — Janeese Lewis George will be the new mayor of Washington, D.C. She practically ran unopposed in Tuesday’s general election after winning the Democratic primary earlier this year.
Now the question is what comes next for the 38-year-old politician who joins Zohran Mamdani in New York City and Katie Wilson in Seattle in a small club of democratic socialist municipal leaders.
Winning was easy as Lewis George breezed past an independent, a Statehood Green Party candidate and 11 write-ins lacking political clout. Now she faces her first potential heavyweight hurdles, including President Donald Trump himself, who has inserted himself in local affairs and denounced the incoming mayor as a threat to the capital city.
Related video: Democrats gain control of the House and Senate. What happens now?
“We will not let it be destroyed by a Communist adherent who has no intention to, MAKE WASHINGTON GREAT AGAIN!” Trump wrote on social media after her primary victory.
Lewis George, for her part, promised that she would work with anyone to keep the city safe “but I will also stand up to Trump.” Come Jan. 2, she will be sworn in as the city’s first new mayor in 12 years.
In an interview earlier this year, she told The Associated Press that her top priority will be addressing “the affordability crisis here in D.C., which the Trump administration has only made worse by unjustly firing federal employees en masse and militarizing our streets.”
The capital city doesn’t have full autonomy
Lewis George, who served five years on the city council, will be the District’s eighth mayor since its Home Rule law was signed in 1973, giving the city’s residents the chance to choose their local officials. She will work with D.C.’s new delegate to Congress, Robert White Jr. He won his race Tuesday and will succeed longtime Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton, who decided to step down under pressure following criticism that she had lost her effectiveness. The election of Lewis George and White mark the first time since 1990 that the city has chosen both a new mayor and delegate.
Lewis George will take over a city of nearly 700,000 and face all the usual challenges of a municipality, in charge of revenue, public safety and affordability and even ceremonial duties like ribbon cutting. But the D.C. mayor faces an added burden. The same 1973 law that allowed her election also preserved Congress’ authority over city affairs.
“They can essentially veto any bill we pass here. Two, they can manipulate our budget without our input. And three, they can legislate directly for us if they want to,” said Emily Cassometus, the director of the Legislation Clinic at the University of the District of Columbia’s law school.
“The Home Rule Act hasn’t changed. It won’t be changing with her inauguration,” said Cassometus, who previously worked on Lewis George’s staff.
During Trump’s first year in office after returning to the White House, Congress blocked the city from spending a billion dollars of its own money by freezing the city at 2024 spending during a federal budget process.
“The fact that a billion dollars of our money was blocked from being spent is huge and has impacts on people’s daily lives,” said Alicia Yass, policy advocacy director for the American Civil Liberties Union of the District of Columbia. “We’ve also seen an exponential increase in the number of bills that Congress is passing or introducing that specifically target the district.”
Control of Congress will shape the city
Key to Lewis George’s tenure will be the outcome of House and Senate elections. If Congress falls into Democratic hands, the city has a backstop against Republican efforts to encroach on local authority.
“It’s Congress, not the president, who has the power of exclusive legislation over the District,” said George Derek Musgrove, an associate professor of history at the University of Maryland-Baltimore County. “I’m suspecting that Democrats will give the mayor some cover, even if they only get the House.”
Lewis George will need to decide how much to defy Trump, particularly on issues like the National Guard deployment and cooperation of local law enforcement with the federal authorities, especially U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.
Outgoing Mayor Muriel Bowser has stayed relatively quiet, even opposing the district council on what role local officers have in holding their federal colleagues accountable. In past discussions she has said her achievements include educational gains and keeping home rule at a time when the district’s autonomy has been severely challenged. Bowser decided not to run again once her third four-year term ends in January.
Lewis George could use Mamdani as a model. Despite early tensions between the two, the New York mayor has occasionally bonded with Trump, asking for the president’s support on some projects while still criticizing many of his policies.
Musgrove said the question is whether the coalition that gave her the primary win and wants her to “fight the president” allows her to be more low key.
Lewis George has praised Bowser for a number of things but opposed her strategy for dealing with the administration, and she promised to end the local police’s cooperation with federal immigration operations.
District of Columbia faces financial challenges
Lewis George will face other challenges, some created by the capital’s relationship with the administration and Congress. The District of Columbia accounted for a fifth of roughly 100,000 job losses in the region in major part because of the Elon Musk-led Department of Government Efficiency overhaul of the federal workforce.
The cuts had a cascading effect, from loss of tax revenue to reduced activity at local businesses and restaurants. The city expects revenue to drop by hundreds of millions of dollars, prompting the district council to consider several tax increase proposals.
The Urban Institute, which is a public policy think tank, estimates that nearly a quarter million families in the D.C. region will be impacted by safety net cuts that will be kicking in after the election as part of Trump’s “big beautiful bill” — a sweeping package of tax breaks, social service cuts and immigration enforcement measures.
There will likely still be National Guard troops on the streets regardless of what Lewis George wants.
The president deployed them in August 2025 and more than 2,900 troops remain. There are plans to keep them there through January 2029.
The legality of that mobilization is now being considered by a three-judge panel with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. A lower court judge ruled in November 2025 that the guard presence was illegal but an appeals court panel stayed that ruling, allowing the military personnel to remain until the case can be decided.

title: Former chief deputy has sizable lead in heated Hancock County sheriff’s race
text:
Former chief deputy and Republican nominee Corey Bagley was headed for victory as Hancock County’s next sheriff early Wednesday morning.
Corey Bagley held nearly a 3,000-vote lead over Dakota Dupuis in the race for Hancock County’s top law enforcement officer at around 1 a.m.
Bagley had 12,917 votes and Dupuis had 10,074 votes with 28 of 37 municipalities in the county having reported unofficial results. Bagley is an Ellsworth police detective and a former chief deputy under outgoing Sheriff Scott Kane, who chose not to seek re-election. Dupuis is a lieutenant at the sheriff’s office.
The race turned particularly divisive in its final weeks after Kane, a Republican, shared a website under his own byline accusing Bagley of steering a county contract to his father. Kane endorsed Dupuis, 31, who is running as a Democrat.
Bagley, 57, said he was not involved in awarding the contract to his father, Rudy Bagley.
The candidates and their allies traded misconduct allegations for weeks before the election.
The race for sheriff — which was the county’s first contested general election to replace an outgoing sheriff since 1980 — jumbled the usual partisan lines. Several Democratic state legislatures endorsed Bagley, while county commissioners were split on their support of the two candidates.
Bagley previously served the sheriff’s office for 31 years before his controversial departure in 2023, which led to a public battle between Kane and county commissioner William Clark, a former longtime sheriff who accused the current sheriff of pushing Bagley out to hire Kane’s brother, Patrick Kane, who previously had served as his chief deputy.
Bagley favors community policing and hopes to add a mental health liaison to the sheriff’s department, he previously said. He also wants to replicate a version of Bar Harbor’s Good Morning program, a free service that provides daily wellness checks to senior residents and adults with disabilities.
If Bagley is confirmed to be the winner, he will begin his four-year term in the position on Jan. 1, 2027.

title: Billionaire Leon Black sues U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia for defamation over Epstein comments
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Billionaire Leon Black on Wednesday filed a federal defamation lawsuit against California Rep. Robert Garcia for public comments the Democratic congressman made tying him to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.
The court filing comes less than two months after the House approved a resolution holding Black in contempt of Congress for defying the Oversight Committee’s subpoenas in its investigation into Epstein.
In June, Black appeared for a voluntary interview at the committee during which he denied any knowledge of Epstein’s sex trafficking network.
Weeks later, Garcia said during a TV interview that “Leon Black is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes” and that Black “was one of the last people to actually interact” with Epstein before he committed suicide in prison.
In addition, Garcia said that he had “talked to survivors that have credibly named Leon Black as someone that was involved in direct abuse of women and was directly involved” with Epstein.
Those statements were false and were made maliciously, Black asserts through his lawyers. The defamation lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York seeks a jury trial and $7.25 million in compensatory and punitive damages.
“Congressman Garcia’s knowing lies have caused real and significant ongoing harm to Mr. Black. His physical safety has been threatened, he has received a barrage of hateful calls, emails, and social media posts, and his business and philanthropic endeavors have suffered,” the filing states.
Garcia’s office didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit.
In September, Garcia called the contempt resolution against Black “an important step toward justice and accountability.”
Black had refused to respond to subpoenas asking him to appear and to turn over any potential nondisclosure agreements involving the investigation into Epstein.
Black’s lawyers have repeatedly denounced the Oversight Committee’s pursuit of the former head of a private equity firm as an abuse of congressional power. They have maintained he had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s criminal conduct.
Black was among several prominent figures, including Bill Clinton and Bill Gates, who had been asked to appear as part of the Oversight Committee’s long-running probe of Epstein. Survivors of Epstein’s alleged sexual abuse have told personal stories of being young women in a trafficking enterprise organized by Epstein and his colleague Ghislaine Maxwell.
Black co-founded the private equity firm Apollo Global Management and stepped down in 2021 during the fallout over his ties to Epstein.
Lawmakers have alleged that Black paid Epstein $180 million during their yearslong relationship.
A 2021 review commissioned by Apollo found that Black paid Epstein $158 million from 2012 to 2017, after Epstein pleaded guilty in 2008 to soliciting prostitution from a minor. The review said the payments were for “bona fide tax, estate planning and other related services.”

title: Star NASCAR driver suspended by own team for final race of season
text:
MOORESVILLE, N.C. (WBTV/Gray News) - A star NASCAR driver has been suspended by his own team for the final race of the 2026 season.
Drivers in all three of NASCAR’s top series will wrap up the racing slate this weekend at Homestead-Miami Speedway.
However, Carson Hocevar, driver of the No. 77 car, will not be among them.
Spire Motorsports announced on Tuesday that Hocevar would be suspended for the Nov. 8 season finale race.
The team-induced suspension comes after some accused Hocevar of intentionally spinning himself to cause a caution during the Nov. 1 race at Martinsville.
The 23-year-old also had a run-in with Austin Cindric as he upheld his reputation as an aggressive driver.
“A decision like this has a lot of variables and a cascading effect across an organization like ours,” Spire Motorsports said in a statement. “The easy thing would have been to leave this in NASCAR’s hands. To us, however, this isn’t about money or points. We believe in respect. Our integrity matters. This is the right decision. Sometimes the right decision for someone you care about hurts in the short term.”
NASCAR veteran and former Spire driver Justin Haley will race in Hocevar’s place.
In a statement of his own, Hocevar called the suspension “an embarrassing day” for him.
“I let the people down that gave me the opportunity of a lifetime to drive a Cup car,” he wrote. “I crossed the line with my on-track actions and gave [owner] Jeff [Dickerson] and Spire Motorsports no option but to put someone else in the 77 car this weekend.”
Hocevar became one of NASCAR’s more popular drivers this season, in part because of his aggressive driving style and charisma.
But he has had numerous incidents involving other drivers in his young career, and was also involved in a viral brawl at Bristol in September.
Hocevar earned his first Cup race win at Talladega on April 26, and advanced to NASCAR’s postseason for the first time this season.
In 35 races this season, Hocevar won a race and recorded 12 top-10 finishes and six top-fives. He sat 12th in the points standings heading into the final race.

title: Lions linebacker Jack Campbell says he has full movement in lower body after suffering neck injury
text:
ALLEN PARK, Mich. (AP) — Detroit Lions All-Pro linebacker Jack Campbell said he has full movement in his lower body and is “continuing to make progress with movement in my upper body,” in his first comments since he was carted off the field on a backboard during a game against Minnesota.
“I know there’s still work ahead, but I remain very optimistic,” Campbell said Wednesday in a statement released by the team. “I’m taking things one day at a time, staying positive, and focusing on getting better.”
Campbell suffered a neck injury early in the fourth quarter of a 19-15 win over the Vikings on Sunday. He was alert when he was taken to the hospital, where he has been recovering since his injury.
Lions coach Dan Campbell said it was powerful that Jack Campbell updated his improving condition himself, shortly before the team’s previously scheduled news conferences with coaches and players.
“That’s good news. That’s positive news,” Dan Campbell said. “We’re all thankful for that.”
Jack Campbell was face down on the turf and not moving after hitting Vikings tight end T.J. Hockenson. He was evaluated by medical personnel before being strapped to a board and carefully lifted onto the cart to a round of applause.
“I especially want to thank the athletic trainers and medical personnel who responded and cared for me on the field,” Jack Campbell said. “I know those were difficult moments, and I’m incredibly grateful for the professionalism, compassion, and care you showed me. The way you handled everything and looked after me when I needed it most is something I’ll never forget.”
The former Iowa star was drafted by the Lions with the 18th overall pick in 2023. Last season, he was an All-Pro selection after becoming the first NFL player in seven years to have 150-plus tackles and at least five sacks and three forced fumbles.
Jack Campbell’s condition has been closely followed since Sunday, a fact that he has felt.
“My family and I want to sincerely thank everyone for the overwhelming amount of love, prayers, and support we’ve received over the past few days,” he said. “It means more to us than words can express.”
The Lions (5-2) play at Miami (1-6) on Sunday.
“The best thing we can do is play the way he would want us to play and honor him that way,” Lions quarterback Jared Goff said.

title: House Speaker Mike Johnson won't seek reelection as Republican leader: AP source
text:
House Speaker Mike Johnson won't seek reelection as Republican leader: AP source
House Speaker Mike Johnson will be stepping aside from Republican Party leadership after the GOP’s wipeout in the midterm election, declining to seek support to stay on as House minority leader in the new Congress, according to two people familiar with his decision who insisted on anonymity to disclose it Wednesday.
Johnson is expected to retain his seat as a rank-and-file member of the House from Louisiana when the Congress convenes in January. He won reelection from his Shreveport-area district for an eighth term in office.
It’s a swift rise and fall for Johnson, often seen as an accidental speaker, who nevertheless drew close to President Donald Trump and led the House GOP during a tumultuous era, with one of the slimmest majorities in modern times. And it sets up a fierce internal party battle for the new GOP leader after Democrats swept to power.
Johnson’s sunny assertions that Republicans would defy history in the midterms, as voters traditionally have punished the president’s party in power, failed to hold. Instead, Republicans were trounced as Democrats swept to the House majority, leaving Johnson without a path to power.
House Republicans are expected to elect their new leader when members-elect gather in Washington next week, in what will likely be a familiar showdown between two who reached for the top spot before — Reps. Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Jim Jordan of Ohio.
The powerful speaker’s gavel now is expected to pass to Democrats, who are preparing to nominate House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York for the job, second in line to the president. The House speaker’s election is among the first votes of the new Congress, on Jan. 3, 2027.
From Shreveport to Washington
Johnson first won the speaker's gavel in 2023 after his colleagues ousted the previous GOP speaker, Kevin McCarthy of California, in a first-of-its-kind coup in House history.
A lower-level member of House leadership, Johnson in many ways fell into the job after Republican colleagues could not agree on a next-in-line successor to McCarthy. He had distinguished himself before the Jan. 6, 2021 attack on the Capitol by organizing support for Trump’s false claims of widespread fraud in the 2020 election he lost to Democrat Joe Biden.
Once in office, Johnson quickly pulled closer to Trump — so close that Johnson candidly recounts their almost daily phone calls and chats, often offering his impressions in the president's voice.
Johnson led passage of the GOP's signature package of tax breaks and social services cuts that Trump signed into law. He protected the president and his administration from embarrassing votes, including a recent effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, by simply sending lawmakers home.
House leadership elections ahead
Johnson's decision sets up a potential repeat of the leadership battles that have played out in recent years between the House GOP's conservative and far-right flanks.
Scalise, the majority leader, has long courted backing from the House GOP's conservative wing, particularly business and energy sector lawmakers. Jordan, the brawling former wrestler who helmed the Judiciary Committee, has long been preferred by the hard right, including some from the Freedom Caucus.
Both Scalise and Jordan reached for the speaker's gavel once McCarthy was forced aside in 2023, but they failed to win majority support from their colleagues, splitting the votes. At the time, Johnson emerged as the consensus candidate who became the House speaker.

title: Chellie Pingree reelected in 1st District, with 2nd District undecided
text:
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine 1st District, won a 10th term in the U.S. House of Representatives, beating Republican opponent Ronald C. Russell by a wide margin.
With 87% of votes counted, the Associated Press said this morning that the 71-year-old North Haven resident won over 66.8% of 1st district voters, compared to 33.2% who went for Russell.
As of Wednesday morning, the count was 225,811 for Pingree and 112,208 for Russell.
For Russell, a Fort Fairfield native and Kennebunkport resident, was new to politics. The defense contractor served 30 years in the U.S. Army.
Working people ahead of powerful interests
Pingree was elected to Congress from Maine’s 1st District in 2008; the first woman to win in the traditionally progressive southern and coastal region of the state, which stretches from Kittery to Waterville and includes the islands east of Rockland.
In her acceptance speech last night, Pingree said her win reflected the widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration and Republican policies, “that have made everyday life more expensive, brought fear and chaos into our communities, threatened our democracy, and damaged relationships with our allies.”
She said voters want leaders who listen, solve problems, “and put working people ahead of powerful interests.”
“My priorities remain clear: bringing down costs, protecting health care and fundamental freedoms, confronting the climate crisis, and defending our democracy. I will work with anyone ready to deliver for Maine,” Pingree said, “and I will fight to hold this administration accountable for its abuses of power.”
2nd District undecided
The winner of Maine’s largely rural 2nd District is expected to hinge on the results of ranked choice voting, and is not predicted to be immediately finalized.
With 85% of votes counted, Democratic state auditor Matt Dunlap has captured 50.1% of the tally, while former two-term Republican governor Paul LePage holds 49.9% of the 296,359 votes currently tallied.
Dunlap’s lead, while small, is still somewhat surprising. Despite his years of experience in Maine government — in addition to his role as state auditor, he served multiple terms as secretary of state and four terms in the Legislature — the Old Town resident has relatively little name recognition.
The Trump factor is likely in play for LePage, who has long aligned himself with the unpopular president.
Trump won the district in 2024, along with its one electoral vote. U.S. Rep. Jared Golden, a Democrat, did not run for reelection.

title: 2 incumbents, 1 newcomer elected to Old Town City Council
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
One new councilor will join the Old Town City Council, and two incumbents will keep their seats.
Linda McLeod, Katrina Wynn and Scott Wilcox were elected to the Old Town City Council Tuesday, beating out Robin Cacace and John Dieffenbacher-Krall.
McLeod and Wynn were the only incumbents in the race.
McLeod received the most votes with 1,803. Wilcox had the second most votes with 1,687. Wynn received 1,623.
Dieffenbacher-Krall and Cacace received 1,217 and 1,540 votes, respectively.
The electees will join a City Council that has been faced with decisions about how to calm rising taxes and whether city positions should be cut. Before election night, the candidates said they were eager to find ways for Old Town to reshape its identity years after the Nine Dragons paper mill closed in 2023.
Candidates pointed to an array of priorities when talking about how they see the future of the city.
McLeod previously said her main priority is bringing in new businesses to Old Town. During her time on council, McLeod has supported a six-month ban on data centers and another ban on automatic license plate readers.
Wynn, who has served on the council for a year and a half, said she wants to bring forward more initiatives to the council. She’s focused on keeping the city affordable for residents and completing projects like adding more accessible sidewalks and removing library late fees.
“I think the biggest issue is we’re a mill town without a mill. We have services built on mill money and no mill,” Wynn said last month.
Wilcox, the former Old Town public safety director, is returning to public service in the city. He currently serves as the CEO of the Old Town-Orono YMCA, and said he wants to work with local businesses to see how the council could bring in other stores.
“I think maybe it’s time that we re-identify ourselves not as a mill community any longer, but try to find something else to go there or work with [ND Paper] to do something different,” he said.

title: McDonald’s US sales fall as more customers struggle with the high cost of living
text:
(AP) - McDonald’s plans to introduce new value-oriented meal bundles early next year after a disappointing third quarter that saw lower traffic at U.S. restaurants.
McDonald’s Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski said Wednesday that the company recently began an eight-week test of mix-and-match and fixed-price bundles at 1,900 U.S. restaurants. Those bundles might feature a McChicken sandwich and small fries for $3.50, for example.
But around 4,000 franchisees have decided not to wait for the test results and have launched meal bundles of their own, he said.
“Customers should see a clear and compelling value proposition every time they consider McDonald’s, whether they’re looking for an affordable individual item, a complete meal or a digital offer in the mobile app,” Kempczinski said during a conference call with investors.
U.S. same-store sales – or sales at locations open at least a year — fell 0.2% in the July-September period, the Chicago burger giant said Wednesday. While that was not as bad as the 0.5% drop Wall Street had expected, it was the first retreat for McDonald’s since early 2025.
McDonald’s restored some regional and national in-app deals and shifted some marketing spending to support value meals, which helped push same-store sales into positive territory in September and October. But the shift in focus at McDonald’s shows how challenging the economic environment has become for U.S. fast food companies, which are losing customers as many Americans struggle with higher gas prices and the uncomfortably high cost of living.
Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant.
McDonald’s has been tweaking its U.S. value offerings for more than two years to try to lure back lower-income customers and better compete with rivals like Taco Bell, which offers a menu of 10 items that each cost $3 or less.
In June 2024, McDonald’s introduced a $5 Meal Deal. The next year, it debuted its McValue menu and Extra Value Meals, which promise a 15% discount for a bundled meal compared to buying items individually. In April, it revamped the McValue menu, adding 10 items that cost $3 or less.
But not all of McDonald’s franchisees — who own 95% of the company’s U.S. restaurants — have been on board. Kempczinski said in August that only 60% of its U.S. restaurants were offering the revamped McValue menu. McDonald’s replaced its U.S. president that same month.
Kempczinski said the company’s previous efforts haven’t been enough because they didn’t offer compelling low-end deals.
“You need to have good entry-level value, particularly with the low-income consumer,” he said.
Globally, same-store sales rose 1.3% in the third quarter. Strong sales in Germany and Australia helped offset weakness in France, which was rocked by protests that began in September.
Revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion for the quarter, short of Wall Street expectations of $7.28 billion.
Net income rose 9% to $2.49 billion. Adjusted for one-time items, the company earned $3.57 per share. That beat analysts’ forecast for a $3.38 per-share profit.
Shares rose more than 5% in morning trading Wednesday.

title: Bath-area voters elect 2 school board members
text:
Bath-area voters on Tuesday elected Woolwich resident Jamie Dorr to the Regional School Unit 1 board, as well as several candidates in uncontested races.
Dorr beat opponent Jennifer Ritch-Smith, 4,063-2,487, with votes from across the district’s four towns: Bath, Arrowsic, Woolwich and Phippsburg. Voters also elected Melissa Martin, who was unopposed, to the Bath seat on the school board.
Bath voters confirmed the election of four unopposed City Council candidates.
For Town Council, they selected Stefanie Veneziano, a newcomer to local politics, for an open at-large seat. Chris Marks was reelected to his post as Ward 1 councilor, as was vice chairperson and Ward 6 Councilor Caitlin McCorkle. Another newcomer, Miles Burleson-Lesser, also ran uncontested and was elected to the Ward 3 seat.
In their responses to the Press Herald Voter Guide, Bath’s council candidates identified affordability and housing as top issues.

title: Vote-scanning malfunction expected to delay vote counting in competitive congressional district until Wednesday
text:
(AP) - A judge has granted permission for elections officials in a major New York county to move thousands of paper ballots to a secure warehouse after a technical problem caused vote-scanning machines to malfunction.
The issue will delay the counting of votes in a competitive congressional district until at least Wednesday.
The New York Board of Elections said machines at locations throughout Westchester County would not accept paper ballots when polls opened Tuesday because of a programming glitch.
Elections officials said the problem happened when they made a software update for one municipal contest after the machines had been prepared and tested. Machines in the other municipalities continued to use the original software and therefore would not recognize the ballots.
Voters were instructed to put completed ballots in bags that would be safeguarded to be processed later. The bags were to be transported under police escort to a county warehouse to be scanned and counted under the supervision of representatives of political parties, election officials said.
The Westchester County Board of Elections said the ballot counting was to begin at 11 a.m. Wednesday.
Westchester County is considered the more liberal-leaning part of New York’s 17th Congressional District, which featured a competitive race between GOP Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley.
Lawler and Conley implored residents to cast their ballots despite the problem and stressed that all votes would be counted.
Lawler said the situation had caused “a lot of frustration, delays, lines and a lot of questions.” But he added at a news conference: “I want to be clear. There’s no shenanigans going on here.”
Despite the delayed counting, Lawler conceded defeat late Tuesday. The Associated Press had not called the race as of early Wednesday.
“When all of the votes are counted tomorrow in Westchester, it’s going to be pretty clear that we will be short,” he said.
Westchester resident Toni Chrystal said she felt “uneasy” after casting her vote Tuesday morning amid the ballot issues.
The real estate broker from White Plains said she completed her ballot around 7 a.m. and then dropped it into one of the designated ballot bags at her polling location as instructed.
“Westchester is one of the richest counties in the state. How does this happen?” she said. “How come they weren’t tested yesterday or a week before? Early voting worked. How does it not work now?”
___
Associated Press writers Anthony Izaguirre and Michael R. Sisak contributed to this report.

title: Freeport voters reject launch of landlocked ship
text:
Freeport residents denied a ballot measure aimed at launching a ship that has been stranded in a Freeport neighborhood for decades.
Voters also filled three Town Council seats Tuesday and elected two to the Regional School Unit 5 board.
According to unofficial vote counts from Tuesday’s election, 3,025 residents voted against the ship launching referendum, while 2,405 voted for it.
The referendum asked residents if they approved a temporary boat launch in the zoning district containing 0 Shore Drive, the planned site to launch the Island Rover, and exempts such launches from certain town environmental and zoning requirements.
Harold Arndt started building the Island Rover more than 30 years ago using scrap materials he got through his job at Bath Iron Works. His dream was to take a group of college students on a trip to the Arctic while showing them creative ways to reuse materials.
But that didn’t happen. Arndt, now in his 80s, and his business partner have been in legal battles with the town and disputes with neighbors for years.
Supporters of launching the 90-foot schooner in September gathered enough signatures to get the issue on the ballot. The same group failed to get the Island Rover on the ballot during the June primaries.
LOCAL ELECTIONS
On the Town Council, two district seats and one at-large seat were up for grabs on Election Day.
Joanna Benoit, the council chairperson, was reelected to her at-large post. Benoit ran unopposed. In District 3, Matthew Pillsbury was the lone candidate and was reelected to his seat.
James DeGrandpre won the only contested seat on the council, for District 2. DeGrandpre received 875 votes while Steve Doran trailed with 319.
Voters also confirmed two uncontested candidates to the local school district board, which covers Freeport, Pownal and Durham. They are Anna Child and Anthony McElligott.

title: Pastor Adam Hamilton ousts GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, Democrats' 1st Senate win in Kansas in 94 years
text:
Pastor Adam Hamilton ousts GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, Democrats' 1st Senate win in Kansas in 94 years
Adam Hamilton, a Democrat and Methodist megachurch pastor, won a startling upset in Kansas over Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, flipping a seat once believed to be safely red in another example of how far unhappiness with President Donald Trump has spread throughout the nation.
Hamilton's victory was historic for snapping a 94-year losing streak in Senate races for Kansas Democrats — the nation's longest — and because spending on the campaign was around $110 million, easily a record in low-cost Kansas. Republicans attempted a massive rescue effort for Marshall, including two Trump rallies in the state in October, but weren't able to save his attempt at a second term.
Hamilton won by appealing to moderate Republicans and independent voters who were frustrated with the rising cost of living and unhappy with Trump's handling of the economy and the war with Iran. He also promised to combat the intense partisanship in Washington.
His fundraising far outstripped Marshall's — particularly when it came to contributions from Kansas residents — and Democratic groups poured tens of millions of dollars into the state. It helped the party overcome efforts by Trump and Vice President JD Vance to animate Trump's political base with rallies down the stretch in Kansas.
Hamilton is the founding pastor of the 25,000-member Church of the Resurrection in the Kansas City area, the nation's largest United Methodist congregation. He brought to the race a centrist persona, a knack for fundraising and a public profile as the author of several dozen books.
Democrats flip a longtime GOP Senate seat in Kansas
Marshall, a retired obstetrician, was elected to the House in 2017 and won his Senate seat in 2020. He remained loyal to Trump throughout the campaign, defending both the war and Trump's tariffs.
Trump had rallies for Marshall on Oct. 19 and Oct. 31, while Vance headlined a rally for Marshall in September and returned Oct. 26.
Republicans spent the final few weeks of the campaign pounding home a traditionally winning message for them: that voting for the Democratic nominee would put liberal Democrats in charge of the Senate. While visiting Topeka, Vance called Hamilton "Chuck Schumer's stooge," though Hamilton said repeatedly that he would not support keeping the New York senator as Democratic leader.
Republicans committed $45 million to television and digital ads in the race, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, but Democrats poured in $65 million.
With only a nominal primary challenge, Marshall's campaign didn't start its ads until late August and his fundraising lagged. Republicans, worried about the national attention that Hamilton was drawing, shifted millions of dollars from North Carolina to Kansas. Democrats continued to invest in the race, spending more than $27 million on television and digital ads in the second half of October alone, according to AdImpact.
Echoing Trump, Marshall blamed high fuel prices on Ukrainian attacks on Russian infrastructure in their war. He repeatedly told voters that the economy was strong and has improved under Trump.
He also faced attacks alleging he had abandoned Kansas to live in Florida. Marshall said he owned a vacation home in Florida so he could spend time with family. Marshall sold the property last month.
Hamilton's victory bucked decades of Kansas history
The last Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas was George McGill, a Wichita attorney, in 1932. There hadn't even been a truly close race since 1974, when future Republican icon Bob Dole won a second term by less than 2 percentage points following the Watergate scandal that forced President Richard Nixon from office.
Republicans portrayed Hamilton as too "woke" for Kansas, in part by highlighting his church's support for LGBTQ rights. In the campaign's final weeks, they also focused on two cases of alleged sexual abuse of teenage boys by an adult leader at annual camps for Hamilton's church, one each in 2005 and 2006.
The church investigated the first incident in 2005 but did not report it to law enforcement when the victims couldn't positively identify the perpetrator, and the man returned for the 2006 camp. The second incident was reported to law enforcement and the church turned over its records on the first case, but the local prosecutor did not pursue criminal charges.
The church changed its child protection policies and since the 2005 case has required all incidents to be reported to law enforcement. Hamilton acknowledged that it was a mistake for the church not to report the first incident in 2005 and for him to not personally check to see that the man didn't return in 2006.
However, along with Trump's drop in popularity nationally, Hamilton benefitted from a recent shift in Kansas politics.
Although the state is often viewed as ruby red, there's a sizable bloc of moderate voters who have regularly swung governor's races to Democrats. Suburbs near Kansas City, Missouri, have become increasingly blue, making it easier for Democrats to win statewide races by carrying just the most populous counties.
Hamilton positioned himself in the political center
Hamilton's comments about Schumer demonstrated the balance he sought to strike in wooing independent and Republican voters. He made a point of describing himself as "independent-minded" and positioned himself as a potential moderate counterweight in Washington.
In another example, he criticized U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement during an event in Topeka but stopped short of calling to abolish the agency.
"They were formed to make sure that people didn't fly airplanes into buildings again," he said, referencing the Sept. 11 terror attacks. "If they stick to what they were created for, I'm grateful for them."
His campaign also hammered Marshall — who uses "Doc" on his stationery — over questions about how he pursued unpaid patient bills before he won a U.S. House seat in 2016.
The New York Times reported that Marshall and his practice sued more than 700 patients during his decades-long medical career. In 81 cases, patients were arrested for missing court dates, and two experts called his tactics extreme, according to the report. During a televised debate, Marshall called attacks on him a "gross mischaracterization" of his professional record.

title: Judge signals lower bail for Milford man accused of manslaughter in toddler’s death
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A Milford man charged with manslaughter in the hypothermia death of his 13-month-old daughter returned to court on Wednesday as his defense pushed for reduced bail.
Shane McLaughlin, 37, faces manslaughter and child endangerment charges in connection with the December death of his daughter, Eleanora Ray McLaughlin. Defense attorneys asked the judge to lower his current $250,000 cash bail and allow him to be released under court-ordered conditions.
Defense Calls State Caseworker
During the hearing, the defense called a caseworker from the Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS), who testified that she was unaware of any prior open cases involving McLaughlin before Eleanora’s death.
However, previous reporting revealed that DHHS had closed an investigation involving McLaughlin’s twin daughters just six days before Eleanora died. Prosecutors questioned the caseworker in court over why no investigation into the two prior cases were pursued.
The caseworker also highlighted McLaughlin’s progress in reunification efforts following his daughter’s death, testifying that his compliance had advanced to unsupervised visits with his surviving children.
Judge Signals Reduced Bail
While the judge did not issue a final ruling on the bail request, they indicated plans to lower the amount. The judge stated that McLaughlin did not intend for Eleanora to die and noted there are no active concerns regarding potential evidence tampering.
A final decision on McLaughlin’s bail conditions is expected at a later date however he remains in Penobscot County Jail on $250,000 bail.

title: Letter: Federal ban on hemp products will harm Mainers
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I’ve been growing plants for as long as I can remember. I started growing medical cannabis in 2010 and began growing hemp in 2023. Today I run Mantis Medicinals, my CBD company, on my farm in Montville, where we make tinctures, salves, teas and body oils from plants we grow ourselves. We were the first woman-owned farm in Maine to earn MOFGA’s Clean Cannabis Certification.
On Dec. 11, a federal ban will take effect that would make most of what we produce illegal. For a small, woman-owned business like mine, that would be devastating.
I think about the customers who’ve written to us. A woman going through chemotherapy who takes our tincture before every treatment and told us it’s eased her side effects. A man who lost his leg years ago and said our salve was the first thing that helped. A neighbor who hadn’t slept well in years until she tried our sleep oil. They found us because they wanted something clean, tested and grown by someone they could meet at the farmers market.
I support rules that keep unsafe, lab-made products off shelves. But a ban that treats a certified organic Maine farm the same as a gas station vape cartridge isn’t protecting anyone. It’s just putting small farms out of business.
Sens. Susan Collins and Angus King can help stop that before Dec. 11. I hope they’ll stand up for Maine growers and the customers who count on us.
Katrina Mascolo
Montville

title: El-Sayed tells AP Michigan rejected ‘hateful, spiteful campaign’ after months of Republican attacks
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed told The Associated Press on Wednesday that Michigan voters had rejected “a hateful, spiteful campaign” after months of Republican attacks on his Muslim identity in one of the nation’s most closely watched Senate races.
El-Sayed said he was “running on adrenaline and caffeine” after his race with Republican Mike Rogers was called early Wednesday, giving Democrats another significant victory in a premier swing state as they won a substantial majority in the Senate in Tuesday’s midterms.
Throughout the cycle, Republicans sought to demonize El-Sayed, who was born in the U.S. after his parents immigrated from Egypt. President Donald Trump repeatedly called him a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists.”
“Michigan proved just how big we are. Rejected a hateful, spiteful campaign that had nothing to say about the issues and only wanted to point to my name and my face,” El-Sayed said. “Michiganders rejected that. Every single county, every single one, pushed against that.”
In a sign of how combative the race had become, Rogers and El-Sayed had not spoken as of Wednesday afternoon, even after Rogers issued a statement conceding the race. In 2024, Rogers called then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin to concede on Wednesday morning, before the AP had even called the race.
El-Sayed, who will become the nation’s first Muslim senator, told the AP by phone that the morning was “a moment of reflection,” including about what his victory would mean to his two young daughters. His 3-year-old, he said, has no idea what happened, while his 8-year-old understands but sees it as normal.
“Now, this is something they read about in the history books,” he said.
With approximately 97% of the vote in, El-Sayed held a 7 percentage point lead over Rogers. Every county in the state shifted toward Democrats compared with 2024, according to AP voting data.
The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of more than 4,500 voters in Michigan, showed that Michigan Senate voters were roughly split on whether El-Sayed’s views were “too extreme,” with about half saying they were.
El-Sayed rose from a double-digit defeat eight years ago in the state’s Democratic gubernatorial election to an upset victory of an establishment-backed candidate in the primary after being outspent by tens of millions. He said his campaign proved that “old-fashioned politics can work if you’re willing to do the work.”
El-Sayed quickly pivoted, though, toward the future, saying his victory is “not the success” and that “the success is what you’re able to do with the seat.”
He would not commit to supporting Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer for another term, saying he did not yet know who else might run. Schumer is expected to retain the leadership position.
“I do believe we need new leadership and I think people are hungry for it,” El-Sayed added.
___
Associated Press reporter Linley Sanders contributed.

title: The fire and the bridge
text:
by Danny W. Howard
I remember – it seems that I start all or most of my stories with “I remember”. I wonder why that is?
Well, anyway, I do remember a time, in what I call my middle years – assuming I live well into my 90s – yes, that’s about right.
At the time I was on the Maine Forest Fire Fighting Crew – and we were called out to a fire way up north – I’ll let you guess who sat in the middle back seat, just over the transmission.
It would have been a pleasurable ride – had the driver of the truck not gone out of his way, it seems, to hit every bump and pothole in the road, plus the fact that we were on the road for three hours before we stopped for a break.
We drove into Ashland, and I thought, “What a great place for a forest fire.” – Ash…land, get it?
We got out of the trucks and did our stretches, one of the guys made a funny noise with his joints, but then again, he was in his “middle” years.
I, after a while, looked up to the sky for some signs of smoke, thinking we were somewhere nearer the fire than we were three hours ago. I was told, as were alltold that we had about 70 miles to go, as the crow flies. I didn’t see any crows.
While we were resting, I told one of the drivers that if it became necessary, the only way to get to the fire was to repel from a helicopter. I would probably do it, but there would be a very long “communication” before I actually did it.
We got back in our trucks to continue our journey down that dirt road, well, gravel road, dusty road. We were going right along when this van passed us like we were parked by the side of the road. It looked more like a bus than a van for all the people in it. “They are certainly in a hurry,” I remarked.
“They are tree trimmers from Nicaragua and Honduras, and they have a long way to go to get to work,” we were told.
“Nicaragua and Honduras,” I said, “no wonder they’re in a hurry, coming from Nicaragua and Honduras, what a commute!”
It took a while for the eye rolling to settle down.
We soon came to a long low bridge. It’s deck was made of wooden planks, with runner planks running across where the truck tires rode. I-beams served as guard rails and I could only imagine what lay beneath to support the great weight it was built for. This was John’s Bridge.
We soon pulled off the main gravel road onto another dirt road and then another dirt road. This one had bushes growing down the middle. By the time we came to where the trees were growing in the road we stopped. The Forest Service had cut a trail into the woods, up hill, always up hill, to the fire site. Now, about this time, it started to rain,well, not a rain, more like real heavy mist that did nothing. It seemed to help in putting down the fire, but it did do a great job soaking our uniforms.
Soon it got dark and we made our way back, always up hill, to the trucks, drove back to John’s Bridge where we cleaned up. Some actually went swimming in the very cold waters of the Allagash River on the night of September 10, 2002.
We then proceeded to the ranger’s cabin where they had set up a 12-man tent beside a very nice log cabin, and sat down to a very large spaghetti meal. I’ve always said, “They feed you well on the fire crew.”
While I was eating I remarked at what a nice cabin this was, as forest ranger’s cabins go.
“Well, we think a bear broke into the cabin that was here before and tripped over the stove, setting the cabin on fire, as we found a badly burned bear in the ashes.”
After eating we went back to the tent where there were 12 Army cots set up with those one time use disposable paper sleeping bags that were surprisingly warm and comfortable. We could have had a good night’s sleep had the temperature not been hovering around 40°. The two pickup trucks, which were outside the tent, were kept running all night with their heaters full blast trying to dry out our uniforms. And let’s not forget the generator on the other side of the tent that kept the lights on in the cabin.
We woke up the next morning, assuming of course that some of us actually slept that night to a breakfast of scrambled eggs, bacon, sausage, toast and the all important coffee. As I said, they feed you well on the fire crew.
We made our way back to the fire site by way of the bridge where we stopped to pick up some litter that we missed when we stopped the night before. The ranger was very concerned about litter in the water way.
We then went back to the fire site where we went about putting out the fire, digging up hot spots laying hoses. When we got the news about the tragedy that had happened at John’s Bridge, it seemed right after we left the area that the van that has passed us the day before had gone off the bridge and into the water, killing all but one. There were 15 men in the van.
The day had become quiet.
We went about our job of putting down the fire and picking up the hoses and tools. We had to go back to the cabin to pick up that area, too. We were told not to go by way of John’s Bridge, so we went cross county where the road seemed to disappear into the forest. I thought, “Gee, I hope the driver doesn’t have a heart attack or we’ll never get out of here.”
We, somehow, made it back to the cabin where we picked up the site, getting ready to leave, and since we didn’t know the area, we made out way toward John’s Bridge, for we knew the way from there.
We were about a mile from the bridge when we noticed cars and trucks parked on both sides of the road. There were three float planes in the river along with three boats, a flatbed truck and a crane. The only thing we didn’t see were any ambulances.
They brought the van, which was upside down, on the flatbed truck. They had covered the van with a canvas, but not enough to hide what lay beneath.
We continued across the bridge where there were three loaded pulp trucks. They were there all day.
We continued up the road with cars and trucks lined both sides of the road for about a mile. This was some eight hours after the accident, and they were still coming in.
I noticed that one of the helicopters seemed to follow us in the sky, as if to remind us of the events of that day, so that day might not be forgotten.
I think it worked.
Responsible journalism is hard work!
It is also expensive!

title: How Troy Jackson beat the odds to defeat Susan Collins
text:
For decades, Susan Collins seemed invincible.
The incumbent Republican had beaten the odds before. In the final weeks of her last race in 2020, polls showed Democrat Sara Gideon with a substantial lead over Maine’s senior senator. Despite those predictions and a Democratic surge that swept Donald Trump out of the presidency, Collins came out on top by nearly 10 points.
This year’s midterms initially looked remarkably similar. The last polls before Election Day showed her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, with a lead similar to Gideon’s. Collins, bolstered by tens of millions of dollars’ worth of outside spending, seemed well positioned to buck the challenge again. Even Jackson supporters predicted she would hold on to her seat, one poll showed.
But unlike 2020, Collins couldn’t defy this year’s “blue-nami,” as some pollsters have called it.
Jackson cruised to a more comfortable victory than many expected. He flipped numerous towns Collins carried in 2020. He narrowed Collins’ margins in Republican strongholds across the state. And he amplified turnout in Democratic areas along the coast.
By Wednesday afternoon, with just over 90% of ballots counted, it all culminated in a roughly seven-point lead for Jackson and a stunning defeat for a Maine institution.
With only 101 days to pick up the pieces following Graham Platner’s exit from the race in July, many thought it improbable for Jackson to organize a winning campaign.
“I don’t know that anyone, including myself, would have thought this was possible,” Jackson said in his victory speech early Wednesday morning.
But buoyed by a small army of organizers, national party infrastructure and growing resentment against Trump, Jackson pulled it off.
Here’s how he did it.
A SEISMIC SHIFT TO THE LEFT
Collins’ electoral strategy always ran through Maine’s reliably Republican rural communities. She won wide swaths of northern, Down East and western Maine by sizable margins in 2020. Holding on to those small towns was crucial to her reelection chances this year.
Early Tuesday night, it was evident that wouldn’t pan out.
Maine’s small, rural towns were among the first to report their totals. Collins still won most of them, but by much smaller margins than in 2020.
The Oxford County town of Hiram went to Collins by a margin of nearly 30 points in her last election. This year, she won it by about 13. Collins carried Rome, in Kennebec County, by 22 points in 2020 but only won it by two this year.
As the night wore on, Jackson began picking up towns that Collins won in 2020. The Penobscot County town of Veazie went to Collins by 13 points in 2020, but Jackson won it by about six this year. Lubec, in Down East Maine, voted for Collins by 15 points in the last cycle before swinging about 17 points toward the Democrat this year.
Still, Collins was performing well compared to Republicans in other states. While stunning GOP defeats in South Carolina, Texas and elsewhere were called early in the night, Maine’s race remained close.
But by midnight on Tuesday, it was evident Collins was on the ropes. The death knell for her campaign arrived when results in the twin cities of Lewiston and Auburn came in.
Collins had won both cities in 2020, by two and eight points respectively. Jackson carried them both this year: Lewiston by nearly eight points and Auburn by about five.
As large, Democratic-leaning southern communities like Biddeford, Brunswick and Portland began reporting results, Jackson’s lead continued to grow. Late in the evening, The New York Times’ election needle gave Jackson a 95% chance of winning.
By 12:30 a.m. Wednesday, Collins had called Jackson to concede the race.
A TALE OF TWO MAINES
Though both Jackson and Collins hail from the northern reaches of Aroostook County, the race was ultimately a tale of two Maines: The smaller, rural communities that lean right and the larger coastal cities that swing left.
Collins’ campaign focused heavily on the value she brought to those smaller towns. In the days leading up to the election, Collins toured several infrastructure projects in rural communities she secured funding for through her role as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
That was Collins’ pitch throughout most of the race: She held a powerful role in Washington, D.C., and she used it to send money Maine’s way.
“I’m the first Maine senator in nearly a century to chair the Appropriations Committee, and I’ve been able to bring $1.5 billion to Maine to support projects just like this one,” Collins said last week while touting new police communications equipment in Winthrop.
Jackson, however, focused on pitching himself as a change agent capable of shaking up politics on a grand scale. He galvanized growing anger with Trump and his administration over the rising cost of living, the war in Iran and perceived corruption among federal officials
His campaign sought to use that energy to run up the score in Maine’s bluest cities. It worked.
Portland, Maine’s largest and most reliably Democratic city, swung hard for Jackson. Gideon, Collins’ 2020 opponent, won the city by 47 points. This year, Jackson carried it by nearly 70.
That trend presented itself in many of Maine’s Democratic strongholds: Jackson won Brunswick by more than 45 points after Gideon carried it by only 25. Bar Harbor voted for Gideon by 35 points and Jackson by more than 50.
During his victory speech in the early hours of Wednesday morning, Jackson acknowledged those swings weren’t just about him. Voters were angry with the country’s direction. And he said he aims to channel that anger into action.
“I’ve known from the start that this wasn’t about Troy Jackson,” he said. “It was about changing the world that we know is wrong, and making life better for all of us.”

title: Democrat Peggy Flanagan wins election to US Senate from Minnesota
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Democrat Peggy Flanagan won election Wednesday to the U.S. Senate representing Minnesota, defeating Republican Michele Tafoya.
Flanagan’s win held a seat for Democrats that the party could not afford to lose as it tried to flip Senate control in Washington.
The current lieutenant governor, Flanagan, who is a member of the Ojibwe Native American tribe, will succeed Sen. Tina Smith, a Democrat who did not seek reelection.
Flanagan’s win also gives progressives a notable victory in a year where Democrats’ left flank has been ascendant.
Tafoya was making her bid for political office after gaining fame as a sideline reporter on NFL football broadcasts.
The Associated Press declared Flanagan the winner at 12:07 a.m. EST.
