title: South Portland rejects public safety referendum, elects City Council and School Board members
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
South Portland residents voted down an $86.6 million public safety overhaul, 8,568 to 5,002.
They also reelected Elyse Tipton and Carter Scott to the City Council. Newcomer Ellen Clancy, who ran unopposed, will represent District 2.
Stephanie Edwards and Eleni Richardson were elected as at-large representatives to the School Board, and Carlton Parsons, who ran unopposed, will represent District 5.
The proposed bond would have provided up to $44.35 million for a new police station to be built on the vacant Walgreens parcel at Cash Corner that the city acquired this year. It would also have allocated $44.25 million for a new central fire station to be built on the footprint of the existing central police and fire station.
The police station, built in 1967, and the fire station, built in 1955, do not meet current codes and have significant mechanical, electrical and plumbing issues. The HVAC systems are past their lifespan, and the evidence room and emergency operation center in the basement regularly flood.
Police Chief Dan Ahern and Fire Chief Phil Selberg have both said the current stations don’t meet modern public safety needs and standards, and their departments are in desperate need of new homes.
Many residents said that the tax impact of a new police and fire station would be too great at a time when they are feeling increasingly pinched by rising costs, including some associated with overdue municipal infrastructure updates.
A median-priced single-family home valued at $514,000 would have been expected to pay an additional $255 in property taxes for fiscal year 2028. By the second phase, property taxes for that household would have increased an additional $244, making the total estimated tax impact about $500 for fiscal year 2030.
The average annual tax impact for the duration of the bond — from fiscal year 2028 through 2059 — would have been about $345, or $28 per month.
Some residents have said they’re struggling to afford living in South Portland without the extra tax burden.
The average resident’s monthly sewer bill is estimated to increase by $9.30 in fiscal year 2027, $11.72 in 2028 and $14.76 in 2029 to fund a new pump station and other wastewater infrastructure improvements as well as the typical operating increases, according to a presentation in March.

title: 'A little bit homeless': Nicolas Cage says a sinkhole swallowed his Malibu home
text:
'A little bit homeless': Nicolas Cage says a sinkhole swallowed his home
Actor Nicolas Cage has said he's "currently a little bit homeless" due to a sinkhole that has opened up under part of his Malibu home.
The Academy Award winner opened up about his current living situation while on a Los Angeles Comic Con panel over Halloween weekend.
"Something happened in my house in Malibu. So, I'm just sort of living in hotels, so I don't have the normal trick-or-treaters I would like to enjoy tonight," the "Face/Off" actor said, according to video recorded by a fan.
Cage is referring to a large sinkhole that opened up in the front part of his Southern California property in September. Authorities are investigating what caused the sinkhole to open, and city officials said it also caused a gas leak.
In an emergency proclamation, the city of Malibu said the sinkhole began forming on Sept. 7 and fully opened up on Sept. 8. The sinkhole measures about 25 to 30 feet deep and 30 by 60 feet wide.
Twenty-four homes in Cage's neighborhood were "red-tagged" due to the loss of "safe vehicular access," and seven homes were tagged due to hazardous conditions.
The city said repairs on the sinkhole are expected to be completed within five weeks, "depending on conditions."
It is not clear how long Cage has been out of the home or when he will be able to return; however, the actor also has properties in New York City and Las Vegas.

title: These are the skin cancer warning signs you may overlook as you age
text:
(Aging Untold) — Skin cancer can appear in more ways than a changing mole.
Warning signs people may overlook
Some of the warning signs that people might overlook are having sores that don’t heal or moles that bleed easily, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Moles can change and that is something people don’t always track, Rogers said, and shared what doctors look for.
“We look at the asymmetry, how symmetric is it? Is it the border of it? Does it change? The color, the color can change. The diameter, and then evolving. Is it changing in its appearance to you?” Rogers said.
Changes matter even for spots people have had for years, gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck added.
“A millimeter can matter a lot,” Cradduck said.
She said people should track whether a mole has grown, changed its symmetry or started to bleed.
Where skin cancer can hide
While people often are told to check sun-exposed areas, Rogers said skin cancer can show up elsewhere.
“You have to look everywhere because they can hide,” Rogers said. “They can be behind your ears, between your toes, underneath the nails.”
She said a doctor’s exam or help from another person can cover places people can’t see, such as the scalp.
“They don’t always look scary,” Rogers said. “But that’s what makes them so dangerous.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke described her own experience when she went to a dermatologist about a brown spot on her cheek.
A whole body scan revealed cancer on top of her head, she said. It was squamous cell, and she had surgery.
Aging well coach Katherie Ambrose said she recently found a dermatologist, had a full body scan, and her husband had one as well.
Rogers suggested that people should check with their insurance, because some plans cover an annual dermatology exam, like a well woman exam.
Risk factors and sun damage
Around three-quarters of O’Rourke’s family has had skin cancer, she said.
Asked whether the risk is genetic or environmental, Rogers said fair skin is a risk factor, along with age and family history.
“So probably both,” she said.
In addressing sun damage, Rogers warned that UVA and UVB light are invisible and can pass through glass.
Melanoma is usually linked to intense, intermittent but deep sunburn, she said.
“It spreads very quickly,” Rogers said. “So you definitely want to pay attention.”
While melanoma presents more like a mole, squamous cell and basal cell cancers are more likely to be pinkish, itchy or sores that don’t heal, she said.
Rogers also addressed a myth: that African Americans don’t need sunscreen.
“Yes, you need sunscreen,” Rogers said.
Sunscreen protects against damage to cells and DNA, she said.
Sun protection
In addition to sunscreen, sun-protective clothing is also available, the hosts said, including rash guards, sun guards, UV clothing and wide-brimmed hats.
Key takeaways
- Skin cancer can show up in unexpected places, including the scalp, ears or under the nails.
- Watch for warning signs, including sores that will not heal or shiny bumps on the skin.
- During your annual dermatology visit, request a full body exam and ask about mole mapping to track changes over time.

title: A woman was arrested for blocking a delivery robot. She says she’ll do it again
text:
A woman was arrested for blocking a delivery robot. She says she’ll do it again
Oct. 14 wasn’t the first time Carolyn Marvin put herself in front of an autonomous delivery robot. It had become, since the wheeled little food vessels were unleashed upon certain parts of Philadelphia, a habit for the 78-year-old: standing in front of one of the robots when she encountered it rolling on the sidewalk, delaying it for a few minutes from delivering its precious lunchtime cargo.
Video above: Carolyn Marvin explains her delivery robot protest
But it was the first time that Marvin, a retired University of Pennsylvania communications professor, was arrested for doing it — in a case that she says raises profound questions about public space and the legal protections extended to robots in our increasingly tech-dominated world.
“I was under the impression that I had more rights than the robot did,” Marvin said, laughing.
Uber Eats launched its self-driving robot delivery fleet in Philly in March, making it the fourth city where meals can be delivered via robot. Not everyone welcomed the heart-eyed little machines: In Philadelphia and elsewhere, videos show people sitting on, vandalizing or kicking the robots.
Marvin says the impact of her one-woman protest is limited. “I have a life, so I don’t have tons of time to stand in front of robots,” she said. If she comes across a robot, and it’s “convenient and possible” for her, she might spend 10 or 15 minutes blocking it, moving as it does, to delay it on its journey.
The only harm that comes from her hobby is that an office worker’s lunchtime bowl “might be delayed for about 15 minutes at the most,” she said.
She views her actions as a symbolic protest against the problems posed by delivery robots: the displacement of low-income delivery workers; the physical hazard the robots pose on the sidewalk; and the privacy concerns posed by the robots’ embedded cameras.
“I also think that I have a First Amendment right to protest the abuses of corporations in public space, in the same public space that the robots are occupying,” she said. In the past, she had protested in favor of civil rights, abortion rights, Black Lives Matter, and for ending the Gulf and Vietnam wars. She views her robot mission as an extension of the same impulse: “It’s what we need to do to make sure the government hears the will of the people.”
Stopping in front of the robots, Marvin said, led to productive conversations with other passersby who asked what she was doing. Most were supportive, or curious. She never considered that she might be arrested, since, as she said, “I wasn’t impeding any persons. I was impeding a machine.”
That’s until the 14th. On the way home from getting her flu shot, Marvin, a jar of enchilada sauce in one hand and chicken biryani takeout in the other, encountered one of the robots and stopped in front of it, per usual. It was in a busy part of the city, and a larger-than-normal crowd began to gather around her. Some were supportive; some were critical. She suspects, she said, that a member of the crowd eventually called the police, who handcuffed her and put her in the back of a squad car, giving her a citation for disorderly conduct.
Marvin said one of her friends put it thusly: “Well, you got a disorderly conduct charge for impeding capitalism.”
Philadelphia police said that they had responded to a report of “criminal mischief involving a delivery robot.” When they arrived, “officers encountered a female who was refusing to allow a delivery robot to pass,” they wrote in an email. “Police issued multiple commands directing the female to move; however, she refused to comply.”
In the aftermath of her arrest, Marvin has found out more about the legal infrastructure that protects robots. In 2020, the Pennsylvania legislature passed a law that classifies autonomous delivery robots — what the law calls “personal delivery devices” — as pedestrians, not vehicles. Democrats, along with labor unions and accessibility advocates, largely opposed the law on the basis that legalizing delivery robots could kill jobs and endanger children and pedestrians; Republicans touted it as an exciting technological advancement.
The law means that a vehicle must yield to a delivery robot on crosswalks, just as it would to a person, said John Mattiacci, a Philadelphia personal injury attorney. Still, in theory humans are at the top of the hierarchy: “Personal delivery devices must yield to other pedestrians and pedalcyclists in a pedestrian area,” he said. Uber Eats didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Marvin sees the proliferation of delivery robots — and the legal protections of them — as another case of machinery and technology infiltrating everyday life. “There’s a way in which we’ve surrendered the streets to cars long ago, and I don’t think we should surrender the sidewalks to machines,” she said.
“Machines in general encroach on our lives,” she went on. “Public space is the most visible place where they’re encroaching on our lives, but they’re going right up the ladder, and lots of people are interested in making that happen.”
Most of the technology people encounter day to day is less tangible: the overwhelming adoption of AI, the mysterious social media algorithms that determine the images and narratives the public consumes. The robots, on the other hand, are a clear and visible symbol of the tech takeover, an easy target for anti-tech rage. Her protest, she said, “makes it visible to people and presents the issue in a way that it might not otherwise be presented.”
Asked if she plans to get back to blocking robots post-arrest, Marvin was succinct: “Oh yeah.” But now she’ll keep an eye out for the cops.

title: Cycling the closed gap in the Eastern Trail through Scarborough and South Portland
text:
I’ve been biking the Eastern Trail for about 20 years. In the past, I occasionally rode north from the Black Point Road trailhead in Scarborough. After a couple of miles, the ride culminated in disappointment when the trail ended at the remains of an old railroad bridge over the Nonesuch River.
Over the years, I heard rumors there was a plan to connect the Scarborough section of the Eastern Trail with the northernmost sector in South Portland, a missing link called “the gap.” I looked forward to that eventuality and the opportunity to finish the entire trail.
When I recently watched a news report that the major effort to “Close the Gap” had been completed, I was intent on finishing my goal. The report stated the 1.6-mile missing trail link had been constructed connecting the off-road sector in Scarborough with Wainwright Sports Complex in South Portland.
I began my outing at the small Blue Point Road trailhead in Scarborough on a partly sunny fall day with moderate northwest winds. I prefer Blue Point Road trailhead because the parking is less congested than at larger facilities.
I rode a mountain bike north on a compacted gravel surface. After a short distance, I crossed Pine Point Road and entered Scarborough Marsh. I consider the marsh to be the most scenic part of the entire Eastern Trail. A moderate headwind was a minor nuisance as I progressed over the marsh bridge and a former railroad causeway where several bird-watchers were in search of the many species that inhabit the extensive wetland. Leaving the marsh I entered wooded terrain and passed Willowdale Golf Course on the left.
Soon after, I arrived at bustling Black Point Road trailhead where there is a large parking area. Just beyond, I crossed the busy road and entered a residential neighborhood. In this area, cyclists travel over paved streets where white lines on the sides of the road separate riders from the relatively slow, light traffic. At the end of Eastern Road, the path transitions to a dirt and gravel surface in a twisting, hilly forested area.
Turning abruptly right on dirt Desfosses Avenue, I approached the Nonesuch River. The new Close the Gap section soon began. Unlike previous trips, I cruised over an impressive new bridge followed by an exquisitely designed sector of trail. Shortly after, a more substantial, steeper bridge traverses high over Amtrak Downeaster railroad tracks and the trail crosses Pleasant Hill Road immediately below.
Continuing north through a serene, relatively level section of trail, I soon passed picturesque Prouts Pond. The trail is paved along the pond and is a very pleasant, scenic ride. Departing the pond and leaving Close the Gap sector behind, I entered Wainwright Recreation Complex, a substantial array of athletic fields.
After Wainwright, the northern portion of the Eastern Trail co-named South Portland Greenbelt Walkway begins. The character of the trail changes on Greenbelt Walkway. The 5.6-mile segment is fully paved and travels through urban South Portland. The number of walkers and runners increased significantly during my ride.
Following a wooded stretch, I entered a residential and commercial area where street crossings were frequent. Traffic was very busy when I arrived at an intersection with Route 77 immediately south of thee Casco Bay Bridge. After completing a two-stage road crossing, I temporarily lost the trail. Once it was relocated, I continued east through Mill Creek Park followed by unobstructed views of Portland Harbor.
After passing through congested Ferry Village, I angled northeast and entered Bug Light Park. I followed the trail through the park and turned abruptly left at the shore of Casco Bay. Views of the many islands in the bay were spectacular as I rode a short distance on a wide trail to historic Portland Breakwater Light (nicknamed Bug Light), the northern terminus of the Eastern Trail. I stopped for a respite while watching numerous runners, walkers, riders and tourists visit the iconic light.
Given my newly acquired knowledge, the return trip through South Portland was problem-free. Once out of the city, I thoroughly enjoyed my predominantly off-road ride back to Blue Point Road trailhead. I score the Close the Gap link a huge triumph.
Read about several more exceptional bike trails around the state and three rides on distant offshore coastal islands in my book “Maine Al Fresco: The Fifty Finest Outdoor Adventures in Maine.”
The author of “The Great Mars Hill Bank Robbery” and “Mountains for Mortals – New England,” Ron Chase resides in Topsham. His latest book, “Maine Al Fresco: The Fifty Finest Outdoor Adventures in Maine” is available at North Country Press and through online retailers. Visit his website at ronchaseoutdoors.com or he can be reached at [email protected].

title: John Nicks, legendary figure skating coach and champion maker, dies at 97
text:
John Nicks, a figure skating coach who shaped generations of US champions, dies at 97
Renowned figure skating coach John Nicks, who won a world pairs championship for Britain with his sister Jennifer Nicks and went on to tutor the likes of Olympic champions Peggy Fleming and Kristi Yamaguchi, died Monday. He was 97.
Related video above: Remembering those we lost in 2026
U.S. Figure Skating, which worked closely with Nicks over the course of his career, confirmed his death in a statement Tuesday.
“The skating community has lost a tremendous ambassador,” U.S. Figure Skating chief executive Matt Farrell said. “John helped shape generations of American figure skaters and his influence extended well beyond the champions he coached.”
Nicks was born on April 22, 1929, in Brighton, England, and began skating at the age of 9 in part because his father wanted to sell skating equipment at his retail store. Nicks soon paired up with his younger sister, who died of a heart attack in 1980, and the two of went on to win six British pairs titles, appear in two Winter Olympics and win four world championship medals.
It was as a coach that Nicks truly excelled, though.
He had already relocated to Canada when Sabena Flight 548 crashed near Brussels, Belgium, killing the U.S. team on its way to the 1961 world championships. After the crash, Nicks was offered several coaching positions in the U.S., ultimately accepting a job at the Iceland Arena in Paramount, California, owned by Frank Zamboni — the inventor of the ice resurfacer that carries his name.
Nicks coached more than 1,200 skaters, including world pairs champions Tai Babilonia and Randy Gardner; world pairs medalists Jenni Meno and Todd Sand; Olympic silver medalist Sasha Cohen; and Olympic bronze medalist Ashley Wagner.
“Mr. Nicks, you were a champion maker,” Wagner wrote Wednesday. “I will forever be grateful for my time with you, the lessons learned and the athlete that you transformed me into. You made me understand that I had to skate for the person sitting in the last row, at the top of the arena. You made me a performer, a skater who learned to care so much more about the total package.”
Nicks was inducted into the U.S. Figure Skating Hall of Fame in 1993 and the World Figure Skating Hall of Fame in 2000.
Along with coaching, Nicks served as the national director of the Ice Capades chalets, a nationwide organization of rinks operated by the ice show company of the same name. And in recent years, a lower-level International Skating Union event co-hosted by the Skating Club of New York and the Skating Club of Boston was titled the John Nicks Pairs Challenge in his honor.
Nicks had a son, Christopher, and daughter, Carolyn, with his first wife, Denise. He later married U.S. ice dancer Yvonne Littlefield, who won the 1962 national championship with her former husband, Peter Betts.
“(Nicks) earned the deep respect of the skating community through a lifetime of dedication to his athletes and to the sport,” Farrell said. "We are grateful for all he gave to U.S. Figure Skating, and our thoughts are with his wife, Yvonne, his son, Christopher, and the many skaters, colleagues and friends mourning his loss.”

title: Democrat Aaron Ford defeats Republican incumbent to become Nevada’s first Black governor
text:
LAS VEGAS (AP) — Nevada’s Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford has won the race for governor, ousting Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo and becoming the state’s first Black governor.
This was one of the most closely watched elections in the country, and Ford’s win marks a major victory for Democrats’ efforts to expand their control of state governments in key battlegrounds. Nevada will play a critical role in the next presidential election.
Ford has served as the state’s top prosecutor since 2019. Throughout his campaign, he described growing up in poverty and going to school hungry. He explained how he became a math teacher before earning his law degree, and highlighted efforts to fight the Trump administration.
“This campaign didn’t happen by accident,” Ford said at a Democratic watch party Tuesday. “It happened because of faith, because of family, because of hard work, and because the people of Nevada decided that our best days are still ahead of us.”
Ford focused his campaign on affordability, promising to tackle student loan debt and crack down on the development of artificial intelligence data centers. He painted his opponent as a staunch loyalist of the president and criticized Lombardo for vetoing bills that Ford said would have helped Nevadans, from restrictions on corporate homeownership to providing free school meals.
Amid voters’ concerns over the impacts of AI data centers, Ford promised to pause new tax abatements for them and oppose projects on federal land in Nevada.
He defended against attacks by the governor, a former sheriff, that tried to paint Ford as soft on crime while he was attorney general. He also deflected Lombardo’s accusations that his policy goals would be too expensive.
Ford got a boost from national Democrats who are eyeing potential 2028 presidential campaigns, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris, who came to the state to campaign for him. Trump won Nevada in 2024 with 50.6% of the vote.
The economy took center stage
During this year’s race, the governor portrayed Ford as a threat to the state’s business-friendly climate. Lombardo sought to tie him to Democrat-controlled California, claiming Ford would bring the “Newsom playbook” of high taxes and more regulations.
Democrats worked to connect Lombardo with President Donald Trump’s tariffs, saying they harmed Las Vegas tourism, which saw a 17% drop in Canadian visitors in 2025. The president has feuded with Canadian leaders, and the two countries are in the middle of a trade dispute.
Ford criticized Lombardo for vetoing legislation the Democrat said would make life more affordable, such as a bill to limit home purchases by corporate investors. Nevadans are grappling with some of the highest gas prices in the country and a shortage of tens of thousands of homes.
The race for governor cast a shadow beyond Nevada
The westernmost battleground state has a distinctive electorate that doesn’t always follow national political trends.
Democratic strength in Las Vegas is counterbalanced by heavily Republican rural areas, and the true wild cards are the nonpartisan voters who make up nearly 40% of the electorate. The steady flow of people into and out of the state, as well as the large number of working-class and Latino voters, make it difficult to predict statewide races.
Although Nevada only has six electoral college votes, both parties have Nevada as an early state in their nominating calendar.
Law enforcement backgrounds were key to the race
Both candidates faced scrutiny for how they exercised their authority in law enforcement.
Ford’s campaign criticized Lombardo after he avoided a traffic ticket in Las Vegas, interrupting the police officer to say “I’m Joe Lombardo.” Meanwhile, the governor’s campaign blasted Ford for sponsoring consideration of a clemency application for a man who killed a pregnant woman in 2017.
Lombardo secured a major boost when the Democratic district attorney for Clark County, which covers Las Vegas, endorsed the governor instead of his fellow Democrat.
The governor served in law enforcement for over 25 years before becoming sheriff of Clark County in 2014. He became well known in 2017 while overseeing the investigation into the Las Vegas mass shooting, the deadliest in modern U.S. history. Lombardo was born in Japan to a U.S. military family stationed overseas and served in the Army and the Nevada National Guard.
Ford, a former state senator, frequently spoke about experiencing poverty as a child and how his father brought home stale candy bars from the grocery store he worked at for the family’s dinner. Since being elected attorney general, he has secured millions in settlements from opioid manufacturers, and he successfully sued a student loan servicer as well as the gaming platform Roblox.

title: Susan Collins’ chief of staff speaks out about her Election Day loss
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - A 30 year run in the Senate will come to an end for Susan Collins.
She called Senate-elect Troy Jackson in the early hours of Tuesday morning to concede the race.
Later in the day WABI spoke with her Chief of Staff Steve Abbott about the outcome and how the evening played out.
Abbott said there was no question the results are a referendum on how the Republican Party has done in the past two years. He also said he was happy with the campaign the team ran.
He didn’t feel they were running against Donald Trump, but that he served as a burden.
Much of that burden coming from gas and oil.
“The one thing we didn’t have an answer for was gas prices, and oil prices. When you consider what people all across the state have been paying in October and now early November to fill up their oil tanks for the first time of the season and you look at what you pay at the pump it’s really tough. We’ve done what we can on that, but there’s not a good answer,” Abbott said.
Abbott said as the numbers rolled in, Auburn results were a bad sign early in the evening, but when the Portland numbers came in, they knew it was over.
“I thought she graciously called Troy Jackson and didn’t prolong this and hold out. She called him and congratulated him on his victory, and then our staff all met in the basement of the hotel last night after she did that. We had a great discussion with the staff and some of the volunteers that I’ve been with us forever. She spent a lot of time with us. Listen, she was disappointed, but she was proud of everything that she had done and everything the staff had done, and told us to keep our heads high, we’ve done good work, and now it’s somebody else’s turn.” said Abbott.

title: Vance blames war in Iran for Republican midterm losses: ‘If you’d like to argue it was worth it ... then do so’
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — JD Vance publicly broke from President Donald Trump ‘s defense of the Iran war Wednesday after the Republican Party’s deep losses in the midterm elections, attempting to distance himself from voters’ clear rebuke of the president as the vice president faces questions about his own political ambitions.
Vance, who has said he would decide after the election whether to run for president in 2028, issued a lengthy social media post blaming the unpopular conflict with Iran for the GOP’s drubbing. Vance said, “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.”
But arguing that the war was worth it is what Trump repeatedly did on the campaign trail, continued to do in interviews as election results came in and did again Wednesday morning. As he led reporters on an impromptu visit to the ballroom he’s constructing at the White House, Trump said, “The Iran thing, we had to do and we continue to do it.”
Trump said he spoke to Vance on Wednesday morning and, when asked about the vice president’s post, he called it “good” and said, “I know how he feels about it,” and “I think it was fine.”
The president also said he “knew the war was going to impact” the midterm elections but again defended his actions.
Vance, who had long advocated for restraint in U.S. military intervention overseas, was lukewarm in his defense of the conflict after Trump launched it and even became the face of an unsuccessful attempt to end the fighting.
Democrats plan to hold Vance accountable for the war
Democrats showed they intend to make Vance own the war.
“If Vance has felt this way all along, why didn’t he speak out forcefully?” Democratic National Committee spokeswoman Rosemary Boeglin said in a statement. “Why didn’t he resign? And most importantly, why didn’t he stand up for Americans?”
The vice president, she said, “will always do what’s most politically convenient for him in the moment — even if it means throwing Americans under the bus. Vance owns this administration’s failures.”
Democrats swept control of both the House and the Senate on Tuesday, defeating GOP candidates even in deep-red areas that Trump carried by wide margins two years ago.
“There’s no doubt this is a repudiation of the last two years,” said Marc Short, who was chief of staff to former Vice President Mike Pence and worked in Trump’s White House in his first term.
He said Vance will still have a big microphone as the sitting vice president, and the election results don’t mean he won’t be the GOP’s nominee for president in two years.
But, Short said, “It certainly doesn’t help his case, that’s for sure. I would argue it does hurt.”
When Pence was in the role, he intentionally tried not to distance himself from Trump and shared his opinions privately, Short said. But Vance’s post Wednesday seemed to be “an intentional separation” from the president despite being inherently linked to him.
“You made that bargain when you agreed to be vice president,” he said.
Vance says reason for loss is ‘obvious to almost everyone’
Vance, in his post, said that Republican voters cast their ballots for Democrats because of the war, the cost of living, America not being prioritized and the U.S. relationship with Israel — a dynamic where he’s also sounded a different note than Trump.
“The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone,” he wrote.
Unlike the president, Vance declined to endorseIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection and this summer publicly chastised members of Israel’s government for opposing Trump’s efforts to resolve the war with Iran.
Vance, who has been a staunch defender of the administration’s immigration policies, also appeared to be seeking some distance from the immigration crackdown that drew a backlash.
“I’m open to the idea that we should change enforcement — by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance,” he wrote.
But he said he rejected any politicians who might propose amnesty for people living in the country illegally.
Voters made it clear they disapproved of the Iran war
About 6 in 10 voters said the U.S. made the “wrong decision” in taking military action against Iran, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 voters in the United States. Most of those voters dissatisfied with the Iran war backed the Democratic candidate in their U.S. House race, but the survey suggested the Iran war was not the leading issue for most voters.
Only about one-third of voters said the war in Iran was “crucial” to their vote for Congress, well below the roughly half who said that about the cost of living or government corruption.
Nearly all voters who backed the Democratic candidate in their U.S. House race said going to war with Iran was the “wrong decision,” while roughly 8 in 10 voters who backed the Republican candidate said it was the “right decision.”
A former Marine who served in Iraq, Vance had been critical of that conflict and said after becoming vice president that a Trump administration would not send troops into the “open-ended conflicts” of the past.
After Trump launched the war with Iran this past spring, Vance was noticeably quiet in speaking about it, a conspicuous change for a politician known for being a pugnacious defender of the president.
This summer, he tried to argue the conflict was worth it, telling conservative podcast host Megyn Kelly in an interview that, “If we transformed the Middle East, this is fundamentally worth it.”
___
Associated Press Writer Linley Sanders in Washington contributed to this report.

title: Why at-home thermometers may differ from what we show on air
text:
Why at-home thermometers may differ from what we show on air
Current temperature readings can vary widely within the same town, especially on very warm days. The temperature displayed in your car or on your thermometer at home will typically read higher than what local meteorologists show on TV.
This is because current temperatures on our maps come from official weather stations (ASOS and AWOS stations) that meet strict standards for where the thermometer is located.
The thermometers at these weather stations are located inside a white slatted box so they are never in direct sun, and the white paint helps to reduce heat absorption. The box must be 4 feet above the ground, in an open field away from trees and buildings.
At home, your thermometer may be in direct sun, picking up heat from your house and surrounding pavement. In the city, this is especially true due to the urban heat island effect.
ASOS weather stations are managed jointly by the National Weather Service, Federal Aviation Administration, and Department of Defense, while AWOS stations are often owned and operated by local airports, municipalities, or private entities. These are where the official, record-book readings are recorded, while it may be warmer in your backyard.

title: DHHS closed 2 investigations into family before Milford toddler froze to death
text:
The Maine Department of Health and Human Services closed an investigation into a family six days before a toddler froze to death in the house without walking through the home.
Shane McLaughlin, 37, is charged with one felony count of manslaughter, as well as three counts of child endangerment, in Penobscot County Superior Court. His 1-year-old daughter, Eleanora Ray McLaughlin, died of hypothermia at the family’s home on Dec. 28.
There was no heat or running water in the house, Assistant Attorney General Jennifer Ackerman said Wednesday in court. It was 18 degrees in the house when first responders arrived on Dec. 28.
Also in the house was Eleanora’s twin sister, now 2 years old, and a now-3-year-old brother. The two children survived and now live with their maternal grandmother.
DHHS started an investigation into McLaughlin on Nov. 14 and closed it Dec. 22 without walking through the house where the toddler died less than a week later, Ackerman said. The department had done a home visit that was announced ahead of time in late November. It was the second investigation into the family that DHHS closed in 2025, Ackerman said.
The new details surrounding the toddler’s death came to light during a bail hearing for McLaughlin. Kirstin Batchelder, a caseworker for DHHS, testified that she joined the case in March. She said she did not read through the case files for the November investigation or another investigation in July for alleged failure to thrive in all three children.
Ackerman described the light layers of clothing the children were wearing that night, including
a short-sleeved shirt for the surviving twin. There were frozen buckets of human waste in the bathtub and animal feces throughout the home, Ackerman said.
That the department closed the investigation in December indicates it found the home was safe, Batchelder said. She said she was unaware of an investigation months earlier in July. That investigation was about failure to thrive and medical concerns for all three children, Ackerman said.
A new DHHS investigation was opened within 24 hours of the toddler’s death and is ongoing, Batchelder said. The surviving children were taken from McLaughlin’s custody and placed with their maternal grandmother, Batchelder said.
McLaughlin worked with the department, taking classes and starting therapy, she said. He worked his way up to unsupervised visits with his kids for 24 hours a week starting in August until his arrest.
The department prioritizes reunifying parents with their children and that is what it was working toward with McLaughlin and the two surviving kids, Batchelder said.
The toddler’s death was ruled accidental by the Office of Chief Medical Examiner.
“There was a tragic death because he lives in poverty,” defense attorney James Howaniec said.
There was no heat in the house and no heating assistance had arrived by that day, Howaniec said. McLaughlin and his three children shared a bedroom, which was heated by a space heater that turned off for unknown reasons the night Eleanora died, Howaniec said.
There was a second space heater that wasn’t being used in the bedroom and extra blankets that weren’t given to the children, Ackerman said.
McLaughlin was originally granted a $250,000 cash bail on Oct. 30. The serious nature of the crime is why McLaughlin’s bail needed to stay high, Ackerman said.
His attorneys argued for a lower bail, explaining how there is no evidence that he is a flight risk, has no violent behavior and no criminal history. Howaniec said McLaughlin’s family can afford about $2,000.
Penobscot County Judge Bruce Mallonee said he will lower the cash bail at some point, but he wants to know more about where McLaughlin will live and who he would be around, as well as more details about how bail conditions would be enforced before he makes a decision to lower bail. He said he doesn’t believe McLaughlin poses a risk to other children.
McLaughlin will remain in the Penobscot County Jail unless he posts the $250,000 bail.

title: Vassalboro select board hears multiple proposals
text:
Vassalboro select board members heard multiple proposals from guests at their Oct. 28 meeting.
Olivia Kunesh, of the Kennebec Valley Council of Governments (KVCOG), and Holly Weidner, chairman of the Vassalboro Conservation Commission (VCC), discussed a new vulnerability study and its implications.
Resident James Poulin recommended reducing the speed limit on a stretch of Route 201 as a safety measure, especially, he said, now that Amish families are moving to town and will be on the road in horse-drawn buggies.
Brian Stanley, librarian at the Vassalboro Public Library, and members of the library’s board of trustees shared a draft document defining the relationship between the library and the town – not recommending changes, they emphasized.
Meetings no longer live streamed
Effective immediately, Vassalboro select board meetings will no longer be live-streamed as they happen. They will be recorded and the recording posted on the website as promptly as technology and staff time allow.
Matthew Weaver, of First National Wealth Management, updated board members on town money invested with his firm and suggested changes they might consider.
Kunesh and Weidner discussed the Vulnerability Assessment Kunesh recently completed for Vassalboro, with help from VCC members and former Town Manager Aaron Miller.
The 28-page document identifies climate-related hazards and areas where they might be mitigated. It stresses planning and upgrades, and identifies grant opportunities.
The next step, Kunesh said, is for the select board to accept the assessment. The next round of applications for grants to implement its recommendations opens in January 2027.
If the town is to have help from KVCOG with grant-writing, Vassalboro must rejoin the organization. In return for annual dues, the town would also receive discounts on some municipal purchases.
Select Board Chairman Chris French said Vassalboro officials discontinued KVCOG membership some years ago, doubting that benefits justified the dues. He invited a KVCOG presentation during the 2027-2028 budget discussions early next year.
Board members voted to accept the vulnerability assessment, with French, Frederick “Rick” Denico and Candy Clark in favor and Dan Bradstreet and Michael Phelps abstaining because they had not had time to read the entire document.
Poulin added a second request for a speed limit study to the one board members received before their Oct. 14 meeting. The former asked for a review of the limit on Hannaford Hill Road and consideration of a four-way stop where Hannaford Hill intersects with Hannaford, Cross and Stone roads.
Poulin said he has lived on the southern end of Route 201, near the Webber Pond Road intersection, for more than 30 years and has watched traffic go steadily faster. Most drivers now go at least 65 miles an hour, and many deer have been killed, he said.
Select board members unanimously asked interim Town Manager Michael Roy to send the state Department of Transportation the necessary written requests for traffic reviews at the two locations.
Results may take up to six months, they warned Poulin. He did not seem surprised.
Stanley asked select board members to approve a document describing the town’s relationship with the library, a private non-profit organization that provides services that in some towns are municipal.
Board members were agreeable, but saw no urgency – Stanley said the library has operated since 1911. They recommended bringing the issue to the new town manager when he or she is hired.
Weaver reviewed the more than $800,000 Vassalboro has with First National, invested mostly in bonds, with some in stocks and cash. If town officials plan to use any of the money within the next two or three years, he recommended transferring funds to CDs, lest there be a “dramatic market decline.”
Candidate accounts for a potential withdrawal are the transfer station reserve fund and the Mill Hill bridge reserve fund, board members said. They took no action.
Later, French proposed going ahead with initially-suggested changes at the transfer station, replacing the present building with a pole barn, and abandoning proposals for larger changes. Roy recommended talking with engineer Jeff Senders, head of Senders science, engineering & construction, of Camden, who has been working with the town on the project. Discussion was postponed to the Nov. 10 board meeting.
French asked Roy how his interim job is going and whether his 24-hour work weeks are adequate. Roy replied yes, on the whole, except for the many FOIA (Freedom of Information Act) requests taking up a lot of his time.
“It’s out of control,” he said. The previous morning, he spent three hours collecting information for responses.
Select board members had interviews with candidates for the town manager position scheduled for Nov. 4 and Nov. 5.
Poulin raised another issue: Vassalboro, he said, is the only area town without restrictions on fireworks. He suggested requiring a permit, which would come with requirements to warn the fire department in advance and to have water on hand.
Because of November holidays, the month’s select board meetings are scheduled for Tuesday, instead of Wednesday, evenings: 6:30 p.m. Tuesday, Nov. 10, before the Veterans’ Day holiday, and Tuesday, Nov. 24, to avoid meeting Thanksgiving eve.

title: This sake combines Japanese and Navajo culture together
text:
HOLBROOK, Ariz. (InvestigateTV) — Atsuo Sakurai and his wife, Heather, make award-winning sake at a shop just off Route 66 in Holbrook.
Sake is a traditional Japanese alcohol made from fermented rice. Its history spans thousands of years. Sakurai’s shop, Arizona Sake, makes the beverage in a 200-gallon vat.
Sakurai said people are often surprised to learn the sake comes from Holbrook, Arizona, on Route 66.
“Oh, yeah. Initially, nobody believed,” he said.
Sakurai is from Tokyo, about 6,000 miles from Holbrook. He worked in the sake industry there before moving to Arizona.
“Initially, I had a dream. Starting a business, establishing a business. Sake manufacturing somewhere in the world,” Sakurai said.
Heather Sakurai is from the Navajo Nation. The couple combine their cultures in the bottle. Sakurai said one of the sakes uses Navajo tea.
“Navajo tea, Navajo tea sake. This is Navajo tea itself, a plant,” he said.
At the shop, workers wash and heat rice in baskets and then put it in vats to ferment.
“When fermentation is done, we press the sake like mash,” Sakurai said.
The sake is squeezed out under pressure. Sakurai said it takes about three months to make one bottle from start to finish.
Sakurai’s sake has won competitions in Japan and around the globe. He makes traditional styles of sake. Some of his creations are sold only in Holbrook.
“The aroma is really beautiful. People describe it as pear or blueberry,” he said.
One taster said she could taste prickly pear in one of the sakes.
“Oh my God, I can really taste the prickly pear. This is about as Arizona as it gets,” the taster said.
Sakurai said the slow, hands-on process brings him peace in a world of AI and automation.
“That kind of business, industry, I want to save,” he said.
Technology threatens how some industries operate, much like the interstate did to some businesses along Route 66. Sakurai said he is confident the story he has written in Holbrook will endure.
Asked whether Arizona Sake will be around in 100 years, Sakurai said, “Hopefully.”

title: New town leaders take the helm in Houlton
text:
Five newly elected Houlton Town Council members took the helm on Wednesday during the Aroostook town’s annual operational meeting.
In recent years, Houlton has struggled to attract candidates for the seven-member council, with most races uncontested. But this year’s midterm election drew eight candidates for five open seats.
Incumbent councilors Sue Tortello, John “J.J.” Schools and Fred Grant were reelected. Challengers Darryl Scott White and Chris Robinson were also elected. Incumbent Grant led the pack with 1,766 votes, followed by Schools with 1,437, Tortello with 1,333, White 1,025 and Robinson with 131.
On Wednesday, the town’s leadership transferred to the new councilors, who were sworn into office by Town Clerk Khylee Wampler.
Robinson was elected chairman.
Prior to Tuesday’s midterm election, Robinson said he wanted to bring a business focus to the council and continue the work he had started as chairman.
“I thought I was fairly effective the last time I was a councilor and chair and because of that I thought I could do it again,” Robinson said in a previous interview. “There were some key deciding votes I made as chair.”
Also on Wednesday, the council confirmed Town Manager Amber Jones’ appointment of several municipal employees including Khylee Wampler as town clerk, election warden, deputy treasurer and deputy tax collector; Tamara Merritt as deputy clerk and deputy election warden; Emily Crofoot as treasurer and finance director; Emily Mills as tax collector and general assistance administrator; and Theresa L. Duff as assessor.
Jones was appointed public information officer and the firm of Severson, Hand, and Nelson as the town attorney.
Attorney Dan Nelson shared information with the town council about open records and public information law. He reminded council members that all communication with the town or town officials, whether by phone, email or in-person, is public record.
“Everything we do is public with a few minor exceptions and it’s important that we let the public know what we are doing,” Nelson said. “People are entitled to it.”
Houlton voter turnout on Tuesday surpassed expectations, with 200 votes cast within the first two hours, according to Wampler. By 3:37 p.m. 1,000 had voted in person and 769 absentee ballots had been processed out of 3,549 registered voters, Wampler said.
Additionally, residents who hadn’t voted for several years re-registered on Tuesday.

title: Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as the first Black woman elected governor in the US
text:
Keisha Lance Bottoms makes history as the first Black woman elected governor in the US
Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected governor of Georgia on Tuesday, making history as the first Black woman to be elected governor in the United States, defeating Republican businessman Rick Jackson and flipping the top job in a key swing state.
A former Atlanta mayor, Bottoms won Tuesday despite a staggering campaign spending deficit driven by the billionaire Jackson tapping more than $200 million of his own fortune. She becomes the first Democrat to prevail in a Georgia governor’s race since 1998.
Related video above: What's at stake for Congress this midterm?
“What we do in this moment will echo through history,” she said ahead of Election Day. Bottoms often sidestepped the barrier-breaking possibilities of her candidacy and instead emphasized her plans to improve an uneven economy and counter President Donald Trump’s administration in Washington.
“Let’s choose hope over fear, progress over division, and come together to build a better Georgia for everyone,” she said.
The outcome bucks voters’ longtime reluctance to put Atlantans in the governor’s mansion, and Bottoms’ victory is the latest example of how the growth of the state’s largest metro area is reshaping Georgia politics. In addition to a Black woman as governor, the state also reelected its first Jewish senator, Democrat Jon Ossoff, to serve alongside its first Black senator, Raphael Warnock.
Jackson told supporters: "Tonight, the voters spoke ... and I respect their decision."
Bottoms will succeed Republican Gov. Brian Kemp, who was barred by law from seeking a third term. It was the third Georgia gubernatorial election in a row with a Black woman leading the ticket. Kemp twice defeated Stacey Abrams, who remains a prominent voting rights advocate and Democratic fundraiser but opted against a third run for governor.
The broken barrier is second to policy
Bottoms was among eight Black major party nominees for governor on the ballot Tuesday. There have been just three Black governors elected in U.S. history, all of them Democratic men. This year, two Black women were vying for governor: Bottoms and Republican Lisa Demuth of Minnesota.
The descendant of enslaved Georgians, Bottoms rarely acknowledged the historic nature of her candidacy explicitly. But she often recounted her family history.
“I am at least a fifth-generation Georgian,” she said. “I say ‘at least’ because we can only trace our family back five generations — to a plantation in Crawfordville.”
She noted that her grandfather moved to Atlanta from rural Georgia and had to “walk through these back doors” of downtown buildings she would later enter through the front as mayor. She said her ancestry “is always present with me.”
Her emphasis was on policy — and on Jackson and Trump
Bottoms called for expanding the Medicaid insurance program to include hundreds of thousands more people and increasing Georgia’s minimum wage to $15 per hour. She wants to raise the pay of teachers, firefighters, police officers and other public employees, pause data center development and repeal Georgia’s ban on abortion after the sixth week of pregnancy.
“This is a life and death issue,” she said of the abortion ban, citing cases of women dying from miscarriage and pregnancy complications because physicians fear criminal prosecution under the abortion law.
She’s called for pausing new data center developments and stopping installation of any additional automated Flock cameras used by law enforcement.
And she pledged to “make sure we are protected from the harmful policies of Donald Trump,” and missed no chance to remind voters that Jackson said he wanted to govern like “Trump with a Southern tone” and become the president’s “favorite governor.”
“I’m not running to be his favorite governor,” Bottoms told voters during the rivals’ lone debate. “I’m running to work on behalf of people like you.”
Bottoms challenged Jackson’s assertions that he understood Georgians’ economic struggles because he’d once had his own. Pointing to Jackson’s company, Jackson Healthcare, and its lucrative government contracts, Bottoms disputed that Jackson was a self-made political outsider. And she accused him of using the money he made from taxpayers to try to “buy this election.”
She withstood Jackson’s attacks on her record as mayor. Jackson’s deluge of TV ads included spots featuring clips of protests after the 2020 police killings of Atlanta resident Rayshard Brooks and Minneapolis resident George Floyd, both Black men, by white officers in their respective cities. Jackson also hammered Bottoms for not seeking a second term as mayor, saying she abandoned the city.
The statehouse dynamic changes
For Republicans, Jackson’s defeat marks a difficult turn in the state’s evolution into a two-party battleground. He began his campaign as a relative unknown but leveraged his personal wealth and outsider appeal to defeat the sitting lieutenant governor, who had Trump’s early endorsement, the attorney general and the secretary of state.
Democrats already had won three U.S. Senate elections since Trump’s first presidential victory a decade ago, and Sen. Jon Ossoff was vying for reelection Tuesday. Yet the GOP has had a statehouse trifecta — holding the governor’s office and controlling both chambers of the General Assembly — for more than two decades.
Democrats were trying Tuesday to flip control of the state House, though Republicans were heavily favored to defend their Senate majority and give Bottoms at least one GOP-led chamber to navigate.

title: SCORES OUTDOORS: Where have all the birds gone?
text:
Where have all the birds gone? That is a question that has been asked of me many times over the last several weeks. My wife first brought it to my attention when we first moved back to town from camp in late September. So, like a good husband, I ignored it. I said that I had seen birds at the feeders. Then, someone called a couple of weeks ago, and asked the same question. Many friends have also brought the situation to my attention.
So, thinking back, I realized I have not seen a single bird at our feeders at home since our move back in from camp. The feeders are usually covered with gold finches, woodpeckers along with many other species. So, where did they go?
Even at camp, we noticed a shortage of birds this season. We did not see any grosbeaks, orioles or cardinals. And the hummingbirds left two weeks earlier than usual. So, where did the bird go?
Research showed me there is no definite answer. One of the reasons could be the loss of insects. Birds are highly dependent on them. When was the last time you had to clean your windshield of insects in the summer as we once did? Even at camp this summer, we noticed a shortage of insects. I haven’t seen a June bug in two years. There were hardly any hickory tussock caterpillars this fall, and definitely a decline in the number of harvestman (daddy longlegs) spiders.
The loss of bird populations in the Western Mountains of Maine includes three major causes. First, there has been a coincidental drop in insect life. No one completely understands how or why this has happened. Another reason is loss of habitat.
Has anyone seen a wooly bear caterpillar this fall. They usually begin to appear in mid-September. I have seen zero, nil, zilch this fall. The only ones I’ve seen are photos sent to me by friends or readers.
Birds are the warning lights that tell us our natural systems are stressed out. Seen as indicator species for the health of America’s natural landscape, they are declining in numbers at an alarming rate.
I think it was in July when we first noticed there weren’t as many birds around as usual. We kept the feeders filled, but the time lapse between fill-ups was getting longer. But, the squirrels and chipmunks were pleased.
Was the summer too cold for baby birds to survive? Also, organized spraying campaigns can kill birds as well as the massive caterpillar population. Or, did the birds just go somewhere else. I guess we shouldn’t take it personally because birds do move from place to place in search of food. Birds migrate, so did they leave to head south a little earlier than normal. Did the hurricane activity this year have an affect on the bird migration? Did the storms mess up the birds’ timing and navigation? I guess the questions are endless on the possibilities.
The best reason I was able to find was from the Audubon Society, along with other bird information sources, insisting that nothing is wrong. That because of the warmer than usual fall weather and the unusually abundant sources of natural food, the birds are still finding plenty to eat in the wild. Also, another explanation was that bird populations naturally fluctuate from year to year and that a feeder that is really “busy” one year may have fewer birds the next.
Many people are under the impression that the birds they see in their yards from day to day are, like the trees and shrubs, constant elements. In fact, however, bird populations are extremely dynamic.
For instance, there are some years when most, if not all, of the summering chickadees, Blue Jays, and other “resident” birds are replaced by a different wintering population. Because individuals of a species look pretty much the same, shifts in feeding birds usually go unnoticed except when concentrations become unusually large or when the out-going visitors are not immediately replaced by a new group of hungry customers.
When struck by a worrisome disappearance of birds in the early fall, people may start searching nearby woodlots and their fears are confirmed. Where recently the woods were full of song birds there is now a pall of silence and inactivity. This, too, is completely normal. Except for unusually loquacious species, bird song essentially ceases by late summer.
Because bird song is such an integral part of our outdoor experience, on a nice day in September we often fail to notice its absence unless we’re listening for it. Once they have left their breeding territories, birds tend to coalesce into feeding flocks, and it is not unusual for extensive sections of the landscape to be bird less when such a flock or flocks are elsewhere. There is nothing alarming about a prolonged silence in the depths of an autumn forest.
Wild foods include berries, weed seeds, mast (acorns and other nuts), and invertebrate sources such as lace bug larvae. These foods are subject to fluctuating availability both seasonally and from year to year. Birds will concentrate in regions where wild foods are particularly plentiful, thus leaving areas where there is less bounty.
The availability of food in the wild will affect the number of winter residents, for example, if there is a poor mast crop, Blue Jays will migrate farther south to where natural foods are more abundant.
It is apparently a universal question in our area right now, and one that seems to have fewer answers.

title: Susan Collins’ Senate Career Lasted Far Longer Than She Originally Promised
text:
Susan Collins’ Senate Career Lasted Far Longer Than She Originally Promised
Let’s take a look back at the pledge the senator from Caribou made when she was seeking election 30 years ago.
👇 KEEP READING: Best counties to retire to in Maine 👇
During her first U.S. Senate campaign in Maine in 1996, Republican Susan Collins pledged to serve no more than two six-year terms.
She made the commitment publicly during a televised WMTW debate while answering a question about congressional term limits.
Collins said she would honor the pledge regardless of whether a term limits law or constitutional amendment passed.
At the time, she argued that two terms would provide enough time to contribute in Washington before returning home and allowing someone else to serve.
Collins later said she changed her position after learning how Senate seniority could increase her ability to advocate for Maine.
She went on to defeat Democratic challengers Tom Allen in 2008, Shenna Bellows in 2014, and Sara Gideon in 2020, extending her Senate career well beyond the two terms she originally pledged to serve.
Democrat Troy Jackson, a former Maine Senate president and logger, defeated Collins in the Nov. 3 election, denying her a sixth term and ending her nearly 30-year tenure in the Senate.
Jackson campaigned on lowering housing and health care costs and supporting workers, while criticizing Collins for not doing enough to oppose President Donald Trump.
And there you have it! A pledge made during Collins’ first Senate campaign remained part of the political conversation all the way through her final race three decades later.

title: Annie Andrews defeats Sen. Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham's sister, in South Carolina Senate race
text:
Democrat Annie Andrews defeats Sen. Darline Graham, Lindsey Graham's sister, in major upset
Annie Andrews won a stunning victory in South Carolina, shattering decades of Republican dominance to become the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from the deeply conservative state in a generation.
On Tuesday, Andrews defeated U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, who has been serving as interim senator since her brother, Lindsey Graham, died earlier this year. The victory also made Andrews, a pediatrician, the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate.
She paused for a few moments, taking in the crowd wildly celebrating the first Democratic win in a U.S. Senate race in South Carolina in 28 years, before she spoke.
"You have shown the nation what is possible," Andrews said. "You have shown the nation that in this era of partisan divides, of vitriol and name-calling, in a politics dominated by billionaires and special interest groups and insiders in Washington, D.C., that we will not bow down."
In Columbia, Graham addressed a subdued crowd of Republican supporters. Her voice raspy, Graham told the crowd they should remain as proud of her brother as she is.
"This is a tough cycle, and all of us need to be involved as we chart a path forward. It is clear that we as conservatives have work to do, and that work starts tonight," Graham said.
Trump's backing couldn't carry Darline Graham to victory
Before facing Andrews, Graham bested better-known Republicans to win a hotly contested special primary. President Donald Trump, a close ally of her brother, endorsed and campaigned for her in the state. Graham again thanked Trump for his support after her loss.
That presidential backing eroded Graham's support from both sides. It bothered some independent voters unhappy with Trump's second term and some Republican supporters who disapproved of the president's involvement in a crowded primary they believed should be left up to the state's voters. Both groups were uneasy about Graham's inexperience and the prospect of turning the seat into a Graham family dynasty.
Andrews benefited from the national wave of discontent with Republicans generally and Trump specifically.
Lindsey Graham was seeking his fifth term, and Republicans felt confident they'd keep the seat before he died. But his sister's status as a political novice, plus Andrews' fundraising prowess, prompted GOP groups to pour money into South Carolina.
Graham faced questions about her experience
About two-thirds of South Carolina Senate voters said Darline Graham lacked the right experience. About 7 in 10 voters who doubted Graham's experience voted for Andrews, according to The AP Voter Poll.
Andrews won a majority of women voters in South Carolina, while Graham won about half of men.
While about 9 in 10 Republican voters in the state supported Lindsey Graham in 2020, according to AP VoteCast, that support from the party's base fell this year, with about 8 in 10 Republican voters saying they voted for Darline Graham.
Andrews had already been campaigning for more than a year and had won her primary outright when Lindsey Graham died, forcing her to rejigger a general election plan centered on ousting the incumbent. After his death, she refocused on the broader GOP field, saying she was ready to debate any of the hopefuls. After the Republican primary runoff, she homed in on Darline Graham.
Andrews was also new to politics. She came up short in a 2022 challenge to Rep. Nancy Mace but has remained visible afterward. Before her Senate campaign, she had never held elected office or run statewide.
The Senate contest's unique circumstances buoyed Democrats as they pursued an elusive statewide victory in South Carolina. A New York Times/Siena poll conducted in October appeared to show a close race and, coupled with criticism of Graham's inexperience, gave Democrats reason to argue the contest had become more competitive this year.
In a Republican primary debate, Graham was asked whether the U.S. has a national security interest in Taiwan and the South China Sea — a longstanding contention of both Democratic and Republican administrations. She struggled to answer before admitting, "National security is not my thing."
She continued facing questions about her qualifications even after squeaking out a runoff win.
Voter Brent Chaplin said he had always supported GOP candidates but couldn't cast his ballot for Graham, saying he backed Andrews and hoped her win would be a "wake-up" call for Republicans.
"You just can't go and say, 'I'm a Republican. I'm just going to vote Republican,'" Chaplin said after voting in Fort Mill. "You've got to put some brain power into it and think about it. So hopefully, it is a message to the powers that be to wake up, pick better candidates."
Before Andrews' victory, Fritz Hollings was the last Democrat elected to a Senate seat in South Carolina, winning his final term in 1998. Republicans had won every U.S. Senate race since then by at least double digits and have held both Senate seats since Hollings left office in 2005.
___
Collins reported from Columbia, South Carolina.

title: 1 killed and 2 others injured when a helicopter crashes into bay near Miami, officials say
text:
MIAMI (AP) — One man was killed and two others were critically injured on Wednesday when their helicopter crashed into Biscayne Bay near Miami, officials said.
The Robinson R44 II helicopter went down late Wednesday morning near Bill Baggs State Park, off Key Biscayne, while on a trip to film boats on the water, the Miami-Dade Sheriff’s Office said.
Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz said during an afternoon news conference that the two survivors were taken to a nearby trauma center in critical but stable condition.
Rescue workers from several local agencies, as well as the U.S. Coast Guard and U.S. Customs and Border Protection, responded to the crash.
When the sheriff’s office marine patrol units reached the scene, they reported finding a Good Samaritan trying to help one of the victims and take him to shore. Miami firefighters attempted to save his life, but he didn’t survive, Cordero-Stutz said.
Meanwhile, border protection officers found the two other men from the helicopter and turned them over to Miami-Dade rescue workers for transport to the hospital.
Cordero-Stutz said the cause of the crash remains under investigation. South Florida has experienced heavy showers over the past few days, but it wasn’t known if the weather contributed to the crash.
Television news video of the crash shows the aircraft upside down underwater with two yellow floats attached to the bottom of its landing skids. Those emergency floats are designed to help keep a helicopter afloat in a water landing.
Officials didn’t immediately identify the helicopter’s occupants. The sheriff said they were still working to notify family members.
On Sunday, nine people died when a Learjet plummeted into the ground near West Palm Beach, Florida, with enough force to create a crater and pulverize the airplane. The NTSB is also investigating that crash.

title: Scarborough becomes latest community to limit employees’ cooperation with ICE
text:
Scarborough is the latest Maine community to prohibit the use of town resources and employees to assist immigration enforcement, except when required by state or federal law or judicial order.
The Scarborough Police Department has had this policy in place for years, but the Scarborough Town Council voted 6-1 Wednesday night to pass a new ordinance that expands this policy to non-law enforcement municipal employees. Councilor Scott Doherty voted against the ordinance.
Other Maine communities have also passed similar ordinances, including Portland and Lewiston, and a state law that took effect in July restricts Maine’s police officers and sheriff’s deputies from coordinating with federal immigration agencies.
This ordinance comes after months of residents expressing their concerns and anger about Immigrations and Customs Enforcement activity in town and the presence of Maine’s only ICE processing facility at 40 Manson Libby Road.
After the killing of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford in July, residents from Scarborough and other Maine communities have consistently shown up at council meetings — often wearing white T-shirts with “ICE” crossed out inside a red circle — to demand action and fight to push ICE out of Scarborough.
Many of them shared their support for the ordinance at Wednesday’s meeting but said it should only be a first step.
“Let’s pass the ordinance, but let’s ensure it can be enforced,” said Jennifer Jortberg, a member of the Community Coalition to Remove ICE.
Residents can bring their concerns to Town Manager Tom Hall if they believe a town employee is cooperating with ICE.
In June, the Town Council had passed a proclamation calling on Maine’s congressional delegation to investigate the facility. In September, Scarborough Democratic Town Committee leadership met with representatives from the offices of Sens. Susan Collins’ and Angus King, along with two representatives from the office of Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-1st District, to discuss reviewing and removing the ICE facility.

title: NASA space telescope plunges to Earth after two decades studying cosmic explosions
text:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — One of NASA’s premier space telescopes plunged to Earth on Wednesday, ending its 22-year investigation of the universe’s biggest explosions.
The Swift Observatory’s demise came less than three months after a long-shot rescue mission failed.
The U.S. Space Force confirmed Swift’s reentry near Indonesia after tracking its sinking orbit, the result of intense solar activity the past few years.
NASA hired a private company to whip together an orbit-boosting effort, but Katalyst Space’s three-armed robotic craft ran into trouble following its July launch and came crashing down in September.
It was not immediately known how much of the 1 ½-ton spacecraft burned up in the atmosphere. NASA anticipated some of the denser pieces surviving.
Swift rocketed into orbit in 2004 on what was expected to be a two-year study of gamma ray bursts and exploding stars. It observed thousands of them over a mission that lasted 11 times longer than planned, serving as a first responder for other telescopes that could probe deeper.
NASA is gauging industry’s interest in mounting a rescue mission for another observatory whose orbit is being chipped away by solar storms: the Hubble Space Telescope. Launched in 1990, Hubble is expected to come crashing down by the mid-2030s, according to recent analyses.
The space agency is looking for input from private companies on whether and how they might boost Hubble’s orbit, upgrade its systems or guide it to a controlled reentry — or all three. Any such mission would need to happen by 2032.
Unlike the rush job with Swift, the space agency has more time to explore options for saving Hubble, said Nicky Fox, NASA’s science mission chief.
“Hubble still has important science ahead of it,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement, “and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible.”

title: York voters approve full slate of referendum questions
text:
York residents voted on six referendums Tuesday, including a special budget item.
Here’s what happened to each of them, according to unofficial results from the town.
YORK AMBULANCE FUNDING
Following a monthslong struggle to find a solution for a significant shortfall in funding, York residents voted to approve a question that grants $500,000 to York Ambulance Association. A total of 7,096 people voted in favor, while 1,291 people voted against the funding.
The town will use $500,000 from its unassigned fund balance to sustain the service through the end of its contract with the town in July 2027. The service will initially receive $300,000 and will earn the rest in monthly installments so long as it can meet a set of conditions established by the town.
Officials say they will continue exploring the possibility of transitioning to an in-house EMS service instead of one that’s contracted.
SINGLE-USE PLASTICS
Residents decided in a 5,921-2,287 vote to make permanent an ordinance banning single-use plastics.
Restaurants and other establishments in York were already required to use earth-friendly or compostable stir sticks, straws and utensils. The ban, first adopted in May 2025, would have expired Dec. 31 because of a clause written into the ordinance.
‘STOP ALPRs’ ORDINANCE
Residents also voted to ban automated license plate reading cameras, or ALPRs, in a 5,386-2,043 vote amid a nationwide debate over the ethics of similar technology.
The York Police Department terminated its contract with the ALPR company Flock Safety in September and removed at least four cameras on public property following a citizen petition that garnered 115 signatures.
Tuesday’s decision implements an ordinance permanently barring any public agency in town from using similar technology. It’s already illegal for public entities to use the technology, per state law.
EMERGENCY MANAGEMENT, WIRELESS COMMUNICATIONS, REVENUE BONDS
Voters also approved an emergency management question that reorganizes disaster relief funds in a 6,896-1,127 vote.
An ordinance redefining requirements for mounting wireless communication antennae passed with 6,130 votes in favor and 1,511 votes against the ordinance.
Residents also considered a question created by citizen petition that would set new parameters for which projects could use general obligation funds and which could be funded by revenue bonds. A total of 3,962 people voted to approve the ordinance, while 3,579 people voted against it.

title: Gas odor shuts down Narragansett school in Gorham
text:
Narragansett School to reopen Thursday after gas odor prompted closure
School officials say no gas leaks were found during an inspection Wednesday
Narragansett School to reopen Thursday after gas odor prompted closure
School officials say no gas leaks were found during an inspection Wednesday
Narragansett Elementary School in Gorham will reopen Thursday after a gas odor prompted officials to cancel classes Wednesday.
In an update to families Wednesday afternoon, Principal Erin Eppler said the building had been cleared for occupancy after an inspection by the Gorham Fire Department, Johnson & Jordan and Unitil.
Officials said no gas leaks were detected during the inspection.
The odor was first detected around 7 a.m. Wednesday. School officials canceled classes out of an abundance of caution while crews investigated.
Officials believe that the odor was caused by an air handler drawing in gas that had been vented outside from the building's regulators.
Additional testing will be conducted prior to students arriving Thursday morning, and officials say they will continue daily checks.
"The message is that safety is the top priority. If there's any thought at all that something may be unsafe, we want to make sure that we're doing everything we can to keep students safe," said Assistant Superintendent Dr. Quinton Donahue.
In December 2025, Narragansett Elementary was evacuated in the middle of a school day and then closed for two straight days following a gas leak.
"They believed the last time it was fixed. Obviously, that was incorrect," said Katie Rustin, whose children attend the school. "Here's to hoping that it gets fixed so this doesn't happen again."
School officials have scheduled a community meeting for Monday, November 9, at 6 p.m. at Narragansett School. District administrators, representatives from Johnson & Jordan and Unitil, and the Gorham Fire Department are expected to answer questions.
