title: Freeport-area schools ask what it means to value education
text:
Lately, I have found myself reflecting on the role of education in our national life and what it means for a community to truly value it. I come to that question from several perspectives: decades spent as a teacher and school administrator, my current role as a superintendent, years as the parent of three children who grew up in public schools, and my own lifelong journey as a learner. Each has shaped my understanding of the purpose and promise of education. As a superintendent, I am also compelled to look beyond individual classrooms and schools and consider education as a vital system that helps define a community. It is one of the most significant collective investments a community makes, not simply in its children, but in the kind of community it wants to be and the values and aspirations it hopes to carry forward. This month, I want to explore what that means in the everyday work of our schools and, in particular, in how we value the people who make that work possible.
I spent many years as a classroom teacher before moving into school administration. It was work that became integral to my identity. I know the particular privilege of being invited into the lives of young people at a time when they are figuring out who they are and who they might become. Teaching is about much more than the subjects we teach. It is about cultivating curiosity, empathy, acceptance, and a passion for learning. It is about seeing potential in children, sometimes before they see it in themselves, and creating the conditions in which they can discover it.
As a parent, I experienced that relationship from the other side. I knew what it meant to send my children off to school each day, trusting that the adults who spent their time with them would recognize their individuality, encourage their interests, challenge them, and care about them. Like most parents, I had moments of deep gratitude for the educators in my children’s lives, and also moments of deep frustration when my children struggled with something in school. Either way, I understood that the people teaching my children were influencing far more than my children’s knowledge and skills. They were helping shape how my children saw themselves and the world around them.
Those perspectives have stayed with me. They have given me an enduring appreciation for the work of educators and for the professional knowledge, skill, and personal commitment that work demands. Teaching is a craft. It requires knowledge, judgment, creativity, patience, and an ongoing commitment to learning. Some of its most important work happens quietly, in relationships and conversations that never show up in an assessment or an annual report. It happens when a teacher recognizes that a child needs something different, when a student discovers a new interest, or when a young person begins to believe in their own abilities.
I believe that, as a society, we need to do a better job of elevating and honoring that work. That means more than occasional expressions of appreciation. It means recognizing the expertise educators bring to their work, respecting their professionalism, seeking their perspectives, and giving teaching and learning a central place in our public conversations. Educators should be among the people we look to when we talk about the kind of community we want to build and the kind of society we want to become.
This matters particularly now. At a time when public discourse is increasingly marked by division, distrust, and too often a diminished regard for expertise and those who serve others, we should be especially mindful of the institutions and relationships that bring us together. Public education is one of those institutions. At their best, schools are places where curiosity is encouraged, differences are respected, possibilities are explored, and every child is regarded as someone worthy of our time, attention, and belief. If we truly value education, that belief should be evident in how we speak about educators, how we listen to them, and the respect we afford their work and professional judgment. Their work is not simply important to our schools. It is important to the fabric of our communities.
I have spent much of my adult life in schools, and I suppose that has given me a particular appreciation for the people who choose to make this their life’s work. I have also seen how much of a difference one educator can make in the life of a child. I imagine most of us can think of someone who made that kind of difference in our own lives. Take a moment to think about that person. What was it about them that stayed with you? What did they give you that you still carry today? And perhaps most importantly, how would you want that person, and the work they devoted themselves to, to be recognized and honored? How might we extend that same recognition and respect to the educators who are making a difference in the lives of children today? I know I am grateful for the educators who have made a difference in my life, in the lives of my children, and in the lives of so many young people in our communities. As we continue to shape the identity of RSU 5, I hope we continue to recognize and honor the profound importance of teaching and learning, and the people who dedicate themselves to that work, in the life of our community.
Tom Gray is superintendent of Regional School Unit 5, which oversees schools in the towns of Freeport, Durham and Pownal.

title: Officials: 2 missing Colorado college students died after 'catastrophic failure' during hike
text:
Missing Colorado college students died after 'catastrophic failure' during hike, officials say
Officials said two college students who were found dead following a hike in Colorado died after a "catastrophic failure" of their equipment.
The Chaffee County Sheriff's Office previously said Kaden Matsuda, 19, from Ridgway, Colorado, and Jackson Donlon, 20, from Queensbury, New York, were located in a basin of the West Apostle Mountain around 3:30 p.m. on Oct. 29.
Both men, who were students at Colorado Mountain College's Leadville Campus, were found dead days after being reported missing by school staff on Oct. 26.
Related video: Suspicious deaths after attacks along Michigan river trail
In an updated statement from the sheriff's office and the Chaffee County Coroner's Office, an autopsy revealed both died as a result of multiple blunt force injuries, saying their deaths "were instant."
An investigation revealed that Donlon was beginning to rappel from a primary anchor point on a rock substrate. That anchor, officials said, appeared to have been backed up by a piton and a secondary anchor made of rock substrate.
Authorities said Matsuda was "attached via his personal anchor device to the same anchor points, as well as the primary anchor point."
"The anchor had a catastrophic failure of unknown cause," the joint statement said. "Both then fell a substantial distance (exact distance unknown)."
Officials said it is unclear whether a heavy snowstorm that had swept through the area had a negative impact leading to the incident. The statement said weather, however, did not play a direct role in their deaths.
“Kaden and Jackson lived life at the highest peaks chasing freedoms and panoramic views that most of us only see in pictures. We hope their families and friends find strength in the memories of their vibrant spirits," Chaffee County Sheriff Andy Rohrich said in the statement. "While their lives were far too short, they spent their final moments together surrounded by the majestic beauty of Chaffee County’s high peaks that they loved. There is also relief knowing neither of them suffered."

title: Trump appears to take credit for stock market rally day after multiple Democratic midterm wins
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray News) - President Donald Trump took to social media on Wednesday to praise the sudden rise in stock prices a day after the midterm elections.
Trump posted to Truth Social, “Stock Market just hit another Record High — 91 Days in just a short period of time — Less than two years. Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”
U.S. stocks went soaring Wednesday following the GOP losing sole control of Washington in the midterm elections.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1,519 points, or 2.9%, with the Nasdaq composite up 1.9% as of Wednesday afternoon.
Stocks are said to generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, but this year’s midterms were harsh to the Republican Party, with multiple GOP states and government positions flipping to the Democrats.
The Democratic Party appears set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, with experts noting Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario, hence the jump in prices seen Wednesday.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
Trump continues to retain executive authority over key areas such as defense, foreign policy and, in some instances, trade.
The president said in an interview with Fox News that he would work with Democrats.
“Congratulations to the Democrats,” Trump was quoted as saying in the interview. “I think the Democrats did a good job. They fought hard. They’ve been fighting me for a long time. This fight’s been going on for ages.”
Trump added when asked about working with Democrats: “I would do that. I think the Democrats want to work with me.”

title: Maine startup develops AI tool for mom-and-pop convenience stores
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
MECHANIC FALLS — For centuries small shopkeepers have tracked inventory by hand, reconciling what’s been sold with what’s still on the shelves and deciding whether to restock.
Even with computers, it remains a painstaking process that requires staffing, time and some comfort with financial risk. Managing all that can be challenging amid rising costs, a tight labor market and narrow profit margins.
A Maine startup aims to ease the struggle with a low-cost, AI-powered system that’s geared toward independent convenience, grocery and liquor stores and other small retailers. It’s one of 97 AI-related projects that the state’s technology incubator has helped to finance since 2020.
Storeveu, built by Fortune Technology Inc., allows storeowners to track products from delivery invoices through front-end sales in a system that’s constantly updating, said Nishant Patel, co-owner and software designer.
The software also forecasts consumer demand and recommends price drops before expiration dates make products unsellable.
“If an item is selling, it predicts how many are needed in the coming weeks,” said Patel, of Lewiston. “If an item isn’t selling, it suggests creating a promotional sale.”
Most convenience stores in the U.S. are owned by companies with 10 or fewer shops, according to the National Association of Convenience Stores. Patel sees strong potential demand among those 95,000 businesses.
“Those owners rarely get software built for them,” Patel said.
Tailored to each store’s needs, the software runs on Fortune Technology’s servers rather than a third-party AI service and uses only data that storeowners provide, Patel said.
Patel began developing the system in January and says it is about 75% accurate. In July, the company got a $30,000 business innovation grant from the Maine Technology Institute to push it closer to 100%.
“Any product line (Storeveu) is unsure of is flagged for a person to check,” Patel said. “The (AI) training is still underway and the number is improving.”
AI PROJECTS FUNDED BY THE STATE
Interest in AI has grown over the last several years, and the state has seen a steady uptick in businesses seeking help to harness its capabilities.
Only three, or just under 4% of applications for IT-related funding from the Maine Technology Institute referenced AI in 2020, compared with 138, or 41% of applications in 2026, said President Brian Whitney. The nonprofit was founded and funded by the Legislature to foster innovation.
“We fund projects that solve a technical or scientific challenge,” Whitney said via email. “We are looking for things that are meaningfully different from existing alternatives. We also look to fund projects that have the potential to create quality jobs and generate revenue growth in Maine.”
Whitney said about 60% of AI-related awards have gone to projects intended to serve a public good, such as healthcare, education, language access and public safety; and about 20% stated an explicit social mission or are a public benefit corporation.
Besides Fortune Technology, other recipients include Alivo Inc. of South Portland, for a home service sales platform ($75,000); Restoration Medicine Inc. of Portland, for a digital health platform to address widespread delays and inaccuracies in pelvic health diagnoses ($30,000); Bluey Technologies Inc. of Portland, for a personal safety app that detects potential risks and connects users to help without constant tracking or data sharing ($50,000); CourseStorm Inc. of Orono, to upgrade and market a class registration platform ($250,000); and ConnectCapable Inc., a Michigan-based company contracted by the Maine Department of Transportation for a traffic management system ($100,000).
Whitney, a member of the Maine Artificial Intelligence Task Force, acknowledged that the technology raises some concerns and risks.
“During this period of rapid and profound change, the pursuit of potentially transformative opportunities from AI must be navigated through the novel or still unknown risks it creates,” a 2025 report by the task force states.
“MTI is not supporting hyper-scalers building out data centers,” Whitney said. “Most of the companies MTI awards have fewer than 50 employees, but they grow over time and together they create high quality, Maine-based jobs and generate significant economic activity for our state.”
FAST-GROWING CUSTOMER BASE
Patel, 26, began developing Storeveu shortly after graduating from Northeastern University with a master’s in information systems.
His business partner is Sanjay Patel, 45, who owns more than a dozen liquor and convenience stores across Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Maine, including Dad’s Place in Mechanic Falls and Phippsburg Center Store. Both are from Gujarat, India, but they aren’t related.
They fine-tuned Storeveu based on Sanjay Patel’s many years of retail experience. They also added video features for store security, theft protection, customer service monitoring and sales of alcohol, tobacco and lottery scratch tickets. He has installed the system in his eight independent stores.
“It has a lot of features that other point-of-sale systems don’t have,” said Patel, who lives in North Andover, Massachusetts. “It’s helping out bigtime. It gives you a clear picture of your sales.”
Storeveu is also a lot more affordable than larger providers, he said, starting at $600 per store for the hardware and $49.99 per month for the software and customer support. One estimate he received from a larger provider was $30,000 to start, he said.
Fortune Technology already has 10 employees servicing 50 stores that are using Storeveu, up from 15 stores when they applied for the grant, and more storeowners are contacting them daily.
The business partners say they are working seven days a week, promoting the system and onboarding new customers.
Last month, they set up a table at the Navratri gathering in Foxboro, Massachusetts, a nine-night Hindu music and dance festival that attracts thousands of people.
“We were there on the eighth night — the most auspicious night — and we got 50 leads,” Nishant Patel said. “Many of them have several stores, so our numbers could grow very quickly.”

title: A pantry cannot depend forever on someone’s spare room
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
by Douglas Vandergraph
For more than three decades, a remarkable part of the China, Maine, community has lived inside a family home. The China Community Food Pantry did not begin with a purpose-built facility or a large operating budget. It grew because Lee and Ann Austin and other neighbors recognized a need and kept showing up.
Now the pantry faces a challenge that many long-serving community organizations eventually encounter: the generosity that carried the work this far cannot be assumed to supply its next building.
The Town Line reported in February [February 5, 2026, issue, article by Jeanne Marquis] that the Austins have made space in their home available for more than thirty years without charging rent. The pantry’s board has been exploring a new location, and its president explained that renting could increase the annual operating budget from roughly $15,000 to about $45,000. The report described about thirty regular volunteers and an average of seventy-five families served each week.
Those numbers reveal a difficult truth. An organization can be extraordinarily successful at serving its neighbors and still be vulnerable because so much of its success rests on an arrangement that cannot last forever.
I live in Fort Collins, Colorado, not central Maine, and have no role in this pantry. What interests me is a responsibility that reaches beyond one town. We need to honor founding volunteers not only by thanking them, but by making it possible for the work to continue when they step back.
The Christian language of stewardship is useful here. Stewardship is often reduced to an appeal for money, but it means something larger: caring wisely for what has been entrusted to us and preparing for the people who will come next.
In the Gospels, Jesus feeds hungry people and then tells His followers to gather what remains. The striking moment of abundance is followed by the unglamorous discipline of not letting resources go to waste. I hear a lesson there for every congregation, pantry and volunteer-led organization.
A food pantry’s mission is not the room where its shelves happen to stand. Its mission is the neighbor who needs groceries, the volunteer who knows how to organize them and the dependable relationships that make distribution possible. A physical home still matters enormously. It must be safe, accessible, practical for deliveries and financially sustainable. But the building should serve the mission, not consume it.
That distinction suggests several questions worth asking before a beloved program relocates. Can churches and civic organizations share underused space? Can a local business offer suitable facilities or logistics expertise? Can several community partners distribute the responsibilities that once fell on a small group of founders? What would a realistic long-term budget look like, including utilities, transport and maintenance?
These are not questions outsiders can answer for the people doing the work. The pantry’s board and volunteers understand details I do not. Their judgment should lead. But community members can help by listening to the needs the organization actually describes instead of assuming goodwill alone will remove practical constraints.
I also hope the discussion keeps the people receiving food at its center. A new location should be judged partly by whether families can reach it and use it without losing privacy or dignity. A cheaper space that is difficult to access may cost neighbors in other ways. Conversely, a more elaborate facility is not automatically better if it threatens the program’s future.
There is a quiet act of faith in planning for a time when the original volunteers will no longer be able to do everything. It acknowledges that our work is not ours to possess forever. We are responsible for handing it forward in better condition, if we can.
Lee and Ann Austin’s gift was never only a room. It was an example of what neighbors can build together. The most meaningful way to respect that example is to make sure the welcome survives the move.
Douglas Vandergraph is a Christian inspirational writer and speaker based in Fort Collins, Colorado. He writes about faith, perseverance and practical compassion.

It is also expensive!

title: China planners schedule public hearings on two applications
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The four China Planning Board members at the Oct. 27 board meeting scheduled future public hearings on both applications before them.
The first application was from Ralph Howe, doing business as BRF (Biorenewable Fuels) on Dirigo Road, to turn an existing house at 15 Alder Park Road into an office and light storage building for his business.
Howe said the previous owner had run a business from the building. After his death, Howe bought and remodeled the building and now wants a similar use.
Asked what “light storage” means, he said things like office supplies.
He anticipates no changes to the property that would affect neighbors, and only a slight increase in daily traffic.
Board members voted 3-1 to hold a public hearing in case neighbors would like to express opinions. Bruce Fitzgerald considered the hearing unnecessary. It is currently scheduled for 6 p.m., Tuesday, Nov 10, the beginning of the next board meeting.
The second application was for a six-lot subdivision of about 144 acres on Two Ponds Road, off Free Man Road, north of Weeks Mills Village.
Surveyor Adam Ellis, representing applicant Daniel Ouellette, explained a map of the subdivision and said minor changes have been proposed. Fitzgerald pointed out that the application consisted of half a dozen statements; he asked if there is a form to be filled out.
Acting Board Chairman Milton Dudley and Codes Officer Nicholas French said there is no form right now; the prior one was so outdated as to be unusable and a new one is not yet ready.
After discussion with Ellis and Ouellette, board members left the public hearing date indefinite – perhaps Nov. 24 – and asked for an updated map and more information beforehand.
Wall resigning
At the Oct. 27 China planning board meeting, former Chairman Toni Wall said she is handing over the chairmanship to co-chairman Milton Dudley and plans to resign from the board at the end of the year.
Dudley praised her for “carrying the weight of the board” for at least eight years. In recent months, Wall has led board members in preparing updated ordinances for voters’ approval.
With the seat vacated by Dwaine Drummond when he retired in August still vacant, the five-member planning board will soon have only three members, Dudley, Bruce Fitzgerald and Peter Nelson, and an alternate, Jennifer Chase.
China Planning Board members are appointed by the select board. Any resident who is interested in serving on the board should contact the town office.
The next regular China Planning Board meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m., Tuesday, Nov. 10, in the China town office meeting room. All meetings are open to the public.

title: Bangor Mall tenants seek alternatives after zero-warning condemnation
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - The sudden condemnation of the Bangor Mall is leaving business owners and non-profit leaders scrambling ahead of the busy holiday season.
The City of Bangor condemned the mall Monday, citing significant health and safety code violations—specifically unsafe electrical conditions, inoperable heating, and a lack of working public restrooms.
While anchor stores JCPenney and Dick’s Sporting Goods remain open through their exterior entrances, all interior mall concourse access is blocked.
Logan Bard, founding member of Some Theater Company says the non-profit has been a mall tenant since 2020 and had zero warning before the doors were locked ahead of their major December production of Les Misérables.
“We love performing there. We felt it was a great central location. We know that over the last year or so, there have been issues that have arisen about the mall in terms concerns about safety and the state of the building. We’re always hopeful that things could be resolved as spaces are not easy to come by, and we just love providing such amazing theater for the community. We’re hopeful that there might be some resolutions in the future. It may not be a forever thing, but we can never hope and put all our hopes on that,” said Bard.
Bard also says that community outreach has been phenomenal, with Morgan Hill Event Center stepping in to offer space.
The company says it will contact ticket holders as it finalizes a performance venue for next month’s production.
The Bangor Mall Craft Fair, a huge draw for locals and vendors across New England, will still be taking place this weekend and the following weekend.
It will be located in the former Furniture Mattresses and More space.

title: Celtics survive a scare from Bucks before collecting win
text:
BOSTON — Paul George scored 25 points and had five 3-pointers, Derrick White added 24 points and seven assists, and the Boston Celtics beat the Milwaukee Bucks 109-102 on Wednesday night.
Tyler Herro scored 18 of his 25 points during the third quarter for the Bucks, who fell to 1-7, including 0-4 on the road. Jaime Jaquez Jr. added 18 points.
Baylor Scheierman had nine points and 11 rebounds off the bench for the Celtics, who survived a scare after being pushed by one of the NBA’s weaker teams.
Boston never trailed through three quarters, opening a 22-point advantage in the second, leading by 21 at halftime and eight entering the fourth. Milwaukee’s best stretch came during the third quarter, with a 26-12 run to make it a single-digit game.
When Ryan Rollins slammed home two of his 13 points, the Bucks trailed 91-89 with 8:17 remaining. George threw the ball away coming out of a timeout, and Nate Ament of Milwaukee raced the other way for a layup that made it 91-91.
The Bucks took their first lead at 92-91 when Ament hit a free throw. With leading scorer Jayson Tatum watching from the bench and Payton Pritchard missing the final quarter because of what the team called a right eye abrasion, the Celtics’ search for late-game offense was answered when White converted a three-point play that put Boston up 102-97 with 2:22 left.
Boston outscored Milwaukee 12-5 over the final three minutes. The Celtics shot 41% from 3-point range (16 of 39) and improved to 5-0 at home.
Tatum (rest) was sidelined for the first time this season. The All-Star forward was coming off a 19-point game during Monday’s 109-93 loss to the Houston Rockets.
Up next
Bucks: Host Toronto on Friday night
Celtics: Open a four-game trip at Charlotte on Friday night

title: Reigning 3-time America East women’s soccer champ UMaine hosts Albany for quarterfinal
text:
Isabella Meadows scored 174 goals in her four-year All-State and All-Region career at Pope Francis Preparatory School in Springfield, Massachusetts, before spending two years at the University of Connecticut.
But in two seasons at UConn, she appeared in only seven games for a combined total of 123 minutes.
Meadows transferred to the University of Maine and has regained her scoring touch, leading the Black Bears in goals with seven and points with 16 to earn All-America East first team honors heading into Thursday’s 7 p.m. America East quarterfinal matchup with Albany at the New Balance Soccer Complex in Orono.
UMaine will be seeking a fourth consecutive conference tourney title and NCAA Tournament berth.
Third seed UMaine is 7-5-4 overall and 4-2-2 in the conference while sixth seed Albany is 5-7-3 and 3-3-2. UMaine beat Albany 2-0 in Orono on Sept. 20, but the Great Danes are unbeaten in their last four games, going 2-0-2.
Junior Meadows was joined on the All-America East first team by senior midfielder Abbey Thornton of Windham, junior defender Olivia Grisdale and senior Luise Reinwald, who was also chosen as the Midfielder of the Year.
It was the first time since 2005 that UMaine had put four players on the first team and also had a Midfielder of the Year. Marie-Andree Canuel won it in 2005.
UMaine head coach Scott Atherley said Meadows has always been a natural goal scorer, and she has regained her confidence after a “valuable experience last spring” in the program after she transferred following the first semester.
“She has good instincts around the goal,” Atherley said. “She knows how to time her runs and how to get into the right spaces.”
He also said she can score with both feet, and she has good speed.
She has two game-winning goals.
“She has been a great find for us,” Atherley added.
Reinwald had three goals and an assist, and Atherley called her the “engine” that makes the team go.
“She does a number of things that have been so impactful for us,” Atherley said. “She wins every second ball, she has exceptional field vision and she knows how to get out of pressure. She can really track the ball.”
Reinwald was an All-America East second team pick a year ago and an All-Rookie team selection her freshman year.
Grisdale has anchored a UMaine defense that has allowed just one goal per game and has held opponents to one goal or less 12 times.
She also has an assist.
“She has exceptional composure,” Atherley said. “She is a converted midfielder so she has a midfielder’s vision. She can see the whole field. She also has excellent speed.”
Thornton has had her best season at UMain, according to Atherley. She had two goals and a team-high five assists.
“She knows how to play off other people,” Atherley said. “And she wins a lot of first and second balls.”
He also said she is surprisingly strong.
Thornton, Reinwald and goalkeeper Elena Barenberg were chosen to the league’s All-Academic team.
Aja Turner (3 goals, 2 assists) and Oklahoma State transfer Sandrine Breault (2 goals, 3 assists) are also among UMaine’s top scorers. Barenberg has a 1.00 goals-against average and a .758 save percentage with four shutouts.
Albany has been led by Sydney Kofton (3 goals, 2 assists) and Kiara Levac (3 goals, 1 assist) along with AE All-Rookie Team choices forward Oluchi Njoku and defender Lila Algarin. Goalkeeper Claudia Volino has a 1.97 GAA, a .698 save percentage and three shutouts.

title: Adam Hamilton projected to become first Democratic US senator for Kansas in 94 years
text:
TOPEKA, Kan. (AP) — Adam Hamilton, a Democrat and Methodist megachurch pastor, won a startling upset in Kansas over Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, flipping a seat once believed to be safely red in another example of how far unhappiness with President Donald Trump has spread throughout the nation.
Hamilton’s victory was historic for snapping a 94-year losing streak in Senate races for Kansas Democrats — the nation’s longest — and because spending on the campaign was around $110 million, easily a record in low-cost Kansas. Republicans attempted a massive rescue effort for Marshall, including two Trump rallies in the state in October, but weren’t able to save his attempt at a second term.
“This is amazing. We really did make history,” Hamilton told his supporters. “We’re not flyover country. We’re the heart of the country.”
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
In his concession speech in Wichita, Marshall said, “I don’t have any answers” and promised to “keep fighting for this great nation.” He called serving in the Senate “the great honor of my life.”
Hamilton won among the state’s moderate voters, with roughly 7 in 10 backing him over Marshall. Marshall only won about one-quarter of this group, down from about 4 in 10 in 2020, according to the AP Voter Poll.
Also, roughly 8 in 10 voters under 30 backed Hamilton. Marshall split that group with his Democratic opponent during his first Senate race in 2020.
Hamilton appealed to voters frustrated with the rising cost of living and unhappy with Trump’s handling of the economy and the war with Iran. He also promised to combat the intense partisanship in Washington. In his victory speech from a Kansas City-area hotel, Hamilton said people were also upset with cuts in health care and food assistance, and President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
“I think the people in Kansas, Republicans and Democrats, are saying that what’s happening in Washington is not OK,” Hamilton said. “Kansans are also fed up with the way politicians divide us.”
Hamilton’s fundraising far outstripped Marshall’s — particularly when it came to contributions from Kansas residents — and Democratic groups poured tens of millions of dollars into the state. It helped the party overcome efforts by Trump and Vice President JD Vance to animate Trump’s political base with rallies down the stretch in Kansas.
Hamilton is the founding pastor of the 25,000-member Church of the Resurrection in the Kansas City area, the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation. He brought to the race a centrist persona, a knack for fundraising and a public profile as the author of several dozen books.
Democrats flip a longtime GOP Senate seat in Kansas
Marshall, a retired obstetrician, was elected to the House in 2016 and won his Senate seat in 2020. He remained loyal to Trump throughout the campaign, defending both the war and Trump’s tariffs.
Republicans spent the final few weeks of the campaign pounding home a traditionally winning message for them: that voting for the Democratic nominee would put liberal Democrats in charge of the Senate. While visiting Topeka, Vance called Hamilton “Chuck Schumer’s stooge,” though Hamilton said repeatedly that he would not support keeping the New York senator as Democratic leader.
With only a nominal primary challenge, Marshall’s campaign didn’t start its ads until late August and his fundraising lagged. Republicans, worried about the national attention that Hamilton was drawing, shifted millions of dollars from North Carolina to Kansas.
Echoing Trump, Marshall blamed high fuel prices on Ukrainian attacks on Russian infrastructure in their war. He repeatedly told voters that the economy was strong and has improved under Trump.
He also faced attacks alleging he had abandoned Kansas to live in Florida. Marshall said he owned a vacation home in Florida so he could spend time with family. Marshall sold the property last month.
Hamilton’s victory bucked decades of Kansas history
The last Democrat to win a Senate race in Kansas was George McGill, a Wichita attorney, in 1932. There hadn’t even been a truly close race since 1974, when future Republican icon Bob Dole won a second term by less than 2 percentage points following the Watergate scandal that forced President Richard Nixon from office.
Republicans portrayed Hamilton as too “woke” for Kansas, in part by highlighting his church’s support for LGBTQ rights. In the campaign’s final weeks, they also focused on two cases of alleged sexual abuse of teenage boys by an adult leader at annual camps for Hamilton’s church, one each in 2005 and 2006.
The church investigated the first incident in 2005 but did not report it to law enforcement when the victims couldn’t positively identify the perpetrator, and the man returned for the 2006 camp. The second incident was reported to law enforcement and the church turned over its records on the first case, but the local prosecutor did not pursue criminal charges.
The church changed its child protection policies and since the 2005 case has required all incidents to be reported to law enforcement. Hamilton acknowledged that it was a mistake for the church not to report the first incident in 2005 and for him to not personally check to see that the man didn’t return in 2006.
However, along with Trump’s drop in popularity nationally, Hamilton benefitted from a recent shift in Kansas politics.
Although the state is often viewed as ruby red, there’s a sizable bloc of moderate voters who have regularly swung governor’s races to Democrats. Suburbs near Kansas City, Missouri, have become increasingly blue, making it easier for Democrats to win statewide races by carrying just the most populous counties.
Hamilton positioned himself in the political center
Hamilton’s comments about Schumer demonstrated the balance he sought to strike in wooing independent and Republican voters. He made a point of describing himself as “independent-minded” and positioned himself as a potential moderate counterweight in Washington.
In another example, he criticized U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement during an event in Topeka but stopped short of calling to abolish the agency.
“They were formed to make sure that people didn’t fly airplanes into buildings again,” he said, referencing the Sept. 11 terror attacks. “If they stick to what they were created for, I’m grateful for them.”
His campaign also hammered Marshall — who uses “Doc” on his stationery — over questions about how he pursued unpaid patient bills before he won a U.S. House seat in 2016.
The New York Times reported that Marshall and his practice sued more than 700 patients during his decades-long medical career. In 81 cases, patients were arrested for missing court dates, and two experts called his tactics extreme, according to the report. During a televised debate, Marshall called attacks on him a “gross mischaracterization” of his professional record.
Many voters appeared concerned about Marshall’s character because of questions about his past debt-collection practices, AP VoteCast found. A slim majority said Marshall did not have the right personal character to serve in the Senate.
—-
This story has been updated to correct that Marshall was elected to the House in 2016, not 2017.

title: Democrats clinch control of US Senate as party notches several major wins
text:
Democrats clinch control of US Senate as Americans signal dissatisfaction with Trump, GOP
The Democrats have clinched control of the U.S. Senate.
The flip in the balance of power ends the Republican Party’s two-year control of the upper chamber. It also signals the American electorate's dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and the first two years of his second term.
Democratic candidates flipped Republican-held seats in North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Texas, South Carolina and Kansas, where the president had personally chosen the GOP nominees or tried to rally voters on their behalf with campaign stops.
The results were also a major reprimand from voters of Trump, who repeatedly urged voters to "pretend I'm on the ballot" as he went into primarily conservative states to shore up Republican candidates and warned of a Washington where Democrats were in power. As he tried to personalize the midterm campaign, Trump also defended his policies on tariffs and the war with Iran that drove up prices.
With Democrats in control, Trump’s legislative priorities will likely be stonewalled, and oversight of the administration will increase. They can also stymie his nominations to Cabinet posts and lifetime federal judgeships.
Trump tried to shift the blame away from himself during a Fox News interview that aired early Wednesday, saying Democrats "did a good job" in their campaigns and blamed GOP candidates for losses.
Trump's choices for GOP races had their own baggage
Despite urging voters to use their imagination when reading names on the ballot, Trump's hand-picked Republican candidates in Texas and South Carolina faced deep skepticism.
Republican Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina after a campaign in which she faced questions about her inexperience.
Republican Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico in Texas, was impeached by his own party over corruption accusations and stained by a very public divorce. But Trump backed him instead of powerful incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, whom he viewed as not sufficiently supportive.
Trump's loyalty pressures also led incumbent Republican Sen. Thom Tillis in North Carolina to decide to retire after clashing with the president. To try to keep that seat in GOP hands, Trump backed his close ally Michael Whatley, who lost to Democrat Roy Cooper.
Trump was also dealt twin defeats in two Midwestern states that had borne the brunt of high diesel prices and his tariff war. Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Roger Marshall in Kansas, while Republican Ashley Hinson lost to Democrat Josh Turek.
In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown regained his Senate seat that he lost two years ago, defeating appointed Republican Sen. Jon Husted in a state in which Trump and Vice President JD Vance repeatedly campaigned.
With Husted, Trump had an odd fixation on his physique, frequently admiring the former football player's body during campaign rallies in Ohio and elsewhere around the country.
Democrats on Tuesday also retained a key Senate seat in Georgia where another one of Trump's endorsed candidates faced controversy.
In that race, Democrat Jon Ossoff defeated Republican Mike Collins, a Trump acolyte who struggled to defend against his ties to white nationalists and an unresolved House ethics investigation.
In 2024, Trump won all seven states — Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina, Ohio, Georgia, Iowa and Kansas.
In another sign of Republican weakness, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, whom Trump had endorsed and repeatedly praised. On Tuesday night, Trump posted on social media that Abbott was to blame for his loss, calling him a "RINO" — a Republican in name only.
Voters blame Trump's economic policies
Placing himself front and center on voters' minds was a major gamble by the president and his political team, who believed it would drive "Make America Great Again" supporters to the polls. Democrats were eager to watch the unpopular president insert himself so fully in the campaign, believing it served as an effective reminder of who should be blamed for the state of the economy.
"Trump's desire to have everyone think that he's on the ballot? Like, it's happening," said Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., who campaigned in key battlegrounds this fall, including Iowa, Georgia and Texas. "Everyone is thinking about him and the harm that he has done to them directly."
The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of the midterm electorate, showed relatively few voters have positive things to say about Trump's performance on the economy. About two-thirds of voters nationally say Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., while only about 3 in 10 said they've improved economic conditions. Similarly, about two-thirds of voters say Trump's tariff policies have "hurt" the national economy, or the economy in their local area.
Views of Trump's priorities more broadly — and his capabilities as a leader — were also mostly negative. More than half of voters say Trump is not a strong leader, does not fight for people like them, does not have the right priorities and does not have the mental capability to serve effectively as president. About 6 in 10 voters say Trump places a higher priority on his own personal interests than he does the country's interests, while about 4 in 10 said he puts more weight on the country's interests.
The president — who faced a Democratic-led House for the latter half of his first term — campaigned aggressively in the final weeks to keep the Republican majorities on Capitol Hill because he knows what the consequences would be if Democrats seize power.
But the president at times shrugged off the prospect of a Republican loss of power in Congress. The president is also keenly aware of the political power he draws from having a foil, leveraging opposition to consolidate support in his party and boost fundraising.
From investigations to impeachment, the stakes for Trump are high
Senior Democrats, as they anticipated a majority in at least one chamber of Congress, have been telegraphing what their top investigative targets would be: the Trump administration's policies, the conduct of its personnel, and interactions between government officials and private corporations who've tried to wield influence with the White House.
Among their priorities are the Trump family's business dealings, the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and broader allegations of corporate corruption.
A Democratic majority will be armed with control of committees, bigger budgets and staff, and subpoena powers that could compel the administration to be responsive to Congress. In response, the White House could reprise its strategy from the first Trump administration, when it slow-walked congressional requests for documents and testimony and asserted executive privilege over certain information.
The president is also bracing for major legislative fights, saying he has a "strong veto." On Tuesday night, Trump posted a picture of his signature red ball cap with "VETO" stitched on it.

title: Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz described as 'cheaters' at trial
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz were described by a prosecutor Wednesday as “cheaters” during opening statements at a New York criminal fraud trial that has cast a spotlight on the threat gamblers pose to America’s pastime.
Assistant U.S. Attorney Rebecca Urquiola told a jury in Brooklyn that Clase befriended a sports betting gambler in the Dominican Republic in early 2023 who shared his interest in dominoes and cockfighting, which is legal in his home country.
Clase eventually agreed to tell “his new friend” what kinds of pitches he would throw in certain games, enabling gamblers to reap at least $460,000 on platforms that allow customers to bet on whether a pitch would be a ball or a strike, she said.
“The defendants, Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz, are cheaters,” Urquiola told jurors. She said they “sold their pitches.”
Clase, the Guardians’ former star closer, and Ortiz, a starter, have pleaded not guilty to conspiracy charges and are on non-disciplinary leave from the club without pay while facing prosecution. They were arrested in November 2025 and have been free on bail since.
Prosecutors said Clase began providing information about his pitches to bettors in 2023 and recruited Ortiz into the scheme in 2025.
Clase, 28, is a three-time All-Star and two-time American League Reliever of the Year who had completed the fourth season of a $20 million, five-year contract when conspiracy and fraud charges against the pitchers were made public in November 2025.
Ortiz, 27, earned $782,600 as a starting pitcher for the Guardians during the 2025 season.
Urquiola said Clase saw gamblers profiting from his pitches and “decided it wasn’t enough to help his friends make money,” so he asked for kickbacks.
She said text messages in which the pitchers described rigged pitches and bets, sometimes using code words such as “chicken” or “rooster,” along with testimony from some gamblers, would prove the government’s case.
Defense lawyers, however, said their clients were innocent and that a gambler who befriended Clase falsely claimed to other gamblers that the pitcher was providing inside information on his pitches and tried to sell them the information.
Michael Bronson, an attorney for Clase, said his client attended school until age 15 in a small coastal village in the Dominican Republic before focusing on baseball and becoming “a standout, a superstar” with a reputation for shutting down teams in the final inning of games.
He said Clase was 25 in the spring of 2023 when he met a 41-year-old gambler, Enoc Pena, who made over 7,000 bets from 2023 to 2025 and had a history of lying to get what he wanted.
Pena “didn’t see a peer, a friend. He saw a mark,” Bronson said.
Soon Pena was bringing Clase food and picking him up at the airport in the Dominican Republic, the lawyer said. The pitcher, in turn, gave him tickets to Guardians games and loaned him money.
As Pena bragged to fellow gamblers that he was close to Clase and tried to sell them information, he was actually guessing which pitches Clase would throw in games and managed with fellow gamblers to lose over 200 bets on Clase’s pitches, the lawyer said.
Pena was “selling lies,” Bronson said, urging jurors to ask themselves if his client would risk “a fortune and his lifelong dream over a few thousand dollars.”
Attorney Samuel Landes, representing Ortiz, told jurors in an opening statement that the pitcher had no contact with gamblers and that only two of his pitches, both balls, are at stake in the trial.
“That’s not a conspiracy. That’s just baseball,” he said.
At one point, Landes asked his client to stand as he introduced him to the jury. Ortiz stood up and waved.
Landes said Ortiz was victimized by Pena’s lies, including allegations that the pitcher — who had received $1.7 million in advance for future contracts and stood to make millions more — had accepted $5,000 for tips about his pitches.
“Why would Luis Ortiz throw all that away for $5,000? He would not,” he said.
Landes said Pena had struck a deal with prosecutors allowing him to avoid prison and stay in the U.S. despite lying to banks and about his marital status on immigration forms.
Although Pena was once listed as a possible witness at the trial, prosecutors said last week that they did not intend to put him on the witness stand.

title: Vote-scanning malfunction expected to delay vote counting in competitive congressional district until Wednesday
text:
(AP) - A judge has granted permission for elections officials in a major New York county to move thousands of paper ballots to a secure warehouse after a technical problem caused vote-scanning machines to malfunction.
The issue will delay the counting of votes in a competitive congressional district until at least Wednesday.
The New York Board of Elections said machines at locations throughout Westchester County would not accept paper ballots when polls opened Tuesday because of a programming glitch.
Elections officials said the problem happened when they made a software update for one municipal contest after the machines had been prepared and tested. Machines in the other municipalities continued to use the original software and therefore would not recognize the ballots.
Voters were instructed to put completed ballots in bags that would be safeguarded to be processed later. The bags were to be transported under police escort to a county warehouse to be scanned and counted under the supervision of representatives of political parties, election officials said.
The Westchester County Board of Elections said the ballot counting was to begin at 11 a.m. Wednesday.
Westchester County is considered the more liberal-leaning part of New York’s 17th Congressional District, which featured a competitive race between GOP Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley.
Lawler and Conley implored residents to cast their ballots despite the problem and stressed that all votes would be counted.
Lawler said the situation had caused “a lot of frustration, delays, lines and a lot of questions.” But he added at a news conference: “I want to be clear. There’s no shenanigans going on here.”
Despite the delayed counting, Lawler conceded defeat late Tuesday. The Associated Press had not called the race as of early Wednesday.
“When all of the votes are counted tomorrow in Westchester, it’s going to be pretty clear that we will be short,” he said.
Westchester resident Toni Chrystal said she felt “uneasy” after casting her vote Tuesday morning amid the ballot issues.
The real estate broker from White Plains said she completed her ballot around 7 a.m. and then dropped it into one of the designated ballot bags at her polling location as instructed.
“Westchester is one of the richest counties in the state. How does this happen?” she said. “How come they weren’t tested yesterday or a week before? Early voting worked. How does it not work now?”
___
Associated Press writers Anthony Izaguirre and Michael R. Sisak contributed to this report.

title: 3 executions scheduled for the same day in Indiana, Florida and Alabama
text:
An Indiana man who admitted killing two children in a house fire was set to be executed in the first of three lethal injections scheduled for Thursday in the U.S.
Florida and Alabama were also set to carry out executions, which would mark the second time this year that three people would be put to death on the same day. The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following Tennessee’s failed execution of Christa Pike, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital last month.
It will be Florida’s 19th execution this year under Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis — matching a record set by the state in 2025 — but the first this year in Indiana, where the death penalty is not as common.
Lawyers had asked for life sentence for Indiana man
Jeffrey Weisheit was convicted of setting a fire that killed his girlfriend’s two children, ages 8 and 5, at a home in the Evansville area in 2010, murders apparently related to the couple’s deteriorating relationship.
Lawyers wanted Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison.
Weisheit’s latest objection centered on the state’s planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said it’s confident “in our ability to humanely carry out” the execution.
Florida on the verge of tying last year’s execution record
In Florida, Jesse Guardado confessed and quickly pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to support his drug habit. She had helped him get a job and housing.
A federal appeals court in 2024 said Guardado, now 64, had received a “full and fair” hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.
Florida has carried out more than half the 32 total executions in the U.S. so far this year. DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has said his goal is to bring justice to families who have waited decades for the death sentences to be carried out.
Alabama man convicted for killings when he was 19
Michael Taylor, 54, faces execution in Alabama, 35 years after fatally beating an older couple with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden home. Police arrested the 19-year-old with the victims’ Cadillac, an hour away in Birmingham. The execution would be the state’s third this year.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor’s sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings. She declined.
“If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life who it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today,” said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.
The state plans to execute Taylor by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.
____
Fischer reported from Fort Lauderdale, Florida and Chandler from Montgomery, Alabama. Associated Press reporter Ed White contributed from Detroit.

title: North Korea launches unidentified projectile toward the sea
text:
North Korea launches unidentified projectile toward the sea
North Korea launched an unidentified projectile toward the sea on Wednesday, South Korea's military said, adding to a recent series of provocative weapons demonstrations by Pyongyang.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said the launch happened off North Korea's east coast but gave no further details, including what type of weapon was fired.
In recent weeks, North Korea has ramped up its weapons tests in a likely bid to increase its leverage in potential diplomacy with the U.S. after President Donald Trump expressed his desire to restore diplomacy with Kim Jong Un.
The latest launch also came a day after North Korea denied involvement in the recent cryptocurrency heist at Binance, dismissing as “a trite provocation” a U.S. announcement that North Korean hackers were behind the incident.
Related video above: President Donald Trump: "We don't know if it's North Korea"
Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, said Friday that hackers stole more than $6 billion in what appears to be the largest cryptocurrency heist on record. The FBI later said the theft was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, attributing the attack to a hacking group known as TraderTraitor, which was also behind a $1.5 billion hack of the Bybit exchange last year.
On Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, issued another statement criticizing the FBI announcement, saying Pyongyang views it as “an extension of Washington’s invariable hostile policy toward” North Korea.
“It is our clear stand that we have no need to sit face to face with such unreliable and hostile persons,” she said. “The choice for peace includes dialogue of course, but this is not surely equated with national interests for us.”

title: Kittery elects town councilors, school committee members
text:
Kittery residents reelected two town councilors in a three-way competition while also voting in new school committee members in an uncontested race.
TOWN COUNCIL
Incumbents Megan Greenwood and Scott Mason were elected to the Town Council, earning 3,925 and 2,504 votes, respectively, defeating challenger William Peirce, who garnered 1,346 votes.
Both Mason and Greenwood were seeking their second terms. They’ll start their new terms immediately.
SCHOOL COMMITTEE
This election cycle’s school committee race was uncontested.
First-time candidates Edie Davis Quinn and Carol James will join the six-member board as Eric Lamont finishes his term on Election Day. Quinn and James earned 3,677 and 3,198 votes, respectively, and will serve three-year terms.

title: Fort Kent and Wisdom Sweep Four Northern Maine Soccer Championships
text:
Four Games, Four Championships: Fort Kent and Wisdom Sweep Northern Maine Soccer Finals
Four games. Four victories. Four Northern Maine championships.
Tuesday was a remarkable day for Aroostook County high school soccer, as both Fort Kent and Wisdom sent their boys and girls teams into regional championship games and all four came away with victories.
And they did it in four very different ways.
Fort Kent's boys needed just 36 seconds of overtime to knock off top-seeded Orono, Wisdom's boys survived a nine-goal championship game, Wisdom's girls got a hat trick from Ellie Cyr, and Fort Kent's girls captured their fourth consecutive regional championship with another impressive defensive performance.
By the end of the evening, four more County teams had punched their tickets to Saturday's state championships.
Here's how Tuesday's Northern Maine regional finals played out.
Girls Soccer
Class C North: Fort Kent Captures Fourth Straight Regional Championship
(1) Fort Kent 3, (2) Orono 0
Four years. Four regional championships.
The Fort Kent Lady Warriors are heading back to the Class C state championship after defeating second-seeded Orono 3-0 Tuesday evening at Hampden Academy.
Fort Kent struck early, and its defense took care of the rest.
Reece Doucette scored twice for the Lady Warriors, while Hayden Plourde added the other goal.
Goalkeeper Trinity Daigle and the Fort Kent defense kept Orono off the scoreboard, securing the shutout and another Northern Maine title.
It was a complete performance from a Fort Kent team that has been one of the most consistent programs in Northern Maine girls soccer.
The Lady Warriors entered the championship after defeating Houlton 5-0 in the semifinals, and Tuesday's victory gave them another shutout against one of the region's top teams.
Now Fort Kent will have an opportunity to bring home a state championship.
The Lady Warriors will face Maranacook, which advanced out of Class C South with a 1-0 victory over Mount Abram.
Four consecutive regional titles are an impressive accomplishment for any program, and Fort Kent has another opportunity to add to that success Saturday.
Eight-Player North: Ellie Cyr's Hat Trick Sends Wisdom to States
(2) Wisdom 3, (1) Dexter 1
Wisdom's girls are Northern Maine champions.
The second-seeded Lady Pioneers earned a 3-1 victory over top-seeded Dexter Tuesday evening at Brewer High School, completing an impressive tournament run and securing their place in Saturday's Eight-Player state championship.
Ellie Cyr delivered another outstanding performance, scoring all three Wisdom goals.
Lakiah Lee scored Dexter's lone goal.
Wisdom's defense was a major part of the victory, limiting the Tigers to one goal and protecting the lead throughout the championship matchup.
The Lady Pioneers had entered Tuesday after defeating previously unbeaten Sumner 5-0 in the semifinals.
That meant Wisdom had to get past two of the region's strongest teams to bring home the Northern Maine championship.
And they did exactly that.
Wisdom will now play for the Eight-Player state championship Saturday in Presque Isle against Southern Maine champion Bangor Christian.
For a program from the St. John Valley, the opportunity to compete for a state championship in Aroostook County makes the next game even more special.
Boys Soccer
Class C North: Dominic Cyr Delivers Overtime Winner for Fort Kent
(3) Fort Kent 2, (1) Orono 1 (Overtime)
Some championship games are decided by a single moment.
For Fort Kent's boys, that moment came just 36 seconds into overtime Tuesday afternoon.
Dominic Cyr converted a penalty kick to give the third-seeded Warriors a dramatic 2-1 victory over top-seeded Orono in the Class C North regional championship at Hampden Academy.
It was an exciting finish to a well-played game between two teams that had battled throughout the afternoon.
Orono struck first when Gabe Lule scored in the 18th minute, giving the Red Riots a 1-0 advantage.
Fort Kent continued to battle, and Cyr delivered the equalizer in the second half to send the game into overtime.
The extra period barely had time to get started before Cyr came through again.
His penalty kick sent Fort Kent into celebration and secured the Northern Maine championship.
It was the second consecutive dramatic tournament finish for the Warriors, who had advanced past George Stevens Academy in the semifinals on penalty kicks.
This time, Fort Kent didn't need a shootout.
The Warriors will now face Hall-Dale in Saturday's Class C state championship after Hall-Dale defeated Mount Abram 2-1 in the Southern Maine final.
And with the Fort Kent girls also winning their regional championship Tuesday, both Warrior soccer teams will be playing for state titles on Saturday.
Eight-Player North: Wisdom Boys Win Nine-Goal Championship Game
(3) Wisdom 5, (4) Piscataquis 4
Wisdom's boys made sure the Pioneers would have two teams heading to the state championships.
The third-seeded Pioneers defeated fourth-seeded Piscataquis 5-4 Tuesday afternoon at Brewer High School to capture the Eight-Player North regional championship.
It was a high-scoring championship matchup, with nine goals between the two teams and Wisdom coming away with the one-goal victory.
The Pioneers had already survived a dramatic semifinal against Calais, advancing on penalty kicks after goalkeeper Bentley Nadeau stopped the final Calais attempt.
Tuesday brought another close finish, but the result was the same.
Wisdom found a way to win.
The Pioneers will now face Telstar in Saturday's Eight-Player state championship after Telstar defeated Pine Tree Academy 5-1 to capture the Southern Maine title.
And just like Fort Kent, Wisdom will have both its boys and girls teams competing for state championships.
That's quite an accomplishment for a small school, and another reason Saturday is shaping up to be a memorable day for the St. John Valley.
The 2026 MPA Soccer Championships on 101.9 The Rock are proudly presented by Pineland Farms in Mars Hill.

title: How Troy Jackson will turn a 100-day campaign into a working Senate office
text:
This story is for subscribers only. Subscribers and donors help fund BDN’s in-depth political analysis, campaign finance investigations, and first-in-the-nation race calls. All election results, live analysis and voting information are free to access as a public service. Subscribe for $1 for 3 months right now.
After upsetting U.S. Sen. Susan Collins on Tuesday in a historic Democratic takeover of Congress, Sen-elect Troy Jackson must rapidly build a transition team before taking office in early January.
The former logger from Allagash and Maine Senate president is no stranger to a quick turnaround. His Senate bid rose from the ashes of a third-place gubernatorial run after oyster farmer Graham Platner’s campaign collapsed in scandal. Jackson charged through a 100-day, 100-plus event campaign to topple Maine’s most powerful political figure.
Organizers who helped Jackson’s rise to Capitol Hill say they expect to be involved in continuing conversations with the senator-elect’s team over the next two months and beyond. Former staffers for Maine’s federal officials say they expect a whirlwind of moves to prepare Jackson for the transition and enable him to help constituents as quickly as possible.
“People expect their senators to be fully functional, and there’s 400 things you have to do in a fairly short, intense period, and none of them are easy,” Kay Rand, the longtime chief of staff for independent U.S. Sen. Angus King in his current office and as Maine governor.
Rand likened it to starting a small business in weeks. The Democrat must hire 30 to 40 people split between Maine offices and Washington, including a solid administrative director who knows the inner workings of the Senate and can help Jackson secure limited office space. He will make choices between loyal Maine Democrats or floaters who specialize in policy in Washington.
He also must make decisions on field office locations, talk to Senate leaders to lobby for desired committees and find a place to live in Washington while officially closing down his huge campaign. Jackson has expressed interest in serving on several committees, including the appropriations panel that Collins chairs. But it’s unlikely he gets every assignment he wants.
King, who was elected to the Senate in 2012, did not move into a full office suite in the Dirksen Senate Office Building until June 2013, Rand remembered. Freshmen senators are often “crunched for space” and often meet with constituents in cafeterias. Jackson’s team will have to establish systems for correspondence, and legislative and policy teams.
“It was a slog, but it’s exciting,” she said.
Jackson could choose to keep Collins’ six field offices across the state or shake things up, Lance Dutson, a former Collins staffer, said. King kept a number of Republican former Sen. Olympia Snowe’s field office staffers, but that’s less likely given the bitter campaign and inherent differences between Collins’ and Jackson’s teams, Dutson said.
The newcomer must also manage the transfer of a constituent service caseload, as senators handle hundreds of cases on Social Security, Veterans Affairs benefits and more. Dutson expected a smooth transition on that front.
“Collins and her team are super diligent on constituent services,” he said. “I would guess despite the party conflict, Jackson is probably going to get handed stuff in a very neat and orderly way.”
Neither Jackson nor Collins spoke publicly Wednesday, but the senator already alluded to the next steps for her and her successor’s teams: “I called Troy Jackson tonight to congratulate him and to assure him that my staff and I will work to ensure a smooth transition,” she said in a statement early Wednesday morning.
King’s office said it had been in contact with both Collins’ and Jackson’s teams as of Wednesday afternoon.
Jason Shedlock, a Jackson confidant and president of the Maine Building and Construction Trades Council, said conversations among labor groups and the senator-elect’s team are sure to ramp up over the next couple of weeks. Engagement with unions will come “before, during and after” the transition, just like it did during the snap nominating race.
“What this campaign did was shed some light for the public in his relationship with labor, but that’s not new,” Shedlock said.

title: 'Everlasting Love' singer Steve Ellis dies at 76
text:
'Everlasting Love' singer Steve Ellis dies at 76
'Everlasting Love' singer Steve Ellis dies at 76
English singer Steve Ellis, known for single "Everlasting Love," died on Friday, Oct. 30. He was 76.
Ellis' death was confirmed on his Facebook page. Although an exact cause of death was not given, the post mentioned that he died "after complications from a chronic illness."
The post also said, "Steve peacefully left the world on the evening of October 30, 2026, in the presence of his loved ones."
He fronted the group Love Affair, which formed in 1966. In January 1968, the British pop group's hit single "Everlasting Love," a cover, knocked the Beatles' hit "Hello, Goodbye" off the top of the charts and surpassed the American original version sung by Robert Knight. Love Affair also had three more Top 10 singles in the U.K., including "Rainbow Valley," "A Day Without Love" and "Bringing on Back the Good Times."
Ellis eventually pursued a solo career in the 1970s and formed his own band with his moniker, Ellis. His music career continued with the group Widowmaker, which saw mild success until the early '80s.
He had a freak accident with a forklift that destroyed his feet, and Ellis spent the next decade in physical therapy. He eventually returned to music.
He performed regularly before his death and recorded several albums, including "A Sort of Innocence," "Best of Days," "The Love Affair is Over" and "Boom! Bang! Twang!"

title: Republican Ashley Moody wins reelection to U.S. Senate from Florida
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Ashley Moody won election Tuesday to the U.S. Senate representing Florida, defeating Democrat Angie Nixon.
Moody first took the seat when Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis tapped her to succeed Marco Rubio when he became U.S. secretary of state in 2025.
A former state attorney general, Moody will serve the last two years of the term Rubio won in 2022.
Nixon, a state lawmaker, is a democratic socialist who tested the strength of Democrats’ left flank in a state where the party has not won a U.S. Senate seat since 2012.
Nixon upset establishment Democrats’ more moderate favorite in the primary. Her general election loss is unlikely to help heal the struggling state party’s internal rift.
The Associated Press declared Moody the winner at 8:34 p.m. EST.

title: Coach Sinclair says he’s grateful for community support as his son is on the brink of returning home
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - This week, Bob Sinclair is doing more than preparing for a championship game, he’s getting ready to welcome his son back home.
On September 30th, his son Tyler was rushed to the hospital after suffering a medical emergency.
“In the middle of the game, he calls me over and he says, I’m having a hard time feeling my foot. He said, I can’t, you know, pick my foot up. It feels numb,”
Tyler suffered a tear in his aorta and was taken in for emergency heart surgery.
“We got it in the nick of time. Thank goodness, thank God. And surgery was successful,” said Sinclair. “He’s a fighter, kid’s a fighter. And he came out of that. and we could feel that we were getting our son back,” Sinclair added.
Coach Sinclair says that the family was flooded with cards, donations poured in, and a meal train was set up.
“When your back’s against the wall, um, in this community, people come out of the woodwork to support you,” said Sinclair.
One of those people is Bob’s friend Rodney.
The two of them worked together to build Tyler a ramp for his return home.
“He’s a retired carpenter and he’s forgotten more about this kind of work than I’ll ever know. I mean, I’m kind of a hack, but he really knows what he’s doing. So I paid attention with him through this project and, uh, very grateful for his, for his help,” said Sinclair.
While Tyler is not ready to come home yet, he does want to greet the team before they load onto the bus Friday night as they get ready to play in the Northern Maine Championship.

title: Sartoris appears on path to reelection as Cumberland County DA
text:
PORTLAND — Democratic incumbent Jacqueline Sartoris has won reelection against challenger Stephanie Anderson in the race for Cumberland County District Attorney.
Across 28 municipalities, Sartoris won by roughly 37,000 votes: 99,178 to 61,527.
“I’m humbled and grateful at the overwhelming support by Cumberland County voters of the progress we’ve made here in adopting pragmatic reform,” Sartoris said in a statement. “I promise to work for everyone to create a more just Cumberland County for all.”
Anderson, the district attorney for 28 years before retiring in 2018, framed her campaign as necessary to restore order at the district attorney’s office.
Anderson, who is now unenrolled but was a registered Republican throughout her six terms as district attorney, said prosecutors and defense attorneys “across the political spectrum” approached her asking her to run. When she entered the race, she said she would drop out if Sartoris lost the primary.
Sartoris, a Democrat from Brunswick, won her party’s nomination in a June primary against one of her former prosecutors.
Elected in 2022, Sartoris has at times been on the defensive. Anderson claimed that the district attorney’s office has been in disarray under Sartoris, leading to a loss of accountability that’s now reflected on Portland streets.
Anderson said in a written statement Wednesday that she was proud of her campaign for exceeding expectations and scrutinizing Sartoris’ leadership.
“Overcoming the partisan politics that have come to define this county was always going to be difficult, but the issues we raised are too important to ignore,” she said. “My hope is that the scrutiny our campaign brought will inspire (Sartoris) to change course, place victims and public safety first while protecting the rights of the accused, and repair relationships with her staff, defense attorneys and law enforcement.”
Throughout the campaign, Sartoris rebuffed claims from Anderson that the county and the district attorney’s office has devolved into turmoil. During a recent forum, she said her office has emphasized “a return to charging” following a pandemic-era dip, and said the county has also seen a decrease in the “return to jail rate,” or people returning to jail within 30 days.
While Anderson said Sartoris was elected as the result of partisan politics, Sartoris continued to cite Anderson’s ties to the Republican Party. After stepping down in 2018, Anderson served as chair of the Cumberland County Republican Committee, ran for the Maine Senate in 2020 and has continued to receive support from Maine conservatives.
Democrats also criticized Anderson for running as an unenrolled candidate, calling it an attempt to distance herself from the Republican Party in a deeply blue county.

title: Roommate of 4 students killed in Idaho says harassment forced her to move repeatedly
text:
Roommate of 4 students killed in Idaho says harassment forced her to move repeatedly
One of the roommates of the four University of Idaho students killed in their home in 2022 says she's endured years of harassment, threats and unfounded accusations and wants to ensure her face is blurred in an upcoming release of investigative video recordings, according to court documents.
Dylan Mortensen, who told police she saw a strange man with bushy eyebrows and a ski mask in the home the night her roommates were killed, detailed the impacts the case has had on her in a court filing in Latah County, saying her life “has changed in ways I never could have imagined.”
Mortensen said in an Oct. 29 affidavit that the “amount of attention and hostility” that she’s received has “affected nearly every aspect” of her life. She said that has forced her and her family to move nine times while enduring “years of hateful messages and threats.”
Related video above: Bryan Kohberger admits to Idaho student murders
Bryan Kohberger was sentenced to life in prison last year after pleading guilty in the Nov. 13, 2022, stabbing deaths that scarred the close-knit community of Moscow, Idaho. He’s currently trying to withdraw that plea.
No motive has emerged for the killings, nor is it clear why Mortensen and another roommate were spared.
Judge Megan Marshall last month ordered the release of records after EWU Media, a company that produces crime documentaries, sued the city of Moscow for them. In Mortensen’s affidavit in support of her motion to intervene in the case, she asks Marshall to help ensure her face is blurred in any police interviews, body-camera footage and other investigative recordings that will be released.
She said people can hear her statements to law enforcement through recordings that have already been released.
“I am already being recognized despite the privacy protections currently in place, and I worry that making additional footage of my face available would make it even easier for strangers to identify me in everyday situations,” Mortensen wrote.
Marshall wrote in an Oct. 20 decision that the city didn’t demonstrate that specific records were properly withheld and ordered the city to disclose them, absent any applicable exemption under the Idaho Public Records Act. Marshall said the act doesn't broadly exempt the identity of witnesses in an investigation.
The Associated Press reached out to the city, via email and phone, Tuesday for comment. The AP also emailed EWU Media and Mortensen's attorney requesting comment.
A motion hearing is set for next week.
Mortensen said she's received “numerous unsolicited messages from strangers accusing me of participating in my friends’ murders, blaming me for their deaths, and making cruel statements about what they believe should happen to me.”
Mortensen said in the affidavit that she used an alias at her job and often introduces herself using a different name. She said she doesn't use her real name for package deliveries because she doesn't want people to know where she lives.
She said that while she knows that there are already photographs and videos online of her and that her identity is publicly known, she believes "there is a significant difference between the photos and videos people have already seen of me and the lengthy police interviews and body-camera recordings taken during one of the most traumatic and vulnerable periods of my life.”
Mortensen said that not only could the release of the "extended footage” of how she talks, reacts and expresses herself make her more recognizable, but that she also does not want her facial expressions used as fodder for people to analyze, criticize or make accusations.
“I want to be able to work, meet new people, attend concerts, celebrate important moments with friends, and enjoy ordinary experiences without constantly worrying about being recognized or confronted,” she wrote.
