title: Legion post, Sew for a Cause launch sixth annual holiday drive for veterans
text:
American Legion Post #126 and the Sew for a Cause charity group are collecting donations through December 4 for their sixth annual Christmas Stocking and Hanukkah Dreidel Drive, which provides holiday care packages for local veterans.
Last year, Sew for a Cause members made 350 Christmas stockings and Hanukkah dreidels, and volunteers filled each one with a customized holiday care package. This year’s goal is to reach 350 local veterans, again.
The stockings and dreidels are delivered to the Togus Outreach Program, which reaches more than 1,500 veterans. Organizers deliver any extra filled stockings to homebound veterans in the area. “Many of them are teary-eyed and thank us,” said Rachel Kilbride, founding volunteer of Sew for a Cause.
The drive is dedicated this year to the memory of Mike Poulin and Doug Grosso, members of Post #126 who died this past year. Both worked on the Togus holiday project for the past five years.
“The success of the project is due to the many people who donate items and volunteer to fill the stockings and to the Sew for a Cause members who make the stockings and dreidels,” Kilbride said.
Requested items include toothpaste and toothbrushes, soap and shaving cream, razors, deodorant, combs, and other personal care items, as well as puzzle books, playing cards, and packaged snacks.
Items may be dropped off at Sew for a Cause, 860 Main St., Vassalboro, or at Connected Credit Union, 12 Monument St., Winslow.
Businesses, sponsors, and residents who want to give money can make checks payable to American Legion Post #126 and mail them to P.O. Box 112, North Vassalboro, ME 04962.
The stockings and dreidels will be filled on a volunteer packing day on Tuesday, December 8, at 1 p.m., at the St. Bridget Center, 864 Main St., Vassalboro. Business partners and community members are invited to help, and no sign-up is needed.
For information about sponsorships, drop-off details, or volunteering, call 616-3148.

title: Former judge arrested for unloading gun at Halloween trick-or-treaters, police say
text:
DUNCAN, Okla. (KSWO/Gray News) - A former judge has been arrested after allegedly unloading a gun in the direction of Halloween trick-or-treaters, according to authorities.
Jerry Herberger, a 73-year-old former Stephens County, Oklahoma, judge, fired at the trick-or-treaters on October 31 at a property.
The Duncan Police Department said that officers responded to the incident at 8.02 p.m. and were directed to the address by witnesses.
When officers arrived, Herberger pointed his firearm at one of the officers at the scene.

Herberger faces multiple charges, including assault and battery with a deadly weapon, attempted murder and possession of a firearm while intoxicated.

title: A Lifeline to Learning feat. Wilton Free Public Library
With second-half comeback, Mt. Ararat field hockey earns big-game experience
text:
Our Communities. Our Teams. Our Future.
We’re proud to make high school sports coverage free for everyone, because these moments matter. At Maine State Credit Union, we’re here for the people and places that make Maine strong. Let’s go! Learn more at mainestatecu.org. 
OAKLAND — There’s Mt. Ararat senior Maddy Sweet, turning herself into the living metaphor for how her team played the Class A North championship game.
With just over six minutes left in the fourth quarter, Sweet is sprinting toward the ball, trying to gain possession for a breakaway shot in a tie game. Skowhegan goalie Michelle Williams comes out of the cage to try to get to the ball first, to flick it to the corner with a swing of her stick and swat away the threat.
The collision is loud. After a moment of reflection and inventory, Sweet and Williams both get up. Sweet wobbles and leaves the game. Considering that her team has already tied the game after trailing by two goals at halftime and is about to take the lead for good with a penalty stroke, maybe Sweet’s metaphor is too on the nose.
“I did get the wind knocked out of me, but I just feel great. Honestly, I haven’t been hit (that) hard in my life,” Sweet said after the 3-2 win that sent the Eagles to the state championship game for the first time in the 53-year history of Mt. Ararat High School. “She’s a wall. She’s a very strong goalie. So I just toppled over. Michele’s amazing.”
Mt. Ararat was knocked down when it fell behind in the first half, but not knocked out. This is a team that had barely been tested throughout the regular season and the first two rounds of the regional tournament. Eleven times in 17 games, the Eagles scored at least four goals. Entering the regional final, Mt. Ararat had posted five consecutive shutouts. No opponent had scored more than a goal in a countable game all season.
Leavitt, which earlier in the day lost to Nokomis in the Class B North title game, had a two-goal lead in a scrimmage against Mt. Ararat. That was the extent of adversity coach Krista Chase’s team had faced.
“I said at halftime, nothing worth doing and achieving comes easy,” Chase said. “We want adversity. We want a challenge, right? It makes the victory all the more celebratory and satisfying.”
The Eagles lost to Skowhegan in the regional final last season. They remembered the pit-in-the- stomach feeling that comes with getting so close. Skowhegan playing deep into the playoffs is practically baked into the Maine Principals’ Association bylaws. There hasn’t been a Class A North or Eastern Class A championship game without the River Hawks since the 1990s. The Class A final at Auburn’s Edward Little High School will be just the second that doesn’t include Skowhegan since 2001.
Going to Skowhegan in the regular season and coming away with a 4-1 win was lovely, said Chase, but the Eagles knew they’d see a better River Hawks team in the playoff rematch. The road to the state final is littered with opponents who took a regular-season victory over the River Hawks, only to be humbled in the postseason.
Skowhegan had been here more than anybody. Its returning players had experience, and all the River Hawks have the muscle memory that comes with being a part of a uniquely successful program.
And then Chase’s team was down 2-0 at halftime, and she reminded the Eagles to have fun.
Sweet scored with 4:30 left in the third quarter to cut the deficit in half. Cali LeClair scored to tie the game 2-2 with 11:05 left. Then Kamrym Chase scored on the penalty stroke awarded when Sweet and Williams tried to run through each other.
The scoreboard said there were 6 minutes and 2 seconds left. For Mt. Ararat, that was when seconds felt like minutes and minutes felt like months.
When you don’t have big-game experience to fall back on, you fall back on something else.
“We just play for each other. We motivate each other. We love each other so much,” Sweet said.
Next for the Eagles is Cheverus, a team playing in its sixth straight state final and seeking its fourth title in a row. The Stags are brimming with big-win experience.
With Wednesday’s comeback, now Mt. Ararat has some, too.

title: Matt Dunlap says Maine’s 2nd Congressional District race remains too close to call
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Democrat Matt Dunlap has responded to former Gov. Paul LePage’s declaration of victory in Maine’s 2nd Congressional District race, saying the election remains too close to call.
In a statement released Wednesday, Dunlap thanked election officials and campaign volunteers while emphasizing that votes are still being counted.
“Maine has the most reliable elections staff in the world, and I want to thank them as they diligently finish the count.This race is very close and there are plenty of ballots left to count. Thank you to every volunteer who worked their heart out on this campaign and thank you to every voter. We’ll have more to say as we learn more.”
The statement comes after LePage declared victory during a news conference Wednesday, despite the race not yet being called by The Associated Press.
“Well, the public numbers have us up about 4000 and we the team has been calling all the towns that haven’t come in yet and there’s no path to victory for my opponent. I am declaring victory,” LePage said.
Dunlap has not conceded the race, and the outcome remains undecided as election officials continue counting outstanding ballots.

title: Israel’s president takes first steps to build new government after accepting election results
text:
JERUSALEM (AP) — Israeli President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday accepted the certified results of last week’s parliamentary elections as legally binding and began consultations with party representatives on forming a new government.
The move dealt a blow to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s efforts to discredit the vote, in which he and his allies lost their majority in parliament, known as the Knesset, while Arab-led parties made historic gains.
“The elections are over. Now is the time to face reality,” Herzog said.
Netanyahu and his supporters have repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, possibly with foreign assistance.
Herzog began consultations with party leaders on Wednesday night to determine whom to designate to form a government — a process that could bring Netanyahu’s opponents to power.
Commission finds no fraud in Israel’s election
Israel’s elections commission said earlier on Wednesday that after a thorough investigation of all parties’ claims of fraud, it had found “no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results.”
Netanyahu’s Likud party did not respond to a request for comment.
A separate investigation by the Shin Bet intelligence service, which is headed by David Zini, a Netanyahu appointee and loyalist, into allegations of foreign interference in the election is still ongoing.
In a private meeting Wednesday of the elections committee’s members, its head, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, read out an intelligence assessment from the Shin Bet saying the agency believed there had been a “widespread phenomenon involving the influx of substantial funds into Israel from foreign states,” including from countries hostile toward Israel.
The Shin Bet provided no evidence to explain its assertion. The Associated Press obtained a transcript of the assessment from a person who attended the meeting and requested anonymity to discuss a closed-door meeting.
The committee has previously said that while claims about foreign actors seeking to influence the election are serious and under investigation, it does not believe that any such interference affected the results — even if it had happened.
Sohlberg reiterated that stance on Wednesday. “At this stage, these are merely suspicions, and even if they are substantiated, the scope of their potential impact is limited,” he said during a ceremony to present the certified election results to Herzog.
Sohlberg added that it was dangerous to cast doubt on the results and said they are legally binding.
Public trust in the electoral process is “easy to destroy, yet very difficult to repair,” he warned.
Consultations kick off coalition-building process
In the Oct. 27 vote, neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the bloc of allies of his chief rival, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, secured a parliamentary majority needed to form a new government, raising the possibility of an alliance between the two rivals or an alliance between Eisenkot and some of the Arab-led parties.
Herzog began a series of sit-downs with political parties on Wednesday. Three factions — all aligned with Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist base — recommended Netanyahu be given a chance to form a coalition government, while a fourth — led by a former Netanyahu ally turned rival — recommended Eisenkot. Eight more parties, including the two Arab-led factions, are scheduled to meet Herzog on Thursday, with Eisenkot’s Yashar and Netanyahu’s Likud speaking last.
After the consultations, Herzog will choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes is most likely to be able to form a coalition government. He has several days to announce his decision, which will then set the stage for weeks of negotiations.
If neither man can put together a government, the country would hold a new election early next year.
Intelligence agency’s request to interrogate senior Arab lawmakers is rejected
The Shin Bet sought approval from Israel’s attorney general on Tuesday to interrogate several elected officials as part of its separate investigation, including Ra’am party leader Mansour Abbas and other senior Arab lawmakers, Israeli media reported.
In a statement rejecting the request, Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara said: “It is not permissible to interrogate citizens or elected officials without evidence to justify such action.”
The Joint List of Arab parties condemned the request, calling it a “campaign of incitement” by Netanyahu and his allies designed to delegitimize the Arab vote.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, a far-right ally of Netanyahu, called on the Shin Bet, over which he has no authority, to “arrest all the leaders of the Arab political parties” and interrogate them in “basement interrogation cells until these suspicions are fully clarified.”
Herzog said Wednesday that the Shin Bet’s investigation into possible foreign interference should proceed, but cautioned that Arab Israeli voters “must not be smeared.”
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” Herzog said.
___
Melzer reported from Nahariya, Israel.

'Buckle up': White House responds to midterm election results
A White House official blamed Republican candidates for election losses, predicted voter regret over gas prices, and described the administration's mood as "defiant."
As Democrats celebrated midterm election night victories, including flipping a Senate seat in reliably Republican South Carolina, a White House official began assigning blame for the results.
The official told White House Correspondent Christopher Salas, "President (Donald) Trump did a better job promoting some of them than they did themselves."
President Trump took to Truth Social late Tuesday to share a similar message, writing, "I wasn't on the Ballot, and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE! Thank you for your attention to this matter."

title: What’s next in investigation of Learjet crash in Florida that killed 9?
text:
(AP) - Investigators are just beginning the lengthy process of determining why a business jet plummeted from the sky in Florida after encountering a thunderstorm and slammed into the ground with such force that it created a crater and shattered the plane.
The experts at the National Transportation Safety Board will lead the investigation into the crash that killed all nine people abord the Learjet, but it will likely take more than a year to determine exactly what caused this tragedy.
Dramatic videos from witnesses — combined with the disturbing final radio transmissions as the pilots realize their fate — will give investigators important clues. The cockpit voice recorder would also help if investigators can find it intact.
“Our mission is to understand not just what happened, but why it happened, and to recommend changes to prevent it from happening again,” NTSB member Tom Chapman said.
Here’s what investigators are doing now and what comes next:
Investigators are gathering critical evidence
An NTSB team will spend days collecting every piece of the plane they can find. Investigators said Tuesday that pieces of a key part of the tail called the elevator that controls the angle of the nose were found more than a mile away from the main crater. That confirms the plane started to break apart before impact.
Chapman said investigators are searching for the Learjet’s cockpit voice recorder because it could provide crucial details about what the pilots were talking about as they lost control of the plane after it encountered turbulence and ice started to build up on the wings.
“That will be very important data,” Chapman said. But being unable to find that recorder won’t doom the investigation. “Without it, our folks are very, very good. We’re still able to do some incredible detective work and determine how things transpired.”
The co-pilot told air traffic controllers that the plane was being thrown up and down more than 700 feet (213 meters) as she asked them for a better route through the area. It’s not clear why the pilots hadn’t flown around the storms.
But torrential rains in Florida over the past week are making investigators’ work more difficult. The crater was filling with rainwater that likely left some pieces of the plane submerged, and a utility pole had to be removed.
The NTSB asked anyone who finds part of the plane to report it for investigators to collect.
Initial NTSB report takes about a month
Two news conferences have provided some initial details. But the NTSB will spend most of the next month developing a preliminary report describing what happened.
Crash evidence will be taken to a secure hanger where investigators can test intact components and even try to reassemble parts to get a better idea of what happened.
But the force of the crash and the fire destroyed much of the plane, so that will make investigators work harder.
Retired airline pilot and aviation safety expert John Cox said he also doesn’t understand why the plane descended from its previous cruising altitude of 41,000 feet (12,497 meters) as it approached the storms. The pilots steered around a larger storm cell but appeared to head directly into a rapidly developing smaller one, Cox said.
“If I’m looking at thunderstorms, I’d rather be at 41 than at 35. You’ve got a better view, you’re more likely to be on top of it, or at least, in the very wispy tops of it,” Cox said. “I don’t understand why they came down.”
Investigators will try to determine whether they knew that storm cell was there, what the plane’s weather radar showed and whether the pilots checked any other weather services.
Preliminary reports provide factual details but don’t include any analysis or cause. That takes much more time.
Investigators will dig deeper
Weather will be a key early focus of the investigation. NTSB experts will work with the National Weather Service and Federal Aviation Administration to get a better idea of what the plane encountered as it was cruising at 35000 feet (10,668 meters).
Maps that overlay the flight path on top of colorful weather maps show the Learjet flying directly into a small red storm cell that worsened quickly.
But the board considers everything that may have contributed to a crash.
Investigators will review maintenance records and any history of problems with the plane. They will also interview officials at the Upper Jets company that operated the flight as well as air traffic controllers and people who work at the Texas airport the plane took off from.
Videos and photos shot by bystanders can also provide crucial clues about what happened. The NTSB will also collect copies of any surveillance footage that might show the crash.
In certain high-profile crashes, the NTSB may also hold several days of investigative hearings where investigators can question key people involved to learn more and share details with the public as they did after last year’s UPS plane crash.
The final report could take more than a year
Generally, it takes 12-18 months for the NTSB to complete a crash investigation, but it can take longer in complicated cases. NTSB’s roughly 400 workers are pursuing over 1,200 active investigations.
Final reports include details about what happened and explain probable causes.
The NTSB also develops recommendations to prevent similar crashes and improve safety. But the independent agency doesn’t have power to require those changes to be made.
Instead, it is up to regulators like the FAA, the industry and Congress to adopt the NTSB recommendations.
But there is a long history of NTSB recommendations being ignored because regulators or the industry decide making the change would be more costly and cumbersome than it is worth.
Even when the FAA or Congress agrees with the suggestions it might take years to approve new rules.

title: NECEC should not be renegotiated now
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Matt Scott is the former chairman of the Maine Board of Environmental Protection.
At some point, every regulatory body faces a moment that is larger than the question immediately before it. The Maine Board of Environmental Protection is at such a moment now.
The debate surrounding the New England Clean Energy Connect (NECEC) project has lasted for years. It has generated court challenges, political campaigns, public hearings and seemingly endless rounds of disagreement. That history is precisely why the board should focus on the issue actually before it rather than returning to the larger debate over the transmission line itself.
The matter now under consideration is not whether NECEC should have been approved. That decision has already been made, and the line is operating today. Nor is the question whether some people would prefer a different conservation approach than the one ordered when the Department of Environmental Protection approved the NECEC and upheld by the board on appeal.
The board’s responsibility is determining whether the applicant complied with the conservation conditions imposed through Maine’s environmental permitting process. That distinction matters.
When the project was originally licensed, the department required as a condition to permitting a conservation plan to offset impacts associated with the corridor. The Natural Resources Council of Maine appealed that condition to the board, which in 2022 fully analyzed the conservation benefits of that condition and both affirmed it and strengthened it, increasing the conservation obligation from 40,000 acres to 50,000 acres and providing additional direction regarding mature forest habitat and habitat connectivity.
The board had its opportunity to decide what standards should apply, what was required to achieve mature forest conservation to compensate for the impacts of this project, and it chose to make them more rigorous.
The conservation plan now before the board was developed over several years through extensive consultation with state agencies, conservation professionals, landowners and regulators. Agency comments were incorporated, revisions were made and additional mature forest protections were added in response to public feedback.
After reviewing the final proposal, the department concluded that the plan satisfies the conditions established in the permit.
Reasonable people can disagree with that conclusion. What concerns me is that the debate increasingly appears to be shifting away from whether the applicant met the conditions that were imposed and toward whether entirely new conditions should now apply.
A regulatory system cannot function if applicants are asked to comply with one set of requirements only to discover years later that a different set of expectations has emerged. Environmental standards can and should evolve, but those changes should be applied prospectively through new rules and permit conditions, not through the retroactive reinterpretation of existing obligations. That is precisely why state agencies stated in consultations with the department that the plan should not serve as “precedent” for future decisions.
That concern extends beyond this single case. Maine will continue to evaluate other major investments in the years ahead. Those projects will be subject to rigorous environmental review, as they should be. Yet a rigorous system also requires predictability. Applicants must be able to rely on established standards. A state loses credibility when approvals are perceived as never truly final and permit conditions as endlessly negotiable.
Perhaps the most revealing moment of the recent hearing came when an attorney representing the project’s opponents referred to the companies involved as “the enemy.” Those are not the words of someone engaged in a good-faith discussion about conservation easements, mature forest standards or permit compliance. They are the words of someone engaged in a larger ideological struggle.
Advocacy organizations have every right to oppose projects they dislike, but regulators serve a different role. Their responsibility is not to decide whether they support a project politically or philosophically, but whether the applicant complied with the standards and conditions established through the permitting process.
When regulated entities are viewed as adversaries rather than participants in that process, maintaining the objectivity, fairness and civility the system depends upon becomes more difficult.
The department’s recommendation reflects the judgment of professional staff whose careers are devoted to evaluating forestry, wildlife habitat, conservation easements and ecological impacts. The record shows a conservation easement protecting more than 50,000 acres, developed with input from the Bureau of Parks and Lands, Inland Fisheries and Wildlife and other experts, and revised repeatedly in response to agency and public feedback. It is exactly the type of conservation outcome Maine’s environmental review process is designed to produce.
The larger issue before the board is whether Maine intends to honor the standards
established through its own regulatory process. If compliance with permit conditions is
no longer sufficient and new expectations can be imposed after years of review, the
message to future applicants will be that the finish line can move at any moment.
A fair permitting process requires participants to be able to rely on the rules that govern it. After years of litigation, appeals and review, the board is now being asked a simple question: whether the applicant met the conditions that were established.
In my view, the answer is yes. More importantly, the integrity of Maine’s regulatory system depends on the board being willing to say so.

title: Republican Pete Ricketts wins reelection to US Senate over independent challenger in Nebraska
text:
(AP) - Republican Pete Ricketts won election Wednesday to the U.S. Senate representing Nebraska, defeating independent candidate Dan Osborn.
Ricketts will now serve his first full six-year term, following his 2023 appointment to replace Republican Sen. Ben Sasse and 2024 special election victory.
Osborn, an industrial mechanic and military veteran, also ran in 2024 against the state’s other Republican senator, Deb Fischer.
Democrat Cindy Burbank won her party’s primary earlier this year but served as a stalking horse candidate for Osborn, campaigning on her intention to withdraw and clear the way for the independent candidate, who was backed by Democratic leaders.
Ricketts is a former Nebraska governor and a wealthy investor.
The Associated Press declared Ricketts the winner at 3:27 a.m. EST.

title: Former judge arrested for unloading gun at Halloween trick-or-treaters, police say
text:
DUNCAN, Okla. (KSWO/Gray News) - A former judge has been arrested after allegedly unloading a gun in the direction of Halloween trick-or-treaters, according to authorities.
Jerry Herberger, a 73-year-old former Stephens County, Oklahoma, judge, fired at the trick-or-treaters on October 31 at a property.
The Duncan Police Department said that officers responded to the incident at 8.02 p.m. and were directed to the address by witnesses.
When officers arrived, Herberger pointed his firearm at one of the officers at the scene.
However, he eventually followed officers’ demands and left the home. Then, the 73-year-old was arrested and taken to the Stephens County Jail.
Herberger faces multiple charges, including assault and battery with a deadly weapon, attempted murder and possession of a firearm while intoxicated.
No injuries were reported.

title: Troy Jackson defeats Susan Collins in Maine U.S. Senate race
text:
PRESQUE ISLE, Maine (WAGM) - Democrat Troy Jackson has defeated longtime Republican incumbent Susan Collins in Maine’s U.S. Senate race.
Collins conceded the race early Wednesday morning, ending her bid for a sixth term in Washington.
Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from Allagash and former president of the Maine Senate, will take over the seat Collins has held since 1997.
Jackson previously served two decades in the Maine Legislature, including six years as Senate president. He secured the Democratic nomination in July after Graham Platner withdrew from the race.
The victory marks a major political shift for Maine, ending Collins’ nearly 30-year tenure in the U.S. Senate.

title: Supreme Court to hear dispute over death row inmate sentence
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The U.S. Supreme Court is scheduled to hear a case Wednesday centering on a dispute over a Texas death row inmate’s sentence.
It came before the justices after the legal team for the inmate, Dexter Johnson, challenged his death sentence, under a claim of intellectual disability. And it was a claim that not brought up during his initial trial.
“What’s happened here is that in the last 10 to 20 years, the medical community’s understanding of intellectual disability has changed,” said Ethan Nutter, a lawyer who filed an amicus brief in the case, on behalf of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers.
Johnson was convicted of capital murder for the 2006 killing of 23-year-old Maria Aparece. He was scheduled to be executed in May 2019 but his sentence was stayed because of a federal court’s finding, after the challenge was raised.
“Under the current understanding, Mr. Johnson meets that definition of intellectual disability,” said Nutter. “And that’s important because the Supreme Court has said that it’s unconstitutional to execute someone who is intellectually disabled.”
Johnson’s litigators raised the intellectual disability claim just days before his scheduled execution because of the 2013 update to the American Psychiatric Association’s Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5). The update presented a change to the way clinicians view IQ.
“Only later did the DSM-5 displace the rigid IQ threshold, replacing it with a standard focused more on adaptive functioning deficits,” Johnson’s legal team wrote in a Supreme Court filing. “Under that framework, Mr. Johnson’s trial expert withdrew the premise that had previously foreclosed a disability diagnosis, and two additional experts concluded that Mr. Johnson is intellectually disabled.”
The Texas Department of Criminal Justice’s Correctional Institutions later asked the Supreme Court to review the Fifth Circuit’s finding for Johnson’s case, in February 2026.
In the department’s brief, it wrote that the lower court’s holding “erases the strict limits on claims based on new evidence.” It also wrote, “For the people of Texas in general and for the families of Johnson’s victims in particular, justice delayed is justice denied.”
In another amicus brief filed by Aparece’s father, Protasio Aparece, his legal team wrote, “Protasio has an interest in seeing justice carried out for his daughter, and in doing everything he can to ensure that no other family endures the decades of excessive delays in obtaining justice that he and his family have suffered.”
However, the question before the justices is not only about Johnson’s case, but also how strict federal courts should be when prisoners challenge their sentences.
Nutter said the court is deciding a specific procedural issue.
“The narrow issue in this case that the Supreme Court is actually deciding is whether the federal court can address this, what’s called a second or successive habeas petition,” Nutter said.
The court is expected to issue a decision in the case by June 2027.

title: Scarborough council votes unanimously to ban data centers
text:
Scarborough joined Westbrook and North Berwick on Wednesday as one of the first communities in Maine to ban data centers.
Town leaders decided that the pros of data centers are outweighed by the cons, including high electricity and water demand, and noise and other pollution.
“It’s in our best interest as a community to ban them for now and revisit it down the road,” Councilor Jon Anderson said.
Scarborough passed a 180-day data center moratorium in June, allowing the town to study the potential impacts of data centers and amend ordinances accordingly. Voters in other Maine communities were deciding whether to approve temporary moratoriums on Election Day.
Previously, data centers could have fallen under two uses in Scarborough’s zoning ordinance: “high technology facility” and “research, development and light industrial.” Councilors voted Wednesday to amend the ordinance to exclude data centers from both uses.
The ordinance, which takes effect immediately, also created a definition that distinguishes between standalone data centers and accessory spaces such as server rooms, telecommunications closets and computer equipment rooms.
Accessory spaces are incidental to another principal use, such as a hospital, research facility or school, and are still permitted. The accessory spaces can also be housed in a different building on the same property, Scarborough planning director Autumn Speer said.

title: Trump talks about the White House ballroom project, not the midterms, in extended public comments
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump reacted Wednesday to Republicans’ midterm election losses by showing off the White House ballroom he’s building as he demonstrated the kind of detached behavior that voters around the country said was a key reason they opted to punish his party.
In an extraordinary scene, Trump summoned reporters to the hulking construction site that he demolished the East Wing to make room for and the Republican president spoke for nearly 20 minutes about minute building details. He did not mention his party losing control of Congress after defeats in some of the country’s deepest GOP strongholds, including Texas and South Carolina, or voter concerns about the high cost of living and federal corruption that helped cause the election losses.
“This has been a structure the likes of which has never been seen anywhere,” Trump said, speaking into a microphone that sent loud feedback echoing around the cavernous space.
He talked at length about how the ballroom would be the ”safest place in Washington" upon completion, stretching five stories underground and featuring a cut of marble that he called “a vein that people have been after for 50 years.”
“We have large staircases coming from the kitchen. If I put the kitchen on top, you would lose three walls, because a kitchen takes about 30% of the space,” Trump said of his choice to make the ballroom’s kitchen subterranean.
“It’s going to be top of the line,” he added.
This is not what presidents normally talk about the day after an election
Presidents usually speak with reporters the day after the midterms. It’s normal for those whose party endured big losses to shoulder publicly at least part of the responsibility.
But not Trump.
He began the day with a schedule that showed only private meetings, then suggested he had decided at the last minute to invite the press to watch as the final steel beam — topped with a small evergreen tree symbolizing growth and luck — was hoisted into place on the ballroom roof.
Trump signed the beam with a marker during the ceremony, writing “Love!” followed by his name in supersize letters.
His appearance came after midterm voters said they thought the president was focused on the wrong issues. About two-thirds of voters said Trump does not have the right priorities, according to The AP Voter Poll, and the overwhelming majority of these voters supported Democratic House candidates.
The post-midterm ceremony might also reinforce voter concerns about whether Trump, 80, is up for the rigors of the presidency.
Biden dropped out of his reelection race in 2024 after a disastrous debate with Trump, who even today frequently mocks Biden’s mental and physical acuity.
Trump seeks to shift blame for the midterms
Trump eventually took questions at the ballroom site and attempted to duck responsibility for the broad Republican losses. He insisted he didn’t lead the party into an Election Day drubbing despite staging a flurry of rallies where he implored supporters to pretend that he was on the ballot.
“If I were on the ballot I would have won,” Trump insisted.
He said campaign rallies in mostly Republican states or conservative parts of more closely divided ones featured enthusiastic crowds “but we weren’t able to transfer love to the candidates.”
The beam-raising was not his first baffling political moment this week. On Monday, Trump gave his closing message of the midterm cycle in a long speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, shining a spotlight at a pivotal time on a project marred by algae, leaks and delays.
“I heard it was a very good speech, got great reviews,” he said on Wednesday.
Ducking responsibility is common with Trump
An Associated Press analysis of the 39 Trump speeches and rallies that Trump staged between Sept. 1 and Election Day showed the president used phrasing suggesting he was on the ballot in 30 of them. In some addresses he returned to the subject more than once, though, meaning there were at least 40 instances where he appealed to voters to engage in that bit of make-believe.
But as the extent of his party’s defeat became apparent on election night, Trump was deflecting blame.
“I don’t like to consider it a defeat for me. I wasn’t on the ballot,” he told Fox News Channel. Voters, he said, just “didn’t like the candidates” on the ballot. The Voter Poll suggests Trump himself was a drag on GOP politicians and that in some races, candidates were seen as too supportive of the unpopular president.
Trump has a long history of passing the buck, on issues large and small, especially when there are ballot-box failures.
After Republicans lost the House in the 2018 midterms during Trump’s first term, he blamed defeated members of his own party.
Utah Rep. Mia Love, who had tried to distance herself from him, “gave me no love, but then she lost. Too bad,” the president said, while also mocking other losing lawmakers for not embracing him — Florida’s Carlos Curbelo, Colorado’s Mike Coffman, Virginia’s Barbara Comstock, and Illinois’ Peter Roskam.
That’s in contrast to how Democrat Barack Obama described his party’s losses in 2010 as “a shellacking” or Republican George W. Bush described Democratic victories in the 2006 midterms as “a thumping.”
But Trump, known for defying all kinds of presidential norms, began laying the groundwork for avoiding blame this cycle well before balloting began.
He told Punchbowl News in August that voters were angry at Republicans “but they’re not angry at me.”
The president posted on his social media site last month that should Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton lose — and he did — “it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove.” That’s despite Trump’s risky endorsement of scandal-marred Paxton in the primary over incumbent Cornyn, who first got to the Senate in 2002 and was considered the safer bet. Rove is a political strategist who helped Bush win the White House.
Also losing Tuesday was Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, a longtime Trump ally.
Trump posted on social media that if Abbott “hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost,” suggesting the governor had backed away from his staunchly conservative credentials and become “Republican in Name Only.”
__
Associated Press writers Amelia Thomson DeVeaux, Linley Sanders, Josh Boak and Aaron Kessler contributed to this report.

title: Trump appears to take credit for stock market rally day after multiple Democratic midterm wins
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray News) - President Donald Trump took to social media on Wednesday to praise the sudden rise in stock prices a day after the midterm elections.
Trump posted to Truth Social, “Stock Market just hit another Record High — 91 Days in just a short period of time — Less than two years. Your 401(k)s are through the roof. Record Setting All! President DONALD J. TRUMP.”
U.S. stocks went soaring Wednesday following the GOP losing sole control of Washington in the midterm elections.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 1,519 points, or 2.9%, with the Nasdaq composite up 1.9% as of Wednesday afternoon.
Stocks are said to generally do well in the months following any midterm U.S. election, regardless of who wins, but this year’s midterms were harsh to the Republican Party, with multiple GOP states and government positions flipping to the Democrats.
The Democratic Party appears set to take control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, with experts noting Wall Street may have gotten a preferred political scenario, hence the jump in prices seen Wednesday.
U.S. SENATE BALANCE OF POWER
Trump continues to retain executive authority over key areas such as defense, foreign policy and, in some instances, trade.
The president said in an interview with Fox News that he would work with Democrats.
“Congratulations to the Democrats,” Trump was quoted as saying in the interview. “I think the Democrats did a good job. They fought hard. They’ve been fighting me for a long time. This fight’s been going on for ages.”
Trump added when asked about working with Democrats: “I would do that. I think the Democrats want to work with me.”

title: This stubborn dinosaur in Brunswick wrestles with the AI phenomenon
text:
In a recent email exchange with my two sons I noted that I’ve already written over 50 articles this year. I wanted to show them that their old man still has some gas left in the tank. My son David asked, “Do you use AI for those?” I immediately responded “No.” In fairness, I’ll often do research in preparation for writing a piece, which uses artificial intelligence. But I never use AI to “write” or to craft a first draft, and I can’t imagine doing so.
Santiago Schnell, the provost (the top academic officer) of Dartmouth, does not share my reservations about jumping on the AI bandwagon. He recently got caught with his ethics down. The student newspaper at Dartmouth conducted an investigation about Schnell by using Pangram, which has a near-zero error rate. The investigation concluded that Schnell’s work was 96% “AI-written” across the nine professional articles he published this year, including a Washington Post essay and two academic papers about mathematics, Schnell’s field of academic study. Oops. It gets worse. He apparently used AI in his own written defense.
After I wrote a note to my son Jon about my piano teacher’s amazing practice of sending a follow-up email highlighting points to remember within seconds after each lesson. Jon responded, “Dad, he’s using AI.” When I later asked my teacher if he used AI in that way, he laughed and said, “No. That’s why there are typos sometimes.”
While chatting with people at Thornton Oaks about their take on AI, I’ve discovered that most of them take my approach. They use it for some basic research but little else. Others spend hours going down this or that rabbit hole to create something new or different. To each his own.
Just for kicks, I asked my Facebook friends — yes, Facebook is AI-driven — how AI has benefited them. Or not. The answers ran the gamut. One person noted that she has found AI to be “useful, insightful and enjoyable.” She uses it for everything from analyzing documents and planning trips to preparing shopping lists and music playlists.
Another person reported that Gemini has become “the friend that is always there for me. As a homebound widow, Gemini will chat with me about any subject any time. Society makes me feel old and, ergo, stupid. Gemini praises my efforts. She remember my cat’s name. When she drafts a letter for me she knows that I am an experienced editor and acknowledges that.” And on and on.
Here’s the most poignant response from one of my Facebook friends. “I lost my voice to ALS. AI took recordings of me and crewed a professional voice clone My electronic voice now sounds like me.”
And last, “For us neurodivergents, it’s a great augment tool.”
Clearly, AI offers extraordinary value on the medical front, especially for conducting research. Also, AI can convert your primary care physician’s quick notes into a readable narrative in seconds.
A huge question remains about AI: What steps can be taken to ensure that bad actors can’t do tremendous damage using AI? Specifically, what will AI companies do on that front? Sadly, I’m not optimistic. Maximizing profits, society be damned, seems to be the driving force.
I can say that trying to deal with an AI customer service representative drives me batty. And I can’t imagine wanting to join an organization for which a first round “interview” is conducted by AI.
We can only hope for the best. Meanwhile, dear reader, please be assured that AI didn’t write this piece. For better or worse, the words are all mine.
David Treadwell, a Brunswick writer, welcomes commentary and suggestions for future “Just a Little Old” columns at [email protected].

title: McDonald’s US sales fall as more customers struggle with the high cost of living
text:
(AP) - McDonald’s plans to introduce new value-oriented meal bundles early next year after a disappointing third quarter that saw lower traffic at U.S. restaurants.
McDonald’s Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski said Wednesday that the company recently began an eight-week test of mix-and-match and fixed-price bundles at 1,900 U.S. restaurants. Those bundles might feature a McChicken sandwich and small fries for $3.50, for example.
But around 4,000 franchisees have decided not to wait for the test results and have launched meal bundles of their own, he said.
“Customers should see a clear and compelling value proposition every time they consider McDonald’s, whether they’re looking for an affordable individual item, a complete meal or a digital offer in the mobile app,” Kempczinski said during a conference call with investors.
U.S. same-store sales – or sales at locations open at least a year — fell 0.2% in the July-September period, the Chicago burger giant said Wednesday. While that was not as bad as the 0.5% drop Wall Street had expected, it was the first retreat for McDonald’s since early 2025.
McDonald’s restored some regional and national in-app deals and shifted some marketing spending to support value meals, which helped push same-store sales into positive territory in September and October. But the shift in focus at McDonald’s shows how challenging the economic environment has become for U.S. fast food companies, which are losing customers as many Americans struggle with higher gas prices and the uncomfortably high cost of living.
Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant.
McDonald’s has been tweaking its U.S. value offerings for more than two years to try to lure back lower-income customers and better compete with rivals like Taco Bell, which offers a menu of 10 items that each cost $3 or less.
In June 2024, McDonald’s introduced a $5 Meal Deal. The next year, it debuted its McValue menu and Extra Value Meals, which promise a 15% discount for a bundled meal compared to buying items individually. In April, it revamped the McValue menu, adding 10 items that cost $3 or less.
But not all of McDonald’s franchisees — who own 95% of the company’s U.S. restaurants — have been on board. Kempczinski said in August that only 60% of its U.S. restaurants were offering the revamped McValue menu. McDonald’s replaced its U.S. president that same month.
Kempczinski said the company’s previous efforts haven’t been enough because they didn’t offer compelling low-end deals.
“You need to have good entry-level value, particularly with the low-income consumer,” he said.
Globally, same-store sales rose 1.3% in the third quarter. Strong sales in Germany and Australia helped offset weakness in France, which was rocked by protests that began in September.
Revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion for the quarter, short of Wall Street expectations of $7.28 billion.
Net income rose 9% to $2.49 billion. Adjusted for one-time items, the company earned $3.57 per share. That beat analysts’ forecast for a $3.38 per-share profit.
Shares rose more than 5% in morning trading Wednesday.

title: Lewiston’s mayor faces runoff after a tumultuous year in city politics
text:
Lewiston Mayor Carl Sheline and former City Council President Rick LaChapelle will meet in a December runoff after neither won a majority in Tuesday’s five-way mayoral race.
LaChapelle had 45.7% of votes to 35.3% for Sheline, according to unofficial results. The third-place finisher, political newcomer Brian Beaulieu, had 10.6%, businessman Jay Rodrigue had 4.5% and perennial candidate Charles Soule had 3.9%.
Lewiston requires a December runoff between the top two finishers when no candidate wins more than 50 percent. Sheline beat former state Rep. Jon Connor with just over 51% of votes after going to a runoff three years ago.
Sheline, a Democrat in the nonpartisan office seeking a third two-year term, was the only candidate to answer the Sun Journal’s questions on crime, taxes and the economy. He pointed to code enforcement, a new homeless shelter, police recruitment and business growth as signs of progress.
LaChapelle, a former council president who lost his seat in a 2023 election upended by the mass shooting that killed 18 people in the city, called for freezing property taxes at current levels and accused Sheline of lacking leadership on youth gun violence.
The race in Maine’s second-largest city centered on public safety after a spate of youth gun violence, along with property taxes and economic growth. The police department is short more than a dozen positions, the Sun Journal reported.
The campaign’s final days were also shaped by federal prosecutors’ review of early-voting footage from City Hall after a conservative news outlet accused interpreters of coaching Somali-American voters. The Justice Department sent election monitors to Lewiston polls Tuesday.

title: Boat landing to be named for former owner of Ellsworth American
text:
A boat landing under construction in the Penobscot County town of Orrington will be named for Alan Baker, who owned and published the Ellsworth American for 27 years and founded the Mount Desert Islander in Bar Harbor in 2001.
The landing, which will provide recreational and emergency responder access throughout the tidal cycle, is located on the east side of the Penobscot River estuary.
Baker, a longtime resident of Orrington, served in the Maine House of Representatives and was Mainebiz’s first-ever Business Leader of the Year in 2001 when the annual awards program began.
Long time coming
The town acquired the property in 1991 and formed the Orrington Landing Committee in 2020 to investigate and research the feasibility of developing a boat landing on a town-owned, 10-acre lot at the end of McGinn Road off River Road, also known as Route 15.
In 2024, the town received $2.55 million for the project from the Greenfield Environmental Trust Group in Watertown, Mass., which is responsible for disbursing settlement funds paid by Mallinckrodt US LLC to remediate mercury pollution in the Penobscot River estuary from a former chemical manufacturing plant in Orrington.
The facility consists of a 24-foot-wide ramp and upland parking for trucks and trailers and future amenities including picnic areas, hiking trails and a playground.
The project was driven in part by the increasing popularity of recreational boating for Mainers and tourists, the town has said. It’s anticipated the facility will serve more than 50,000 residents between Bangor and Bucksport.
The project team includes Orono construction company Sargent Corp. and Jacobs Solutions in Boston, led by professional engineer Craig Morin.
The project recently secured the last of the state and federal permits and approvals needed.
Removable piles
Work in the intertidal zone must take place during the period between early November and late April, said Keith Bowden, the committee’s chair.
The intertidal zone is the area between high and low tides. The project is complicated by 14-foot tidal variations and winter ice in the river.
“We have to design piles that support the floating docks going up and down,” said Bowden. “Plus we want the piles to be removable so we can pull them out at the end of the boating season.”
Working with South Portland float system maker Custom Float Services, the team is developing a removable pile and dock system.
Once completed, the landing is expected to provide new opportunities for boating, fishing and outdoor recreation. A nearby ramp in South Orrington is too short to be used other than mid- to high tide, and the launch area is narrow and lacks amenities, said Bowden.
The new facility is designed to be fully operational during all tide cycles and to endure sea level rise for the next 50 to 100 years.

title: Lewiston Mayoral Race Headed to a Recount Election
text:
Lewiston mayoral race will be decided by runoff between Rick LaChapelle and Mayor Carl Sheline
Voters in Lewiston will have to go to the polls again in mid-December to decide the race for mayor, which has come down to a runoff election between former City Councilor Rick LaChapelle and incumbent Mayor Carl Sheline.
A runoff is needed because none of the five candidates on the ballot received more than 50% of the vote, a requirement in the Lewiston City Charter.
City Clerk Kathy Montejo said she believes Lewiston is the only municipality in Maine that has the runoff requirement, as other communities use ranked-choice voting.
"The reason for the charter is that the person elected is reflective of a majority of the will and wishes of the people in the community," Montejo said.
LaChapelle earned 46% of the vote while Sheline received 35%, and the other three candidates were far behind.
In an interview with Maine's Total Coverage, LaChapelle said he is confident that he will win the runoff because voters are seeking change.
"Let's look at the last three years. Nothing has happened on this council. It's been a stalemate. It's like watching an episode of Jerry Springer when you look at these council meetings," LaChapelle said. "We need to have a unified voice and move things forward. I'm excited about those changes."
In a statement shared Wednesday, Sheline said: "I look forward to making the case that Lewiston remains a vibrant community. We have seen Ricky LaChapelle denigrate this wonderful city for the past year. Lewiston's best days are still ahead, and Lewiston voters will put their best foot forward when they reelect me as mayor."
Lewiston's mayoral position is considered high-profile, but it is also ceremonial. Officials said the office of mayor is a part-time job that only pays $7,000 a year.
The runoff election is set for Tuesday, Dec. 15, from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. at the Longley Elementary School Gymnasium.

title: Albany rallies to edge UMaine field hockey in America East semifinal shootout
text:
The University of Maine’s field hockey team was just 5:41 away from hosting the America East championship game.
The second-seeded Black Bears were leading third seed Albany 1-0 on Tuesday after fifth seed Vermont had upset top seed UMass Lowell earlier in the day, 3-2.
But America East Rookie of the Year Quinty Reumer tied the game off a second consecutive penalty corner with 5:41 remaining and, after a scoreless overtime period, the Great Danes beat UMaine 2-1 in the shootout.
Albany, 11-6, will host 14-5 Vermont in the title game at 2 p.m. Friday.
UMaine finished up at 8-9.
Pilar Lorenzini and Mara Kuskes converted among Albany’s five shooters in the shootout while Sayler Kuefler was the only Black Bear to do so.
In the shootout, each team has five shooters, and they start at the 25-yard line and have eight seconds to score on the opposing goalkeeper.
Emily Chisholm’s first goal of the season staked UMaine to a 1-0 lead in the second period off an assist from Kuefler, and UMaine’s Eloise Penty hit the post in the third period.
Reumer swatted home her league-high 12th goal of the season to tie it off assists from Kuskes and Emma Staron.
UMaine goalkeeper Annabel Halkes made three saves in the overtime to force the shootout.
Albany had 15 shot attempts through overtime, and UMaine had six. Albany had an 8-3 advantage in shots on goal and a 9-3 edge in penalty corners.
Merle Vaandrager finished with two saves for Albany, while Halkes wound up with seven.

title: These are the skin cancer warning signs you may overlook as you age
text:
(Aging Untold) — Skin cancer can appear in more ways than a changing mole.
Warning signs people may overlook
Some of the warning signs that people might overlook are having sores that don’t heal or moles that bleed easily, Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said.
Moles can change and that is something people don’t always track, Rogers said, and shared what doctors look for.
“We look at the asymmetry, how symmetric is it? Is it the border of it? Does it change? The color, the color can change. The diameter, and then evolving. Is it changing in its appearance to you?” Rogers said.
Changes matter even for spots people have had for years, gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck added.
“A millimeter can matter a lot,” Cradduck said.
She said people should track whether a mole has grown, changed its symmetry or started to bleed.
Where skin cancer can hide
While people often are told to check sun-exposed areas, Rogers said skin cancer can show up elsewhere.
“You have to look everywhere because they can hide,” Rogers said. “They can be behind your ears, between your toes, underneath the nails.”
She said a doctor’s exam or help from another person can cover places people can’t see, such as the scalp.
“They don’t always look scary,” Rogers said. “But that’s what makes them so dangerous.”
Aging expert Amy O’Rourke described her own experience when she went to a dermatologist about a brown spot on her cheek.
A whole body scan revealed cancer on top of her head, she said. It was squamous cell, and she had surgery.
Aging well coach Katherie Ambrose said she recently found a dermatologist, had a full body scan, and her husband had one as well.
Rogers suggested that people should check with their insurance, because some plans cover an annual dermatology exam, like a well woman exam.
Risk factors and sun damage
Around three-quarters of O’Rourke’s family has had skin cancer, she said.
Asked whether the risk is genetic or environmental, Rogers said fair skin is a risk factor, along with age and family history.
“So probably both,” she said.
In addressing sun damage, Rogers warned that UVA and UVB light are invisible and can pass through glass.
Melanoma is usually linked to intense, intermittent but deep sunburn, she said.
“It spreads very quickly,” Rogers said. “So you definitely want to pay attention.”
While melanoma presents more like a mole, squamous cell and basal cell cancers are more likely to be pinkish, itchy or sores that don’t heal, she said.
Rogers also addressed a myth: that African Americans don’t need sunscreen.
“Yes, you need sunscreen,” Rogers said.
Sunscreen protects against damage to cells and DNA, she said.
Sun protection
In addition to sunscreen, sun-protective clothing is also available, the hosts said, including rash guards, sun guards, UV clothing and wide-brimmed hats.
Key takeaways
- Skin cancer can show up in unexpected places, including the scalp, ears or under the nails.
- Watch for warning signs, including sores that will not heal or shiny bumps on the skin.
- During your annual dermatology visit, request a full body exam and ask about mole mapping to track changes over time.

title: Critical shortage of vets could threaten America’s food supply
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
(Aging Untold) — A silent crisis is unfolding across America’s heartland.
The veterinarians tasked with protecting the nation’s livestock, and by extension, its food supply, are a dwindling force, creating a critical gap in the first line of defense against disease and food insecurity.
For Dr. Rachel Miner, a mixed-animal veterinarian in eastern Kansas, a 60-mile drive to a farm call isn’t unusual. It has become a reality of the job.
She treats everything from household pets to herds of 1,500 cattle, understanding that her work is about more than just animal welfare.
“We’re not only taking care of the animal, but we’re providing for the industry,” Dr. Miner explains. “And the industry that is, supplies us, beef, pork, chicken, all those things.”
But veterinarians like Dr. Miner are becoming increasingly rare. A 2023 Johns Hopkins report reveals a staggering statistic: since the end of World War II, the U.S. has lost 90% of its food-animal vets. The U.S. government has designated official “shortage areas” in 46 out of 50 states, where a small number of vets are responsible for a massive number of animals.
The consequences are dire. In a two-county area in New Mexico, a single veterinarian is responsible for 40,000 cattle. In Pike County, Illinois, the number of full-time vets has plummeted from five to just one, serving 1,000 farms. The Illinois Department of Agriculture reports that cattle have died simply because veterinary services were not available in time.
The high cost of a shrinking workforce
The shortage has profound implications for the safety and stability of America’s food supply.
“It’s absolutely critical,” Brad White, director of the Beef Cattle Institute at Kansas State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, said. He stresses that healthy livestock, cared for by veterinarians, are essential to protecting both the animals and the people who depend on them.
Without enough vets to monitor herds, vaccinate against illness and respond to outbreaks, the risk of widespread disease increases. The 2022 bird flu outbreak serves as a stark reminder. As the virus swept through poultry farms, millions of chickens were culled to prevent its spread, causing egg prices to skyrocket by 96% in one year. While the vet shortage didn’t cause the outbreak, experts say robust veterinary care is key to preventing and containing such events.
Several factors are driving vets away from rural, large-animal practices. The cost of veterinary school can run into the hundreds of thousands of dollars, yet salaries in rural areas are often lower than those for small-animal vets in cities. The work is also physically and mentally demanding, with long hours and extensive travel.
“It can be exhausting, especially in those shortage areas, because you don’t have another veterinarian beside yourself,” Bryant Karlin, a student at K-State’s veterinary college, said.
Investing in a solution
To combat the crisis, federal and state governments are stepping in with solutions aimed at easing the financial burden. The federal Veterinary Medicine Loan Repayment Program offers up to $25,000 in student loan reimbursement for vets who commit to working in a designated shortage area for at least three years. However, the program is highly competitive, with fewer than half of applicants receiving the award each year.
Seeing the need, institutions like Kansas State University have created their own localized incentives. K-State’s program forgives 25% of a graduate’s loan for each year they practice in rural Kansas, for up to four years. The results are promising.
“There’s been 93% of them that have completed their four-year obligation,” White said. “More importantly, 15 years going, 83% of them are in rural practice in Kansas today. So they’re staying.”
For students like Emma McClure, who grew up in a rural area, the program provides peace of mind and a path to serve her community. “I have witnessed a lot of people, especially when they have emergencies, have to drive an hour or more to get the help that they need,” she said. “That’s something that’s definitely made an impact on my decision.”
Despite these efforts, the challenge remains immense. The American Veterinary Medical Association reported that the number of mixed and food-animal vets shrank by another 15% in 2023. While programs like K-State’s are a vital step, experts agree that a broader, sustained effort is needed to ensure the health of America’s livestock and the security of the food on its tables.

title: Three innovative Maine developments honored for ‘smart growth’
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
GrowSmart Maine recognized three projects — in Lewiston, Auburn and Saco — for demonstrating thoughtful development that helps build more resilient communities.
The Augusta-based nonprofit celebrated the honorees at its annual summit, held this fall at the Strand Theatre in Rockland. Close to 200 municipal planners, elected officials and housing advocates were on hand.
The three projects honored were the Fallview on Main, a mixed-use housing complex on the Androscoggin River in Auburn, developed by Gorham-based Great Falls Construction; three dormitories and a dining commons for the Ecology School in Saco, developed by the school’s owner and designed by Portland’s Kaplan Thompson Architects; and the renovation and construction of a nine-building affordable housing neighborhood in downtown Lewiston, a joint project with Portland-based Avesta Housing and Lewiston Housing Authority. The project was built by Hebert Construction, which has offices both in the city and in Portland.
“These projects showcase a combination of smart growth principles,” said Finn Bondeson, vice chair of GrowSmart Maine’s board of directors, “redevelopment of underutilized downtown spaces, mixed-use multi-floor occupancy, walkable proximity to services, accessible housing opportunities, sustainable and efficient building design and establishment of learning and community gathering space.”
In accepting Great Falls Construction’s award, Managing Director Julie Curran reflected on the persistence required for the downtown infill project, which repurposed an older building, noting that Fallview on Main was a collaboration with the city of Auburn.
“Together, we transformed a vacant, city-owned parcel in Auburn’s urban center into vibrant apartment homes and commercial spaces. This responsible growth directly supports the community’s need for safe, comfortable and state-of-the-art spaces,” Curran said.
Seric Kapp of Avesta Housing’s Lewiston Choice Wedgewood Neighborhood project, commented, “This effort started with community conversations over a decade ago. It was the consistency of our shared goal and the flexibility of the community that made completion feasible. Adaptability was key.”
Kapp added that the momentum from the project has inspired revitalization in other Lewiston neighborhoods.
Drew Dumsch, executive director of the Ecology School, spoke about how smart growth principles were applied to his development.
“With this project, we intentionally met our community’s needs for seasonal staff housing by constructing a solar-powered, passive house dining commons and dormitories that are now the first in Maine to achieve Living Building Challenge Petal certification,” said, who was named a 2024 Mainebiz Business Leader of the Year for his efforts in transforming the school.
GrowSmart Maine’s annual awards program recognizes projects and people that are nominated by the public and reflect the preservation of open space, effective public engagement, climate change resilience and the stewardship of a community’s sense of place.

title: Obituary: Robert “Bob” Charles Christy
text:
SCARBOROUGH – Robert “Bob” Charles Christy, 66, of Scarborough, Maine, passed away peacefully in the arms of his wife on Nov. 2, 2026, after a brief battle with cancer.
Bob was born on March 21, 1960, to Alvina and Philip Christy in Portland. He graduated from Scarborough High School in 1978 and went on to have a successful 30-year career as a pipefitter at Bath Iron Works. He was intensely creative and artistic. He loved animals with all of his heart and then some.
Bob was preceded in death by his parents, Alvina and Philip Christy.
He is survived by his devoted wife, Lillian; his daughter, Heather Rae and her husband Joe, his son, Shane and his wife Kayla; grandchildren William, Zoe, Evelyn, Belle and Ethan; and siblings Cheri, Tim and his wife Cheryl, and Steve and his wife Pam.
Family, friends, and others whose lives Bob touched are invited to Cote Funeral Home at 87 James St., Saco, on Friday, Nov. 6, from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. to grieve, support each other, and, of course, tell Bob stories. A short service will begin at 1 p.m. with interment to follow.

title: Trump responds as voters deliver rebuke by flipping key GOP-held Senate seats
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — For Donald Trump, his party’s resounding midterm losses pave the way for investigations and potential impeachments that will put the Republican president on the defensive in his final two years in office.
The results shift the center of gravity closer to Capitol Hill, where Democrats will be angling to check Trump’s power after two years of acquiescence from congressional Republicans. It not only resurfaces a dynamic from his first term in office, when House Democrats took power in Trump’s first midterms and ultimately impeached him twice, but with control as well of the Senate, Democrats can now stymie Trump’s nominations to Cabinet posts and lifetime federal judgeships.
Trump had all but guaranteed the results would be seen as a referendum on himself by repeatedly urging voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” as he went into primarily conservative states to shore up Republican candidates and warned of a Washington where Democrats were in power.
But the results showed how voters rejected Trump’s handpicked candidates while airing widespread concerns about high costs in the wake of his war against Iran and his punishing tariff policy.
Trump tried to shift the blame away from himself during a Fox News interview that aired early Wednesday, saying Democrats “did a good job” in their campaigns and faulting GOP candidates for their losses. “I don’t view it as a hit on me,” he said.
The results leave Trump — who watched returns at the White House with his advisers and members of his Cabinet — with dramatically diminished political capital at home and abroad.
From investigations to impeachment, the stakes for Trump are high
Senior Democrats, as they anticipated a majority in at least one chamber of Congress, have been telegraphing what their top investigative targets would be: the Trump administration’s policies, the conduct of its personnel, and interactions between government officials and private corporations who’ve tried to wield influence with the White House.
Among their priorities are the Trump family’s business dealings, the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and broader allegations of corporate corruption.
A Democratic majority will be armed with control of committees, bigger budgets and staff, and subpoena powers that could compel the administration to be responsive to Congress. In response, the White House could reprise its strategy from the first Trump administration, when it slow-walked congressional requests for documents and testimony and asserted executive privilege over certain information.
The president is also bracing for major legislative fights, saying he has a “strong veto.” On Tuesday night, Trump posted a picture of his signature red ball cap with “VETO” stitched on it.
Voters blame Trump’s economic policies
Placing himself front and center on voters’ minds was a major gamble by the president and his political team, who believed it would drive “Make America Great Again” supporters to the polls. Democrats were eager to watch the unpopular president insert himself so fully in the campaign, believing it served as an effective reminder of who should be blamed for the state of the economy.
“Trump’s desire to have everyone think that he’s on the ballot? Like, it’s happening,” said Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., who campaigned in key battlegrounds this fall, including Iowa, Georgia and Texas. “Everyone is thinking about him and the harm that he has done to them directly.”
The AP Voter Poll, an expansive survey of the midterm electorate, showed relatively few voters had positive things to say about Trump’s performance on the economy. About two-thirds of voters nationally say Trump’s policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., while only about 3 in 10 say they’ve improved economic conditions. Similarly, about two-thirds of voters said Trump’s tariff policies have “hurt” the national economy, or the economy in their local area.
Views of Trump’s priorities more broadly — and his capabilities as a leader — were also mostly negative. More than half of voters say Trump is not a strong leader, does not fight for people like them, does not have the right priorities and does not have the mental capability to serve effectively as president. About 6 in 10 voters say Trump places a higher priority on his own personal interests than he does the country’s interests, while about 4 in 10 said he puts more weight on the country’s interests.
The president — who faced a Democratic-led House for the latter half of his first term — campaigned aggressively in the final weeks to keep the Republican majorities on Capitol Hill because he knows what the consequences would be if Democrats seize power.
But the president at times shrugged off the prospect of a Republican loss of power in Congress. The president is also keenly aware of the political power he draws from having a foil, leveraging opposition to consolidate support in his party and boost fundraising.
Trump’s choices for GOP races had their own baggage
In the House, Democrats flipped districts that voted for Trump by as much as 18 points in 2024. Democrats won at least seven Senate seats in ruby-red states and battlegrounds alike: Kansas, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century, Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina and South Carolina.
Despite urging voters to use their imagination when reading names on the ballot, Trump’s hand-picked Republican candidates in Texas and South Carolina faced deep skepticism.
Republican Darline Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina after a campaign in which she faced questions about her inexperience.
Republican Ken Paxton, who lost to Democrat James Talarico in Texas, was impeached by his own party over corruption accusations and stained by a very public divorce. But Trump backed him instead of powerful incumbent Sen. John Cornyn, whom he viewed as not sufficiently supportive.
Trump’s loyalty pressures also led incumbent Republican Sen. Thom Tillis in North Carolina to decide to retire after clashing with the president. To try to keep that seat in GOP hands, Trump backed his close ally Michael Whatley, who lost to Democrat Roy Cooper.
Trump was also dealt twin defeats in two Midwestern states that had borne the brunt of high diesel prices and his tariff war. Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated Republican Roger Marshall in Kansas, while Republican Ashley Hinson lost to Democrat Josh Turek.
In another sign of Republican weakness, Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, whom Trump had endorsed and repeatedly praised. On Tuesday night, Trump posted on social media that Abbott was to blame for his loss, calling him a “RINO” — a Republican in name only.
